IN THE
FOURTH SESSION OF THE THIRD PARLIAMENT OF NORTHERN IRELAND
APPOINTED TO MEET THE EIGHTH DAY OF MARCH, IN THE
TWENTY-SECOND YEAR OF THE REIGN OF
HIS
MAJESTY
KING
GEORGE V.
VOLUME XIV.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

---

Tuesday, 8th March, 1932.
The Fourth Session of the Third Parliament of Northern Ireland, appointed to
meet 8th March, 1932, in the Twentysecond year of the Reign of King George
V, was opened by the Governor (His
Grace the Duke of Abercorn, K.G.,
K.P.) in person.
The House met at Ten Minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Right Hon. H. G. H. Mulholland, M.P.)
in the Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod
(Major T. Dalby Hackett, D.S.0.) was
announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman Usher said:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Three
of the Clock, and then resumed.

Sessional Orders.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within
one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return or Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such Bribery or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any persons hath been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime or
misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant at
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND
RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings,
and Records of this House be printed,
being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and
that he do appoint the printing thereof;
and that no person but such as he shall
appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered: That a Committee of Privileges be appointed.

King's Speech
King's Speech
8 MARCH 1932
KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear his Grace's Speech, on behalf of His Majesty, to both Houses of
Parliament; of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The Speech is
as follows:
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I view with concern the repercussion
of the world economic crisis upon those
major industries of our Country which
are dependent upon international commerce.
Nevertheless, the textile trade
has benefited to a certain extent by
the recent change in the fiscal system
of the United Kingdom of Great
Britain and Northern Ireland. I trust
this improvement may be maintained,
that its sphere may be extended to
other industries in the near future, and
that by these factors together with the
continued exercise of strict economy
in Government and local administration the foundations for an increase of
prosperity may be laid.
I am glad to observe that since a
year ago the improved state of trade,
apart from shipbuilding, has been reflected in a substantial decrease in unemployment, the Registers of the
Exchanges having recorded a fall of
13,657. It is satisfactory also to note
the amicable relations existing between
employers and employed; important
wage adjustments have been negotiated
within the last few months in a commendable spirit of reasonableness.
our
The prolonged depression in
staple trades, upon which so large a
section of the people is dependent, has
thrown into bold relief the desirability
of a wider diversity in our industrial
activities. My Government will continue its efforts to encourage the
establishment of new industries and in
pursuance of this policy legislative
proposals will be laid before you for the
purpose of empowering it to grant free
sites to firms desirous of establishing
new undertakings in Northern Ireland.
Proposals have been formulated dealing with Local Government Reform
and have been circulated to the various
organisations of Local Authorities in
Northern Ireland. Any representations received from them will receive
the most careful and sympathetic
consideration.
In framing these proposals my
Government have anxiously endeavoured
to avoid any possibility of imposing
additional charges on the rates.
In the meantime, I am glad to learn
that my Government, in co-operation
with Local Authorities, have been able,
by administrative measures, to effect
considerable reforms in the direction of
closing down Workhouses and of establishing up-to-date District Hospitals.
It is proposed to introduce a Bill
prolonging the restrictions on rents of
the smaller type of houses, and remedying, as far as possible, certain abuses
which have been brought to light in the
recent Report submitted by the Select
Committee on Rents.
A Bill will also be introduced for the
purpose of continuing for a further two
years a modified principle of Government Subsidy for working-class dwellings and enabling Local Authorities, as
heretofore, to co-operate
with the
Government in the encouragement of
the building of these houses.
The Bills which were introduced last
Session dealing with necessary reforms
of the Lunacy Laws and the Consolidation of the Law relating to Joint
Stock Companies will be reintroduced
during the forthcoming Session.
Other Bills will be laid before you
dealing with the following matters:-
Law of Landlord and Tenant.
Poultry Diseases.
Valuation of Railways.
Amendment
of the Slaughtered
Animals (Compensation) Act,
1928.
Garden Allotments for the Unemployed.
Members of the House of Commons.
The Estimates for the Public Services will be laid before you in due
course.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I recognise the serious hardship
which has been experienced by the
farming community through the severe
fall in agricultural prices which has
occurred as
result of the world
economic depression of the past few
years. A measure of protection is,
a
I
Debate on the Address
King's Speech
HOUSE OF COMMONS
however, being afforded to farmers
through the imposition of duties on
imports of certain classes of agricultural commodities including potatoes.
oats, eggs, poultry and dairy produce.
It is the policy of my Government to
seize the opportunity afforded by these
duties to extend, by all practicable
means, the market for our agricultural
produce in Great Britain.
It has been announced that as soon
as a scheme for the reorganisation of
the bacon industry has been prepared
a measure for the quantitative regulation of imports of bacon into the
United Kingdom will be introduced.
My Government trusts that farmers
will put themselves in a position to
take advantage of the regulation of
imports as soon as it is put into
operation.
I am gratified to learn that substantial progress is being made in the
initial stages of the scheme of comprehensive electricity development authorised by recent legislation. I look
forward with confidence to the beneficial effects of this scheme both to
industrialists and to private citizens
throughout Northern Ireland.
And I pray that the blessing of
Almighty God may rest upon your deliberations.
Debate on the Address.
Mr. JOHN JOHNSTON (in morning
dress): I beg to move:
"That an humble Address be presented to His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland as followeth :
"Your Grace,
"We, His Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland, in Parliament assembled,
beg leave to offer our humble thanks
to your Grace for the Speech which
your Grace has addressed to both
Houses of Parliament."
The King's Speech, which we have
just heard, is in some ways rather remarkable, as it takes up so much space
with the present economic crisis. This
crisis has crowded out nearly all other
subjects from our thoughts, and those of
the world. It is in every Ruler's mind,
in every Government's Exchequer, and
has got into all our pockets.
I am safe in saying that no Government in the world except our own will
balance its budget this year. In
In our
case it has been made possible only
by the patriotism shown by all the
British people in such a crisis as
this. They have shown themselves
to be truly an imperial race, and
one to be relied upon in time of trouble.
Our people have displayed to all their
determination to pay their debts, and to
sacrifice their all for their country's
cause. This spirit must be supported by
our leaders and rulers, and every effort
made by the Imperial Government and
our own to second the effort made by the
common people of this land.
I am glad to see in this respect, the
King's Speech asks for strict economy in
government and local administration,
and I hope the coming Estimates will
give a lead to all our local administrators
in this respect, and that the Members of
this House will support heartily the
economies foreshadowed. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I trust that the Government will be ruthless in economy where
necessary, and that they will not hesitate
to cut down expenditure. I think the
people of this Province, owing to the
spirit they have shown in the recent
crisis, should be helped, and we call upon
the Government to do so this year.
I have always been of the opinion that
our administration expenses have been on
too high a scale, and rather ambitious for
such a small State as we have to administer, and now that the Government is
"up against it," I will welcome, and I
am sure this House will welcome, a substantial reduction in the forthcoming
Estimates. I hope the Government is in
earnest about this, and will not hesitate,
as I said, to reduce relentlessly where
such is necessary. We are all convinced that reduction is not only
necessary, but inevitable, if Northern
Ireland is to pay its way.
I rejoice, with the King's Speech, in
the improved state of our local textile
trades, and hope the improvement will
continue with increased vigour during the
coming year. I am confident that the
worst is past, and our unemployment
register should show a distinct reduction
during the year. World unemployment
is very much increased over a year ago
in every country except our own. Anybody who cares to look into the figures
regarding the state of unemployment in
the world will see the favourable position
we are in.
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
8 MARCH 1932
Mr. NIXON: Question.
Mr. JOHN JOHNSTON: I believe
that with improved trade conditions
our shipbuilding will also have its turn,
and should share in the returning prosperity of the world, which must come
sooner or later. This House will welcome the efforts which the Government
intend to make of introducing new trades
and industries into Northern Ireland by
the offer of free sites for such industries,
and I hope their efforts will be crowned
with success.
That is one Bill that I
hope the Government will not hesitate to
introduce at once, because it is a case of
first come, first served, and if Northern
Ireland is first in the field with the offer
of free sites we will get some of these
new industries which we are so anxious
to secure, and which are so necessary for
our surplus employees. I believe the
Government will find it much easier to
offer facilities for these new industries
owing to the fact that cheaper power will
be obtained from the electricity lines
which are spreading all over the country.
If the Government had offered free sites
two or three years ago I think they
would have found a difficulty in getting
people to come, because if we want to
establish industries here we must offer
the same facilities as can be obtained
elsewhere. Formerly, if people wanted
to start an industry they had to build
a chimney and install steam engines and
boilers, but now they have simply to
attach a wire to one of the lines of the
Electricity Board. A great field of
opportunity is here open, and I hope the
plans of the Government will meet with
the support deserved.
An ambitious scheme for the reform of
local government is also foreshadowed,
which will, I trust, meet with the
approval of this House. The abolition of
the workhouse will meet with all our
support, and a good hospital in
each district instead will be a great
boon to the rural community. I
hope the Government can take into
account the co-ordination of the policies
of local government bodies, particularly
in the case of roads. I would prefer
that all main and second-class roads could
be taken over by a Road Board for the
whole Six Counties, and thereby making
the road policy one instead of six or
more.
Mr. BEATTIE: A united Road Fund.
Mr. HEALY: That is anti-partition.
Mr. JOHN JOHNSTON: Nothing, I
think, has given rise to more controversy
in this House than the Rent Restriction
Acts and the housing subsidies, and I
see the Government intend to tackle
both in the coming Session. Until a
sufficient number of houses are available
to meet the demand, I suppose rent restrictions are necessary, but the restrictions should not be necessary in a
healthily housed country. They are
symptoms of a disease which should be
remedied as soon as possible. The Government remedy is to continue the housing subsidy. In spite of all financial
difficulties they propose to continue for
another two years the principle of payment of subsidies for the building of small
houses. We are all aware of the enorin
improvement
the housing
situation which has taken place during
the last few years, mainly due to the
generous financial assistance given by the
Government in conjunction with the
grants made by local authorities, but the
job is not yet finished.
mous
I fear that the local authorities may
slack off in their housing schemes, owing
to their many other duties and financial
troubles unless a strong lead is taken by
the Government to urge the building of
small houses suitable for our workers.
Up to the present the Government has
contributed no less a sum than 21
millions towards the provision of houses,
and over 25,000 houses have already been
built. Notwithstanding all this the
housing conditions in many urban and

This House is aware of the financial

the building of the smaller type of houses
which can be let at low rents to the

Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. John Johnston]
I cannot stop without referring to the
great change in the fiscal policy of this
country, which has just taken place. It
will profoundly affect all of us in Northern Ireland, and none more so than
the farming community. For the first
time in over 80 years the farmers' produce will get some protection, and not
be liable to the disastrous flood of foreign
importation as hitherto, particularly
potatoes, oats, eggs, poultry, and dairy
produce. This will give our people a
preference in the home market, and a
similar boon is foreshadowed for the
bacon industry.
This Speech winds up on a subject in
which I have personally taken a great
interest, the development of electricity.
This, if properly done, will mean everything to Northern Ireland when industry revives. It puts power and light
into every small town and village, and
makes the establishment of new indus-
I
tries an easy matter. It will improve
the amenities of the country side out of
all knowing. I have not seen eye to eye
with the Government in this matter.
felt it would have been better to develop
along the lines of private ownership
rather than under Government control,
but the Government in their wisdom or
unwisdom, have decided to do both.

In County Antrim there is private

will be Socialistic. It will be interesting

cannot help thinking that the money for

have been more easily procured by
private enterprise, and the drain on
the credit of Northern Ireland would
have been relieved considerably. The
Chancellor of the Exchequer could
tell us. I congratulate the Government on tackling the problem notwithstanding my quarrel with their
method, and I am sure Northern Ireland will reap the benefit four-or-five
fold in a few years. Once the habit of
using electricity is learned, it cannot be
given up. In the countryside it will
mean light, heat, and the banishment of
drudgery from many homes.
I learn that this is the opening of the
last session of Parliament in our present
buildings. For the past ten years or
more this Chamber has been filled with
the noise of controversy. Opinions strongly
held, and strongly expressed, have resounded around these walls for the last
time. I hear that in September next it
will be occupied by a very different community entirely unconnected with the
sport of politics. Students of theology
will take our places, and I sincerely hope
that none of the virus of infection from
our sometimes violent disputations will
remain to disturb the serenity of the
future occupants. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
Mr. MINFORD (in morning dress): I
rise to second the Address, and in doing
so acknowledge the great honour that has
been done to my constituents by asking
me to perform this pleasant duty. The
House will, however, allow me also to
indicate my appreciation of the personal
honour done me.
My constituency
has within its confines
some of the
largest industrial concerns in Northern
Ireland which afford employment in
prosperous times for many thousands of
Ulster's typical working people, as well
as a rich and extensive
acreage of
arable and pastoral land, tilled by
a careful and shrewd agricultural
community. All those classes of people
have borne with commendable fortitude
the calamitous result of the economic
crisis referred to in the opening sentences
of the Gracious Speech.
Whatever views hon. Members may
take on the great question of Free Trade
versus Tariff Reform, I think it will be
agreed that Free Trade in the circumstances in which we were placed would
never have extricated us from the serious
position into which we had drifted, so we
now turn with renewed hopes that the
measure of Protection mentioned in the
Gracious Speech will result in a greater
industrial activity and secure for the
agricultural community such a condition
of things as will bring to them a greater
measure of prosperity and contentment
than has hitherto been their lot.
It is a matter of great gratification,
not only to Members of this House, but
to the workers in Northern Ireland, to
learn from the Gracious Speech that the
Government propose to extend that
policy of subsidy to working-class
dwellings. I feel confident that local
authorities will co-operate with the
Government in the building of these
houses. We all know and appreciate the
fact that our lives are invariably influenced by the nature and character of
our homes. Knowing this we should
spare no effort to secure for our working

men and women homes worthy of them,
and which will influence their lives with

I have no doubt that the Bill foreshadowed in the Gracious Speech to

May I say that I respectfully share the

so that farmers will recognise and take

The world economic depression of the

other class of people. I think I can

products or commodities.

When one thinks of the unfair competition to which farmers were subject in

would offer them. I sincerely hope that
the policy of the Government outlined in
the Gracious Speech will result in a
stabilised market for our agricultural
produce.

Minford) on the very excellent speeches.
which they made in proposing and

John Johnston) said that this was our
last meeting in this building, and therefore, perhaps, I may take the opportunity
of saying that that is so, and that when
we meet again it will be in the new
Parliament House at Stormont. What
the Government propose doing is to have
no Autumn Session this year, but to
clear up all the work that has to be done
before we rise, keeping the House alive,
if hon. Members will realise what I mean,
by not proroguing there and then,
finishing the business and proroguing at
later date when
we are definitely
certain when it will be convenient for the
ceremony of opening the new House to
take place. Then when we meet at
Stormont we will begin the Session of
1933, reply to the Speech from the
Throne and get over the Address, because I feel, and I am sure every Member
will feel, that it would be inappropriate
to wind up the Session after having the
a
opening ceremony. We would prefer to
open the new building at the same time
as we open the new Session of Parliament. I think it will be more appropriate for the distinguished member of
the Royal Family-whom I hope and

Mr. DEVLIN: Would it not be well
and more appropriate if we had a dissolution first before we open the new

The PRIME MINISTER: My experience of the Ulster people is that they
do not care for a great many changes.
They are quite satisfied to carry on as
they are. I know that the hon. Member is very anxious to have a Nationalist
Government, but as we are practically
two to one in the House, representing the
country, I think we will be able to manage quite well without dissolving Parliament. We will prorogue it in the
ordinary way.
Now, I come down here at the opening
of each new Session with a certain amount
of trepidation. I have never known
when I sit here what the chosen Leader
of the Opposition is going to attack the
Government upon. It is kept a dead
secret up to the last moment, and no
one knows what heavy guns will be
trained on us by the champion of the
Opposition. We shiver to think of our
past misdeeds, our sins of commission and
omission, and therefore I was somewhat
relieved to find that the first shot of the
Session is a complaint against apples.
After all, when one thinks of a community which is a very live one, occupied
with subjects of varied interest and great
importance, and finds that the combined
brains of all these clever men opposite can
only just bring up the question of apples,
or something about pottery works, and I
think a reference to loans, it provides a

at present.

to deal with the question of flax. At any

The PRIME MINISTER: I presume
that the hon. Member (Mr. Devlin) will
admit that his party chose the hon. Member (Mr. Healy) to fire the heavy guns,
even if he himself comes along afterwards
as the infantry or some other arm of the
force. May I first deal with what the
leader (Mr. Healy) on this occasion has
said. He says we ought to be more
generous in our loans to the farming
community. I can guarantee that no
Government or Minister has been as
generous to the farming community as
my right hon. Friend (Sir Edward
Archdale). Bring a just case before him
and he will treat it with the greatest
generosity as far as the limit of the financial resources of our country will admit.
But behind all this has been the consistent policy of the Government since we
took office to get the farming community
out of debt, and, if possible, to see that
they would never get into debt again.
I think all those who have lived in the
country and who realise the life of the
farmer know that there is nothing he
dreads more than being in debt, either
to the Government, or to a bank, or to
his neighbour. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). I think it is an awful thing to
have debt hanging over his head all the
time.
What have the Government done?
With the assistance of the Exchequer on
the other side, land purchase has been
practically completed. There is hardly
a holding that has not been vested in
the tenants, and that means that the
reduction from the rents to the instalments that are paid is a considerable
advantage to the farming community.
Nobody who is honest can deny that.
Then, on top of that, the Government
provide a sum of £900,000 a year in order
to relieve the farmers of rates on agricultural land and farm buildings. That is
no small matter. Coming on the top of
that is the £450,000 spent by the Government on social services, which the farmers in the country generally enjoy just
as much as the Corporation of Belfast or
any of the other local authorities. Those
two sums alone are of the utmost assistance to the farming community. Over
and above that, I find that £150,000 has
been availed of for special cases which
have been brought before the notice of
the Ministry. The hon. Member (Mr.
Healy) therefore, can rest quite satisfied.
and not be so gloomy in the future when
he knows that no effort will be spared
to help the farmers along the very
difficult road which they are travelling.

with seed potatoes?

HOUSE OF COMMONS

We have decided in all the circumstances, and especially in view of the
reduced cost of building material, to fix
the subsidy at £25 per house, which we
hope will be an incentive to local
authorities and private builders to continue the erection of workmen's dwellings.
In considering the proposals which we
will lay before the House, we have had
to bear in mind that the efforts which
have already been made to meet the
housing shortage have entailed the expenditure of a great deal of money, and have
placed upon the Exchequer a heavy
burden, which must continue for some
years to come, and however much we
may desire to hasten the building of more
houses we must exercise caution in placing
too severe a strain upon our resources.
Since the matter was taken in hand
by Parliament and the Government,
upwards of 25,000 houses have been
erected under the Housing and allied
Acts, and a sum of not less than approximately 2 millions has been contributed
out of State Funds to secure the erection
of these houses. The figure for Belfast
is £1,400,000, and that for the rest of
Ulster £1,390,000. For the current year
the burden upon the Exchequer in respect.
of this expenditure is £156,000, a figure
which will be appreciably increased in the
coming financial year. In formulating
our proposals we have had to bear these
figures in mind, and the assistance which
we suggest should be given for the next
two years is, in our opinion, the most
generous that is possible, having regard
to financial considerations.
The Government has given anxious
thought to the question of rents in connection with houses built with the assistance of a subsidy, but we are still of
opinion that this question of rents in such
cases cannot be adjusted by governmental
action, and that the only means by which
satisfactory results in this connection can
be obtained is by encouraging the building of these smaller workmen's dwellings.
In other words, we feel there must be
an encouragement of building, and to
hamper in any way the freedom of those.
who are prepared to undertake the task,
whether it be the Belfast Corporation or
any other local authority, or private

money invested in the building of houses
fly out of the country the financial extension of the City of Belfast and of
other towns is bound to suffer, and our

difficulty owing to the want of foresight
on the part of their predecessors. Therefore, we feel it quite impossible, as I
say, to do anything more than to hold
out a hand of assistance to those who are
less able to help themselves.

agricultural difficulties, certain

conditions of the people will be lowered.

contact with thousands who are in utter

The local authorities were carrying out
work of great public utility to the

I will tell you why they do not sign.
If a man has no dependents-the Minister
of Labour is here, and will correct me

chance whatever of any of those men
getting work through the Labour
Exchange.
I wish to denounce the Labour Exchange. I am sorry to have to do it, but
I wish to indict it on the question of unemployment benefit. The Labour Exchanges have changed the charge-if I
may use the expression-that they put
against a man when they are going to
deprive him of his benefit. Here is the
charge they put against a man now. This
is the charge that was put against a man

Springfield Road, where Arthur Trew
lived. The charge now is-
"You have not proved that you are
normally in insurable employment and
will obtain your living by insurable
employment in future."

prove that. How can he prove that he
will obtain his living by insurable employment when he can get no employment at

place to place asking for work. He is in
an impossible position before a court of
referees because he cannot prove it. None
of them can prove it. The Minister himself could not prove what he will do in
the future. If he cannot get insurable
employment he cannot make his living by

public assistance committee, and on the

a court of referees, and that court found
that
"You have not proved that you are

When the Prime Minister was standing
at the Table he talked a lot about flax.

Britain-and I am a man who stands for

efforts in getting the Protection taken off

the taking off of that duty would destroy

Mr. BEATTIE: I desire to move as an

"But profoundly regret that no

to deal with the evergrowing problem
of poverty and unemployment now
widespread in Northern Ireland."
I think this is one of the most important subjects that any House of this
kind could spend its time in discussing. In
moving the Amendment, I am going to
try to outline the plight and position in

the present moment. This state of affairs
has been brought about solely by the
harsh regulations which the present Government, who are confronting us now,
have brought into being as far as the
question of unemployment insurance is

One out of every five shipbuilding workers

That is not through any fault of their

In regard to the anomalies aspect of
the work, one would think that when a
man had worked 30 or 40 years in industry that would be his normal occupation, especially in the case of a skilled
man like a blacksmith, shipwright,
caulker, joiner, boilermaker, or electrician.
Such men have served an apprenticeship, and during that period of apprenticeship they received no wages. Their trade
is their profession, and they should not
be lightly asked to leave that profession
and take up work belonging to another
class of people in the community.
,,
A skilled man has a calling, but a man,
such as an engineer, is now classified in
a grade where his trade is given as his

Brown, a labourer; alternative occupation, boilermaker.' That is a most
ridiculous position in which to place any
man of that kind. He only took general
labouring work because he could not get

The whole thing, in my opinion, is

back to normal times the shipyards would

Then we come to the new Act passed
during the last Session of this House.
I have been told that the Anomalies Act
was placed on the Statute Book by the
Labour party. Placing a Bill on the

placed there to remove anomalies, I hold

salary between this side of the House and

that side.
smiles. I will show him an anomaly

Take the case of a married woman.

Miss Margaret Bondfield made that statement. It was also said that dockers were
drawing unemployment benefit after

Those statements were all exaggerated.
The Committee investigating the statements found that the practice was not as
extensive throughout Great Britain and
Northern Ireland as appeared from the
Press. The Press is solely responsible

in the Plaza, in Belfast, two nights a

person coming within the meaning of the
Anomalies Regulation No. 2."
I do not know how they could say that,
because I do not think a waitress is a
seasonal worker at all. The waitress who
resides in a seaside town and who never
leaves that town to look for any other
class of employment is a seasonal worker,

to a seaside town to get employment during the summer months and then returns
to a district where work of her kind is
available cannot be graded as a seasonal
worker. Nor did the framers of the
Regulations ever intend her to be included within the scope of Section 2.
The whole thing is being misinterpreted
and mismanaged to the detriment of
those justly entitled to receive benefit.

I will give you an instance of how I
believe the officials of the Ministry go to
the very extreme in order to put people
off unemployment insurance benefit. A
couple of years ago in this House I raised
a particular case regarding officials employed in the municipal baths at Warrenpoint, and the same state of affairs exists
to-day. There are probably not more
than half a dozen persons employed in
those baths, but the Ministry of Labour
have been guilty of a most indefensible
act in holding that while some of these
officers have to be insured, others have
not. For instance, the boilerman has
not to be insured under the Unemployment Insurance Acts, while the superintendent of the baths, who is a full time
officer, has to be insured. This question
has been before the Ministry before now,
and an explanation of their action has
been given by the Ministry which I think
this House would hardly care to endorse.
However, the view taken by the Ministry,
or by officials of the Ministry, has deprived certain of these officers of benefits
that otherwise they would be entitled to.
This is an extract from a letter from one
of the officials of the Ministry of
Labour:-
I have to inform you that the boilerman, female attendant, washerwoman,
and the boy who cleans the boxes, etc.,
are not required to be insured under
the Unemployment Insurance Acts.
Contributions under these Acts are.
however, required to be paid in respect.
of the Baths Superintendent and the
ticket collector.
That seems to me to be cutting the
thing very fine. The baths superintendent is a full time officer and never has
received unemployment benefit. The
other officers referred to are not full time
employees, but are what are called
seasonal workers, and yet they are not
required to be insured, and are therefore
not elegible for benefit. I think that
such a decision on the part of the Ministry
is indefensible, and it only goes to show
the extremes to which the officials of the
Ministry will go in order to prevent people
receiving benefit. In a further letter
from the Ministry the official says:—-
I have to inform you that the reason
the boilerman at the Municipal Baths
is excepted from the scope of the Unemployment Insurance Acts is because
his duties are of a domestic character.
The Superintendent of the Baths is,
however, required to be insured, as his
duties are other than of a domestic
character.
Both these persons are in the same
employment, and while one is never unemployed, and never receives unemployment benefit, he is required to be insured,
while the other, who is only seasonally
employed, is not required to be insured
and therefore is never entitled to receive
unemployment benefit. I say that this
is a typical example of the effort of the
Ministry of Labour to employ every device
possible to prevent people from securing
the benefits which Acts like this are designed to give them. There surely can
be no difference between the case of a
boilerman who is employed for six months
in the year at the baths, and a man who
is employed as a boilerman in any other
firm during the winter months. I have
mentioned this case to show that some
alteration should be made in the conditions necessary to secure unemployment
benefit. This practice of simply cutting
people off benefit cannot be justified in
the present state of affairs. My own
impression is that the Ministry of Labour
could administer the present Acts with a
good deal more advantage to the insured.
people, and that no new legislation is
required to remedy these grievances.
However, if any new legislation is considered necessary the Minister should come
to the House and ask for it, because you
cannot allow people to remain in a state
of absolute starvation. Therefore. I think
it is the duty of the House now, at the
beginning of their new Session, to alter
their Unemployment Insurance Acts so as
to secure that no person will be allowed
to die of want.

That is my first point. The business of
the Government is to secure work or

people and therefore they should give

comfort and dignity, aiming at higher

This public assistance committee,

subsistence level. This public assistance committee, therefore, respectfully

My considered judgment as convener
of public assistance in a great industrial
constituency is as follows: The reduction
of the dole from 26s to 23s 3d. is a
tragedy. From a bare subsistence level
thousands of our countrymen are now
at their wits' end to keep the house
going, and are definitely in the poverty
With 26s the house could be
kept going barely. There is not a
halfpenny over for clothing, boots, replenishments, etc., with 23s 3d. The
means test has been effective in cutting
out masses who have not been requiring
extra money, and the saving over the
country must be enormous; but in the
case of decent workers, idle through no
fault of their own, it is a scandal that
recipients of poor-law relief are sometimes in a better position than they
are.

at all. The Minister of Labour realises

on behalf of those people, because I believe there are no people in the world like
the people of Northern Ireland. They
would suffer anything for their loyalty,

you about hundreds of Shankill Road

turned down by the gentlemen the

after this transitional benefit.

I say no. You have one market that is
closed against you.
You cannot send any
of the commodities that are made in
Northern Ireland into the Free Stato
without being taxed. Therefore, that
market is practically cut off. Then if
they send their goods to England they
have to compete against the rings in
England, and the right hon. Gentleman
knows something about the cement rings
and different other rings. He knows
how powerful they are. Immediately the
goods are sent into England there will be
a combine to smash the sale of goods
made in Northern Ireland. Again, the
question of freight has to be taken into
consideration, and it is a very important
factor. Here are the first things that
have to be done. How many philanthropists in any part of the world are
prepared to come to Northern Ireland
and, just because they are going to get a
free site, sink £20,000 or £30,000 in the
construction of buildings? If it is going
to be an industry that will employ any
men or women at all they will have
to spend £20,000 or £30,000 on
buildings. Then they will have another
£10,000 or more to spend on installing up-to-date machinery, and a
very large sum for other requirements,
such as motors-

MR. DE VALERA.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the order prohibiting Mr. De Valera, President of the
Irish Free State Executive Government,
from entering any part of Northern Ireland, except County Antrim, is still in
force.
SECRE-
The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): No, sir.
Mr. HENDERSON: Arising out of

Northern Ireland on
any occasion he
likes?
Mr. HEALY: Also arising out of that
will the hon. Gentleman tell us what the

SHORT LEAVE IN THE ROYAL
ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether short leave granted
to members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, under Barrack Regulation 11,
has in some cases been curtailed by an
order made on May 3rd, 1931, which enjoins that any such leave already granted
would be cancelled when an inspection
by the Commissioner or District Inspector
was notified, except leave granted for
urgent reasons; whether such order causes
inconvenience and hardship to men who
have made arrangements before the inspection was notified and who have not
time to cancel those arrangements.
Mr. HANNA: Short leave is a
privilege, the taking of which involves
no elaborate previous arrangements, and
is granted only subject to the condition
that it does not involve interference with
or absence from any particular duty.
Apparently the impression appears to
have prevailed in certain quarters that
this short leave was a right rather than
a privilege, and the directions issued by
the Commissioner of Police in May last
were intended to correct this wrong
view.
There are no grounds for the suggestion that attendance at inspections causes
inconvenience or hardship to the men,
who are fully aware that the granting
of the privilege of short leave is contingent on the due performance of such
duties as may be necessary.
MARKETING OF AGRICULTURAL
PRODUCE.
3. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Prime Minister whether he is prepared to set up a
committee, representative of all parties
in the House, to devise an agricultural
policy for Northern Ireland, with special
reference to the marketing of agricultural
produce.
The PRIME MINISTER: The Government is confident that the far-sighted
policy which my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Agriculture, is pursuing
adequately meets the requirements of the
farming communtiy, and that as a result
of the various Acts prescribing the
marketing of agricultural produce already
on the Statute Book, satisfactory progress
is being made. I am not convinced that
any advantage would be gained by adopting the suggestion of the honourable Member. However, needless to say, if any
Member can put forward constructive
suggestions they will be carefully and
sympathetically considered by my right
honourable Friend,

PROVISION OF SEED POTATOES.
4. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he has received
from his inspectors and also from the
Board of Guardians of Enniskillen and
Lisnaskea Unions, respectively, reports
concerning the pressing need for seed
potatoes for small farmers and labourers;
and whether he will endeavour to carry
out the wishes of these Boards and have
potatoes provided in accordance with the
Seed Potatoes Supply Act of 1925.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I have
received representations from the boards
of guardians of the Enniskillen and
Lisnaskea Unions regarding the supply
of seed potatoes as suggested by the hon.
Member. A report furnished by an
inspector sent down by me to investigate
the position is to the effect that there is
no general shortage of seed potatoes in
the area. It is, however, apparent that
growers in some cases have not been able
to save sufficient seed potatoes from their
1931 crop to meet their requirements in
the coming planting season, and that in
certain instances such growers may have
difficulty in purchasing the seed potatoes
they require owing to a shortage of ready
cash. To meet
meet this difficulty I am
arranging for the granting of loans for
the purchase of seeds, and also artificial
fertilisers on the same easy terms as in
previous years. As the hon. Member is
probably aware, the Seed Potatoes
Supply Act of 1925 applied to that year
only.
Mr. HEALY: Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that the average amount
of loan necessary will be from £2 to £3,
for which three persons may be required
to go security?
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: Two
persons.
Mr. HEALY: And
the borrower.
That means that to borrow £100 would
require 150 people as sureties. Does the
right hon. Gentleman think that that is
a practical solution of this problem in
view of the crisis that is facing these
small farmers?
Sir EDWARD: ARCHDALE: I do
not agree that the figure given by the
hon. Member is the amount required.
The small farmers have nearly all got
enough seed potatoes. The larger farmers between Lisnaskea and the Lough
shore are the ones who have suffered
damage by flooding, and they are well
able to get sureties.

Gentleman prepared to act on the recom
mendation of his own inspector against
the recommendations of two boards of
guardians who know the locality and who
recommend a certain course of action? In
other words, are the wishes of public
representatives who are going to bear
the responsibility to be turned down because you prefer to act on the recommendation of a single inspector who does
not know the locality?

ordinary procedure under circumstances

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I think it will be admitted

desire to be judged, and judged alone.
on what we have done, and what we are

frankly.
In the first place, he asked me what was
our policy as regards the payment of
unemployment benefit. It is very easy,
indeed, to answer that. It is that as regards unemployment benefit, both in
relation to legislation and administration.
we should keep on similar lines to Great
Britain so that equal conditions should

exist throughout the whole of the United

What are the facts? As regards unemployment benefit alone, approximately
£25,000 a week is being paid. As regards

£15,000 a week is being paid. In other

There has been a great deal of talk

and threequarter millions was paid last

and old age. When the Government representing this small area is putting up
that huge sum, almost half of our total

Mr. ANDREWS: I come a little further. The public assistance committees
have been referred to at considerable
length. It has been suggested that their
administration has been harsh and cruel.
I am not responsible for their administration because Parliament has decided that
they, and they alone, shall have the charge
of deciding not whether a person is entitled to benefit but, if the courts of referees and umpire decide that the person
is entitled to benefit, they decide the
amount the person is to receive weekly
having regard to his actual need. Now,
why was that change made? Simply because the Unemployment Fund in Great
Britain had got into debt to the extent
of £115,000,000. An hon. Member said
a few minutes ago that the Northern
Government should not have been afraid
to pledge our resources in order to help
the unemployed. He evidently forgot
that our Unemployment Fund is overdrawn to the extent of approximately
£5,000,000, so that the two funds taken
together, were overdrawn to the extent of
£120,000,000-an enormous sum which
was affecting the whole financial structure
of the Kingdom. Borrowing could not go
on indefinitely; there had to be a change.
What was the change that was made?
It was decided that insured persons should
receive the statutory benefit to which they
were entitled on the contributions which
they had paid upon an actuarial basis.
and that meant that the maximum amount
in any one year, which an insured person
was entitled to receive as standard benefit
was for twenty-six weeks. It was recognised in Great Britain and here as well,
that when the twenty-six weeks came to
an end the position of many homes might
be serious if some further provision was
not made. How could that provision be
made most justly and most fairly? By
what was called the means test? That
means test was to be applied with the object
of placing in those homes where there is
the greatest need, such money as is available, and I want to say here clearly and
frankly, that I feel that the public assistance committees have, without fear or
favour, and with a great deal of public
spirit, undertaken this duty. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). They are not
acting harshly, and I can prove that is so,
for the position is simply this. In all,
the public assistance committees have
reviewed 24,463 cases. They have not
deprived everybody of payment, quite
the contrary. They have given full
benefit to 9,218 persons or to 38 per cent.
of the entire number reviewed. They have
given reduced benefit to 10,718 persons,
or 44 per cent. of the cases reviewed, and
there have been "nil" determinations in
only 4,529 cases or 18 per cent. What of
those cases that have got benefit on a reduced scale? On the average, they have
got two-thirds of their statutory allowance

question to which the Prime Minister

That is the development of the whole
system of agriculture on scientific lines.
I have the greatest possible sympathy
with him in regard to that, but I would
remind him of this fact that the country
that has made the greatest progress in
agricultural development inside the last
eighty years or so-less than that, the
last sixty or seventy years-Denmarkhas done so not through legislation but
through education. Denmark was practically down and out in 1864 when the Germans took the two duchies from them, but
they started to educate the people, and
through education the great farming cooperative movement grew. It is due to
that, and to that alone, that the agricultural condition of Denmark is what it
is to-day.
I listened to-day-and I read the debates of yesterday and the day beforeto Members, especially Members on the
opposite side appealing to the Government to intervene here, there, and everywhere. I most respectfully ask the
Government, as far as possible, to keep
their hand out of ordinary business and
to leave it to the people who are
interested in business. It is not the
function of the Government, nor have the
Government the means, to deal with these
things as the people engaged in the industries have. There was a case referred
to several times during this debate, the
marketing of fruit. I made some
inquiries on my own behalf in regard to
that matter, and I went to a man whose
name has never been mentioned in connection with the controversy in Armagh,
one of the largest growers in that county,
who stands very high in the opinion of
the Department of Agriculture, and who
probably has got more cups for growing
apples than any man in Armagh or indeed in Ulster.
I asked him frankly what would be the
result of the Marketing Act, and he said
this year, so far as he was concerned, not
more than 30 per cent. of the apples he
grew and by the way he told me that he
had sprayed them nine times during the
season-would qualify for the grade that
had been laid down, and that so far as
70 per cent. of his apples were concerned
he had got to sell them for 3s a unit,
whereas Covent Garden would gladly have
given him 25s. I only mention that to
show that the interference of the Government in the ordinary flow of trade does
harm instead of good. Reference was
also made recently-I think by the
Prime Minister-to marketing conditions
in New Zealand. I happen to be pretty
familiar with the development of New
Zealand, and I have read the official
documents with care.
So far as New Zealand is concerned,
there was an Act brought in appointing
a board to deal with apples in 1924. One
of the first conditions laid down in that
Act was that before the Act was put into
operation the majority of the growers
should vote in favour of it. The result
was that every district in New Zealand,
with one exception, voted in favour of
this board, and with regard to the board
for local control practically every district
turned it down. But the New Zealand
Government guaranteed to those who export apples to Great Britain and other

a
countries a minimum of one penny
pound. There is no guarantee of that sort
given here. I do not for a moment doubt
that the intentions of the Government
in these matters are the very highest and
best, but I do say that if they pursue
their operations they will discover that
they are hindering the trade instead of
helping it.
I was glad to notice in the King's
Speech a reference to the question of
leaseholders, a question that I raised as
far back as 1925, and on which the
Megaw Committee reported three years
ago.
It has been referred to before in a
King's Speech, and I do hope that this
time something is going to be done.
During the debate that has just ended a
good deal was said with regard to providing employment. I wish to speak of one
class it is a small class, undoubtedly,
but it is a
very important class-the
fishermen around our coast. If the
Government can see their way to do anything more to help these people I am
sure they will do it. I appeal especially
to the Minister of Commerce, and I
should like at the same time to thank him
for what he has done already in my own
constituency, but there is a good deal
more that can be done to help these hardy,
thrifty, industrious men to earn even a
precarious living. They do not want to
get something for nothing. They do not
want to be put on the dole. They want
to be able to earn their own living.
The conditions that exist, for which
no Government can be responsible, are
serious enough. I am neither an optimist nor a pessimist; I am a realist. I
want to face the hard stern facts that are
before us. I know that it is only by hard
work, by thrift, by keeping our expenditure to the very lowest possible limit that
we can extricate the country from the
terrible position into which it has fallen
as a result of the war and of world
complications. There is no secret road to
prosperity, and I do sincerely hope that
the Government mean during this
Session and in the future to exercise the
strictest economy, to get rid of all unnecessary interference with trade, and to
let the people help themselves, because it
is only by helping themselves that they
can bring back that condition of
prosperity that I am sure we all pray for.

He

That is what I consider Couéism.
There was a Professor Coué who said if
you kept on suggesting to yourself that you
were getting better if you were financially

disease you should forget about it and say

the past eight years. Day by day, was

day in every way I am getting better

Six Counties is the one outstanding
memorial of Professor Coué. Day by

worse and worse.
I want to refer particularly to a certain aspect of the discussions in this

this Government has got of a Belfast

Mr. DEVLIN: A few days ago I ventured to raise in the House the, to me,
all-important question of the marketing
of agricultural produce, with special
relation to transit, and the Prime Minis
ter-I think he was impressed with the
importance of the matter at the timethen said he would discuss the matter with
me. I waited for the invitation to discuss the matter from then until now, but
the invitation has not been extended. I.
therefore, put a question upon the Order
Paper to-day. I notice the Prime Minister has entirely changed his attitude. I
do not know why he has done so, because
in my judgment if we had less talk in this
House and elsewhere of our interest in
the farmers and in agriculture, and more
practical work for the farmers and agriculture, it would be far better for us.
I had not before me at the time the
fact that I have since discovered-and
which I discovered largely because the
matter was mentioned by the Prime
Minister that this question has already
been dealt with. The question I am
raising now is a matter of pressing public
importance and is most vital to all our
interests. It was really so vital and
important six years ago that the Prime
Minister set up a Committee for the purpose of taking evidence and of coming to
conclusions upon the basis of that evidence as to the best way in which this
matter could be dealt with. That Committee, I gather, was composed of a
number of political and other supporters
of the Prime Minister. Its chairman
was Mr. John M. Mark, M.P.; the next
most important member of it was Mr.
William Grant, M.P., and the other
gentlemen whose names are here are, with
one exception, i understand, strong political supporters of the noble Lord.
That Committee was appointed, and
the terms of reference were very simple:
in fact, they were practically on the same
lines as the question I put to the Prime
Minister. It was a Committee to inquire
into
(a) The cost of transit of farm
produce;
(b) the causes of the difference in
prices obtained by producers and the
prices charged to consumers; and
(c) the methods of marketing agricultural produce generally.
If the government, of which the noble
Lord, the Prime Minister, is the head,
thought it important six years ago, when
agriculture was in a less parlous condition
than it is to-day, to set up a Committee
of this character to explore the question
and submit recommendations as to the
result of their explorations and inquiries,
surely it is rather a contemptuous thing
for the Prime Minister to treat my suggestion in the way he has done, at the
end of six years, during which time agriculture has passed through a period which
has caused much disquietude to those engaged in that occupation?
That Committee sat and heard evidence,
and I would like to read to the House
one of the paragraphs in their Report.
The Committee animadverted upon the
fact that several vested interests refused
to be represented or to give evidence befor it. They seem to be a very powerful
body. They seem either to have stupefied
the Government or prevented them from
making a single improvement. After
animadverting upon the action of several
public bodies who refused to give evidence
or be represented before the Committee,
the Report states:-
"The Committee have, however, received general evidence from reliable
and very varied sources to the effect
that the present costs of transit, even
if they can be shown to be compatible
with working expenses are nevertheless
so high as to constitute a very grave
impediment and, in some cases to which
we shall refer later, a virtual bar to
the marketing of Northern Ireland
farm produce."

CLASS IV. No. 2.
NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum, not exceeding £2,400, be granted
be granted to His
Majesty for the service of the year ending
on the 31st of March, 1932, to defray the
grant-in-aid of the cost of Benefits and
Expenses of administration under the
National Health Insurance Acts."
Mr. GORDON: I feel that I will have
the support of every Member of the Committee in presenting this Supplementary
Estimate, and more especially will I have
the support of my hon. Friend (Mr.
Beattie) who sits on the Front Opposition
Bench.
Under the National Health Insurance
Act, 1931, provision is made for the prolongation in health insurance of certain
classes of persons who would otherwise
lose their health and pensions rights.
The additional charge on the funds of
approved societies resulting from this
prolongation is met by the Exchequer, which
pays over to the approved societies a sum
representing the value of 36 contributions
for each member benefiting by prolongation. The total charge on the Exchequer for these contributions is now
estimated at £2,400-the amount shown
in the Supplementary Estimate.
This sum will meet the cost of prolongation up to 31st December last-the
date fixed by the National Health Insurance Act (Northern Ireland), 1931.
The cost of the further prolongation to
31st December, 1932, under the National
Health Insurance (No. 2) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1931, is included in the 1932-33
Estimates for Health Insurance. I beg
to move.

Private Business.
RANDALSTOWN AND DISTRICT
ELECTRICITY SPECIAL ORDER,
1932.
Resolved: "That the Special Order
made and confirmed by the Ministry of
Commerce for Northern Ireland under
the Electricity (Supply) Acts, 1882 to
1931, in respect of the Townlands of
Randalstown, Lisnagreggan, Feehogue,
Ballygrooby, Lurgan West, and Shanes
Castle Park, in the Rural District of
Antrim, and the Townland of Ballytresna, in the Rural District of Ballymena, all in the County of Antrim, is
hereby approved."
THE LISBURN GAS ORDER, 1932.
Resolved: "That the Special Order
made by the Ministry of Commerce for
Northern Ireland under Section 10 of the
Gas Regulation Act, 1920, with respect
to Lisburn Urban District, is hereby
approved."

Oral Answers to Questions.
ELECTRICITY IN EAST DOWN
AREA.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Commerce whether he can
state in what areas in East Down will the
Electricity Board operate, and give an
approximate date when current will be
available.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): My hon. and gallant
Friend will appreciate that the Electricity
Board is an independent entity and not
under the control of my Ministry. I
have, however, had inquiries made and
am informed that work is at present proceeding on the construction of a 33,000
volt line which will link Belfast with
Newtownards and Comber, and thereafter
form a junction with the existing Belfast,
Holywood, and Bangor line at Bangor.
The Electricity Board propose to put in
hand very shortly the construction of an
11,000 volt main transmission line
to connect Bangor, Groomsport, Donaghadee, and Millisle, and also a 33,000 volt
line connecting the Board's system at
Poyntzpass with Newry.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
Α contract has also been placed
for the provision of low tension distribution systems in Newtownards,
Comber, Groomsport, and Millisle, and it
is anticipated that supplies of electricity
will be available in these centres before
the winter of 1932-33.
The Board is not at the moment in a
position to give an exact date when its
main transmission system will be extended to the remainder of the eastern
portion of County Down. I am informed,
however, that the necessary surveys are
being gradually undertaken.
The question as to the extension of the
Board's supply system to particular areas
is largely dependent upon the extent of
the load available. If, therefore, my
hon. and gallant Friend has in mind any
particular area where a supply of
electricity is urgently desired, I would
suggest that the residents in that area
may assist to expedite consideration of
their claims by furnishing to the Board
statistical data as to the potential demand
in their area obtained as a result of a
canvass.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of the first part of the reply, is the
Minister not responsible under Section 4
of the Act of 1931 for collecting the information?
Mr. BARBOUR: I will endeavour to
do so in this case.

3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of

5. Mr. McCARROLL asked the Minister of Finance whether his attention has
been called to the resolution of the
Londonderry branch of the Typographical
Association, stating that it is the intention to have Government printing
executed in London, and strongly protesting against such an injustice; and

amount of unemployment in the printing

Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONE
Mr. POLLOCK: My attention has
been directed to this resolution, and I
would take this opportunity of informing
the hon. Member that the matter has
been somewhat exaggerated.
It is the normal practice of this
Government to ensure that such printing
requirements as can be entrusted to, and
undertaken by, the printing industry in
Northern Ireland shall be so allocated,
and in pursuance of this policy, I may
state that 97 per cent. of the total printing orders for this Government, during
the last financial year, were assigned to
Northern Ireland firms and executed in
Northern Ireland. In the instance which
has given rise to this question, it was
decided to produce certain lists, which
had previously been printed, by a duplicating process in London, in order to effect
substantial financial economy, a course
which will, I think, commend itself
generally, and this accounts for the printing of those particular lists not being
continued.
It might, perhaps, be of interest for
hon. Members to know that, as I am informed, printing firms in Northern Ireland are not excluded from participation
in, and, as a matter of fact, have secured
orders for Government printing for
United Kingdom requirements.
Mr. McCARROLL: Do I understand
the Minister to say that this work has
been done in London?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes, at a saving of
£140 out of a total of £300. They have
a peculiar duplicating plant which is not
in existence here. It is not printing.
Mr. McCARROLL: Do the same rate
of wages apply?
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not know.
Mr. COLLINS: Oh!

GOVERNOR'S ANSWER TO THE
ADDRESS.
The Prime Minister (at the Bar) reported that His Grace the Governor,
having been attended with the Address
of 10th March, has been pleased to give
the following answer :-
I have received with great satisfaction the expression of your thanks for
the Speech with which I opened the
present Session of Parliament.

MAYO STREET SENIOR P.E.
SCHOOL.
1. Mr. McNEILL asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he can state if the
following statistics of floor space in Mayo
Street Senior Public Elementary School
are correct-One room, fifty-six feet by
twenty-four feet; one, seventeen and
three-quarters feet by fifteen and a half
feet, providing total accommodation for
199 pupils.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): According
to the official returns furnished by the
school manager, this school consists of
three rooms whose measurements are:-
56 feet x 25 feet,
173 feet x 173 feet, and
173 x 15 feet respectively.
As a class in a school such as this
usually has an attendance of over 40
pupils, the Ministry does not regard the
smallest of the rooms mentioned, which
contains only 275 sq. feet of floor space,
as suitable for teaching purposes, and
does not now recognise it in the
authorised school accommodation, which
is sufficient therefore only for 171 pupils.
2. Mr. McNEILL asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether any official communication as to the sufficiency of the floor
space in Mayo Street Senior Public
Elementary School, was sent to the
Manager of the school by his Department immediately following the appointment of Mr. David Gamble as
Vice-Principal, or at any time subsequently during Mr. Gamble's tenure of
office.

REARRANGEMENT OF SCHOOL
ACCOMMODATION - STATUS OF
TEACHERS.
3. Mr. McNEILL asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he can state if it is
the policy of the Ministry to reduce in
status teachers in schools affected by the
rearrangement of the school accommodation in the immediate neighbourhood, and, if so, to give the names of
teachers so reduced.
Mr. ROBB: The answer is in the
negative, but in cases of amalgamation
or reorganisation, where two or more
schools are combined, as only one of the
principals concerned can be principal
teacher of the reorganised school, it is
usually necessary that the other principals should become assistants, but in
such cases they are given a privileged
position which ensures reasonable protection against financial loss.
GLENWOOD SCHOOL-MR. DAVID
GAMBLE.
4. Mr. McNEILL asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he is aware that Mr.
David Gamble denies that he volunteered
Vote on Account
Housing (Grants) Bill
15 MARCH 1932
to go as an ordinary assistant to Glenwood School, and can he state the
evidence upon which the Belfast Education Authority made the assertion that
Mr. Gamble volunteered to accept the
inferior position.
Mr. ROBB: With regard to the first
part of the question, the Ministry understands that Mr. Gamble denies that he
volunteered to go to Glenwood School as
an assistant.
In regard to the latter part, the Ministry is informed that the evidence consists
of oral statements, which passed at the
time between Mr. Gamble and an officer
of the Belfast Education Committee, and
the fact that he signed an agreement in
September, 1930, with the Belfast
Education Committee, agreeing to serve
as an assistant teacher in any school
under that Committee's management.
Mr. Gamble entered upon his duties in
Glenwood in August, 1930, without
making any appeal to the Ministry.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In considering the
present proposals which are now before
the House, in regard to the future of
housing in Northern Ireland, the Government took into their earnest consideration
the views expressed in the Report of the
Select Committee presented to the House
in the month of December last dealing
with the question of rent restriction. It
is proposed to bring in a Bill dealing with
this matter at an early date and, therefore, I propose to refer only to one paragraph of that Report in this connection.
Towards the end of their Report the
Committee used these words:-
"In referring to this matter of the
shortage of houses the Committee desire, even at the risk of overstepping
their terms of reference, to suggest
that the greatest need at the moment
is for houses which can be let at low
rents, i.e., not exceeding 6s per week,
in
and housing subsidies future,
whether made by the Government or
by local authorities, should be made
conditional upon a rent not exceeding
a certain limit being charged for a
prescribed period."
I may say at once that the Government
concur in the first part of that Report.
Indeed, it has been, and is, the policy of
the Government, since they introduced
their first Act dealing with the question
of housing in 1923, and it was with the
object of trying to get the type of house
within the means of the working man that,
in 1927, the Government, when introducing the Bill in that year fixed the
minimum area of houses qualifying for
subsidy at 650 superficial feet. We had
found at that time that the practice of
the builders was to build to the maximum
allowed under the Acts, and therefore
the attitude of the builders defeated to a
large extent the object the Government
had in view of providing a type of house
within the means of the working man.
It will be within the recollection of
hon. Members that, in deference to the
wishes expressed from all parts of the
House, the Government agreed to increase the maximum area to 700 superficial feet, but the result of the working
of that Act has been that this Amendment hinders the supply of houses which
the Government regarded as most urgently
needed. I would like hon. Members to
take a note of these figures relating to
houses built by private builders between
1930 and 14th March, 1932. In regard
to houses between 500 and 550 superficial feet only 1 per cent. built under
the Acts came under that description.
When we come to the next stage, houses
between 550 and 600 superficial feet, the
proportion was 27 per cent., then between
600 and 650 we find it was 32 per cent.,
and within the last limit 650 to 700
Housing (Grants) Bill-

percentages show that the contention I
put forward is the correct one.
As will be seen when I come to explain

the Government have come to the conclusion that a still greater limitation in
the maximum size of the houses eligible

With regard to the second part of

should be dependent upon a condition.
limiting the amount of rents charged,

subject to restricting conditions of this
kind.
I have said over and over again at

by obtaining an adequate supply of
houses, and by encouraging people to invest their money in houses, and unless
we can succeed in getting people to put
their money into houses, a shortage will

There is, of course, very direct financial

Hon. Members will, therefore, appreciate that we have made large strides
towards meeting the deficiency in housing
accommodation, and that in doing so we
have incurred serious financial liabilities.
As I have already pointed out, our
liabilities in respect of subsidies under the
Acts passed by this Parliament amount
to over £2,000,000, and this will entail
an annual charge on the Estimates of
£169,000. In addition, we have to meet
annual sums amounting to £21,000 in
respect of liabilities incurred under
previous housing legislation.
In formulating our future policy we
cannot but have regard to these liabilities,
and to the present financial situation.
Our resources are limited, and we have
therefore to attach great importance to
the financial aspect of the question.
Balancing these various considerations,
we have come to the conclusion that the
utmost assistance that we can give in this
matter is a subsidy of £25. We have also
come to the conclusion that the maximum
area under the existing Acts of 700
superficial feet is too high-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear) and we therefore
hear)-and
propose that the subsidy shall only be

500 superficial feet and a maximum of

comfortable houses can be provided within
these limits is proved by experience.

It has hitherto been our custom to

only, and this has had the disadvantage
state of unof leaving builders in a

thus slowing up the preparation of plans
for new buildings during that period.
For these reasons we think it better to
legislate for a period of two years, and
accordingly if this Measure is accepted

What are the Government doing at the

policy of the Government is to prevent

employment. The proof of that is in
my hand. Here is a letter from the

"Grants from the Road Fund,"
and here is the circular:
Minstry of Home Affairs,
Stormont,
Circ. No. R179.
Belfast.
25th January, 1932.
Sir, I am directed by the Minister
of Home Affairs to state that the
question of the grants to be paid from
the Road Fund in respect of the programme of work for the financial year
1932-33 by local authorities has been
receiving his earnest consideration in
the light of the fact that the reserves
in the fund have been completely exhausted and of the growing demands
on the Fund.
In these circumstances, the Minister
was at first constrained to feel that it
would be necessary for him to reduce
the percentage of rates of the grants
in respect of the three classes of roads,
but, after most careful and anxious
consideration as to the effect of such
change on the finances of local government authorities, particularly having
regard to the fact that in the majority
of cases the Estimates have already
been prepared in the expectation of
receiving the grants at the existing
rates, it has now been decided to retain
for one year more the present scale of
grants, i.e., 60 per cent. on 1st Class
roads, 30 per cent. on 2nd Class roads,
and 15 per cent. in respect of certain
3rd Class roads.
The retention of these rates for a
further year, which, as has already
been explained, has been decided upon
in order to avoid any dislocation or
disturbance of the accounts of local
authorities, will inevitably have the
effect of producing a very substantial
deficit in the fund during the course of
the year.
Accordingly, the Minister feels that,
while the grants at the above rates will
be paid, it will be necessary, as far as
possible to effect economies by curtailing, where practicable, the road programmes of the various local authorities
on the different classes of roads, i.e
by deferring works which are not of
really essential and urgent character
for a year at least, and by reducing, or
in special cases by abandoning the works
altogther for the present.
In particular, the Minister feels
constrained to impose a reduction in
the amounts of the grants which nor-

schemes, but the Derry scheme would
have been carried out if this Government
had never come into operation. It would
have been carried out by the Corporation
in Londonderry.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have a certificate
from the Corporation of Derry to the

Mr. NIXON: I do not like to intervene, but did not the Minister say before
now this afternoon that these schemes are
when they are not
only subsidised
necessary for at least three years?
Mr. McCARROLL: The position in
regard to the Derry scheme is perfectly
plain. In order to get a certain grant
the local bodies certify that the schemes
are necessary and owing to the financial
stringency they could not carry on.
There is no doubt about that. That is
the position. The Minister says there is
a certain amount of dishonesty in that.
I do not admit it. The conditions are
such that these local bodies could not
carry on. At any rate they would not
get assistance if they did not give the
certificate. That is the position. In
other words the entire expenditure in
relation to the scheme would be put on
the local authority. In a city like Derry,
where the rates are 18s in the pound, it
is perfectly obvious they could not carry
on without assistance from the State.
I say there was, to my mind, condemnation of these non-productive
schemes. I do not think it is fair to
condemn them. I think, whether these
schemes are productive or non-productive,
it is the business of the Government to
try to carry on and provide work for
these people in Derry, and other places.
It is much better to give them something
to do, and particularly to bring in the
young element who are doing nothing and
who have never done anything. Unfortunately there is an element that get work
for a short period, and when they qualify
for unemployment benefit they cease work
and never do anything. Since the war
that element has grown greater in this
area, and if the Government can do anything to drain it and give that element
employment they would do a great service.
Mr. ANDREWS: I would just like
to point out that the responsibility of
promoting these schemes, in the first instance, rests with the local authorities.
It has always rested with the local
authorities, both here and in Great
Britain. It is perfectly futile to talk
about the Government promoting schemes
and carrying them out themselves. They
would have to engage a huge staff, and,
further, they would have to go into the
area of the local authorities in order to
do the work which the local authority
was elected to carry out with their own
staff. To hear hon. Member's talk you
would think the Government's hands had
to be forced in connection with this matter. We do not require any force at all,
because I am justified in saying that in
Relief Schemes
Relief Schemes
15 MARCH 1932
all these ten years my Department has
scarcely turned down a scheme. We have
not turned down a single scheme which we
felt to be a scheme of public utility and
a scheme which we knew would provide
work for the unemployed. Therefore, if
there have not been more schemes it is
not the fault of the Government. It is
the fault of the local authorities who
have not promoted more schemes.
I have always said this, that I have
appreciated very much the way the local
authorities have carried out this matter
with the Government. That is why this
Amendment is down. This Amendment
simply means that that friendly cooperation should continue in order that
useful work should be carried out and
work should be found for the unemployed
as far as possible in the district that the
scheme is intended to benefit.
Now, hon. Members opposite have indicated-I will not put it further than that
-that no schemes are going on. At the
present time there are in operation in
Northern Ireland, and the greater number in Belfast, 78 schemes, involving a
Government grant of £664,000. Actually,
at the moment, 2,110 men are engaged in
this area, and further still, there are 94
schemes that have been sanctioned that
have not been started by the local
authorities and that involve a Govern.
ment grant of £131,000 odd. If these
schemes were started to-morrow, they
would provide for one year work for 2,700
people. So that I am justified in saying
that nowhere else is so much being done.
If there is any hold-up in this matter,
the hold-up is not due to the Government.

In Great Britain, somtimes they have

they have been carrying out schemes to
a lesser extent than they were doing some
years before. But here in Northern Ireland, continuously for more than ten
years, we have been sanctioning practically
every scheme put up by the local
authorities.
