FROM ULSTER FIRMS.
3. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether the Government propose
to introduce legislation to enable public
authorities to give a preference up to 10
per cent. to Ulster contractors tendering
for public contracts and thereby give
practical effort to the slogan, Push
Ulster Goods "
""
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked to
reply.
The hon. Member is evidently not
aware that this question formed the subject of a circular which was issued to every
local authority in May, 1927, and in
which local authorities were requested,
when considering tenders, to give preference, as far as possible, to firms
supplying goods manufactured in Northern Ireland, even where the prices
quoted by the Northern Ireland tenderers
were slightly in excess of those quoted by
other firms
For the guidance of the local authorities in determining what would be a
reasonable preference to allow, it was
indicated that it was the established
practice of all the Government Departments, other things being equal, to give
a preference up to the limit of 5 per cent.
It is not considered desirable or
expedient to interfere any further with
the discretion of local authorities, or to
lay down any hard and fast rule, in
matters of this character. It must therefore be left to the local authorities to deal
with each particular contract on its merits
and to decide on their own responsibility,
having regard to the lead given by the
Government, to what extent they will
extend the preference to Northern Ireland goods and to Northern Ireland
contractors.
Mr. NIXON: Would the Minister consider the advisability of raising the preference to 10 per cent. instead of 5 per
cent. under the conditions laid down?

March), "That the Bill be now read a
Second time."-(Sir Dawson Bates).
Question again proposed.
Mr. HEALY: The statement that the
Minister made yesterday in introducing
this Bill gave us a good deal of information as to the position from 1923 to
date. The Prime Minister sometimes
says that Members on this side of the
House are unwilling or reluctant to give
the Government credit for anything they
do. I do not think that is precisely
correct, because I am prepared to admit
that the Government have gone a long
way in providing houses for the working
classes where the local authorities have
been willing to co-operate. In that connection, I must say I have been very
much impressed by the figures given with
regard to the work of the Belfast Corporation, and if the urban councils in the
remainder of the Six Counties had cooperated to anything like the same extent,
I should not have a single word to say
to-day by way of criticism.
I differ from some of my hon. Friends
on this side in another respect too. I
think that the great matter is to provide
houses for the working people in whatever may seem to be the best way.
Probably it is unfortunate that the
recommendations of the Committee
appointed by the Government have not
been carried out, but I recognise that
there may be a difficulty. It may be a
monetary difficulty. We on this side of
the House are preaching economy, and the
most logical thing in the world would be
for the Government to adopt some of the
suggestions made from the Opposition.
Probably the work of economy would have
been done in the most inconvenient

The Minister, however, made another
prophecy yesterday in addition to the
many prophecies made from the Government Benches. He prophecied that within
a reasonable time they would have a
sufficiency of houses. Well, that remains
to be seen. The worst of prophets is that
when they embark on a journey into the
future they do not take a return ticket.
I am afraid it sometimes happens that
hon. Members on this side fall into
exactly the same errors in this matter
of prophecy. However, I am not going to
prophesy on this occasion. My difficulty
is with regard to housing in rural and
municipal areas. I know that large sums
of money have been allocated for the
purpose of providing houses, but urban
councils have not used that money in
providing houses for the people who are
unable to provide houses for themselves
-that is the working classes. They
erect a sufficient type of house which is
occupied by the professional or semiprofessional class.
Sir DAWSON BATES: What size?
Mr. HEALY: Up to 750 superficial
feet, and the rents of these houses are
anything up to £1 a week. Anybody who
knows the conditions in the country towns
will realise at once that it is not possible
tradesman's
for any man earning a
wages to pay a rent of this kind. Therefore, we have the extraordinary spectacle
of the Government wasting money, spending large sums of money, to which the
working classes must contribute their
quota, to subsidise the building of houses
for people who ought to be in a position
to build them themselves. At the same
time, in the urban area of Enniskillen,
with which I am particularly concerned,
there practically has not been a single
house erected that would fall within the
compass of a working man's dwelling.
That brings us again to another point.
Under the Labourers Acts for providing
housing accommodation there
was an
element of compulsion. It was open to
the applicants to make representations to
the district council, and if they were unwilling to perform their obligations they
could appeal to the Local Government
Board. A like provision, I suggest,
ought to be inserted in this Bill with
regard to urban areas which have not
been carrying out their duties to the
working classes as the Legislature contemplated they should. I think there
should be an element of compulsion in
this Bill, and that working people in an
urban area, who cannot find housing
accommodation and for whom there is no
provision made, ought to be able to come
to the Minister of Home Affairs and, in
putting up a scheme, he ought to be in
a position to come to their aid.
Generally speaking, I am not in favour
of coercing local authorities where those
local authorities take a broadminded and
enlightened view of their responsibilities.
But we have to recognise the fact that
there are many public bodies, such as the
Enniskillen Urban Council, which will
never rise to their responsibilities in this
matter unless some element of compulsion
is added. It is unfortunate that all
public representatives do not take the
public-spirited view of the members of
the Belfast Corporation in regard to the
provision of houses for the working
classes, but we have to deal with facts
as we find them. In Enniskillen the
Urban Council have refused to vote a
single penny of money on their own
account to the subsidising of labourers'
dwellings, although they have been prepared to take all the money the Government voted, utilise it, and then charge
rents that will ensure that there will be
no loss on the rates. In other words, the
Urban Council of Enniskillen-and in
this respect, I suppose, it is not any different to many other urban councils-are
not prepared to do anything for the working classes. They are prepared to utilise
the Government grants for the erection of
dwellings provided the rent will bring
them in a sufficient return to cover depreciation and sinking fund interest. In
other words, there is no sympathy whatever with the working classes in that particular area. The result to-day is that a
working man living in Enniskillen has no
chance of securing a house, but he must,
as a taxpayer, contribute his quota to
provide houses for other people who can
afford a rent of £1 per week.

Under the Chamberlain Act they built

considered programme of providing

that the information which I had received was incorrect I was perfectly prepared to withdraw it. But now, on the

Member denied that he had taken no
useful steps, and he said that he carried

Mr. BARBOUR: The valuation of
railways in Northern Ireland is at present
ascertained by reference to the Valuation
Act of 1852, which fixes the valuation on
the basis of net annual value, that is to
say, the rent for which, one year with
another, the same might in its actual state
be reasonably expected to let from year
to year, the probable average annual
cost of repairs, insurance, and other expenses, if any, necessary to maintain the
hereditament in its actual state, and all
rates, taxes and public charges, if any,
except tithe rentcharge, being paid by
the tenant.
The valuation of a railway must,
therefore, be based on the rent which a
hypothetical tenant would normally pay
for the land and buildings comprising
the railway's property, but the definition
of value cannot be applied to ascertain
the annual value of a railway in the same
way as it is applied in finding the value,
Railways Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
for example, of a shop. In valuing a
shop there is usually no great difficulty
in finding sufficient evidence of rental
value, but in the case of a railway there
is no such evidence, as the companies who
occupy railways are also the owners.
A special method-usually referred to as
the "revenue principle"-has therefore
been devised for applying the statutory
definition of value in the case of railways
and other properties, such as gas and
electric light undertakings. The method.
is the outcome of numerous law cases
which have been before the courts for
many years past, and it has become so
firmly established that it possesses almost
the same legal sanctity as the statutory
definition which it purports to apply.
This method of arriving at railway
valuations worked well so long as the
railways enjoyed a reasonable degree of
prosperity. Modern industrial depression and the competition of road transport have been severely felt by the
railways, and the resulting fall in their
revenue has been so great that if the railways were to insist on their strict legal
rights under the "revenue principle" the
result might in many cases be a nil
valuation. In recent years the whole
fabric of railway valuation has only been
maintained by makeshift informal agreements, having no foundation in strict
law.
This position is felt to be impossible,
and it is considered that the whole question of the valuation of railways should
be revised and put upon a clear statutory
basis, which, while securing fair treatment for the ordinary ratepayer, shall
not impose too harsh conditions upon the
railways. The fact that a railway is
actually working is an indication that it
is of some value to the company working
it, and this renders it inequitable that it
should escape altogether the burden of
rating which is levied to support those
services which it enjoys in common with
other ratepayers.
I should, perhaps, mention here that
unlike industrial hereditaments, a railway undertaking does not gain in actual
financial benefit from the derating legislation of 1928 and 1929. The threefourths relief which it obtains must,
the statutory freight rebates
under
scheme, be passed on to users of the
railway.
It will readily be appreciated that
under the "revenue principle" of fixing
valuation, the larger the amount allocated to interest on tenant's capital, the
smaller will be the balance of receipts
which may be considered as landlord's
rent or valuation. Judicial decisions
have established that for the purpose
of calculating the interest on tenant's
capital, the capital value of plant, rolling
stock, stores, etc., is to be their present
value in terms of modern money values
and not their original cost. The result
is that, in addition to the rapidly shrinking revenue of the railways, the position
has been complicated by the fact that,
owing to the decreased value of money,
the allocations for interest on tenant's
capital have had to be very largely increased. Thus, rental value under the
present system entirely disappears and a
nil valuation is the result.
The first part of this Bill gives a statutory basis to the "revenue principle" interpretation of the Act of 1852, while
freeing it from the judicial qualifications
which have been grafted on to it, such
as the necessity for allowing fixed percentages for interest and profit on tenant's
capital. There are to be quinquennial
revisions of railway valuations. For the
purposes of such a revision, the Commissioner of Valuation is, in accordance with
Clause 5, to ascertain the average of the
net receipts of each railway company as
a whole for the first five of the six completed accounting years next preceding
the date on which such revaluation is to
come into force. Having arrived at this
average, he is to use it as the basis of the
letting value of the railway, and the
annual rent thus arrived at is to be the
valuation for the next five years.
It is possible however, and, if the
present decline in revenue continues, even
probable, that the foregoing formula may
still involve a nil valuation. The Bill
provides against such an eventuality, because, as I have already stated, so long as
a railway runs, it must be considered
to have some value. A minimum valuation is accordingly specified which is to
operate in the event of the receipts of
the railway companies falling beyond a
certain point. Clause 7 of the Bill details the method of arriving at such a
minimum valuation.
In the case of the actual railway track
itself, the minimum valuation is to be
the valuation which would have been
placed on the land under the Act of 1852
if it had not been adapted for use as a
Railways Bill-
Second Reading
21 MARCH 1932
railway. In the case of other portions of
the railway, such as goods sheds and so
forth, the minimum valuation is to be
arrived at on the annual basis of letting
value, but on 1914 standard and reduced
by two-thirds.
Having now, in language as little
technical as possible, described the general
aim of the Bill, I will reply to a question
which doubtless many Members have been
asking themselves, namely, is Northern
Ireland the only part of the British Isles
that has had to face this problem? The
answer is that it was faced in Great
Britain in 1930, when the Railways
(Valuation for Rating) Act was passed.
That Act in the main corresponds with
the Bill before this House, save that it
does not provide for a minimum valuation. In the Irish Free State, a Bill
was passed towards the close of last year,
and the present Bill corresponds more
closely with it than with the British Act,
by reason of the fact that the Irish basis
of valuation and case law on valuation
differ in many respects from that which
operates in Great Britain. Moreover, a
differing system of railway valuation in
the two parts of Ireland would be bound
to lead to confusion, owing to the inter-
State character of a number of the railways.
I have confined myself to the main
outlines of the Bill. The more technical
aspect of the various Clauses can best be
dealt with in Committee. I beg to move.

New Industries (Development) Bill.

Mr. BARBOUR: The prolonged industrial depression through which Northern Ireland in common with the rest
of the United Kingdom has been passing
has brought home to us in a most forcible
manner the greater vulnerability of an
industrial community like our own almost
entirely dependent on one or two major
industries. Although the depression has
affected all industries, without exception,
it has weighed most heavily of all perhaps
on shipbuilding, and almost as heavily on
the textile trades. Northern Ireland,
therefore, has been in an exceptionally
exposed position, and relatively she has
suffered more than a comparable area
possessing a broader industrial basis.
Accordingly, the Government has been
turning its attention to the special opportunities of broadening the Northern Ireland basis presented by the recent change
in the fiscal policy of the United Kingdom, and the Bill now before the House
represents an effort to take advantage of
those opportunities.
The Bill is very simple in character.
It empowers the Ministry of Commerce,
under certain conditions, to pay to any
person or company establishing a new industry in Northern Ireland within the
five-years period, 1st November, 1931, to
31st October, 1936, an annual sum not
exceeding what the Ministry considers to
be equivalent to a reasonable annual rent
for the site on which the undertaking is
established. It also empowers local
authorities to exempt from payment of
rates any premises erected on a site in
respect of which the Ministry of Commerce has agreed to make the annual
payment to which I have referred.
For the purposes of the Bill a "new
industry" means one devoted to the production of goods of a kind which were
not being produced in Northern Ireland
before 1st November, 1931. The maximum period during which the Ministry
of Commerce is empowered to continue
making the annual payments, and the
local authorities to continue exemption
from rates, is twenty years, reckoning
from the date which the Ministry's
annual payments began.
Hon. Members will appreciate the
necessity of restricting the benefits proposed by the Bill to industries concerned
only with goods of a kind not previously
being made in Northern Ireland.
It may
be, of course, that the opportunities of
successfully establishing a factory for the
the production of something already
being made in Northern Ireland are quite
as good as those for the establishment of
one engaged in producing something
entirely new. The restriction of the
benefits to new industries, therefore, must
not be taken as implying that in the
Government's view the only industries
which stand a chance of successful development are those already existent here. By
confining the benefits to new industries
the Government avoids an injustice to our
existing industries.
In the exercise of its functions under
the Bill the Ministry of Commerce will
have the assistance of an Advisory Committee, to which it may refer applications
for the benefits allowable under the
Measure. The Ministry, however, will
itself make the decision on each application, and that decision shall be final. In
any case in which the Ministry considers
that an annual payment should be made
the Ministry will obtain the consent of
the Ministry of Finance before such a
payment is made.
New Industries Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
The Bill provides that, in order to
qualify for payments, the undertaking
must in every case appear to the Ministry as likely to afford substantial employment. The Bill also provides for the
Ministry of Commerce prescribing such
other conditions attaching to the acceptance of an application as the Ministry
may think necessary. Hon. Members will
observe that provision is also made to
enable the Ministry of Commerce to expend money, up to such amounts as the
Ministry of Finance may sanction, for the
purpose of making known the facilities
provided under the Bill.
Those are, briefly, the objects and
machinery of the Bill. In the Government's view the present is a most opportune moment in which to endeavour to
attract new industries to our territory.
The recent change in the fiscal policy of
the United Kingdom is likely to lead to
the establishment of branches of foreign
industrial undertakings within the United
Kingdom, and the object aimed at in the
Bill is to offer just that extra inducement
which often decides the locating of a
factory in one place rather than in
another. I beg to move.

Shooting Affair in County Derry.

Mr. McCARROLL: I desire to raise
a question in regard to the shooting that
occurred on St. Patrick's Day in a part
of County Derry, when two Catholic
young men, who were members of a procession proceeding to a railway station,
were fired upon and seriously wounded.
Most of the facts in connection with this
diabolical affair have already appeared in
the Press, and I should like to know what
steps the Government propose to take to
apprehend the perpetrators of this outrage, to ensure that there will not be a
recurrence of such a terrible affair, and
that adequate measures will be taken to
safeguard the lives of the Catholic people
in these parts and to allow them to live
in the enjoyment of their rights as free
citizens.
I do not know that there is at all an
adequate appreciation of the terrible
character of this outrage. These men,
members of a procession, were proceeding in a legitimate way in the morning,
in broad daylight, to the railway station
at Magherafelt, when they were fired
upon by a large party. I understand
that there were several members of a
party lying in ambush and they opened
fire in this murderous fashion on this
unarmed body. Those men could not
have congregated there, in my opinion,
without the knowledge of the police
authorities in that area. Moreover, I
am bound to say that it was within the
knowledge of the Ministry of Home
Affairs that there was in this area a
reign of terror that has existed for a considerable period. There has been a good
deal of shooting, and there has been a
good deal of interference with the
Catholic people in that area.
These facts
were, I understand, brought to the knowledge of the Government, and I suggest
that the Government either ignored
entirely the representations that were.
made to them in regard to this state of
affairs, or that they failed absolutely to
do anything to provide adequate protection for that procession which, as I
say, was proceeding, as it was entitled to
do on that particular day, to the railway station.
There can be no question as to the right
of members of that procession to congregate at their hall and proceed, on St.
Patrick's Day, to the railway station and
there entrain to participate in a demonstration. I do not think there will be any
question as to their rights in this respect
when they were proceeding in a peaceable
way, and when they were unarmed. When
they were doing so this, as I call it,
murderous attack was made on them.
Those men with rifles congregated on
either side of the road, along which this
procession was proceeding, could not have
dropped out of the air. The police must
know the conditions in the locality. They
must know who the persons are who
possess these rifles, and this assembly of
armed men could not have taken place
without the knowledge of some of those
who are supposed to be the guardians of
law and order in that area. I suggest
that it is quite impossible that these men
could assemble there in broad daylight
and commit this atrocious crime without
the knowledge of either the regular police
force or the Special Constabulary in that
area.
I regret exceedingly the necessity of
raising this matter. There has been
growing up in Northern Ireland a spirit
of peace and goodwill. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). This and other
incidents of which we have had to complain in this House have a very serious
and disturbing effect on the peace of the
country, and create alarm and apprehension in the minds of the people we
represent. I do say that the Government cannot be absolved entirely from
responsibility for permitting to be created
the situation in which this attack was
made upon inoffensive and unoffending

think it is the duty of the Minister of

Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: Since

Friend did come to me on this subject,

Creamery purchases manufacturing milk,

pays its producers a price which compares.
very favourably with the price paid by

one between the management committee

On the question of housing the Government has spent large sums of money
for the purpose of assisting the local
authorities and builders with the object
of providing homes for the people who
require them. I think the Government's
policy on the housing question is wrong,
because it did not get sufficient houses
when you were giving £100 plus £40 from
the Corporation, and to-day you are only
giving £25 with no prospect of anything
from the Corporation. I think that £25
will be lost. It will really be futile so far
as the private builders are concerned. It
has been always claimed by myself and
the representatives of the party I have
the honour to represent in this House,
that no public money should be given to
any individual without a voice in its
administration. Now, in house building,
I think the Government when they make
subsidies should have a voice in fixing
the letting value of the houses, and until
the Government do that we will never
get houses fit for the working classes.
You will get them fit for living in, but
not fit for paying for. It is a paying
proposition the working classes are looking for at the present moment. There
are plenty of houses. There are houses
built by the Corporation. I was round
an avenue last night where there are
ten nice suitable houses vacant. Why
are these ten houses vacant and people
three streets away living in a room?
is because a pound or 22s 6d a week is

If I had known there would be a debate

to sympathy than blind people.
Members: Hear, hear.) Blindness is one
of the greatest afflictions anyone could
imagine or conceive. It is very remarkable that most blind people take an
interest in football and every other form
of sport, and in politics and everything
in which an ordinary person takes an
interest. I remember spending a night
with the members of one of the blind
person's organisations, and, after we had

was no subject in which they did not
take an interest, or which they were not

about you, and to be able to take no part
in it.
It is humiliating to any country that
blind people should have to go out on the
street and beg or importune persons, or
hold out a can to get money. I do not
know how it comes, but I have seen some
of that in Belfast lately. I cannot
understand how it is necessary. We

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Mental Treatment Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Although in England
a comprehensive statute which in effect
consolidated and brought up to date the
law in regard to lunacy was passed in
1890, and a subsequent Measure-the
Mental Treatment Act-was passed in
1930, bringing certain valuable reforms
into operation, lunacy law in Ireland
for all practical purposes has remained
unaltered since the passing of the Act of
1875. Although I am glad to say the
actual care and treatment of this malady
is no less enlightened and efficient in Northern Ireland than in any other part of
the world, the fact remains that our
legislation dealing with the question is in
some respects archaic and has not kept
pace with modern developments.
While, no doubt, the progress of medical
science and the growth of an enlightened
public opinion have revolutionised the
treatment of the mentally afflicted, there
is still a tendency to regard to mental
illness as something carrying an indelible
stigma, and although we may congratulate
ourselves that we are no longer living in
an age which considered fetters and a
straw pallet as the suitable equipment for
the treatment of the insane, the deepseated idea that persons of unsound mind
are to be regarded as lepers or pariahs to
be shut off from society still survives to
a certain extent. Consider, for example,
as evidence of this the existing procedure
for dealing with dangerous lunatics, to
which I shall again refer, which would
seem to imply that there is something
actually criminal in mental infirmity.
It is of the first importance that this
entirely wrong and cruel idea should be
got rid of. As has been well said in the
Report of the Royal Commission on
Lunacy, which sat in 1926:-
:--
"The keynote of the past has been
detention, the keynote of the future
should be prevention and treatment."
It is essential that mental illness should
be considered in its true perspective as a
serious malady requiring sympathetic
and specialised treatment, and one which
does not necessarily carry in its train
any greater reproach than any ordinary
physical disability. Mental disease, like
other forms of disease, is in many cases
curable and the chances of effecting a cure
are infinitely improved if treatment is
undertaken in the incipient stages of the
disease. Under existing conditions, and
as the law now stands, it is almost
inevitable that any disposition towards
mental disability will be concealed as
long as possible on account of the prejudice which unfortunately still obtains
in regard to this malady.
To endeavour to combat this false impression and to provide for the early
treatment of sufferers is one of the main
objects of this Bill. Hitherto the specialised treatment provided in our public
mental hospitals has been confined to persons definitely certified as of unsound
mind, and the preventive value of such
treatment has been denied to those who
may be merely threatened with the
disease or who may be suffering from
some temporary form of mental instability which does not amount to actual
insanity.
549 Mental Treatment Bill-

23 MARCH 1932
Second Reading
The object of Part I of our Bill is,
therefore, to enable such cases of incipient.
mental disease to be treated in mental
hospitals without any necessity for certification and without undue formality or
the intervention of anything in the
nature of judicial proceedings. The provisions in this respect have been adopted
with little alteration, from the corresponding provisions of the Mental Treatment Act of 1930 now operating in England. These provisions provide for
voluntary treatment and also for temporary treatment.
With regard to voluntary treatment,
it is provided that persons who are desirous of submitting themselves for
treatment for illness of a mental nature
may voluntarily avail themselves of the
benefit of treatment in mental institutions and may submit themselves to such
treatment without the necessity for
certification.
It may be interesting to note that, in
connection with this matter, evidence was
given before the Royal Commission, to
which I have already referred, of several
distressing cases of people who felt that
they were becoming mentally unstable,
and in whose cases rest and special treatment in a mental home would have been
invaluable, but who were unable to avail
themselves of this advantage until their
illness had progressed to the point when
they became certifiable. Had it been
open to them to receive the necessary
treatment in the initial stages of their
illness it is possible that its progress
might have been arrested and the necessity for certification might never have
arisen.
The provisions dealing with temporary
treatment are intended to meet the case
of persons suffering from some temporary
form of mental disorder which, in the
opinion of their doctors, would be likely to
yield to the specialised mental treatment
in a mental home. The patient in such
cases, although possibly suffering from some
purely temporary form of mental illness
may nevertheless be incapable at the
moment of volition and unable, therefore, to avail themselves of the provisions
relating to voluntary treatment to which
I have just referred.
The procedure proposed under which
such cases may be received in a mental
hospital provides for an application to
this effect being made by the husband,
wife, or relative, or, if made by some
person other than such relatives, the
application must indicate the connection
of the person making the application
with the patient. The application must
be supported by a certificate from two
doctors to the effect that the patient is
suffering from mental illness and is likely
to benefit by temporary treatment. The
patient may then be accepted for a period
not exceeding six months as a temporary
patient and this period may be extended
for further periods of six months with
the consent of the Ministry, if it appears
from medical evidence that recovery is
likely as a result of further temporary
treatment. It will be noted that, in this
case as in the case of a voluntary patient,
the patient is not certified to be of unsound mind, nor is the intervention of
judicial authority required. The
reasons underlying these provisions for
voluntary and temporary treatment will,
I think, be fairly obvious.
a
It may be appropriate if I here refer
to proposals which are in the nature of
a logical corollary to this system of preventive treatment in the incipient stages
of the malady. I allude to the provisions in Part IV. of the Bill which
will enable public mental hospitals to
provide clinics at which extern patients
may obtain advice and treatment, and
which will also enable patients who have
been discharged from the institution to
receive advice and treatment which may
be of the greatest benefit in preventing
a recurrence of the illness.
Apart from these provisions the opportunity has been taken to effect various
amendments in the general law relating
to mental disorder, which will have the
effect of bringing the law in Northern
Ireland more into line with the more
modern English code, and which will also
simplify the existing procedure. I do
not at this stage propose to go into
elaborate detail, but I would like to mention a few of the more important points
where it has been thought desirable to
introduce such amendments.
It is first of all proposed, with the
object of removing anything which may
tend to keep alive the unfortunate prejudice which we know still exists in regard to mental disorder, to abolish
certain terms which have hitherto been
employed in connection.
connection with mental
illness, and which have acquired a sinister and objectionable significance. The
term "lunatic" will pass into oblivion, and

[Sir Dawson Bates]
the expression "person of unsound mind"
will be used to designate persons suffering from this form of illness. Similarly,
"lunatic asylums" will in future be
more accurately described as "mental
hospitals," and the objectionable terms
"pauper" or "poor" in relation to inmates of public mental hospitals will be
replaced by the expression "rate-aided."
It will be observed that a considerable
portion of Part II. of the Bill deals with
the procedure in regard to the admission.
to and discharge from institutions of
patients. With regard to admissionsthere are no fewer than 7 different forms
of procedure for the admission of persons
of unsound mind into mental institutions.
The most common method is that employed in the case of ordinary admissions
to public mental hospitals, and the conditions governing these are, strange to
say, not at present laid down by statute
but are prescribed in the regulations.
made by each individual asylum committee
and approved by the Governor.
The
conditions so laid down by regulation are
in short an application supported by a
medical certificate on which a recommendation from a justice for the admission of the patient is obtained.
In the case of so-called dangerous
lunatics admitted under the provisions of
the Act of 1867, unfortunately a comparatively numerous class, although in
many instances the individuals are not
dangerous in the ordinary acceptance of
the term, the procedure laid down is entirely contrary to the whole trend of
modern opinion in regard to mental illness.
Under this statute, alleged dangerous
lunatics are, if I may put it in this way,
arrested, brought before two justices,
charged with being dangerous lunatics,
convicted and committed to an asylum.
They are, in fact, treated as criminals.
Mr. BEATTIE: Did you say alleged

Sir DAWSON BATES: May I put a

case to my hon. Friend?
going along the street sees a man behaving

The

Mr. BEATTIE: He is not an alleged

Sir DAWSON BATES: In the case of

It is, therefore, now proposed, following
the practice which has obtained for many
years in England, to adopt a common
procedure for admission under which persons of unsound mind may be received
into mental institutions on a simple order
of a J.P. supported by a medical
by a
certificate.
In order to provide for cases where it
may be desirable that the patient should
be removed at once to a mental institution,
provision is made that, if the doctor
certifying the patient is satisfied that he
should be removed forthwith to the
asylum, this may be done in anticipation
of the justice's order. In such cases, however, the authority to detain the patient is
limited to seven days unless, meanwhile,
the full procedure for admission has been
completed.
There is also the further type of case
where a person of unsound mind is found
actually behaving in such a way as to
constitute a danger to himself or to
others, and to meet such cases machinery
is provided, as in the English Act, which
will enable the patient to be placed under
restraint, pending certification and completion of the necessary formalities to
enable him to be received in a mental
institution.
The proposed provision,
which, as I have said, follows that in
the English Act, gives power to the
police to bring such persons for safe
custody to a workhouse, pending the completion of the order for their admission
to a mental hospital.
It has also been thought desirable to
adopt provisions which appear in the
English Act whereby cases of persons of
unsound mind, believed to be cruelly illtreated or neglected, can be brought under
notice of a justice, who can then set
machinery in motion to have the matter

to be detained in the institution.
re-
Such a contingency is no doubt most
unlikely to arise in institutions so admirably conducted as our present day mental
hospitals, but it was, nevertheless, considered necessary when the English Act
of 1890 was passed to insert provisions
safeguarding beyond a
a possibility of
doubt patients in mental institutions.
from being detained after recovery. It
has been thought well to include in this
Bill provisions corresponding to those in
force in England. Under these, a
ception order, which will in future be
the authority for the detention of the
patient, will remain valid in the first
instance for one year only, and thereafter for successive periods of 2, 3 and 5
years. Before the termination of each such
period the medical officer of the institution must certify that the patient is
still of unsound mind, and sanction must
be obtained from the Ministry for the
continuance in force of the reception
order for the subsequent period. This
procedure ensures that every individual
case must be brought up for examination
and review at comparatively frequent
periods.
The existing provisions in regard to
discharge, as in the case of admission,
are partly governed by regulations and
partly by statute, and show a similar lack
of uniformity. Provisions similar to
those in the English Act of 1890 have,
therefore, been incorporated in the Bill
and while no radical change in principle
is effected, this arrangement will, it is
believed, prove more convenient in
operation and for purposes of reference.
Part III. of the Bill deals mainly with
a proposed alteration of the system under
which private establishments are authorised to receive persons of unsound mind.
The existing arrangement is that laid.
down in the Private Asylums Act of
1842, and, as may be imagined, can
hardly be regarded to-day as entirely up
to date.
The system of licensing laid down in
that Act under which proprietors of
private asylums must apply annually at
Quarter Sessions for licences has been
subjected to criticism. So far back as
the year 1846 the inspectors of lunatics
in their annual report stated that the
procedure was found to be attended with
inconvenience and was open to objection.
Such decision must necessarily depend
mainly upon medical and technical considerations, and it is, therefore, now proposed to substitute in place of the system of licensing at Quarter Sessions a
system of registration by the Ministry,
who will be advised by their inspectors.
Part IV. of the Bill comprises various
amendments of the law relative to public
mental hospitals.
I have already dealt with those relating to extern treatment and after-care,
and I hardly think that it is necessary
at the moment to refer to any of the
other Clauses save those relating to the
parliamentary grant in aid of the maintenance of persons of unsound mind in
public mental hospitals and the settlement and chargeability of rate-aided
patients.
With regard to the parliamentary
grant, I may explain that, prior to the
establishment of the Northern Government, the parliamentary grant was made
by way of a capitation grant of half the
net charge of maintenance subject to a
maximum of 4s per week. These grants
were payable out of the Local Taxation
Account, but for many years the funds
in this account were insufficient to meet
the entire amount of the required charge,
and the actual payments did not amount
to the authorised maximum.
On the establishment of the Northern
Government, when the Local Taxation
Account was wound up, it was decided
to stereotype the grant at the average
amount paid during the three financial
years from 1918 to 1920, and this

deavoured to produce a method for fixing

I have not endeavoured to give a detailed résumé of the contents of all the

hitherto adopted.

The other Clause to which I referred
is Clause 54, which deals with the financial assistance to be given to the local
authorities. That has already been dealt.
with by a number of Members who have
spoken, but I think it is a matter of some
importance. The provision of finance as
between the Exchequer and the local
authorities commenced as far back as
1875. The original idea was that half
the expenses of the maintenance of rateaided patients should be borne by the
Exchequer and the other half by the local
authorities. The idea was that the total
cost per week was a matter of 8s, 4s of
which would be borne by the Exchequer
and 4s by the local authority.
That was all very well at the time,
but owing, as the hon. and gallant Member for East Down (Lieut.-Colonel
Gordon) has mentioned, to the failure of
the Local Taxation Account the amount
which was contributed by the Exchequer
got less and less-that is, after the passing of the Local Government Act-and
eventually in 1923 the matter was compromised by this block grant which has
been referred to. It was no longer a
capitation payment, but a block grant.
The hon. Member for the University has
referred to this block grant as the beginning of the local authorities' trouble.
I do not believe it was the beginning of
the trouble at all. I think that it was
merely to put a brake on the tendency
which had gone on for years and years
by which the Exchequer contributed a
smaller and smaller proportion and the
local authorities were forced to contribute a larger and larger proportion of
the cost of the patients.
The local authorities have naturally
objected to a system which has been
their contribution
gradually raising
from 50 per cent. to 80 per cent. or 90
per cent. of the cost of maintenance.
The House will recollect that in the report of the Financial Relations Committee, presided over by the hon. and
Member for South Derry
gallant
(Captain Chichester-Clark), there was a
recommendation that this grant should
be very substantially increased. Nothing has been done towards increasing the
amount, and in this Bill we have the
provision in Clause 54. Now, the Minister of Home Affairs has given the House
the assurance that it is not intended to
decrease the amount of the block grant,
but the wording of Section 54 is surely
very alarming to the local authorities.
The wording is as follows:-
"The Ministry shall, by regulations
made with the approval of the Ministry of Finance, provide for the payment out of moneys provided by
Parliament, to each council of a county
or county borough, in respect of the
expenses of the council on account of
the maintenance of rate-aided patients
in the public mental hospital established for such county or county
borough, of annual grants of such
amounts and subject to such conditions
as may be prescribed in the regulations,
and such regulations may provide for
the discontinuance of grants payable to
such a county or county borough council
under section ten of the Local Government Act (Northern Ireland), 1923 (as
amended by subsequent enactments),
and for the application of any provisions of that section to grants payable under this section."
Therefore, instead of having what they
have at present, an Act of Parliament,
a statutory provision, entitling them to
a certain block grant every year what is
in this Bill, as it is now drafted, is a
provision by which the Minister of Home
Affairs and the Minister of Finance may

I quite agree it would be a mistake to

prescribed by the Act of 1923. That

But while I do not think there should

I think everybody will welcome the departure from the expression "lunatic" to

a
"lunatic" became the butt of ridicule and
the subject of gibes and jokes. This
sprung to a large extent from the manner in which the law itself regarded him.
It is not so very long ago since the provincial newspapers used to publish details regarding the committal of a lunatic
in exactly the same way as they published
details regarding the committal of a thief

It is a grand thing to be able to get

the opposite direction. With regard to
the committal of mentally diseased persons, they should certainly not be brought
up as criminals are brought up, and when

it generally is, the police should be plain
clothes policemen and not uniformed
officers of the law.
Regarding the remark of the Member

statistics furnish proof that from the
farming community more than from any
other part of the community the greatest
number of mentally diseased persons is
drawn. The moral is very obvious. If
the conditions of the farming community
were much brighter and happier and the
farmers were more prosperous than they
are to-day, it is inconceivable that they

On the contrary, they may justifiably be
forced to the conclusion that the present
Government is not only a menace to the
physical health of the farmers, but a
menace also to their mental condition.

24 MARCH 1932
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 24th March, 1932.
The House met at Twelve of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
BANK RATE IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state why the
Bank rate in this country is one per cent.
greater than in Great Britain, and
whether the Government is prepared to
make representations to the banking
authorities to have the same rate made
applicable here as across the Channel.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I cannot state why the Irish bank
rate is, at the moment, precisely one per
cent. greater than the Bank of England
rate.
I would suggest, however, that international considerations have much to do
with the fixing of the Bank of England.
rate, and obviously, such have little significance in Ireland. Moreover, it must
not be assumed that the English Banks
charge their borrowers merely at the
English Bank rate.
Having regard to these considerations,
the answer to the second part of the question is in the negative.
Mr. DEVLIN: If we are to have the
step by step policy in regard to other
matters surely, in view of the fact that
we are an integral part of Great Britain,
we ought to have the same terms in the
banks as Great Britain.
Mr. POLLOCK: We have no evidence
that we do not follow the English practice. While I do not wish to be very
assertive in the matter, I am perfectly
satisfied that no English bank is willing
to accept the official English bank rate
for advances made to customers in
ordinary trading. If the advances are
made against Government securities it is
a different matter. Here our banks would
be willing to treat customers quite as
fairly as the banks do in England. So I
am advised.
Major HALL-THOMPSON: Surely it
is a fact that for an overdraft, which,
unfortunately, is necessary in commercial
affairs at the present time in many cases,
the banks of Northern Ireland do charge
one per cent. more than do the banks on
the other side of the Channel. Is that
not to the disadvantage of the development of business in this country?
Mr. POLLOCK: The Irish banks here,
I think, would answer that question by
saying that their arrangements are on
an entirely different basis in regard to
overdrafts, that interest is charged from
day to day by Irish banks upon the exact
overdraft, whereas in Great Britain it is
charged on the amount pre-arranged, and
that, therefore, the position of the Irish
banks is quite as favourable to their
customers as is that of the English banks.
Mr. DEVLIN: Would it not be within
the province of the right hon. Gentleman to have these banking arrangements
made similar as between Northern Ireland and Great Britain?
Mr. POLLOCK: That is a matter for
the banks. They are not national
banks.
Mr. DEVLIN: I wish they were.
Major HALL-THOMPSON: It is possible, and it is the practice for the English
banks to allow overdrafts on exactly the
same terms as overdrafts are allowed in
this country, with the exception that one
per cent more is charged.

Sir DAWSON BATES: If the Government were to accept the Amendment proposed by my hon. Friend it would defeat the very object he has in view. My
hon. Friend seems to have misunderstood the effect of this Clause. Under
the Clause, for the protection of the
patient, the medical officer has to send in
at the end of one year-that is from the
date of the admission of the patient-and
then after two and three years, and thereafter every five years, his report on the
condition of the patient. What my hon.
Friend proposes should be done is that
on the 1st January of every year all the
medical officers connected with these
institutions should send in reports on all
the people under their care. There are
something like 4,600 inmates in mental
homes in Northern Ireland, and that
would mean that for a period of about
three months the superintendents in
these institutions would be busy writing
a report on each particular case.
these 4,600 reports would come into the
Ministry of Home Affairs which, although
it is suggested that we are overstaffed, has
only two medical inspectors. Would my
hon. Friend tell me when these medical
inspectors could deal with these 4,600
reports? What we want is to get these
reports in from day to day, that is to
say that if a patient is admitted on the
1st January his report will come in on
the 1st January following, and if on the
2nd January then on the 2nd January
following; in other words that the reports will flow in daily to the Home
Office. I hope my hon. Friend now
appreciates the situation. He and I are
really trying to get at the same thing,
but I think that my way is better than
his.

Sir DAWSON BATES: One of the
great objects of this Bill is to take away
the criminal taint from those who are
mentally afflicted. It was with this
object that this Clause was framed. If
my hon. Friend looks at the Clause he
will find that these powers are not given
unless an officer or constable of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary is satisfied that their
exercise is necessary for the public safety
or for the safety of a peon alleged to
be of unsound mind. If people have to
look for a sergeant, a head constable, or
a district inspector, or even a county inspector, it might be that the poor
individual would have committed suicide
or killed somebody before he is removed.
It surely is better that he should be
treated as mentally unsound and taken
to the infirmary, which, after all, has
not the pauper taint, rather than that
he should be taken to the cells and treated
as a criminal. If my hon. Friend can
suggest any other way to meet such a
situation as I have described I will be
only too glad to consider it.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Why take him to
the workhouse?
Sir DAWSON BATES: We must take
him somewhere. I hope the term "workhouse" will disappear in course of time,
Mr. STEWART: I was going to suggest to the right hon. Gentleman that he
should delete the word "workhouse" here
and insert "infirmary."
Sir DAWSON BATES: There may be
a technical difficulty about that, but if
I can do it without any difficulty I will
be only too glad to fall in with the suggestion of the hon. Member.

do not want to ask the police to interfere

HOUSE OF COMMONS

Prime Minister on the Adjournment of

the second British Note, dated 9th April,
from the Secretary for the Dominions to

Executive Council of the Irish Free State.
The paragraph in question reads:-
"It is true that the 1921 Settlement
did not result in the establishment of a
united Ireland, but the Treaty itself
made the necessary provision for the
union at that time of the two parts of
Ireland if both had then been ready to
accept it.
"As to the future, His Majesty's
Government in the United Kingdom
feel it sufficient to state that, in their
opinion, there can be no conceivable
hope for the establishment of a united
Ireland except on the basis that its
the
allegiance to
Crown and its
membership of the British Commonwealth will continue unimpaired."
It is particularly with reference to the
last part of the paragraph that I, and I
think the House, and the country, would
like to hear the Prime Minister, if he
can see his way to make a statement this
afternoon. Without any comments from
me, I think that very clearly implies
that the Imperial Government might
united Ireland under
contemplate
certain circumstances.
a
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): I have had very short notice.
of the intention of the hon. Member to
raise this question in the House this
afternoon, and I would prefer not to
have it raised just quite so soon.
Mr. NIXON: To-morrow.
The PRIME MINISTER: If the hon.
Member will be kind enough, perhaps
next week I can make a statement. That
will give me an opportunity to inquire
into the whole matter in the meantime.
I will only say this, that by the action
of the British Parliament, and by the
action of the Free State Parliament, as
it then was, the position of Ulster was
made abundantly clear. I had no knowledge whatever of the terms of the communication with the present Free State
Government, and I have hardly had time,
as I was travelling up this morning from
a distant part of County Fermanagh,
even to digest the exact meaning of the
words used in the communication.
Therefore, I think it would be better not
to make any pronouncement at the
moment, except to say that we here in
the Ulster area stand to-day exactly
where we stood through the past eleven
years. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
No change has taken place in the desire of the people, no change has taken
place in the determination of the present
Government of Northern Ireland to remain an integral part of Great Britain
and the Empire. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). No change has taken place
-I reiterate that and, therefore, if
some words have been used which would
give a different impression they must
have been made under a complete misapprehension. I do not think it would
be proper for me to go further than that
to-day because, as I say, I really have
not had an opportunity of either consulting my colleagues or even of analysing the
exact terms used, but I will carry on
with my colleagues exactly the same in
the future as I have done in the past.
Nothing can change my attitude towards
our feelings of loyalty to the King, to the
Constitution, to Great Britain, and to the
Empire-nothing under any circumstances whatever. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Mr. NIXON: I thought it was a question the Prime Minister might have been
able to answer right off the reel and
without making up his mind, but, of
course, he is the judge, and since he
would like to make up his mind as to
how he should answer that question I can
offer no objection.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): If hon. Members will
refer to the summary as set out on page
131 they will observe that there is an
increase in these Estimates of £5,875,
as compared with those which I placed
before the Committee for the year
1931-32. The increase is,
is, however,
mainly in respect of grants in aid of
works which had been actually com
menced, as in the case of the Newry Ship
Canal, or of expenditure on works to
which the Government had already agreed
to contribute part of the expenditure
involved, as in the case of the Ballycastle Harbour. Apart, however, from
the increase on those items I am glad to
be able to inform the Committee that the
Estimates now presented show a reduction in most items as compared with
those for last year, which, as hon. Members may remember, represented a total
reduction of 27 per cent. as compared
with those in 1930-31.
In reviewing the various functions of
my Ministry, I shall first deal with those
touching what I may call the commercial
aspect. The services afforded to the
commercial community, with the details
of which the Committee are already
familiar, have been freely utilised during
the past year by our exporters, and many
of these have received effective assistance
in building up their selling organisations
abroad. In addition, much useful information regarding trade conditions,
calls for tenders, commercial openings,
and the like, has been issued to firms
to whom the information was likely
to be of most practical service. The
utility of the services thus afforded by
the Ministry can, perhaps, best be
gauged by the increasing frequency and
confidence with which Northern Ireland
firms are, after ten years' experience of

it in the public interest to encourage the

I can assure hon. Members that my
Ministry maintains an active and sympathetic interest in all fishery matters.
throughout and around our territory.
The executive action in regard to the
enforcement of fishery laws is, of course,
taken in the main by the Boards of Conservators constituted for this purpose.
There are, however, many matters of detail which come at some stage directly
before the Ministry, and the fishery bylaws, which from time to time appear
on the Table of the House, are in every
case the sequel to careful investigation
and consideration. I have no doubt,
also, that hon. Members have seen
references in the
the Press recently to
attempts that are being made to establish Portrush as a fishery centre. I do
not wish at this stage to say anything

and that Portrush, and Northern Ireland
generally, will ultimately benefit.
Hon. Members may be interested to
know that the issue of fishery loans from
the Government Loans Fund continues,
twenty-six further loans to the amount
of £709 having been issued during the
calendar year 1931, bringing the total.
advanced since April, 1926, to £5,650.
These loans have been a definite help to
our inshore fishermen, and it is greatly
to the credit of the borrowers that, notwithstanding the difficult years recently
experienced, they have, with few exceptions, met their obligations in the matter
of instalments.
The summer herring
season last year showed considerable improvement over its predecessor, and our
fishermen being now adequately equipped
to take advantage of any opportunities
offered, there is ground for hope that,
given favourable conditions, the coming
season will bring increased prosperity in
our fishing centres.
In introducing these Estimates in
previous years I have spoken of the
participation of Northern Ireland in the
exhibitions which are organised in
London and large provincial centres by
the Empire Marketing Board. The
public interest in these exhibitions does
not appear to flag, and the demand for
samples of Northern Ireland produce
with which we have been met in the
"Empire Shops" in which we have
participated during the past year has
been a matter for astonishment as well
as gratification. The exhibitions are
now tending to fall into two definite
categories on the one hand trade shows,
aimed at the trade buyer rather than the
general public, and on the other Empire
shops, the primary appeal of which is to
the retail purchasing community.
The Ministry has taken pains to include in each exhibition, in addition to
our staple exports, new food products
of Ulster origin and valuable initial
publicity for these products has been
obtained. Through the medium of the
trade shows we were able last year to
introduce to important trade buyers,
amongst other commodities, liquid eggs,
which Ulster is now canning in competition with China and other foreign
countries.
The success which has attended the
shops, at which samples are sold direct
to the public, has caused the Empire
Marketing Board to concentrate more
and more on this type of advertisement,
as it has been found that these shops, in
addition to selling thousands of samples
direct to the consumer, attract the retailer, and, through him, the wholesaler.
On last year's figures, the average cost
of each exhibition was some £70, a cost
which, in my opinion, is almost negligible
in comparison with the value of the
publicity obtained. Moreover, I would
remind the Committee that it is not
merely trade publicity which we are
getting from these exhibits. They have
served to make familiar to our
patriots throughout the length and
breadth of Britain the name of our
Province and the place we hold within
the United Kingdom. I am confident
that the Committee will approve the continuance of this work.

Before I leave the subject of trade and
commerce I should like to refer to a
factor which is exercising a rapidly increasing influence upon our economic and
social life, and that is the development
of tourist traffic. The competition between the countries of the world to
attract visitors to their shores is becoming
more intense from year to year, and it
would be a calamity if our Province,
with its natural attractions, failed
receive the attention which it so well
deserves.

cutions where information of a suitable

little railway will manage to weather the

am more particularly concerned with,
the interests of the City of Londonderry.
I say, speaking from a knowledge of the

a knowledge of the commercial importance of that little line, that this grant
that has been made from year to year,

made by our Government, has served a

line to weather the storm up to the

to weather the storm in the future.

SHOOTING AFFAIR IN COUNTY
DERRY.
1. Mr. LEEKE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state if any
progress has been made with the investigations into the attack on the Hibernians
at Ballinderry on St. Patrick's Day.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Inquiries and
investigations are still being actively
instituted into the circumstances of
the deplorable incident referred to
in the hon. Member's question, with
the object of tracing the culprits,
but the hon. Member will appreciate that,
under the circumstances, it would be
inexpedient to make any statement as to
the nature and extent of the steps which
are being taken.
Mr. LEEKE: Arising out of the
answer, can the right hon. Gentleman
assure us that any progress has been
made? He has not let us know that.
He has given only a formal reply.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The only
object in not giving information is that
to do
so might defeat the course of
justice.
Mr. COLLINS: Has the right hon.
Gentleman any hope that his people will
be more successful than they were in
tracing the Annahugh gentlemen?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am an
optimist.
Mr. McALEER: Arising out of the
answer by the Minister of Home Affairs,
I would like to ask is it a fact that every
class of crime has been detected in Northern Ireland except the destruction of
Hibernian halls and these murderous onslaughts on Hibernian demonstrations?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I wish that
was the case.

CLASS VI. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £49,989 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending on 31st March, 1933,
for the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Agriculture (15 and 16
Geo. V., c. 3, s. 4 (N.I.); 16 Geo. V.,
c. 4 (N.I.))." (Note-£17,000 has been
voted on account.)
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I am in the
happy position of presenting Estimates.
for my Ministry which for the second
year in succession show a substantial if
not a large saving. If hon. Members
will refer to Vote I. they will find that
in all but two items economies have been
effected. The net increase in Vote I. of
approximately £2,400 is accounted for by
the necessary increase in our veterinary
staff and consequential travelling expenses. No one regrets this increase more
than I do, but, unfortunately, we have
no option in the matter. Following the
regretted outbreaks of foot-and-mouth
disease in the Downpatrick area in June
of last year, the Ministry of Agriculture
and Fisheries issued an Order requiring
the mouth of every animal leaving Ireland to be examined by a veterinary
surgeon before shipment. The net increase in Vote I. is more than accounted
for by the requirements of this Order.
I should like to take this opportunity
of paying a tribute and expressing my
gratitude to the veterinary staff of the
Ministry and to all those who helped
them for the extraordinarily able manner
in which this outbreak was handled.
Similar outbreaks in Great Britain have
cost millions of pounds to suppress, and
I attribute the fact that this serious outbreak, which might well have spread over
the country, was put down at a total cost
of £14,500. mainly to the very able manner in which our chief veterinary officer
and his staff handled a most difficult and
dangerous situation.
Before I leave this aspect of the
question I should like to acknowledge our
great indebtedness to the police for the
very efficient manner in which they cooperated with us in this difficult task.
But for the very able and tactful manner
in which they controlled the movement
of animals in this district it might well
have been impossible to prevent the
spread of the disease over the whole
Province. Northern Ireland has long
been free from this plague, and I sincerely hope we may never experience
another outbreak.
The sources of infection have always
puzzled veterinary surgeons and perhaps
the most disturbing feature of the
numerous outbreaks in Great Britain has
been the failure, owing to the great
difficulties in the way, to trace the
probable source of infection. I am,
therefore, particularly glad that we were
able, after a most exhaustive inquiry to
trace the source of infection. It was
found to be due to Dutch broccoli or
cauliflower, imported through the port of
Leith, the refuse from which was, unfortunately, thrown on a rubbish heap
to which the cattle at the farm on which
the first outbreak occurred had access. As
hon. Members already know, Holland is
never free from foot-and-mouth disease.
Whilst there is a certain amount of
satisfaction to be derived from being in
the position to present to the House
reduced Estimates for two years in
succession, I should be failing in my duty
if I did not point out that the services
for which I am responsible cannot be
further curtailed without serious injury
to their efficiency. Moreover, I must
emphasise the fact that if we in Northern
Ireland are to take full advantage of
the opportunities which may arise through.
the change in the fiscal policy of the
United Kingdom a material increase in
agricultural expenditure is inevitable in
the immediate future.
The agricultural situation has loomed.
very prominently in the Press during the
past few months and, whilst I do not
desire to review the situation in detail,
there are one or two important aspects
to which I should like to refer before I
sit down. The greatest difficulty our
farming community in Northern Ireland
has had to face during the past few years
has been the almost catastrophic fall in
the price level of agricultural produce.
Fortunately for Northern Ireland this
Ministry of Agriculture 686
Estimates-
14 APRIL 1932
fall in prices has been much more marked
in the case of cereal than in animal
products, and the fact that 80 per cent.
of our agricultural income is derived
from stock and stock products has enabled
the Northern Ireland farmer to weather
the storm in a much more satisfactory
manner than farmers in other parts of
the world. I am very happy to think
that all the signs indicate that the removal of the pound from the gold
standard, together with the operation of
the 10 per cent. tariff imposed by the
Import Duties Act, has definitely checked
the fall in the price level of agricultural
commodities. Without being unduly
optimistic, I think I can with confidence
express the view that prices have touched
bottom, and that the agricultural situation
is definitely on the mend. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
Even to the lay observer it must be
obvious that the agricultural industry is
on the threshold of a new era.
I am
sure the Committee will be glad to know
that we have played our part in the efforts
which have been made to shape a new
policy for agriculture. I am under a
great debt of gratitude to Sir John
Gilmour for agreeing to an officer of my
Department acting as a liaison officer
between me and the Imperial Cabinet on
agricultural policy. By this means we
have been able to keep in close touch
with developments, ensure that our
interests have been properly understood
and, in particular, play a not unimportant part in securing the recognition.
of the fundamental importance of live
stock and live stock products in United
Kingdom agriculture.
The imposition of a 10 per cent. tariff
on certain agricultural produce, together
with the duties which have been imposed
on foreign potatoes and horticultural
produce generally under the Horticultural
Produce Emergency Duties Act, have
been an advantage, but I attach more
importance to what may be described as
the long-range policy in connection with
which His Majesty's Government in the
United Kingdom has undertaken to limit
the importation of pig products if a satisfactory scheme for the re-organisation of
the bacon industry is brought into
operation in the United Kingdom.
Progress has already been made and
officers of my Department are working
in close collaboration with the Ministry
of Agriculture and Fisheries in the
elaboration of an acceptable scheme of reorganisation.
It is too soon to speak with any degree
of certainty, but I am not without hope
that the promise to limit quantitatively
the import of foreign bacon will in due
course be extended to foreign beef and
mutton. If we are to secure such important concessions to agricultural development it is essential, owing to
complicated treaty obligations, that there
should be a high degree of organisation
amongst Northern Ireland producers,
and on that task my Department is concentrating all its energies. Our task has
been simplified by the lead we have
taken in stock improvement and marketing legislation. I am aware that these
developments have given rise to a certain
amount of criticism amongst the less enlightened members of the community. It
is a curious fact that all progress brings
in its train a band of irresponsible critics
whose main contention is that everything
has been perfect, is perfect, and will be
perfect, if only no change is made, and
the good old methods allowed to continue
indefinitely.
Mr. COLLINS: Hear, hear.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: The way
of the reformer is not an easy one, and
I am in the rather peculiar position of
seeing the efforts which we have made
extolled in the agricultural Press of
England and Scotland as a model of
progress and efficiency, whilst a very
vocal, but, I am glad to think, small
minority at home attribute to them all
the ills and misfortunes which have beset
the agricultural industry. Be that as it
may, I am convinced that the agricultural situation is definitely on the mend.
Improvement may be gradual, but it
will be none the less certain and beneficial, and I sincerely trust that I may
continue to count on the whole-hearted
support of the vast majority of the farmers in Ulster in the efforts which are
being made to ensure that Northern Ireland secures its full share and, if possible,
more than its full share of the opportunities which will arise through the
quantitative limitation of the imports of
foreign agricultural produce. It will, as
I have hinted, entail a still higher degree
of marketing organisation than we have
yet reached and closer combination and
concentration of action amongst producers. But the prize is well worth
striving for, and I am confident that
the farmers in Northern Ireland will rise
to the occasion. I beg to move.

With regard to the pork industry,
something should be done to level up

50s. The following day in another
market it is 54s, and on the next day it
is down again to 50s. Some consideration should be given to the farmers,

being at the mercy of a few buyers who

the pork. I look upon the small farmers,
for whom I wish to speak, as virtually
labourers. Small farmers have a great
deal more difficulty in getting loans

They must get two guarantors at present, and as a result very often they fail
to obtain the loans. The Minister should

With regard to the flax industry, as I

and other countries? During the war
very good crops of flax were produced in
this country, and it paid the farmers.
Why cannot flax be grown now? About
two years ago a very large farmer told
me that he had 100 stones of flax, and
that he did not know whether he would
scutch it or not. Scutching, he said,

to obtain work, people who are getting

SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION IN
AUGHNACLOY.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether the Ministry is fully
aware of the serious condition which has
arisen in the town of Aughnacloy owing
to insufficient school accommodation for
the pupils of that district; and whether,
in view of the fact that the Regional
Committee for that area has approved of
a new school to replace two existing unsatisfactory buildings, he will see that
the Ministry expedite the building of the
proposed new school, and if any inquiry
is necessary see that it is held at the
earliest possible moment.
SECRE-
The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF EDU-
CATION (Mr. Robb): The Ministry is
fully aware of the urgency of the need
for a new school in the town of Aughnacloy, and it has already approved the
sketch plans of the proposed new building, with a view to the preparation by
the Regional Education Committee's
architect of the detail of the plans. The
erection of the new school is a matter for
the Regional Education Committee.
Objections have been received by the
Ministry from certain bodies of ratepayers
in the area to the application of the
County Council, as the Education
Authority, for sanction to the raising of
the necessary loan. Some of these
obiections were subsequently withd, awn,
but as some still exist it will be necessary
to hold a public inquiry into the application. Arrangements are being made
to hold this inquiry at the earliest possible date.

FEE FOR BIRTH CERTIFICATES
FOR SCHOOL CHILDREN.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he is aware that a fee
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
of 3s 7d is charged at the office of the
Registrar of Births in the Belfast Union
Workhouse for issuing certificates of birth
required by children entering secondary.
schools; whether one shilling of this
amount is for searching the registers,
whereas no search is usually necessary;
whether he considers this an exorbitant
charge, having regard to the small
amount of work involved; and what steps,
if any, he proposed to take to have birth
certificates, demanded, by secondary
schools, issued at a reasonable price, so
that parents wishing to
give their
children a secondary education may not
be burdened with this charge.
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): I have been asked to reply.
The charge for a certified copy of an
entry of birth issued by a Registrar, a
Superintendent Registrar, or the General
Register Office is fixed by Statute and is
made up as follows:
Search Fee
Certified copy of entry
Stamp Duty
...
1/-
2/6
1d
3/7
In most instances a search in the
indexes is necessary before the issuing
officer is in a position to make a copy of
the entry in the register. If, however,
the number of the entry in the
register and the date of registration are
given by the applicant, a search in the
indexes is not required, and in such cases
no search fee is chargeable.
Fees received by registrars and superintendent registrars for the issue of
certified copies of entries form an
integral part of the remuneration for
registration work, and, in my opinion,
are not excessive.
Provision has been made by various
enactments for the issue of copies of
birth entries for certain specific purposes
at cheap rates, but the resulting loss of
remuneration to the issuing Officers has
not been made good, and I cannot view
with favour any extension of the system
of cheap certificates. Moreover, I do not
regard a single payment of 3s 7d as a
hardship on parents.

CONNECTION AT DUNDONALD.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister

for a considerable time past the proposal
to have a connection made with the Belfast Corporation sewer at Dundonald has
been before the Castlereagh Urban
Council and the Belfast Corporation and

whether up to the present anything has
been done, and, if not, whether he will
endeavour to have this work expedited,
in view of the present system of drainage
being a serious menace to the health of
the inhabitants of this district.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am aware that
negotiations are going on between the
Castlereagh Rural District Council and the
Belfast Corporation in connection with
the sewerage of Dundonald. Some rather
intricate questions regarding the share
of the cost to be borne by each authority,
the size of the sewers to be constructed,
and other matters have to be determined.
These have been referred to the engineers
to the two authorities, and a report is
expected at an early date.
to
I am satisfied that the authorities concerned are fully alive to the importance
of the matter, and that they are anxious
find a solution to this somewhat
difficult problem. If necessary, my
Ministry will render every assistance in
their power to bring about agreement.
