ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Rent and Mortgage Interest
(Restriction) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: I cannot but
regret the necessity for introducing
further legislation dealing with this very
difficult question of Rent Restriction.
In 1923 I appointed a Committee,
which was representative of all shades of
opinion, to advise as to the course to be
pursued with regard to this subject. The
members of that Committee differed on
many aspects of the problem, but on one
proposition they expressed themselves as
unanimously agreed, namely,
"that
recontrol of rents should be removed at the
earliest possible date." With that conclusion most of us will agree, because it
is generally recognised that rent
striction-the artificial control of rentsare only
is in itself an evil, and we
justified in promoting legislation of this
kind on the ground that it is the lesser
of two evils.
In considering this matter, it is important that hon. Members should keep
clearly before them the course of events
which has led up to the present situation.
The control of rents was instituted, as
hon. Members are aware, in 1915.
building of dwelling-houses had come to
an end owing to the exigencies of the
Great War.
All
Prior to that date, rents
for dwelling-houses in Northern Ireland
and particularly in the City of Belfast
were extremely moderate; in fact, our
city enjoyed the position of being the
most moderately-rented city in the United
Kingdom. In 1915, however, partly
owing to the cessation of building, and
partly owing to other causes, the demand
for houses here and elsewhere began to
exceed the supply, and, as there was no
means of catering for the increased demand, rents began to rise. It was
found necessary, therefore, to control the
letting prices of houses in the same way
as in the case of the prices of many other
commodities at that time.
The control imposed by the Act of 1915
I was limited to the cases of houses of £26
valuation and under. This legislation.
remained untouched until 1919, when the
limit of control was extended to £52, or
just twice the original figure, and this
Act was followed in 1920 by further
legislation, which is the foundation of
our present code extending the limit to
£78 or three times the original figure,

It is important to consider the causes
which have prevented the realisation of
the hope which was generally entertained, that by now there would have
been sufficient houses to enable us to allow

In the first place, the intense economic
depression which has afflicted this area

the larger type of houses to seek less

the effect of the higher rates and taxes.
In the cities and towns many of the

The advent of the cheap motor-car,

The cost of building, while it has

There is another very important cause,
and it is one of the evils inherent in

the upper limit of £26 are occupied by

These people are, however, content to
occupy houses at a controlled rent, even
though they could easily make other

answer the argument that it is inequitable that such people should be protected
from the operation of the ordinary
economic law of supply and demand,

I pass now to another point dealt with
by the Committee. Hon. Members will
recollect that, where a landlord pays the
rates on a house to which the Rent Restriction Acts apply, he is entitled under
the Act to pass on any increases of rates

tenant of any decrease, and he is made

Clause 5 deals with a matter which

There is already a remedy at common

As hon. Members will appreciate, we
have gone very far to carry out the recommendations of the Committee. In
two particulars we have not been able to
follow their recommendations. One of
these is the re-imposition of control on the
houses which had actually come out of
control. This I have already dealt with.
The second point related to sub-letting
of rooms in controlled houses. If hon.
Members will look at the Report of the
Committee they will see that the recommendation is couched in very general
terms, and there is no hint as to the
method by which this recommendation
should be carried out. I am not surprised
that the Committee abstained from entering into particulars, because, after a very
careful study of the subject, I have come
to the conclusion that there is no effective
means of dealing with it. Any provision
giving a landlord power
to resume
possession of the house, if his tenant is
sub-letting rooms at an exorbitant price,
would, of course, be quite inoperative.
No landlord is going to the trouble and
expense of resuming possession of the
house merely to re-let it at the same rent
simply because his tenant is charging exorbitant rents. If the provision that, on
the landlord obtaining possession, the
house went out of control remained, it
might be a different story. This might
have a deterrent effect in the case of
houses between £8 and £26 valuation,
but this provision will be gone if the
House passes this Bill, and, therefore, the
power of resumption of possession by the
landlord gives no remedy. In any event,
it would be extraordinarily easy to evade
any provision with regard to sub-letting
of rooms, because the Committee themselves state that the recommendation was
not intended to apply to furnished rooms
as defined by the Rent Restriction Act
of 1927.
We have spent much labour and thought in
trying to meet the Committee's views with
regard to this matter, but I and my
advisers have been unable to evolve any
satisfactory method for dealing with it.
I am, however, quite open to suggestions
in the matter.
May I before sitting down reiterate my
firm conviction that the real and permanent solution of the question that we
have been considering does not lie in restrictive legislation. Legislation of the
character which I have introduced this
afternoon may be necessary as a temporary
expedient in spite of its manifest and
manifold disadvantages, but, in my
opinion, and I may say in the opinion of
the Government, the only true and the
only satisfactory solution to the problem
of rents is that every encouragement
should be given to people to invest money
in house property, so that more and more
funds may be provided for the building
of houses until a sufficiency is provided to
meet all reasonable needs of the community. When the supply of houses is
equal to the demand, there will be no
further necessity to introduce Rent Restriction Bills, and I would appeal to
every Member of this House to do nothing
and to say nothing which will discourage
enterprise in the building of houses, and
thus promote confidence and enterprise
in the building industry. I beg to move.

they again face the people of Northern
Ireland. This is not a grievance against
decent landlords. We have no grievance
against them. I can quote cases where
landlords got an opportunity to increase
the rents, but they did not put on a
150 per cent. increase. Some relet their
houses at the old rents. Now you are
going to protect the 15, 20 or 30 per
cent. unscrupulous landlords and allow
them to continue their nefarious work.
Under this Bill you are still going to
allow them to extort £1, 25s, or 30s a
week from 5,000 or 6,000 tenants. I
hope the Government, even at this late
hour, will see that these people be not
allowed to go scot free, that they will be
subject to paying the whole amount back
and also to imprisonment for illegal exactions from the poor tenants, who,
out of unemployment benefit of 25s a
week, have to pay 15s a week in rent.
I say that in itself warrants the Government extending the Measure a little bit
further.

Rev. PROFESSOR CORKEY: I wish
to congratulate the Government on introducing this Bill. I think it will go a
long way to meet the complaints made in
regard to overcharging in the way of
rents for houses that have been decontrolled. It is a very thorny subject.
People are very sensitive where their interests are touched, and I feel that the
Government deserve thanks for the way
in which they have tackled it. They
have gone a long way to introduce a Bill
which will do away with many of the
things which people justly complain
about. I support the re-introduction of
control, because I think the owners of
these houses are in fact, in possession of
a monopoly. A great deal has been done
to build houses, but all the ingenuity of
the builders has not enabled them to
erect houses which could be let at a rent
comparable to the rent charged for the
working classes prior to the war.
Before the war rents ran from 3/- to
6/- for houses of £8 valuation, and these
houses constituted about half the number
of houses in the whole community. The
rents charged for houses from £8 to £26
valuation ran from 6/- to 12/-, and these
houses constituted one-third of the total
number of houses in the whole country.
If these houses were allowed to become
decontrolled, and
and the rents were increased, the houses which would have
been available for the workers would have
become increasingly less. I think, therefore, there is reason in the action which
the Government have taken, in bringing
in this process of decontrol so far as these
houses are concerned. It is really the
working-class houses which constitute a
monopoly.
Further than that, it appeared
to those who were members of the Committee that the controlled rent gave a
fairly reasonable return on the money
invested in houses-that is to say, in the
average case. Here, for example, is a
typical case, one of many which came
before the Committee. A house was
built at £150. The supposed value of
the house at present is £250, and the
poor-law valuation is £10 10s. The controlled rent for that house was £25.
When that house goes out of control the
rent may be £35 or £45 or £50. The
controlled rent, however, was £25. If
you take half that as liable for charges of
one kind and another the rent coming
to the owner of the house represents
eight per cent. of the cost of the house...
the money expended on the cost of the
house-and five per cent. on the present
value of the house. That, I say, is a
typical case. These people are getting
a reasonable return on their money. No
doubt they are not getting as much on
their money as they would get if the
houses were entirely decontrolled, but the
enhanced value of the houses is due to
scarcity. If they could be decontrolled
without any hardship to anyone I do
not see that anyone would raise objection
to decontrol. I therefore congratulate
the Government on handling this subject
in a courageous way. I think the Bill
deserved a more enthusiastic welcome
than the one given it by the hon. Member (Mr. Beattie). Although it is not
ideal from every point of view, I do not
suppose any Bill ever is.
The question has been raised as to
whether the Government ought not to
have brought back under control those
houses between £8 and £26 valuation,
which actually have been decontrolled.
I have some sympathy with the attitude
taken up by the Minister-that the reimposing of control once houses have been
decontrolled raises a great deal of discontent. There is a procedure in Ireland
known as splitting the difference when
people are making a bargain, and it
occurred to me that if the Government,
instead of reimposing entirely control of
houses decontrolled, had brought them
back and allowed the owners to charge
the standard rate, plus 50 or 60 per cent.,
it might have been a gesture which would
have been in the nature of a compromise
and satisfied a great many people.
However, that is only detail. The Bill,
as a whole, does reimpose control on a
great majority of houses.
With regard to these agreements,
about which a good deal has been said, I
am gratified at the Clauses which have
been drafted to prevent exploitation of
people who want working-class houses
under such agreements. I am inclined
to think that the Clauses, as drafted, are
not adequate to prevent this exploitation.
The first section of Clause 3 is the governing section of the Bill, and it prevents
owners charging more than 7 per cent.
interest on the amount outstanding,

I agree with the Minister that the only

Government will at some future time

Here is a fact, which I can prove, and
I would commend this remark to those

more houses, we need twice
as many
houses for the working classes as we have

whatever, then they have ten times a
greater right to put restrictions on the
rent of houses built with the assistance of
public money. I was in a subsidy house
no
797 Rent Restrictions Bill-

19 APRIL 1932
Second Reading
a short time ago, and a man who is
better able to judge house property than
I am, assured me absolutely that the
house did not cost £140 to build, although
the builder or landlord got £140 for it,
and is charging a rent of 11s a weekfor a house that cost him nothing.
The Government say, "Go ahead, Mr.
Landlord, we will not interfere with you,
we are a landlords' government."
There never was a Government that
occupied a more ridiculous position than
this Government occupies in respect of
this question, because if there are any
houses at all on which the Government
should place restrictions surely they are
the subsidy houses. In this particular
house-I can take any man to it-the
ceiling is done with pressed paper, and
everything is done in the plainest possible
manner. There is a street of these
houses built in the same way, and there
is not a house in the street which cost
the builder £140, I am assured, and yet
the rent of these houses is 11s a week.
That money, which was voted by this
House, is being passed on, not to the
pockets of the tenants for whom it was
intended, but to the pockets of the landlords, who built the houses.
It is not too late even yet for the
Government to see the folly and the
injustice of what they are doing in this
case, and for them to bring forward an
Amendment to include subsidy houses.
Someone says,
"How could that be
done?" It is very easy to do it. It is
very easy for some competent person to
assess what it actually took to build the
houses, and to subtract the subsidy from
that amount-that is, if the subsidy does
not already exceed the amount, and it
does in some cases I know of-and then
allow the landlord or the builder a fair,
I would say, a good, interest on his
money, making all allowances for ground.
rent, income tax, and anything like that
that may arise. There could be no hardship imposed on anyone. You could give
the landlord 10 per cent., or perhaps
more, on his money, and yet get a substantial reduction of the rent of the
houses.
There are subsidy houses in Glencairn
Street that were the subject of debate in
this House before I came into it, and
they are a perfect disgrace. The timber
was carted up out of some old building in
Howard Street and put in under the
noses of Government inspectors and Corporation inspectors. Some people bought
those houses, and were robbed. Some of
them lost their work since they purchased, and had to forfeit the money they
put into them and walk away. That
was debated in this House. I understand that the Parliamentary Secretary
of the Ministry of Home Affairs was himself to go up and look at those houses,
and I was told the other night that he
never went. That is only hearesay from
me. I know that other Members have
dealt with other phases of this subject.
I am not going to touch on the other
points that have already been dealt with.
Now I have helped to open the door so
that any Member may express his opinion
on that subject, and I hope there will be
such a volume of opinion as will force the
Government to take the necessary steps.

there is a difficulty in finding tenants

Those conditions handicap not only the
decent tenant but the decent landlord,
and they arise to a large extent, if not
entirely, in the unsettlement and uncertainty that spring from the present
chaotic state of industry in the Six
Counties. People do not know exactly
where they are, what they should invest
in, or whether it is safe to remain in the
Six Counties at all or not. That is
attributable to this Government's incompetence and selfishness, and its want of
sympathy with matters that vitally concern the people. It springs also from
this other issue, that in the rural districts
you have got poverty of a very abnormal
kind. You have got an extraordinary
amount of depression, and people are
flying to the cities and towns in abnormal
numbers, thinking they will there escape.
from the conditions of starvation with
which they are confronted. They come
into the towns to compete with the townspeople in regard to labour and make the
housing conditions infinitely more chronic
than they have ever been.
That, in brief, is how I would answer
the question asked by the Minister of
Home Affairs, when he was moving the
Second Reading of the Bill. He asked
how was it that greater advantage was
not taken of the subsidies. My reply is
that greater advantage is not taken of the
subsidies because of the chronic conditions
that exist in industry, amongst the working classes, amongst the employing
classes, amongst all sections of the community, that they are alarmed, that they
feel that insecurity is so great. That is
daily demonstrated by the removal of industries from this territory to the Free
State. They are afraid to put any stake
whatever in the country, and they have
merely become quiescent and submit to
whatever conditions prevail. My contention is that as these inequalities
began at the very beginning of this Government, they can only end by the fall of
the present Government from power.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): This Estimate is to be found
on pages 23 to 33. Hon. Members will
note that, as explained in paragraph 5
of the general foreword to the Estimates,
the abolition of "duplicate voting" now
takes effect in the case of all works
services, and not only in the case of headquarters of Ministries, and that this
change has necessitated certain alterations
in the form of this Estimate. Works
expenditure incurred on behalf of Northern Ireland Ministries is now borne
finally on this Vote, and is not recoverable
from Departments. Two works items do
not appear here, however, namely, expenditure on ancient monuments and on
harbours, the reasons being clearly set
out in the foreword mentioned. There is
a decrease in the Estimate this year as
compared with 1931-32 of approximately
£126,000, of which £116,000 is under
Section I and is due mainly to the fact
that the buildings at Stormont are nearing completion.
The anticipated expenditure (Sub-head
D) in connection with the portion of the
new Law Courts which will house the
Ministry of Commerce and other sections
of Departments remaining in town,
accounts for an increase of about £14,000,
and this may be regarded as indicative
of the acceleration of work on that building. It is anticipated that the transfer
of staffs to the building will take place
towards the end of the current financial
year. The increase in Sub-head B for
furniture and fittings is accounted for by
the provision required for the fitting out
of the new Parliamentary portion of the
Stormont Building as well as the cost of
furniture for the Departmental offices in
the Law Courts. It will be recollected
that under Section 34 of the Government of Ireland Act all the above expenditure is repayable to the Exchequer
of Northern Ireland from Imperial
Funds.
Expenditure under Section II shows
a gross decrease of £13,000, new works
expenditure being down by £18,000. It
will be observed that provision is made
for the payment of the balance of the
contribution due from Northern Ireland
funds in respect of the provision of
accommodation for staff at Stormont surplus to the agreed numbers for whom the
British Government has provided accommodation. The estimated total provision
under this head is £30,000. An item of
£1,250 in connection with the new Law
Courts Building reappears here too, owing
to the fact that the Northern Government
agreed to contribute from Northern Ireland funds towards the increased cost of
the Law Courts, due to the use of stonework externally. A balance of £1,250,
Public Works and Buildings 812
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
as I said a moment ago, is here provided for. There is also a sum of £1,045
provided for the cost of the accommodation for the Incorporated Law
Society. These two works account between them for a reduction of £10,000
on the 1931-32 figures.
One of the largest increases under this
sub-head is £2,000 for the erection of
four cottages at Stormont. These are for
the use of the ground staff, as difficulty
would otherwise be encountered by them
in finding suitable accommodation in the
neighbourhood. Undoubtedly, it will
be advantageous to have some of the staff
There
resident on the Stormont estate.
is also the sum of £2,000 provided for

for mentally deficient children. This is
a provisional estimate only, and £1,000
is a re-vote as there was no expenditure
in 1931-32.
Under the heading of Maintenance,
Repairs, etc., there is an increase of
about £6,500, which in the main is due.
to anticipated expenditure for the
periodical repainting and decorating of
Royal Ulster Contabulary barracks built
two or three years ago, and to increased
dredging which it is proposed to perform
in connection with the navigation on the
Lower Bann. During the last two years
the Ministry has, under the provisions
of the Drainage Act, 1929, taken over
the functions of the Lower Bann Navigation Trustees and the Lough Neagh
Drainage Trustees, and a gradual reconditioning of the navigation channel is
being undertaken on the work, spread
over a period of years. This dredging
is essential to the carrying out of the
Bann drainage contract.
The expenditure in connection with
the Bann Drainage Scheme will be found
under Sub-head I. Under the provisions
of the Drainage Act of this year the
expenditure on the schemes is to be met
by borrowings, repayable over 25 yearsthat is. until 1957-by means of
annuities charged on the Vote. The
amount provided in the Estimate each
year represents a level annuity charge
required to meet the loan charges due
to the Government Loans Fund. Hon.
Members will be interested to know that
despite the rather unfavourable weather
last summer progress on the main
drainage scheme may be regarded as
being satisfactory on the whole, and that,
given reasonably good conditions in the
future, the completion of the scheme
should not lag behind the contract date.
The new sluice gates at the Cutts, at
Coleraine, and two out of four at Portna
are now operating, and constructional
operations on the five new gates at Toome
will re-commence as soon as the weather
conditions become favourable. The
approximate total quantity of soft
material dredged to date is 1,000,000
cubic yards, and a new type of pumping
apparatus is yielding very good results as
regards output of soft dredging. Progress made on rock excavation is satisfactory, having regard to the bad weather
conditions last year accentuated by
abnormal winter floods.
The reduction in receipts appropriatedin-aid is more apparent than real. The
main cause is the fact that certain works
in connection with the training colleges,
prisons, etc., the cost of which falls
finally on Capital Fund No. 2, are
practically completed, and therefore the
amount to be drawn from that fund is
a diminishing one. The apparent "loss'
is offset by a corresponding reduction in
the expenditure under Sub-head E. I
beg to move.

The PRIME MINISTER: The hon.
and gallant Member has mentioned the
subject of getting on with subsidiary
drainage schemes over and above the
actual larger work on Lough Neagh and
the River Erne, and I would like to
explain to him that the Government are
not anxious for the local authorities or
for the Government itself to prosecute
these minor schemes at the moment. We
feel very strongly of opinion that until
such times as the work has been completed on the main Bann drainage scheme
it would be foolish to invite more water
into Lough Neagh and Lough Beg, because there, in the first instance, we
would have the difficulty of getting it
away in a flood season, and in the second
instance, we might be advancing the work
along the various tributary rivers to
which the hon. and gallant Member has
referred too fast for the main work. It
might not be quite completed before the
minor work is completed.
Another point is that all our machinery
in connection with the larger work is
fully occupied at present, and it would
not be possible to ask any of the contractors to go on with the subsidiary work,
and it would be impossible for us ourselves to spare such machinery as we have
for carrying out the smaller work until
the larger work is completed. I only
mention that because I have been twice
over the work itself in order to understand everything that is going on, and I
am putting in very simple language probably what an engineer would be able to
explain more specifically. We are
merely holding back these other schemes
until the major work is completed, and
after that every possible assistance will be
given to help County Armagh and other
places drained by the river itself.

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON:
not got a suitable lecture room?
Mr. ROBB: There is no suitable

thing to bring 40 or 45 children to
strange surroundings, to a place to which
they are not accustomed and put them
down before an audience with a professor
to lecture to them in order to show the
students how to teach. The far better
plan is to take the students out to the
school, put them into a workaday school
so that they may see the children in their
ordinary environment, instead of in a
strange place, and so see the effect of a
good lecture given to those children in
an ordinary school at their ordinary desks.
The advantages of a school of that sort
are enormous as compared with having a
class of specially-selected children brought
up from time to time into a strange
place. By our method the students
from the college see the children working in their own environment, in their
Own school, and with their Own
teachers.

for £20,413. Hon. Members will understand how very closely the probable expenditure this year has been estimated,
and so there is little margin to any of
the items in order to make up for such
purely legitimate unforeseen expenditure
as may arise during the year.
The hon. Member (Mr. O'Neill) was
also anxious to know when those officials
who are at present accommodated at 15
Donegall Square West will be able to
move into their new quarters. In my
remarks in moving the adoption of this
Estimate, I told the Committee it is
hoped that during the present Treasury
financial year we may be able to move
into the new apartments provided for us
at the Law Courts.
While I am mentioning the accommodation at the Law
Courts I should like to assure the hon.
Member (Mr. Byrne), that in selecting
the Departments to be accommodated at
the new Law Courts, attention has been
given to those offices which are frequently
visited by members of the public, and
those particular activities will be located
in the new Law Courts. Naturally the
Government is desirous of serving the
convenience of the public in every way
they can.
As regards the furnishings at Stormont
the hon. Member (Mr. O'Neill) also
wished some information about them.
This is an expenditure which is unusually
large this year owing to the fact that in
such a short time we will be occupying
the new deliberative Chambers at Stor
mont, and this represents the furnishings.
and equipment of those apartments at
Stormont which will be devoted to the
usual purposes of what we regard as the
Houses of Parliament, that is the House
of Commons and Senate. These are being
provided for by the Government at Westminster at their expense and are part of
the building itself.
The hon. and gallant Member (Major
Shillington) and many other Members
showed the interest that they feel, as do
so many of our fellow-countrymen in
Northern Ireland, about the rate of progress of the works in connection with the
Bann drainage. I am glad to know that
the hon. Member (Mr. John Johnston)
was SO interested that he is going
to organise a tour of inspection in
order to show some of his friends the rate
of progress being made. That is apparent
to anyone who has the time and sufficient
interest to go and see for themselves the
major work being carried out and alsc
estimate the rate of progress which the
contractors have been able to effect. Personally, I utilised Easter Monday for that
particular purpose, and I thought that
the work done at Coleraine Cutts was of a
very extensive character, and revealed to
me more than I appreciated before what
a very important engineering undertaking
this is.
I think the contractors have been more
influenced by their desire to provide for
the suitable egress of the water at the
lower end than they have been with the
works on the Upper Bann. In other
words, they are most anxious to provide
for the outlet into the sea than to facilitate the inlet at the upper end of the
works into Lough Neagh and Toomebridge. The hon. and gallant Member,
who is anxious that the work should be
accelerated. must realise that the contractors have provided such an amount of
dredging and land plant as they consider
suitable for dealing with the work within
the specified time that it would not be
possible to remove such plant at the pre-

20 APRIL 1932
sent time from the lower reaches of the

As regards the practising school at
Stranmillis, I am much indebted to my
hon. and learned Friend (Mr. Robb) for
explaining to the Members of the Committee the necessity for this school. After
all, that is a matter for the Ministry of
Education, subject, of course, to the will
of this Committee and House, but the
Ministry of Education do feel that it is
necessary that a practising school should
be provided as a necessary adjunct to the
Stranmillis Training College. The fact
that we have come here for a number of
years and asked for a Vote of money
towards providing this necessary facility,
and the fact that it has not been expended
does not in any way indicate our estimate
of the necessity that this school should be
provided, but my hon. and learned Friend
(Mr. Robb) explained to the Committee
the difficulties they were confronted with
owing to the subsidence of part of the
site on which they intended to extend this
practising school and the necessity for a
change in the plan. Difficulty is experienced in the case of every public body
that is under the unfortunate necessity
of having to acquire land from some
private owner. It nearly always means
protracted proceedings and even considerable expense. The provision of this
training school has been delayed much to
our regret and on this account.
I think I might speak at some length
in connection with the playing-fields
which have been criticised, but I must
say that personally I share the view
expressed, that while our young teachers
are in training at Stranmillis they should.
have a recreation ground. The course
they have to go through there is intensive
in character, and it is right that they
should have opportunities for necessary
exercises and recreation in order to
develop them physically as well as
mentally in the way we would like to
see them developed. It is quite true, as
was said by the hon. Member (Mr.
Crawford), that hitherto we have been
dependent on hired ground, but, as has
also been stated, owing to building
development we could not rely on being
able to rent this ground in the future,
and consequently, at the request of the
Training College Committee and the
Ministry of Education, the Ministry of
Finance took the necessary steps to
acquire suitable ground. The Ministry
of Education asked for a ground of 5 to
6 acres in extent and convenient to the
Men's Hostel in Balmoral Avenue. It
was intended to ask for three playing
pitches.
A suitable area was found but the
owner would not sell the small portion
that was required unless we were to purchase the full extent of ground which he
owned, which was about 18 acres in
extent. As it was considered that
a portion of the ground could subsequently be let for building, the purchase was approved and a price of £5,000
was paid for the fee-simple. Of this
ground, the portion furthest away from
the road, covering about 12 acres, is
intended to be laid out as a sports'
ground, and the part of the purchase
price apportioned was £2,800. The
remainder of the
the ground is being
retained until a favourable opportunity
arises for its sale for building purposes.
The 12 acres is intended to contain
tennis courts, which have been already
laid out, a pavilion, a Rugby football
ground, and a ground available either
for hockey or association football. Owing
to the shape of the ground there is some
loss in the lay-out, and in particular,
there is between the tennis courts and
the football grounds a steep dip, which
renders at least three acres useless for
any purpose. This was, of course,
realised when purchasing, but this
portion could not be omitted from the
take.
The total expenditure on the ground
is anticipated to be:-Purchase, £2,800;
laying out of grounds, £770; pavilion,
£300; extras, £30, making in all £3,900.
I do not think hon. Members will consider
that an unreasonable sum to provide a
recreation ground of this character, seeing
that it has to be provided within the
boundary of Belfast.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I would like to

When a Government starts economies
it really ought to start them in the right
place, namely, at the top. When the
Government of the Free State started

their own salaries. Every man from the

The President of the Executive Council

Northern Ireland to show the people
that, when he speaks of sympathy with

There are approximately 318,309 male
people between the ages of 20 and 65 in

take the

UNEMPLOYMENT-BENEFIT
CLAIMS REJECTED.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he will state the total
number of claims for unemployment
benefit rejected during the past twelve
months by Courts of Referees and
umpires, including deputy umpires, on
the grounds that the claimants were
"not normally in insurable employment"; and whether he will state if there
is any legal or other definition of the
expression or formula quoted.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): In the twelve months ended on
the 31st March, 1932, the Courts of
Referees disallowed 21,891 claims to
benefit on the grounds that the claimants
had not proved that they were normally
in insurable employment and would
normally seek to obtain their livelihood
by means of insurable employment.
During the same time and on the same
grounds the umpire disallowed 2,977
claims, but he allowed 1,641 of the claims
disallowed by the Court. The total disallowance, therefore, during the period on
these grounds was 23,227.
The umpire has not given any definition
such as is asked for in the question. He
has, however, various decisions laid down.
principles upon which the words are to
be interpreted and applied.
Mr. NIXON: Can the Minister explain to the House how any human being
could prove that in future he would be
engaged in insurable employment?
Mr. ANDREWS: It is not my duty to
explain that to the House.

OF COURTS OF REFEREES.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Loans Guarantee (Money).
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to amend the Loans
Guarantee Acts (Northern Ireland), 1922
to 1931, by extending to the 31st day of
March, 1933, the period within which
the Ministry of Finance may give
guarantees under the Loans Guarantee
Act (Northern Ireland), 1922."-(Governor's Recommendation signified.-Mr.
Barbour).
Mr. BARBOUR: The Government
have decided to recommend Parliament
to adhere to its policy of keeping alive
the Loans Guarantee machinery, and this
Resolution has, accordingly, been tabled
as an essential preliminary to the introduction of the requisite legislation. The
activities of the Ministry under this
machinery during the past year have
necessarily been limited owing to the
stagnation in industry, and hon. Members will have observed from the returns
which have been tabled from time to time
that they relate to two transactions only,
namely, a supplemental guarantee to the
Oceanic Steam Navigation Company to
enable the "Georgic" to be completed,
and a guarantee in connection with the
construction of a fruit boat. Satisfactory security has been obtained in each
case.
The
Looking to the future we find in the
realm of shipping an unhappy prospect.
In Northern Ireland-a community
boasting the biggest shipbuilding concern
in the world-the yards have not a single
slip occupied at the present time. In
this, of course, we are not alone.
yards in Great Britain are suffering in
the same way, and although subsidised
contracts continued to be placed long
after British shipowners had ceased to
place orders
orders for new tonnage, the
shipping depression has now reached a
point at which even foreign shipbuilders
are experiencing
almost complete
paralysis of their activities, despite the
operation of out and out subsidies.
such a time as this our Government is
called upon to consider its future policy
in regard to the grant of credit facilities
under this Act. The issues are threefold-Firstly, the employment position;
secondly, the nature of the security that
can be offered by the applicant, and
thirdly, the difficulties which already face
the Exchequer in respect of past loans
guarantee commitments.
At
It is quite obvious that, looked at from
the employment position alone, the need
for credit facilities is as great as, if not
greater than, in the past. Unemployment
amongst shipyard workers is in the
region of 60 per cent., and with the completion of the "Georgic" in two months'
time we fear that matters will be worse.
The Committee will appreciate that the
Government do not claim that the continuation of these facilities will of themselves restore to any appreciable extent
the activities of our shipyards in the
coming year. British and foreign shipowners have been temporarily forced to
retire from the new tonnage market as a
result of the serious shrinkage in revenue
from passenger traffic, illustrated by
drastic cancellations of liner sailings, and
by a grave curtailment of the staple
cargoes on which merchant shipping de-
Loans (Guarantee) Money-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
pends. The fact that 4 million tons of
deadweight capacity were still out of
commission at the end of last year provides
eloquent testimony to the loss of cargo
traffic.
One comforting thought, however,
emerges, namely, that much of this laid
up tonnage has become obsolete, so that
when indications of improvement appear
on the horizon shipowners must undertake commitments in the way of new
tonnage. The Government desires, therefore, to retain the statutory powers so as
to be able to give some assistance when
this time comes, bearing in mind that
are to be found
even to-day there
prosperous shipping concerns which are
maintaining and even developing their
trading position. We must not imagine

It will be within the
general terms.
knowledge of the Committee that during
the last fifteen months the Royal Mail
voting trustees have been grappling with
the task of salving the biggest shipping
group in the world, comprising one-sixth
of the British Mercantile Marine, and
their work has been made progressively
more difficult by the world depression.
I should like to say, on behalf of the
Government, how deeply we are indebted
to them and all those associated with
them for their work in this connection.
The scheme proposes a sort of moratorium for three years, during which
time the various groups of secured
creditors, including Governments, are
asked to withhold their rights of foreclosure. In the meantime the relative
rights of these parties are preserved
essentially unaltered. It provides for a
reorganisation of management, both at
home and abroad, involving substantial
economies more important still, it introduces a new spirit of co-operation.
The Government is to remain liable under
its guarantees, but the income from its
specific securities is to be available for
the service of the guaranteed loans. In
this connection it should be pointed out
that even under the present depressed
conditions the group companies in
general are not losing money so far as
direct trading expenses are concerned.
The Ulster Government and the
British Government, who are jointly
concerned in most of the transactions,
have been in consultation with the
sponsors of the scheme from the time of
the very first draft, and both Governments are satisfied that on general principle the scheme is sound, and that it
provides a satisfactory solution of the
problem. In the opinion of this Government, given some improvement in
world shipping conditions, taken in corjunction with the substantial economies
and improved management, there is no
reason why ultimately any serious sacrifice should be entailed on the part of
this Government. As a temporary
Measure the Government will, in all
probability, be called upon to make advances under its guarantees in any cases
where net earnings for the time being
prove to be insufficient to meet the service of the guaranteed first mortgage
loans, but if such should be the case the
scheme provides that such payments
shall rank in the preferential position
which is given under the scheme to those
who, like the Government, are fortunate
enough to be covered by first mortgages

Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: This is
a small Bill, which I hope will not take
up much of the time of the House. At
the outset it may interest honourable
Members if I give some facts which will
enable an accurate appreciation to be
made of
of the immense and growing
economic importance of the poultry
industry to the agricultural community.
The following figures for the year 1928
indicate the annual value of the output
from the leading agricultural commodities:-

It will be seen from these figures that
the poultry industry is worth 3 millions
sterling a year, almost as much as the
cattle and pig industries combined.
Further, poultry production is capable
of almost unlimited further development.
In this connection it may be pointed out
that the United Kingdom imports
annually poultry and poultry products
to the value of about £20,000,000. That
shows the possibilities, more particularly
now that at last home produce looks like
obtaining a favoured position in the
British market.
Although poultry rearing is important
to the farming community of these islands
generally, it is of vastly greater relative
importance to the small farmers of Northern Ireland, and the development of the
industry in this country in recent years
has been remarkable. For example, in
1904 the poultry population of Northern
Ireland was estimated at 4,351,344, but
in 1930 it had risen to 8,807,516. The
number of poultry in proportion to
acreage is also considerably higher in
Northern Ireland than in Great Britain
or even the Irish Free State. The following figures in this connection are
illuminating:-

At present I regret to say that this
valuable industry is menaced by serious
disease. Bacillary White Diarrhoea at
the moment constituted the gravest
danger to our poultry flocks. The effect
of the disease is that within three weeks
of hatching the young chicks die off
rapidly, the rate of mortality being any
thing from 90 to 100 per cent.; consequently where outbreaks occur practically
the whole of the young stock is lost.
Moreover, surviving birds, although
apparently healthy, act as carriers of
the disease, the germ being transmitted
in the eggs and thus hatches in subsequent years are reinfected.
Poultry Diseases Bill-
Second Reading.
21 APRIL 1932
Unfortunately, there is no known cure
for this disease. The only method of
coping with it is to determine its presence
by bacteriological examination and then.
to weed out the reacting birds. The
Ministry has done much in recent years
to prevent the spread of this disease
within Northern Ireland, and the results
on the whole are satisfactory. Poultry
stations under the schemes of County
Agricultural Committees are obliged to
have their flocks tested and, in addition,
we have a voluntary scheme whereby
private breeders can have birds tested at
a small charge.
Private breeders are fully alive to the
advantages of the scheme, and are having
birds tested in increasing numbers. For
example, in 1927-8 the number of blood
samples tested for private breeders was
2,606, whereas in 1930-31 the number
was 22,851.
I am glad to be able to say that many
breeders who found it impossible to rear
chicks in 1928 have, as a result of our
scheme, had no difficulties in this connection in 1932.
All our efforts and expenditure in endeavouring to eradicate bacillary white
diarrhoea disease within Northern Ireland will, however, in the end be nullified unless steps are taken to exercise
some control over the imports of breeding
poultry, day-old chicks, and hatching
eggs. It is futile to stamp out disease
one day if we allow it to be introduced
the next. I may say in this connection
that practically all outbreaks of bacillary
white diarrhoea in Northern Ireland can
be traced directly or indirectly to such
imports. All the important poultryproducing countries in Europe have now
regulations in force to prevent the introduction of disease, and as these countries
are our chief competitors on the British
market we are going to be seriously handicapped if we simply fold our hands and
look on without taking
without taking similar precautions.
It seems to me quite extraordinary that
while the Diseases of Animals Acts give
ample power to protect other live stock,
such as cattle, sheep, swine, etc., from
contagious disease, no provision has heretofore been made for the safeguarding of
our poultry flocks which are of at least
equal importance from the financial point
of view. Probably the explanation is
that when the Diseases of Animals Acts
were first contemplated poultry were regarded as of little economic importance
and, consequently, they were left outside
the scope of that splendid legislation.
that has freed us from such scourges as
pleuro-pneumonia, which within living
memory was a very serious disease in this
country. It is also to the Diseases of
Animals Code that we owe our comparative immunity from such diseases as
foot-and-mouth disease, swine fever, etc.
All I now ask for is authority to protect
similarly our poultry industry and, if this
proposal is approved, I look forward to
equally satisfactory results. Members will
observe that the Bill is what is known as
an enabling Measure, that is, that it gives
us the necessary powers to make Orders
without specifying in detail what those
Orders shall be. In that respect it
follows precisely the lines of the Diseases
of Animals Acts already referred to, and
it is difficult to see how a question of
disease could otherwise be efficiently dealt
with legislatively. However, in case
hon. Members desire to know what
Orders we have in mind at the moment,
I may say that we propose, in the first
instance, to secure as far as practicable
that breeding poultry, day-old chicks, or
eggs imported for hatching, are not
carriers of bacillary white diarrhoea. It
is not at present proposed that disease in
poultry should be made notifiable, or to
schedule areas on account of disease, because the measures we are already taking
are reducing the incidence of disease, and
are adequate to cope with the position so
far as the internal situation is concerned
at present. Disease might, however,
suddenly get out of hand, and a particular district might become a plague spot
contaminating a whole area. In that
case it might be necessary in the interests
of the industry to resort to drastic
measures, but we do not contemplate such
action at present, and I am hoping that
it may not be necessary. At the same
time, as in the case of the Diseases of
Animals Acts, we must be prepared to act
if, unfortunately, an emergency such as
we have indicated should arise. I beg to
move.

fowls, pigeons, and any other kind of
live poultry which may be specified in
an order made under the powers conferred by this Act."
I would like to know from the Minister
how they are going to watch pigeons flying from Southern Ireland into Northern
Ireland, or how they are going to inspect
every hen, duck, goose, or turkey, or
other class of poultry that may be brought
across the Border, because to enforce this
Bill properly they will have to do that.
That is one of the points the hon. and
gallant Member (Lieut.-Colonel Gordon)
has made, and has made well. While
this legislation may be desirable it should
be avoided, unless you are in a position to
give effect to it, because it brings the law
into contempt to place an Act that cannot be enforced upon the Statute Book,
or that would take half the population
of the country to enforce. There is
plenty of that kind of legislation on the
Statute Book. There are any number of
Acts of Parliament passed from time to
time in this Parliament and other Parliaments, which it has never been possible
to put into force.
The Minister should make some arrangement other than the present for the

bringing of these Orders before the
House. The present arrangement I think
is to place them in the Library for a
certain number of days, and if any Member of the House wants to see them he has
to go into the Library, or perhaps they
may appear in some part of Hansard.
The right way to bring these things
before this House would be for the
Minister to bring them in here and read
them and allow hon. Members to comment on them.
There is no doubt about it that the
people are sick, sore, and tired of inspectors. On the last day when we were
discussing the Estimates the Minister
almost suggested the possibilty of inspectors having to look in the mouths of
poultry later on. At the present time
they have to look into the mouth of every
animal, including pigs, imported, and if
this legislation goes on we will soon have
them looking into their mouths and
counting their teeth. I will not oppose
the Bill. I know it will pass.
Any Bill
brought in here by the Government will
pass, no matter what it is like, but when
it is passed I hope that this Bill will
be enforced with moderation and consideration.

Captain CHICHESTER
What I think both this House and some

which might be called anti-inspectoritis.
I saw a most extraordinary case in a certain agricultural committee the other day
in regard to this very question. It was

coccidiosis, did not exist, that there were

that they declined to pass the resolution

Scourge. That shows the position we have
arrived at when the question of another

have said this, and I will say it again,

when I see that inspectors are going to
help our farmers, when they are going
to improve their produce and help to

Captain CHICHESTER CLARK:
The point I want to make is that in

Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: The
hon. Member for South Fermanagh (Mr.
Healy) spoke of the damage done to the

said we were going to impose great restrictions on poultry breeders. We are
not going to impose any restrictions on

What we want is to keep diseased poultry
and eggs out of Ireland. (Hon. Memhers: Hear, hear). We are not going to
appoint any officials. The Bill does not
authorise the appointment of any officials.
In some counties where there are a great
many poultry, like County Down and
County Antrim, we may perhaps, require
another woman or someone to make tests
for a short time. But what we really
want is not to let diseased poultry or
diseased eggs into Northern Ireland.
We want to keep our breeds free. Both
in Northern Ireland and the Free State
at the present time, I am thankful to
say, there is no real disease, except that
contracted from birds imported from
England, and that is the thing we want
to prevent. In all our egg stations and
in the counties the birds are tested by
our poultry instructresses, and that
keeps those eggs pure. But we want
power over any bird that may come into
Northern Ireland. For instance, a man
may see a great advertisement of a poultry

We want to prohibit imports of infected

Animals Act is an old Act, but we had
no great poultry industry at the time it
was passed, and so there were no inspectors for the purpose. Now poultry
has become must valuable to everyone.
The hon. Member for Mid-Tyrone (Mr.

If our eggs fetch as high a price as any

You cannot run up the price of eggs by

My hon. Friend, the Member for Mid-

is found in a flock of fowl all the fowl

not always possible to lay any Regulations that may have to be made on the

26 APRIL 1932
PREPARATION OF DOG LISTS.
2. Mr. McCARROLL asked the Minister of Finance whether he has received
a communication from the Derry Branch
of the Typographical Association renewing the protest against the transfer to
London of printing work hitherto done in
this country; whether, before the decision
referred to was arrived at, opportunity
was given to firms in this area to tender
on an equal basis; whether it is not contrary to statutory provisions to have the
printing of the lists of dog licence holders
executed outside Ireland; and whether,
in view of all circumstances, it would not
be desirable to revert to the former position, under which the employment was
provided at home.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The communication to which
the hon. Member refers has been received
and answered.
Since the hon. Member persists in referring to this work as printing, might
I again point out that, as I explained
fully in a reply given to him on the 14th
ultimo, the printing of the lists has been
discontinued, and they are being copied
by duplicating process in the Stationery
Office, London. As a result of the
change, the Exchequer has made a
saving estimated at more than 40 per
cent. of the previous cost.
I am not aware that there are any
firms in Northern Ireland which could
compete for work of this nature, but if
there are, I am prepared to undertake
that they will be given an opportunity
of tendering for future contracts.
There is no statutory provision which
prohibits the printing or duplicating of
these lists outside Ireland.
The answer to the concluding portion
of the hon. Member's question is in the
negative.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether
it is a fact that by Statute these dog
lists must be delivered by 15th April
each year; whether the right hon. Gentleman is aware that under the new
arrangement these lists have not yet
been delivered, and what steps he proposes to take in regard to this matter?
Mr. POLLOCK: It is a fact that
under an Act of 1865, the date mentioned
by the hon. Member, 15th April, is included as the date on which these lists
should be prepared, but it has never been
the case, or has not been the case for
many years, at any rate, that that has
been complied with. It is regarded as
an archaic Act. The period between 13th
March and 15th April this year, whether
on account of the number of dogs I do
not know, was quite insufficient to prepare the lists. That is the answer to my
hon. Friend from Tyrone. There is no
special obligation as to date, except that
contained in this archaic Act of 1865.
Mr. McCARROLL: May I ask the
Minister, having regard to the use to
which these dog lists are put, if the proposed method is considered a correct one?
They will be used very extensively by the
people, and will they be as suitable for
the purpose as the old ones? May I also
ask whether the decision of the Government in respect to this is consistent with
the desire to maintain employment in
Northern Ireland?
Mr. POLLOCK: It has been found in
practice that there has been no difficulty
in respect of the circulation of these lists.
They are intended for the police and must
be posted up at the doors of petty sessions
courts, police barracks, and such places.
No one will want to examine these lists
except someone to see about his own dog.
No inconvenience has really been caused
by the method adopted.
Mr. HEALY: Is it a fact that the
paper suitable for cyclostyle work is not.
suitable for posting up?
Mr. POLLOCK: That is a technical
matter which I am not prepared either
to accept or to deny.
Mr. HEALY: Can the right hon.
Gentleman tell us what the actual cost
previously was?
Mr. POLLOCK : Yes. The actual
cost was £340, and it has been reduced
to £200 by the change.
THE MEANS TEST.
3. Mr. McCARROLL asked the Minister of Labour to state the total number
of cases in which, since the regulations
under the Economy Act came into force;
the means test for transitional payments
has been applied, up to and including
the 31st March; the total number in
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. McCarroll]
no
which full rates have been allowed and
are being paid; the total number in which
partial rates were paid and are being
paid, and the numbers in which
allowance has been made; and also
whether any steps will be taken to secure
greater uniformity in administration, and
in the amounts allocated by public
assistance committees.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The total number of determinations received from public assistance
committees up to the 30th March last
(the latest date for which figures are
available) was 31,197. Of these 11,668
were allowed at normal benefit rates,
and 14,415 at rates lower than normal
benefit rates, while in the remaining
5,114 cases the needs of applicants were
held not to justify payments.
A conference was held to co-ordinate
views in administration in certain areas
where discrepancies existed. Allowing
for the variation in local conditions I am
not now aware of any serious lack of
uniformity in the administration.

ployment exchanges service in Northern

Mr. ANDREWS: A friend of mine
suggested to me this forenoon that this
was my big day.
Mr. BEATTIE: Your pay day.
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
26 APRIL 1932
Mr. ANDREWS: My reply was that I
did not look upon it as that, that I looked
upon it as the big day of the Opposition.
However that may be, it is the one
occasion in the year when I have the
opportunity of referring to the general
policy of the Department and its many
activities in a great number of directions.
I think I should, in the first place, remind hon. Members how greatly the work
of the Deparment has increased during
the last few years. When we took over
our powers from His Majesty's Imperial
Government more than ten years ago we
became responsible for industrial
relations, trade boards, the factory and workshops code, the Truck Acts, and workmen's compensation. In addition to that
we had dual control with the approved
societies in connection with health insurance matters, and we became responsible for the employment exchanges and
for the unemployment insurance. Since
then there has been added to the duties
of the Department, old age pensions (contributory and non-contributory), widows'
and orphans' pensions, employment services, such as relief schemes, juvenile
training centre, etc. Our control over
health insurance matters has been
strengthened and medical benefits have
been added to this scheme. This, of
course, has involved an increase in our
Estimate, and in addition to that it has
involved the Department in a great many
additional duties of a very important
kind in the public interest.
May I say that the general policy remains what it always has been, namely,
that in connection with these four great
social services which my Department is
charged with the responsibility of dealing
with, to remain in step or in parity with
Great Britain. That was the policy
which the Government decided upon when
we took over our powers more than ten
years ago, and from that policy we have
never varied, either as regards administration or legislation. Of course the Department is frequently criticised, very
often from two very different standpoints
at the same time. I am told that we
cannot afford the great expenditure involved, that we are a poorer part of the
Kingdom than that which lies across the
Channel, and that we ought to cut our
coat according to our cloth. The reply
of the Government I think is very convincing. It is that because we have for
certain services a Parliament of our own
that is no reason why our working
people should suffer as regards benefits
and privileges which their fellow countrymen in Great Britain enjoy, and which,
if we continued to be governed from
Westminster, they would also enjoy.
Besides, if the Government were to do
less in connection with these matters, I
do not think it would involve any saving,
because it would simply mean that the
local authorities would have to bear a
heavier burden as the rates would have
to make up the difference. The attack
on the other side is that the Government are not doing half enough to
deal with the situation as it now exists.
In fact, hon. Members opposite have
stated from time to time that the Government is doing nothing.
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: And I observe that
a Member of a local board the other day
said the same thing. Well, of course, a
statement like that is really foolish, as
almost every sentence which I utter to-day
will show. There is the less extravagant
statement made that we are not doing
enough. The answer to that is that we
are doing everything which has been done
in Great Britain, and more than is being
done in any other country in the world,
and that we cannot afford to do more.
May I say at this stage that I particularly desire to-day to remove a misunderstanding which, I fear, is too
general, namely, that the Ministry of
Labour Estimates show an actual increase
in State expenditure this year of £217,703
against last year. This is, however, only
part of the story. It is true that we ask
the Committee to vote under all heads, as
shown on page 83 of the Estimates,
£4,002,411, as against £3,784,708 for the
previous year. It should be remembered
in this connection that last year the Unemployment Fund borrowed £841,000,
while this year we are estimating on the
basis of paying our way. In other words,
instead of borrowing to make up the
deficiency as between the income of the
Unemployment Fund and the actual expenditure as happened last year, the State
is to make up such difference as there may
be. A correct comparison, therefore, discloses a reduction of £623,297, less certain
adjustments, under the Re-insurance
Agreement, which can only be correctly
ascertained at the end of the financial
year.

On this occasion it might interest the
Committee if I reviewed as briefly as
possible the various activities of the Department and their importance to the
people generally in Northern Ireland. The
first service to which I desire to refer is
that of our industrial relations branch,
in other words, the preservation as far as
possible of industrial peace. It is always
a pleasure to me to refer to the harmonious relations which exist between
the workers and their employers in Northern Ireland and the few strikes and lockouts which we have. We are much more
fortunate in that direction than they are
in Great Britain. During the past year
important questions arose affecting both
the spinning and weaving ends of our
staple industry. Through the machinery.
of conciliation and negotiation, which
was established some years ago by my
Department in connection with the
spinning branch of the trade, and with
the goodwill of both employers and
workers in that branch, certain differences
were adjusted; and wage reductions also
resulted from the negotiations, it being
recognised by all concerned that the state
of the industry at that time required
that some sacrifices should be made by
the workers in order that we might be in
a better position than we were to compete with the fierce foreign competition
to which we were subjected.
In the weaving end of the trade it is
true that a strike occurred and lasted
for a few weeks in Lurgan. I am glad
to state that it did not spread to other
districts, and after a few weeks' time,
under the auspices of the Department,
matters were adjusted on a satisfactory
basis. In the building trade, under the
auspices of the Department again,
settlements were arranged of a good many
At our docks,
outstanding difficulties.
I
quite recently, there was a certain trouble
associated with our cross-Channel trade.
Here, again, the Department was successful in bringing about a settlement.
think I am entitled to say that I am
particularly gratified that our chief conciliation officer, by his patience, tact, and
ability in dealing with matters of the
kind, has earned the confidence of both
employers and employees to a very remarkable degree throughout Northern
Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Largely owing to the influence of the
Department, therefore, I think I can
claim that we have averted strikes which,
if they had occurred, would have cost
our Province many hundreds of thousands
of pounds.
I need only refer briefly to Trade
Boards. There are in Northern Ireland
eighteen of these Boards, composed, as
they are, of representatives of employer
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
26 APRIL 1932
and employee, with a neutral appointed
member as chairman. They exist for the
purpose of settling wages and conditions,
and they affect 3,000 firms and 50,000
of our employed persons. When I became Minister of Labour I remember in
this House I was very frequently attacked
on the ground that these Boards were a
perfect pest, that they never should have
been established, and that they were unacceptable both to employers and working people. We legislated on the matter
in this House, and owing to reasonable
administration I am glad to think that
these Boards are now looked upon by both
employers and employed as a very satisfactory way of dealing with labour matters in those industries to which the
Boards are applied. At any rate, there
has been absolutely no trouble in those
industries since we here became a Parliament.
There are one or two things I would
like to say about our Factory and Workshop code. Our employers have been cooperating in a most generous way with
the Ministry in this connection, with the
result that, I am glad to be able to
state, through improved ventilation,
sanitation, lighting, etcetera, and the
shorter hours which they now enjoy, the
health of our industrial workers in Northern Ireland has improved to a remarkable degree. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). But there is one thing which I do
not look upon as satisfactory, and that
is that there are in Northern Ireland far
too many accidents. Many of these
accidents, I believe, are avoidable. There
were no fewer than 1,195 last year, and 13
persons were fatally injured. These accidents involved payment by employers
during the year to the average amount per
week of £1,000. My Department has been
urging for some time that employers
should to a very great extent protect moving parts of their machinery in such a
way as
to lessen the probability of
accident, and that their foremen and
workers generally should be instructed as
to the importance of not taking unnecessary risks. In our shipyards safety committees have been established and have
been most useful in this respect.
I now come to the question of pensions.
It may surprise hon. Members to know
that in this little area of ours we have no
fewer than 94,297 pensioners receiving
pensions every week.
Mr. BEATTIE: How many paid for
them?
""
Mr. ANDREWS: They range from
under one year to over ninety, and I can
assure the Committee it is no light task
to see that the conditions which Parliament has laid down are fulfilled when
these pensions are granted, and work is
rendered more difficult through the everchanging circumstances in the lives of the
pensioners. These pensioners are scattered
all over Northern Ireland. They live in
our city streets and they live high up on
mountain sides. They reside in the
island of Rathlin and also on the islands
of Lough Erne. Administration under
the circumstances is, therefore, a very
difficult matter indeed. My inspectors
from time to time hear funny statements
made. For instance, the other day a
woman was asked to try to think of
some evidence with regard to her age
which she could give to qualify her for
the old-age pension. Her reply was:
"Well, I cannot get my birth certificate,
and I cannot get my baptismal certificate.
I really cannot think of any evidence I
can give. Our inspectors are always
ready to help a claimant, and the inspector in this case said: "Well, now,
just think again, because if you cannot
give some proof, of course, you cannot
get the pension." "Well, she said, "I
remember when I was a little girl being
taken to the opening of an Orange Hall,
and above the door of that Orange Hall
there was a date." So the inspector said:
"Yes. That might be very good evidence."
He went and looked at the Orange Hall
and found the date on the stone was
1690. (Laughter.) Although that made
the woman rather over 200 years of age,
I do not know that it was taken as satisfactory proof of her actual age. Again,
when a claimant was asked to try to give
some proof of her age, she said: "Well,
the truth of the matter is, I have a very
bad memory for these things, but my
mother is inside, and she probably remembers the event better than I do. She
will, no doubt, tell you what my age is."
However, that may be, I can assure you
that every effort is made in order to ensure that justice is done in connection
with these matters.
Mr. DEVLIN: Are these the tests
that are applied to blind persons?
Mr. ANDREWS: I shall refer to that
later on. As regards health insurance
matters, I am sorry I cannot say that all
is well. The health insurance scheme is
giving great anxiety to the Ministry of
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
Health in Great Britain, and it is also
giving a considerable amount of anxiety
to us here. I remember that, when I became Minister of Labour, the health insurance scheme was very often criticised
on the ground that the reserves were far
too large, and that it was a foolish thing
to go on creating these immense reserves.
My answer always was: "Well, we are
in close contact with the best actuarial
authorities in the Kingdom on these
matters, and they assure us that the reserves are necessary to liquidate the contingent liabilities which are certain to
occur from time to time, especially as the
scheme goes on to function."
Now, nobody makes an attack on the
ground that the reserves are too large;
no one suggests that the benefits should
be increased or that the contributions
should be lowered, because I think everyone realises that the liabilities upon the
scheme in these days have been increasing
beyond what was first expected. As hon.
Members know, there is a valuation of
the assets and liabilities of the approved
societies made every five years, and the
last valuation which was reported upon
some months ago disclosed the fact that
the societies' financial position had gone
back a good deal. That is exactly what
is causing the anxiety at the present time.
I may say, however, that I should be
much more anxious about the position if
it were not for the fact that we are so
closely associated with the British scheme,
and therefore we are on a much sounder
foundation than if we had to depend on
our position here alone.
The demands on the approved societies
have increased, I think, largely owing to
the fact that when the scheme was started
it was the first contributory scheme of
the kind which was launched. A great
many people did not know very well how
to make a claim. They had never made
claims of the kind before; they hesitated
to make them, and if they could carry
on for a short period without making a
claim upon the health insurance funds
they did so. Now they have come to
realise and nobody can blame themthat, as it is a contributory scheme to
which they are paying when they are
working, they are entitled to get benefit
when they are ill, and so the claims have
vastly increased.
In addition to that, due to unemployment, the contribution income has fallen
off to a very considerable extent, so that
the approved societies have been hit both
ways to a rather startling degree at the
same time. The claims of married
women have mounted up to an alarming
extent, as the following figures disclose.
The expenditure in 1931 upon men was
£1 2s per head. The expenditure upon
single women was £1 5s 1d per head,
while the claims for married women
amounted to no less than £3 4s 10d per
head. In other words, married women
paid into the fund 17s 4d per head, and
during the year to which I am referring,
namely, 1931, they drew out on the
average no less than £3 4s 10d.
The general position, however, has improved as between the year 1929 and
1930. The claims upon the approved
societies in 1929 amounted to £681,359,
and last year they amounted to £623,092,
or a reduction of approximately £60,000.
So far, so good. Of course, the great
difficulty in health insurance matters is to
be sure when a person is really entitled
to draw benefit and when a person is not
entitled to do so. We are largely dependent on the certificates which are given
by the local doctors, and in recent years
our medical referees' service has been
greatly strengthened, with the result
that the approved societies-and they are
paying for this scheme themselves-can
have a second opinion when they so desire. In addition, this service is of a
consultative nature, because when the
medical referee finds something wrong
with the patient which the local doctor
may not have discovered, he communicates his views to the local doctor, very
much, I am sure, at times to the advantage of the patients who are the insured
persons.
I am very pleased to acknowledge the
very helpful way in which the Central
Insurance Practitioners' Committee cooperate with my Department in connection with this very important social service.
As hon. Members know, a year or so ago
there was attached to this service a medical benefit scheme, and I am pleased to
say that that scheme is working very
smoothly and satisfactorily, and that
complaints are few indeed.
Only six
complaints of sufficient importance to
necessitate their being considered by the
Medical Benefit Council have been received since the scheme
was started.
Four hundred and ninety-nine doctors,
and 405 chemists are working the scheme,
and I am confident that it is of incalculable value to insured persons, due to
Ministry of Labour
Estimates-

the fact that there is brought within the
reach of the insured person when ill, medical advice, which, no doubt, in many instances, shortens the duration of the

I come now to unemployment insurance. We have so frequently discussed
this matter in the House-and quite recently--that I am afraid there is not
much new that I can say upon the matter.
But, at the same time, if I did not refer
to the scheme and its working at some
length I probably should leave myself
open to the reproach that I had run away

should like to say at the beginning of
my remarks on this subject that last year
we estimated on the basis of 25 per cent.
unemployment. As a matter of fact, it
worked out at 26.8 per cent., and I venture to suggest that it was a very close
estimate, having regard to the fact that
the year was an abnormal one. How
abnormal it was will be gathered from the
fact that during the financial crisis of
August last unemployment rose in our
area to 28.5 per cent., but on the suspension of the gold standard and the
adoption of the abnormal importation
duties it fell again towards the end of
the year to 24.1, and it is rather less
now, I am glad to say.
However, we are estimating on the
basis of 25 per cent. unemployment for
this year, which, unless something unexpected happens, we think is a conservative
estimate. The reason we are budgeting
for 25 per cent. unemployment is thisalthough, as I have said, it is rather
lower at the moment-the whole world's
industrial and financial position is very
uncertain, indeed, and in addition to
that our shipyards, I admit with great
regret, are in an unfortunate position at
the present time, through no fault of
those controlling the destinies of those
yards, of those who work in the yards, or
of the Government. As I have already
said, we are not borrowing for this year.
We are paying our way-with the result
that our Estimates are apparently increased by £260,000.
In
Several changes have been made in the
scheme, as hon. Members know. The
contributions income has been increased
from each of the three contributors.
addition to that, it was necessary to reduce the benefits paid by approximately
10 per cent., and even then it was found
that the expenditure would be largely in
excess of the income if benefit were paid
under the old conditions. Therefore it
was considered necessary that the standard
benefit should be limited to 26 weeks, and
that, after that, if the claimant found
that a further payment was necessary he
could receive it provided that he was able
to show in the first place that he was
normally in insurable employment, and
would normally seek to obtain his livelihood thereby. And the second condition
is that he can show to the public assistance committees that he is in need of what
is, after all, not insurance benefit but a
free State grant. Now a great deal of
criticism has been directed against this
needs test, but the object of it can be
defended, and it is to conserve what
funds there are for those who need them
most.
As regards the scheme, the first condition to which I referred is adjudicated
upon by the machinery of the Department,
and as regards the latter condition,
namely, the needs test, that is applied by
the Public Assistance Committee. And
although there may be features connected
with that form of administration which
are not acceptable to many of us, yet at
the same time I am entitled to say that
I
think these public assistance committees all over Northern Ireland have
played a very honourable part. They
have shouldered a heavy burden and I
believe that they are discharging their
responsible duties with great care and in
a purely public-spirited way. Their
duties are unpopular. They knew they
would be unpopular from the start, and
I think they deserve all the more credit
for shouldering what they were
would be an unpopular task to perform.
aware
And how are they performing their
task? Just let me tell the House. Up
to the 30th March they have reviewed
31,197 cases. They granted full payments to 11,668 claimants. They gave
assistance to 14,415 claimants and they
found in 5,114 cases that public assistance was not necessary. Now, on the
average, therefore, they have given twothirds of the benefit rates to those who
claim this form of State grant. How can
it be said fairly or with truth that these
public assistance committees are not endeavouring to do what is right in the
public interest by conserving the money
available, as I have said, for those who
are able to show that they require this
form of help, after having exhausted the
benefit which they were entitled to receive on the actuarial basis from the Unemployment Fund itself?

I shaved myself with a razor-blade which

Now, I desire, in conclusion, to say

in asking the Committee for the means to

asking what hon. Members on both sides

freely give. I beg to move. (Hon.
