do so because the average coming into
the home has exceeded 8s per head. If
you think that is a proper way to adminis
ter Exchequer grants I fail to agree.
I ask the right hon. Gentleman to use
his good influence with the Government
to change their policy of having the administration of the Exchequer grants
carried out by the body called poor-law
guardians. If he does that he will be
coming more into line with Great Britain.
This is something which, perhaps, the
Minister knows but does not want to hear.
There is no fear or dread in Great Britain
of an unemployed man being disallowed
at the Public Assistance Committee, because there they have their scale of relief
under the exceptional distress order,
ranging as high as £2 5s for a man and his
wife and family of four. The scale
under the exceptional distress order was
always higher than it ever was under poorlaw relief in Northern Ireland. No man in
England will be allowed to starve, because
the secretary of that distress committee
can give a chit right away the moment
a man applies for it, and that chit is for
money as well as goods. But here we
are subject to an authority which has been
cutting down to the lowest possible figure
the amount of relief that should be given
for keeping life within the body. The
right hon. Gentleman wants to tell the
public assistance committees that they
must increase their scales of Exchequer
grants, or, failing that, that he is prepared to recommend the abolition of the
public assistance committees and the
appointment of a more humane committee
to take over the administration. The
right hon. Gentleman has those powers,
and, if he wishes to use them, I am sure
many thousands of citizens of Northern
Ireland will welcome the change.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have not those
powers.
Mr. BEATTIE: You have power under
the Privy Council Order to abolish the
Public Assistance Committee from the
administration of Exchequer grants and
to set up a more humane and more
sympathetic committee.
Mr. ANDREWS: No. I have not.

Mr. BEATTIE: Another point which
I want to make is that the policy of the
Government is not to keep work in
Northern Ireland on the high level on
which it was when labour was a little scarce.
The Government are taking advantage of
the depression in trade and the surplus of
workers. In the Minister's own Exchange they employ a head porter to do
duplicating work. The right hon. Gentleman actually employs the man who is in
charge of the hall to do work which girls
could be and should be paid for doing.
Labouring men should not be doing such
work in the Labour Exchange. The man
is a head messenger or porter, and he
should not be called upon to do the work
of a typist or duplicater. There are any
amount of girls signing the unemployment
register who would be very glad to fill
such a position.
With those arguments, I have the
greatest pleasure in moving the reduction
of the items mentioned, the law charges
included, because this system is making
criminals of every man who happens
technically to tread over the line. This
year the right hon. Gentleman estimates
for £625 for pursuing those unfortunate
individuals, some of whom cannot read or
write and others of whom do not know
they are making mistakes. We are asked
to pass this charge of £625 to pursue these
unfortunate individuals, who should be
guided and advised by the managers of
the respective exchanges and who, while
that advice is not there for them, make
these technical blunders; and then you
pursue them to the courts, have them imprisoned and so manufacture criminals out
of innocent people. I beg to move the
reduction of the Vote by that amount.
Question proposed, "That a reduced
sum not exceeding £8,240 be granted to

Hon. Members must remember that out
of that £217,000 there are two items

I was somewhat conthe employed.
cerned as to whether or not I should

the question whether or not the conditions of the unemployed which obtain
in Northern Ireland are any worse, or

are

that the conditions which prevail in the

worse than the conditions which prevail
in Great Britain.
Then I asked myself a second question.
Having regard to the position in which
we are placed in regard to Great Britain,
are we in a position to deal with the
problem of unemployment in a comprehensive manner? I am of the opinion
that no State which is not a Sovereign
State can do other than, at the very best,
tinker with this great subject. Even if
this were
a Sovereign State I doubt
whether as a Sovereign State we should
be able to provide a remedy to deal with
this great problem. I am inclining to
the view that the problem of unemployment is not a problem for a Federal
State such as this, nor for a Sovereign
State, but that it is a collective problem
which must be tackled and dealt with by
a combined council of civilised countries.
There is one thing, I think, which
strikes the casual observer in looking at
these Estimates, and in comparing these
Estimates with the Estimates of 10 years
ago, and that is, the enormous increase
in the cost of the social services. In
1923, I notice, the Estimates of this
House for social services amounted
approximately to two million pounds.
To-day, not including education, they
amount to substantially over four million
pounds. These social services include,
as the Minister pointed out, all branches
of social service in our midst. They
include unemployment benefit;
benefit; they
include transitional benefit; they include
health insurance; they include widows'
and orphans' pensions, and they include
the contributory pensions which are now
paid to the insured persons who attain
the age of 65.
This cost is enormous. Ever since I
entered this House, some three years ago,
the cost has been increasing year by
year, and it is only during the past year
that an attempt has been made to arrest
this somewhat startling tendency. We
had last year, if I remember aright, an
attempt I believe a perfectly sincere
attempt by the Prime Minister and by
the Members of the Cabinet to reduce
the cost of administration, and at the
same time to reduce the cost of social
services. I myself, so far as I have been
able to study the subject of economics,
do not agree with the postulates of such
a policy. I do not believe that we are
going to solve the problem of unemployment, if it can be solved at all, by any
cheese-paring policy. By saving £20,000
or £30,000 a year we cannot deal with
the subject or even deal with the fringe
of the subject, no matter though our
intentions are of the very best.
I am somewhat concerned, when I reflect upon what this House did last year
with regard to unemployment benefit. I
am somewhat concerned that not merely
did we reduce the unemployment benefit,
the weekly benefit, by 10 per cent., but, as
the Minister himself pointed out to-day,
we also increased the contributions from
the State, from the employer, and from
the employee. In addition to the reduction of 10 per cent., we compelled the
insured population to subject themselves
to what was in reality a far greater reduction. Hitherto they had been allowed
to draw benefit for several years, but we
fixed a limit to the period of time during
which benefit might be drawn, a limit
which, if I remember aright, was six
months, so that it seems to me to some
extent that we are all responsible for
having imposed upon the working population a greater burden than we imposed
upon ourselves. We imposed upon ourselves the burden of a reduction of 15
per cent., which I am glad to say was
carried out pretty well universally and
without exceptions, but we imposed upon
the employed population, the industrialists, a far heavier burden, and I am
sorry now to reflect that in my opinion
that burden was somewhat heavier than
they could be expected to bear. This
burden, which is not estimated by a reduction of 10 per cent., has deprived them
of such material advantages under this
great system of legislation which began in
1911, these National Insurance Acts, that
I should say their total loss amounted at
least to 25 per cent. or 30 per cent.
There are other aspects of the Estimates
to which I should like to refer; in fact,
there are so many that I find the question
of a choice very difficult. The question of
new industries was raised by the right
hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Labour.
I doubt very much whether this policy
of new industries is going materially to
help new industries here in Northern
Ireland. I am afraid that the Government and the House generally or perhaps
the Cabinet-act upon the assumption
that the function of industry is to provide
employment. I have never looked upon
industry as necessitating such a function.
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. McNeill]
In my opinion the purpose of industry is
to produce goods and to render services,
and the purpose of every Sovereign Parliament in the world to-day is to enable
those goods and services to be distributed.
And when I reflect upon the material
wealth of the world in civilised countries,
and it must be remembered that the
world is all one single market--and when
I reflect that there is a superabundance of
raw material, and a superabundance of
manufactured articles, and that there is
an unlimited capacity to produce whatever articles the community needs, I come
to the conclusion that what we want in
Northern Ireland and elsewhere in other
countries, is not new industries, but the
distribution of the goods and services which
have been brought into being by existing
industries.
And even with regard to new industries
I do not think it is a proper policy to
take a country which is primarily agricultural, like Northern Ireland, and which
is situated within easy reach of the world's
greatest industrial markets-I do not
think it is a sound policy, considering the
particular genius of this country, to try
to convert it into an industrial country.
I would be sorry to see cities scattered
about the midst of County Tyrone and
other parts of Northern Ireland. I would
rather see rolling fields of grain and long
drills of potatoes. And I believe that
what we want to-day in Northern Ireland,
if we are to exist as a separate entity, is
to devote our energies very largely to
fostering what is at hand, namely, agriculture.
With regard to industries in agricultural districts I may tell this House that
I have been very favourably impressed by
the existence of smaller industries in certain agricultural districts. I do not know
if hon. Members have ever visited Belleek
or the pottery there. I spent some time
there last summer, and I was immensely
impressed by the potentialities of the
small industry operating there within
That industry has not
narrow limits.
converted Belleek into an industrial city.
It provides employment; it provides
goods and services; and yet the character
of the place remains as it always was.
And I was also impressed with a visit
to West Donegal by such local industries
And when we talk
as that at Ardara.
about fostering industries in Northern
Ireland by giving free sites to persuade
industrialists to come across,
my own
opinion is that small industries are the
only industries which we should seriously
attempt to implant here in Northern
Ireland.
There are not many other points that I
can conveniently raise at the present
time, because we must make certain concessions to time which never loses time,
but I should like whole-heartedly to compliment the Minister and the Department upon one particular branch, and
that is the Juvenile Employment
Department in Alfred Street. And I
should like to ask every hon. Member
here to visit that Department and to see
the work that is being carried on.
As
the Minister has told us, that Department exists for boys and girls-I shall
call them youths-from 16 to 18 years of
age. They undergo during these years,
perhaps, three or four months valuable
training under skilled teachers and in
useful subjects.
When I had the privilege of visiting
this Department I was immensely encouraged to see that the physique of these
students appeared to me to be of a high
standard, and others have also told me,
who have visited this branch, other skilled
observers from England and Wales, that
they admired the physique of the young
people undergoing training. I think
that there we have the germ of what may
prove to be a very useful institution. I
wish we had the means to see its benefits
extended. I wish we had the means to
increase the age limit so that young
people over the age of 19 should be able
to benefit by the services which are
rendered there, because although we cannot provide employment, although those
of us who have studied the problem know
that unemployment is a permanent
feature of modern life, and that perhaps
the State with the greatest amount of
unemployment can be regarded as the
most successful State-although we know
that, yet I believe from the moral point
of view it is our bounden duty to train
the young citizens who are brought up in
our midst, and I am very glad and
gratified to see that the Minister is trying
to the fullest extent competent with his
means to perform that very important
duty.
Those are all the observations I feel
impelled to make at the present time,
but I may say, in conclusion, that I do
not think that a strong case can be made
out by any Member in this House against

The Parliamentary Secretary made a
point about the police protecting some
man who was executing distress
warrant. I recollect reading in the
newspapers where some man was successfully sued before the courts for levying
a
distress he had no right to levy. I
want to know if the police are being used
to protect a man who is doing something
he has no legal right to do. If a man is
legally executing a distress warrant and
has his legal warrant with him, then it is
right to use the police force to carry out
the law; but I understand that in this
particular case the man was violating the
law, that he was acting outside the law,
and that instead of executing distress he
was doing something he had no right to
do, and for which he was successfully
sued in the courts. Am I to understand
that the police are being used to protect

there any instructions given to the

Mr. HANNA rose.
Mr. SPEAKER: The Member for
Larne has already spoken once on the
Adjournment.
Mr. HANNA: By leave of the House
I would like to correct what might be
a very erroneous impression. In the
case the hon. Member (Mr. Nixon) refers
to, the mistake was made in the actual
carrying out of the distress. It is one
of the principles of our law that if a
man abuses an authority or licence given
to him by law he becomes a trespasser
from the very beginning. If a man sets
out to carry out a warrant of distress,
which was a perfectly good warrant, but
in carrying it out he does something that
is irregular, his whole entry is a trespass.
The presence of the police is, as I said,
for the purpose of preventing anything
in the nature of a breach of the peace.
That is their constant duty. They do
not go to help in the carrying out of
distress, but for the protection not only
of those engaged in the carrying out of
the distress but of all other interested
parties. They are not on one side or the
other.
Mr. NIXON: Do they protect a man
in an illegal act?
Mr. HANNA: No. They have no responsibility for any illegality. It must be
understood that a man is entitled to police
protection from others even though he is
engaged in a transaction that is not a
worthy one.

raised by the hon. Member for Mourne

Member for East Down (Lieut.-Colonel
Gordon), the effect of which was to

order is under the Bill required to be

gallant Friend had tabled a Motion with

is not contemplated to alter in any way

My right hon. Friend, the Minister of

Amendment tabled by the hon. and
gallant Member, but undertook to
examine the question in collaboration
with himself, and this discussion has
taken place. As a result of this disand subsequent Departmental

People when they want a house only

First of all, a house is a thing with a
limited term of life. It does not last
for ever. The occupant will find he is
not in the house very long-not a great
number of years-until it begins to show
signs of deterioration, and if the payment for the house is spread over
excessive number of years the purchaser
may find when he has completed his payments that there is no house for him to
possess. The stairs have become shaky,
the slates have blown off the roof and
the floors are untrustworthy. Take, for

being sold. The seller of the house is
unreasonable and makes a provision that
the annuities be paid over a period of
forty years. That is to say, when the
purchase will be completed the housea working-class house-is 90 years old.

economic circumstances, which are no
fault of his, becomes unemployed and has
no income coming into the home he should
be immediately cast out into the street?
If
you fail to accept this Amendment that
is the principle which you stand for. I
think that where a man has become unemployed and the position is created within his home, that he is not able to pay the
rent, after it is thoroughly investigated by
an authority, he should remain under protection until such times as he is in a position to pay the rent, because he is only
the victim of circumstances. But, assuming that you drive that man into
the street by your act,
where do
you drive him to? To the workhouse? What is the cost of a man and
his wife and family in the workhouse
on the rates? Compare that with the
amount that the landlord or agent is going
to forego to the unemployed person.
think the principle is one that the whole
House will agree with.

Mr. POLLOCK: The discussion of the
Money Resolution which was the natural
precedent of this small measure was so
very exhaustive, and I hope illuminating,
that I think to attempt a repetition of
the arguments used pro and con would
only weary the House unnecessarily. The
object of the Measure is to ensure the
continuance of the operation of the Loans
Guarantee Act for another year, to 1933
-as a matter of fact to 31st March, 1933.
It is a one-clause Measure, and is to enable the Ministry of Finance, that is, the
Government, to take advantage of any
opportunity that may arise, subject to
the limitations which are necessarily imposed, to provide work for any industry
that is regarded as suitable, and where
the security is sufficient. I do not think
I need offer any further comments. I beg
to move the Second Reading of this Bill.
Mr. BEATTIE: Could the Minister of
Finance give us any hope that this Bill
will be brought into operation immediately to get some orders for our shipyards? I do not know how far the statement which I am going to make is correct,
but I believe portion of it is correct. I
understand there was an order for the
Belfast shipyards of a class at Lloyds,
but owing to the failure of the Northern
Government to give the covering required, the building of the ships in
Belfast did not take place up to the
present. I said I did not know how far
that was correct, but if there is any
prospect of this Measure being applied
within a month or two weeks, or within
a period of days, I would ask the Minister
to get into touch with these people immediately who desire to be covered by it.
I ask the Government to extend themselves in every direction and to make
every possible move to have a ship or
two for our shipyards.
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not think it is
necessary for the hon. Member to press
the Government in that respect. If I
saw there was any prospect at the moment
that this Measure could be utilised for
the purpose of providing work for the
shipyards, I can assure you nothing would
give me so much pleasure standing at this
Box to-night. But there is no use in
disguising the fact that the outlook is
bad. I am not yet able to assure the
House that there is any prospect at the
moment of any work in consequence for
the shipyards. I regret very much to
make that statement.

Oral Answers to Questions.
"CUTS" IN SALARIES OF P.E.
TEACHERS.
1. Mr. McALEER asked the Minister
of Finance whether he has seen the many
resolutions adopted by county and district meetings of the teachers in public
elementary schools in Northern Ireland
complaining of the "cut" in salaries
which took place last year, and whether
it is the intention of the Government to
give special consideration to the many
strong appeals made for the restoration
of the amount deducted from the salaries
of this very useful body of civil servants.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have seen a number of such
resolutions, but regret that in the present
state of public finance the Government
is unable to reconsider the question of
the reductions made in teachers' salaries
last year. I might add that the position
of teachers is not by any means unique
and that many classes have suffered from
the prevailing economic depression to a
greater extent.

purchase annuities form a most important part of the revenue of the Province,

the Ancient Order of

Sir DAWSON BATES: As it was
apprehended that the band parade in
question would give rise to a breach of
the peace, the responsible organisers were
warned by the police that the parade
could not be permitted to take place.
A dangerous riot was narrowly averted

instance, no such parades have been held
in Caledon for some fourteen years, and

arose.
With regard to the latter part of the

Roman Catholics, but I have no information as to the number of these who are
supporters of the band.

state what is the position in relation to
preserving the amenities of the Antrim
and other coast roads under the Planning
and Housing Act, 1931.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Under the
Planning and Housing Act, 1931, the
county council of any county can formulate a scheme for planning the area under
its jurisdiction or any part of it for the
purpose of preserving amenities. The
council may, at the request of a rural
district council, delegate their
under the Act to the rural district
powers
council concerned.
No schemes have so far been submitted
to the Ministry. This is not surprising
having regard to the short time that the
Act has been in force. Such schemes
require a considerable amount of preliminary consideration and preparation, and,
in view of the financial stringency at
the present time, local authorities have
to be cautious in entering into fresh
liabilities.
Mr. DEVLIN: Did the right hon.
Gentleman not issue a circular from the

Act into operation? The beauties of our

scheme of ugliness seems to destroy the

Sir DAWSON BATES: That may be
so, but my hon. Friend will appreciate
that even a local authority cannot take
away the rights of people without compensation.

offset by provision for the

During the year the Ministry lost the
services, through retirement, of Mr. W.
H. Welply, the senior chief inspector of
schools. Mr. Welply was 36 years in the
public service as inspector of elementary
schools, during the last 15 of which he

Each elementary school pupil in Northern

average rate in England and Wales was

In considering the cost of education it
is interesting to note that, notwithstanding the very considerable improvements
made in our educational system and the
great extension of educational facilities
provided by our local education authorities, the Estimates now presented to
Parliament do not differ much in amount
from those put forward eight or nine
years ago. To-day we are spending from

in 1923-24 our Estimates under the two

£11,000 more than to-day. It is true
that the salaries of our elementary
teachers have been twice reduced in the

at some figures of the substantial progress that has been made.

When the present Ministry took over

20,000 more pupils present in our schools

compulsory attendance an addition of
some 2,000 pupils was caused also by the

The addition of 20,000 pupils to the
daily attendance might have been expected to require about 640 new teachers
to cope with the larger numbers, but
thanks to the policy of amalgamation of
small schools steadily followed by the
Ministry, the teaching strength has
actually been increased by only 258.
This policy was greatly assisted by the
efforts of our local education authorities
in building new central schools, without
which the amalgamation of schools on
any considerable scale would have been
impracticable in a large number of cases.
Besides the amalgamation of boys,
girls' and infants' schools under the same
roof, which was extensively effected by
the Ministry, the most useful form of
amalgamation is the combination of two
or more schools in the same urban centre,
and this has been carried out in many of
the towns as well as in Belfast, and the
In such cases

the need for new premises is imperative,

of school architecture.
Up to the present date 55 new schools
have been built and opened for use by
the Education Committees. Eleven of
these schools, with accommodation for
over 10,000 children, have been erected
in Belfast, and 44 are situated in the
rest of the area of Northern Ireland. In
the nine years, between 1922 and 1931,
the number of separate elementary
schools in Northern Ireland has decreased
by 199, from 2,066 to 1,867, that is to say,
about 260 old schools have been struck off
the roll, and some 60 new schools, allowing
for some under voluntary management,
have come into operation.

While I am referring to this matter,
I might remind the Committee of the
great saving in cost of staffing the schools
which is secured by the policy of eliminating small schools in favour of large ones.
It will be realised that as two schools of
50 pupils each are entitled to employ
four fully qualified teachers, and as a
single school of 100 pupils needs only
three teachers, the building of a new
school which enables an amalgamation of
this kind to be carried out results in the
saving of a teacher's salary, at an
average cost of £317 for a man teacher
and £238 for a woman teacher. This
saving is not always realised immediately
on amalgamation as the existing teachers.
are usually retained as privileged assistants in the amalgamated school, but on
the retirement or resignation of a member
of the staff normal conditions are restored and a saving is effected. As a
rule, redundant members of the staff tend
soon to disappear.
While the effect of amalgamation in
producing economy is greatest in the
smaller schools, substantial savings are
secured in nearly all cases, and it is for
this reason that in the Ministry's opinion
the expense of new buildings, which some
people consider an extravagance in these
days of financial stringency, is really recovered through the saving in salaries,
and, in the long run, proves a really
economical measure. And the advantages
secured in this way to the pupils' health
and educational efficiency are so selfevident that, even were there no saving,
the work would be worth doing for its
own sake. A careful line is drawn by
the Ministry in these matters between
what is essential and what can be done
without, and the pros and cons in each
case are very carefully weighed.

The Committee will observe that the
Estimate for the Training College this
year is £22,265, showing a decrease on
last year's Vote of £2,855, equivalent to
11.4 per cent. Apart from some small
economies in organisation, this decrease is
mainly due to the fact that the numbers
in training are much lower than in
previous years. In the present session
we have a total of 323 students in training; last year we had 357; in 1929-30 we
had 381, and in 1928-29, 398. There are,
therefore, 75 fewer students in training
now than three years ago. There was
reason to believe a year or two ago that
we were training somewhat too many
teachers; a considerable diminution has
been made which I hope will not prove
to have been a mistake, for I would impress upon the Committee that the precise
adjustment of supply to demand in this
matter is not the easy problem that it
may appear to some hon. Members.
May I be allowed to develop this point?
It might be supposed that the Ministry
has sufficient data in its possession over
a long term of years to enable it
accurately to estimate the number of new
teachers required every year. But on
examination of the figures of teachers
leaving the service it is found that these
figures vary considerably from year to
year, and are subject to
are subject to substantial
fluctuations which are not always easy to
explain and are generally very hard to
foresee. Deaths and retirements on pension are accountable for about half the
teachers leaving the service; the number
of deaths is small, from 10 to 15 a year,
but the retirements have been affected by
changes and reductions in the salary
scales, which have been not infrequent in
the last dozen years and which influence
materially the rates of pension. The
increasing of salaries to such a substantial
extent just after the war caused many
teachers to retire prematurely before
serving the full term of years; recent reductions in the scales have had a somewhat
similar effect on teachers wishing to be
pensioned before the lower rates of salary
took effect. These factors have made a just
estimate of the demand for teachers that
might exist three years ahead rather
difficult, but the problem is rendered still
more difficult through uncertainty in the
number of resignations on marriage of
young women teachers, and also through
the fact that many teachers who resign
their positions return later to the service
and form portion of the still available
supply. Then, even supposing that
officers of the Ministry can form, in spite
of these uncertain factors, a fairly
reliable estimate of the number of
teachers leaving the service annually, the
problem of the requirements of the
schools is further complicated by the fact
that school attendance is improving in
most places, which, of course, requires
more teachers, and, on the other hand,
that beneficent process of amalgamation
of schools to which I have already referred diminishes the need for teachers,

purpose which

in the best interests, either of

No person or association of persons
has any right to special representation
in the control of that institution.
Parliament, which is the constitutional
representative of the people, has laid

That was the principle laid down by the

am not. I raise this question in this

education, but also with the religious
future of Northern Ireland. And I
cannot conceive that it is in the interests of Northern Ireland that clergymen, merely as clergymen, should be

three, and by three only. And I say it
is
an extraordinary thing that three
members of the one profession, or of a

Before the clergy were appointed, the

But what is the position to-day? Not
merely do the clergy look after the

Stranmillis College, but they claim to be

clergymen. Now that they are on the

They would have the power to dismiss
teachers. They will have all the powers
proper to a management committee, and
I have looked in vain in the records of
Great Britain and Ireland in connection
with Protestant education for a similar
precedent and I cannot find any.
I have in my hands a Government
pamphlet issued by the Department of
Education in Scotland, and it is very interesting to note that in connection with
Scottish primary education, the national
committee which looks after the training of
teachers is composed entirely of members
from the different education authorities.
throughout the length and breadth of
Scotland. It does not include in its

there on the central executive committee

a single clerical member present on that

I think that this is a very important
question. It is a question of vital importance to education in Northern Ireland. It has caused
a great deal of
misgiving in the minds, not merely lay
minds, but the religious instincts of the
Protestant Ulster people in Northern
Ireland. As I said before, I trust that a
reasonable explanation will be given by
the noble Lord, the Prime Minister, and
that he will explain to this House how it
is that a matter which was a question of
principle in September, in October, in
November, ceases to be a question of
principle six months later.
I do not know whether I should be
justified in prolonging discussion along
those lines. I have made my point. I
have heard no explanation, nor has any
explanation appeared in the Press to
account for this sudden change of front.
I have heard it said, though I do not
credit it, that the Prime Minister simply
wanted to close up the ranks and create
union in Northern Ireland, and that he
imagines that by acting in this way and
going back on a question of principle he
is going to create union. I can hardly
credit such a policy. I should like to
give the noble Lord, the Prime Minister,
credit for being a statesman, but I
cannot conceive of a statesman who
changes a question of principle from day
to day.

Captain CHICHESTER-CLARK: I
should like to congratulate first of all the
Parliamentary Secretary upon his clear
and illuminating statement on the Estimates for his Department. I was frankly
surprised at the speech which has just
been delivered by the hon. and learned
Member for the University, because it
seemed to me we were being led away on
what was purely a question of detail, and
that we were being drawn away from
what we are going to consider to-daythe financial aspects of education. To
put it in legal parlance to suit the hon.
and learned Member, I think he made
what I might call a petty sessions case
into a State trial. I do not want to be
led away along those lines. But I cannot refrain from saying that it was a
great pity when all the agitation was
going on about this vexed question, that
those who felt as he felt did not raise
their voices. They allowed the objective
of the general attack to be bombarded
by all sorts of people without saying one
word in its support. Personally, I am
not ashamed to say here and now that
I think the solution the Prime Minister
has arrived at is an excellent one, and
I always thought it was the simple one.
To return to the question which I
really think concerns the House-the
financial aspect of education-I know
that I am going to do something that
has never been done on this Estimate
before. I am going to criticise it from
the point of view that it is too great
in comparison with the efficiency. I do
so not in any carping spirit, but with the
object of bringing to the fore the real
object of education. Personally, I have
always taken a deep interest in education. I have been on a regional committee ever since they were inaugurated,
when the Education Act first came into
being, and I hold education as being a
most important thing. It will probably
be thrown up against me when I sit down
that I am trying to cut away the money
necessary for education, and that I am
against education and a reactionary.
Nothing of the sort. I want to criticise our expenditure on education because I regard education as a means to
an end, and the end we want to achieve
is the welfare, prosperity, happiness, and
recreation of our young people. But if
we are going to let the means, which is
education, increase
to such
enormous
preponderance in the way of expenditure
Estimates-
Ministry of Education
28 APRIL 1932
that we are going to upset and bankrupt
the ship of State, then I feel we are
doing no service to the young people.
Education surely must be the very best
value we can get for the money, and our
expenditure must surely be in perspective with our means at the present time.
We cannot afford to go on increasing expenditure year after year on particular
services while the nation's revenue is
sinking steadily, with the prospect of
sinking for many years to come.
It is generally thought in this House,
or, at least, that is how I have gauged
the feeling of Members, that as long as
money is spent recklessly education is
being improved. That is not always so.
The most expensive house is not always
the best to live in. The most expensive
stock bull does not always rear the best
calves. The most highly dowered wife
may not be the most suitable. There are
many people who think if you spend
money you get the best results. I have
noticed in this House a feeling that as
long as we are throwing money in all
directions we are doing the right thing,
even if we are bringing the country to
the verge of bankruptcy. Again, this
education is having a tendency, I think,
to lead people into professions to which
they are not suited, into professions
which, in spite of the Parliamentary
Secretary's assurance, are overstaffed and
will continue to be overstaffed. We are
inclined, through this system of education, to attempt to get them away from
the paths they should follow. We can
see the day, and it is not very far distant, when the ploughman may be a good
deal more useful than the professor,
because we must have the ploughing of
land and the hewing of wood and the
drawing of water for all time. We
should let our expenditure on education
be reasonable, efficient, and suitable to
what we can afford, otherwise it is only
a question of a few years before this
country goes down in general bankruptcy.
Now, I cannot help referring to the
Estimate in detail. True, the Estimate
for this year is actually down by the
immense sum of £249 out of £2,000,000,
compared with last year, but the Committee should remember that that reduction is due entirely to the cuts in
wages and reductions in salaries. Obviously, therefore, the Estimates otherwise must have very considerably increased compared with last year.
Yesterday the London County Council
were considering their Estimates for the
coming year, and it is not uninteresting
to notice the reductions they made.
They have made a reduction in their
Estimates for the coming year of
£1,500,000 out of a total of £10,000,000,
a very big proportion, and only half of
this reduction is due to the 10 per cent.
cut in teachers' salaries. These salaries
actually represent two-thirds of the total
expenditure, so we can see that the
London County Council have certainly
shown that efficiency and economy, even
without reducing salaries, can still go
hand in hand. When I remind you that
the London County Council are responsible for the education of one-seventh of
the whole of the children of England and
Ireland you will realise what a wonderful
reduction that is.
Here are we, unfortunately, with what
is practically an increase in our Esti
mates. The Parliamentary Secretary did
refer to the fact that we spent considerably less per head on education. The
only answer I have to that is that the
income per head of the population in this
country is two-and-a-half times smaller
than the income of the people in England.
In order to try to advance my point a
little further, as to the necessity of
changing our policy and reducing our
expenditure on education without reducing
our efficiency, I would like to refer to
one particular instance, and I do this in
no critical or unfriendly spirit.
What I want to refer to is the salary
in fees that is paid to the architect of one
particular county, and the reason I refer
to the architect is because it is on the
question of his fees that you can obviously
arrive at the size of the general increase
year by year of the building programme
of any particular county. A question I
put down recently elicited the fact that
the architect employed by the County
Down Educational Authority, who is
only a part-time officer-I am not questioning whether he is paid too much or
too little, because that is the business of
the County Down Educational Authority
-but in 1929 he received in fees £1,162.
In the year 1930 he received £2,250,
practically double, and in the year 1931
he received the very large sum of £3,104.
If you work out the fees on a 5 per cent.
basis you can see the rate at which the
County of Down is increasing her building programme, and is saddling herself
with overhead charges from year to year.

Mr. NIXON: Two speeches have been
made in reply to the Parliamentary
Secretary, one by the hon. and learned
Member who sits beside me (Mr. McNeill),
and the other by the hon. and gallant
Member who has just sat down (Captain
Chichester-Clark). I do not know which
of the two I will attack first.
What
seems to be troubling the hon. and gallant
Member for South Derry is that the
people will all get educated and, in his
own words, there will be no ploughmen,
no hewers of wood, and no drawers of
water. There will be no line between
the people of so-called aristocratic birth
and the common people. There will be
no common people to lift their hats to
your honour when he is going along the
road, because education wipes out all that
and it puts the snob and the nob and the
ordinary person on one footing. That is
what seems to be troubling the hon. and
gallant Member. Long may education
continue, and long may the ordinary
people be educated, because when they
are educated they do not recognise any
difference, and the reason they do not
recognise any difference is because there
is no difference. The sooner this snobbery
is wiped out of this little part of the
British Empire the better for all, including the snobs. I know myself that it is
regarded as an impertinence for anyone
to appear in this House other than
imaginary aristocrats and hired retainers.
But the democratic people have willed it
otherwise, and that is why I am here.
On the whole, I can congratulate the
Ministry of Education so far as the
Ministry itself is concerned. The officers
of the Ministry, the inspectors of the
Ministry, and the teachers employed by
the Ministry do their duty faithfully
and well by the rising generation of
Northern Ireland, notwithstanding the
discouragement the teachers got a year
ago when their salaries were reduced,
not with their consent, as was stated at
the time, but against their will. With
regard to Stranmillis Training College,
I entirely disagree with the speech of
the hon. and learned Member who sits
beside me (Mr. McNeill). It is quite true
that the Prime Minister, as usual, showed
a bold front in what he was going to do,
but I knew at that very time, as well as
I know now, that he would surrender,
because I knew he would have to surrender, and rightly so. There is no use
in talking about non-sectarian education
in Northern Ireland, because it does not
exist. The Roman Catholic Church do
not surrender their schools. They retain
sectarian education, and their teachers
must satisfy the Roman Catholic Bishops
on the question of religion. That being
so, I see no reason why the representatives
of the Protestant Churches should not
insist on having the same privilege so far
as they are concerned.
They have insisted on it, and I am very glad to hear
that they got what they insisted on
getting. If they have not fully got it
the time is coming when they will. There
is no question at all about that, one way
or the other.
There was no use in the Prime Minister
and the Minister of Education shouting
last July, and August, and September
about what they would do on this sub
ject, because they had to surrender,
and they did surrender, not by any means
for the first time. I cannot understand
the attitude of the Prime Minister and
the Government on this question of religion and religious teaching in the
schools. You would imagine that the
Estimates-

object of this Government from the time
it was set up had been to subvert the
Protestant religion in Northern Ireland.
That they have not been allowed to do
and will not be allowed to do, and I hope
the Government will take a lesson from
what has happened and will not put
themselves in the position of being compelled to surrender yet another time.
One is never sure of what they will do,

and immediately after it was supposed to

Now I may pass from that and make

Rev. Professor CORKEY: I would
like, first of all, to congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary on the interesting
statement he has given us. I always
enjoy the statements made by the Parliamentary Secretary on this subject. They
are always lucid, and they are always
concise and informative. To begin, I
would like to say that all legislation is
experimental. Every law is an experiment and has to be tried out in actual
experience. The politician or the statesman legislates not blindly, but in the
light of all the facts which are at his
command, and he may find that in spite
of all his wisdom the law which he designed was not at first perfect. Even
the 1920 Act, the Act by which we
operate here, was found not to be perfect and has been modified once or twice
to bring it into conformity with the circumstances which have developed since
1920.
The chief critics of the educational
policy of the Northern Government seem
to forget that, and they seem to imagine
that in regard to education the Government should have been able to establish
a Utopia which would have been perfect
from the first and which would not have
demanded the slightest modification from
then until now. But that is not how
laws are framed. That is not how satisfactory educational systems are developed. I have great confidence and
belief in the educational system which
has been developed during the last ten
or twelve years in Northern Ireland. I
think it suits Northern Ireland, and is
about as wise a system as any man could
devise for the education of the people
here. It has been modified from time
to time, but it has been modified in the
light of facts which have emerged in the
actual working of the system, and it
seems to me, therefore, that there is very
little point in complaining of slight
changes of policy and of the alteration of
the system in detail.

attraction of other and more popular
things in the evenings that has led to less
concentration or less willingness on the
part of the pupils to attend these evening
schools, but the fact remains that the
Ministry does make grants to evening
schools. That the amount of the grants
is diminishing the Minister regrets.
With regard to what the Member for
Derry said, touching the general expenditure, might I point out to him that
out of the total amount expended,
£1,900,000, almost £1,663,000 goes in
payments to teachers, and I think he
would be a bold man who at the present
moment would suggest that now another
cut should be made in the emoluments of
teachers. That seems to be the only
direction in which possibly the Education
Estimates can be reduced in any way
worth doing.
As to the fees that were paid to the
architect in County Down, may I say that,
so far as the Ministry is concerned, no part
of that expenditure comes upon this Vote,
and our Vote has not been increased,
even if County Down has been extravagant in the payment of fees to the
architect, because for some time we have
been paying County Down the limit of
the eightpenny rate. But I might point
out to the hon. Member and to the Committee that these fees did not
cover
simply and solely the personal remuneration of the architect. These fees covered
the amounts he had to pay for draughtsmen and others whom he has had to
employ. The whole of that money does
not go into his own pocket, and it is
rather accident that in this particular area these fees amount to such a
large sum.

Captain CHICHESTER-CLARK:
just want to say, I tried to make it

Mr. ROBB: I see the hon. Member's

This is non-recurring expenditure. It is

programme of building. It started that

it is non-recurring expenditure. We are
not going next year to erect another
school at Newtownards costing £15,000,
and another one costing £30,000 or
£40,000 at Bangor. Those schools that
have recently been built in those towns
are going to last for a hundred or two
hundred years.
Their cost will be spread
over whatever period the loan was granted
for.
I think the hon. and gallant Member
is looking at this question from a wrong
point of view. I would like to ask him
if he has gone about the country and
examined the hovels in which the children
were taught. Does he not think that
almost any expenditure and any sacrifice would be worth while if it improved
those wretched hovels? The new schools
that have been erected and those that
have been renovated ensure that for the
next two generations at any rate our
children will be educated in well designed, sunny, and well ventilated
buildings, and in cheery, healthy, and
stimulating surroundings, instead of in
the wretched hovels that were formerly
such a great blot on our educational
system in the North of Ireland.
When I first took up the position
which I now have the honour to hold
I was, of course, interested in education
generally, but I did not know much
about the buildings in which our children
were being educated, except a few in
Belfast. I have taken it as part of my
duties to investigate, as far as the opportunities presented themselves, the state
not only of the curriculum, but especially
of the school buildings. I started with
a sort of luke-warm enthusiasm for the
provision of better buildings, and if
Ministry of Education
Adjournment
28 APRIL 1932
there is one thing that will give me more
satisfaction than anything else when I
come to vacate my present office it will
be that during my connection with the
Ministry the buildings in which our
children are being educated have been
revolutionised. They are being revolutionised, and no better work could any
man put his hand to.
Both the Member for Central (Mr.
Devlin) and the Member for South Fermanagh (Mr. Healy) have said that in
their view the system of education that
was inaugurated by the 1923 Act has
failed. In the most emphatic manner I
challenge any such statement.
The Act
was passed in 1923, and it came into
operation only in 1925. That is seven
years ago. We have had only seven years
in which to set up local education authorities and get them started on their work.
Already in those seven years one-third of
the total pupils in elementary schools in
Northern Ireland are working in schools,
either provided or transferred, controlled by the Education Committees.
think that is a very good result for the
time we have been at work. We hope
that this result, which we regard only as
a beginning, will mean the dawn of a
new era not only for the pupils I have
referred to but for all the pupils in
Northern Ireland.

Mr. ANDREWS: During the three
years ended 31st March, 1932, 713 persons ceased to draw blind persons'
pensions for the following reasons:
295 pensioners died or left Northern

as to blindness, and there were 71
cessations for miscellaneous reasons.
I regret that exact figures are not
available for earlier years.

are very capable and, further, their

CLASS III, No. 1.
MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £39,149 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1933, to
defray the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Home Affairs (15 & 16 Geo.
V., c. 3., s. 4 (N.I.); 16 & 17 Geo. V.,
c. 31 (N.I.), etc.)."-(Note-£13,000
has been voted on account).
Sir DAWSON BATES: In presenting
to the Committee the Estimates of the
Ministry of Home Affairs, I am glad to
be in a position to refer to the fact that
we have been able to effect substantial
reductions in the various services for
which the Ministry is responsible, the
total of the reductions being £21,146. It
is a fact, of course, that on the contrary
we have an increase of £22,658 in connection with our grants to local authorities, the net result being that while we
are increasing our grants to local authorities, we have reduced the cost of our own
administration by substantial amounts.
As regards the Estimate for the Department of the Ministry of Home Affairs,
it will be observed that the decrease is
£940, which is due to the fact that we
have been able to effect a substantial reduction in the number of our staff. It
will be observed on page 52 that, for the
current financial year, the total number
of staff attached to the Ministry is 140,
as against 150 for the year 1931-32, but
it should be explained that this gross
reduction of 10 includes 3 officials who
were formerly attached to the Ministry
when it was located at Ocean Buildings
but who are now transferred to the
general pool, the result being that we
have a net reduction of 7 officials.
The fact that it has been possible to
effect this substantial reduction in
numbers and consequent expenditure, in
Ministry of Home Affairs 1124
Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
spite of the increasing responsibilities
and duties imposed upon the Ministry by
new legislation, will, I feel sure, demonstrate to the Committee that every care
is being taken to reduce the work of the
Department as far as possible, consistent
with efficiency.
on
Turning to the general work of administration, I have pointed out
several occasions of a similar character
that our work generally falls under two
heads Home Office Administration and
Local Government Administration. Home
Office Administration is a wide comprehensive term, involving police, prisons,
law and order, asylum administration, as
well as a multitude of other minor but
still important services, such as Wild
Bird Protection, Reformatory, Industrial
and Borstal Schools, the Pharmacy Acts,
Explosives, the Petroleum Acts, and so
forth.
All these services-in fact, one might
say the main activities of the Home Office
division of the Ministry of Home Affairs
resolve themselves into a consideration of
the question of law and order, and in
this connection I am glad to be able to
say that in Northern Ireland there is
much reason for satisfaction in connection
with the prevalence of crime, although
there has been a slight increase in the
number of cases specially reported by
the police, yet these are mainly attributable to what one might regard as less
serious crimes, such as petty larcencies,
etc.
The Judges of Assize, on their visits
to the various counties as well as in the
City of Belfast, have been able to report
that a normal state of affairs has existed
during the past year and that, from the
calendars that came before them, they
had no cause for anxiety. In fact, the
presiding judge at the opening of the
Down Summer Assizes stated that "
unusual and unprecedented state of peacefulness" existed, and at the Spring
Assizes at Derry the judge made special
reference to the decrease which he
noticed in charges arising out of drunkenness.
an
Another important aspect of administration in connection with crime during
the year is the fact that the percentage
of persons made amenable for crimes
committed during the year was 68.7.
This is the highest percentage reached
during the past five years, and reflects
the utmost credit on the Royal Ulster
Constabulary who have continued to
carry out their duties in a thoroughly
efficient and
and satisfactory manner, in
spite of the fact that, on the grounds of
economy, the strength of the Force is
being steadily reduced.
I will now turn to the question of
drunkenness, which I have already referred to, and I submit that the judges'
remarks are fully borne out by the
following figures, which show clearly that
the lurid pictures which from time to
time are given by certain enthusiasts in
the cause of temperance have no real
foundation in fact. The number of convictions for drunkenness in Belfast has
decreased from 2,326 in 1927 to 1,642 in
1931, which is a reduction of as much as
33 per cent. The number for Northern
Ireland, excluding Belfast, has decreased
from 2,423 in 1927 to 1,984 in 1931.
It
During the year 1931, 2,356 prisoners
were committed to prison, as against
2,283 in 1930, and 2,661 in 1927.
will thus be seen that the numbers, while
slightly more than last year, are considerably less than the numbers five years ago.
At the same time, although the numbers
committed last year were slightly more
than the year 1930, there were a greater
number of short-term cases, the result
being that the average number of
prisoners in custody for the whole of the
year 1931 was only 307, as against 336 in
the previous year. These figures in themselves speak volumes for the improved
conditions in Northern Ireland, and show
clearly that, while troubled and unsettled
conditions may prevail elsewhere, the
people of Northern Ireland are becoming
on the whole more law-abiding.
While I am dealing with the question
of our prison population, I think it well
to state that the expenses of maintaining
our prisons is being kept down as low as
possible. Our cost per head for the year
1930 was £67 7s Od as compared with
£63 7s Od for 1929, and £67 16s Od for
1928. These costs are, as I have explained on a previous occasion, somewhat
in excess of the comparative English
figures, i.e., £53 19s Od for 1928;
£50 8s Od for 1929; and £49 2s Od for
1930, but it would be unfair to our prison
administration to attempt to draw hasty
conclusions from a comparison between
these figures, having regard to the exceptional conditions under which the
administration is carried on in Northern
Ireland. It is an established principle
Estimates-
Ministry of Home Affairs
3 MAY 1932
in prisons administration, as well as in
the administration of other institutions,
that the per capita cost tends to decrease
as the numbers increase, or, in other
words, the cost is lowest in the case of
large institutions.
As the Committee is aware, fortunately
the numbers in our various prisons are
comparatively low, and, accordingly, in
the interests of efficient supervision we
are compelled to maintain a staff which
would be capable of dealing with considerably larger numbers. In addition
to that we are not able, as in Great
Britain, with our limited resources to
maintain a series of institutions of a
specialised character for the various
classes of prisoners. In point of fact, on
the contrary we are compelled in Belfast
Prison to cope with several different classes, each of which class requires separate treatment and consideration. In other words, we are endeavouring in Belfast Prison to carry on work
which in Great Britain would be dealt
with in many different institutions, such
as first offenders, prisoners on remand,
short-term prisoners, old offenders, convicts, who are divided into different
categories. While we cannot go to the
same extent in the way of segregation in
different institutions, we endeavour to
put into effect, so far as is possible, this
very desirable and indeed necessary principle, and we must therefore maintain at
Belfast Prison a larger staff than if the
institution were used for one class only.
The same principle applies also in the
case of the Londonderry Prison, which, as
the Committee is aware, is used not only
as a prison for short-term prisoners committed from the north-west areas, but
also as a criminal lunatic asylum.
In
I have taken a special interest in our
prison administration, and I am satisfied
that our prisons are being run efficiently
and economically, and I am glad to have
this opportunity of expressing my appreciation of the manner in which the prison
staffs, from the governors downwards,
have carried on their onerous, monotonous
and sometimes unpleasant duties.
other countries the Governments have
been able to provide buildings of modern
type in proper surroundings, with suitable appliances and conveniences for the
different classes of inmates with which
they have to deal, and under these circumstances I feel that we have reason to
be satisfied that we are making the best
use of our facilities.
The years that have gone by have been
full of difficulties in connection with
prison administration, not only in Northern Ireland but in other countries, and,
on the whole, great credit is due to
our prison staff, and, if I may be invidious
for a moment, I would like to refer to
Major Long, of Belfast Prison, who has
had during his administration a very
anxious and difficult task, which I regret
to say has seriously impaired his health
and caused him and us very considerable
concern.
The various prison industries continue
to be maintained, and some months ago
we were able to make arrangements under
which prisoners were afforded a longer
period of exercise away from their cells
than had been possible previously. The
new workshops, to which I have already
referred, are giving complete satisfaction,
and the industries are now being carried
out under the healthiest possible conditions, under light and airy circumstances.

cannot speak too highly of the continued

The Discharged Prisoners' Aid Societies.

which I have made regarding the staff
of our prison service apply equally, if

Criminal Lunatic Asylum is now 7, and
I am glad to find from the reports of the

I will now turn to our Borstal Institution, which is associated with the
Reformatory School at the Malone Training School. The committals to the
Borstal Institution still continue to show
an increase, as may be seen from the
following figures in respect of the last
five years:

The number of inmates at present
under detention is 71, as compared with
30 a few years ago.
This increase may,
perhaps, seem alarming and may indicate
an increase in juvenile crime, but it
would be wrong to arrive at any such conclusion. The real meaning of the increase is that the courts are taking greater
advantage of a system of disclipinary and
technical training which the Borstal
Institution provides, and while we have
not had, perhaps, sufficient experience of
the system in Northern Ireland to enable
us to judge accurately the value of this
principle, yet from our limited experience.
we are satisfied that the principle is a
sound one and tends on the whole to make
better citizens of the boys who have completed their period of training than the
old system of sending them to prison,
which tended on the contrary to make
criminals of them.
I have been afforded opportunities
from time to time of coming into personal contact with the boys, and I have
followed their after-history with the
utmost care. I am glad to be able to
state that a substantial number of them
have justified the training and discipline
which they have received at our training
school, and that only a small proportion-about 30 per cent.-have come
unfavourably under the notice of the
police since their return to ordinary civil
life. Even in these few cases the offences
were, for the most part, of a trivial
nature and did not indicate a return to
criminal habits or tendencies. The expenses of running the Borstal Institution
have been controlled with the greatest
care, and the figures for 1930 show a
very substantial reduction over those for
1929, the cost per head for 1930 being
£52 9s 6d, as compared with £66 8s Od
for 1929. In England the comparative
figures were £65 14s Od and £68 8s Od.
The educational and moral welfare of
the boys continues to be looked after
satisfactorily, and, in addition to the
teaching afforded by the staff, we have
a considerable number of voluntary
teachers and lecturers who go to the
school in their spare time and interest and
instruct the boys on all manner of
subjects, from boxing to architecture. I
am sure I am expressing the view of this
Committee when I say that the Government and the whole community are indebted to these ladies and gentlemen, and
also to the ladies and gentlemen who
have, at their own expense, provided
entertainments and excursions. The
kindly human touch which is brought
into the lives of the boys by these ladies
and gentlemen cannot but have the
utmost effect on the boys' minds. Finally,
I must refer to the work of the Visiting
Committee of this school. It is largely
owing to their efforts and the efforts of
their welfare officer that employment is
found for the boys on discharge, and I
must once again publicly extend my
heartiest thanks to all the members of
the committee for their interest, not only
in the boys while at the school, but also
on leaving.
Although the Reformatory boys at
Malone Training School are kept entirely
separated from the Borstal boys, the remarks I have made about the staff and
the activities of the school apply equally
to the Reformatory side of the school,
and the Chief Inspector of Reformatory
and Industrial Schools has been able to
give a satisfactory report of the work
done in the Reformatory side of the
school during the past year.

Having dealt with the subject of law
and order, it is impossible not to make
a reference to our police forces, including
the regular Royal Ulster Constabulary as
well as the Special Constabulary, and I
think the community has reason to be
satisfied with, if not proud of, these
forces, the perfect discipline which has
been maintained, and the active steps
which have been taken in connection with
the prevention and detection of crime.
Mr. CONNELLAN: Does the right
hon. Gentleman say that the police force,
the R.U.C. and the Specials, are to be

enacted at Ballinderry?
The CHAIRMAN: I think interrogatories at this stage are not very desirable.
The Minister is stating the policy of his
Department in a considered speech, and
it would conduce to more orderly debate
if criticism was deferred to a more appropriate stage.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The ordinary
man in the street, if he thinks
of crime at all, thinks of it only
in relation to the detection of crime, and
few people pay proper attention to what
is, in our minds, more important—that is,
the prevention of crime.
I think I have already satisfied the
Committee that, according to our statistics of crime and convictions compiled for
the last few years, we are becoming a
more law-abiding people. That satisfactory process is due to several causes-it
is perhaps inherent to ourselves—it is
perhaps due to the moral training which
we received from the churches and from
our fathers and mothers, but I think it
is only fair to say also that it is largely
due to the watchfulness of our police
forces, and also, perhaps, to the fact that
there is a closer understanding in Northern Ireland to-day between the community as a whole and the police than
one could have ever contemplated under
the old regime. This is a most gratifying
feature of our social order, and in itself
it is due to several causes.
In the first place, our regular police
force is drawn from our own people; it
is composed of men who understand our
people, who have sympathy with our
The
people, and who know our people.
old antagonism between the police and
people has gone, and now, as I have already said, there is understanding. This
understanding has introduced a new and
satisfactory element into our life. The
people now assist the police, whereas the
contrary principle was more noticeable in
the old days.
To a large extent the constitution of
the Special Constabulary has contributed
to these happy relations between the
police and the people. So many of our
citizens have been associated with the
Special Constabulary that it is felt a
point of honour in their civil capacities.
to assist the police in maintaining law
and order.
As was explained in this House during
the course of our debates on economy last
year, recruiting for the Regular Constabulary has been suspended and will continue to be suspended for some time yet,
until we have effected a substantial reduction in the strength of the force as a
whole. We have also suspended our
general barrack reconstruction scheme,
and are confining ourselves at present to
reconstruction of a few cases where the
existing circumstances call for immediate
amelioration.
While we are, in the essential interests
of economy, effecting a reduction in the
strength of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, I am satisfied that we are not impairing the efficiency of the force, and the
Committee may rest assured that no steps
will be taken which will in any way
prejudice the maintenance of law and
order.

We have for several years
enjoyed immunity against outrage of
a serious nature, and, while it
is a regrettable fact that there
have been one or two isolated cases
which have caused us great concern, I
think it will be admitted that comparing
Northern Ireland with other countries we
have suffered considerably less from armed
raids and other outrages of a similar
nature.
Turning to the Local Government Department of the Ministry, I think that,
generally speaking, the administration of
local government affairs in Northern
Ireland during the past year has been
satisfactory. Considerable attention has
been directed towards the formulation of
proposals for local government reform.
As the Committee is aware, the first step
in this direction has been taken by the
introduction of the Bill dealing with the
reform of the Lunacy Laws, and, following that step, the Ministry prepared and
circulated to the various local authorities
in Northern Ireland, and to their organisation, a Memorandum setting forth the
proposals which the Government had in
mind in connection with the reform of
other local government services, including
poor relief, medical relief, hospitals,
public health, and general local government services.
In the formulation of these proposals
every possible care and attention was
directed towards the imperative necessity
of endeavouring to work out a scheme
which would not impose any further
additional financial burden on the rates
or on the Exchequer, but, in spite of that
fact, we find that most of the local
authorities in Northern Ireland, as well
as their organisations, apprehend that
additional burdens will be cast upon them
in the event of comprehensive changes in
the structure and machinery of local government.
The representations and views submitted by the associations and by the
individual local authorities are at present
under consideration by the Government.
with the object of arriving at a decision
as to whether, under the circumstances,
it would not be expedient to defer, for
the present at any rate, introducing legislation involving comprehensive changes in
our local government services.
It will be appreciated by the Committee.
that if there was a growing need for reform in any particular direction, the
Government would be entirely justified,
even against the wishes and expressed
views of the local authorities, to proceed
with the new legislation, but on the whole
the system which is in operation to-day
is one that has become firmly established
and understood, and while possibly in
certain directions and in certain points of
detail, it may be necessary to effect
changes, on the whole there are sound
reasons for deferring until a more favourable opportunity the breaking up of what
has been, after all, a good system, with
the object of introducing a new and untried system which would not, at the
present moment at any rate, commend
itself to the local authorities.
Even if we have to defer the introduction of the legislation, we can at the
same time, under the existing laws and
by administrative methods, effect considerable improvements in the system.
These improvements have been going on
quietly, slowly, and steadily for several
years past in connection with our hospital
system. Several of our old antiquated
workhouse infirmaries have been converted into new and up-to-date district
hospitals, and there are further proposals
before us at the moment.
These proposals are being carefully
considered in the light of the existing
conditions and of the needs of the inhabitants, but I would like to point out
that in the consideration of these proposals we are keeping steadfastly in our
minds the future requirements and the
necessity for conforming with a wellbalanced and logical system of hospitals
in each county.
Only a few days ago the Newtownards
Board of Guardians were in a position to
open their new district hospital, and I
must congratulate that Board on the
vision and courage with which they faced
up to this problem, and with the excellent results that they have obtained.
A hospital is now provided for the inhabitants of the Newtownards Union
which will rank as one of the best hospitals
in Ulster, and I would particularly like
to refer to the care and attention which
the Board of Guardians gave to the
subject of securing a proper medical and
nursing staff.
The Banbridge Board of Guardians
have also, with our approval and encouragement, converted their old workhouse into a district hospital of excellent

design and properly fitted up and
equipped to deal with the needs of their
Union. As I have already said, there
are other proposals under consideration
at the moment, and pending a solution of

Perhaps the most important aspect of
local government administration is that
relating to roads and road traffic. The
Committee is aware that for the last few
years we have by financial assistance been
steadfastly encouraging the road authorities in Northern Ireland to face up to the
problem of improving the road systems
in their various areas.
As the Committee is aware, our road
systems were in a most unsatisfactory
condition following the war and it became necessary to spend large sums of
money on making up the various classes
of roads to that standard which is
warranted by the traffic passing over
them. I am glad to be able to say that,
with the hearty co-operation of the local
authorities and with the substantial
grants which we decided to accord to
them, our road systems now compare
favourably with those in other countries
of similar character.
Our difficulties were not made any
easier by reason of the fact that the
number of motor vehicles in the Province
continued to increase year by year at
such a substantial rate-in fact, we
found that it was difficult for us to keep
pace with the increase in motor traffic,
but from the reports which I have
received I am inclined to think that we
have now reached a point at which the
work we have done in the past will enable
us to keep abreast of the traffic in so far
as the maintenance and improvement of
our roads services are concerned.
Owing, as I have said, to the poor condition of the roads and the necessity for
meeting the situation at once, at all
costs, we found it necessary during the
last few years to encroach heavily upon
the resources of the Road Fund in order
to accord to the road authorities the
utmost financial assistance possible. I
would remind the Committee that we continue to contribute 60 per cent. in respect
of first-class roads, 30 per cent. on secondclass roads, and 15 per cent. on thirdclass roads, which are used for motor
traffic.
As a slight index of the expense of
road reconstruction work in Northern
Ireland, in connection with which we have
in the past been giving grants of 72 per
cent. on Class I. roads, I would like to
point out that this special reconstruction
work has cost no less than £1,063,000.
On the other hand, it has enabled us to
provide on the more important roads in
Northern Ireland 100 miles of new
foundation, 70 miles of reinforced concrete
roads, and 22 miles of asphalt macadam
surfaces. The result is, as the Committee
will appreciate, not only better roads but
lower future maintenance costs.
Apart from the improvement and reconstruction of our road systems, considerable attention has been devoted to
the cutting of hedges and the roundingoff of corners and the improvement
generally of vision at such corners.
In addition to these measures which
have been taken with the object of improving traffic conditions and of lessening
the risk of accidents, a forward step has
been taken, particularly in Belfast, in
connection with the establishment of
automatic road signals. The Belfast Corporation have cordially co-operated with
the Ministry in the establishment of these
signals, and have received grants from
the Road Fund amounting to 50 per cent.
of the cost of setting up and of maintenance.
I saw it stated in one of the papers
this morning that no saving has been
effected by this system as regards the
utilisation of pointsmen. I think that is
wrong. I have had the figures taken out,
and they may be of interest to the Committee. I find that, to provide for
interest and sinking fund, cost of operation, maintenance, and general supervision involves an annual sum of £134.
As against that, to work a point where
you place an automatic signal would
require the equivalent of the services of
one and a half policemen per day, which
would work out at a cost of £480 per
annum, which means that there is a
saving of £346 per annum at every point.
But, apart altogether from the economical
side of it, I think it will be admitted
that these signals have proved a great
boon and blessing and that their development not only in Belfast but in other
centres is strongly called for.

on the question of accidents. While the
number of accidents reported for the

Another very important feature in connection with road traffic administration
is the fact that so few accidents occur
in which drivers of omnibuses and motor
coaches are concerned, and when we take
into consideration the fact that these
vehicles are constantly on the road I think
that this circumstance constitutes a strong
tribute to the care and skill of the drivers
of these vehicles. I could only wish that
the drivers of ordinary private vehicles
would show the same skill, care and
courtesy which is displayed from day to
day by the drivers of these public service vehicles. Out of a total of over
1,500 accidents only 32 were caused by
motor omnibuses and motor coaches.
The use of the double-decked motor
omnibus has proved very popular in Northern Ireland, and it is prehaps unfortunate that we have not found it possible,
up to the present at any rate, to extend

traffic, as well as the effect that they have
on the road surfaces.
