Mr. HEALY: Although we may have
to complain of a good deal in these Estimates, in other respects I do not think
anyone in this Committee will cavil at
the minuteness with which the Minister
has gone into the details of his Department. He has made the most of the
matter placed at his disposal. He has
taken an hour and ten minutes
practically to deal with the activities of
the Department of Home Affairs, and I
am afraid that we shall be in the position,
in which we sometimes find ourselves in
this Committee, that when we have
spoken, which we do at no great length,
there will be no opportunity for the
Minister to reply to the various criticisms
that will be offered from this side of the
Committee.
The Minister has discovered, not I think
for the first time, that the Ulster people
are law-abiding. That is a discovery that
even the Opposition made a good while
ago, so that I think the Minister is just
a little belated. It is rather curious that
the Minister records a steady decrease in
crime just in direct ratio to the decrease
in the Royal Ulster Constabulary and the
practical elimination of the Specials.
We have always been told that the existence of the Specials was our assurance
of the security of the people of the Six
Counties. But they have disappeared for
all practical purposes from the Estimates
-that is, excepting the officers-and, notwithstanding that, the peace of the Six
Counties not only remains unimpaired,
but continues to improve day after day.
Therefore, it will be of the greatest interest for hon. Members of this Committee
to turn back to the speeches of the
Minister of Home Affairs in introducing
his Estimate for former years and compare them with his speech to-day.
But I find that, notwithstanding the
Minister's congratulations, he has still on
his pay roll 2,846 persons at headquarters
costing the country about £635,000.
That is a fairly large figure for a comparatively small area such as the Six-
Counties. I do not think if there were
a referendum of the people taken they
would stand for anything like a charge of
that kind. I do not think they can afford
it, and I do not think it is necessary.
Therefore, the first thing to which the
Minister should devote his attention is the
reduction of those figures at the earliest
possible moment.
We are as much interested in the preservation of peace in the Six Counties as
any Member of the Government can be,
because in the past when there has been
any departure from that peace we have
been the people who have suffered, and
I have no doubt that if there should be
any similar happening in the future we
would be in exactly the same position.
But we have a right to call the attention
of the Committee to what I think the
Minister has rather carefully skimmed
over, namely, the administration of law
and order in the Six Counties. I would
like to direct the Minister's attention to
two particular incidents in this connection.
The first is that which occurred at a place
called Annahugh in County Armagh
some years ago, and which was repeated
on subsequent occasions down to last
year, namely, the destruction of a hall by
armed men in a district where the population are all of the political faith of the
Minister, and where one-half of the ablebodied men of from twenty-one to sixty
years of age are in the Special Constabulary and, therefore, presumed to
have arms. In that district an outrage
which meant the demolition of a public
building on no fewer than three successive
occasions took place, and on each occasion
the ratepayers had to pay.
If the police force had been half so
efficient as the Minister has indicated he
would have had no difficulty in putting
his finger on the guilty person or persons,
because there was a whole set of circumstances in connection with the affair
which pointed clearly to the probable
source. I need not weary the Committee
by going over the details. They were
pretty familiar a short while ago, but
one notable fact was that the people who
came to destroy this hall knew the local
surroundings and also knew fairly well.
whether they were likely to meet with any
opposition. It was noticed, too, I think,
by some people whose information was at
the disposal of the Ministry, that on the
night of the outrage lights were seen in
some local halls at an unusually late hour.
The Parliamentary Secretary at the
time told us that no efforts would be
spared to bring the guilty people to
justice; in fact, he almost indicated that
if we kept silent and did not do anything
to upset the equilibrium of the specialists
of the Home Office, who were investigating the matter, we would have the
culprits by the leg in a day or two. And
so we have kept silent all these months-
I might say all these years but the
people who perpetrated these outrages are

The Minister referred to reformatories, and anything I say about that
matter is not to be taken as a criticism
of the Ministry, because it is not so intended. The Ministry, I believe, are
carrying on the reformatories to the best
of their ability, but there is a misconception about these institutions. I have
given this matter very close attention;
and what I say is that no person on a first
appearance before a court should be sent
to a reformatory unless he has no proper
guardians to look after him. Under such
circumstances there is nothing else to do
but send the boy to the reformatory.
The reason I say that is this—and this is
no reflection on the managers of reformatories or the Ministry I hardly
ever knew a habitual criminal who did
not graduate in a reformatory. Suppose
a boy is sent to a reformatory for three
years, and after leaving it goes to look
for a position, the very fact that he had
been in a reformatory would nail his
chances on the spot. There is nothing
else then for him to do but commit again
the offence which put him into the reformatory first of all.
I want to make myself clear before
leave that point. I knew a case recently
where two boys who had never been before
the Court before were sent to a reformatory. The Ministry released them,
and they did one of the best day's work
they ever did since they took up office in
Northern Ireland, because these boys have
gone back to homes where they will be
looked after and brought up properly.
If they had been kept in the reformatory

nothing before them.

There is another class of person I would

I think there should be some information given to the Committee on the

I cannot see but that the base rate will

agreed upon as being fair and reasonable between the companies operating

£2,222,000 to the Ministry of Home
Affairs I can assure the Committee that
the two millions are of very little concern
to the constituents I represent to-day.
The town of Newry is in a state of consternation owing to the new tariffs put
on on the other side of the Border. They
will close some of our mills. But I want
to call the attention of the Committee to
a matter referred to by the hon. Member
for Central (Mr. Devlin), namely, law
and justice. As the hon. Member for
Central said, it is for one side of the
community. I want to make a definite
and serious charge against the Minister
of Home Affairs in the following circumstances:
There is a family residing in my
district whose friendship I am proud to
have. This is a family named Murney.
One member is a minister in our church.
Another is a professor in the Christian
Brothers' School at Dundalk. He is a
man who loves his country. He was a
follower of the man who died on this day,
and whose anniversary we celebrate,
Padraig Pearse. When this Government
was set up and things settled down it was
found that he could not get a position.
inside the Six Counties, so he went to the
Free State and took up a position as a
professor in Dundalk.
He is an Irishman who loves his home.
He has a beloved mother living below
Ballyedmond Castle, Killowen. That
mother he goes to see every week-end.
On Friday last he arrived at Newry by
bus. He got into the Kilkeel bus to
bring him to his home in Killowen, and
when he arrived at the village of
Rostrevor he was pulled from the bus by
the police. He was brought down to the

of Police and all others in authority,

You do not interfere with Orange
demonstrations on 12th July, and what
right had the police to interfere with a
labour demonstration at Shaftesbury
Square on Saturday last, when they broke
the ranks of a procession. It was
fortunate for the officer in charge that
he broke the ranks of the right class,
because if he had broken the ranks behind
that section there would have been a
riot, and he would not have been living
to tell the tale. I say it is an outrage.
We demonstrated last Saturday as we
had a right to do. We kept the law,
but we were interfered with at every
point. Our procession was broken up
and disconnected. I have watched the
12th July demonstrations, and not once
have I seen the police breaking up that
procession or disconnecting the ranks
throughout its whole journey, either inside the city or outside. All I ask for
labour is the right to demonstrate without interference from the police as long
as they keep within the law. I hope
you will take a note of that, and draw
the attention of District-Inspector
Stratford, of Donegall Pass Barracks,
to it. He had no right to break the
procession at Shaftesbury Square and
Wellington Place.
The outdoor relief question has been
raised by the Member for Mourne. I
want to tell the Minister that the sooner
he educates boards of guardians throughout Northern Ireland as to their duties
in this respect the better for all concerned. There are thousands of people
starving in Northern Ireland through the
fault of the Government in issuing regulations which deprive the unemployed
of the right to benefit. The only
alternative left to those people is outdoor relief. How many boards of
guardians or local authorities in Northern Ireland have applied to the Ministry of Home Affairs to have Section 13
of the Act of 1918 put into force. Only
about four proving conclusively that the
remainder of the boards of guardians are
prepared to allow the people to starve.
I say that such a thing should not be
allowed to take place in a Christian
community.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I beg to move, in
page 14, lines 28 and 29, to leave out
the words "the institution" (in paragraph c) and insert the words "a registered institution or house to which the
patient is admitted."
This Amendment is introduced as a
result of representations made to me by
an hon. Member, and I am sure that it
will greatly assist in the administration.
Under the Clause, as it stands at present,
it is not possible for the resident medical
superintendent of a public mental hospital, or the medical officer in charge of
a registered institution or house, to sign
the medical certificate of a person being
admitted to such institution. It has been
pointed out to me, however, that while
this restriction is a very desirable one in
the case of registered homes, yet, were the
resident medical superintendents of a
public mental hospital not allowed to
examine and certify patients who may
later be admitted to their own institutions, considerable difficulty, delay, and
expense might ensue. In practice, I am
aware that the services of the resident
medical superintendents in Northern Ireland are called upon frequently in connection with the examination of many
persons who must ultimately become inmates of their institutions. I think it
is only natural that these gentlemen who
have wide experience of mental illnesses
should have an opportunity of certifying
when it becomes necessary.
Amendment agreed to.

CLAUSE 21 (Removal of persons of
unsound mind to workhouse for reasons
of safety).
If any officer or constable of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary is satisfied
that it is necessary for the public safety
or for the safety of any person alleged
to be of unsound mind that such person
should be forthwith placed under care
and control he shall remove such person
to the workhouse of the union in which
the person alleged to be of unsound
mind is resident or is found, and the
master of the workhouse shall admit
such person to the workhouse and shall
forthwith have such person examined
as to his state of mind by the medical

Exported Animals (Compensation) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be read a Second time.'
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): The Slaughtered
Animals (Compensation) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1928, passed by this House
four years ago provides for the payment
of compensation in respect of animals exported from Northern Ireland ports and
slaughtered in British landing places by
reason of the requirements of the British
authorities in consequence of foot-andmouth disease. The fund from which
such compensation is payable is constituted by a small levy as follows paid by
shippers on each animal exported:- -Each
head of cattle, 24d; each sheep, d; each
pig, ld.
The arrangement is therefore
a very sound form of insurance to which
the State is not asked to contribute.
For a considerable time past the cattle
trade associations have been pressing for
an extension of the legislation, so as to
provide compensation not only for
slaughter but also in respect of the
extra lairage and feeding charges payable
in British landing places whenever,
owing to foot-and-mouth disease or
suspected disease, whether in Great
Britain or Northern Ireland, animals
sent through our ports are detained in
British landing places beyond the usual
detention period of ten hours. For
example, last June animals consigned
from Northern Ireland were held in cross-
Channel landing places for prolonged
periods, during which the owners had to
pay considerable extra sums in respect of
lairage and feeding. It has been estimated that in consequence of the June
outbreak, such additional charges falling
to be borne by exporters through Northern Ireland ports amounted to about
£2,000. This Bill will enable that
amount to be paid to the shippers concerned from the insurance fund. Further,
the
measure protects traders against
similar risks in the future.
Section 13 (1) of the Act provides that
whenever the compensation fund amounts
to £5,000 the Ministry may make an
order for the suspension of payment of
the export levy per head on each animal
shipped. In view of the increased
liability now proposed to be placed on the
insurance fund, it is the intention that
the sum of £5,000 referred to should be
raised to £10,000. This increase has
been approved by the trade interests
concerned.
After careful consideration, I am of
opinion that this proposed legislation is
sound and I have, therefore, great
pleasure in commending the Bill to this
House. I beg to move.
Mr. MINFORD: I rise to support this
Bill. I think that any Bill brought in
by the Minister of Agriculture deserves.
the support of both sides of the House.
This Bill will clear away many difficulties
in regard to the shipment of cattle.
Last year the shippers of cattle experienced great delay for a considerable
period at the English and Scotch ports
owing to the outbreak of foot-and-mouth
disease which cost the exporters a sum of
£2,000. The Insurance Fund, which
amounted to £5,000 and which has not
been spent, was contributed to by the
exporters, who had to pay hundreds of
pounds extra for serious losses incurred.
Any loss derived by cattle shippers is a
direct loss to the farmers.
Might I
mention two items in regard to the landing of cattle on the other side. When
cattle are landed on the other side the
shippers have to pay 4d per head for
inspection fee and 3d per head for
tagging. I would like some explanation.
in regard to that. It may be a small
sum, but in the aggregate the amount
concerned between 1924 and last year was
£152,000 for all Ireland. Last
the
year
total for Ireland was £24,720. I consider
that these fees should be paid by the
English people themselves, because on
this side they have no veterinary fees
to pay at all. The only charge here is
4d per head for hay and 3d per head for
lairage. When
Irish shipper has to pay a total of 7d per
head, and that these tags cost only 3d
you
consider that the

dozen I think the charge is ridiculous.
I hope the Minister of Agriculture will

comes indirectly out of the pocket of the

Motion made, and Question proposed:

Mr. O'NEILL: I wonder if it would
be possible to get any reply to a question.
I raised yesterday during the debate on
the Estimates of the Ministry of Home
Affairs with regard to the position in
Castlewellan and Annsborough. I do not
see either the Minister of Labour or the
Minister of Home Affairs in the House.
The House will remember that I brought
forward cases of great hardship and want
in this district. I understand that some
of them are cases of almost absolute
starvation. The Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs did
state in reply that he would have inquiries made, and probably the time has
been too short to make those inquiries
or to have had a reply to them. There
is no doubt that in this district for some
time past there has been a good deal of
distress due to unemployment in the mills
at Annsborough and to other causes, and
there are a lot of people on the brink
of starvation, if not in absolute starvation. I think when such distress occurs
on a scale like this it is the business of
the Government to inquire into the matter immediately and to afford instant
relief. The complaint I have received
not only in regard to outdoor relief but
in regard to the Ministry of Labour is
that people have been cleared off unemployment benefit wholesale, with the result that both those who are insured and
those who are not are in dire distress at
the present time. I would like to know
what has been done, because this is not
the first occasion I have raised the question in this House, and things have not
improved in the meantime. Perhaps the
Parliamentary Secretary would tell us
exactly what the position is.
Mr. BYRNE: In the City of Belfast
there are a great many cases of distress
as bad as those to which the Member for Mourne has referred. Those of
us who are mixing with the working
people encounter nothing but the direst
distress wherever we go. We know that
under recent Acts of Parliament an unemployed person can draw unemployment
benefit for only six months, and then he
has to go before a public assistance committee which, I am sorry to say, is not
very sympathetic towards him. When
they have drawn four or eight weeks'
benefit their case comes before a Court of
Referees, and their claim for further
benefit is turned down entirely. This is
a very serious matter for the working
people of this city. Some time ago there
was a prospect of an improvement in the
linen trade which we hoped would relieve
unemployment considerably, but I am
sorry to say that according to reports I
have heard within the past week hundreds
of people have been paid off. I am told
that this is due to the reduction of the
tariff on linen from 50 per cent. to 20
per cent.
During the whole of my public life I
never heard of more distress than exists
in the city at the present time. Something should be done for these people at
once, because there is nothing but starvation staring them in the face. When
their transitional benefit is exhausted the
only thing left for these unemployed
people is to go before the Board of
Guardians, and everyone knows that
decent working people, who are unemployed through no fault of their own,
are very reluctant to be mixed up with
pauperism. If they are granted outdoor
relief they have to perform a certain
amount of work, and people have told me
they would starve rather than apply to
the guardians for relief. I sincerely
hope the Government will take some
effective steps to promote employment for
the large number of people who are now
practically in a state of starvation.
Major HALL-THOMPSON: It is a

to what is the fundamental duty of

ought to do something to keep them from
destitution and, perhaps, from starvation.
I would like to ask the Government
whether they propose to take any steps
to deal with these cases where people are
refused transitional benefit and are left
either at the mercy of the Guardians or
practically without any means of livelihood at all. There is no use in saying
you can just leave this matter as it is.
It would be far better to deal with it before the people become too vocal, and
when I say too vocal I mean before they
become so resentful of the conditions
under which they are compelled to live
that, perhaps, their organised vocal protests may take the much more concrete
form of revolutionary action. If they
cannot secure a means of livelihood the
people are not entitled to starve, and
the alternative may be presented to them,
and it may be an alternative very dangerous to the State.
What is in the minds of these people?
When the Great War broke out they
were told that the people who left these
islands would come back to a land fit for
heroes to live in. They do not expect a
land fit for heroes to live in, but they do

there is no doubt that it will be a very
serious situation that will present itself

Oral Answers
5 MAY 1932
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 5th May, 1932.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
JUVENILE EMPLOYEES OF
JOHNSTON & CO., BELFAST.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state how many
boys of the age of 15 years have been
engaged through the Juvenile Exchange
by the firm of Johnston & Co., Ravenhill
Road, Belfast, and what are their periods
of employment; whether these boys have
been employed as labourers by this firm
on municipal and Government contracts
at a wage of from 6s to 7s per week;
whether he is aware that this firm has
been blacklisted by the Belfast Corporation; and whether he will see that no
more contracts, subsidised by public
funds, will be given to this firm until they
receive a clean bill of health from the
National Union of Operative Heating
and Domestic Engineers and General
Metal Workers.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): In the unavoidable
absence of my right hon. Friend I have
been asked to reply. The Ministry of
Labour's available records show that in
the last three years the Belfast Juvenile
Exchange filled vacancies for apprentices
or helpers in the case of ten boys of about
the age of 15 years with the firm in
question. Of these one has been employed
for ten months, while two others reregistered at the Exchange after seven
months and three weeks respectively.
The Department has no information as
to the actual wages paid to the boys or
as to the work on which they were engaged.
With regard to the latter part of the
question, the matter is at present under
consideration between the representatives
of the Union and of the Government
Department concerned.
CARCASES OF PIGS CONDEMNED.
2. Mr. GAMBLE asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state how
many carcases of pigs have been condemned by the Inspectors of Pork since
the introduction of the Act.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): The Agricultural
Produce (Meat Regulation) Act (Northern Ireland), 1930, came into operation
on the 1st May, 1931. During the
twelve months ended 30th April, 1932,
274 carcases of pigs were condemned
under the provisions of the Act.
REVALUATION OF
AGRICULTURAL LAND.
3. Major McCORMICK asked the
Prime Minister whether the Government
propose to introduce legislation for the revaluation of all agricultural land now outside the scope of the Revaluation Act.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked to take this
question, the answer to which is in the
negative.
LANDLORD AND TENANT
LEGISLATION.
4. Major McCORMICK asked the
Prime Minister whether it is the intention of the Government to introduce
legislation on the lines of the Imperial
Parliament's "Landlord and Tenant Act,
and in accordance with the recommendation of the Departmental Committee set
up to consider this question.
SECRE-
The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): In the absence
of my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson
Bates) I have been asked to reply.
I have to refer the hon. Member to the
answer given to a similar question asked
by the hon. Member for Mid-Londonderry on the 28th April, to which I have.
nothing to add.

area. Such tables were never before
prepared for Ireland separately from
Great Britain, but are now available for

The

Another thing I want to take exception.
to is the ruling out of ordinary civil

who pass
the examinations and who get

Service examination in his life.
He was
not a civil servant, and had no training
whatever in business. A few years ago
most people were inclined to bow to a
gentleman, no matter where he was, if
he had a great financial reputation. But
events in Great Britain and elsewhere
have dissipated that idea once and for
all. We know that a great many financial reputations are spurious, and there are
several people in this House at the present
moment who know that to their cost.
There is no man worth £1,800 a year at
the present time under any circumstances,
more particularly a man with no training whatever in the business.
It would be a very big job, indeed, for
me or anyone else to commence reading
out the numerous and well-paid posts
created by this Department. At the
present time I think that would be rather
superfluous in view of the fact that there
is a very good book on the subject which
I had not the pleasure of reading yet
and which is published at twopence. It
is a book, I believe, from what I hear,
that is making an impression. I remember raising a question to which I still
take exception. When young men pass
the Civil Service examination and have
their marks allotted to them, I think after
they pass the doctor they should be
appointed in order of merit. I have every
reason to believe that the examinations
as conducted by the Civil Service Commissioners are fair and above board. I
have every reason to believe that the
marks given are fair, but I object
absolutely to candidates after they have
got good marks from the Civil Service
Commissioners being brought before
another board and questioned, and being
knocked up or down or off the list.
That is not to be taken as reflecting
on the members that form that board.
I know some of the gentlemen, and I am
not reflecting on them in the slightest degree, but I do say that no man can sit
here or in a room, and after asking a
candidate a number of questions then
decide on the ability of that candidate.
If it is a question of physical appearance
or something like that, then there should
be a medical test set up. Candidates
have to be medically examined, and that
is quite proper, but for a number of
gentlemen to call themselves an investigation committee and hurl all sorts of
foolish questions at the candidates brought
before them is absolutely absurd, because
some of the candidates might be nervous.
I am sure they would be. What would
make them more nervous is that this Committee and, again, I mean no personal reflection on the gentlemen of the Committee-have the reputation of knocking
off people that should not be knocked off,
and of putting people on whose marks

coming before them nervous.
I suggest that it would be more honourable and above board to appoint the

CLASS 11. No. 9.
MISCELLANEOUS EXPENSES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £1,790 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1933, to pay
certain miscellaneous expenses, including
certain Grants in Aid."-(Note-£500

Mr. BARBOUR: There is little that
calls for comment in this Estimate.
Grants-in-aid have been fractionally
reduced in accordance with the general
economy cut principles that have been
applied all round. Sub-head I calls for
some more detailed comment. The explanation of the proposed grant is that
the former Clones Union was partly in
County Monaghan and partly in County
Fermanagh. On the setting up of the
Northern Ireland Government, the Union
was divided, about one-third of the area
being attached to Lisnaskea Union in the
North, but no division of assets and
liabilities was made. The failure of the
Imperial Government to have such an
apportionment made has not, however,
been of material consequence, as items
such as superannuation allowances have
been accepted as a final charge by the
body where the office of the former
guardians was situated, while matters
such as the adjustment of payments due
for treatment of inmates from transborder areas have been left to settle
themselves on the assumption that assets
and liabilities in general cancel out.
The present case, however, is in a
different category. It is a case of a bank
overdraft which the former guardians
owed but which now, owing to severance,
cannot be legally accepted or legally enforced, so far as one can judge. For a
considerable time past the bank concerned has made representation that it
was
not equitable that it should be
penalised merely because the three Governments concerned had left a transborder problem unsettled. My right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Home Affairs,
and myself have accordingly come to the
conclusion that in equity the bank should
not be left in this position. On the
other hand, only one-third of the former
Clones Union is situated in Northern
Ireland, and our normal liability should
be confined to that proportion of the
debt. Technically this amount might be
held to be owing by the Lisnaskea Union,
but it cannot legally be imposed upon
them, and, in any event, if the amount
were paid from the rates, it would, in
all probability, owing to derating, be
paid as to 80 per cent. by the Government in the long run. The grant,
therefore, is an ex-gratia payment in
respect of a moral obligation arising out
of the establishment of separate Governments in Northern Ireland. I beg to
move.

Oral Answers to Questions.
BUILDING PROGRAMME FOR NEW
SCHOOLS.
1. Major McCORMICK asked the
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Education whether, in view of the
heavy expenditure in the building and
equipment of schools, he proposes to curtail or stop the building programme for
new schools other than those already in
hand.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The answer
is in the negative, but I may explain that
as a result of personal representations
made by the Minister in December, 1930,
the building programme has, in view of
the financial stringency, already been curtailed or delayed.
Except where they merely replace
existing unsuitable schoolhouses, the
building of new schools results, through
amalgamation, in the concentration of
pupils in larger school units, which can
be more efficiently and economically
staffed, and I may add that the consequent saving in teachers' salaries is much
greater than the annual loan charges on
the money borrowed for new or enlarged
schools.
INCREASED BUS FARES.
asked
the
2. Major McCORMICK
Minister of Home Affairs whether, in
view of the increased bus fares put into
force on almost all routes, he will make
representations to the Bus Fares Tribunal to have the scales reconsidered.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The hon. and
gallant Member appears to be under a
misapprehension regarding the activities.
of the Tribunal referred to in suggesting
that the Tribunal has put in force increased bus fares on almost all routes.
The facts are that after considering
the representations made by certain
operators and formal objections lodged by
local authorities and other interested
parties, and having weighed up carefully
expert evidence tendered by persons of
experience and knowledge in connection
with the operation of motor omnibus
services, the Tribunal has formulated certain basic principles on which they consider bus fares should be regulated in
Northern Ireland in future.
The practical application of these principles to various routes is at present under
consideration, and a further session of the
Tribunal has been arranged to consider
and decide as to the practical working out
of their general principles in connection
with these specified routes which all interested parties can attend and be heard.
The Tribunal is an independent body
and in connection with its activities must
be guided by the evidence placed before
it by applicants and objectors, and it
would be out of place for me as Minister
of Home Affairs to make any general
representations to the Tribunal of the
nature suggested by the hon. and gallant
Member.
Major MCCORMICK: May I ask the
Minister if he is aware that these increases inflict great hardships upon many
people who have gone to live permanently
in the country?
Sir DAWSON BATES: As I have
already pointed out, these applications
will come before the Tribunal, when, no
doubt, my hon. and gallant Friend's
friends will be present and will put forward their views.

is a fact that men employed on distress

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.

1928, which corresponds to a provision in

There is one other item, and that is with

machine the police has failed in that

There is no doubt that the police have

failures should take place without the

It is, therefore, the duty of the Minister

go lawfully and legally about their
business, and who have given no offence

tell the reason why that has occurred.

Mr. BYRNE: I would like to support
the hon. Member (Mr. O'Neill) in this
matter, and there are many reasons for
doing so. I can quite understand these
restrictions in all cases satisfying those
who are opposed to any person getting
any refreshments. We require revenue
at the present time, I think, as much as
any other part of the country, and the
drastic restrictions in connection with the
licensing laws operating in the Six
Counties are driving hundreds and
thousands of people out of the Six
Counties with their money which is being
spent in other parts of the country. I
think the Government should consider
this matter. Even when excursionists
come to a hotel in Belfast or the Six
Counties they are denied reasonable refreshments. This means sometimes that
the law is being broken. People in this
age like liberty, and if you deprive them
of that liberty it makes them go to extremes and they break the law. Would
it not be far better that people could get
reasonable refreshments in their Own
district than that they should go by bus
to another area and thereby deprive us
of the revenue, which I am sure would
be very useful to us at the present time?
We have the cry about economy, and
we have the cry about the want of money.
More revenue comes from the liquor trade
than any other business, and yet the
people engaged in it are more publicly
abused on public platforms than any
other class of the community. No class
of the community contributes more to
the revenue of the country. Those in the
trade at the present time are practically
tax-gatherers. They are the people that
collect the tax for the Government, and
yet the people are not allowed to get
fair and reasonable refreshments. I am
in the trade and I detest and abhor any
man who takes too much drink. I would
rather that those who cannot take refreshments in moderation would take
none at all, but I say the ordinary
traveller-the ordinary excursionist-who
comes here should get reasonable refreshments, and be encouraged to come
again. It is well known to many in this
Committee that large numbers of people
go out of the area at the week-ends and
visit other places where they can get
reasonable refreshments. I appeal to the
Government to consider this matter. The
laws here are more drastic than in any
other country in the world.

The traffic on the roads is so complicated
and so dangerous that really I would
imagine it is an easier job to drive a
steam locomotive on a railway line than
it is to drive a bus on the public road.
After all, all the engine driver has to
look out for are the signals, and that is
not nearly so hard a job as that of a bus
driver looking out for traffic on the road
and not knowing where it is going to or
where it is coming from. An engine
driver has to be at his shed half an hour
before his engine leaves the shed, and his
time is counted as beginning from that
hour; and he is allowed another half hour
when he arrives back at night. All that
is included in his eight-hours day. If by
chance his run during the day exceeds
eight hours he is paid overtime, and, as
far as possible, the railway companies try
to keep him reasonably near the eight
hours. Another point is that if a driver
exceeds 120 miles in a day he is paid
overtime.

Another thing I wish to mention is that
there are many courts of inquiry being
held that are quite unnecessary, in my
opinion. The other day I read of a
district inspector going into a sergeant's
house and finding that the sergeant had
been, perhaps, a quarter of an hour off
his patrol. The sergeant had some excuse
for going into the house. He was brought
to the barracks, and a statement was
taken. A court of inquiry was assembled
to investigate this most serious charge of
a sergeant going into his own house to see
his wife who was ill. I submit in the
interests of the police-I do not say this
by way of criticising the Governmentthat the district inspector would have
served the police force far better by telling the sergeant not to let the like occur
again, instead of assembling a court of
inquiry for the purpose of taking
evidence that food was consumed in the
house. It might have been that the
children had taken their supper before
going to bed. This was all opened up.
I hope sincerely that the police and the
district-inspectors will never have anything more important than that to deal
with. That is a very trivial thing. I
do not know a single one of the persons
concerned; not a single one of them
approached me on the subject.

do not know how it will be taken, and,

Mr. O'NEILL: There is a matter I
wish to raise on the Adjournment, although I have not given notice of it. I
am sure the Minister of Labour or his
Parliamentary Secretary will give some
reply to the question. It is with regard
to this matter at Annsborough. Up to the
present I have only been able to get at
Distress and Unemployment 1306
Adjournment-
10 MAY 1932
the Minister of Home Affairs because his
Department had responsibilities in this
matter just as the Ministry of Labour
have. Indeed, I think the Ministry of
Labour have been the real villains of the
piece, in that they have carried on the
sins of commission, while the Ministry
of Home Affairs have only carried on the
sins of omission. The Minister of Labour
must know that for some time past there
has been a great lot of distress in Annsborough district. It has been brought
under his notice in this House. The
latest information I have from Castlewellan is in a letter from a clergyman
there, and these are his words:
Only yesterday (14th April) I have
been informed 14 persons without
notice and without benefit for a fortnight have been put off the dole. I
am also informed that these people
cannot, owing to the regulations and
red tape procedure, receive any help
inside the next two weeks.
I would have thought that the Minister,
considering the condition of affairs there,
would have been more lenient, and that
he would have given instructions that no
more reductions in unemployment benefit.
would take place there until things would
right themselves in some way, but
evidently he could not do that. The
complaint I have to make boldly with
regard to the administration of the
Ministry of Labour is that they are not
sympathetic. It is not sufficient to say
you cannot do it. You could do it well
enough, although you would not strictly
be within legal limits. Then with regard
to pensions to blind persons, we were informed in an answer to a question that
during the past three years almost 400
persons have been deprived of blind
pensions. These people, according to
your own admission, had been illegally
receiving these pensions up to
period. No one took exception to that,
and even if they had been still receiving
the pensions no one would have taken
exception to it. I will mention
particular case in regard to a blind person's pension. The man lives at Warrenpoint, although I think he comes from
Gilford. His name is McCusker. He
was a railway worker in Scotland for
many years for twenty years I thinkand belonged to some of the railway
benevolent societies. His health became
defective, and his eyesight became
defective, and he was pensioned off with
that
one
a pension of 14s or 16s a week. Ultimately
his sight became so bad that he also
received the blind pension, and has been
in receipt of that blind pension up to
about a fortnight ago. Now the Ministry have notified him that his blind pension has ceased. This is a case I know
myself. I know the individual and have
seen him often. As a matter of fact, I
saw him to-day. And when the Ministry
decides that he is not entitled to a blind
pension, of course, his other disability
pension would also disappear. This is a
man who has been in the Benn Hospital
in Belfast for over a year at a time, and
has gone under six operations in respect
of his sight. As a matter of fact, he has
lost one eye, and the other eye is such
that a famous eye specialist here, Dr.
Craig, has stated on paper that he cannot find glasses to suit him to read with.
There is a man whom you have deprived of his blind pension, carrying with
it in all probability the discontinuance
of his other pension. You leave this man
absolutely unfit for anything but the
workhouse. That is one particular case.
There are many other cases, but I have
just given the House an idea of the
methods by which the Blind Pensions Act
is administered by the Ministry of
Labour. I think the House is entitled
to an explanation, not only in this particular case but in others, and also, I think,
the House is entitled to an explanation
as to why so many people have been
deprived of unemployment benefit in the
Castlewellan and Annsborough districts.
Mr. HEALY: I just want to say one
word in reference to blind pensions.
Since the regulations of the Ministry
went forth I have had numerous instances
of people, who had been in receipt of the
blind pension for a number of years, being
suddenly deprived of it. These people
must have furnished some satisfactory
medical evidence to the Ministry once
upon a time, and must have satisfied
them that their sight was so defective
that they could not carry on their
ordinary work, or otherwise they would
never have had the pension. One learns
from one's experience of such things
that failing sight does not improve with
the years. If these people were sufficiently
bad to enable them to get the pension,
say six, seven, or even as long as eight
years ago, surely it can hardly be claimed
that they have improved in the interval.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Healy]
When the Ministry send down a gentleman who is an eye expert it is hardly
fair to the people, because he goes there
Iwith the definite idea in his mind that
the Ministry have instructed him that a
number of people have been receiving
pensions whose total blindness does not
reach the limits fixed by the Ministry.
He goes down predisposed to find as many
facts as he possibly can in favour of his
employers. It is not a reflection on the
expert or on his judgment to say that he
finds in favour of the Department, because there is kept in front of him all
the time the fact that there is an excess
number in receipt of the blind pension,
among that number being some people
who are not entitled to it. Therefore,
he goes to the country with a predisposition against the people. We know pretty
well that what actuated the Ministry in
that course was probably the Ministry of
Finance. It was to save funds.
know that very well. If times were
better in Northern Ireland there would
be no such thing as a revision of blind
persons' pensions. But every penny
must be saved, at all events on the social
services.
even
man.
We
The people have only one remedy, and
I suggest that it is a very unfair remedy
to offer them. The Department will not
take the certificate of any country
practitioner as against that of their own
expert. Not
when people have
produced three certificates from three
independent doctors would the Ministry
except those as against the certificate of
their own
Therefore, the people
are driven to the extremity that they
have to get the certificate of an expert
whose name will overbear that of the
expert of the Ministry. That entails a
big fee. It entails a special railway
journey to Belfast and the attendance of
somebody along with them, because they
are so blind that they could not make
their way. I suggest that that is an inhuman position to take up. No Government should take up an attitude of that
kind. If the evidence on which the
original pension was granted was sufficient,
then it is sufficient to enable them to
continue to receive the pension.
I suggest that in a case where two local
doctors, acting absolutely independently,
certify that a person has a degree of,
say, 65 per cent. lack of sight the Minister ought to accept that and ought not
to put these poor people to the expense
of travelling to Belfast and all that that
entails before they can succeed in persuading the Ministry that they are blind.
There have been people who have succeeded in persuading the Ministry, but
only when they have got another expert
whose name carries greater weight in the
medical world than even that of the expert of the Ministry. But suppose they
were not in a position, or that their
friends were not in a position to provide
that, they would still be without the
pension. It means that the wretched,
poor people who cannot afford an eye expert are never going to be restored to the
pension, and that is the most callously
cruel thing one can possibly conceive. I
hope the Ministry of Finance will not
issue any instructions to the other Ministries to economise at the expense of the
blind people, the poor, old people up and
down the country who have been receiving this pension for years and who had
every anticipation, every hope, and every
belief that they would go on receiving it
till the day of their death. I hope the
Ministry of Finance will find some better

The hon. Member for Mourne went on

is so. But the degree of blindness very
frequently changes. Eyes may get worse
or eyes may get better. In very few
cases do eyes remain stationary, as I, for
instance, know. Sight may improve in
one direction, and may get worse in
another. The fact that a person gets a
blind person's pension one year does not
mean that that person is necessarily entitled to a blind person's pension as long
as that person lives.
The proof that my Department is administering these social services sympathetically is to be found in the enormous

NOMINATION OF DELEGATE FOR

have to announce that the Secretary of

of Finance has kindly consented to act.

Act.

Minister's Statement
11 MAY 1932
""
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
THE BUDGET.
Financial Statement, 1932-33.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That this House approves the proposals
of the Government for meeting the
financial requirements of the year.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Hon. Members will, no doubt,
recall the depressing conditions existing
a year ago, when it was found necessary
to resort to unusual expedients directed
to balancing the Budget of Northern
Ireland for the year which then lay ahead
and which closed on 31st March last.
To accomplish that result, important
sacrifices on the part of all those in receipt
of public money were demanded, and in
the main cheerfully conceded as a patriotic
necessity and duty. The figures of the
past year, which are already in the hands
of Members, and on which I propose to
comment later on, bear witness to the
success which has followed this act of
renunciation, and afford the satisfaction
which always follows the consciousness of
right-doing, that Britain and our little
Province almost alone of all the countries
in the world have faced the situation with
courage and success. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
The year 1931 will long be remembered
as a year fraught with momentous,
political, economic and commercial consequences to the Kingdom and Empire.
It will be written in history as the year
of the resurrection of our people from the
grave of apathy and indifference, and may
well prove a turning point in the fortunes
of the Kingdom, in its relations to that
great confederation of nations and peoples
which we call the British Empire.
Furthermore, from the point of view
of commerce and industry, the year 1931
must be reckoned as in some respects one
of the blackest in our history. In its
earlier months all hope of recovery seemed
abandoned, and a feeling amounting to
despair had taken the place of expectation
and confidence. However, the very
acuteness of the economic and financial
situation was, beyond doubt, something
in a nature of a blessing. It aroused the
British people to a sense of the serious
danger to the entire structure of the
Commonwealth, and in its rebound overthrew all the fiscal traditions of one
hundred years, and opened up possibilities
of a new and prosperous era in the life
story of Britain.
In such extraordinary circumstances,
involving radical changes in the whole
political, fiscal and financial outlook of
the country, it could not be expected that
our Province could be free from its
natural reaction on every feature of our
Provincial life, but especially in the
domain of finance.
The House will, I am sure, appreciate
the difficulties and confusion resulting
from these changes, and feel that it is
matter for congratulation that we have
emerged from this fateful year of 1931
with our current obligations met, and a
margin of contribution to the Imperial
Services greater than we undertook to provide in our Budget calculations.
House has had presented the figures
relating to the revenue and expenditure
for the past year, and it may be thought
that these figures require little further
explanation.
The
But, following my usual practice in presenting our annual accounts, I feel it will
be convenient if I analyse these figures of
income and expenditure, and call attention
to some interesting comparisons between
the estimates made in the Budget of last
year, and the ultimate outcome as shewn
on the Financial Statement issued on the
last day of the financial year, 31st March.
If hon. Members will turn to Table I of
the White Paper, which has been circulated, they will find statements comparing
the estimated with the actual outturn of
last year's finance.
EXPENDITURE, 1931-32.
Dealing first of all with the expenditure
during the year 1931 we find that Consolidated Fund Services, apart from the

REVENUE 1931-32.
The first source of revenue which I will
touch upon is the transferred taxes, that
is, those taxes which produce revenue
which are imposed by us and collected by
us.
These amounted to £1,008,000; that
is £30,000 less than the Budget Estimate.
The details are:-Estate duties, or death
duties, as they are generally called
£676,000, realising £9,000 in excess of
the Estimate; stamp duties, £201,000, or
£36,000 less than was estimated, and excise duties (that is income tax and licences
of various kinds) £131,000, or £3,000 less
than the Estimate.
I cannot but wonder at the fact that in
a year when the value of all securities has
been depressed to a level which a few
years ago we would have regarded as
phenomenally low, the yield of estate
duties has not only fulfilled, but has exceeded our Estimate by £9,000. May I
remind the House that estate duties are a
very variable and uncertain method of
raising revenue as it depends entirely
upon the rate of mortality during the
period. It happened that we were fortunate in receiving an item of £30,000 late
in the month of March. We regarded
that as a sort of windfall.
The yield of stamp duties reflects only
too truly the chaotic state of the world
and its reactions on business transactions
of all kinds. Hon. Members will realise
that the great bulk of our stamp duties
arise from stamps on transfers of securities
and from the buying and selling of securities. There is no doubt that until world
confidence is restored, the returns from
this duty must continue to show a shrinkage, and perhaps give us
reason for
thought. Motor taxation, as I have stated
above, produced £559,000.

The Budget-
Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS

of £14,000 on the working of the Post
Office, from which we receive £890,000
revenue, as against £876,000 expenditure.
A significant part of my comment is that
this is the first time in our autonomous
career that the Post Office has paid its
way, and the occasion is surely worthy
of more than a mere passing notice,
having regard to the importance of the
service.
I have watched this commercial
department of our public life from year
to year with more than ordinary interest.
I can recall in one of my Budget statements, some four or five years ago, congratulating the House that the loss on
the working of the Post Office had been
reduced at that time from a considerably
larger figure to £20,000. At any time.
I had hoped and expected that we were
approaching a period when that loss on
the Post Office Service would be turned
into a profit, but the depression of recent
years falsified that hope, until to-day,
when we find, as I have said, that we
have turned the corner, and can report
a profit, however small, having regard to
the magnitude of the service, on the
operations of last year. This result is
all the more remarkable when we call
to mind the year of general commercial
difficulties through which we have passed.
I think it is possible to regard the Post
Office as a very important barometer in
respect of the conditions of trade, and
although in these depressing times it is
hard to see any blink of sunshine yet
the Post Office, if it do give any indication of trade, would show that we are
not so bad as perhaps some of our neighbours in respect of economic conditions.

11 MAY 1932
SUPPLY.
The House has already had the Supply
Estimates under detailed examination,
and I need not, therefore, take up very
much time on this subject. A certain
amount of disappointment has been expressed at the fact that the total
£8,937,000 is in excess of last year's total
by some £108,000. To those people who
have expressed dissatisfaction at any increase, I should like to point out that in
the current year our Supply Estimates
make provision for meeting in full from
revenue the cost of unemployment insurance. We borrowed last year £840,000
for current unemployment needs for which
no provision whatever appeared in our
Estimates. But this year we have provided out of the Exchequer the necessary
money to provide for the transitional
benefit outlay. I am sure the House will
agree that it is wiser and sounder policy
that a matter of this kind should be
covered from year to year out of revenue
rather than that a huge debt should be
piled up. (Hon. Member: Hear, hear.)
The Consolidated Fund items of last
year were:-Interest, £133,000; Sinking
Funds, £195,000; Road Fund, £570,000,
and other Consolidated Fund charges,
£160,000, making a total of £1,058,000.
The interest charge contains £95,000 for
Treasury Bills and £38,000 for Ulster
savings certificates. This figure is a net
amount after the appropriate withdrawal
of £24,000 from the Interest Sinking
Fund. The gross interest to be paid on
Ulster savings certificates during the year
is estimated at £62,000. The House will
understand that it is necessary that we
should provide from year to year for the
payment of interest and also the increase
in the value of these savings certificates
as years go on.
The Sinking Fund payments, it will be
seen, are £105,000 in excess of last year.
£85,000 is due to the restoration of the
normal allocation to the Land Purchase
Sinking Fund established for the purpose
of preserving in perpetuity the annual
value of the existing land purchase
annuities. The House will remember
that it was necessary in the exigencies of
the position a year ago to utilise a sum of
£85,000 by withholding for a year the
contribution to the Sinking Fund on our
land purchase annuities. The excuse for
that was that we were ahead in regard to
the necessary provision for extinguishing
the land annuities at the time we expected they would expire, and we argued
from that that it was a perfectly justifiable
withdrawal, having regard to the necessity
of balancing our accounts. But this year,
on the other hand, I propose to make the
ordinary provision, amounting to £85,000,
and the restoration of that will keep the
fund in its proper condition. The remainder of the increase is due to normal
growth in the allocations to the Sinking
Fund for meeting the interest payable in
respect of Ulster savings certificates.
The figure of £160,000 for other Consolidated Fund issues contains provision of
£150,000 to meet possible liabilities
in connection with loan guarantees.
Although, as I have stated in the House
on previous occasions, the Government is
convinced that the reorganisation scheme
which has recently been adopted for the
future management of the Royal Mail
group of companies has reasonable prospects of success, I feel that, having regard
to the fact that this will be the first year
of the scheme's working, and to the continued depression in shipping, it is only
prudent to make this provision against
possible losses, not only on Royal Mail
guarantees, but on guarantees to any other
companies on which losses may arise.

INLAND REVENUE.
The prospects of the Inland Revenue
show, unhappily, a very different state of
affairs. I have already mentioned that
the abnormally large collection in 1931-32
was in large measure due to the fact that
payments had been made by numbers of
taxpayers at an earlier date than usual.
Although this factor influenced last year's
revenue substantially to our advantage,
hon. Members will readily realise that it
has a converse effect on the revenues of
the present year. I need not enlarge
upon the general shrinkage of incomes
suffered by all classes of taxpayers last
year on account of the appalling state of
industry and trade. Clearly we must,
on that account, apprehend a substantial
reduction in the yield of Income and Sur-
Tax this year, which is assessed on last
year's incomes.
From these two causes, I am unable to
rely upon the Inland Revenue, which last
year produced £3,810,000, for more than
£3,250,000.

I do not, however, regard this balance
as sufficient, and I propose, therefore, to
ask my colleagues to join with me in

of economy, a saving of at least £50,000
on the Supply Estimates. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). It will not, I am

task should not prove impossible, granted
the good-will of our people, and a recognition by all of the fact that in times such

measures of economy must be adopted
and services curtailed to an extent which

submitted. Not only is there no room for

In addition, I would like to point out

to the extent of £250,000 annually. We

Ireland with the fee simple of their

I cannot think, therefore, that the

Imperial Services is not by any means inconsiderable.
I am happy to say, finally, that our
credit on the London Market stands
deservedly high, as always, and we have
now a keen competition for any Treasury
Bills we may require for our temporary
needs.

On thing we very often hear in this
House is that Northern Ireland is too
small an area to have a Parliament, as
the expenses would be too great on
account of its area and the size of its
population. That view is often put forward by the Opposition, which is nonexistent at present. I wish they were
here. I myself was under the impression
that Northern Ireland was a very small
and a very insignificant place when I
looked at it on the map, but on making
enquiries, to my amazement I found that
seven of the thirteen New England States
which formed the Federal Government
of America were comparable in area with
Northern Ireland. They are Vermont,
New Hampshire, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Delaware and
Maryland. Of those seven States only
one at the present time has a larger
population than Northern Ireland, that
is Massachusetts.
That fact fortifies the opinion that Northern Ireland has an area big enough,
and is populous enough to govern itself,
and I am sure that we will not listen to
any more of these stories that Northern
Ireland is too small an area to have a Government. That brings me to a point which
I think the Chancellor of the Exchequer
touched upon rather lightly, that is,
the crisis through which this world is
passing and which is not over yet. He only
touched on it lightly, because of the fact
that happily we are linked with the
finances of Great Britain.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Mr. JOHNSTON: The right hon.
Gentleman when there is nothing in one
pocket can put his hand into the other.
This time he has done so to nearly the
fullest extent. It is nearly emptied now,
as there is only a small surplus of £70,000.
It is so small that the Minister thinks it
might disappear during the year. He is,
in consequence, determined, if it is possible, to add another £50,000 to it. That
brings me to the main point in my speech.
I believe that our Government and the
Government of Great Britain will be
compelled, whether they like it or not,
to economise much more than they have
done. I want to make sure the Government are going to do this.
No matter what Government are in
power they will not next year get the
money from the taxpayers the same as
they did last year. The limit of taxa-
The Budget-

tion has been reached (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). If any more taxes are put
on, or if the existing taxation is increased, instead of the Government getting more money they will get less
money. Therefore, I say that the Governments of Great Britain and Northern
Ireland will have to economise in both

shortly following the example of Great
Britain in appointing a Commission to
go into the expenditure of the various
Departments.
I can quite see that is coming on the
other side, and I hope this Government
will not hesitate to take that course too.
It is high time they did it. I am of the
opinion, and have been of the opinion for

Northern Ireland could be very much
greater without in any way interfering

Service. There is one thing you can have.
You can have too much of a good thing.
The Civil Service is a splendid organisation, but you can have too much of a good
thing. I believe the curtailment of some
of the operations of the Civil Service
could very well be effected without loss of
efficiency.
Captain CHICHESTER-CLARK: I
would like to add my tribute of congratulation to the right hon. Gentleman, the
Minister of Finance, for the able and
lucid way in which he introduced the
Budget for the coming year.
If I may
say so, with all respect, he brought it in
with all the pep, and energy, and dash of
a very young man. But the curious
action of the Opposition has rather left
us dumbfounded. I feel I would not be
wrong in congratulating that party on
having done the best thing they have ever
done, that is retiring and letting us get
on with the debate.
I know that a few years ago it would
have been thought, and perhaps it is still
thought, a very presumptuous thing for
a private and humble back bencher to get
up and criticise, or even talk upon, the
nation's Budget. But times have
changed since then, and the people upon
whom we looked as kings of finance have
faded away.
A few years ago if a man's
name began with H-Harrison, Horne,
or Hatry or even if it had been Kylsant
or Kreuger, we should have listened to
him with great reverence, and we would
have tried to follow out the financial
schemes he was recommending. But, as
I say, times have changed and those men
are with us no longer.
Their schemes have failed, and it is
left, I think, perhaps to the humble
simple man to criticise and to deal
with questions of finance. What I
think we want is the plain man and plain
simple finance. Recent events have shown
the loyalty and patriotism of the
very small body I have referred to, the
sur-tax payer and the income-tax payer.
Had it not been for their patriotism and
for the fact that they came forward in the
nation's need this country would at
the present time have shown very different
returns as regards inland revenue. Today, I think, is the day when that very
small and yet absolutely necessary
minority should have most to say on the
situation, because it is they who pay the
piper whilst other people are so very
ready to call the tune.
There can be no doubt-and I feel that
perhaps I am wasting my eloquence, as
the Opposition are not here that legislation in the past ten years has been
legislation for one class only. I am not
disagreeing with that. I am glad to see
the sort of legislation which has been
passed and which has so greatly improved
the lot of the poorer people of the world,
but there can be no denial that legislation
has been for one class only. During the
history of the British Empire we have
seen legislation first of all by the feudal
class, then by an absolute monarch, then
a limited monarch, and in recent years
and the years during which Great Britain
has made wonderful strides to prosperity,
the ruling classes have been the middle
class, and it is through their wise rule that
Great Britain is now the country it is
to-day.
Unfortunately the rule of the middle
classes is passing away. and the country
is being ruled by universal suffrage, and
universal suffrage is up against the acid
test of whether they are fit to rule or
whether they are going on and on into
the clouds while, at the same time, they
are knocking away the absolutely
necessary props on which the structure is
built. Sir Robert Horne, who was speaking on the Budget in another place, made
this very interesting remark. He said
"it is going to be a close thing as to
whether the survival of our civilisation is
going to continue or as to whether it is
going to decline." And to-day we have
to bear in mind that we are budgeting

But the last three years have shown that

I fail to see, and Sir Robert Horne
failed to tell us, what advantage the
possibility of being able to borrow cheap
money will bring if he cannot at the same

mention that a policy of inflation will increase the cost of living. It will increase
the cost of living of the wage earner and
of the man with a small salary. Consequently, one need not be carried away too
much by the advice of great financiers
to-day, because they have so often in the

In the last 25 years, that is to

-they have sliced off a sum of
£2,000,000,000 of the country's capital,

It is safe to say that if this sum had not

For the

These are the direct results. The indirect results are much greater and spread
much further, but I want to stick strictly
to actual facts and figures, so I will content myself with showing what the direct
results were. The action on the labour
market and the action on unemployment
of these death duties suddenly operated
have been exactly the same as a catastrophe like the fire on the Bermuda. I
think from the calculations I have made
that every thousand pounds collected in
death duties means one more man on the
unemployment register or it keeps one
man on who otherwise might come off.
By every thousand pounds of death duties
we are adding one more man to the Minister of Labour's troubles.
The reason I raised this question so
definitely at the present time is this.
During the years preceding the war, and
I might even add a few years after the
war, there was a certain prosperity in the
land, and there was a chance for the
thrifty and hard-working to replace
capital that had been snatched from the
country by the operations of these taxes.
There was a chance for every man during
his lifetime, if thrifty and saving, to be
able to put back a little of the capital
previously taken away. Now, and here
is the point, there is no possibility in the
days of bad trade for replacement, and
nobody can save anything. Apart from
the complete destruction of any incentive
to thrift, most people, most firms, and
most industries are living on their
capital. There will be no hope of any
real saving for several years to come.

Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS

in which he opened his Budget. This is
the last Budget which will be opened in
this House, and I am sure I am expressing the feelings of all hon. Members of
the House when I say that we hope that
when we come to open a new Budget in
new surroundings that Budget will be
opened by the same Chancellor of the
Exchequer, to whom we have always been
so indebted in the past. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I had not intended to rise to-day. I
had hoped that there would have been a
considerable amount of discussion and
that I would have had an opportunity
this evening to assimilate and to digest
the figures that have been presented so
admirably by the Minister of Finance.
These figures are in many respects
astounding. In some respects I think
they are matter for congratulation.
Reference has already been made by the
Chancellor of the Exchequer himself to
the fact that, for the first time since the
inception of the Government of Northern
Ireland, the Post Office services have paid.
That is a matter for congratulation-
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)—because, if
I remember rightly, last year on that particular reserved service there was a deficit
of £16,000. This year that deficit,
through circumstances which I cannot
estimate or understand, has been changed
to a balance of £14,000.
But there is one factor in this Budget
to which I think it would pay to draw
attention, and that is that, in spite of all
our lip service to economy in the past, our
estimated expenditure for the year upon
which we have just entered is slightly
higher that it was for the year which has
just passed. I have the exact figures here
for the past three or four years since I
had the honour to become a Member of
this House, and I think they are somewhat significant. I find that for the year
1928-29 the expenditure of this Parliament amounted to £9,861,000, that in the
following year it increased to £11,109,000,
that last year our expenditure was
£11,411,000, that for the past year our
expenditure was slightly higher at
£11,577,000; and for the year to come,
taking down the figures which have been
supplied by the Minister, I find
that our estimated expenditure amounts
to £11,760,000.
I mention these figures with some degree
of apprehension. I do not blame the
Minister of Finance. That is not his
duty. His duty is, in accordance with
the financial decisions of this House and
in accordance with the Votes in Supply,
like a prudent accountant to arrange if
possible for a balance on the credit side.
But the figures are somewhat significant
of the tendency of what we may call the
modern state. That tendency has already
been referred to by the hon. and gallant
Gentleman (Captain
(Captain Chichester-Clark)
who has preceded me, that tendency
towards socialisation, towards the increase
of the Supply Services and the social services. That tendency, it seems to me, is
a dangerous tendency unless there is some
prospect of a check somewhere.
I am not for one moment criticising
the payments made by this Government
to those who are in need of State assistance. We all sympathise with those who
are unemployed. We all sympathise with
the widows and orphans for whom we now
provide benefits benefits, if I remember
rightly, amounting to about £300,000 a
year. But, looking back on our commitments, it seems to me that there are certain commitments which are not justifiable. I refer in particular to the commitments which this House undertook
three years ago in respect of derating.

I join with the other Members who

after deductions, is somewhere about ten

seven millions on social services. It is
certain that taxation has reached a peak
and it is a burden that can no longer be
borne at its present rate. I would remind the hon. Member (Mr. Beattie) that
it is on taxation the social services depend. Taxation comes out of industry.
The social services depend on the wheels
of industry turning round. If you cog
those wheels and hinder the machinery
of industry by over-taxation you are
travelling in a vicious circle. Industry
cannot go on carrying a burden which is
stopping it working.
In the past this country, I think, was
known and had a reputation far and wide
for a characteristic, and that characteristic was thrift. On that thrift was
built our agricultural, linen, and shipbuilding industries. I think we want an
example from the Government in order
to bring back this thought that used to
be the leading point in our social life.
We have built up here in Northern Ireland a structure which, I think, in years
of plenty can be carried on, but this
structure is too heavy for these lean years.
I think it is somewhat top heavy, and
we have got to come down to plain finance
and thrift to get back so that the wheels
of industry may turn faster in the future.
This can only be done when all in Northern Ireland realise that the Government
has no inexhaustible supply of money.
The limit of taxation has been reached,
and to get back to our old position of
work and thrift we must realise that
sacrifices have to be made by all who live
in this country. May I say that the basis
of the social structure-economy, thrift,
industry and commerce-depends on one
thing, and that is social security, and so
long as we maintain and have our connection with the British Empire we have
that social security which we on this side
all stand on.

I was also asked a definite question

approximately, is a debt on the Unemployment Fund, and it is right perhaps

deficit, and that when Great Britain

to the specific question asked.
