PROROGATION.
Message from the Senate.
A Message was delivered by the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:
I am commanded to inform this
honourable House that the Proclamation of his Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland proroguing this
present Session of Parliament is to be
communicated forthwith, and, further,
I am commanded to invite this honourable House to attend in the Senate
in order to hear the said Proclamation.
The House went, and having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER: This House has this
day attended in the Senate, when the
following Proclamation proroguing this
present Session of Parliament was read
by the Speaker of the Senate: :-
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR
OF NORTHERN IRELAND.
A
PROCLAMATION
For Proroguing the present Parliament
of Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by Section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said Act,
that the Governor of Northern Ireland
shall in his Majesty's name summon,
prorogue and dissolve the Parliament of
Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that
this present Parliament of Northern
Ireland should be prorogued to the
twenty-second day of November, One
thousand nine hundred and thirty-two:
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, KNIGHT OF
THE MOST NOBLE ORDER OF THE
GARTER, KNIGHT OF THE MOST
ILLUSTRIOUS ORDER OF ST.
PATRICK, Governor of Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do publish
and declare his Majesty's Pleasure that
the said Parliament be, as from the
Prorogation
Prorogation
HOUSE OF COMMONS
reading of this Proclamation in the
Parliament of Northern Ireland, prorogued
to Tuesday, the twenty-second day of
November, One thousand nine hundred
and thirty-two.
AND I do hereby further declare his
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall on the said
twenty-second day of November, One
thousand nine hundred and thirty-two,
assemble and be holden at Stormont for
the despatch of divers urgent and
important affairs, and the Senators and
Members of the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland are hereby required to
give their attendance accordingly.
Given at Baronscourt, County Tyrone,
this twenty-ninth day of September, One
thousand nine hundred and thirty-two.
(Signed by his own hand)
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
End of the Fourth Session (opened

Tuesday, 8th March, 1932) of the Third
Parliament of Northern Ireland in the
twenty-third year of the Reign of his
Majesty King George the Fifth.

Tuesday, 8th March, 1932.
The Fourth Session of the Third Parliament of Northern Ireland appointed to
meet on 8th March, 1932, in the twentysecond year of the Reign of King George
V, was opened by the Governor (His
Grace the Duke of Abercorn, K.G.,
K.P.) in person.
The House met at Twelve of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER (the Rt. Hon. Viscount
Bangor, O.B.E., D.L.) in the Chair.
KING'S SPEECH.
His Grace the Governor, being seated
on the Throne, commanded the Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod to let the
Commons know "It is His Grace's
pleasure that they attend him immediately
in this House."
The Commons being at the Bar with
their Speaker, His Grace delivered the
following Speech from the Throne:-
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I view with concern the repercussion
of the world economic crisis upon those
major industries of our Country which
are dependent upon international commerce. Nevertheless, the textile trade
has benefited to a certain extent by
the recent change in the fiscal system
of the United Kingdom of Great
Britain and Northern Ireland. I trust
this improvement may be maintained,
that its sphere may be extended to
other industries in the near future, and
that by these factors together with the
continued exercise of strict economy
in Government and local administration the foundations for an increase of
prosperity may be laid.
I am glad to observe that since a
year ago the improved state of trade,
apart from shipbuilding, has been reflected in a substantial decrease in unemployment, the Registers of the
Exchanges having recorded a fall of
13,657. It is satisfactory also to note
the amicable relations existing between
employers and employed; important
wage adjustments have been negotiated
within the last few months in a commendable spirit of reasonableness.
The prolonged depression in our
staple trades, upon which so large a
section of the people is dependent, has
thrown into bold relief the desirability
of a wider diversity in our industrial
activities. My Government will continue its efforts to encourage the
establishment of new industries and in
pursuance of this policy legislative
A
King's Speech
King's Speech

THE SENATE
proposals will be laid before you for the
purpose of empowering it to grant free
sites to firms desirous of establishing
new undertakings in Northern Ireland.
Proposals have been formulated dealing with Local Government Reform
and have been circulated to the various
organisations of Local Authorities in
Northern Ireland. Any representations received from them will receive
the most careful and sympathetic
consideration.
In framing these proposals my
Government have anxiously endeavoured
to avoid any possibility of imposing
additional charges on the rates.
In the meantime, I am glad to learn
that my Government, in co-operation
with Local Authorities, have been able,
by administrative measures, to effect
considerable reforms in the direction of
closing down Workhouses and of establishing up-to-date District Hospitals.
It is proposed to introduce a Bill
prolonging the restrictions on rents of
the smaller type of houses, and remedying, as far as possible, certain abuses
which have been brought to light in the
recent Report submitted by the Select
Committee on Rents.
A Bill will also be introduced for the
purpose of continuing for a further two
years a modified principle of Government Subsidy for working-class dwellings and enabling Local Authorities, as
heretofore, to co-operate with the
Government in the encouragement of
the building of these houses.
The Bills which were introduced last
Session dealing with necessary reforms
of the Lunacy Laws and the Consolidation of the Law relating to Joint
Stock Companies will be reintroduced
during the forthcoming Session.
Other Bills will be laid before you
dealing with the following matters:-
Law of Landlord and Tenant.
Poultry Diseases.
Valuation of Railways.
Amendment of the
Slaughtered
Animals (Compensation) A ct,
1928.
Garden Allotments for the Unemployed.
Members of the House of Commons.
The Estimates for the Public Services will be laid before you in due
course.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I recognise the serious hardship
which has been experienced by the
farming community through the severe
fall in agricultural prices which has
occurred as a result of the world
economic depression of the past few
years. A measure of protection is,
however, being afforded to farmers
through the imposition of duties on
imports of certain classes of agricultural commodities including potatoes,
oats, eggs, poultry and dairy produce.
It is the policy of my Government to
seize the opportunity afforded by these
duties to extend, by all practicable
means, the market for our agricultural
produce in Great Britain.
It has been announced that as soon
as a scheme for the reorganisation of
the bacon industry has been prepared
a
measure for the quantitative regulation of imports of bacon into the
United Kingdom will be introduced.
My Government trusts that farmers
will put themselves in a position to
take advantage of the regulation of
imports as soon as it is put into
operation.
I am gratified to learn that substantial progress is being made in the
initial stages of the scheme of comprehensive electricity development authorised by recent legislation. I look
forward with confidence to the beneficial effects of this scheme both to
industrialists and to private citizens
throughout Northern Ireland.
And I pray that the blessing of
Almighty God may rest upon your deliberations.
Then His Grace was pleased to retire,
and the Commons withdrew.
House adjourned during pleasure.
House resumed.

Address in Reply to His Majesty's
Most Gracious Speech.
Mr.
SPEAKER having read the
King's Speech,
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH (in
morning dress): I beg to move "That an
humble Address be presented to His
Grace in the following words:-
"Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and
loyal subjects, the Senate of the Parliament of Northern Ireland, beg leave
to offer our humble thanks to Your
Grace for the speech which Your Grace
has addressed to both Houses of
Parliament."
and
Filling for the time being, as I do, the
office of chief magistrate of the capital
city of Northern Ireland, I appreciate
the honour conferred upon me
through me upon the Municipality of
Belfast, in my being permitted to move
the Address. It is appropriate that the
main theme of the Gracious Speech should
relate as it does to economics. The position
called loudly for the best intellects which
the country could produce, and the
response came from the people themselves, who made possible the constitution of a National Government at
Westminster, whose wise administration
has its reflex in the words of one phrase
of the Gracious Speech we have heard,
namely, "the recent change in the fiscal
system of the United Kingdom of Great
Britain and Northern Ireland," whereby
our industries are
very materially
assisted. The question, or rather, the
problem, presented by the call for
reduction of expenditure, is one that
may be termed a two-edged sword and
must be handled by experts, as
there can be unwise, as well as
wise, economy; for if, in response
to the call for economy, the internal
expenditure of the nation is substantially
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
THE SENATE
[Sir C. McCullagh]
reduced, the industry of the country will
have a continuous tendency to reduce in
volume, with the result that unemployment will steadily increase. Obviously,
the cutting of expenditure, which reduces
the demand for labour should, where
possible, be avoided. The decrease in the
figures of unemployment referred to in
the Gracious Speech is a hopeful sign,
and we pray that the fall may continue.
We rejoice to know that Measures are to
be presented which will have for their
object the attraction of new industries
to Northern Ireland, and we sincerely
hope that the people will see that it is
to their interest to assist the Government in this most laudable movement.
I do think if everyone would assist new
industries I do not mean competitive
industries however small they may be
at the moment, there is no knowing how
big they may be in time, it would bring
more employment.
The Measure which is to be presented
dealing with Local Government Reform
will, no doubt, be carefully and sympathetically considered by all local authorities, and, if facilities are given for the
joint consideration of the proposals by
the experts and the practical exponents
of Local Government, the outcome should
materially improve the present system,
which in some respects might be described
as antiquated. The necessity for the
continuation of the restrictions on rents
of the smaller types of houses is obvious,
and the people of Northern Ireland will
appreciate the wisdom of the proposals.
in this respect foreshadowed in the
Gracious Speech. Also the continuation
of the principle of Government subsidy
for working-class dwellings, if restricted.
to houses which can be let at low rents,
will be welcomed by that class of workers
whose incomes are small and whose claims
have hitherto received little attention.
As regards the subsidy, perhaps I
should say my mind goes back to the first
subsidy on these houses. Then it was
thought that something like three years
would be sufficient to bridge over the
difficulty, that is to say, that private
enterprise would come in again and start
building. Unfortunately, many years
have passed since it was forecasted that
private enterprise would start to build
again in three years' time. As it is today we have made great headway.
we have not yet got to the point when
the supply is equal to the demand.
Still
The amendment of the Lunacy Laws
has been delayed too long, and it is hoped
that the Measure to be submitted dealing
with this subject, which is really one of
National rather than local interest will,
when it reaches its final stages, be satisfactory to all concerned.
The consolidation of the law relating
to joint stock companies should prove of
material advantage to the industrial and
trading concerns of the Province. The
other legislation promised will be looked
forward to with interest, while at least
some of the Measures mentioned will be
gladly welcomed.
an
It has been a matter of satisfaction to
the Corporation, over which I have the
honour to preside, that their electricity
undertaking has proved to be
important factor in assisting the Government in its scheme of comprehensive
electricity development. In this connection I should like to pay a tribute to
the Harbour Board for the facilities
given to the Corporation by that Board
for the acquisition of the splendid site.
on which the principal electricity
generating station now stands with ample
room for extensions to meet the requirements of Northern Ireland for many
years to come. I beg to move.
Mr. JOSEPH CUNNINGHAM (in
morning dress): I consider it a great
privilege to have this opportunity of
seconding the Address of Thanks for the
Gracious Speech from the Throne, which
has been proposed with such well-chosen
words by the right hon. the Lord Mayor
of Belfast. As a working-man representative of this House, I much appreciate
the great compliment paid, not to me
personally, but to those honest workingclass people with whom I have lived and
worked for the greater part of my life.
As usual, the words contained in the
Gracious Speech again convey to the
people of this Province the anxiety and
interest which His Grace continually
entertains for their welfare, and I am
sure all Members of this House will join
in the fervent hope that the improvement
which is noticeable as a result of the
recent change in our fiscal system will
bring about increased prosperity.
It is most gratifying to note the great
reduction in our unemployment figures,
and I have no doubt that this is princi-
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
8 MARCH 1932
pally due to the improvement in our linen
industry. The people are now reaping
the benefit of the Government's active
assistance with the advertising schemes
which were carried on for a number of
years in co-operation with the linen trade
organisations. I wish some means could
be discovered to help to restore employment in our shipyards. The employers
are doing all that is humanly possible,
but they are meeting with little success.
We have the best-equipped yards here,
and a plentiful supply of good, willing
workers, who are certainly very reasonable to deal with.
I sincerely hope that the Government
will be successful in their efforts to encourage the establishment of new industries in this area. There is none who
will appreciate their efforts more than
the unemployed men and women,
are so anxious to obtain work.
who
The proposals regarding Local Government reform, and the Bill dealing with
rent restriction will, I feel sure, be carefully considered by the Members of this
House, and followed with great interest
by the electorate. It is a pity that
further legislation is required to prolong
restriction, but owing to the conduct of
a few unscrupulous property owners it is
evidently considered necessary. I am
glad to know that it is proposed to continue for a further period the subsidy for
working-class dwellings. I believe it is
necessary to encourage the building of
these houses, so that a good supply will
be available for the poorer classes.
might then be possible for the local authorities to deal successfully with the clearance of slum property if other accommodation could be offered. In the end it
may prove the most economical.
It
There are other Bills mentioned which,
if passed into law, will prove very beneficial to the people of Northern Ireland.
The conditions of the farming community
are also mentioned, and the serious hardships with which they have to contend.
These are sympathetically recognised, and
with a little patience and perseverance
I believe agriculture as well as industry
will again prosper.
Mr. CAMPBELL: We have had the
views of the supporters of the Government presented to the House by the right
hon. the Lord Mayor of Belfast and by
Senator Joseph Cunningham in becoming
and suitable language. If I may say so,
I think the one did it more with the charm
of art, and the other with the grace of
nature. I am delighted that the Lord
Mayor has been chosen by his party for
this honour, although I must say I have a
strange feeling when I think about the
last Session of Parliament and that
wonderful Revaluation Bill over which we
spent so many agonising hours, and the
bold attitude taken by the Lord Mayor in
connection with that Bill. We are told
that a Corporation-and the Lord Mayor
represents a Corporation-has neither a
soul to save nor a body to kick, but it
certainly has one cheek to turn to the
smiter who has struck the other cheek.
For the Lord Mayor personally I entertain feelings of the highest regard, and his
intervention in debates in this House is
always straight to the point.
With regard to Senator Joseph Cunningham, I am very glad he is sitting in
front of me to-day. He usually sits
behind my colleagues and myself,
although we know he is never behind
us in spirit. He has one great
advantage over us, because he always
speaks after us and therefore I am not in
a position to tell him what I think of him
publicly. What I think of him privately
is another matter altogether, but the more
I think of the policy he advocates the less
I think of it. He has told us here today, not in so many words, but he has implied that a Government such as the
present Government of Northern Ireland
has not existed since Governments were
first established. I would say the same,
but I would say it in another sense.
have recognised in the hon. Senator
sparks of independence, and I only hope
he will not damp down those sparks.
I
The jejune speech from the Throne contains a freezing reference to the control
of rents and no reference at all to the repercussion on Ulster of the revolutionary
changes in the fiscal system of the United
Kingdom on Leap Year Day when the
Free Trade flag was hauled down from the
masthead after fluttering there for ninety
years a fitting day for a leap in the dark.
You will not be celebrating the day next
year. (Laughter).
(Laughter). The scandals of exorbitant rents, usurious sub-lettings, oppressive lettings under colour of purchases
and key money ought to be put an end to.
If the promised legislation comes up to
expectations, I shall be agreeably surprised. Accompanying decontrol, rents
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
THE SENATE
[Mr. Campbell]
in many cases have been increased fifty
per cent., one hundred per cent. or more.
I notice that the Wrexham Urban District
Council are letting substantial threebedroomed houses with parlour and a
large living room at a rent of 8s 6d a
week, including the consolidated and
water rates and are actually making a
small profit.
What a prospect that would be if a
similar state of affairs could be brought
into being in the City of Belfast.
The Speech holds out some hope that
security of tenure will be given to leaseholders in urban areas in Northern Ireland. That is a reform that is long overdue. The recommendations of the Committee which sat and investigated that
matter have been pigeon-holed now for a
very long time. Will the Bill which is
foreshadowed give protection to building
tenants against confiscation of their improvements? Will it give security to
short-term leaseholders? If it does not
the Bill to a large extent will be an idle
and futile Measure.
If Parliament dare speak its mind
openly and frankly it will not be silent.
as to the urgent necessity of checking the
orgy of extravagance into which the Government has been plunging by the almost
interminable process of broadcasting
guarantees in favour of shipping and shipbuilding concerns. Six years ago the
British Government put a stop to this
process, but the local Government has
gone on heaping guarantee on guarantee,
and piling liability upon liability. It is
the money of the people of Ulster that is
being pledged and perilled with spendthrift profusion. The total of these loans
guaranteed by the Northern Government
was £11,300,000, of which close on
£3,000,000 has been repaid, leaving a
liability of about £8,500,000 still outstanding, a staggering load for our small
community. It is a Nemesis of public
finance that the Northern Government
should probably be far and away the largest
creditor of one huge combine. Yet, such
is the utter and unquestioning submissiveness of the servile majority in Parliament
that the Government will likely have the
hardihood to ask leave later in the Session to pour another million or two of
hard won Ulster money into some bottomless pit. It is rather significant that the
Government's guarantees for all other
concerns are about one-hundredth of its
guarantees for shipbuilding adventures.
The speech says nothing about any effort
by the Government to secure to the
farmer in Ulster advantages corresponding to the advantages given to the farmer
in Great Britain by the Imperial Wheat
Bill, or to protect the people of Ulster
against the higher prices of bread consequent on the operation of the Bill. How
are they to protect the people of Northern
Ireland from the high prices that are
bound to result in this area from the
operation of that Bill? That Bill ensures
to the British farmer for his wheat an
average price of 45/- a quarter by a levy
of so much a sack on millers and flour
importers who will in turn recoup themselves by increasing the prices to their
customers. If, as is anticipated, this Bill
for the benefit of the British farmer raises
the price of the 4-lb. loaf by one halfpenny, it will mean an extra charge of
£600 a day, or £200,000 a year on the
people of Ulster without one penny of
benefit to the farmers of Ulster, who grew
last year only 3,000 acres of wheat.
Must we interpret the silence of the Speech
on the subject as a sign that the Government is lethargic to the effect upon Northern Ireland of the recent revolutionary
changes in the fiscal system of the United
Kingdom? During the last few weeks
tariffs have sprung up with a rush like
mushroom growths. Very few of the
imports upon which tariffs have been
levied come direct to the ports of Northern Ireland, like Belfast, Larne, or
Londonderry. The goods and commodities
enter London and other cross-Channel
ports in bulk. If the tariffs are a means
of raising revenue from the foreigner,
what revenue will they bring to Northern
Ireland? Is any share of the new tariff
revenue allotted to Northern Ireland?
Inevitably the tariffs will mean that the
people here will have to pay more for the
imported goods. People are apt to forget
that the Parliament of the United Kingdom, which levies and collects 75 per
cent. of the taxation of Ulster, will levy
and collect almost 100 per cent. of the
tariff revenue of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
Mr. MCALLISTER: I should like to

could have handled the goods at his

command with greater skill and ability.

of Mr. Joseph Cunningham, who

I think it would be opportune for one
who has more or less rural area interests
to intervene at this period to voice something of the views of the rural districts
and the country classes in Northern Ireland, and I make no apology for once
again deploring in this House that no
real, substantial, or comprehensive effort
is contemplated or forecasted by the
Speech to regenerate agricultural industry. And I make no apology for
again trying to impress upon this House
and the Government that agriculture is
the very foundation and indispensible
industry and the one hope of success for
the people of Northern Ireland. Living
in an urban area I would never be jealous
of the progress and prosperity of the City
of Belfast or any other city. But what
I would like to impress upon the House
is this: the urban and rural areas comprise the greater part of Northern Ireland. There is no doubt whatever that
if you can stabilise the agricultural
industry, if you can bring it back to anything like its original prosperity you will
stabilise upon a sound economic position
the whole towns of Northern Ireland,
and if you put them in a sound financial
and economic position that is bound to
have its reflection also on the city of
Belfast, the city of Derry, and other
towns.
I note reference has been made to the
reorganisation of the bacon industry. I
think all those who have any knowledge
whatever of the bacon industry of rural
and urban Northern Ireland will agree
that the time has come when something
should be done to stop the abuses of that
system. There can be no justification for
the fluctuation of the prices from day to
day and from town to town by a ring
of buyers who have a monopoly in this
industry, and who pay the farmers whatever they agree upon on the morning of
the market. I hope, at whatever cost,
whatever scheme may be necessary to
destroy that unhealthy, unfair and unjust
piece of tyranny on the farming community will be adopted, and if the
Government in their reorganisation of the
bacon industry will take steps to stop
that abuse I am sure they will have the
support not only of this House but the
right-thinking people of Northern Ireland. A Bill is foreshadowed on the law
of landlord and tenant in Northern Ireland. Now, if this is to be a Bill merely
to put into statute form the existing law
of the land, a great many people of
Northern Ireland will be very much dissatisfied and disappointed. I know there is
a widespread and almost universal feeling
amongst leaseholders that this Bill will
afford relief to the building leaseholder.
I should like to warn those people whom
my voice may reach, and who are not
familiar with legal technicalities, that if
it is the intention of the Government
merely to put into statute law the existing law it will be no relief for the man
who takes a lease of property for 50, 90,
or 100 years with a covenant in it to build
a house at a certain price. If this contemplated legislation is not to safeguard
what is known as the building leaseholder who forms 99 per cent. of the
householders and property owners of
urban Ireland, if it is not to protect him
from the abuse of high, exorbitant, and
unjust rents being imposed upon him on
the termination of the lease, then this
Bill will be of no benefit good, bad, or
indifferent to the leaseholder of Northern
Ireland.
Surely no one could justify the position
-I do not want to discuss the forecast of
the Bill in detail-but no one could
justify the position of a man taking a
lease of property for 50 years, at say £4

you pay me £20 or £30 ground rent, instead of the £4, you will have to vacate
the premises and I will take them over"
-the man's buildings worth £2,000 or
£3,000 and his whole life's work and the
business he has built up. I do press the
Government to meet that class of case in
this legislation, because if they do not I

seems to me that we hear the voice of our

sure he has earned that in his representhe

tative capacity, but I think we are unanimous, as I said just now, in feeling that
in this case the compliment has been

(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
And now to come to another matter.
I am sure that we all feel, sitting here
to-day, that we are to some extent
perhaps at a disadvantage, and we are
certainly sitting with a feeling of regret
in our hearts at the absence of the noble
Lord, the Leader of the House. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). We miss the
noble Viscount. We miss him as a Leader;
we miss him perhaps more as a man.
The duties of leadership, as we know,
are in competent hands, and we owe much
to the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr.
Long) for the manner in which he discharges them, but the charming geniality
of the noble Viscount is exclusively his
own, and our sittings are the poorer for
the absence of that personality.
As regards the Gracious Speech itself,
one notices that economy has been placed,
so to speak, in the forefront of the battle.
Economy is, as indeed the Lord Mayor
has reminded us, a two-edged sword.
Undoubtedly a most rigorous, if not ruthless economy is required at the present
time owing to the fact that during the
past twenty years or so national expenditure has outrun the constable. But
that economy must be regulated according to well understood rules; that is to
say, administrative economies must never
go beyond the limit as regards proceeding without due Parliamentary sanction.
That is a matter which must from time
to time necessarily engage the attention
of one House or the other.
Again, that economy has to be both
national and local, for it must be remembered that whether we are dealing with
taxes or rates either one or the other extracts from the pockets of the citizens
certain sums of money which are required
for the purposes of administration and
government. The two interests are not
necessarily opposed, although it has been
stated here more than once, I think by
a former Member of this House, that it
is the duty of Parliament to safeguard
the taxpayer rather than the ratepayer,
while those who sit on local authorities
are expected to endeavour to safeguard
the ratepayer at the expense, if need be,
of the taxpayer.
That particular contrast is, I am afraid, not one which
we could do away with even if we would.
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
8 MARCH 1932
A good deal is said in the Gracious
Speech on the subject of our new fiscal
arrangements, and much has been said,
relatively much, on the advantage which
may be expected to accrue to the agricultural industry. Poultry, dairy produce,
and potatoes are specifically referred to,
and a scheme for the re-organisation of
the bacon industry is adumbrated.
Former speakers have dealt with what I
may call the pig products of the North of
Ireland farmer, and it is a matter which
awakens widespread interest in the agricultural community. But in any effort.
made for ameliorating the conditions,
whether it be as regards eggs, pork, or
bacon, it ought constantly to be borne
in mind that the primary object ought to
be to benefit the farmer who produces the
eggs, bacon, or potatoes. There is too
much danger-and it is brought to our
notice again and again-of any increased
price that may be obtainable, say in the
London market, finding its way into the
hands of the handler or middleman, and
not going back to the producer, as it
ought to.
So it may happen that although your
Ulster egg or Ulster pig may command
the highest possible price in the London
market, the producer of the Ulster egg
or pig might not be receiving a relatively
commensurate return for his responsibility, expense, and trouble. I do venture to hope that that particular matter
of the profits of handler or intermediary
will be very carefully watched, and, if I
may use the expression, intensely watched
as tariffs tend to produce alterations in
prices.
There is no concrete Amendment before
the House. I do not know whether it is
the intention of the hon. and learned
Senator (Mr. Campbell) to divide the
House at a later stage on the main question, but the fact that there is no Amendment before us makes it a little difficult
to refer in any detail to the remarks
made by the hon. and learned Senator
(Mr. Campbell) and Senator McAllister.
I may however, perhaps say that the bulk
of the complaints made seem to me to
relate to subjects which have been previously discussed in this House and, if
I may say so, on a more appropriate
occasion. For instance, to take the first
complaint on the Revaluation Bill, that
was
more appropriate to the discussion
of the Bill, which has now become an
Act, and the matter of the guarantees
has certainly been before us on several
previous occasions.
As regards the general remarks on
fiscal matters, if the hon. and learned
Senator will pardon me for making a
suggestion, I do not think he attached
sufficient importance to the injurious
effects of what is known as dumping.
That is a term which we all well understand, and that dumping is a thing at
which the new fiscal arrangement is particularly aimed. As regards the question
of the proposals made by the Imperial
Parliament for establishing something
in the nature of a wheat quota, one cannot but remark that, as we know from
previous assurances in this House, the
amount of wheat which could be produced in Northern Ireland is absolutely
negligible and we cannot, I think, admit
that an alteration in the tariff arrangements in Great Britain will be without
their repercussion-to borrow a word used
in the Gracious Speech, and which is my
excuse for once more using the word in
this House-the tariff arrangements cannot be without their effect on the finances
in Northern Ireland. There is such an
inter-dependence between the two financial systems that what benefits one must
directly or indirectly benefit the other.
As regards the possibility of any particular tax hitting the locality of Northern Ireland harder than Great Britain as
a whole, or some particular locality in
Great Britain, we must of course to some
extent take our chance, but in doing
that we may always rely upon what one
might describe as most favoured locality
treatment, and we have had proof that
for that treatment we shall not look in
vain. We have received a great concession in the matter of the proposed duty
on maize, and we have received a further
concession as regards a certain class of
fibre. What has happened in the past is
an indication of what we may expect in
the future, and I do not think the future
is one to which we may not look forward
with confidence. In conclusion, it only
remains to join heartily in the terms of
the humble Address proposed to be presented to His Grace.
Mr. BARCLAY: I would like to

THE SENATE
[Mr. Barclay]
like to join with the hon. and learned
Senator (Mr. Leslie) in his expression of
sympathy with the noble Leader of the
House, whom we would all like to see

likelihood that he will soon be amongst

the absence of the Leader of the Senate.
This is practically the first occasion
since I became a Member of this House
that hope for the future seems to have
taken possession of the hearts and minds
of the people. At the beginning of every
Session there was always a dark cloud
of some kind hanging over the whole
country, but in the Gracious Speech read
to-day there is a ray of hope for the
future. In Northern Ireland we find today that trade is improving and that the
number of unemployed has decreased by
13,657 people who have found work
within the last few months. That is
something to be thankful for, and I believe it is only the beginning of the
good times that are ahead.
The Speech from the Throne makes
reference to the question of the adjustment of wages. In this respect a little
bit of wisdom is required on the side of
both the employer and the employee. I
hope both sides will use a little discretion
and not place any obstruction in the path
of progress on which we have entered. I
have not the least doubt that both parties
will do their best to settle this question
in the proper spirit.
Then I find again that in the Gracious
Speech reference is made to a Restriction
of Rents Bill going to be brought in. I
am very pleased to know that it is the
mind of the Government to continue rent
restriction on the smaller houses, because
a great number of the people who live in
the smaller houses are unemployed to-day.
Others are earning very small wages, and
cannot really afford to pay any more rent
than they are doing at the present time.
I am very glad to see also that the Government is going to take steps regarding
those who have abused their privileges in
the matter of rents. We passed a Bill
here some time ago removing rent restriction from certain classes of houses,
from £8 to £26 and so on. But when we
passed that Bill we passed it in the faith
at least I voted for it in good faiththat those who owned these houses would
play their part decently. But as the
seconder of the Motion said there were a
few who did not do what was right, and
so I am very pleased to know that the
Government intends to take steps to bring
those who have abused their privileges to
toe the line and do what is right.
Senator McAllister made reference to
rents having gone up by 50, 100, or sometimes 150 per cent. more than they were
previous to rent restriction coming off.
Some of these people who live in these
houses are very important citizens I
might say. They are the thrifty citizens,
and if you are going to penalise the
thrifty people you are going to penalise
the best citizens we have.
Then again the continuance of the
subsidy on working-class houses, in a
modified form, is mentioned in the
Gracious Speech. I have expressed myself
previously in this House regarding these
subsidies. I have not the least doubt
that in the city of Belfast these subsidies
are necessary, for there is a great deal of
slum property which is unhealthy and
bad for the people living there, and for
bringing up children in, and that becomes a weight on the ratepayers later
on. But I would say that in the rural
districts, as far as I can see, there are
sufficient subsidy houses. I hope that
when the Government comes to bring in
this Bill they will take that into consideration, and not be handing away
money to owners of land to build houses
and pocket the subsidy and sell the houses
at a profit, or let those houses they do not
sell at 11s or 12s a week. The working
man is not getting any benefit whatever
from the subsidy as far as I know.
As far as I remember the subsidy was
given for the benefit of the working class,
but instead of the working class benefiting
it is the speculative builder. I hope that
when this Bill comes before this House
these people will be protected, and
that the money will not be thrown away,
because the ratepayers to-day are groaning beneath rates, and also taxation, that
they cannot afford. There has been
some reduction in rates, but I think there
is no district that could not do with a
great deal more reduction than it has
received.

There is another Bill mentioned here.

There
be unwise as well as
may
economies. During the last eleven years

I may say that we hope to have him back

My first duty is to offer my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the
Address on their eloquent and admirable
speeches. The Lord Mayor is specially

Ireland, which was mentioned in the

valuable contribution to the debate, which
has been marked with his usual knowledge, judgment and good sense.
In regard to the matters which are
mentioned in the Gracious Speech, I
would like to refer to the definite improvement which has taken place in the
linen industry in recent months. Unem-
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
8 MARCH 1932
ployment in this industry has declined.
from the figure of 20,000 persons in
September to 10,840 in January last, and
the various subsidiary industries also
show a welcome advance. It is hoped
that this improvement will still further
develop and will extend to other industries as well. I may here make a
reference to the Bill which is to be introduced, empowering, on the one hand, the
Government to provide free sites for the
establishment of new industries offering
substantial employment and, on the other
hand, empowering municipalities to grant,
should they consider it desirable, complete
or partial remission of rates on the property concerned. One of our main
difficulties has, of course, been that here
in Northern Ireland in the past we have
been inclined to concentrate on a few
major industries and, as a result, we have
felt unemployment all the more severely
when these particular industries became
depressed.
Perhaps the most prominent matter
which has been in the mind of the Government and the public generally during the
last few weeks, has been the very important effects on our Province of the new
Imperial policy, so far as it concerns
our own trade, including agricultural
products.
Since the close of the last Parliamentary Session, certain developments.
of the very greatest importance have
taken place in connection with the outlook for the agricultural industry. The
intentions of the National Government in
regard to agricultural policy have been
made available, and it has become
necessary for our Ministry of Agriculture
to consider carefully the action which
will be required to enable farmers in Northern Ireland to take the fullest possible
advantage of the new economic conditions
in regard to the industry which have come
into being as a result of the passage of
the Import Duties Bill and which will
arise as soon as the detailed statement of
agricultural policy which has been outlined by Sir John Gilmour has been
brought into operation.
As hon. Members are aware, a measure
of protection will in future be awarded
to various classes of our agricultural
produce on the British market.
Eggs
and poultry, milk and dairy produce,
oats, fruit, potatoes and grass seed imported from foreign countries into the
United Kingdom will all be subject to a
10 per cent. duty. As a consequence, the
demand for these classes of our produce
on the part of the British consumers is
likely to be increased, and I can assure
hon. Members that no effort will be
spared by the Government of Northern
Ireland to extend by all possible means
the market for these classes of our
produce. The advantage which a 10 per
cent. duty on produce such as eggs and
poultry, milk and dairy produce and
potatoes will be to our farmers will be
realised when I state that approximately
50 per cent. of the agricultural output
of Northern Ireland is derived from the
production of these commodities.
Along with the duty upon imports I
would remind hon. Members that farmers
will continue to obtain their most important feeding stuffs and fertilisers from
abroad without any imposition of tariff
duty. Moreover, there is a definite
prospect that in the very near future
further advantage will accrue to the
farming community when the Imperial
Government's policy has been fully
worked out. It is hoped that at no late
date a scheme for the quantitative control of imports of bacon will be put into
operation. This scheme will be dependent upon a satisfactory reorganisation of
the bacon industry in the United Kingdom being effected, so that home producers will be in a position to guarantee
that if they are allocated a definite
percentage of the home requirements for
bacon and hams the necessary supplies of
pigs will be forthcoming. So far as we in
Northern Ireland are concerned, the
Government is confident that no difficulties will be experienced in extending our
production of pork to meet whatever
quota percentage is required. I may also
say that the question of doing something
to steady the pork market is receiving
the attention of our Government.
Senator McAllister referred to the
fluctuation in prices, and I may mention
that in my own case the fluctuation has
ranged from 38s to 116s. As is well
known, one of the handicaps to pork
raisers at present is the uncertainty of
the market, and my right hon. Friend,
the Prime Minister, hopes to call a conference at an early date of the producers
and the pork merchants with a view to
seeing whether something can be done.
towards stabilising prices by mutual
agreement.
Meantime our own Government are
continuing their efforts to protect the interests of our farmers, especially as re-

gards the risk of the introduction and

The serious losses which our farmers may
experience as a result of disease were
brought vividly home to every member of
the community last year when an unfortunate outbreak of foot and mouth
disease occurred. As hon. Members are
aware, we have a definite code of legislation which enables us to deal with
disease amongst animals, and this legislative power has been of the very greatest
service to us in the maintenance of our
stocks of cattle free from many of the
worst and most contagious diseases to
which live stock on the continent of
Europe are so frequently subject.
defect in the code of existing legislation,
however, is that no provision exists to
enable us to safeguard ourselves against
the risk of the introduction of poultry
diseases.
A
In recent years poultry have become of
such great value to our farmers that if
has become more and more necessary to
legislate against the danger of diseases of
this character. Within the past few
years the prevalence of bacillary white
diarrhoea amongst our poultry has been
a matter for very grave concern to my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Agriculture, and unfortunately it appears
that this disease has been imported from
Great Britain, where many of our
breeders obtain eggs for hatching purposes and also day-old chicks and stock
birds. At the moment we have no power
to intervene, but a Bill will be introduced during the present session to
enable us to control the very grave risks
which at present exist in regard to the
introduction and spread of this and other
serious diseases which, if left uncontrolled,
might speedily do untold harm to the
poultry industry of the country.

Another Bill which will be submitted
for your consideration is in connection
with the compensation of exporters of
stock who experience losses due
animals being detained in British lairages
on account of a sudden outbreak of footand-mouth disease. An insurance fund
is already in existence whereby cattle
shippers are recompensed for any losses
which they experience through animals
for export being slaughtered on arrival in
Great Britain on account of foot-andmouth disease being prevalent at the
landing place. It is now proposed that
this insurance measure should extend to
cover abnormal expenses incurred in the
detention of animals for prolonged periods
at British ports.
Referring to other legislation which is
foreshadowed in the Gracious Speech, I
should like to draw particular attention
to the question of local government reform. For some considerable time past
the Government have had under consideration the recommendations which
were submitted by the Departmental
Commission on Local Government Services
in 1927. The recommendations made by
that Committee were of a most valuable
character and embraced the whole ambit
of Local Government Services. The whole
position, however, was very much altered
owing to the introduction of the principle
of derating and also of the institution of
the medical benefit, known as the panel
system, and it became necessary to reconsider the Committee's recommendations in the light of these more important
factors.
At the same time the Government felt
that it was imperative that in the consideration of any reforms extreme care
should be exercised in estimating the
financial effect of such reforms or changes,
as, having regard to the present financial
situation it is desirable-if not essential
-that no changes should be effected
which might in any way be liable to increase the burden on the local authorities
or on the Government. Finally, after
careful consideration and deliberation, it
was found necessary to depart, in detail
rather than in principle, from the general
trend of the Committee's recommendation,
and to formulate proposals which, as far
as could be ascertained, would not impose
additional burdens on the ratepayers.
These proposals were embodied in a
circular letter which was addressed to the
representative organisations of local
authorities some months ago, and the
whole question is at present receiving the
careful attention of the authorities and
their organisations. As far as can be
ascertained at present, it would appear
that local authorities themselves apprehend the possibility of additional charges
being imposed on them by the introduction of even the modified scheme formulated by my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Home Affairs, and I would
like to give this assurance, on his behalf,
that if it should transpire that the local
authorities as a whole-who are, after all,

It will be within the knowledge of the
Members of this House that a Parliamentary Select Committee was set up last
Session to inquire into certain anomalies
and hardships arising out of the operation
of the Rent Restriction Acts. The Committee has submitted its report to Parliament and the Government, and it is the
intention, as indicated in the Gracious
Speech, to introduce at a very early date
a Bill giving effect, where possible, to the
recommendations of the Committee, with
the object of removing abuses, rectifying
hardships and prolonging the period of
control for a further period of years.
It will also have been observed in the
Speech that the Government propose to
continue the principle of paying subsidies.
for the building of smaller types of
houses for the working classes. Pending
the introduction of the proposed Measure
it would be out of place for me to enter
into any details, but it is the intention
of the Government to focus attention on
these smaller houses, and, as heretofore,
to grant to local authorities power to
supplement the Government's efforts in
the encouragement of building. The
Government is still satisfied that the
question of rents cannot be adjusted by
Governmental action, and that the only
means by which satisfactory results in
regard to rents can be obtained is by
encouraging the building of smaller
houses.
The Bill dealing with the reform of
lunacy laws which was introduced into
Parliament last Session, but which for
want of time, could not be proceeded
with, will be re-introduced this Session.
During the interval an opportunity has
been taken by my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Home Affairs, to consider
views which have been put before him
by experts on these matters, namely,
officials and members of asylum committees and by others who are best
qualified to judge, as a result of which
considerable improvements have been
made in the Bill. The re-introduction of
this Bill marks the first step in the process
of reforming our local services. Without
going into details, I may say that it is
intended to bring the whole service into
line with the system which now prevails
in Great Britain, and which has been
generally based on expert advice and investigation extending over many years.
Modern research and modern thought
have shown that mental disorder requires
the same shades of treatment as any
physical disorder, and treatment directed
towards cure is now the dominant factor.
Finally, I might refer to the consolidation of the law relating to Joint Stock
Companies. Hon. Members will recollect
the somewhat lengthy Measure which
was introduced last Session. This is
being re-introduced and opportunity has
been taken to embody some Amendments
in the original draft. These are being
circulated and a Second Reading will be
taken as soon as they are available and
have been studied by hon. Members.

I should like to point out to

Campbell) that the change of fiscal
policy in the United Kingdom does
not involve a change in the general financial arrangements between the Exchequers
of Northern Ireland and the United
Kingdom. The new fiscal policy relates
entirely to customs duties which are collected by the Imperial authorities.
regard to the yield of the duties, however, I would refer the hon. and learned
Member to the provisions of Section 22
of the Government of Ireland Act which
enables the Joint Exchequer Board to
apportion the yield of such duties,
whether collected in Great Britain or in
Northern Ireland so that each country
will receive the amount
attributable to each area. This function
of the Joint Exchequer Board has been in
operation constantly in regard to the
yield of all reserved taxes, of which the
new duties will form only a small part.
I cannot, of course, deal with the
amount of Northern Ireland's prospective share of the new duties, as
it would, in fact, be improper for me to
attempt to make any premature disclosures of this sort, but I am informed
that my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Finance, is in communication with the
Treasury on the subject with a view to
agreement before presenting a
mendation to the Joint Exchequer Board.
The hon. and learned Member may rest
assured that the Government is fully
alive to the issues involved.

THE SENATE
[Mr. Long]
As regards Loans Guarantees, the hon.
Senator has made an assumption to which
the Government is not prepared to subscribe. He has assumed that Northern
Ireland's financial interests, which have
arisen by reason of guarantees given
under the Loans Guarantee Acts, are
likely to be jeopardised. Given even a
slight return to normality in shipping
conditions, there is no reason why any
ultimate sacrifice should be entailed on
the part of Government.
The hon. Senator has criticised the
application of the Wheat Quota Bill to
Northern Ireland, and apparently considers that the Government has been to
blame in allowing this Measure to apply
to Northern Ireland. The Wheat Quota
Bill, however, must be considered as a
part of the whole agricultural policy of
the Imperial Government. It is easy to
seize upon particular aspects of a comprehensive policy such as that which has been
put forward by the Government, and
suggests that one or other feature of that
policy is detrimental to certain interests.
We have just recently had evidence of the
way in which a comprehensive Measure
such as the Import Duties Act, designed
to benefit the community as a whole, may
prejudice certain local sectional interests.
The agricultural policy which has been
enunciated by the Minister of Agriculture.
and Fisheries must be considered as a
whole, and in conjunction with the
benefits which agriculture is deriving
from the passage of the Import Duties
Act. When this is done we find that,
first, a ten per cent. duty has been imposed upon imports of eggs, poultry,
milk and dairy produce, and potatoes.
Approximately 50 per cent. of the value
of our agricultural output is made up of
these commodities. Imports of oats,
fruit and grass-seeds will also be subject
to duty.
Secondly, as a result of the
efforts of our Government, maize-the
most important feeding stuff used by our
farmers will be admitted free of duty.
Thirdly, a definite promise has been
given by Sir John Gilmour that at an
early date a scheme for the quantitative
control of imports of bacon will be put
into operation. When this is done our
farmers will reap very definite advantages
in view of the important facilities we enjoy for the feeding and rearing of pigs.
Along with these aspects of agricultural
policy to which I have referred, the
of
Imperial Government were most anxious
to do something for the wheat growers in
East Anglia, where the incidence
agricultural depression has probably been
more severe than anywhere else. Since
wheat has not been included under the
Import Duties Act the Wheat Quota Bill
has been introduced. It would have been
impossible for the Wheat Quota Bill to
have been made applicable to Great
Britain alone. To have done so would
have rendered the scheme unworkable,
and it had to be made applicable to the
whole Customs union of Great Britain
and Northern Ireland.
Even in England and Wales some
areas will derive like benefit from
the Wheat Quota scheme. In Scotland it is estimated that the cost
of the scheme will be £750,000, and
that only £250,000 will be returned
to the grower. But areas such as the
West of England, Scotland, and Northern
Ireland
are deriving benefit in other
ways through the 10 per cent. import
duty and through the quantitative control of imports of bacon which will
subsequently be introduced.
I should like to say, therefore, and I
am sure hon. Senator McAllister in his
concern for farming interests will agree,
that the Government are doing all
possible in the interests of agriculture.

beg to ask the Leader of the House if the
Government would consider the advisability of introducing legislation to remove the liability from public bodies of
having to pay for losses for malicious
injuries.
In asking this question I should like
to point out that we in Northern Ireland
are the only people who have such a law
as this. If a fire takes place in England

or Scotland the owner of the premises
destroyed is expected to be insured, and
if he is not he has to stand the loss.
think the necessity for our law arose at a

not so good as it is now. Since that time
our police force has developed into the

old days if people saw a disturbance and

LICENSING OF FILMS.
The following Question stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Mr.
Campbell:-
To ask the Leader of the House
whether his attention had been drawn to
the serious warning to the film industry
contained in the report of 1931 of the
British Board of Film Censors regarding
films which call for drastic action, and
whether the Government will consider the
advisability of holding a comprehensive inquiry into the arrangements for
licensing films so as to insure uniformity
of treatment for particular films and
prevent different licensing authorities
acting independently.
Mr. CAMPBELL: A grave warning
to the film industry regarding "sex"
films, which, it is stated, are becoming
more and more daring, is contained in
the report for 1931 of the British Board
of Film Censors.
421781
The report declares:-"There has
unquestionably been a tendency of
late, for films to become more and
more daring, the result probably of the
large number of stage plays which are
now presented on the screen, and of
the licence which is to-day allowed in
current fiction.
"Subjects coming under the category of what has been termed 'Sex'
films, others containing various phases
of immorality and incidents which tend.
to bring the institution of marriage into
contempt, show a marked increase in
number.
"The president has come to the
definite conclusion that more drastic
action will have to be taken with regard to such films in the future."
The number of films to which exception was taken by the British Censors and
of films definitely rejected showed a
marked increase in 1931. No fewer
than thirty-four films were totally rejected, the reasons being:-
Blasphemy and comic treatment of
religious subjects.
Travesty of religious rites.
The institution of marriage treated
with contempt.
Death treated with vulgar flippancy.
Gross and brutal travesty of prison
life.
Hospital scenes treated with vulgar
levity.
Unrelieved sordid themes.
Prolonged and gross brutality and
bloodshed.
Lives of thoroughly wicked men and
women.
Stories in which criminal element is
predominant.
Habitual youthful depravity.
Habitual immorality.
Offensive political propaganda.
Gross and objectionable dialogue.
A uniform system of licensing films in
this area is necessary. The influence of
the cinema upon the young is undoubted.
The official distinction between films
which might be shown to children and
films which might not be shown to
children is idle and futile. Some police
authorities think the censorship of films.
is not work for them. Some people say
that the public is the best censor, and I
think this is the opinion of the Government. But the cinema exhibitors say
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
THE SENATE
[Mr. Campbell]
that the films to which exception is taken
are shown because of a public demand
for them.
As the law stands there is no means of
ensuring the uniform black-listing of a
banned film. Different licensing authorities take different views of a film, or a
licensing authority may be utterly indifferent to, or practically ignorant of its
duties. The result is that a film may be
banned on one side of the street and blazoned
by posters for exhibition on the other. At
various cinemas showing films marked as
fit only for grown-up persons, children
are allowed to attend if accompanied by
a parent or a responsible adult. If a
film is unfit for a child's view is it fit for
an adult's view? What difference does
the presence of the adult make if the film
is objectionable? The "responsible "
adult is often a fictitious person.
Another aspect of the films appears in
a report presented lately to the London
County Council by its Education Committee on the attendance at cinema performances of children from 29 elementary
schools distributed all over London.
Nearly 9 per cent. of all children attending school, from the age of three to 14,
went to the cinema twice a week, and 30
per cent. once a week. Another 48 per
cent. went at irregular intervals. Only
about 13 per cent. did not go at all.
Of children under five, 63 per cent.
attended the cinema, 30 per cent. at least
weekly, and 7 per cent. twice a week. It
was quite common for children to be
admitted to performances of films which
were for adults only. As to the effects
of attendance at the cinema, one distinct
evil lay in the fear and dreams caused
by films depicting acts of violence. The
evil was mentioned with such frequency
by inspectors and teachers and with such
specific examples as left scarcely any
doubt of its existence. There can be
little question that war pictures, gruesome and terrible details of which are
undoubtedly remembered, and "gangster"
plays have undesirable and possible permanent effects on children. The report
also suggests that it may be right to prevent, altogether, the attendance
cinemas of children under the age of 7
or 8. This is a matter of serious importance nowadays, and I feel that the
greatest defect in our law at the moment
is that the system of licensing fails to
secure the outlawry, all round, of undesirable films in Northern Ireland.

Mr. LONG: In asking the House to
give a Second Reading to this Bill, it will
not be out of place if I give a brief
account of its origin. As long ago as
the year 1925 it was becoming increasingly clear that the code of company law
embodied in the Statutes, and more particularly in the Companies (Consolidation) Act, 1908, required some revision
to bring it into harmony with the modern
conditions, and in that year the President of the Board of Trade set up a very
committee
representative
under the
Chairmanship of Sir Wilfred Greene,
K.C., with terms of reference sufficiently
wide to enable the whole field of company
The
law and practice to be reviewed.
Committee presented their Report in
May, 1926, and stated that in their view,
while the existing company law had on
the whole worked well, further legislation
was necessary for the better regulation of
the formation and management of companies, and the more satisfactory and
uniform presentation of information
regarding the affairs of companies. They
made many recommendations for the
amendment of the law. The Report of
the Committee found acceptance by the
Imperial Government, and its chief recommendations were embodied in the
Companies Act, 1928, the operation of
which, with the exception of one or two
sections, was suspended in order to avoid
difficulties of reference and interpretation until such time as all the provisions
of the code might be embodied in one
Act. This was done when the Companies
Act 1929 was passed.
In Northern Ireland, the Government
felt that it was necessary to adopt a
similar course, and it will be within the
recollection of hon. Members that a Com-
Companies Bill
Poultry Diseases Bill
THE SENATE
[Mr. Long]
panies Act was passed two years ago on
the lines of the British Companies Act
of 1928. With the exception of two
sections, numbers 54 and 96, the provisions of that Act were suspended until
such time as a consolidation Measure
could be prepared and submitted for legislative sanction.
Hon. Members will appreciate that the
task of preparing this Consolidation Bill,
containing as it does, 339 Clauses and 10
Schedules, has been one of considerable
magnitude. It was complicated by
various legal problems, which had to be
considered in the light of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, and the
Adaptation Orders made under that Act.
The body of Statutes that were being consolidated, with the exception, of course,
of the Companies Act (Northern Ireland),
1930, were for the most part of general
application to the United Kingdom, and
it was necessary to examine with meticulous care all the provisions of the various
Acts bearing on company law and
administration, so as to bring in all that
was relevant to Northern Ireland and to
exclude all that might be deemed to have
application only to England or Scotland.
This task was complicated by various
points of constitutional law that arose.
Some idea of the difficulties that arose
on the consolidation of company law by
the Imperial Act of 1929 may be gathered
from a remark of Lord Muir Mackenzie,
who presided over the Joint Committee
of the House of Lords and the House of
Commons. After a lengthy discussion.
on Clause 79, regarding the treatment of
mortgages and charges on land in
Northern Ireland created by companies
registered in England he said, "Then I
may take it that we only pass from the
horrors of 79 to the almost slough of
despond, Clause 80."
Some conception of the range of the
provisions which have been brought
together in this Bill may be gathered
from a perusal of the Tenth Schedule to
the Bill, which contains a list of the
enactments that are being repealed. The
arrangement of the subject matter of the
Bill differs very considerably from the
arrangement followed in the Companies
(Consolidation) Act, 1908. There are
sound reasons for the adoption of this
course, but the best reason of all is the
importance of keeping our Northern
Ireland Act as far as possible in conformity with the Companies Act, 1929,
of the Imperial Parliament. The rearrangement of the sections in the latter
Act was carried out after consultation
with eminent company lawyers, who
expressed their approval of the suggested
change. The Clauses of the Bill now
before the House correspond with the
Sections of the Imperial Act as far as
Clause 71. There is thereafter a divergence, slight at first, but increasing as
the Bill goes on, which is due to the fact
that some of the provisions necessarily
contained in the Imperial Act, as, for
example, matters relating to the Companies' Winding-up Department, which
has no counterpart in Northern Ireland,
and to the Stanneries, find no place in
the Bill. Bearing in mind, however, the
fact that the general arrangement
remains the same, those who have
occasion to use the published text books
on company law will be able to do so
without much inconvenience.
I have stated that this Bill is a consolidation Measure and, this being so, it
does not involve any amendment of
law nor introduce any new principle. It
is highly technical, and the detailed
examination of the Clauses and the Schedules will fall to be dealt with by the
Committee on Consolidation Bills. I do
not think that I can usefully add anything more at this stage and, accordingly, I beg to move.
On Question, Motion agreed to.

Mr. LONG: An outstanding feature
of Northern Ireland agriculture in recent
years has been the remarkable development of the poultry industry. In the
year 1904, the poultry population of Northern Ireland was estimated at 4,551,344.
In 1931 this population had grown to
8,690,758. In Northern Ireland poultry
is of incomparably greater importance
than in other parts of these islands. The
following figures illustrate this statement:-

When we come to compare the annual
values of the output of our chief agricultural products, poultry occupies the
same commanding position both absolutely and relatively. This statement is
strikingly illustrated by the figures which
I will now read of the annual values of
the chief farming products of Northern
Ireland in recent years:

Important, however, as the poultry
industry is at present, it is still capable
of almost unlimited further development
and never were the prospects more favourable than at this juncture, when at last
the home producer is being placed on a
proper footing on the British market.
When it is recalled that twenty million
pounds' worth of poultry and poultry
products are still imported to Great
Britain, the potentialities of that market
become apparent.
There is, however, one aspect of the
question which is now causing the Ministry grave anxiety, and that is the fact
that no adequate means exist for preventing the introduction to Northern
Ireland of serious poultry disease, or of
checking the spread of such disease within
the Province.
Bacillary white diarrhoea at the
moment constitutes a very grave danger
to the poultry industry. The effect of
the disease is that within three weeks of
hatching the young chickens die rapidly,
the mortality rate being between 90 per
cent. and 100 per cent. As a consequence, where outbreaks occur, practically the whole of the young stock is lost.
Moreover, surviving birds, although
apparently quite healthy, act as carriers
of the disease, the germ being transmitted in their eggs, and thus the infection is carried on. A survey by the Ministry leaves no doubt of the fact that the
disease is prevalent in each of the Six
Counties, and is unfortunately spreading.
There is no known cure for this disease,
and the only present method of coping
with it is to determine its existence by
bacteriological examination, and to weed
out infected birds
In view of the spread of the disease,
the Ministry has been compelled to make
it a condition that all poultry stations
coming within the terms of any of the
Ministry's schemes should have their
flocks tested twice a year, and all reacting
birds disposed of By this means the
Ministry has been able to ensure the
soundness from a disease point of view
of all hatching eggs sent out from a
poultry station. A scheme is also in
operation whereby for a nominal charge
birds are tested for private breeders, who
are thus afforded a ready means of eradi
cating this disease Increasing numbers
of such breeders are, we are glad to say.
availing themselves of this method of
cleaning their flocks.
Practically all the outbreaks of bacillary white diarrhoea in Northern Ireland can be traced directly or indirectly
to imports of hatching eggs, day-old
chicks or stock birds, and unless steps are
taken to control such importations the
benefits accruing from the testing scheme
will be largely nullified, and the Ministry
will be unable to succeed in its efforts to
eradicate this disease from Northern Ireland. Such failure would seriously
imperil the poultry industry of this
country.
Fowl paralysis is another serious
poultry disease against which protective
measures will be necessary, although
further research into the nature of this
disease will be required before the best
methods of protection can be devised.
In passing, it may be said that practically
every country in which the poultry
industry is being developed has armed
itself with appropriate powers to prevent
the introduction and spread of disease.
It should be noted that the Diseases of
Animals Act of 1894 affords ample protection for our other live stock, such as
cattle, sheep, swine, etc. At the time of
the passing of the Act in 1894, however,
poultry were apparently regarded as of
so little economic importance that it was
not then thought necessary to bring them
within the scope of the legislation.
is, however, evident that such necessity
now exists and, accordingly, the present
Measure is commended to the consideration of the House. I beg to move.

REAR "STOP" LIGHTS ON BUSES.
The following question stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Major
Dobbs :-
To ask the Leader of the House whether
the Government will make it obligatory
on all motor omnibuses to be equipped
with a rear "stop" light to be brought
into operation whenever the foot-brake is
depressed.
Major DOBBS: In asking this question
I would not like hon. Members to imagine
that if such a regulation was made there
would be a big reduction in motor accidents, but I do think that a contributory
cause of accidents would be removed, and
that the amenities and comfort of road
users would be enhanced. Imagine
travelling behind a motor bus going at
30 to 35 miles an hour. One is perfectly
happy. One does not want to pass the
bus, but that bus will suddenly put on
its brakes. You cannot tell the bus is
going to stop suddenly, because you cannot see the road in front, nor can you
see the signal of the driver, supposing
he does signal. The back of the bus blots
out the whole road. It is very much
like the elephant in the pass which
Rudyard Kipling spoke of. When the
bus suddenly stops, what are you to
do? You have either to jam on your
brakes or swing your car out to the right
to pass.
If the road is greasy and you
jam on your brakes you stand a very good
chance of skidding. If you swing out to
the right you may cause an accident to
people coming from the other direction.
I would remind hon. Members of the
bad accident that took place on the
Basingstoke Road about twelve months
If the motor bus has a rear "stop"
light, as soon as the driver starts to put
on his brake the red light shows, and a
person driving behind immediately sees
it. I have confined this question to
motor buses, although I should like to
see every motor car equipped with a rear
"stop" light. Motor buses, however, are
unlike other road vehicles, because they
are continually stopping.

PROVISION OF FOOTPATHS.
Mr. CAMPBELL asked the Leader of
the House whether, in view of the
number of road accidents in this area,
the Government will take note of the
strong demand now arising in England
for the diminution of the appalling
figures of road fatalities by the provision,
where possible, of footpaths immediately.
near main roads, and of more footpaths
away from main and other roads, by
which people, who walk, can escape the
peril of the roads.
Mr. LONG: The importance of the
provision of adequate footpaths has been.
fully appreciated by the Ministry of
Home Affairs. So far back as January,
1927, the Ministry issued a circular to
the Road Authorities emphasising the
necessity for providing footpaths and, in
March, 1929, the matter was again
brought under the notice of the local
authorities. The hon. and learned Member will, no doubt, have observed that
footpaths have been provided in the case
of most of the roads which have been
recently re-constructed.
While proper footpaths will undoubtedly contribute to the safety of pedestrians on the roads, an examination of
the statistics with regard to accidents for
the past few years does not seem to
indicate that any very appreciable proportion of the accidents to pedestrians
are caused by lack of footpaths, but that
such accidents rather occur where traffic
is dense and where adequate footpaths
are in existence. Accidents of this kind
are mostly caused by want of care, either
on the part of the pedestrian in stepping
off the footpath or in crossing the road,
or on the part of the motorist.
