Adjournment-
Shooting at Ballinderry
THE SENATE
Adjournment.
The Shooting Affair at Ballinderry.
Mr. LONG: I beg to move "That this
House do now adjourn until 12-5 tomorrow" for Royal Assent.
Mr. MCALLISTER: I beg to ask the
Deputy-Leader of the House a question
of which I have given private notice,
namely, has he any information to supplement the statement made by the
Government in another place, in reference
to the brutal outrages at Ballinderry. I
can say in regard to this question that it
is always with the greatest possible reluctance that I feel compelled to raise a
question of this description. I think it
is a humiliating thing at this hour of the
day for a public representative of the
minority to be forced to deal with matters
of this description.
When I entered
public life seven years ago I had a profound conviction that the resources of
the State socially and materially could
only be fully developed by the wholehearted co-operation and goodwill of this
small population of 1 million people.
Therefore, it is only from the highest sense
of duty that I raise this question.
I would say in passing that I happened
to be one of the speakers invited to
address this meeting at Kilrea on this
occasion. Perhaps some Members of the
House who have listened to me might
say it was sufficient punishment to listen
to me without having the people shot in
addition. Perhaps some would go further and say shooting was the lesser of
two evils. However, I can safely say
that I never witnessed a more orderly or
better disciplined, or more peaceful meeting or procession in my life. I think the
whole House will agree with me in condemning the depraved mentality, and
brutal and barbaric nature of the men who
went behind a hedge and fired upon what
they knew to be an unarmed body of men.
They used recognised rifles. That is a
very disquieting fact to me, and I am
afraid I must say it is a reflection on a
great many people. These were either
local people or strangers who perpetrated
this outrage. If they were strangers they
should be known as strangers, and some
people should be able to give a description
of them to the police. If they were local
people there must have been quite a
number of local residents who knew these
people were there to perpetrate that outrage. I do think that is one of the most
humiliating and serious aspects of this
whole question.
The fact is that rifles were found, and
there is a feeling amongst the people whom
I represent they profoundly believe itthat when these rifles were found there
should be no difficulty in finding those
in whose possession or custody they were.
That is the feeling, whether well founded
or not, that is universally felt. It is a
strange thing that through all the vicissitudes and trials of the internecine
strife of recent years the Hibernians
were the one organisation that through
the stress abided by their constitutional
principles and yet they, defenceless and
unarmed, are singled out for attacks of
this description.
Mr. JOSEPH CUNNINGHAM: By
whom?
Mr. MCALLISTER: I would suggest
that my hon. Friend who interrupts me is
in a better position to answer that question than I am. He does not suggest for
a moment that a Nationalist public representative had any part in attacking
a Nationalist body? Surely he has more
commonsense than that. However, I
just want to stress the point that there
has been quite a number of these outrages in recent times, in County Armagh,
in Ballinderry, in Portadown, and various
other places, and none of the perpetrators
of these outrages have been brought to
justice. That, undoubtedly, is creating
a
feeling of uneasiness and anxiety
amongst a large section of the people in
Northern Ireland. I put it on a broader
issue. I say on behalf of all the people
of Northern Ireland that it is absolutely
essential that whoever perpetrated this
outrage should be brought to justice immediately, because we all know where a
spark may lead to, and I am very anxious
in dealing with a question of this nature
that no word of mine should foment any
discord, or raise any passions, or create
any feeling of mistrust. But merely from
a sense of duty, and on behalf of those
I specially represent, I wish to impress
upon the Government the anxiety of the
minority that they should be assured that
there will not be a repetition of these unfortunate and brutal incidents that have
occurred so frequently of late.
Mr. BARCLAY: I sympathise with
the hon. Senator on this question which
he has raised. I personally am a man
Adjournment-
Shooting at Ballinderry
23 MARCH 1932
who goes in for peace, and I would not
in any way encourage such actions as have
taken place in the past. But the question
arises in my mind, who was it that committed this deed? From the report I
read in the paper on that evening from
one of the officials who came with the
wounded men to the hospital here in the
city of Belfast, I gathered that this
official, in communication with the Press,
stated that this was a Roman Catholic
district that the procession was passing
through and where the men were shot. I
naturally came to the conclusion that it
could not be the Protestant population
that went out into a Roman Catholic
district and shot at the procession that
was passing by that way. I also came to
the conclusion in my own mind that there
are two political parties connected with
that religious persuasion, and there is the
other probability that others fired instead
of those who are blamed.
It is up to the people in that district
to come forward if they have evidence
or if they have any information to give
to the police. I am sure the Government of Northern Ireland will do all
they possibly can to bring to book these
men who have committed this deed. The
Government is not out to encourage the
like of that. We passed through enough
ten or eleven years ago, and I should not
wish to have a repetition of that kind of
thing. I sympathise with the processionists and with the men who were wounded,
and I am sorry that such a thing should
take place. I thought peace had come
and that every section of the community
were going to work together for the good
of each other and the well-being of the
Province.
Mr. LONG: In reply to the question
of the hon. Senator I wish to say that
the answer is in the negative. The
matter was discussed in another place and
there is no further information to give to
the House. The Government is making
every effort to bring the perpetrators to
justice. Every right-minded person in
Northern Iraiand deplores this outrage
and earnestly trusts the miscreants will
be brought to justice. The presiding
justice at Derry, in regard to the matter,
had expressed the hope that the inhabitants would co-operate with the constabulary in detecting the offenders. I should
like to reiterate the hope of the hon.
Senator who asked the question that, in
the interests of the people of Northern
Ireland, they would do their best to
stamp out outrages of this character.
Question put and agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at
a Quarter before Four
o'clock until 12-5 p.m.
to-morrow.

Questions to Minister.
WAGE OF WEEKLY WAGE
EARNERS.
The following question stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Mr.
Dorman:
To ask the Leader of the House whether
it is a fact that the changes of weekly
wage earners in Northern Ireland are not
set out in the Twentieth Abstract of
Labour Statistics of the United Kingdom, and if so, whether the Government
will take steps to have these figures
published.
Mr. DORMAN: The question which
stands in my name on the Paper follows
naturally a question I put some time ago
with regard to the reduction of wages in
Northern Ireland. I understand that it
was found to be almost impossible to
ascertain the exact reduction in wages of
the weekly wage earners in the area of
Northern Ireland during the last eleven
years. I think it is important that such
figures should be available for the purpose of investigating the relationship
between the lowering of the purchasing
capacity of the consumers in our area
and the volume of unemployment which,
unfortunately, we all regret to know, has
been greater in Northern Ireland than in
other parts of Great Britain. The increase in the number of unemployed in
Northern Ireland during the last three
years has been over seven points, having
been raised from 20 to 27.9.
For a
number of successive years, from 1921 to
1931, there has been a consecutive reduction in the wages of weekly wage
earners in Great Britain, and last year
the reduction amounted to £399,500,000.
It is utterly impossible for us to ascertain what proportion of that volume
of reduced purchasing capacity in the
community is applicable to Northern
Ireland. That is the reason I have
put this question on the Paper. I do not
intend to go further than to ask the permission of the House to quote from a
celebrated economist who wrote on this
subject nineteen years ago.
He said at that time:-
"Nothing can be so disadvantageous
to any people as a permanent depression
in the rate of wages, or a decline in the
purchasing power of the labouring class
respecting the articles necessary for their
subsistence. No country can be
flourishing where wages are low, and
none can be long depressed where they
are high. The labourers are the
thews and sinews of industry. Their
numbers are not estimated, like those
of other classes, by hundreds, by
thousands, or even by hundreds of
thousands, but by millions. It is by
them that our machinery is constructed and kept in motion, that our
agriculture, manufactures, and commerce are successfully carried on.
Oral Answers
New Industries Bill
THE SENATE
[Mr. Dorman]
Everything, then, that may have the
slightest tendency to depress their condition, or sink them in the social scale
should be most particularly guarded
against. Those who feed and clothe
the rest should themselves be well fed
and clothed. They are the foundation
of the social pyramid, and so long as
the standard of wages is high this
foundation will be solid and secure."
That covers the ground and the reasons
why I have put this question on the
Paper, and I hope to get a satisfactory
answer.
Mr. LONG: The number of workpeople in Northern Ireland reported as
affected by changes in weekly full-time
rates of wages and the aggregate amount
of such changes during the period 1924-
1930 are included, but not shown separately, in the Twentieth Abstract of
Labour Statistics of the United Kingdom, dated March, 1931.
In view of the fact that in a considerable number of important industries such
changes are arranged on a national basis
and separate statistics for Great Britain
and Northern Ireland are not obtained,
it is regretted that it is not practicable
to publish information relating to wage
variations in Northern Ireland.
HIGH TENSION WIRES ALONG
ROADS.
Mr. LESLIE (for Major Dobbs) asked
the Leader of the House whether he considers that the safety of the public is
sufficiently safeguarded, where high
tension wires for the supply of electric
current are carried by the side of the
public highway.
the
Mr. LONG: It is not usual for high
tension overhead lines to be carried along
a public highway in Northern Ireland
but, where such is the case,
electricity undertakers must comply with
regulations designed to secure the safety
of the public. I am advised that such
regulations are adequate and, I may add,
that, in the matter of the safety factor
required, the regulations in force in
Northern Ireland are in all respects
similar to those in Great Britain, where
high tension distribution is undertaken
on a much wider scale.

New Industries (Development) Bill.
Moved, "That this Bill be now read a
First time."-(Mr. Long.)
On Question, Motion agreed to.
Mr. LONG: I am sure that this House
will welcome the attempt which is made
in this Bill to encourage the establishment of new industries in Northern Ireland. The past few years have served
to show the extent to which the general
prosperity of our Province is dependent
on at most two or three major industries. Unfortunately, the industries
upon which we have been obliged mainly
to depend are amongst those which, of
all United Kingdom industries, have
suffered most during the prolonged trade
depression. It will not be disputed that
Ulster's position generally would be
greatly strengthened by the accretion of
new industries, especially if those industries can be developed sufficiently to provide employment for a large number of
our workers. The Bill which is presented
to you, is, therefore, designed to make
Ulster specially attractive to the industrialist contemplating the establishment
of a new industry.
The methods by which it is hoped to
attain the end in view are, briefly, to
relieve a new industry, for a maximum
period of twenty years, of the burden of
site rent and rates. The Bill empowers
the Ministry of Commerce, subject to
certain conditions, to make an annual
grant to any person or Company establishing a new industry in Northern Ireland, between 1st November, 1931, and
31st October, 1936, not exceeding what
the Ministry regards as the reasonable
annual rent of the site on which the industry is established. It also empowers
local authorities up to the same maximum period of 20 years, to exempt from
rates any site in respect of which the
Ministry of Commerce has agreed to
make an annual grant.
In the sense of the Bill, a "new industry" is one engaged in producing goods
of a kind which were not being produced
in Northern Ireland before 1st November, 1931. Existing industries, as the
New Industries Bill-
Second Reading.
12 APRIL 1932
House will see, are, therefore, not being
placed at a disadvantage, as only an industry which is not devoted to producing
something which is already being made
in Northern Ireland can qualify for the
benefits proposed by the Bill.
In dealing with applications made to
it under the Bill, the Ministry of Commerce will have the assistance of an
Advisory Committee, but the Ministry
itself will make the decision on each
application, and, where the Ministry
considers that a grant should be made,
the consent of the Ministry of Finance
will be obtained before payment is actually made. In order to qualify for payments the industry must, in the opinion
of the Ministry of Commerce, be such as
promises to afford substantial employment
in Northern Ireland. Further, an applicant is required to comply with such
conditions as may be prescribed in Regulations made by the Ministry, and the
Ministry is empowered to discontinue
payment of the annual grant at any time.
if, in its opinion, the conditions attaching to it have not been, or are not being,
satisfied.
As the House will appreciate, the
success which is likely to attend the Government's efforts to attract new industries by the methods provided for in the
Bill must depend very largely upon the
extent to which the benefits are brought
to the notice of interests outside Northern Ireland itself. To this end the
Ministry of Commerce is, therefore, empowered to expend money up to such
amounts as the Ministry of Finance may
sanction for the purpose of making
known the facilities provided under the
Bill. Although no expenditure has yet
been incurred the House will, no doubt,
be pleased to learn that the Ministry has
already taken steps to secure publicity
for the provisions of the Bill, in the Continental and Dominion Press.
What I have said describes briefly the
aim and the machinery of the Bill. Of
all the times which might have been
chosen for the introduction of such a
Measure the present is, I think, the most
opportune possible. Britain's adoption of
a policy of protection for her home industries can scarcely fail to bring about
the establishment of branches of foreign
industrial undertakings within the United
Kingdom, and the Bill which is now before you may have the effect of making
Ulster the most attractive area within
the United Kingdom when the selection
of a site for a new industry is being made.
That is the hope underlying the Government's present effort. I beg to move.
Question proposed: "That this Bill be
now read a Second time."
Mr. LESLIE: I am sure that the Bili
which the Parliamentary Secretary has
brought before the House this afternoon
is one which will naturally evoke not only

all agree that if anything can be done
further to promote the prosperity of our
Province that is a thing which this House
would be very anxious to do. The Bill
is, I think, of a somewhat novel character.
I do not think it has any counterpart
across the water in Great Britain,
although I think something of the same
nature has been attempted across the
Atlantic in the Western Hemisphere, but
as to that I have no details to lay before
the House.
The question of novelty comes before
us in another way. The industries to
which attention is directed in the Bill are
not to be, as I understand, necessarily
novel in the world. All that is required
is that they shall be novel in Northern
Ireland, that is to say, they are to be
industries which have not hitherto been
promoted in this area. The object of the
Bill, as I have said, is a very excellent
one, and I think we shall all agree it is
very desirable, indeed, that power should
be taken to expend a certain amount of

amount of money-to advertise the benefits it is hoped the Bill will secure. But

the House will be unduly inquisitive.
Passing from that I cannot but admit
that the Bill seems to me, or rather the

I do think there are some

be made to date from the acquisition of
the site, or is it to be suspended until the

House will, I am sure, remember the
difficulties inherent in the situation.
There is nothing in the Bill, as I read it,
to require that the site should be what I
may call prairie land. It might perfectly
well be one of the silent factories which
are too prominently before us at the present time. There are all these difficulties

I can appreciate, as I am sure the

in the work they are seeking to undertake;

Slaughter of Animals Bill. (S.).
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg to move the
Second Reading of this Bill. Its object
is to assimilate the law of Northern
Ireland to the existing law of Scotland
and to what I believe will very soon be
the law of England and Wales. In Scotland they have the Slaughter of Animals
Act, 1928, which has been a marked success.
This Bill is framed on identical
lines. In December, 1930, Colonel
Moore secured the Second Reading in the
House of Commons at Westminster of a
like Bill for England and Wales, and the
Bill would undoubtedly have reached the
Statute but for the crisis which last year
led to the dissolution of Parliament, in
consequence of which the Bill came to an
end. Colonel Moore has just re-introduced the Bill with a backing of the
strongest character from every section of
opinion in the House. Some of the
backers are Mr. Lansbury, Mr. Macpherson, Sir Rennell Rodd, Miss Lloyd
George, Sir Hugh O'Neill, former
Speaker of another place in this Parliament; Sir William Davison and Sir
Robert Gower. There is well grounded
hope that the Bill will shortly become
an Act. Parliament has had the experience derived from the working of the
Scottish Act, which is altogether in
favour of the use of the humane killer.
•
The object of the Bill is to ensure that
all animals, except swine, slaughtered in
slaughter-houses and knackers' yards in
Northern Ireland, whether for human
food or otherwise, should be humanely
killed.
433 enlightened English local authorities have adopted model by-laws for
slaughter-houses making compulsory the
use of mechanical instruments. This
Bill applies those by-laws to Northern
Ireland. There are local authorities in
England who have not taken that enlightened stand. There have been seven
local authorities in Northern Ireland
who have made by-laws making the use
of the humane killer compulsory. They
are, Belfast, Bangor, Ballymena, Larne,
Lisburn Urban and Rural, and Cookstown. In each of those areas the bylaws enforce the compulsory use of the
humane killer, and these by-laws have
worked well, have given satisfaction, and
have been the cause of no complaint.
This Bill simply seeks to apply generally
to local areas in Northern Ireland the
same by-laws in a statutory form. Ι
do submit to the House that it would
conduce to the public well-being if those
by-laws were in force in the area of
every other local authority here. Most
local authorities would welcome the
general use of the humane killer. Some
of them are not quite free to adopt it
owing to local influences and local
prejudices in matters of that kind, but
taking them as a body most of the local
authorities would be glad to be brought
into line by means of general legislation.
There are about 1,600 private slaughterhouses in England and Wales, about 520
in Scotland, and about 400 in Northern
Ireland. The number in the Free State
is not actually known. Many of them
are very dark, il ventilated, without
water or sanitation, and without much
equipment for handling live animals or
meat.
I would like to state in a very few
words the recent history of this subject.
In 1908 an influential and independent
Admiralty Committee was set up to
inquire into the whole system of the
slaughter of animals, and reported
unanimously that in every case of animal
slaughter the animal should be stunned
before being slaughtered. In 1923 a
Cabinet Committee was appointed by the
Coalition Government to go into the
whole subject, and as a result of their
exhaustive investigations it was announced that the Ministry of Health
would continue to approve of model bylaws, the essential one of which was that
where a local authority so desired every
animal slaughtered in its area should be
stunned before being killed. There is
humane slaughter. There is also inhumane slaughter. No right-minded
person would defend or permit inhumane
slaughter. People do not go to see
slaughter-houses. If they visited some
primitive ones their instincts of
humanity would be roused.
Slaughter of Animals Bill-
THE SENATE
Second Reading
[Mr. Campbell]
The case for the humane killer does not
rest on sentimental grounds. Cool reason
and public necessities require its adoption.
The most distinguished physiologists, the
authorities of leading veterinary institutions, eminent doctors, progressive public
authorities, and thousands of up-to-date
practising butchers and bacon curers are
decisively in favour of its use. The ever
strengthening forces of enlightenment and
education are arrayed on one side. The
ever weakening forces of prejudice and
ignorance are marshalled on the other
side. The unprogressive forces need to
be educated up to the level of the progressive elements.
Hundreds of thousands of animals are
slaughtered in Northern Ireland every
year. The majority of them are slaughtered at the abattoir in Belfast, where
the use of the humane killer is obligatory.
That abattoir is in every way a credit to
the city of Belfast in respect of cleanliness, up-to-date methods and quick and
humane despatch of the animals. I do
not know of any slaughter-house in the
United Kingdom that can compare with
it in matters of efficiency and economy.
Animals to the number of hundreds of
thousands are slaughtered every year in
Northern Ireland. This is necessary to
the subsistence and health of man. What
right-minded man or woman will gainsay
the proposition that every person engaged
in the slaughtering of any animal should
in the process take such precautions as
may be necessary to secure the infliction
of as little pain or suffering as practicable? None of us wish to visit any creature with unnecessary pain. The exquisite
physical torture of the methods of surgical operation
the wounded
on
at
Trafalgar or Waterloo would have seemed
unutterably barbarous in the Great War.
Modern surgery has scored its distinctive
triumph in the discovery of anesthetics.
The humane killer is the anesthetic of the
slaughter-house. The brute creation
must be subservient to the use of man,
but the House will agree that it is but
humane that they should be freed from
the consciousness of pain before or at the
moment when their death stroke is given.

must be wielded by an expert who knows
his job, but even the expert, if he shows

-a very easy thing to do in one of these
slaughter-houses having regard to the
condition of the floor-or if he misjudges
his aim, however slightly, or if the animal
has room or scope for any degree of restlessness or movement, may cause severe
and unnecessary cruelty. The pole-axe is
a primitive weapon. Success depends on
the skill and strength and long practice
of the wielder. The spot he has to aim
at is not larger than a golf ball.
When the human factor or the animal
factor is at work there is the risk
of cruelty-unintentional no doubt in the
average case. The Health Department
of the London Corporation carried out
investigations in 1923 and found that 400
animals which were pole-axed required
655 blows. Witnesses will tell you of
four or five or six blows having been required. In some cases as many as seven,
eight, nine, and twelve and thirteen blows
have been necessary, because the skulls of
old animals of the larger type are very
dense, and the skulls of different types
vary. Even the most expert slaughterer
may fail to strike on the proper place
with the maximum mechanical advantage. If he strikes on the proper spot
he produces unconsciousness. The skull
is cracked and the brain is penetrated
and all sense of pain is gone, but if he
misses the spot by a quarter of an inch
and strikes elsewhere the animal may not
be stunned, and may suffer excruciating
pain.
The modern humane killer is as perfect an instrument as science can devise.
It is safe and simple in operation, and
mercifully sudden in effect. There are
two kinds of humane killers. There is
the bullet-firing killer and the captivebolt killer. The captive-bolt killer fires
a bolt which cracks the skull and penetrates the brain, and the bolt recedes into
the barrel again. This kind is portable.
and easy to handle and keep clean. Anæsthesia from it is instantaneous. There is
no risk of misadventure. It eliminates all
unnecessary suffering, and involves no
danger whatever to the carcase. It
means no danger to the operator himself.
From the years 1920 to 1930 only six
accidents in England had been traced
to the humane killer, and the majority
were cases of suicide. Its cost compared
to the work it performs is unappreciable.
It can be bought for 19/6, and the best
type costs five or six guineas. Two or
three would doubtless be an adequate
supply for an average small local area.

25, but the number of animals despatched

The whole cost of the use of the humane
killer for every animal in England and
Wales, distributed all round, would not

When an animal is shot with a humane
killer the upper and lower brain cease
to function almost simultaneously. Effective stunning acts as a perfect and instantaneous anæsthetic. The stunned
animal is lost in unconsciousness before
there is time for the blow which produces
it to be felt. There is no risk of a
return of the stricken animal to consciousness. Consciousness of pain only
continues so long as the brain remains
uninjured.
Cattle are slaughtered here under the

brought into the slaughtering place with

As to the reality of the unnecessary

John Dodds.
He says: "I have seen three, four,

oft repeated blows cause the head to

another blow. At Belfast-he mentions
other places I have
examined heads with many punctures
and also witnessed more suffering than
my readers could bear to hear described."

should like to show the House the poleaxe. It is perfectly safe.

I have also here a captive bolt pistol.
It is not loaded, but even if it were
loaded it would be perfectly safe. It
holds a captive bolt which is released by
the discharge of the cartridge. The bolt
speeds outwards and pierces the brain of
the animal. It is held quite close to the
head. Once the bolt has done its work
it recedes into the barrel. The captive
bolt pistols vary according to the size of
the animal to which it is to be applied.
The weapon is sure and immediate in
its operation.
It causes no apprehension to the animal, involves no danger to
the operator, requires little skill, and
makes only a slight noise. The animal
falls to the ground, all consciousness gone.
No injury is caused to the carcase.
Useful experiments have proved this
fact, as well as the experience gained

which was passed because the public
opinion of Scotland demanded it should
be passed. Reliable experiments show

I mentioned that this Bill applies
only to places, slaughter houses and
knackers' yards. It does not extend
to individual farmers at all. I am told
that few farmers nowadays kill for their

to them.
Jews are exempted. It may be asked
why? The Jews have their own method
of slaughter, and this Bill does not trespass except to say that in it all
unnecessary suffering must be avoided.
There is also an exemption in the case of
Mohammedans. We have none resident
in our area at the present time, but from

and these men have their convictions.
Besides, it is a matter of interest to see

from India selling silks and other articles.
Some of them may be Mohammedans.
Germany, Switzerland, Holland, and

The Netherlands export to these islands
something like £7,000,000 a year of pig

English local authorities' districts 318,000

I submit that the use of the stunning

Just one or two words with regard to
the clauses. Clause 1 provides for instantaneous slaughtering or for effective.
stunning by a mechanically operated
instrument, worked by a person who is
the holder of a licence from
a local

Clause 5 makes provision for the revocation of local by-laws so far as same
are inconsistent with the provisions of the
Bill. Clause 6 contains the saving for

Clause 8 is aimed at preventing any clash

which it embodies affect local sanitary
authorities throughout the area—that is,
the urban and district councils, and it is
the Government's view that these authorities should be consulted to see what their
opinion is on this question. This is in
accordance with pledges repeatedly given
to them. The Minister of Home Affairs
is accordingly prepared to consult the
Association of Municipal Authorities and
the Association of Rural District Councils
and when their views have been received,
the Government will definitely be in a
position to define its attitude towards the
proposed legislation. Meanwhile, the
Government has no objection to the
Second Reading being taken, but only on
the understanding that the question of
further progress remains in abeyance until
the views of the local authorities have
been received.
Colonel SHARMAN - CRAWFORD :
I think the hon. and learned Senator
(Mr. Campbell), has pleaded for a cause
of which we were all in favour before he
made his speech. Personally, I am in
favour of the Bill, and I shall support
the Second Reading. At the same time
there are one or two points in the Bill
which I think ought to be explained on
the Committee stage. For instance,
Clause 1 is left rather too open. It refers
to animals being "stunned by a mechanically operated instrument." It seems to
me that under that Clause an instrument
of any kind, which is mechanically operated may be used. I have heard of
several mechanically operated instruments
which are not very successful, and I
should like to be assured that any
mechanically operated instrument that is
permitted to be used under this Bill will
be approved by some competent authority.
Then in connection with Clause 2 I think
it is essential that such an instrument
should be used by a person trained to
operate it. It is just as easy for an untrained man to make a mistake with a
pistol as it is to make a mistake with the
hammer. I wondered why swine were
omitted from the Bill, and I should like
to quote the experience of a man I know
very well, but whose name I will not
mention, to show that all mechanical
killers are not perfect in their operation
This man was slaughtering swine on his
own farm, and after three shots from the
pistol the swine was not killed and they
had to send for a man with a hammer to
finish the job. This is an actual case I
myself know of. We are all in favour
of this Bill, but before it is passed it
should be tightened up in the several
directions I have indicated and made more
perfect than it is at present.
Colonel PAKENHAM: I should like
to detain the House for a few moments
in giving my support to this Bill. I
think that any means by which you increase the humanity of killing animals is

Question to Minister.
BUILDINGS ON ANTRIM COAST
ROAD.
The following Question stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Colonel
Pakenham:-
To ask the Leader of the House whether
the local authority has taken any steps
under the Planning and Housing Act of
last Session to stop the erection of unsuitable edificies on the Antrim Coast
Road.
Colonel PAKENHAM: Before formally
asking this question I would like to bring
a few facts to the notice of Members of
the House, of which they may not be
aware. We know that the Antrim coast
road is one of the beauty spots of Northern Ireland. I do not think any Member from any other county will
trovert that statement.
At the present
contime, taking a short stretch of that road
from Larne to Ballygally Head, a distance
of about five miles, there are at present
erected in that short stretch of the Antrim
coast road 120 houses. Fifty of these
houses are built of wood and are nothing
more than shacks, s-h-a-c-k-s, and of those
fifty shacks, some eight or nine are built
on the sea side of the coast road, and
stand right in the way of any view over
the sea.
The other seventy are of the
bungalow type, in cement, brick, and
some in wood, and to add to the offence
of the whole lot, there has lately been
erected opposite Ballygally Castle, an
old Norman stronghold, a large modern
villa, standing in all its flaming newness
and blocking the view of the sea, not only
to the people on the other side of the
road, but to anybody driving along the
road.
I submit that this is the worst class
of building and ribbon development to be
found in any country, and at present
there is nothing to prevent the whole of
the Antrim coast road from Larne to
Glenarm, and from Glenarm to Ballycastle being developed in the same way.
You will eventually get long lines of these
buildings stretched along this coast road
and spoiling for ever one of our finest
suburban views.
These new houses have all been erected
and finished since the passing of the
Planning and Housing Bill in this House
last Session. I think the matter is of
sufficient importance to acquaint the
Government of the fact that there are
a good many people who are disgusted
with the way building is going on along
that coast road.
Mr. LONG: The County Council of
Antrim referred the consideration of the
Town Planning Act to their Finance and
Law Committee on the 3rd November last,
but this Committee does not yet appear
to have reported, and I am informed by
New Industries Bill-
Committee
THE SENATE
[Mr. Long]
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Home Affairs, that, so far as he is aware,
no steps have been taken by the County
Council to formulate any plan in respect

As the hon. and gallant Member is no

for any particular area is a matter primarily for the County Council, and the
Ministry of Home Affairs has no compulsory powers. I would suggest that this
is a matter upon which he might appropriately approach the County Council.
Colonel SHARMAN-CRAWFORD: I
take a great interest in this matter, because the same thing is happening along
the County Down coast, and if it is
allowed to continue in the way it is going
on, the whole coast line will be completely
ruined from the point of view of scenery.
We cannot accept the present position
lying down, and I think the Government
ought to compel the County Councils to
take some action in the matter. It is a
most serious thing at the present time.

CLAUSE 1 (Grants in respect of sites
for new industrial undertakings).
Mr. LONG: In the course of his remarks on the Second Reading of this Bill,
Senator Leslie raised certain matters
which he thought deserving of consideration by the Government, before the
Committee Stage was reached, and
although no promise was made at the
time, I am sure that he will be glad to
hear that his suggestions have in the
meantime been carefully examined.
The hon. Senator asked when a new
industry was to be regarded as established, and whether the annual grant
would run from the date of the acquisition of the site or from the time when
the undertaking was definitely started as
a going concern. The answer to that
question is that the date of the commencement of the grant will be fixed by
the Ministry with regard to the actual
circumstances of each case. Normally,
it is thought that the date will be that
from which the applicants become liable
for rent. The Bill provides that the
Ministry may attach such terms and conditions to the making of the grant as it
considers advisable and, where a grant
is made to begin from the date on which
the site was required, it will be open to
the Ministry to require the applicant to
give satisfactory guarantees as to the
erection of the factory and the carrying
out of the intention upon which the
application was based. I do not think
that it is possible to be more definite
than this, as, in order to achieve the
purpose in view, the Ministry must
obviously be left a certain amount of discretion in such a matter.
As regards the question as to whether
it is the intention to follow the practice
laid down in the case of loans
guarantees and to acquaint Parliament
year by year of the amount of the grants
made under the Bill, I am advised,
subject to the ruling of the Speaker on
this point, that an Amendment of Clause
1 in this sense, as well as in regard to the
submission to Parliament of the Regulations made by the Ministry, would be
outside the competence of this House.
At the same time I need hardly assure
the hon. Senator that any information
in regard to progress or procedure, which
he or any other Member of the Senate
might desire to have, will be readily
forthcoming at any time when he may
care to ask for it.
The hon. Senator pointed out that
local authorities might not be inclined to
give exemption of rates for the full
period of 20 years, and suggested that
consideration should be given to the
question whether the provisions of the
Bill were ample to allow a local authority
to limit its contribution to some shorter
period and to make such adjustments
for the repayment of rates as might be
required. I am advised that, as regards
the powers of a local authority to restrict
exemption from rates to a period shorter
than the maximum of 20 years allowed
by the Bill, Sub-Section (1) of Clause 2
fully meets this point. If a Council or
Commissioners under Sub-Section
allow exemption for a shorter period
than that fixed for the Parliamentary
grant, they will presumably make it.
begin or end with their own rating
period.

Railways (Valuation for Rating) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. LONG: I do not propose to take
up very much time in moving the Second
Reading of this Bill. Its provisions are
not of a controversial nature, and it is
designed to give statutory force to a
system of valuation for railways in Northern Ireland which is regarded as a
reasonable and fair solution of the
difficulties which have been experienced
in administering the law on this subject
as it exists at present. The railway companies have been consulted in regard to
the general principles laid down in the
Bill, and, indeed, it is only with their
goodwill that a complex Bill of this sort
could have been prepared.
The valuation of railways in Northern
Ireland, according to the Statute at
present in force, that is, the Valuation
Act of 1852, falls to be ascertained on
the basis of net annual value, namely
the rent for which one year with another
the hereditament might in its actual
state be reasonably expected to let from
year to year, the probable average
annual cost of repairs, insurance and
other expenses necessary to maintain the
hereditament in its actual state, and all
rates, taxes and public charges being paid
by the tenant.
The difficulty of assessing a rental for
railway property-which will be obvious
to hon. Members-led to the adoption of
a special method. for applying the
statutory definition of value in the case
of railways and other properties, such as
gas and electric light undertakings; this
method, usually referred to as the
"revenue principle," is founded upon
numerous law cases and proved to work
satisfactorily in those days when railways enjoyed a reasonable degree of prosperity. I need not dwell upon the
factors which have caused the decline in
the revenue of railway undertakings; it
is sufficient to say that the resulting
position has a severe reaction upon the
revenue principle of assessing valuation,
in that the application of this principle
would result in many cases in a nil valuation. Such a result is regarded as inequitable, because we must regard the
Railways Bill-
Second Reading
THE SENATE
[Mr. Long)
fact that a railway is actually working
as an indication that it is of some value
to the company by whom it is worked.
The anomalous situation which has
arisen has already been dealt with in
Great Britain by the Railways (Valuation for Rating) Act of 1930, and in
the Irish Free State, where a similar
Act was passed towards the close of last
year, and the Bill which is at present
before this House proposes to place on
a definite statutory basis a system of
valuation for railways which for the
most part corresponds with a system in
force elsewhere throughout the British
Isles. Hon. Members will readily appreciate the desirability of a common system of valuation for railways in the two
parts of Ireland, having regard to the
fact that a number of the railways own
property both in Northern Ireland and
in the Irish Free State.
Many of the provisions of the Bill are
of a highly technical character, and I do
not, therefore, propose to deal with the
Clauses in detail. Briefly, the Bill gives
a statutory basis to a form of the
"revenue principle" interpretation of the
Act of 1852, modified to meet the present
day circumstances, and provides for the
quinquennial revision of railway valuations.
Clause 5 lays down the procedure by
which the valuer is to arrive at the letting
value of the railways for the purposes of
revision.
Provision is made in order to avoid a
nil valuation being arrived at in respect
of a working railway-a possibility which
I have already stated might well arise
in existing circumstances. Accordingly
the Bill provides for a minimum valuation, to be ascertained as provided in
Clause 7. It will be seen that in the
case of the railway track, the minimum
valuation is to be the valuation which
would have been placed on the land under
the Act of 1852 if it had not been adapted
for use as a railway, and in case of
hereditaments other than the actual
track, the minimum valuation is arrived
at on the usual basis of letting value,
but on the 1914 standard and reduced by
two-thirds. These provisions regarding
minimum valuation should prove reasonable both from the point of view of the
rating authority and of the railway company itself.
As I have said, the subject matter of
the Bill is of a highly technical nature,
I
and I have therefore confined myself to a
brief outline of the object of the Bill.
shall be pleased to furnish any detailed
information which hon. Members may
desire on the Committee stage of the Bill.
I beg to move.
Mr. CAMPBELL: This is an interesting Bill. It is a Bill which marks a
contact between Northern Ireland and the
Irish Free State. It deals with the railway system which is common to both
territories, and I see among the companies
affected by the Bill is the Joint Committee of the Donegal railways. The
object of the Bill is, I understand, to
determine that the valuation of the undertakings worked by the railways for their
primary purpose as carriers shall be
decided by the revenue basis and the
revenue basis alone. In other words, it
is a railway relief Bill. Well, what
railway at the present time does not
require relief?
Times were when the premier railway
in Northern Ireland territory, the Great
Northern Railway shares and stocks,
stood as high as 170 and 180 for the £100
stock. To-day the condition of things is
so serious that the same stock is being
exchanged in the local markets at
£8 10s. The same fact applies to the
great magnificent British railway, the
London, Midland and Scottish. Its
shares sold just as high, and to-day they
are almost as low. One sad fact about
it is this, that in those days hard-working
industrious men put their money,
practically all their savings, into these
railways for the sakes of their children
and widows after their day, and those
widows, knowing very little of the commercial world or the stock exchange or
ordinary mercantile affairs, held on to
those stocks and shares right through all
those days and never dreamt of parting
with them, and to-day they are in a
plight which deserves the sympathy of
the community. If this Bill does nothing
more than bring some kind of relief to
that very large and silently suffering
class, I am very glad to support it.
There is another class that has also
been hit very hard. The money of many

There is another reason also. I do

competition with road

Colonel SHARMAN CRAWFORD: I

Housing (Grants) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. LONG: The Bill which I now
present to the House forms one of a series
which have been introduced annually into
this House since 1923. The policy which
underlay the earlier Acts underlies this
Act also, and the Government would
submit that the large Measure of success
which has been achieved by this policy in
the past justifies the provision which it is
proposed to make in the Bill now before
the House.
The general housing policy of the
Government has been directed towards
two ends:
First, the abatement of the present
housing shortage; and second, the
gradual reduction in the rents of the
cheaper type of house as a result of the
operation of the law of supply and
demand.
As regards the latter point, hon.
Members will be aware that a Select
Committee which was set up in another
place re-affirmed in its report the principle
to which the Government has been
endeavouring to give effect, namely, the
necessity-if profiteering in rents is to be
prevented-of increasing the number of
dwelling-houses available at reasonable
rents. This has been the consistent aim
of the Government, and the figures which
I shall give you in a moment or two will,
I believe, convince you that a large
measure of success has attended the
Government's efforts.
Since housing operations were commenced after the war 25,563 houses have
been completed with assistance from
State funds. Although generous assistance was available between 1919 and
1923, both under the Housing Acts and
from the Unemployment Relief Funds,
the total number of houses erected during those years was only 2,155, of which
498 were erected by private builders and
1,657 by local authorities. The series of
Northern Ireland Acts to which I have
referred under which housing subsidies
have been payable began in 1923, and
from that date until the 31st March last
no less than 23,408 houses have been
completed, of which 21,561 were built
by private builders, and 1,847 by local
authorities. I have no doubt that the
House will agree that as these figures
indicate, the Government has already
made a great effort to meet the shortage
in houses, but perhaps the magnitude of
the effort will be more apparent if we
convert these figures into money. Up
to the end of the last local financial year
-31st March, 1932-subsidies were paid
under the Housing of the Working
Classes Act, 1908, amounting to £12,730,
and under the Housing (Additional
Powers) Act, 1919, amounting
£58,850. Under the Housing (Ireland)
Act, 1919, the amount paid to date is
£281,149, while disbursements from the
Unemployment Relief Fund account for
approximately £200,000. Payments in
respect of subsidies under the Housing
Acts passed by this Parliament amount
to £2,090,180. This makes the total
State assistance some £2,642,909.
to
As hon. Senators are
aware, these
figures do not fully represent the total
sums expended out of public funds
towards the erection of houses. Many
local authorities have given supplemental
grants in respect of houses erected under
the Housing Acts, and in some cases
local authorities have embarked on
schemes themselves towards which they
have got assistance from the State, but
which, even with this assistance, entail
charges on the rates.
Housing (Grants) Bill-
Second Reading
THE SENATE
[Mr. Long]
I will now proceed to give a brief
account of the provisions of the Bill.
Clause 1 (1) provides for the payment
by the Government of grants at the rate
of £25, in respect of the construction of
houses completed before the 1st April,
1934, being of the kitchen or small parlour type.
The houses in respect of
which grants will be payable fall into
two classes, the first of which is dealt
with in paragraph (a) of sub-clause (1),
and the second in paragraph (b).
Paragraph (a) refers to houses commenced before the 9th March, 1932, and
the limitations of size in the case of these
houses are those obtaining under the last
Housing Act, under which grants would
have been payable if the houses had been
completed before the 31st March, 1932.
Paragraph (b) provides for the more important class of houses commenced after
the 9th March, 1932. In the case of
these houses the maximum dimensions
will be 550 superficial feet, and the minimum 500. The houses are to contain
four apartments, scullery, sanitary
accommodation, and the usual offices.
is also provided that plans showing the
lay-out of the site, the type, design, and
method of construction shall have been
approved by the Ministry of Home
Affairs before the house is commenced.
The object of this provision is to be sure
that builders will not find themselves in
the position of having to alter the plans
of houses after operations have commenced.
It
Sub-clause (3) provides for the payment of supplemental grants of £25 per
house by local authorities, that is, county
councils, county borough councils,
borough councils, urban district councils,
and rural district councils. The maximum amount obtainable by any builder
will, therefore, be £50 per house.
At this point I may perhaps be expected to deal with some of the criticisms
which have been directed against the
provisions of this Bill. The first criticism is that where a grant is paid by the
Government or local authority in respect
of any house the rent obtainable for that
house by the builder should be in some
way restricted. As I have already
pointed out on other occasions, it has
always been the deliberate policy of the
Government to impose as few restrictions
as possible upon the builders of houses.
If, as is our desire, a large number of
cheaply rented houses are to be provided for the working classes it will only
be done if those who build them are
free to let them at the best rent that
they can obtain at any time.
If any
restrictions are put upon the amount of
rent chargeable houses will not be built,
and persons desiring to invest money will
be deterred from using it for the purpose
of financing building operations, and this
would defeat the whole object of our
Housing Acts. As is well known, private enterprise has in the past provided
cheap houses for the working classes in
Belfast, and it is our belief that if
a sufficient number of houses can be made
available the operation of the law of
supply and demand will ensure that they
will be let at reasonable rents.
As regards the second criticism, that
the size of the houses is too small,
I would say that experience shows that
it is possible to provide decent and comfortable houses within the limits which
have been imposed. The houses recently
erected by the Corporation on the Seaview site afford a good example of such
houses, as the size of the houses on this
site approximates to the maximum which
we have laid down. A house containing
four living rooms, that is, a kitchen, a
sitting-room, and two bedrooms
alternatively, a living room and three
bedrooms, can be built within these
dimensions. Moreover, if a larger type
of house is to be built it will certainly
cost considerably more than a house of
the size which I have indicated. The
result of this would be that the rents
chargeable would be higher, and, as I
have already pointed out, one of our
objects is ensure that the rents
chargeable shall be as low as possible.
to
or,
The third criticism is that the amount
of the subsidy is too small. I have
already pointed out that a sum of over
two million pounds has already been
spent by the Government in aiding the
provision of working-class houses. Our
liabilities in respect of subsidies entail
an annual charge on the Estimates of
£169,000 and, in addition, we have to
meet annual sums amounting to £21,000
in respect of liabilities incurred under
previous housing legislation. In formulating our future policy we cannot but
have regard to these liabilities and to
the present financial situation.
Our resources are limited and we have, therefore, to attach great importance to the
financial aspect of the question. We
have, accordingly, come to the conclusion
105 Housing (Grants) Bill-

19 APRIL 1932
Second Reading
that the utmost assistance that can be
given in this matter is a subsidy of £25,
and in order that the greatest possible
benefit may accrue from this subsidy to
the classes of persons who are most in
need of housing accommodation, and who
are least able to provide it for themselves,
we are satisfied that the size of the houses
in respect of which the subsidy would be
payable must be strictly limited.
I may point out in conclusion that the
Bill now before the House proposes to
authorise the payment of the subsidy over
a period of two years. Hitherto it has
been our custom to legislate for one year
only, and this has had the disadvantage
of leaving builders in a state of uncertainty towards the end of the year and
thus slowing up the preparation of plans
for new building during that period. I
beg to move.
Mr. CAMPBELL: This is the class of
legislation that would have appealed to
Lord Beaconsfield, the anniversary of
whose death is, I believe, to-day, and I
am surprised to see such a small proportion of the Members of this House
paying a tribute to his memory. The
classes in whose interests he desired
legislation, were the working classesthe genuine working classes. I have
always felt that the results which
have so far been achieved by the various
Housing Acts that have been passed by
the Government of Northern Ireland
have not benefited the working classes in
the community for whom they were
primarily intended. Many builders have
benefited under these Acts. Many
builders have received high rents in
addition to substantial bonuses. The rents
of these houses are, beyond any dispute,
far beyond the means of the poorer
members of the working classes. All
along the line the rents have been beyond
their means, and it is indisputable that
they are beyond their means at the present time. I do not think this Bill will
in any way mitigate that evil.
We are told it is the conviction of the
Deputy Leader of the House, and of the
Government, that the law of supply and
demand will eventually regulate the
rents of houses. That is the old doctrine
of the Manchester school of sixty or
seventy years ago, and it is amusing to
see a Government which has repudiated
all doctrines of that class, Free Trade included, still holding on to this law of
supply and demand. I do not think any
business man in Belfast believes that the
law of supply and demand will ever
regulate the rents of working-class houses.
No capitalist or builder will build a house
to-day in the hope that he will be able
to realise any profit on it. It will not
pay him, and he can only do it with the
assistance of the State. Yet the State
has taken no steps whatever to control
the rents which may be demanded from
the working classes, except so far as they
are sheltered by the Rent Restrictions
Act.
This Parliament passed last year a
Planning and Housing Act. It purported to follow the English Act, but it
departed from it in one vital matter.
One great object of that Act was to
abolish the slums, to put an end to slum
areas, to pull down unsanitary houses and
in their place erect decent houses to
accommodate the people who were living
in the slums. In England, in order to
accomplish that, the Government supplied
a financial stimulus and
gave local
authorities financial assistance over a
series of years. The Northern Government under their Act did not give the
local authorities
one
penny for this
purpose, and the net result of that has
been that I do not think a single order
has been made by any local authority
in Northern Ireland declaring any area
unhealthy and ordering the houses to be
pulled down, not to speak of erecting
houses in their place. I think that is a
very unsatisfactory condition of affairs.
The Bill now before the House may be
the last of these Housing Acts, and it
is simply the climax of a series of unsatisfactory Acts which have brought no
real help and assistance to the class which
needs it most, the humbler working class.
The slums are still there, and they are,
apparently, going to continue. The better class artisans have got something, the
builders have got more, but the particular class of people the State intended
to make provision for has gained nothing.
Colonel PAKENHAM: As a trustee
of the Irish Sailors' and Soldiers' Land
Trust I should like to take this opportunity of thanking the Government of
Northern Ireland for having treated us
so decently and honourably as they have
done under one Clause of this Bill. The
Government have been very good to us.
They have always given us every assistance in carrying out our responsibilities,

Order for Third Reading read.
Mr. LONG: I beg to move, "That this
Bill be now read the Third time.”
Mr. CAMPBELL: We shall all be delighted if this Bill achieves any practical
results, but one question does occur to
one, and that is whether at a time such
as this there is really any probability of
this Bill bringing about early useful results. Under this Bill we are endeavouring
to attract new industries into our area.
That is quite right and very desirable,
but at the same time we know that all
around us tariff walls are being raised
higher and higher. People who have
been on the Continent in recent years
will tell you that in almost every capital
on the Continent business is practically
stagnant and international trade has
almost ceased to flow. One country is
sending up tariff walls against another,
and the other country retaliates by sending its tariffs higher. We are doing
the same thing. We want to trade with
other countries, but we are doing our
best to shut them out. They want to
trade with us, but they are doing their
best to shut us out. That is going on
all over Europe to-day, and for this
reason I am afraid early fruits of this Bill
will be negligible.

Question to Minister.
LOADING AND UNLOADING OF
LIVESTOCK.
The following question stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Mr.
Quigley:-
To ask the Leader of the House
whether the Government will make it
obligatory that all motor transport
lorries used for the conveyance of livestock should be provided with a gangway
for loading and unloading.
Mr. QUIGLEY: I have put down the
question standing in my name with a
view to preventing a form of cruelty
which exists in regard to livestock conveyed by motor transport lorries. The
unloading of animals from such lorries is
most painfully carried out.
The common procedure is for a man to remain on
the lorry and to place each animal in
such a position that a man on the ground
can get hold of it, usually by its tail,
should it be a pig. The animal is jostled
about until it is dropped to the ground.
When pigs are being unloaded the men
unloading them seem to think that the
tails are handles for swinging the pigs
about. From the amount of squealing
raised by the pigs it is obvious that considerable pain is occasioned to the hapless
animals. If motor transport lorries were
provided with gangways for loading and
unloading animals such unnecessary
suffering would be prevented. Suitable
gangways could quite easily be fitted to
the rear of the lorries.
Sheep are similarly coarsely treated.
I have witnessed the transfer from lorries
of sheep, and I think the only difference
in the procedure I have referred to is
Oral Answers
Railways Bill
THE SENATE
[Mr. Quigley]
that the sheep are encouraged to jump
from the lorry to the ground, a distance
of between four and five feet. Sometimes they miss their jump and fall to
the ground. Others which are not inclined to jump are pulled from the lorry
by two attendants in waiting. I am
aware that some motor transport lorries
are provided with equipment for the
loading and unloading of cattle and
horses, but not all are provided with such
equipment. I beg to ask the question
standing in my name.
Viscount CHARLEMONT: An Order
has recently been made by the Ministry
of Agriculture regulating the transit of
animals by road vehicles generally. This
Order provides, inter alia, that motor
vehicles used for the conveyance of livestock shall be provided with suitable
loading and unloading facilities. The
Order is at present being printed and
will shortly be on sale. I am, however,
posting to the hon. Senator a copy of
the Clause which deals with the particular point that he has raised.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I think the hon.
Senator (Mr. Quigley), who has brought
this question forward, deserves credit for
drawing attention to an aspect of cruelty
which we are apt to overlook very largely
as a matter of habit and frequent usage.
The Order to which the noble Leader of
the House has referred marks a distinct
advance, and I am very glad to hear that
such an Order is about to be promulgated.
I think the hon. Senator, who raised the
matter, will agree that the men who are
engaged in this work are not cruel or
callous, but they do their very best with
the equipment they have at hand.
Mr. HILL DICKSON: I would not
like it to go forth that cruelty exists in
all these cases, because although a motor
lorry may not have a gangway there is
usually a beach level with the back of
the lorry, and on to which the animal
walks on the level. Such beaches are
provided at Messrs. Robson's, and at
Balmoral and other places, including my
own place at home. At such places there
is no need for a gangway, because the
animals walk from and to the lorry on a
level beach. Although I have no doubt
that in some instances there is cruelty
involved, I want to make it quite clear
that it is by no means universal.
Mr. McHUGH: Certainly not.

Viscount CHARLEMONT: When this

asked for an assurance to be given at a

Clause 10 of the Bill by reason of the

Valuation Acts Amendment Act of last

the issue of general revaluations.
I am happy to give to the hon. and
learned Senator the assurance which he
is seeking. The object of Clause 10 is,
as he is aware, that the special quinquennial railway valuation is to be included every year in the document which
the Clause describes as "the revised
valuation lists to be issued by the first
day of March next following.' Now, in
every year there will be a document corresponding to this description. In a year
when no general revaluation is to come
into force, the ordinary revised valuation
lists will come within this description.
This will also be the case in a year when
a general revaluation is to come into
force. The Act of last year provided for
the issue of a general revaluation on or
before the first day of March, except in
the case of the first general revaluation.
The first general revaluation is to be
issued on a prescribed day, but is not to
come into force until the first day of
April in the following year.
In the year
in which this prescribed day falls, the
ordinary revised valuation lists are to be
issued on or before the first day of March,
and by the first day of March of the
year after, the general revaluation must
have been out at least two months, and
will thus come within the description in
the Clause.
In short, by the first day of March in
every year there will be a set of lists with
which the railway valuations can be incorporated under this Clause. I beg to
move, "That this Bill be now read the
Third time."

to the noble Viscount for looking into

the explanation just given before them,

on the wording of the particular Clause.

Railways (Valuation for Rating) Bill.
Viscount CHARLEMONT: Before I
move, "That this Bill do now pass,' I
should like to give a reply to a question
raised yesterday by Senator Armstrong.
The provisions of the Railway Valuation Bill are intended to apply only to
hereditaments of such a nature that their
net annual value can properly be found
by reference to the net receipts derived
from railway undertaking. The definition of railway hereditament has been
framed, therefore, so as to exclude such
premises as offices or receiving depots,
situated in town and not forming part of
the railway station, because the letting
value of such premises can be found by
ordinary methods, and is not governed
by the earning power of the railway
company. Such premises are excluded
by paragraph (a) of Sub-section (1) of
Clause (1).
The Bill prescribes a method of valuation for railway hereditaments only, and
paragraph (b) of the section is inserted to
exclude premises used for other purposes,
such as road or sea transport. Lest the
exclusion should be too wide, it was
agreed with the railway companies to
introduce limiting words to ensure that
any parts of such premises used for
goods or parcels services directly connected with railway transport, and the
annual value of which could only properly
be found by reference to the net receipts
of the company, should be excepted from
such exclusion.
Broadly speaking the distinction between paragraphs (a) and (b) is that
paragraph (a) refers to premises possessing a letting value quite apart from their
occupation for the special purposes of a
railway company, while the words in
brackets in paragraph (b) relate to those
parts of hereditaments which, although
the main use of the hereditaments themselves is for subsidiary purposes, being
directly connected with a railway station,
Local Bills.

or by railway with the company's system,
ought properly to be included in the
premises which contribute to the earning
capacity of the undertaking, and are
valued on the revenue principle. I hope
this explanation will satisfy the right
hon. Senator. I now beg to move, "That
this Bill do now pass."

THE MEANS TEST.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg to ask the
Leader of the House, whether, owing to
the means test for the unemployed,
mothers are suffering from under-nourishment, particularly in families where there
are a number of children; whether, before
the means test was adopted, standard
benefit was often eked out by relatives
helping one another; whether this has
now become impossible by reason of the
stringent conditions of the test; and
whether the Government will take steps
to ensure that families are maintained
on a subsistence level.
In putting this question may I say I
think there is a tendency at present to
slur over unpleasant facts in connection
with the means test. It is not always
safe to shut one's eyes to those facts.
As far as my information goes many
families in this area have now nothing
but standard benefit to live upon. That
benefit is not enough to maintain families
in a decent standard of subsistence,
particularly where the wage earner has
been long out of work. Then families are
going into debt. It is not deep debt
because they cannot get long credit, and
they cannot get large credit, but it is
deep enough to spread abroad a feeling
of despondency among many of the
working-class people. Clothing is being
worn almost threadbare. One thing I do
submit to the House is that mothers and
children should not suffer from want of
nourishing food, because, and for no
other reason, their men folk through no
fault of their own cannot find employment. It would be wrong that these
things should exist, and I do suggest that
it would be a wise thing to increase the
children's allowances at least where most
needed, and to give a liberal interpretation to this means test.
Viscount CHARLEMONT: The Government is not aware of the facts as
alleged by the hon. and learned Member.
As a measure of necessary economy certain
changes in the unemployment insurance
scheme were brought into operation in
C

November, 1931. The means test, which
was designed to secure that the money
available should be distributed amongst

rate assessed by a public assistance committee on the grounds that his circumstances are such that whilst unemployed
he has need of assistance by way of such

The public assistance committees are

COST TO VOLUNTARY HOSPITALS
OF MOTOR ACCIDENTS.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg to ask the
Leader of the House, whether, notwithstanding that the Motor Vehicles and
Road Traffic Act, 1930, imposes liability
in certain events on insurers and owners
of motor-cars for expenses of hospital
treatment of persons injured in accidents,
the position of the voluntary hospitals remains unsatisfactory in respect
of
accident cases; whether in only a small
percentage of such cases do the hospitals
obtain any payment for maintenance
expenses, and whether the Government
will take steps to lighten this heavy
burden on the hospitals.
I am sure the House will recognise that
the voluntary hospitals in Northern Ireland are each and all rendering indispensable services to the entire community.
They are struggling hard to make ends
meet, and the heaviest load they bear
to-day is due to a cause that was not
anticipated until a few years ago, and
that is the appalling number of people
who are killed or injured by motor
vehicles on highways. I see that in
Great Britain last year 18 people a day
were killed on the roads, and 553 people
a day were injured. The number of nonfatal accidents in Great Britain rose last
year by 24,000 to the staggering total of
202,119. There are more people killed
and injured in a year as a result of motor
accidents on highways in Great Britain
than were killed in the three years of
the Boer War. It is a most remarkable
fact that taking the entire British killed,
wounded and died of disease in the Boer
War from 1899 to 1902, they were not
as numerous as the British people killed
and injured in 1931 in motor car accidents.
The figures for Northern Ireland are not
known to me at the moment, but they are
by no means reassuring. This class of
accident is now proving a heavy and unfair drain on the resources of these
voluntary hospitals, resources which are
very rapidly decreasing. In the larger
proportion of these cases the hospitals
can get no return whatever. They take
the patients in, treat them, maintain
them, and spend money in providing
skilled medical and surgical treatment,
while they themselves are almost crippled
financially and they do not get one penny
return in the vast majority of cases. The
Motor Vehicles Act (Northern Ireland),
1930, gives some little relief, but it is
very inadequate, and I do submit that
this is a matter that requires very urgent
consideration by the authorities.
My attention is also drawn to the fact
that a large number of commercial lorries
now take traders and their wares to the
provincial towns in Northern Ireland, and
their third-party insurance is limited to
goods only. They set down
down thirty
traders and their goods in a market town,
and if an accident happens, as a rule
there is no person of substance to sue.
The injured party is taken to hospital,
and the hospital is left in the air as far
as any return for their services is concerned. I do say this has become
a matter of very definite urgency.
Viscount CHARLEMONT: The Government have no definite information as
to the percentage of the cost of treating
accident cases which is recovered by the
hospitals, but it is understood that it is
not great. While the Government
sympathise with the difficulties of the
hospitals in this matter, they cannot see
their way to introduce further legislation.
Mr. HILL-DICKSON: There is no
difficulty in finding out the number of
cases that come into voluntary hospitals
through motor accidents, and I do not
admit they are of a negligible quantity.
Not only voluntary hospitals but district
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
10 MAY 1932
hospitals and county infirmaries are
affected in the same way. Perhaps a
person is injured by a motor lorry
driven by a person from another
district altogether and I think all
hospitals are entitled to have the first
claim on the insurance company in respect of the treatment of an injured person. I think the answer given by the
Government to the question on the Paper
is very unsatisfactory. I hold that in
twenty-five per cent. of these accident
cases there is no recovery by the hospitals
of the cost of treatment, and I think it
is high time the insurance companies
should be called upon to pay it as a first

NOTICE OF OFFICIAL VISITS.
The following question stood on the

-:
To ask the Leader of the House whether
the Government will consider the advisability, in cases where Government valuers
or other officials are sent to visit dwellinghouses for the purpose of making valuations or performing other public duties,
of giving timely notification of such visits
to occupiers, particularly in rural areas,
unless the public interest should otherwise require.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I may say at once
that in putting down this question I have
no intention of making the slightest insinuation, directly or indirectly, against
the officials, who do their duty most
efficiently. The only aim of the question
is to bring to the notice of the Government the fact that sometimes people
living in rural areas in Northern Ireland receive visits from persons who are
perfect strangers to them. The fact that
such visits are unexpected is sometimes a
matter of considerable embarrassment and
inconvenience. So many people now visit
private houses for different purposes that
it is quite natural that an elderly lady
or gentleman living in a secluded area
in Northern Ireland and seeing an official
for the first time in his or her life may
not be quite sure about his identity for
the time being or whom he represents,
but an officially written postcard in advance would prevent any uncertainty as
to his identity.
Mr. HILL-DICKSON: I quite agree
with the hon. and learned Senator that
when an official visits a house the tenant
or owner should have due notice of his
visit, but if we received a notice in the
case of visits of every official we would
be getting postcards every morning.
Mr. CAMPBELL: That is not my experience.
Viscount
CHARLEMONT: Having
regard to the large number of dwellinghouses and other properties to be inspected for the purpose of revaluation,
and to the uncertainty of any official's
programme of work owing to weather and
other conditions, it is quite impracticable
to give individual notice to the occupiers
of the proposed visit of a valuer. Moreover, the expenditure of time and money
involved in the issue of such notices
would not be justified.
I am assured, however, by the Commissioner of Valuation, speaking from
long experience, that no practical difficulty is likely to arise. Every effort is
made to consult the convenience of ratepayers in these matters, and they, on
their part, are found willing to offer all
reasonable facilities to visiting officials.
A valuer is always ready to make a
special appointment for the purpose of
an inspection or to revisit premises when
that course is found to be necessary.
For the information of the public, it
may be stated that the work of inspection
in the rural districts of Counties Antrim
and Down is likely to be commenced in
the immediate future. Having regard to
the courtesy extended to his officials in
the past by owners and occupiers of
property, the Commissioner of Valuation
does not anticipate any difficulty in carrying out the work.
Message from the Commons.
The Commons agree to the Amendments made by the Joint Committee to
Hall's Divorce Bill, without Amendment;
they agree to the Poultry Diseases Bill
without Amendment; they have passed
the Loans Guarantee Bill, the Rent and
Mortgage Interest (Restrictions) Bill, and
the Mental Treatment Bill, to which they
desire the concurrence of this House.

Viscount CHARLEMONT: This short
Bill seeks to extend the powers of the
Ministry of Finance in regard to loans
guarantees for a further year, namely,
until 31st March, 1933. The Government feel that it is advisable to continue
this legislation so that the necessary
facilities may be available in case they
are needed, though I regret to say that,
so far as shipbuilding is concerned, the
position is almost as bad as it could be.
We can only hope that some new orders
may be received in the not too distant
future, and that it may be possible to
put the machinery of the guarantees into
operation. There is a further reason for
keeping these facilities alive, namely,
that they are applicable not only for
shipbuilding but also for other industries
as well, and it is possible that with the
introduction of tariffs some new factories
may be established in our area which
might satisfy the conditions required for
the loans guarantees. For these reasons
I commend this Bill to the House and
beg to move that it be read a Second
time.

Bill.
