a First time."-(Mr. Long.)
On Question, Motion agreed to.
Viscount CHARLEMONT: On rising
to move the Second Reading of this Bill
it is necessary, I think, to go back a little
to see the course of the legislation on the
whole question of rent restriction which
has taken place since it was first introduced in 1915. Control of rents was of
course necessitated by war conditions
when the building of houses had come to
a sudden stop. The Act of 1915 was
limited to houses of £26 valuation and
under and this limit in valuation was extended in two subsequent Acts passed in
1919 and 1920, the maximum being so
raised to a valuation of £78. The
amount of increase in rent which was
allowed was fixed at 40 per cent.
This control was renewed yearly until
1925, when our own Government here
reconsidered the whole question and introduced a Bill in which it was prescribed
that houses should go out of control on
definite specified dates; those of £52 valuation and over on 1st November '26;
those between £26 and £52 on 1st May,
'28, and those £26 and under on 1st May,
1930. There is also a provision that any
house over £8 valuation should automatically become decontrolled on coming into.
the possession of the landlord, and there
was the additional change that the permitted increase in rent was reduced from
40 per cent. to 30 per cent. In 1928 it
was felt that for houses of £26 valuation
and under it would not be advisable to
remove the control and an Act was passed
extending the period of restriction until
1933.
In view of the large number of houses
which have been built by means of the
subsidy it was hoped, and, indeed, it was
expected, that in 1933 we might finally
see the end of this whole difficult business of control. There has been, however, as hon. Members are aware, a good
deal of feeling and apprehension among
smaller householders as to what will
happen if all control were taken off next
year, and the other House last Session
thought it advisable to set up a Select
Committee to inquire into the rents now
being charged for houses which are at
present controlled and also those which
have become decontrolled, and to report
whether these rents were excessive. The
report of this Select Committee was
published in December, and there is no
doubt that the situation as it was revealed to them in the evidence which
they received from the various interested
parties called for some further legislation.
That legislation is contained in the present Bill now before the House.
I propose to make a few remarks on
the various Clauses of this Bill, taking
them in order. Clause 1 seeks to continue the operation of the existing legislation until 1936. Clause 2 of the Bill
takes the matter somewhat further. If
the present legislation were merely continued, houses between £8 and £26
would become decontrolled on coming into
the possession of the landlord; that is the
arrangement as it stands at present. This
Clause, however, provides that all the
houses in this category will remain controlled until 1936, irrespective of whether
they come into the landlord's possession
or not. The Select Committee in their
recommendations went even farther than
this and suggested that houses between
£8 and £26 valuation, which had already
become decontrolled, should be again
brought into control, certain provisions
being recommended to deal with cases of
those in which a change of ownership has
taken place since they went out of control.
But the Government have been unable
to accept this part of the recommendation
as they believe that it would be quite
unworkable.
Clause 3 of the Bill deals with the prevention of evasions of the Rent Restrictions Acts. There were certain gross
abuses revealed in the course of the
Select Committee's inquiries which could
not be tolerated. The first of these is
dealt with under Sub-Clause (1) of
Clause 3, the period of payment of instalment where a house is being purchased
on the instalment system being limited to

I think the Government has gone as
far as it possibly can to deal with the
undoubted abuses which were revealed by
the Select Committee, and also to deal
with the general question of the extension of control which we would all like
to see ended, but which, I am afraid, it
is necessary to continue in the case of
some classes of houses for a little time
yet. The Committee, it may be remembered, proved without doubt that the rents
of houses between £8 and £26 valuation
which have been coming out of control
have been in a large number of instances
increased to an exorbitant extent. The
only final cure for all this is that the
ordinary economic laws of supply and
demand should operate, and I may conclude by expressing the hope that when
this extended legislation comes to an end
in 1936 there may be a sufficient supply
of houses of all classes to render further
control unnecessary. I beg to move.
Mr. CAMPBELL: The Government
has stopped a good way short of producing a satisfactory Bill dealing with
In the first inthis question of rents.
stance, it is a disappointing Bill, because it
fails to give protection of any kind to large
numbers of tenants-there must be many
hundreds-whose houses have been decontrolled by the operation of the Rent Restrictions Act of 1925, in the course of the
last seven years.
In this respect the
recommendation of a majority of the
members of the Select Committee has
been ignored. It was the complaint of
this class of the community that led to
the formation of that Committee. It was
their grievances that brought the
iniquities referred to by the noble Leader
of the House to light, and now at the
end of it all they find a Bill laid before
this House in which they are left out in
the cold. That is not a satisfactory condition of affairs when we reflect that many
of these tenants are paying exorbitant
rents and are at present suffering very
great hardships. The Government offers
them no relief whatever. In other words,
the Government is sheltering those landlords who, during the past seven years,
have put the screw on their tenants. I
know of no valid reason for that except
that the Government has a soft spot in
its heart for the landlord class.
It takes its stand on the plea that
it cannot interfere with contracts,
that contracts have been made during
the past seven years which it would not
be wise or expedient to interfere with.
But these Rent Restrictions Acts for
years and years past have been interfering
Rent Restrictions Bill-
Second Reading
10 MAY 1932
with contracts, and the very basis of these
Acts is the settled policy of interfering
with contracts between landlords and
tenants in the interests of the community
at large. If the same argument had
prevailed in the year 1881 we should
never have had the historic Land Act of
that year, and if the same argument had
prevailed in 1906 we should never have
had the Town Tenants Act of 1906. Both
of these Acts interfered in a most serious
way with the sanctity of contracts, but
they did it in the interests of the State
and the community at large. I do submit to the House that the tenants of all
houses between £8 and £26 valuation
should be put on the same level, and that
there is no reason in fairness and equity
in discriminating, as Clause 2 does, between the tenants of this particular
class of house. There is no reason
either why the landlords of this
class of houses should be differentiated
between. They in turn should be put on
the same level.
Then there is no provision in this Bill
against profiteering by tenants. That itself
is a very insidious and widespread evil.
There is a new class of landlord springing into existence in Belfast. He takes
houses to which these Acts apply and
proceeds to split them up into different
apartments and rooms, and he charges
the highest rent he possibly can to the
sub-tenants. That is a very gross evil
against which this Bill makes no provision whatever. Again, in failing to
guard against profiteering of that kind
this Bill falls very far short of expectations.
Mr. LESLIE: I am afraid that for the
reason suggested earlier in the afternoon
the remarks I have to address to the
House will be more disjointed than I
could wish, although it is a fact, as was
stated, that a copy of the Bill did reach
me last Thursday. My post-bag contained other Parliamentary Papers,

One of those Papers was a Bill already
referred to, containing 71 Clauses, ten
times the length of this Bill; consequently I have not been able to devote
as much of the past week as I could have

However, I must say that I dislike this
Bill intensely. I had hoped that we had
seen the end of control, or rather that
we should see it when we came to the
1st May, 1933, on which date we had
reason to believe it was intended that
control should cease. I dislike the continuance of control to such an extent that

facts already alluded to; that is to say,
that a Committee appointed by those who
sit elsewhere has recommended its continuance, the Government have accepted
its recommendation in that respect, and
the other Chamber has passed the Bill.
Moreover, one has to recognise that
although it might be well to get rid of
control at once, that is, next May, there
will be certain disturbances, no doubt,
following the cessation of control, and it
may be that the time then will not be as

I hope
myself that one of the results of revaluation will be to move towards the general
object which we all had in view, and that
is the provision of a sufficient number of
houses for the lower incomed classes
or poorer classes at rents which
they can afford to pay.
That is really
what all these measures are aimed at,
and this particular Bill may be termed
one of the paving stones leading in that
direction. Therefore, the Bill as regards
its object will have the sympathy of all
of us.
The object is all right, and, as to the
manner of its execution, I think we will
have to consider whether there are not
proposals in this Bill which will militate.
against the provision of additional houses
of the class I have alluded to. The
Bill seems to me, having got over its first

years, to proceed on the lines that every

who takes one of these houses is good.
Neither of these theories is borne out

and bad tenants. But the landlords con
cerned in these particular houses were
alluded to by one of the hon. Senators
on my left, I think when the Bill of 1925
was before the House, or perhaps 1927,
as being landlords not in an extensive
sense but very small people indeed.
Very often the landlord of other
labourers' houses is a labouring man
himself. That, so far as I have been told,
has been borne out by the report of the
Committee as well as by the evidence
brought before the Committee to which
I have alluded.

THE SENATE
[Mr. Leslie
Moreover, the Bill makes no effort
whatever, as the hon. Senator in front of
me said, to deal with the evil of subletting. I do not know how far hon.
Senators have been able to dip into the
evidence before the Committee. There is
nothing to deal with the sad case of a
young woman about to become a mother
who went and wept in Mr. Armstrong's
outer office, because she was asked to pay
15s a week for a room in a house, the
total rent of which was something about
6s. That case is not dealt with in the
Bill before us. I, myself, can see no
reason whatever why the landlord of that
house, whatever he may have done,
should be penalised as against the tenant
who dealt in that manner with this particular woman. And those cases, I understand, are typical.
Moreover, I think we have to remember that although some of those agreements and, of course, we shall all think
naturally of Appendix A of the Reportsome of those agreements, probably 99
per cent. of them were harsh and unconscionable and were not, in all probability,
agreements at all. Some of them were
genuine. Most of them were pretty bad,
and at once the Committee and Parliament rises up and condemns the person
responsible, or alleged to be responsible,
and Parliament forgets to condemn itself.
Parliament does not remember, or, at
least, there is no indication in the Bill
that it does remember, that Parliament
itself is to blame in this matter. Parliament has dealt with restriction of rents
since 1925. Two Parliaments, the Parliament across the water and our own, have
been at this game since 1915, and this
particular Parliament has dealt with
abuses as regards letting small houses
with furniture, but nobody in this Parliament foresaw the ingenuity and tricks
that people outside have practised to
their own interest and the detriment of
others.
Parliament did not foresee. And this
provision seems to me unjust, however
immoral these proceedings may be. I am
not defending them. But we have to remember that those acts, so far as they
went, were acts which our own made law
could not touch. As to the contracts, I
may say something about them later on.
But the general proceedings were not prohibited by law. The proposal now is to
turn round and inflict penalties on the
assumption that what we are going to
enact now
was law when these things
were done.
It is impossible to stand over
that, or, at least, to go very far in that
direction. I will say more about that
if I may at a later date. There are, undoubtedly-and most of us knew it before
the Committee reported, but the evidence
has brought it more home to us-many
things wrong about this matter and we
are anxious to put them right, but two
wrongs, or forty-five wrongs or more,
do not make one right.
And, therefore, when our sympathies
are aroused to the highest pitch, one
might say for these poor people whose
faces have been ground by inconsiderate
landlords we ought, as I think, to be exceptionally careful that we do not do an
injustice to any individual person. One
thing in the report of the Committee was
the direct statement that some of these
arrangements-I do not like to call them
agreements were, no doubt, genuine.
That is not recognised at all in the Bill
before us. The Bill proceeds to deal with
these cases in the lump as though they
were all necessarily immoral, if you like,
and does not provide any protection for
that minority which may have been honest
purchase agreements. I think it will be
admitted that the number of these cases
where these arrangements came into existence that could be described as legitimate
would be very small indeed.
But still there may be some left, but
owing to the fact that the bad will very
heavily outweigh the good I think we
might deal with the matter not by requiring in the ordinary way that the
person alleged to be wronged should
prove the iniquity, but by asking the
person who made the arrangement to
prove it was a genuine arrangement.
There ought to be some loophole provided, and I think we ought to be the
more ready to do that because, as I say, we
are not entirely free from blame in the
matter. These matters we did not foresee and it is scarcely for us to turn round
and say to a man: "We did not mean you
to do that. You have done it, and you
shall pay for it." And then we have got
to keep before us very prominently the
point, is what we are going to do likely
to conduce to our end, that is, the provision of suitable houses at a suitable
price, or is it going to drive people out
of the trade. Are people going to stop
building houses because they are no
longer profitable? Are these smaller
people referred to in the report going to
Rent Restrictions Bill-
10 MAY 1932
Second Reading
stop investing their savings in house
property because there is not going to be
any more inducement to build houses?
I must draw attention to Clause 2,
because of a remark of the noble Viscount
which, I confess, I did not expect him to
make. I hope he did not mean it. But I
rather gathered from the earlier portion
of his remarks about Clause 2 that he
intimated that Clause 2 is not to cease to
operate when the Rent Restrictions Act
ceases to operate, that will be, assuming
the Bill becomes law, in May, 1936. I
thought myself that the Clause bore out
my view that when the Rent Restrictions
Act expired in 1936 Clause 2 will expire
also. The noble Viscount spoke of a
further extension.
I think the hon. Senator in front of me
made some other remarks on Clause 2
about the matter of the £8. I do not
think I need say anything about that.
I think his suggestion was that the house
under £8 was differentiated in this Clause
from the house above £8 and under £26.
Passing on to the first Sub-Clause of
Clause 3 there is some difficulty in understanding the reference to the interest on
the instalments. I imagine the intention
is that 7 per cent. is to be paid or to be
payable on so much of the purchase money
as is outstanding. I think that is the
intention, but I confess it is not very
clear.
I presume also the intention is that the
cost of these copies of the agreement is to
fall on the person who for this purpose
may be called the grantor. The Bill
does not say. A copy of an agreement
such as that cannot possibly be supplied
without cost to somebody. I am inclined
to think the grantor is to pay for it. We
have required that the agreement is not
to be an agreement unless it is signed,
and we have to go into details as closely
as that. I gather from the report of the
Committee that it is necessary to provide
for things like that. From the report we
really have got to provide that the agreement shall be signed.
Now we come to Sub-clause (2) and
there we begin, I think, to hit out on the
assumption that an agreement providing
for an option cannot possibly be an
honest agreement. I agree that if paragraph (a) and paragraph (b) are disregarded I should hesitate to believe that
there was anything to be said for the
person on whose behalf I am for the
moment speaking, that is, the person
who under paragraph (c) has to
repay the deposit with interest and
to lose under paragraph (d) his right
of action to recover rent. It does seem
to me apparently possible that an option
may be given, and a deposit taken in a
perfectly genuine action. I think saving
clauses should be put in to meet cases of
this sort if, in fact, there are some. We
are not told how many good cases there
We are told, or it is reported, that
some of these agreements are genuine.
are.
Again, passing on to Sub-clause 3, I
understand from the noble Viscount that
Sub-clauses 3 and 1 were not in any way
related to each other, and it was clear
from the report of the Committee-at
least I think it is clear-but it is one of
the matters I was not able to finish investigating, but it does
that some
appear
of these arrangements, at all events, did
provide for due payments to the landlords, but failed to provide that at the
expiration of the payments the tenant
should get anything for which he had
paid. That is to say, a man was to pay
his instalments, and when he had done
so he was not to get the house. Naturally,
when Parliament is dealing with these
matters, that class of agreement is likely
to come in for rather severe attention.
Again, it is proposed to provide here
that the agreement shall not be determinable by the owner except for wilful
injury to or destruction of the dwellinghouse, or where default is made in payment of any part of the periodical
instalments. In those events the deposit
and all instalments are to be repaid to
that man who has destroyed his house,
and the owner of the house is not to
bring any action against him until he has
paid over the deposit and instalment.
That is to say, he is providing the man
who has wilfully destroyed his house with
money to run away with, and the owner
is left to whistle for compensation for
damage to his house. I do not know
whether that is the intention of the Bill,
but it does seem extraordinary. As it
stands, it appears to me you are weighting
the dice in favour of the tenant who
deliberately damages his house and then
runs away.
Now we pass to Sub-Clause 4, as to
which there is no reason to cavil. A man
ought to execute his agreement, and
ought not to enter into an agreement
which contravenes the provisions of the
Rent Restrictions Bill-
Second Reading
THE SENATE
[Mr. Leslie]
section. There is no particular difficulty
about his liability to a fine, as that is
already the law in other circumstances
under, I think, the Act of 1925 or 1926.
I forget which. Now we come to Sub-
Clause 5, which, speaking generally,
seems to me to be not unreasonable, and
it would become perfectly reasonable if
the saving Clause I have spoken of for
the honest letter is put in.
When we come to Sub-clause 6 I am
afraid I do think very seriously that this
House ought to resist the temptation to
accept this particular Sub-clause.
That
is, the Sub-clause dealing with the case of
an arrangement which is past and done
with. A man, perhaps, has been unfairly
treated. The suggestion is that when all
that is over the former occupier should
go back and recover the money which he
would not have had to pay if this Bill
had then been law. But this Bill was
not law, and he was required to pay it
and did pay it. I cannot agree that it
is right to re-open those proceedings. If
the House passes that particular provision they will be doing the greatest
possible disservice to that cause I spoke
of, that is the cause of getting a proper
number of houses built of the class you
want. If you support retrospective
legislation of that kind you will discourage anybody from putting their
money into house property. They will
say, "No doubt control expired in 1936.
There is no control now, but how do I
know the 1946 Parliament will not reimpose control and that they will say,
'You built these houses in 1936. If you
built them to-day the conditions would
have been so and so and so. You must
pay back the money you got for the past
ten years.
That is the precedent you
are setting, and it is a most dangerous
precedent, and I shall have to press it
most seriously on the attention of the
House at a later date. I ought not to go
further into the matter now, and I am
more willing to leave it, because
Clause 4 deals solely with iniquities as
regards payment for rates, in which I
entirely support the Bill.
As regards Clause 5 there is nothing
to be said. It is, in fact, an extension
of what Parliament did before as regards
rates, I think, in 1927. There is no
reason whatever to allow abuses to continue in regard to that matter, and I
think we can deal with that quite easily
as it stands. Clauses 6 and 7 are normal
as well as formal. On the whole, the
Bill recognises what is true enough, that
those contracts which are not contracts
ought not to be sustained. I mean by
that an arrangement or agreement where
there was
no agreement between two
minds in the same sense.
When there
was no proper contract undoubtedly one
may intervene, but you must preserve the
rights of anybody who may possibly be
honest. You must give then a chance of
establishing their innocence before the
appropriate court, and protect them from
the loss of damage. Generally you must
remember there is all the difference in
the world between transgressing the law
on the Statute Book and simply transgressing something which is not there
then but which you are about to adopt.
I do not propose to oppose the Bill,
because I am in sympathy with its objects,
even though I doubt very much if it will
help to the end we have in view
Mr. ARMSTRONG: I feel a great deal
of sympathy with the criticisms the hon.
and learned Senator has just delivered
with regard to this Bill. It seems to me
that the Bill has been drawn with a view
to Belfast conditions alone, because if
there is any discontent in the country
with regard to the working of the Rent
Restrictions Acts it has not reached my
ears. I do not think there is a feeling
in the country that landlords have tried
to evade the Acts-at least I have not
heard of such cases. I have noticed that
very few people build houses with a view
to letting. They sell them as soon as they
are built, and I am afraid this Measure
may have the effect of discouraging building.
In Belfast there has been an
enormous increase in the amount of money
put into savings banks. I believe it has
increased to the extent of a million
pounds, and that is the class of people
interested in these small houses. That is
not a very good thing, because houses
are very badly wanted, and it would
seem that, as time goes on, we shall have
them entirely provided by the public
authorities. Again, I think that would
not be desirable. I think the present
condition of affairs in Belfast is very unsatisfactory, because there are evidently
some landlords who have tried to evade
the Rent Acts. At the same time I think
this Bill will cause a great deal of
trouble, and instead of being an advantage it will prove a disadvantage.
Rent Restrictions Bill-
Second Reading
10 MAY 1932

Mr. DORMAN: I do not think this
Bill will give any satisfaction to that
large class of tenants whose outcry
against the injustices inflicted upon them
by landlords caused the setting up of
the Committee which inquired into the
rents charged in Belfast and elsewhere.
A large number of houses between £8
and £26 valuation have had their rents
increased to such an extent that the
Government had to pay some heed to the
outcry against the injustices to which the
tenants were being subjected. On previous
occasions I have given striking instances
of the exorbitant increase in the rents of
houses that have become decontrolled.
now want to draw the attention
Members to three particular cases in
different parts of the City of Belfast.
One is a street of houses built fifty years
ago at a cost of £150 per house.
controlled rent is £24 per year, and houses
in that street which have become decontrolled are now paying £36 a year. In
another part of the City there is another
street of houses erected forty years ago
which cost £220 per house. The controlled rents are £26, while the tenants
of houses that have become decontrolled
are paying £40.

of
The
In yet another part of the City the controlled rent of houses erected forty years
ago at a cost of £225 per house is £26,
and £45 is being charged for houses in
the same street that have become decontrolled. It was cases such as these that
created the outcry against the removal of
control, and the object of this Bill ought
to be to bring these houses back under
control. I do not see how a provision of
that kind could operate against the
building of new houses if you allowed
these individuals to have a reasonable return upon the value of their property.
Fancy houses which cost £150 fifty years
ago and they have not increased in
value in the meantime-being let at £24
under control, while the same house that
has become decontrolled is let at 33 per
cent. more These tenants must continue
to pay that exorbitant rent until the
Government take some steps to protect
them.
There is one admirable provision in the
Bill, and that is that the Government
have fixed the maximum rate of interest
upon borrowings under these hire purchase agreements. I would suggest
that if the Government would take into
consideration the advisability of setting
up a fair rent court to fix a fair rent as
between landlord and tenant they would
do more than they are doing in this Bill
to establish just relations between the
citizens of Belfast.
Mr. QUIGLEY: I am very much disappointed that the Government did not
accept and adopt the Rent Committee's
report in its entirety. The Government
are quite aware that quite a number of
house agents and landlords took advantage of the people to a greater extent
than even the Government expected.
Rents were increased from 60 to 100 per
cent. and over by some house agents and
some landlords. I did hope that control
would be reimposed and would apply to all
houses of £8 to £26 valuation. It is most
unfair and unreasonable to find tenants
paying 15s and 17s 6d weekly while other
tenants in the same street for identically
the same houses are paying something
like 7s 6d or 8s a week. Such anomalies
are bound to cause dissatisfaction, and i
think the Government should have made
some provision in the Bill for these
people. There is one matter I am not
quite clear about, and which I would like
to know from the noble Viscount, the
Leader of the House. If a house, the
valuation of which exceeds £8 and which
came into possession of the landlord after
1928, again becomes vacant, say in June,
1932, will it then be decontrolled?
I am
not clear upon this point in the Bill.
While not fully satisfied with the Bill, I
am very pleased that they have gone so
far in control and in safeguarding the
tenants.
Viscount CHARLEMONT: The criticism of this Bill on the one hand
is that the Government have gone too far
and on the other hand that they have not
gone far enough. It is a very thorny and

also like to answer Senator Quigley with

the Government came to the conclusion

of this abuse could be effected I am certain the Government would consider it.

CLAUSE 71 (Penalty for personation
of shareholder. [1908, s. 38 (1) (ii).]).
If any person falsely and deceitfully
personates any owner of any share or
interest in any company, or of any
share warrant or coupon, issued in pursuance of this Act, and thereby obtains
or endeavours to obtain any such share
or interest or share warrant or coupon,
or receives or endeavours to receive any
money due to any such owner, as if the
offender were the true and lawful
owner, he shall be guilty of felony, and
shall on conviction thereof be liable, at
the discretion of the court, to be kept
in penal servitude for life or for any
term not less than three years.

CLAUSE 100 (Power for Company to
keep Colonial Register. [1908, s. 34]).
(1) A company having a share
capital, whose objects comprise the
transaction of business in a colony,
may, if so authorised by its articles,
cause to be kept in any colony in which
it transacts business a branch register
of members resident in that colony (in
this Act called a colonial register).
(2) The company shall give to the
registrar of companies notice of the
situation of the office where any colonial
register is kept, and of any change in
its situation, and of the discontinuance
of the office in the event of its being
discontinued.
(3) For the purpose of the provisions of this Act relating to colonial
registers the term "colony" includes
British India.
Companies Bill-
Committee
THE SENATE
Mr. LESLIE: The Clause we are now
approaching, and the two following
Clauses, 101 and 102, are referred to in
the special report that the Committee
submitted to the House. The Committee
felt that having regard to the trend of
legislation of recent years across the
water, the expression "colony" and
"colonial" is one that ought not to be
used again, being entirely out of date.
Consequently, following the example set
across the water in the Companies Act of
1929, and sundry other Acts which I need
not refer to, the proper course was to
leave out the words "colonial" and
"colony" wherever they occurred and
substitute "dominion." The first opportunity of bringing that to the notice of
the House occurs at the top of this page.
If the Committee accepts that Amendment it will follow that an Amendment
must be made to sub-clause (3) of Clause
100 by altering the expression "colony"
and the definition of it to "dominion,"
and giving a definition of "dominion."
In giving the definition to "dominion"
I may say the Committee followed as
closely as practicable the wording in the
Interpretation Act of 1889. It
also
follows that as a necessary saving one
must provide that references to a colonial
register occurring in Articles of companies registered before this Act was
passed shall be construed as if they were
references to a dominion register. The
new Sub-clause is taken directly from the
Act of 1929. I beg to move the Amendments on the Paper.

CLAUSE 101 (Regulations as to
colonial register. [1908, s. 35.]).
(1) A colonial register shall be
deemed to be part of the company's
register of members (in this section
called the principal register).
(2) It shall be kept in the same
manner in which the principal register
is by this act required to be kept, except that the advertisement before
closing the register shall be inserted
in some newspaper circulating in the
district wherein the colonial register is
kept, and that any competent court in
the colony may exercise the same jurisdiction of rectifying the register as is
under this Act exercisable by the
court, and that the offences of refusing
inspection or copies of a colonial register, and of authorising or permitting
the refusal may be prosecuted summarily before any tribunal in the
colony having summary criminal jurisdiction.
(3) The company shall transmit to
its registered office a copy of every entry
in its colonial register, as soon as may
be after the entry is made; and shall
cause to be kept at its registered office,
duly entered up from time to time, a
duplicate of its colonial register, and
the duplicate shall, for all the purposes
of this Act, be deemed to be part of
the principal register.
(4) Subject to the provisions of this
section, with respect to the duplicate
register, the shares registered in a
colonial register shall be distinguished
from the shares registered in the
principal register, and no transaction
with respect to any shares registered
in a colonial register shall, during the
continuance of that registration, be
registered in any other register.
(5) A company may discontinue to
keep any colonial register, and thereupon all entries in that register shall
be transferred to some other colonial
register kept by the company in the

Mr. LESLIE: I beg to move in
page 177, lines 22 and 23, to leave
out the words, "whether limited or not,
and to insert, "not being a limited partnership. There is only one Amendment
on this Clause, but there are others on
the following Clause, and I may say at
once that this is perhaps the most technical and the most difficult part of the
Bill. I can best, I think, explain Clause
292 by reference to Clause 293. We have
to make the same provisions here, as
nearly as we can, as have been made in
Great Britain for other companies, and
we have to do it without relying in any
way on rules made by the Lord High
Chancellor of England, such as are referred to in paragraph (g) of Clause 293.
The position is that by the Act of 1908,
which is the principal Act we are consolidating, power is given to the Lord.
High Chancellor of England to make rules
dealing with this matter, applicable not
only to England but also to Ireland. In
due course the Act of 1920 came on the
Statute Book, and the Lord High Chancellor of England rather faded out of
the picture as regards Ireland.
But no Adaptation Order was made to
deal with this particular case, and when
the matter was considered it was seen
that an Adaptation Order could not possibly be made in that connection because the
matter that had to be dealt with was not
a matter which arose out of the establishment of the Northern Ireland Parliament. Consequently the Committee was in
a great difficulty in dealing with this
matter, and we felt it necessary to call
the attention of the House to the matter
specially, as was done in the report. It
seems to us that the winding up of a
limited
company belongs to the code
applicable to bankruptcy rather than to
the code of companies. We could not go
beyond our jurisdiction as a consolidating
Committee by inserting the words in the
text, that is, a direct reference to the Lord
Chief Justice of Northern Ireland in place
of the Lord High Chancellor of England.
We could not do that without the leave
of the House, and it did not seem to
us to be worth while to ask leave for an
extenion of our powers, which could
only result in an unsatisfactory solution
of the difficulty.

Mental Treatment Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
a
Mr. LONG: In moving the Second
Reading of this Bill, in the absence of
the noble Leader of the House, I think I
should, in the first place, remind
hon. Senators that the principal enactments under which treatment of
mental cases in Northern Ireland is
being carried out were passed in the
year 1875, and when I say that it
was found necessary in England to pass
a Consolidating Act in 1890, and
further Mental Treatment Act in 1930,
it will be appreciated that it is time we,
in Northern Ireland, brought our law in
this respect up to date. I do not wish
to suggest for one moment that the treatment of mental diseases in Northern
Ireland is less efficient or less successful
than elsewhere, because I am satisfied
that the treatment given in our mental
hospitals is, so far as the law at present
permits, as satisfactory as it can possibly
be.
One of the chief objects of this Bill is
to emphasise the fact that persons suffering from mental disease and cared for in
mental hospitals are invalids suffering
from afflictions of the mind, and are just
as
blameless and deserving of every
sympathy as persons in hospitals suffering
from and treated for afflictions of the
body. I think we should all endeavour
to remove the old idea which, unfortunately, prevails even now that mental
disease is something disgraceful, and that
persons of unsound mind should be kept
entirely away from society and looked
upon as being outside the pale of society.
Unfortunately, the procedure followed in
sending persons of unsound mind to
asylums in Ireland has rather tended to
give the ordinary person the impression
that they are committed as criminals, but
as a result of this Bill it is hoped that the
idea that to be of unsound mind is a
criminal offence will die out.
Under the provisions of this Bill persons of unsound mind may be divided
into three categories:
(1) The voluntary patient;
(2) The temporary patient; and
(3) The person certified to be of unsound mind.
To take the first of these categories,
there have not in the past been any facilities for persons who may be suffering from
a mild form of, or mere tendency to,
mental trouble to submit themselves for
voluntary treatment in institutions
specialising in the treatment of such
disease, and there is not the least doubt
that, like every other form of disease,
prevention is better than cure.
Under the provisions of Part I. of the
Bill it will now be possible for persons to
obtain specialised treatment by voluntarily entering an institution or hospital,
nursing home or place approved by the
Ministry of Home Affairs on that person's own written application, accompanied by a medical recommendation. In
the past it has not been generally possible
for persons suffering from a form of
mental instability which does not amount
to actual insanity, to obtain the benefits
of such treatment.
To come to the second category, which
is called temporary treatment, this again,
as its title implies, enables persons who
are in all probability suffering only temporarily from mental illness to be received
on the application of a near relative, or,
if there is no near relative, on the application of the relieving officer of the district, into an institution where special
treatment for this illness would be given.
This application must be accompanied by
two medical certificates, and one of the
conditions of temporary treatment is that,
in the opinion of the examining doctors,
the patient is likely to recover within
six months.
In this category, as in the first category
-I refer to that of voluntary patients-
Mental Treatment Bill-
Second Reading.
THE SENATE
[Mr. Long]
there is no actual certification of insanity,
and, consequently, there can be nothing
of the stigma which, unfortunately, has
come to be attached to an actual certification of insanity. It is to be hoped that
the benefits to be given under this Bill
in providing for such voluntary and temporary treatment will be taken advantage
of, and thus, by dealing with the various
forms of the disease at the early stages,
avoid the necessity in very many cases of
patients being definitely certified as of
unsound mind. It will also be observed
that in neither of these cases is there any
intervention of a judicial authority.
These provisions may be regarded as
preventive measures,
and it
be appromay
priate if I allude here to certain provisions under Part IV. of the Bill, in
which provisions are set out which will,
we hope, have the effect of helping to
prevent a recurrence of the disease in
cases where patients have been discharged
as cured. I refer to Section 48, under
which clinics at which extern patients may
obtain advice and treatment may be established by public mental hospitals.
As regards the third category, beyond
the alteration in the nomenclature which
hon. Senators will find in Part II. of the
Bill and which I know will be welcomed
by everyone, many simplifications have
been made in the existing code of procedure. I do not wish to examine in
elaborate detail the various simplifications
which will follow the passing of this Bill,
but, as an example, I might mention that
at the present time there are no fewer than
seven different forms of procedure for the
admission of persons of unsound mind
It is proposed
into mental hospitals.
now to adopt a common procedure for admission under which persons of unsound
mind may be received into mental institutions on a simple order of a Justice of
the Peace, supported by a medical certificate.
To meet the case where it is expedient
that a patient should be admitted to a
mental hospital at the earliest possible
moment, the Bill provides that a patient
may, on the certificate of the certifying
doctor that it is desirable that removal to
an institution should take place forthwith, be removed to a mental hospital in
anticipation of a justice's order, but the
authority to detain such a patient is
limited to seven days unless in the meantime the normal procedure for admission
has been completed.
Provision is also made under Part II.
of the Bill for the immediate removal of
persons of unsound mind to the nearest
infirmary or district hospital as a preliminary to medical examination and certification in cases where such removal is
necessary either for the safety of the
persons themselves or for the public
safety, and, again, provision is made to
cover the case of persons of unsound mind
who may not be under proper control or
who may be cruelly treated or neglected.
In the latter cases the facts will be laid
before a justice, who may himself visit
the place where it is alleged a person is
being cruelly treated, and he must, in any
event, obtain the opinion of a doctor on
the point, and if the justice is satisfied
that the case is one for removal to a
mental hospital on the ground that the
treatment being given is insufficient, or
that there is an element of cruelty in the
case, he shall direct the necessary steps
to be taken for the admission of such
person to a mental hospital.
Another new system which I think may
be of interest to hon. Senators is that of
periodic examinations of persons detained
in mental hospitals. Where questions of
personal liberty are involved it is essential that every precaution should be taken
to ensure that no person is improperly detained in an institution, although I admit
at once that such a contingency is most
improbable in institutions so admirably
conducted as our present day mental hospitals. This system which we propose has
been in force in England for many years
and has worked admirably. Shortly, the
reception order on which a patient is
admitted will remain valid in the first
instance for one year only, and thereafter for successive periods of 2, 3 and
5 years. Prior to the termination of each
period the medical officer of the institution must, after examination, certify
that the patient is still of unsound mind
and is a proper person to be detained
under care and treatment, sanction for
this course being obtained from the Ministry of Home Affairs. This procedure ensures beyond all doubt that every
individual case is brought up for examination and review at comparatively frequent periods.
Part III. of the Bill deals mainly with
the licensing of the registered institution
or house in which patients may be treated.
The Act under which the licensing of
such institutions is at present carried out
was passed in 1842, and can hardly be
181 Mental Treatment Bill-

11 MAY 1932
Second Reading
regarded as up-to-date. Under that Act
the licensing of these houses was a matter
for quarter sessions-a system which has
long been regarded as not entirely suitable. It is now proposed that the Ministry should be the licensing authority. As
will be readily understood, the decision
in these cases depends mainly on medical
and technical considerations which are in
fact the special province of the Ministry's
inspectors, and it is, therefore, appropriate that the licensing should rest with
the Ministry.
Finally, I would refer to the provisions
which appear as Part IV. of the Act
relating to settlement and chargeability.
Hitherto in Ireland there has been no
Law of Settlement, and the mental hospital of the district in which a person
of
unsound mind is found must receive and
maintain such person. This has been
found to press hardly on some mental
hospitals which have to maintain an
undue proportion of persons who really
belong to some other part of the country.
The law in England and in Scotland is
very complex on this question, but under
the provisions of this Bill the Government
has done its best to introduce an arrangement which will be both simple and
effective. In short, it is that the mental
hospital in whose area a person of unsound mnd is found shall prima facie be
responsible for his maintenance, but if
the committee of that hospital can show
that such patient has not been resident
in their district for a period of three
years, and has been continually resident
in some other district for three years, the
liability will then be thrown on that other
district and the patient may be transferred to the mental hospital thereof or
a suitable financial arrangement entered
into between the two districts.
I have not endeavoured to give a detailed résumé of the contents of the
various Clauses, because many of them
are self-explanatory, and a substantial
number are, moreover, really re-enactments of the existing law with minor
amendments-a course which has been
followed to avoid the necessity, as far as
it is possible, for legislation by reference.
I can only express the hope that this
Bill, which to a certain extent clarifies the
very involved existing code of laws relating to lunacy, will prove to be a
stepping-stone to a complete codification
at some future date.
It would not be right were I not to
inform hon. Senators that, in connection
with the preparation of this Bill, the
Government has received much valuable
help from many of the resident
medical superintendents, and also from
the late Chief Medical Officer of the
Ministry of Home Affairs. As a
result of the assistance and advice
which has been so ungrudgingly given
to the Ministry engaged in the preparation of this Bill, I trust, and I
believe, that the Measure will be a really
useful one, not only in the administration
of the laws, but still more important, in
the actual treatment of unfortunate
people who may suffer from mental illness. I beg to move.
Mr. CAMPBELL: I am sure this is a
Bill which will command the support of
every section of the House. It is a wellthought-out Bill. It is a Bill to which
apparently the greatest care and attention
have been given with regard to details,
and I think it will elicit commendation
from every quarter of this Province. The
Bill is mainly for the benefit of a most
helpless section of our community, the
class which can do least for itself, and I
look upon it as the forerunner of a series
of enactments which will bring our local
government system, especially in its
medical aspect, thoroughly up to date.
A great deal has been done under Acts of
Parliament that at present exist for the
amelioration of the mentally afflicted,
and one aspect of this Bill that will commend itself to the community is that
there should be an end of all feeling of
disgrace in connection with the troubles
of people who have suffered permanent or
temporary mental eclipse. There should be
no sense of humiliation and no sense of
shame in regard to such persons, and one
aim of the Bill before us is to blot out
altogether old ideas of that kind.
We
are now getting rid of those opprobrious
words asylums and lunatics," and
we recognise that these people are
mentally afflicted often through no
fault of their own or of anyone else.
Having heard the very lucid explanation.
of this Bill, I am glad to say that it is
in every aspect a thoroughly good and
commendable Measure.

only mention this because the case shows

Clause 67 is the Clause which protects

As regards the general structure of the

County of Antrim and District Electricity Special Order, 1932.
Mr. LONG: I beg to move,
"That the Special Order made and
confirmed by the Ministry of Commerce
for Northern Ireland under the Electricity
(Supply) Acts (Northern Ireland), 1882
to 1931, in respect of certain parts of the
County of Antrim and certain parts of
the County of Londonderry, be hereby
confirmed.
on
The Special Order will confer
the Electricity Distribution Company,
Limited, statutory authority to supply
electricity throughout the greater part of
the County of Antrim and the eastern
half of the County of Londonderry. The
Electricity Distribution Company is a subsidiary of the Antrim Electricity Supply
Company, which, in December, 1928,
obtained powers from this Parliament to
supply electricity on comprehensive lines
throughout practically the same territory.
The parent company, however, has no
general powers of retail distribution, its
powers being restricted to the sale of
electricity in bulk and to power users.
Following the policy which has been
recently adopted by other companies
similarly situated in Great Britain, the
Antrim Company decided that powers to
undertake retail distribution in this area
should also be sought, and the subsidiary
company was formed for this purpose,
the application for a Special Order being
lodged in November, 1930.
This application was opposed by certain
companies and persons already supplying
electricity in the area affected, as well as
Antrim District Electricity

by some local authorities and other
private interests, whilst competing applications for statutory powers were received
in respect of four towns in the area, viz.,
Ballyclare, Ballymoney, Randalstown and
Whitehead. In the circumstances, it was
necessary to hold a formal Inquiry. This
Inquiry, which lasted ten days, was conducted by Mr. J. C. Davison, K.C., M.P.
My right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Commerce, has given the most careful
consideration to the report of this
Inquiry, and he is fully convinced that
the proposals of the Electricity Distribution Company to deal with the supply
of electricity in this area on comprehensive lines constitute the only policy
which will ensure that the benefits of a
supply of electricity will be made available throughout the area for industrial
and domestic purposes at attractive rates.
Experience has shown that piecemeal
development by small generating plants,
centred in the various towns and villages,
can
never hope to provide adequate
supplies of electricity for power purposes,
nor for domestic purposes, other than
lighting, on terms within the reach of the
smaller householder. The whole trend of
development, both in Great Britain and
on the Continent, is towards the elimination of the small generating station and
the development of supply over large
areas by means of main transmission lines,
and it is only by this means that supplies
can be made available on reasonable terms
in rural areas.
In granting a franchise of this nature
over such an extensive area to one company, it is, of course, necessary that we
should be satisfied that the promoters of
the scheme are in a position to carry out
the obligations that would be placed upon
them. This aspect of the question has
been the subject of special investigation
and attention on the part of the Ministry, as a result of which satisfactory
evidence has been received that both the
parent company and its subsidiary are
now, as a result of re-organisation, controlled by two British companies with
ample capital resources behind them, and
expert knowledge of the problems of electricity supply.
As regards the objections, the Ballyclare Urban District Council came to
terms with the Electricity Distribution
Company at an early stage in the proceedings, and withdrew their application.
In the case of Randalstown, there was an

failing agreement, to be determined by
arbitration.
The Order was duly granted by the
Ministry on 6th April last, and notice.
of the intention to confirm the Order was
published. An objection to confirmation
was received from the Electricity Board
for Northern Ireland, in which the Board
asked for a slight re-arrangement of the
Southern boundary of the proposed area
of supply, to which the company agreed.
This re-arrangement provided for the exclusion of a portion of the Rural District
of Lisburn contiguous to the main transmission line between Belfast and Lisburn,
now owned by the Electricity Board, and
for the exclusion of a portion of the
Rural District of Magherafelt, including
the village of Moneymore, which can be
more economically supplied from the
Board's system. These amendments,
which were agreed by the Electricity
Distribution Company Limited,
approved by the Ministry of Commerce,
and the Order was confirmed accordingly.
I beg to move that the House now approve
the Special Order.

VOLUNTARY HOSPITALS AND
MOTOR ACCIDENTS.
Mr. HILL DICKSON asked the
Leader of the House, whether, in view of
the fact that in many cases of motor
accidents, voluntary hospitals are unable
to claim payment for treatment, the Government will consider the advisability of
introducing legislation to enable voluntary hospitals to claim compensation in
respect of such cases.
Viscount CHARLEMONT: As was
pointed out in this Chamber on the 10th
instant in reply to the hon. and learned
Member (Mr. Campbell), who sits
opposite, the Government have no definite
information as to the percentage of the
cost of treating motor accident cases which
is recovered by hospitals.
Having regard to the various classes of
hospitals in Northern Ireland which deal
with these cases, and to the different
systems of administration and control,
that is, private, general, voluntary, and
rate-aided, it will be difficult to collect
and prepare accurate statistics in such
form as would be of much practical assistance in connection with the consideration
of this question.
a
When the Motor Vehicles Act of 1930
was under consideration this aspect of
according assistance to the hospitals was
carefully considered in all its bearings,
and it was felt that the provision which
was inserted in the Act, Section 124 constituted the utmost limit to which Parliament might reasonably be expected to
go. It should be pointed out that
similar considerations and circumstances
have arisen in Great Britain, and the
corresponding statutory provisions in
Great Britain are of a similar nature to
those which appear on our Statute Book.
It must be remembered that the question of the recovery of expenses is one
primarily as between the hospitals concerned and the patients, and to interfere
further than has been done under the
existing law would involve a consideration
of similar principles being applied to all
other cases of accidents treated in the
hospitals, thereby conflicting and interfering with the well-recognised voluntary
principle upon which most of our larger
hospitals are organised and conducted.
I
Mr. MCALLISTER: I would like to
support the principle involved in the
question put by the hon. Senator.
think it is a very unjust thing that the
subscriptions to voluntary hospitals should
be appropriated to the medical treatment
and nursing and maintenance of an individual injured in a motor accident.
Whether his case is determined by law
or settled voluntarily he usually bases a
substantial proportion of his claim on the
cost of hospital treatment, and I think
there should be some means of enabling
the hospital to claim from him the cost
of his treatment. Those of us who are
associated with the legal side of these
motor accident cases know that one of
the principal items put down by a
claimant in his claim for damages is the
cost of his medical and nursing treatment, and I think it is very unjust and
unfair that a person should be able,
whether his claim is settled by the court
or out of court, to have the advantage of
basing at least part of his claim on expenses which he is not compelled to pay.
It is also unfair that subscribers to voluntary hospitals should have to pay for the
medical and nursing treatment of such a
person when that person is able to claim
the cost without being compelled to refund it to the hospital. Some simple
means should be found to do away with
an injustice of that description.
Colonel SINCLAIR: It is rather disappointing to learn from the reply to the
question that we need not expect in the
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
THE SENATE
[Colonel Sinclair]
near future to get any change in the
legislation already framed to deal with
this problem. The voluntary hospitals
are finding great difficulty in meeting
their financial obligations, and they really
do not see their way to finance a number
of things that are provided for by the
National Health Insurance Acts. So far
as I know no voluntary hospital has been
able to recover more than 25 per cent.
of the cost of treatment in the case of a
motor accident, and, after all, that is
only a moiety of the expense that is incurred. Motor accidents are on the increase, and no one expects a hospital to
shut its doors in the face of tragedy when
the ambulance arrives with these cases.
That is not the time to raise any question
of financial consideration. It is a case of
the best being done that the medical and
surgical staff can think of.
Of course,
when the time of urgency has passed inquiry may be made as to whether the
patient will be able to pay anything, but
in the vast majority of cases they leave
the hospital without paying anything
whatever. Usually the patients or their
friends contribute a niggardly sum of
about 10 per cent., but under the most
favourable circumstances 25 per cent. is
the greatest amount they pay. There is
a maximum sum of £30 that can be recovered for the treatment of injuries
under the National Health Insurance
schemes.
Having regard to the financial stringency in the country and the fact that
voluntary subscriptions have become less
and less, the boards of management and
staffs of hospitals look forward to something being done to amplify the provision that has been made hitherto, and
to which the noble Leader of the House
alluded, so that the work of these fine
institutions may not be crippled or closed
down, and so that some pressure should
be put on the people concerned to contribute a little more than they have been
doing towards the upkeep of these voluntary hospitals. I hope that before many
years have passed some reconsideration
will be given to this subject so that some
relief may be given to the precarious
finances of these hospitals.
Mr. CAMPBELL: May I express the
hope that Senator Hill Dickson will not
lose sight of this question. This problem
of the strain that is put upon voluntary
hospitals by motor accidents is a problem
of quite recent years. It was unforeseen
ten years ago, and it was still more un foreseen some fifteen years ago. I am informed on what I regard as very good
authority that several of the oldest established and voluntary hospitals in London
are in desperate financial straits, due,
apparently, to the unexpected influx of
fatalities and non-fatalities arising from
motor accidents on public roads. Within
the past week one of the very oldest
established hospitals in London, which
has kept open doors for all accident cases
for upwards of two hundred years, has
been compelled to notify its extern
patients that it will be obliged in future
to make some charge for treatment. That
hospital deals with 120,000 cases in the
course of a year. This is a question that
will undoubtedly have to be faced by the
State in the near future.
Mr. HILL DICKSON: The reply
which has just been given by the noble
Viscount-
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member is
not entitled to make another speech. He
can ask a supplementary question.
Mr. HILL DICKSON: The point I
want to make is that a person walking
along the street who meets with an
accident is not insured, and therefore
there is no question of the recovery of
the expense of his treatment, but a person
driving a motor car who meets with an
accident is bound by law to be insured.
And that is my point, that the hospitals
should have first claim on the insurance
people for maintenance. The hospital
may have no claim on the person walking
down the street who is not insured and
who gets injured, but by law the motor
men must be insured.
Viscount CHARLEMONT:
In reply
the remarks of hon. Senators I can do
nothing more than express my sympathy
with their views. The Motor Vehicles
Act of 1930, which contributed some
assistance to the hospitals by its implications, was in some degree an experimental
Act, and as the hon. and learned Senator
opposite said, this question has only
thrust itself forward to public notice in
the last few years. We cannot reasonably
expect that the present condition of
affairs will continue indefinitely if the
strain on the hospitals is so great as to
force some of them to close their doors.
I can only promise to bring the views of
hon. Senators before the Government,
but I cannot promise any legislation as
being likely in the immediate future.

SUSPENSION OF TRANSITIONAL
PAYMENTS.
Mr. QUIGLEY: The question standing
in my name concerns quite a number of
our unemployed people. Prior to 11th
April of this year, when claimants
attended at the Courts of Referees for the
consideration of their claim in respect of
the normal aspect of unemployment, if
the courts decided against continued unemployment benefit the claimants were
allowed payment up to the day previous
to the hearing at the courts.
A different procedure has been introduced since 11th April, and claimants
attending for their weekly unemployment
benefit at a certain stage receive payment for days varying from one to six,
and then are informed by their box
clerks at the Labour Exchange that
further payment has been suspended. On
their attending on the next week, and so
on for a few weeks, they are notified to
attend at the Courts of Referees for the
consideration of their different cases. If
at those courts the decision is against
continued benefit no payment is made
from the date of suspension. This is, I
think, most unfair, as the claimants fully
expected that they would receive payment
of benefit up to the hearing at the courts
as has been done up to 11th April. I
think it is unfair and, under all the circumstances, I think that benefit should be
paid up to the day previous to the hearing at the court.
If a change of procedure was found
to be necessary, I think it would be very
much better if the claimants were
notified to attend at the courts just
before payment was about to be suspended, and then they
then they would know
exactly where they stood.
stood. Quite a
number of such cases as I have referred
to have come under my own personal
notice in representing the unemployed
people at our Courts of Referees, and I
have felt very keenly for these people
when they realised that they were not
going to get payment up to the day
before they attended the courts. I beg
to ask the Leader of the House if he can
state why claimants whose unemployment
benefits have been suspended, pending
decision at the Courts of Referees, are
not paid up to the hearing and decisions
by the courts.
Viscount CHARLEMONT: No change
has been made in the procedure governing claims to unemployment insurance
benefit and, I presume, therefore, that
the hon. Member refers to applicants for
transitional payments.
Mr. QUIGLEY: It is. Yes.
Viscount CHARLEMONT: Before the
Unemployment Insurance (Economy)
(No. 2) Order (Northern Ireland), 1931,
was made, a claimant whose title to
benefit was based on Section 18 (2) of the
Unemployment Insurance Act (Northern
Ireland), 1928-which embodies what are
known as the transitional provisions for
allowing benefit to persons with less than
30 contributions to their credit in the
two years preceding their claim-was entitled to continue drawing benefit up to
the date on which the Court of Referees
decided on his claim, whether that
decision was adverse or favourable.
Article 1 of the Economy Order repealed that Section and consequently
cancelled any rights arising out of it and
substituted the provision of transitional
payments for persons who proved that
they satisfied the ordinary conditions for
drawing unemployment benefit and, in
addition, proved that they were normally
in and would normally seek to obtain
their livelihood by means of insurable
employment.
The present position, therefore, is that
where any doubt arises as to whether a
person satisfies these condition, payment
automatically ceases until that doubt is
settled by the machinery provided by the
Act-that is, in the first instance, by a
Court of Referees, and sometimes
eventually by the Umpire. If the Court.
decides against the claimant, no further
payments can be made unless the decision
is subsequently reversed by the Umpire
on appeal; but if the Court allows the
claim payment is continued from the date
on which it was suspended, except in
cases arising out of trade disputes in
which the insurance officer may appeal to
the Umpire. This last special exception
(which is very rare) is provided for by
Section 8 (9) of the Unemployment
Insurance (Amendment) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1930.

The bigger fleas have little fleas,
Upon their backs to bite 'em ;
The little fleas have lesser fleas,
And so ad infinitum.
That is the position, and that is what
we are going to do if we pass this Sub-

Viscount CHARLEMONT: I beg to
move, after Clause 4, to insert the following new Clause:
5. In the form of notice contained in
the First Schedule to the Increase of
Rent, and Mortgage Interest (Restrictions) Act, 1920, the following paragraph
shall be inserted after the words
express liability": -
an
"Should you consider that the
premises are not in a reasonable state
of repair, you can apply to the Sanitary
authority for a certificate to this effect,
if the condition of the premises is not
due to your neglect or default, and, if
such certificate is granted, you can serve
a copy thereof on the landlord. Having
done so, you will have a good defence
to any claim against you for the payment of any increase of rent permitted
under heads (c) and (d) above, and the
certificate will be sufficient evidence to
the court that the premises are in the
condition mentioned in the certificate,
unles the contrary is proved."
The intention of this Clause is to bring
the First Schedule to the Increase of
Rent and Mortgage Interest (Restrictions)
Act, 1920, into conformity with the provisions of Section 7 of the Rent and
Mortgage Interest (Restrictions) Act
(Northern Ireland), 1925. The schedule
to the Act indicates what the position
of the tenant is under the 1920 Act,
when a statutory increase is made
in his rent. The 1925 Act, however,
made certain alterations with regard to
the tenant's rights in such a case, and it
is to make provision for the insertion of
these rights in the notice which is served
on them that this Clause is inserted. It
is really a technical matter.
Mr. MCALLISTER: I rise to oppose
this new Clause more on account of the
principle involved than because of its
immediate effect on the Bill. I think it
is a bad proposition in law to put the
sanitary authority in a position to do
something they have no special qualifications to do. It is more or less putting
them in a judicial or semi-judicial
position, and I think that where a question of fact has to be determined by a
court of law it should be so determined
untrammelled by the certificate of a
sanitary authority. The onus of proving
whether or not there have been reasonable repairs to premises should not be
placed on one individual but should be
decided by the court itself. From the
purely legal point of view I am entirely
opposed to this principle because I think
it is a bad precedent to introduce, and
one that cannot be justified.

Exported Animals (Compensation) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Viscount CHARLEMONT: This is a
very short Measure and, I think, we shall
have time to take the Second Reading
now. The Slaughtered Animals (Compensation) Act of 1928 passed by this
House provided for payment of compensation in respect of animals exported
through Northern Ireland ports and
slaughtered in British landing places by
reason of the requirements of the cross-
Channel authorities in consequence of
foot-and-mouth disease. The fund from
which compensation is payable is constituted by a small levy (23d on each
head of cattle) on animals exported. It
is, therefore, an excellent example of
practical co-operation financed by the
traders concerned and involving
charge on the public Exchequer.
no
or
Apart, however, from the risk of
slaughter in British lairages already provided for there is the further risk that
animals may be held up in landing places
for prolonged periods, because of action
taken by the British Ministry on account
of foot-and-mouth-disease, actual
suspected. For example, last June large
numbers of animals from Northern Ireland were held up in British landing
places, and it has been estimated that
the additional charges falling on our exporters amounted to about £2,000. The
object of the Bill is to protect shippers
against similar risks in the future. It is
proposed that the present Bill should be
made retrospective so as to cover the
June charges.
Section 13, Sub-Section 1, of the Act
provides that whenever the compensation
fund amounts to £5,000 the Ministry may
make an Order for suspension of payment
of the export levy on each animal shipped.
In view of the increased liability now
imposed on the insurance fund, it is the
intention that the sum of £5,000 referred
to should be increased to £10,000. For
a considerable time past the Live Stock
Exporting Associations in Northern Ireland have been pressing for this Measure,
which it is now felt should no longer be
delayed. I beg to move.
Mr. LESLIE: I suppose we can take
it from the noble Lord that this is an
agreed Measure. As the noble Viscount
may remember, when the principal Act
was before us, from every quarter of the
House came reports of attacks that had
been made on individual Members in
order to get these provisions inserted,
that is to say, it was wanted at the
beginning to make the fund cover detention as well as slaughter. Now,
apparently, we are going to get it. The
only conceivable point that may arise is
the expenditure of funds already accumulated.
Viscount CHARLEMONT: I do not
think there is any limit to what persons
in Northern Ireland will say on any
conceivable subject, and I can quite
understand there may
be a certain
amount of discussion when this Bill has
been passed, as has been the practice on
every other occasion I have been concerned with. It is an agreed Measure.
Mr. HILL DICKSON: I understand
this compensation is only for disease.
