Land Law (Miscellaneous Provisions)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Viscount CHARLEMONT: As the
title indicates, a number of matters not
directly related to each other are dealt
with in this Bill. The first point is one
which arises out of the transfer of
functions from the Land Commission in
Dublin to the Ministry of Finance in
Northern Ireland, and deals with the
distribution of the proceeds of the sale of
a holding which has been sold by the
Ministry by reason of the registered
owner defaulting in the payment of
his annuity under the Land Purchase
Acts. Before the setting up of the
Government of Northern Ireland the
Land Commission dealt with this matter,
and had drawn up an elaborate set of
rules of procedure. Since, however, the
administrative structure of the Land
Commission was entirely different from
the structure of the Ministry of Finance,
the existing rules have been found to be
not wholly satisfactory to administer, and
it has been deemed best to make fresh
provision by legislation for a more suitable
procedure.
It is unnecessary to detail the proposals
as they are set out in Clause 1 and in the
Schedule of the Bill, but I might draw
attention to two salient points, the first
being that the solicitor to the Ministry
will take all the action necessary, and the
second is that in very small cases where
the balance of the purchase money does
not exceed £15, the procedure has been
simplified with consequent lessening of
the costs. I might also mention that
aggrieved persons are being given the
right of appeal to the county court when
the amount involved is over £30. The
amounts to be dealt with as the purchase
money of holdings for which the tenants
have been unable to pay the annuities
are usually very small, but, nevertheless,
a precise method of dealing with the
money is desirable.
Clause 2 relates simply to administrative
procedure in the Ministry of Finance to
lighten the routine work of higher
officials. It allows the authentication of
the Seal to the Ministry to be delegated
to some person other than those officers
authorised by the Ministries of Northern
Ireland Act, 1921. The certifications to
be authenticated relate to the amounts
due by defaulting tenants each gale day.
Land Law Bill-
Second Reading
THE SENATE
[Viscount Charlemont]
The third Clause deals with tithe rentcharges and variable rents payable to
persons other than the Ministry of
Finance. It will be remembered that
the Tithe Rent-charge and Variable Rents
Act, passed by this Parliament in 1930,
reduced such rents payable to the Ministry by 8 per cent., and allowed voluntary
agreements in other cases. These charges
and rents, I may explain, are those which
according to old custom were variable
according to the price of agricultural
produce. Later, in 1920, the method of
variation was changed so as to relate
variations to the average change in
judicial rents ascertained by the Land
Commission. Since the fixing of these
judicial and fair rents was abolished by
the Northern Ireland Land Act of 1925,
it was necessary to find a substitute for
the reduction to be made every 15 years,
and the figure of 8 per cent. was arrived
at on the best data available. It has now
been thought desirable to regularise the
position of tithe rents payable to private
interests by making the reduction of 8 per
cent. applicable to them also in respect of
every gale day after 1st May, 1932.
beg to move.
I
Mr. MCALLISTER: I rise to oppose
this Bill as strenuously as possible. In
the first instance, it introduces a very
dangerous and difficult system of administration into the affairs of the country.
It seeks to transfer from the judicial
tribunals to an official of the Ministry
the administration of purely judicial
matters. If there is one thing the courts
have been up to the present, they have
been the safe and efficient buttress, protecting the public generally in their rights
of property against the Government or
the official administration. I think it
is a very dangerous principle to say that
where rights of property are involved
these should be transferred from the
courts properly constituted to be administered by an individual in the offices of
the Government.
In offering this criticism, of course I
do not refer to any particular civil servants or member of the administration.
I think this House should be very slow
to support the principle of usurping the
functions of the courts. In the second
place, why should this Bill in certain
respects be made retrospective? If there
have been no mistakes made by the
Ministry in the past, why do they
If
require the sanction of this House to
legalise administration in the past.
this Bill is not introduced, amongst other
reasons, to legalise maladministration and
inefficient administration in the past,
why is it made retrospective? I do say,
after considerable experience, that to say
that the solicitor of the Ministry of
Finance should apportion out the balance
of the money, after payment of the costs
due to the Ministry, on the evidence of
a copy of the folio of the land registry is
ludicrous, absurd, and primitive in the
first degree. That is not evidence upor
which any tribunal would act. No
judicial tribunal, no court, would act
upon any such evidence in paying out
money to claimants.
Supposing, as is the case in the majority
of instances, that the land in question
had been registered subject to equity,
there is to be no investigation of title of the
registered owner, good, bad, or indifferent.
The registered owner, in many cases, has
no legal title at all to the land in question. His name appears as the registered
owner, and we are told by this Bill that
on the mere production of a copy of the
folio showing him to be the registered
owner, without any investigation of evidence, the money is to be handed over
to him. I do repeat that as a legal
proposition that is perfectly absurd and
primitively futile. If we pass this Bill
we are depriving people, in certain instances, of the right of appeal against
an official determination of how the purchase money should be distributed.
I would ask the House very seriously
to consider before they take from the
courts their proper function, and hand
over to the administration the rights of
property which have always been the
care of the courts efficiently and properly
constituted. I think the Bill as it
stands is bound, in many cases, to work
grave injustice. As I say. the evidence
on which it is proposed that the solicitor
of the Ministry of Finance is going to
allocate the balance of the funds is quite
insufficient, and it is not evidence on
which any properly constituted court
could act with safety.
Mr. McCORKELL: I find myself in
the rather peculiar position of largely
agreeing with the hon. Member who has
just spoken. I was struck by the fact
that the noble Viscount, the Leader of
the House, told us there were three
Land Law Bill-
Second Reading
19 MAY 1932
salient points in this Bill, one of which
is the distribution of this money is to be
decided by the solicitor to the Ministry
of Finance. The second salient point is
that if the amount does not exceed £15
it can be paid away practically without
inquiry. I agree these are salient points,
and for that very reason I object to the
Bill in the main.
We have courts of justice in this
country, I venture to say, that are second
to none, and we should be proud of them.
They are not carried on by individuals;
they are carried on by a number of
people and by a system which has given
great satisfaction and which I think we
can hold up to the world as an example
of what courts should be. And yet we
now propose to take away the ordinary
citizen's rights and hand them over to
an individual. I agree again with the
last speaker in not saying anything
against such individuals. The individuals
at present are, undoubtedly, very good,
but what may the individuals be twenty
years hence.
We are taking away from
the ordinary citizens the right of appeal
to the courts and placing him in the
hands of one individual, whoever he may
be, and twenty years hence he may be
very bad.
The second salient point refers to the
matter of a sum not exceeding £15 that
can be paid away by the Ministry. Of
course £15 is a mere bagatelle to anybody
in the Government, but it is a very large
sum of money to a small farmer who may
be interested in this matter. It is the
price of a bullock, which may be onethird of his entire stock, and if there are
many sums of £15, in the aggregate it
really becomes a very substantial amount.
I see no reason-and I know there are a
great many people in Northern Ireland
who agree with me in this why the
ordinary citizen's rights, which have been
safeguarded by the courts in the past, and
for all we know to the contrary will be
safeguarded in the future, should be
taken away and placed in the hands of
one official, whoever he may be. I feel
bound to say I think this is a bad Bill, or
rather an unnecessary Bill, and I feel
obliged to enter my protest against it.
The very fact that aggrieved persons have
the right of appeal where a sum of over
£30 is involved establishes the principle
that there should be the right of appeal,
and £30 may mean a great deal less to one
man than £15 does to another man.
think that is the most illogical part of the
I
Measure. Why should one man have the
right of appeal while another man has
not that right? That is a most illogical
situation, and on its two salient points
the Bill is condemned.
Colonel PAKENHAM: I should like

that if there is one thing I dislike more

than another it is depriving the ordinary

ments exceeding £30 been made by the

That is to say, is there anything

Again, connected with the same Clause,

As regards Clause 2 we have nothing

Mr. CAMPBELL: I rise to join in
the protest that has come from different
quarters of the House against this Bill,
and I do so on one or two main grounds.
The Bill seems to vest in the solicitor to
the Ministry of Finance certain judicial
powers in reference to the distribution of
purchase money. I am sure that that
is a thing this House will be very jealous
of. It is one of the series of steps by
which the administration is encroaching
on judicial powers. It is a matter of the
very utmost importance that we should
preserve as far as we can the freedom of
the courts, and to check as far as we can
any encroachment on the part of the
Government. Then again, these judicial
functions involve the determination of
the rights of property. The solicitor to
the Ministry of Finance is made the final
tribunal in many cases, which means that
there is no right of appeal from him. As
the Mayor of Derry has pointed out, a sum
of £15 may mean a small amount to
many, but to others it is a very substantial sum. I do not think this Bill
has been carefully thought out, and I
do not think it is a Measure that ought
to be accepted by this House. In
my opinion the Government ought to
withdraw it in view of the opinions expressed in opposition to it from all parts
of the House.
Viscount

said the first point was one which arose
out of the transfer of functions from the
Land Commission in Dublin to the Ministry of Finance in Northern Ireland.
That is the position at the present
moment. It is not proposed to transfer
anything the courts can deal with to
some Government Department where
they cannot deal with it. This is merely
a Bill to simplify the procedure in the
Ministry of Finance and to enable them
to deal with these cases in the future
as they are doing at the present time.
The Bill takes nothing from any
court. I understand quite well what
hon. Members have said about appeals in
respect of sums under £15, but the fact
remains that although, as has been said,
£15 may mean as much to some people
as £30 does to others, it would be a most
uneconomical procedure to take cases involving these very small amounts to
court, because the expense of the proceedings would swallow up the money,
with the result that no one would get
anything.
With regard to the questions raised by
Senator Leslie, if he will allow me I will
answer them at a later stage of the Bill.
On the whole, I do not think this Bill
will in effect be so unfair as hon. Senators
have tried to make out, though I agree
it may not be a Bill that will appeal to
popular sentiment.

Allotments Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Viscount CHARLEMONT: This Bill is
a comparatively simple one and its various
Clauses require little in the way of explanation or comment; its subject matter
is not, I think, of a controversial nature.
In brief, the object of the Bill is to enable
local authorities either themselves to
provide allotments for unemployed and
other poor persons, or to assist voluntary
organisations in the provision of allotments for such persons.
Hon. Members who have had any
acquaintance with the excellent work
which is being done by some of the
voluntary plotholders associations will
know the great benefits which plotholders
derive from their plots. Not only do
they obtain opportunities for healthy
exercise and a means of providing food
for their families, but they also are
furnished with a source of interest which
may help to divert their minds from the
depressing conditions arising from unemployment. Possession of a plot also ensures that the holder will, when work
comes his way, be better able to pursue
his ordinary means of livelihood.
It is the hope of the Government that
local authorities will use to the full the
powers with which the Bill will provide
them. The Government is encouraged in
this hope by the fact that the Belfast
Corporation passed a resolution
some
time ago asking for the introduction of
legislation on the lines of this Bill. The
General Council of Municipal Authorities,
which is the representative organisation
of urban authorities, have also expressed
their approval of the proposal to provide
allotments for unemployed and impoverished persons.
I understand that some persons in
receipt of unemployment benefit have.
been reluctant to apply for plots provided
by voluntary organisations in case their
claim to benefit might be prejudiced. I
am advised that such persons need have
no fears in applying for any allotments
which may be provided under this Bill
and in selling any surplus produce, provided always that they remain ready to
accept any suitable employment which
may be offered to them. The size of the
allotments provided under the Bill will
be limited to one-eighth of an acre and
only one allotment may be held by any
person. The work involved in cultivating
an allotment would, therefore, appear to
be such that it could ordinarily be carried
out by a man in employment outside his
ordinary working hours.
Moreover, any
profit from the allotment could not
possibly exceed the statutory limit fixed
under the Unemployment Insurance Acts
as a bar to eligibility for unemployment
benefit. I am, therefore, in a position to
confirm the assurance given in another
place that none of the unemployed need
have any hesitation in obtaining an allotment or in selling any surplus produce
which he may not require for the use of
his own family, provided only that he
remains ready to accept any suitable
work which may be offered to him.
To take the Clauses in order, Clause 1
of the Bill indicates the local authorities
upon whom powers are proposed to be
conferred, that is to say, county borough,
borough and urban district councils.
These authorities, subject to the approval
of the Ministry of Home Affairs, may for
the purpose of providing allotments take
on lease land, or use for that purpose
land already in their possession. They
may also fence or drain land and adapt it
any other way which would be necessary
for the purpose of making it suitable for
allotments.

conditions to be observed by local

know they were held up to a certain

Motor Vehicles (International Race)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Viscount CHARLEMONT: This short
Measure is concerned with the Tourist
Trophy Motor Race which is to be held
here this year, and its objects, I think,
are fairly apparent from the text of the
Measure itself.
The reason for introducing the Bill is
that the Royal Automobile Club, on receiving an invitation to repeat the race
on the Ards circuit in 1932, was obliged
to inform the Government that they
would require to receive a substantial
guarantee against contingent loss, as
they had actually a substantial loss in
1931 and could not face this state of
affairs again. The Government and the
local Race Committee considered every
possibility by which funds could be raised
to carry out these requirements, and
after exploring the various possibilities
they came to the conclusion that the best
solution would be to seek the necessary
legislation so that the motor cars attending the race should pay a small charge
for doing so, the amount not to exceed
half-a-crown. The area within which this
charge would be payable will be fixed by
the Inspector-General of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary, and badges or some such
indication will be issued to the drivers of
the motor vehicles who have paid the
necessary fees so as to enable them to
enter this limited circle.
I may also say that it is expected to
raise some further funds by the sale of
badges to other spectators who are not
actually in charge of cars, although there
will be no legal requirement to this effect.
It is hoped, however, that this will be
well supported and that the charge of
half-a-crown for cars, together with the
a
voluntary subscriptions, will raise
sufficient guarantee to satisfy the Royal
Automobile Club, whose demands I may
say are only reasonable in the circumstances.
It will be noticed that in Sub-Clause
(3), of the first Clause, there is power
for the Ministry of Home Affairs to
exempt particular motor vehicles from
the necessity of having a badge to enter
the limited area. This is meant to cover
the cases of residents inside that area and
other people, such as milk men or breadservers, whose occupations may take
them there during the time when the
roads are shut, or even for doctors whose
professional duties may require them to
do so.
The Bill, as hon. Members will notice
from the preamble and from Sub-Clause
(6), of the first Clause, is only to apply
to the race which is to be held this year.
If there are any funds left over after
such liabilities as have to be met have
been satisfied they will be held in trust
for the purpose of further future motor
races in Northern Ireland.
In conclusion, I would just like to express in this House the thanks of the
Government to all those who in the past
have done so much to assist us in promoting this competition. There is no
doubt that it is a great attraction for
visitors from across Channel, and even
from abroad, and our thanks are due to
the Royal Automobile Club in the first
instance, and to all the generous supporters who have helped us in the past.
I might mention especially Lord Wakefield who presented the prize money last
year, and Lady Houston who is very
kindly doing the same this year. I beg
to move.

scheduled area it might be found that all
the badges available had been bought up
by unauthorised persons, and were being

to which the Kent Restrictions Acts apply

tunity of having their individual case

I put down the Amendment which appears
on the Paper it has been pointed out to
me that it is necessary to define the expression "court" which I use. I was under
the impression at first that the provisions.
of the principal Act of 1920 were sufficient,
but I am told it would be better to say,
"the court having jurisdiction in the

have also been told that the exemption
to be given to the one just lamb should be

differs slightly from that on the Paper,
but only in wording, not in principle.
The exact Amendment I now beg to move
is:-
--
At the end of Clause 3, page 6, after
line 19, insert the following new subsection:-
"(7) Notwithstanding anything contained in the foregoing provisions of this
section any person, at any time within
twelve months from the passing of this
Act but not afterwards, may apply to
the county court having jurisdiction in
the place where the premises are situate,
for a certificate that any agreement to
which such person, as the landlord of
a dwelling house to which the Rent Restrictions Acts (as amended by this Act)
apply, was a party, was executed by
him in good faith and for adequate
consideration and was not entered into
as a means of obtaining a greater sum
in respect of the use and occupation of
the dwelling house that such person
would have been entitled to charge as
rent if the dwelling house had been let
by him as landlord.
The county court, after giving all
parties to the agreement an opportunity
of being heard, may, if it sees fit, grant
such certificate; and thereupon, in such
case, the foregoing provisions of this
section, or such of those provisions as
the county court may specify in the
certificate, shall not apply as against
the person named in the certificate in
respect of the dwelling-house concerned."
I venture to hope that the insertion of
these words will commend themselves to
the sense of justice of this House.
Viscount CHARLEMONT: I am glad

Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg to move the
insertion of this new Clause in the Bill in

Second Reading, and I venture to commend it to the favourable consideration
of the House. I think it is recognised
that the evil of profiteering by tenants at

be checked. Some might say that this

they would go farther and deal more

by tenants, holding that profiteering

to curb and control these exorbitant
may
rents. The Clause applies only to

will mean that they will have the shelter

National Health Insurance and Contributory Pensions Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Viscount CHARLEMONT (Leader of
the House): The matters proposed to be
dealt with under this Bill concern in
general the finances of the Health Insurance system. The recent valuation of
the assets and liabilities of approved
societies disclosed that during the five
years from 1924 to 1928 covered by the
valuation there had been on the one hand
a steady drop in the contribution income
of approved societies due to unemployment, and on the other hand a steady
increase in claims. Both these factors
have operated since 1928, and the Government Actuary has advised that the
scheme is no longer able to bear the
strain imposed upon it. It is, therefore,
necessary to take immediate steps to restore its financial stability. A careful
analysis has revealed that the principal
cause of loss is the very high rate of
claims
insured
experienced amongst
women, and particularly married women.
Figures are contained in the White
Paper circulated to hon. Members, which
show the position for the whole of the

Northern Ireland than in Great Britain.
The Government Actuary has advised

Disablement benefit for single women
and widows from 7s 6d a week to 6s a

Sickness benefit for married women
from 12s a week to 10s, and
married
Disablement benefit for

The other main cause of the present
difficulties of the scheme lies in the effect
of unemployment. Prior to 1928 insured
persons were required to make certain
payments in respect of periods of unemployment if they wished to continue full
title to benefits. With the gradual improvement in the employment position it
was thought in 1928 that the very considerable sum of money
which had
accumulated in respect of unclaimed contributions would be sufficient to recoup
approved societies for the loss of contribution income due to unemployment, and
since then unemployed members have been
relieved from the necessity of making any
payments themselves. The sums available
from this source are, however, no longer
adequate, and the actuary advises that it
will be necessary to revert to the old principle and to require members to make
some payment themselves in respect of
their arrears of contributions if they wish
to retain their title to full benefits.
Societies will be called on to bear half the
loss of income due to unemployment, and
if this should threaten a deficiency on
valuation the loss so caused will be made
good from the Central Fund to which the
balance of the moneys representing unclaimed contributions is being transferred.
Amendments are being made at the
same time in the provisions relating to the
duration of insurance. One of the principal of these requires the payment of
eight contributions in two consecutive half
years before a member who has been
subject to unemployment can requalify
for the extensions of insurance which the

present provisions allow.
time, however, steps are being taken to
preserve for
a further period the
contributory pension rights of genuinely

As regards the other matters raised, I
quite admit that I do not like procedure
by Order in Council, especially when the
Bill has only got a Second Reading in
Great Britain, but it was inevitable for
two reasons. In the first place, our insurance year begins on 1st July, and
therefore this Bill has to become law before that date, just as the British Measure
will have to become law in Great Britain.
Our House will not be sitting when the
Measure does become law in Great
Britain, and so we would have required
special sittings in order to pass this Bill
if we waited until it became law across
the Channel.
But, after all, it does not make any
difference, because it is necessary that the
Bill should be passed here exactly on
similar lines to the British Measure, and
Orders in Council do not give the Government power to do just what they like.
They do not give the Government a blank
cheque. They give the Government
power to follow Great Britain in this
matter, and that undertaking I am
pleased to be able to give to-day. Now,
why must we follow Great Britain in this
connection? Simply because our health
insurance scheme is one for the United
Kingdom and cannot be divided. Our
insured persons are largely in international societies. Societies called by
that name are those which act both
here and in Great Britain. I think
I am right in saying that about
52 per cent. of our insured persons are in
these international societies. It is unthinkable, for instance, that they would
accept different contributions from or pay
different benefits to their Northern Ireland members to what they would pay to
their members in Great Britain.
Again, we here are members of the
Joint Committee which really is the overriding authority in connection with all
health insurance matters, and, further,
the reserve funds which have been
accumulated, such as the Central Fund,
are available to help societies here in
times of difficulty and deficiency, just in
the same way as they are available for
societies similarly placed in Great Britain.
I could give figures to show what a great
advantage it is to our insured people in
Northern Ireland that this is a scheme
which applies to the whole of the United
Kingdom, because English societies do
transfer large sums, which may be looked
upon as the property of their insured
members in Great Britain, in order to
preserve the same standards as regards
benefits here for their members as they
give to their members across the Channel.
Also, some of our smaller societies are
not in a particularly strong position and
do require help from the Central Fund to
a very considerable extent.
The other matters raised were mainly
connected with unemployment insurance.
This Bill does not really deal with unemployment insurance, and I do not propose
to deal with that great service in detail
to-day. I may say that my great difficulty in connection with all these social
services is this. I am told on the one
hand that they are costing far too much,
far more than Northern Ireland can
afford to pay; and on the other hand I
am told we are not spending enough, with
the result that great hardships are being
imposed upon many of our people.
My Department is budgeting this year for
no less a sum than £5,635,000 in connection with these social services-

Mr. DORMAN: It strikes me that no
attention is being directed to the underlying causes leading up to this demand
for the victimisation of married women
in order to save the Insurance Fund. We
are inconsiderately making married women
the victims of the industrial and financial
crisis through which the nation has passed,
and we are really not prepared to consider why, from one point of view, this
unreasonable amount of claims is arising
from the married women. Anyone
accustomed to, and acquainted with, the
habits of the working class will know that
the working class wives and mothers sacrifice themselves for their husbands and
their children, and that the crisis through
which we have passed inevitably meant
an abnormal amount of incapacity through
sickness on the part of the wage-earning
married females of the country. Wages
have been reduced in Great Britain and
Northern Ireland by £577,000,000 per
annum, and behind that reduction in the
purchasing capacity of the exchequers of
the working-class homes of the country
there has been an enormous amount of
self-sacrifice. Hunger and sickness are
produced as a result, and now in consequence we are asking the married women
to shoulder the responsibility of this crisis
and these conditions.
The noble Lord, the Leader of the
House, has told us that he could not give
us the figures with regard to Northern
Ireland. When the insurance scheme
was set up a separate set of Commissioners
were appointed for Ireland, and all
the international societies to which the
right hon. Gentleman referred were compelled to set up committees for the regulation of their business in Ireland. I fail
to see why the Government should not be
in a position to differentiate and give this
House and the country in general particulars with regard to the percentages of
claims between the married women and
the unmarried women and other classes
in Northern Ireland, just as I cannot
understand why the Government cannot
differentiate with regard to the reductions
in wages that have taken place.
I have been endeavouring to ascertain
what that amount has been during the
last ten years, and I estimate that there
is at least from £15,000,000 to £20,000,000
per annum less going into the homes of
insured individuals in Northern Ireland
now than there was ten years ago. Those
acquainted with the purchases made in
the homes of the working class and with
the proportion set aside for the purchase
of food and clothing, and so on, must
know that if you reduce the necessary
clothing and thereby reduce the temperature of the human organism you expose
it to unnecessary sickness and disability.
Mr. JOSEPH CUNNINGHAM: That
is in the case of women.
Mr. DORMAN: If the hon. Member
would just bear with me a moment he

Mr. CAMPBELL: I beg to move in
page 2, line 33, leave out from "that"
("Provided that") to "any" ("any

Hon. Members will realise what the
purport of this Bill is. It provides for
the distribution of the proceeds of sales of
holdings which are permitted to be sold
Land Law Bill-
Committee
24 MAY 1932
by the Ministry of Finance under any of
the powers vested in them by the Land
Purchase Acts, and then it provides for the
appropriation of the proceeds of the sale.
The proceeds are to be applied in payment, first of all, of all moneys certified
to be due to the Ministry in respect of
the holdings; secondly, of all costs and
expenses incurred by the Ministry in relation to the sale or the distribution of
the proceeds of the sale or otherwise in
relation to the holding, and thirdly, the
balance of the proceeds of the sale is to
be paid to the person to be determined
by the solicitor to the Ministry of Finance
in accordance with the provisions of the
Schedule to the Bill. Clause 1 (5) gives a
right of appeal from the decision of the
officer of the Ministry in any case where
a determination is given and the balance
of the proceeds of the sale exceeds £30.
An appeal is only given where the
balance exceeds £30. My Amendment, if
the Committee will think it right to give
it approval, gives an unrestricted right of
appeal to any private citizen, no matter
what the balance may be. I do not for a
moment mean to convey the least reflection
on the solicitor to the Ministry of Finance.
He is a very competent official, and I am
certain he will do his duty well and
thoroughly; but I think we are putting
too heavy a burden on him-a burden of
which he himself might be glad to be eased
-if this right of appeal to the county
court judge from a decision of his is not
given. He is the final arbiter in all cases
where the balance is under £30. He is
practically put in complete control of
cases of that kind.
It is a very heavy
responsibility, and I do submit to the
Committee that an error may arise in regard to the proceeds of a sale where the
amount is under £30, just as it may occur
in a case over £30. I think the Committee would look with jealousy on any
effort made to take from the poorest subject of the King his right to be protected
by the King's courts.
I do not think the right of appeal would
be often resorted to. I feel certain it
would be very seldom resorted to; but
would it not be well that the right of
appeal should be given so that if a mistake
arose and through some inadvertence some
person, who was entitled to under £30,
was left out, he would have the right to
go beyond the Ministry of Finance and

should not lightly set aside the authority.
of the courts.

concerned. With regard to the

asked to determine on this question?
It is
He has
is a question of title.
to determine who is entitled to the

the property and the proceeds of the
property.
After all, that is a power which you do
not give to any court in the land. You
do not give that to the county court or to

Court. There is an appeal in all questions of title from the county court to the
assizes or to the Court of Chancery. There
is an appeal from the King's Bench or

Here, in this particular case, you are
restricting the interpretation of the law
in the very involved question of title-the

jurisdiction to an official of the Ministry

case. You bring to the notice of those
concerned all the publicity of the hearing

of facts and the legal aspects of the case.

The very method by which it is proposed to test this question shows the inadvisability of the procedure being
adopted. The solicitor for the Ministry
is authorised on production of a copy of

up the

British justice when we say that, because

I would
Viscount CHARLEMONT:
like to give the hon. and learned Senator

No person could possibly be deprived of
any right he may at present possess without his consent and without compensation,
because, in fact, this Bill only deals with
rents which are subject to periodical revision. These revisions took place at
periods of fifteen years, and followed the
average change in the level of fair rents
fixed by the Land Commission, then by
the Ministry of Finance. As the fixing
of fair rents was abolished by the Land
Act, 1925, as close as possible an estimate
has been made of what the variation would
have been, and the reduction arrived at is
eight per cent. as inserted in this Bill.
Accordingly, it would be logical to say
that had the old conditions continued,
that is to say, if there had been no 1925
Land Act, the reduction by approximately
eight per cent. would automatically have
taken place without legislation.
On Question, Motion agreed to.
Clause ordered to stand part of the
Bill.

Mr. LESLIE: I am sorry that this point
should arise at this late stage. I think
the House will, perhaps, agree that
although it is quite right that a tenant of
an allotment who misbehaves in any of
the manners suggested in the earlier part
of the Clause before us should be subject
to disciplinary power, I think the House

allotment. The Bill is not a temporary
one; it is to endure. Therefore, I think
the provision suggested in the words on
the Paper should be made, in order to
meet the case of a man having done wrong
in the past making amends for that wrong
and wishing to start afresh.
I cannot myself find that there is any
provision for the man in any other part of
the Bill. Accordingly, I beg to move in
Clause 3, at the end of Sub-clause 2, to

Health Insurance Bill-
Third Reading
26 MAY 1932
Mr. CAMPBELL: Even at this belated
stage I would like to say that I am not at
all impressed with the change that this
Bill seeks to make in the national health
insurance scheme. The object of the Bill
is to bring back the scheme to a condition
of financial stability, and that object is
achieved by reducing the benefits-disablement benefits and sickness benefits-in the
case of unmarried and married women. In
the case of unmarried women the sickness
benefit remains at 12/- a week, but the
disablement benefit is changed from 7/6
to 6/-a diminution of 1/6. Again, in
the case of married women, the rate of
sickness benefit will remain at 10/-, but
the disablement benefit will be only 5/-.
The matter is of great importance because the textile industry is far and away
more important in Northern Ireland than
in any like area in Great Britain. There is
a far higher percentage relatively of women
employed in the textile trade in Northern
Ireland than there is, I think, in any
corresponding trade in an area in England
comparable with our area here. This
Bill, though the diminution is small, is at
matter of moment to these poor women.
They are living practically on the margin
of subsistence. They are enduring keen
hardships, especially where there is a
small family, and I do think it is a pity,
even in these hard days, that a Bill of
this kind should be thought necessary to
be brought forward by the Government,
and that they should try to restore financial stability to this scheme by reducing
these benefits. For that reason, even on
the Third Reading, I venture to enter a
strong protest against the principle underlying the Measure.
Mr. DORMAN: Since the Second Reading of this Bill, on which occasion I voted
against it, I made myself conversant with
the Section giving the actuary's figures
referred to in the Memorandum accompanying the Bill. Table 13 referred
to in the Memorandum sets forth
the actuary's estimate of the payment
ratio for men and women under the Insurance Acts, and the estimate for men
was over-estimated by eight per cent., and
that for women was under-estimated by
four per cent. The actual percentages of
claims for men were 99.2 per cent., and
for women 104 per cent. for sickness
benefit and for disablement benefit 90 per
cent. for men and 138 per cent. for
women; but in turning to another table
in the actuarial report, I discovered that
there is a considerable surplus in the
working of the Acts on both sections. For
instance, there are 554 societies catering
solely for women, whose figures are given
in this report, and there is a surplus of
£4,271,304 and a deficiency of £149,550.
I find on deducting that deficiency from
the surplus that there is a net surplus of
£4,121,754.
That is in respect of the societies that
cater solely for women. But there are
other sorts of societies that cater for men
and women. There are 3,627 such societies and the returns show a surplus of
£13,065,989 and a deficiency of £244,677.
On deducting the deficiency from the
surplus it will be seen that there is a net
surplus of £12,821,312. Adding the two
surpluses together there is a surplus of
£16,943,066. I cannot see what justification there is for victimising the most helpless of the insured people because of a
temporary setback in the percentage of
claims over and above the valuation of the
actuary. I take it that all insurance
companies and collecting societies collate
these reserves for the purpose of meeting
unexpected ratio claims under-estimated
for in the actuarial return, and I have
yet to learn after fifty years in connection
with the industrial insurance business that
any society having large reserves has proceeded to reduce the risks upon the existing policy-holders by an effort similar to
what the Government is proposing in this
Measure. Therefore, I feel it is my duty
to divide the House against this Measure
in consequence of these facts I have placed
before the House.
Mr. JOSEPH CUNNINGHAM: I am
sure no Member of the House is content.
any more than the last two speakers that
it is found necessary to reduce the benefits
of this particular class of insured person,
but there has been no suggestion put forward as to how we will meet the difficulty.
If it is allowed to go on it means that the
benefits are bound to be reduced both for
men and women. It is evident that the
greatest drain on these insurance societies
is the married women. The actuarial
figures prove that, and the recommendation made by the actuaries is that women's
benefit only be reduced. When you take
into consideration that it is married women
are affected it is not such a hardship as in
the case of single women. In the case of
a married woman her husband is a worker
and expected to provide for the woman if
sick. It is not such a hardship in that
case. Then it is stated that the Govern-
Health Insurance Bill-
THE SENATE
Third Reading
[Mr. Joseph Cunningham]
ment has not kept faith with the insured
workers. That is hardly the fact, because
when the insured workers first entered insurance they were only entitled to sickness
benefit; but since then they are receiving
other benefits such as widows' and orphans'
pensions. They are also receiving the
widows' pensions at a much earlier age
than was contemplated in the early stages
of the Insurance Acts. I think there is
nothing to complain of. For myself, I
know that there are many who will feel
the pinch. As I said the other day, there
are some genuine cases of hardship, but
there are others who will not suffer in any
way. I do think the Government is acting
properly in reducing the benefits of the
particular class that are the greatest
drain on the Fund, rather than reduce
the sickness benefit of men and single.
women as well.
Mr. LONG: In reply to the hon.
and learned Senator (Mr. Campbell), who
introduced this matter, I should say that
it is with regret that the Government
feel that the reduction alluded to is
necessary, but I am afraid it cannot be
avoided if we are to keep the Fund in

that it is necessary, of course, to keep
on the same lines as Great Britain in
these matters, and for this purpose the
Bill is an absolute necessity. I suggest
that the hon. Senator (Mr. Joseph
Cunningham), who has last spoken, has
very effectively answered Senator Dorman's
contention. As
to the hardship on
married women, which has been alluded
to, hon. Members will recollect that the
The Lord Mayor of Belfast.

Armstrong, Mr. H. B.

Minister of Labour said on the Second
Reading the other day that we were
faced with the alternative of doing what
is in the Bill or reducing all round, and
the Government in Great Britain have
chosen what I believe is the lesser of two

Mr. LESLIE: The White Paper, circulated with this Bill, contains four
divisions-A, B, C and D. The speakers
who suggested to us this afternoon that
the Bill should be rejected based their
comments on division A of the White
Paper, but they have not drawn our
attention to the fact that if we reject the
Bill before us now there will exist no
power for bringing into operation here
the proposals contained in divisions B,
C and D in the White Paper. Those
latter divisions do seem to me to confer
a very distinct benefit on the classes to
whom they relate and, therefore, I know
I was not unduly enthusiastic in my
support of the first part of the Measure
in the Imperial House, which is only part,
of course, of what will be covered by the
Measure we are passing to-day. Leaving
that aside there remain these three subsequent divisions of the proposals, the rejection of which, to my mind, would
entail serious loss to those who can very
ill afford it. Consequently, I think it is
our duty to support the Bill for these
reasons in addition to those given by the
Parliamentary Secretary.

WHITEWELL P.E. SCHOOL.
""
Mr. LONG: I beg to move, "That this
House do now adjourn until such time as
Mr. Speaker may appoint. In any case,
the Senate will meet for the Royal Assent
to Bills at five minutes past Twelve on
7th June.
Mr. BARCLAY: I wish to draw the
attention of the House to a grievance
under which the parents of the children
at Glengormley labour. Some three and
a-half years ago the school at Whitewell,
which was used by the children of Glengormley and district, was burned down.
Since then there has been practically no
accommodation for those children except
in the old tea room in the Bellevue
grounds. This building was constructed
some twenty or thirty years ago, and is of
corrugated iron. In the winter time it
is cold and draughty, and in the summer
time it is over-hot and stuffy. In this
temporary school there are 200 children
and seven teachers, while a school of the
size should have accommodation for only
100 children.
I raise this question to-day in the
hope that the Ministry will make an
effort in some way to bring pressure to
bear upon the Lisburn Regional Committee. I have made inquiries as to why
the Regional Committee did not make a
move sooner to provide a school for those
children, and I have been informed that
they are under the impression that the
Belfast city boundary will be extended in
the near future, and that Glengormley
will be taken in. If Glengormley is
taken into the city area, then it will be
the Belfast Corporation that will be responsible for erecting the school there. I
cannot understand the Regional Committee, because if they have not already
agreed they have almost agreed to build
a school at Finaghy, and it is quite
probable that when the boundary is extended Finaghy will be taken in also.
I cannot see where the wisdom comes in
in building a school at Finaghy and
leaving Glengormley to stand alone with
200 children and seven teachers crowded
into a small place. I raise this question
in the hope that the Ministry will get into
touch with the Regional Committee, and
that something will be done in the near
future for the children and teachers at
Glengormley.
Mr. LONG: In reply to the hon.
Senator, I think the matter he has
alluded to is one primarily for the
Regional Education Committee of the
area, but I will bring his remarks on the
subject to the notice of my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Education.
On Question, Motion agreed to.
Adjourned accordingly at
a quarter before Four
o'clock until such date
as Mr. Speaker shall
appoint.

Prorogation of Parliament.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have it in command
from his Grace the Governor to read
forthwith in this Chamber to the Senators
and Commons of Northern Ireland therein
assembled his Grace's Proclamation for
proroguing this present Parliament.
(6
Resolved, That the Gentleman Usher
of the Black Rod be commanded to inform
the Commons that the Proclamation of his
Grace the Governor proroguing this present
Session of Parliament is to be read forthwith, and that this House invite the
Commons to attend in order to hear the
same." (Viscount Charlemont.)
The Commons, being at the Bar with
their Speaker, the Proclamation was read
to both Houses of Parliament by the
Speaker of the Senate (in pursuance of
his Grace's command) as followeth:-
A PROCLAMATION
For Proroguing the present Parliament
of Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by Section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said Act,
that the Governor of Northern Ireland
shall in his Majesty's name summon,
prorogue and dissolve the Parliament of
Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that
this present Parliament of Northern
Ireland should be prorogued to the
twenty-second day of November, One
thousand nine hundred and thirty-two:
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, KNIGHT OF
THE MOST NOBLE ORDER OF THE
GARTER, KNIGHT OF THE MOST
ILLUSTRIOUS ORDER OF ST.
PATRICK, Governor of Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do publish
and declare his Majesty's Pleasure that
the said Parliament be, as from the
reading of this Proclamation in the
Parliament of Northern Ireland, prorogued
to Tuesday, the twenty-second day of
November, One thousand nine hundred
and thirty-two.
AND I do hereby further declare his
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall on the said
twenty-second day of November, One
thousand nine hundred and thirty-two,
assemble and be holden at Stormont for
the despatch of divers urgent and
important affairs, and the Senators and
Members of the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland are hereby required to
give their attendance accordingly.
Given at Baronscourt, County Tyrone,
this twenty-ninth day of September, One
thousand nine hundred and thirty-two.
(Signed by his own hand)
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
End of the Fourth Session (opened

Tuesday, 8th March, 1932) of the Third
Parliament of Northern Ireland in the
twenty-third year of the Reign of his
Majesty King George the Fifth.

Tuesday, 22nd November, 1932.
The Fifth Session of the Third Parliament of Northern Ireland, appointed to
meet at Stormont, 22nd November,
1932, in the Twenty-third year of the
Reign of His Majesty King George the
Fifth, was opened by the Governor
(His Grace the Duke of Abercorn, K.G.,
K.P.) in person.
The House met at ten minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Right Hon. H. G. H. Mulholland,
M.P.) in the Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black
Rod (Major T. D. H. Hackett, D.S.O.)
was announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman Usher said:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.

Sessional Orders.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return or Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such Bribery or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any persons hath been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime or
misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant at
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear His Grace's Speech, on
behalf of His Majesty, to both Houses
of Parliament, of which I have for
greater accuracy obtained a copy.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
It gives me particular satisfaction to
inaugurate this Session of the Parliament of Northern Ireland while the
hearty welcome to His Royal Highness
The Prince of Wales is still ringing in
our ears.
His gracious act in coming to us and
declaring this building open, on behalf
of His Majesty The King, and his
visiting the people, has endeared him
still further to them, who deeply
appreciated the opportunity afforded
them of again demonstrating their undying devotion to the Throne. The
enthusiasm and rejoicings of the community were striking features of the
happy occasion.
I desire to record my appreciation
of the services rendered by the Forces
of the Crown and to congratulate the
Royal Ulster and Special Constabulary,
as well as the Stewards who lined the
route, on the admirable arrangements
made for the convenience of the public.
I congratulate you on the amenities
of your new habitation, in which you
will be privileged in future to conduct
the legislative affairs of this part of the
United Kingdom.
To turn to matters affecting the
future-the state of agriculture, linen
and ship-building, continues to be
governed by those adverse World conditions which for several years past
have exercised so baneful an influence
upon every country. It is my ardent
hope that the ratification of the Agreements reached at Ottawa may mark the
beginning of fresh prosperity for the
farming community and those of our
industries upon which the well-being
of the people so largely depends, and
may lead in turn to the removal of
some of the obstacles which have
hitherto impeded the development of
our trade with countries outside the
Empire.
While the number of persons seeking
employment through the Employment
Exchanges showed an increase during
the first half of the year, I am gratified
to learn that in the summer a turning
point was reached, since when a steady
fall has been recorded. The increased
employment was mainly due to the
activity in the linen trade and available evidence leads me to expect that
this may be maintained.
As regards shipbuilding, there is an
improvement to record and it is to be
earnestly hoped that, with the progressive obsolescence of tonnage, new
contruction will become inevitable and
that our local firms will secure the
share to which their high reputation
entitles them.
King's Speech
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
I should like to refer to the valuable
contribution to employment which
local authorities and public bodies are
continuing to make, by putting in
hand, with the assistance of my
Government, works of public utility,
which will prove of general and lasting
benefit to the community.
I am pleased to learn that, as a
result of anxious consideration and
negotiations which have been in progress for some considerable time
between my Government and the responsible local bodies, steps have been
taken to formulate a revised basis or
standard of outdoor relief in respect of
certain areas which should alleviate
the present distress.
My Government have carefully considered the views of local authorities on
the subject of proposals for local government reform. In deference to their
views and the fear that any comprehensive scheme might involve additional burdens being imposed on the
rates, my Government have decided
not to do more than introduce a
measure dealing with matters of an
urgent character and remedying
certain defects and anomalies in the
various codes bearing upon local
government administration.
Legislation will be introduced during the session to enable schemes for
the marketing of agricultural produce
to be promoted in Northern Ireland.
A measure will be laid before you
to give effect before the 31st March
next to the various operations on our
funds necessary to implement the Budget proposals approved last Session,
including power to make advances
from the Consolidated Fund to the
Road Fund.
A Bill will also be introduced for
the better regulation of moneylenders,
together with measures dealing with
the following matters:-
Amendment of the Bankruptcy
Law.
County Officers and Courts.
Dangerous Drugs.
Destructive Imported Animals.
Fisheries.
Regulation of Stormont Estate.
Unemployment Insurance.
Members of the House of Commons.
The Estimates for the Public Services will be laid before you in due
course.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
Notwithstanding the many difficulties with which our manufacturers
have been confronted the industrial
life of the community continues to be
substantially free from interruption by
trade disputes. The accommodating
spirit shown by employers and employees in settling questions of wages
and conditions without recourse to a
stoppage of work is most praiseworthy.
And I pray that the blessing of
Almighty God may rest upon your
deliberations.
Debate on The Address.
Rev. Professor CORKEY (in morning
dress): I beg to move:
"That an humble Address be presented to His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland as followeth :
"Your Grace,
"We, His Majesty's most dutiful
and loyal subjects, the Commons of
Northern Ireland, in Parliament
assembled, beg leave to offer our
humble thanks to your Grace for the
Speech which your Grace has addressed
to both Houses of Parliament.”
I appreciate very highly the honour
which has been done to me and those
whom I represent in asking me to move
this Address on this historic occasion
when we
as a Parliament meet for the
first time in this splendid building,
which has been presented to us by our
Imperial authorities, and which has
been declared open by His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales amid such
enthusiasm and rejoicing. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
The first word which I would utter on
this occasion is one in appreciation of
the goodness of His Royal Highness in
coming over here to declare this building
open, and to take part with us in the
solemn dedication of the house to those
services for which it was built. The
events of the last two or three days can
have left no one in any doubt as to the
strength of the loyalty which the people
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
22 NOVEMBER 1932
of Northern Ireland feel towards the
Throne of England-(Hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-or as to the admiration
which they have for His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, the heir to
that Throne.
The interest which the Prince took
during his visit here in all our industrial
activities and in all our social and
philanthropic works deeply impressed
everyone, and was a great stimulus, I
can imagine, to those who are engaged in
such work. During his brief stay here
he found time to glance at almost every
side of our industrial and our social life,
finding opportunity, I am told, for inspecting one of those wonderful orchestras known as drumming parties. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). I can imagine
that the brief lesson which His Royal
Highness had at Hillsborough in the art
of beating the big drum may be of service to him in the coming days in that
high propaganda work in which he is so
often engaged. I am quite confident
that his visit to Northern Ireland will
help to strengthen the ties of loyalty and
affection which bind Northern Ireland to
Great Britain and to the whole Empire.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
My second word would be one of
appreciation of the courageous men who
twelve years ago, in days of anxiety and
uncertainty-
Mr. NIXON: Broke the Covenant.
Rev.
Professor CORKEY-carried
through those negotiations which
founded our constitution here and which
made possible the foundation and
erection of this House. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). It was a great joy
to the whole Ulster community to have
with us, on the occasion of the opening
of this House, Lord Carson-(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-looking almost
as gay and as vigorous as ever.
(Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). And it must
have been a singular gratification to Lord
Carson to have been able to be present
at the opening of this building, which
was the consummation of one of the
greatest triumphs of his whole career,
when he pleaded a cause, not before a
jury of twelve men, but before the whole
public of the United Kingdom.
My third word would be one of
appreciation of the work of our Prime
Minister and the members of his Cabinet
!
who, for the last twelve years, when this
building was in course of erection, have
been, with great wisdom and foresight,
firmly laying the foundations of our
Government's authority here and buttressing our position so that, thanks to
their efforts, their loyalty and their
devotion, that position now can be said
to be impregnable and secure for all time.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) And
they have made our position not only
secure as a political unit but they have
made possible, I think, a prosperity and
welfare for the people of this area which,
in spite of present depression, would
have been otherwise altogether impossible.
I am quite sure that the course of events
in other parts of Ireland will not prompt
anyone to regret the action which was
taken twelve years ago by our leaders
then, and which has been consistently
developed by those same leaders from
that time until now. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
The Gracious Speech from the Throne
congratulates the Members of this House
on the amenities of the habitation in
which their future activities will be
carried on. Those who have inspected
this building realise that there are
grounds for that congratulation. It is a
magnificent building, magnificently constructed on a magnificent site. Speaking for myself, hon. Members will understand me when I say that I think I felt
as much at home in the Assembly
College as I am ever likely to be here,
and it is possible that I shall miss the
moral courage which I was wont to get
from the pictures of the venerable
patriarchs who looked down upon us at
our work in that building. Nevertheless, as a Parliament we are to be congratulated on the gift which we have
received from our Imperial authorities of
this splendid building. It will stand
here for years to come, as our Prime
Minister has said, upon its foundation of
granite, as a symbol of the alliance
which binds us and will bind us, I
hope, for centuries to come to Great
Britain. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It will stand as a testimony to our indebtedness to our Imperial authorities,
not only for this House, but also for the
liberties and privileges which, as citizens
of the United Kingdom, we enjoy.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) It was a
magnificent gift. It is fitting that
Parliament should have a worthy environment. If our legislation in the
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Professor Corkey]
coming days is in accordance with the
character of this building in which that
legislation is conceived and formulated
and discussed, then our legislation will
be symmetrical, well balanced, and fair
to all parties. It will be perfect in detail
and will be elevating to the lives of all
those who are affected by it.
an
Coming to the details of the gracious
Speech, it puts in the forefront
expression of the hope that the agreements reached at Ottawa will inaugurate
a new era of prosperity for our agriculture and for our other industries. I
leave the details of criticism of these
agreements to others who are more conversant with them, but I would just like
to say that if these agreements encourage our people to remain on the land
or even of they will induce a part of our
over-swollen population to return again to
the country, they will be worthy of all
praise and all support. For the last hundred years in this country there has been
a steady drift to the towns. People have
been attracted by the prospect of larger
incomes and brighter lives. Surely it is
time that this drift towards the cities
should come to an end, and I think anything that can be done ought to be done
which would encourage the people to
maintain their homesteads in the country,
where they would have a far better opportunity of health and independence, of a
secure means of livelihood and an increasing degree of all the amenities enjoyed by those who live in our towns.
The Speech also refers with appreciation to works of public utility which have
been initiated in the interests of the unemployed by many of our local authorities. Surprise is sometimes expressed
that the local authorities do not initiate
still more extensive schemes of this
character-schemes so far-reaching that
practically all our unemployed might be
absorbed. Those who make this criticism
of our Government and local authorities
forget that it takes four or five times as
much in the way of immediate charges
to keep a man in work of this sort as it
does to provide a man with unemployment insurance, so that unless this public
work is of genuine utility, or unless there
is some guarantee that it will be remunerative in the not too distant future, it is
absolutely impossible for our public
authorities to undertake more than a
limited amount of work of this kind.
At the same time we endorse the sentiment in the gracious Speech when expressing appreciation of these public
authorities that have initiated work of
this kind and enabled a larger number of
our people to find that work in which alone
they can have satisfaction and a decent
livelihood.

The Speech goes on to refer, also with

which have been carried through recently
between our Government and the local
authorities, whereby a higher standard.
of outdoor relief has been established. I
would like to congratulate the Government on the prompt action which they
took in this matter. It is just another

for the working people conditions, so far

not be inferior to the conditions enjoyed
by their fellow workers in Great Britain.
I may say, speaking from personal experience, that a few weeks ago there was
considerable amount of discontent
in
smouldering
city-discontent
which at the time seemed to me not
unnatural, and there was a possibility of
that situation being exploited by
agitators who had not the welfare of the
city or the people at heart. If I may
say so, it is my opinion that great service was rendered to the community at
that critical moment by certain representatives of our Churches, who lent an
ear to the complaints of these people and
who interpreted their need in a reasonable way, and who thus snatched the
leadership from the hands of those
agitators and baffled their evil designs.
While I say that, I repeat what I said
before, that the whole credit for the
speedy passing of the unrest is due to the
Government.
Mr. BEATTIE: Question.
Rev. Professor CORKEY: The Speech
also reminds us that the Government has not forgotten the proposals
made some time ago on behalf of extensive local government reform. There
will, I am sure, be no surprise in the
mind of anyone that the Government
does not propose at the present moment
to launch out on any such extensive local
government reform. The times are
peculiar. The cost of our public services at the present time, especially of
our social services, is very excessive and
very unusual.
I understand that every
Debate on the Address

Debate on the Address

week our Northern Government
spending about £100,000 upon unemployment insurance claims and industrial
pension claims. When the cost of maintaining our social services at the moment
is so excessive-and, after all, these
charges are a first charge on the community-there need be no surprise or regret expressed anywhere that our Government is unwilling to undertake at
this juncture a vast scheme of local government reform, which would probably
involve a good deal of immediate expense.
In regard to the various Bills which
are foreshadowed in the Speech from the
Throne, it is true to say that while they
are of a somewhat minor character, they
will be beneficial to the various classes
of our community who will be affected
by them. I have not sufficient inside
knowledge of the intentions of the Government in regard to
any of these
Measures to be able to give a forecast
of their contents, but some of the titles
are provocative of a good deal of interest. For example, there is to be a
Measure which will enable new schemes
for the marketing of agricultural produce to be promoted. I think we all feel
that the Measures which have been
launched in this House during the last
number of years by our Minister of Agriculture have been a great benefit to the
agricultural community, and the results
have, it seems to me, confounded the
critics. I am certain that this new Bill
will also be a boon to those who have
products to market.
Then there is to be a Bill which will
deal with dangerous drugs. I do not
know whence the suggestion for this
Bill came. Perhaps it came from
Geneva. If so, it is very suggestive and
very instructive of the trend of world
affairs. I hope that this Bill dealing
with dangerous drugs will be very comprehensive, and I would be glad to think
that it would include some strict regulations as to the vending of all the various
nostrums which might be properly so described.
We are also to have a Measure which
will deal with unemployment insurance,
and which will confer upon the people of
Northern Ireland further benefits in conformity with the benefits conferred by
the recent Act passed by the Imperial
Parliament. I observed an item of news
in the newspapers the other day.
It
was that in consequence of the arrangement we have with the Imperial
authorities in regard to unemployment
insurance, this country during the last
seven years has benefited to the extent
of some three and a half million pounds.
In that state of affairs no one out of
Bedlam would surely suggest that anything should be done here which should
weaken the ties we have with those
authorities, or which would jeopardise
our relationships with them in regard to
this great service.
As a whole, the Speech foreshadows a
limited amount of cautious legislation,
and I think in that respect the Speech is
one on which the whole country may
congratulate itself. This area of ours-
Northern Ireland-lives, and moves, and
has its very being in the social and industrial régimes which are maintained
by the Imperial Parliament at Westminster, and I think it would be very
unwise for our Northern Government,
in these times of uncertainty and
anxiety, to launch out on great schemes
for the remodelling of our whole industrial or social system, schemes which at
the present moment may be hazardous in
themselves and which might in future
create difficulties in our adopting and
applying to ourselves Measures which are
likely to be adopted by the Imperial
authorities for dealing with the peculiar
situation in which the people now stand.
I beg to move.
Mr. GAMBLE (in morning dress):
I rise to second the Address in reply to

entirely agricultural constituency. This

Friend, the Member for University, in

Hon. Members will agree that this
Session will be a memorable one. All
who were present on Wednesday of last
week, when his Royal Highness the Prince
of Wales, as representing his Majesty

the King, declared this building open,

I am

would add that we can still rely on these

The Gracious Speech goes on to refer to
matters affecting the future, namely, the
state of agriculture, linen and shipbuilding. I propose to deal briefly with
agriculture, as this is the subject with
which I am most conversant. I may say
that I am an optimist and firmly believe
that brighter times lie close ahead for
the agriculturist. The agreements
reached at Ottawa will, I hope, mark the
beginning of an era of prosperity for the
farming community, and will open the
way for further discussion, which may
lead to the removal of some of the
obstacles which have stood in the way of
the development of our trade outside the
Empire. It is proposed to introduce
legislation during the present Session to
enable schemes to be promoted for the
better marketing of agricultural produce
in Northern Ireland. That, combined
with a regulated quota of imports, ought
to go a long way in giving the farmer a
steady market at remunerative prices
without unduly raising the cost to the
consumer. (Hon Members: Hear,
hear.)
The linen trade, according to latest
reports, has slightly improved, and I
hope this improvement will be maintained. Every effort should be put forth
to help the production and sale of linen.
Mr. NIXON: Flax.
Mr. GAMBLE: I am pleased to know
that the co-operation of local authorities

been dealt with largely by my hon.
Friend who moved the Address, I will

It has been decided to introduce a

bearing upon local government administration, and I would urge upon the

at the present time. The House will

I beg formally to second the Address in

Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to extend my congratulations to the mover
and seconder of the Address in Reply.
I might say that the King's Speech, to
my mind, is a very difficult document to
diagnose. I certainly appreciate very
much the amount of talking that was
done by the mover on a document that
contains absolutely nothing of interest
to the people of Northern Ireland.
(Hon. Members: No, no.) I am quite
prepared to say that, as has been previously stated in this House, we have
come to the period when the Government
who now control the destinies of Northern Ireland are bankrupt of ideas. We
never had documentary evidence to prove
such a statement until to-day. This
document to me is proof of the bankruptcy of the Government in its outlook
for the people of Northern Ireland.
What do we get other than a few palliatives in the form of an extension cf
the pauper idea, namely, that people who
have been long in employment will have
their position enhanced by a further
period of unemployment benefit?
Nothing of a practical nature has been
set out by the Government. What have
they in mind for the future of the
thousands of people previously employed
in the shipbuilding industry and who
never more will be employed in that industry? What have they in mind for
the linen workers of Northern Ireland
who have been ousted by foreign competition? Not a solitary word has been
said as to the future of those people,
and I claim that the bankruptcy of the
minds of the Government has been
proved 100 per cent. by this document.
In it we get appreciation of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary. How do the Government value services rendered? They
value them from the shipyard worker's
point of view by sending him to the Lisburn Road, and they also value it from
the linen worker's point of view by sending him to the Lisburn Road too, and in
regard to the Royal Ulster Constabulary
by giving them a cut in their pay. That
is the way the Government appreciate
services rendered. To-day we are sitting
in a House-one of the finest I may say
in the world-which is due to the workmanship of the people of Northern Ireland, and not one solitary word has been
said to the credit of those people who
built this House and who have honoured
the Province by the result of their craftsmanship. Not one word has been said
in this Speech about the men who are
now walking about depending on
charitable relief as their only means of
existence.
I should have thought that after the
time spent at Ottawa and the agreements
reached there some brighter ideas
would have sprung from the minds of the
Government. I will take shipbuilding
first. I should have thought that the
Minister of Finance during his sojourn
in the Dominion would have made every
effort to get some of the shipbuilding
orders that have been floating about in
the world's markets from the Soviet
Government of Russia. You are smiling
at the idea, but I say to you, give the
shipyard workers ships to build and they
will not care whether they are Russian or
American. They care not what country
the order comes from so long as they get
work. The commercial traveller does
not care about the views of the man to
whom he sells his goods. He gets paid
for the goods, and you get paid by the
Russian Soviet to-day. (Hon. Members:
No, no.)
Hon. Members opposite need not get
angry when Russia is mentioned. It is
not so long since they were making
representations to the Imperial Government for the free entry of Russian flax.
They were successful in those representations. Therefore, if the free entry of
Russian flax is good for Northern Ireland,
the three million pounds worth of shipbuilding which Russia had to give out
would have been good for it too. The
Russians were on the market for ships in
1930, in 1931, and right up to February
of this year.
No effort was made by the
Government to get the construction of
one of those ships for Northern Ireland.
Efforts were made by the employing
class to bring them here, but owing to
the Trades Facilities Act not being
extended, the work did not come here.
If the Government had brought into
being a Trades Facilities Act and given
an extension of one or two years I am
satisfied that the hammers would still be
humming in the Queen's Island, and that
men would be constantly employed building ships, no matter what country they
might be for.
