Debate on the Address

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
Another remark in this Speech refers
to undying devotion to the Throne.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I do not
think that undying devotion to the
Throne has ever been disputed by anyone
in this House, but certainly the Government have lived on that undying devotion
to the Throne, and have thrived very
well on it. If the British Government
refused financial assistance to Northern
Ireland the loyalty of the Government
would disappear. That has been proved
time after time from the year 1912 right
up to date. Where was your undying
devotion to the Throne in 1912 when you
rebelled against the forces of the Crown-
(Hon. Members: No)-when you made it
possible for people in this country to
take a gun and ammunition and shoot
down those who did not agree with them?
Was that undying devotion to the Crown?
My hon. Friends, I hope, will learn sense
at some future date, and will not prattle
any more about their undying devotion
to the Throne.
The Mover of the Address moved a
humble Address to His Grace for the
elaborate display of good things contained in this King's Speech. Those
words are mine. I should like to know
why we should humble ourselves to anyone for something to which we are entitled. I understand that the hon.
Gentleman who moved the Address (Rev.
Professor Corkey) is classified in some
circles as a social worker. He has told
us to-day that he is thankful for the
small mercies contained in this document.
If he is, I certainly am not satisfied with
the crumbs, if there are crumbs, from
any party's table. The crumbs from
any party's table are not good enough
for the class I represent. I certainly was
surprised at his begging leave to move
this humble Address. I cannot see that
we, as human beings, have the right to
be thankful for anything we are getting
at the present moment. The old saying
that the rich are getting richer and the
poor are getting poorer is coming truer
and truer.
The state of chaos that exists in our
midst and in the midst of other countries
is due solely and simply to the class of
government we have been getting, and
the class of legislation that has been enacted has not removed any of the evils
that exist. Where did anyone ever agree
that unemployment benefit was a remedy
for unemployment? You are continuing
in this strain, that you are paying
£100,000 a week in social services. A
great part of that is due to unemployment benefit, but will any Member of the
Government tell me that that is a remedy
for unemployment? I fail to see that
that type of legislation is going to meet
the present or future requirements of the
unemployed. I do not think that we had
ever before in the history of this country
boys up to the age of 23 who have never
found one day's employment. That
state of things is not decreasing. It is
increasing, because of the scarcity of
employment in Northern Ireland, because
of the dying state of the shipbuilding and
linen trades, and because of the nonfulfilment of the pledges made by the
Government to establish new industries
to take the place of the old.
The Government are going along from
day to day, and are not paying the
attention required for the alleviation of
this great menace which has crept slowly
upon them. But they will, perhaps, pay
attention to it when the evil day comes,
the evil day of revolt against the trying
conditions which you are perpetuating.
I heard the Mover of the Address state
that he was pleased to know that the
lawful authorities had taken the position
out of the hands of the mob orators and
agitators who were responsible for trying
to overthrow constitutional order in this
city. Perhaps I happen to be one of the
mob orators spoken of by the hon. Member for the University (Rev. Professor
Corkey). I am not ashamed of any
assembly of people with which I was
associated during the outdoor relief
workers' strike. I am not ashamed of
any
services that I rendered in compelling
the Government to come down and feed
the hungry when the hungry demanded
to be fed, because up to that date the
Government were holding out a stone to
the hungry when they were asking for
bread.
Does the hon. Member for the
University say that men of this type
should be despised and scorned as traitors
to constitutional law? If that is the
theory of the University then I am
pleased that I never passed through it.
That is the intelligence that comes from
that great assembly called the University.
I want to say that if it had not been for
the unemployed workers, who demanded
through the Government consideration of
their needs and requirements, the city
would, perhaps, have been in a worse
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
22 NOVEMBER 1932
position than it is in to-day. The Government allowed deaths to take place; they
allowed destruction; they allowed riot
when they could have avoided it. Not
a death should have taken place in the
city of Belfast, no man should have received an injury. If the Government had
done their duty and it was their duty
to take action-they should have compelled the Board of Guardians to bring
into operation, three weeks earlier,
treatment for the unemployed on parallel
lines with that meted out in Great
Britain. The thing which they did in
the last week under compulsion and the
threat of a general strike, should have
been done three or four weeks earlier, and
not a life would have been lost. The
city would not have had to go through
the scenes of riot caused by the neglect
and carelessness of the authorities who
control that institution.
The next thing I want to speak about
is the reference in the Speech to
dangerous drugs. Do I take it that they
are going to put more drugs within the
confines of a particular class of people, in
view of the fact that so many thousands of
people in this part of the world are tired of
life owing to the trying economic conditions through which they are passing!
Are the Government afraid that the
people of Northern Ireland are so tired
of this material world that they might
take to drugs? There are drugs in our
midst to-day about which the Government
have taken no action. I know that the
notice of the Government was brought to
a very serious drug, and they took no
action-a thing that is causing grave
trouble in the lives of the people of
Belfast who are addicted to it. I refer
to the drug called "Red Biddy.
Mr. CRAWFORD: What is that?
Mr. BEATTIE: I never tasted it.
The hon. Member for Mid Antrim (Mr.
Crawford) may be a connoisseur. I hope
that that drug will be included in this
Bill to deal with dangerous drugs, and
that its sale will be prohibited in Northern Ireland.
Mr. NIXON: And drugged speeches.
Mr. BEATTIE: I want to go further
and to say that the unemployment insurance scheme that has been suggested
for Great Britain is not a suitable one
for Northern Ireland. I hope the Government will not follow the lines of Great
Britain in this respect. If they follow
the lines of Great Britain so far as unemployment insurance is concerned, and
bring insurance on to a solvent basis,
they will deny the right of 75 per cent.
of the unemployed workers of Northern
Ireland to participate in the new scheme.
The new scheme lays it clearly down that
a reduction of the twenty-six weeks'
benefit is to take place, and that the
twenty-six weeks is to be replaced by
thirteen weeks. This is the new Bill.
But a person who can show a good industrial record may still qualify for a
further period than thirteen weeks.
They have brought down the figure to
thirteen weeks and it is possible for any
man or woman who, because of depression in trade, has not a very good industrial record to be the victim of that
thirteen weeks' provision. I hope the
Minister responsible for this scheme will
endeavour to remedy the grievances of
the class for which I am speaking at the
moment.
I would have also thought that legislation would have been foreshadowed in
this Speech in the form of an Economy
Bill for landlords. We have now given
a privileged class in our midst the right
to exploit rents to the extent of thirty
per cent. clear profit. They have never
yet come forward and made any sacrifice for the nation in the bad times
through which we are passing. Is there
any reason why legislation should not
have been included in this Speech to reestablish house rents at the pre-war rate?
Mr. SPEAKER: That matter is not
included in the Speech, and the hon.
Member for Pottinger must move an
Amendment in order to introduce it into
the debate.
Mr. BEATTIE: It is not contained in
the King's Speech, but there is so little
in the Speech that one is inclined to be
rather despairing. The landlord classes
have the best vested interest I know in
Northern Ireland at the moment. They
should be asked to make some sacrifice,
and I hope the Government will include
in the next Session of Parliament a Bill
restoring pre-war rents retrospectively to
the tenants of Northern Ireland.
The last point I wish to make about
this Speech is that it is not true. It is
pretty harsh to say that anything is untrue, but when I see it in writing I must
repudiate a position which I know to be
untrue. It is stated in the Speech:

Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Beattie]
"While the number of persons seeking employment through the employment exchanges showed an increase
during the first half of the year, I am
gratified to learn that in the summer a
turning point was reached, since when
a steady fall has been recorded. The
increased employment was mainly due
to the activity in the linen trade, and
available evidence leads me to expect
that this may be maintained."
I want to say that during the summer
very harsh regulations were operating in
the Minister of Labour's Department.
By compiling the number of claims made
in Great Britain through the medium of
the "Gazette" and taking the number of
claims made in Northern Ireland for the
twelve months ending October, 1932, I
have discovered that there was an active
industry in Northern Ireland during the
summer months. That industry took the
form of courts of referees, before which
applicants for unemployment benefit had
to appear. Taking the figures per
1,000 people in Great Britain and the
same ratio in Northern Ireland, it is surprising to find that for every 1,000
persons making claim to unemployment
benefit in Great Britain eight are disallowed, while for every 1,000 persons
making claim to unemployment benefit
in Northern Ireland twelve are disallowed. In other words, under the
Unemployment Insurance Acts there are
fifty per cent. more people disallowed in
Northern Ireland than in Great Britain.
Certainly your industry in that direction
was very active, and was playing the part
of un-step-by-step with Great Britain
instead of step-by-step on this occasion.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews)
may try to challenge these figures if he
wishes, but they are unchallengeable.
The official figures are there, and we have
recently had a very large deputation of
representatives of the workers appearing
before the Minister and drawing his
attention to the serious state of affairs
caused by this drifting away in Northern
Ireland from the Unemployment Insurance Acts as they are carried out in Great
Britain. That has been proved beyond
the shadow of a doubt by those figures I
have quoted and by the representations
which have been made. I hope that,
instead of continuing active in that way,
the Minister will pull up now and reduce
his number per thousand so as to make
up the leeway that has been caused by
having a greater percentage of disallowance in Northern Ireland than there
is in Great Britain.
We
We have had a very long Recess.
had a very long holiday, if you like to
call it a holiday. To some hon. Members,
I presume, it was a holiday; to others it
was not, because when the House is not
meeting some Members are hard at work.
To others, however, it is a period of enjoyment.
But I would have thought
that a Speech of this kind would have
given us some hope, would have given
us some inspiration, would have given us
some of the old industrial grit, as I may
call it, of the industrial classes of
Northern Ireland, and would have given
a lead to the industrialists of Northern
Ireland outside this House. But the
Prince came, the Prince went, and the
Prince's orders were nil.
It was understood by many that the
Prince was the greatest traveller Great
Britain ever possessed. It was thought
by many that when he did arrive he
would arrive with his pockets bulging
with orders. But the only order we got
was one that was delivered in a very
mysterious way, one that was delivered
from London to the headquarters of the
Unionist Association. Whether it was
genuine or not I am not in a position to
say, but I hope it is genuine. But it was
one anyway which should never have
been sent to that address. In my
opinion, the business man who adopts a
political game of that kind is not fit to be
in a business community, because he is
playing the game of politics in his
business, not with the object of giving
any assistance to the Government, but for
the sake of some other perquisite or something else in the near future. I hope
that the orders, when they do come, will
come to the business addresses of the
firms for whom they are meant.
I understand that we are to meet now
for about six days. Then we are to
adjourn again, and the unemployed
worker and the destitute people will go
on, and not one word of mention has
been made of the class of persons for
whom we fought during the outdoor relief workers' strike. No mention is made
of the single person in lodgings about
whom I have been in close touch with the
Ministry of Home Affairs. Up to the
present, I regret to say, they have failed
to put in force the terms of the agree-

ment arrived at. I hope the Government will take immediate action to have

(Hon.
I can hardly stand at this box without
feeling thrilled all through by the fact
that I have still beside me and round
me here those trusty colleagues who

One is that I believe that the great benefit

one of the greatest revolutions in the

suddenly from a completely Free Trade
country into the position of foreign
countries by having tariffs for protection
or for revenue purposes. Nobody can conceive any greater scheme that has been
carried out.
If, as I hope, the change to a tariff
country brings about general prosperity

engaged, and who, with the prosperity
following, will be able to spend more

that in itself will be a result most satisfactory to Northern Ireland. It will
also be the first stage of showing the
great benefits that have emerged from

other words, we need not be pernickety

I now come to the serious affairs of
Ulster, and I would like to say there
are one or two very difficult corners still
to be rounded. Perhaps the most
difficult of all will be the railway situation which gives me and my colleagues
considerable perturbation. The difficulties in connection with railways are world
wide, and in Great Britain, as here,
the situation is causing anxiety in the
minds of all those who have to do with
railway management. I can only say
it is one of those problems which crop
up like so many others throughout the
world which have to be solved as soon
as possible. I believe that we can tackle
it as satisfactorily as any other part of
the United Kingdom.
We are a small, compact area. We
have the whole picture before us, we
have very able men in control, and we
also have, I think, as satisfactory a settlement of road traffic as is to be found anywhere in the world. It only requires us
to round off the great triumph of my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Home
Affairs, in connection with motor traffic,
to be able to say that difficulty is out of
the way.
We will have to ask considerably more patience from the public in
connection with this matter. It touches,
as everybody knows, a very wide part of
our area and is, in my opinion, a very
difficult nut to crack. We want all the
help we can get from every wise head in
order to solve a problem that to-day presents so much difficulty.
In conclusion, I would like to say that,
so far as the Government are concerned,
throughout the past eleven years we have
invited all the criticism, the help, and
encouragement we could get from the
people of the country. We shall continue
to do the same thing. We hope that
through our Members, who have so well
represented their constituencies in the
past, we shall be able to keep our fingers
very closely on the pulse of public
opinion in the future. We have come
through an extraordinarily difficult
period, but perhaps the Union Jack flying on this noble building for the first
time may presage a period of prosperity
and happiness such as we have not known
since we took on the government of the
country. At any rate, I can only say,
in resuming my seat, that no one will be
more satisfied and no one will be more
happy than I shall be if anything can be
done to improve the Ulster we have
known, the Ulster of which we are so
proud. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

Monday, 28th November, 1932,
will be the ninth anniversary of the
Prime Minister's famous speech on the
question of unemployment, when he said.
that if the Imperial Government would
not solve the problem of unemployment
he would do so. Every year since that
he has repeated that promise. Notwithstanding the figures quoted to-day, the
position so far as men are concerned was
never worse. I will not be contradicted
when I state that the number of unemployed men signing the register in Belfast
alone is over 28,000. I have no hesitation
in saying that several thousands can be
added to that of men who did not sign because they have no chance whatever of ever
obtaining employment through the labour
exchange. It is a fact which is not disputed that a single man without responsibility when his benefit ceases has no
use signing on because he will never get
work, and therefore ceases signing on.
Every Member on that side of the
House who has given serious consideration
to the matter knows as well as I do that
in about five or seven years the problem
of unemployed men in Belfast will be
terrific. It is bad enough at the present
time; but every year-I think I am safe
in saying so, although I hope I am wrong
-half the young men leaving school are
going on the labour market. They will
get no work and never will. There are
men up to 25 years of age in Belfast, and
through no fault of their own they never
got a day's work and never will. No attempt whatever has been made to meet
that situation. Somebody certainly will
have to meet it later. In about five years'
time the position will be so acute that
something will have to be done. I have
often been asked what could I do. I
think the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr.
Gordon) asked me that some few years
ago in respect to the matter of unemployment. I said at that time that for one
thing I would subsidise the growing of
flax; that I would put a flat rate per acre
on all flax put in by the farmer. By
doing that there would be more employment in the country and in the scutch
mills. Then you would have your own
flax for your own country and for your
own mills.
just
The Parliamentary Secretary
turned that down. There are some experts in the flax industry in the House,
and I think they will admit to-day that
flax is dear abroad. Seeing that we are
off the Gold Standard it means of necessity
that it is dear when you go abroad. There
is no flax at home. If my suggestion had
been followed at that time there would
have been flax; and yet look at all the
millions paid away year after year as dole
for distress relief and the like, and nothing
useful is done; nothing that is productive.
If I had my way I would approach some
shipbuilding company that usually builds.
ships in Belfast and I would say: "Prepare your plans; come along and build
ships in Belfast. We will pay you 50 per
cent. of the wages paid." That would be
an inducement. That would be something
better than telling the House and the
country and the world-"We do a lot for
unemployment because we pay so many
millions on social services." Somebody
will have to do something like that. The
Government with all their influence were
not able to bring the Olympic to Belfast,
where she was built, for repairs. I sometimes doubt their influence, and I doubt
the interest that they take in these
matters.
I have a right to doubt it, because a
few years ago, when I told the House
that one of the yards was to be closed,
I was contradicted and criticised, and yet
before a week an order closing one of the
yards was posted up. As a matter of
fact it was in print when I told the House,
and I knew it. But the Government did
not know it, simply and solely because
they were not minding their business as
they should be minding it. They were
not taking the interest in the people they
should take. I know the Government
have a great majority. I know that while
the Government lasts they will have a
great majority, but there is not much
difference between this Government and
other Governments. There is not much
fear of them losing an election, but some
time they will lose it. If the Conservative Government across the water lose
an election they win another, and vice
versa. I am afraid if the Northern
Government lose an election it will be the
last and only one they will lose. Instead
of sneering and laughing at the distress
of the unemployed or anguish of the
parents of babies, that the medical officer
of health has proved are dying of starvation, they should try to do something on

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I had not intended to intervene at this early stage in the discussion
on the King's Speech, but circumstances
have arisen which compel me to be in
London to-morrow, and, therefore, it will
be necessary for me to leave the House
earlier than I had hoped. I had hoped
to give my hon. Friends the results of
the Ottawa Conference, but as I must
leave the House I am afraid that will be
impossible. I should like very much to
have been able to reply or afford information to hon. Members on this subject
myself, but, as I say, that would be impossible. With regard to the Conference
itself, perhaps hon. Members will recall
that when the British and Dominion Governments released the information in respect of the results of the Ottawa Conference, I handed to the Press a precis of
these results, which were then published
in full. As these results are common
knowledge to-day, I propose to limit my
observations to the circumstances which
brought the Ottawa Conference into
being, and also to the work of our delegation and the treatment which was
accorded to the views of our Ulster Members on that delegation.
If we are to view the results of the
Imperial Economic Conference which met
at Ottawa in their proper perspective, we
must carry our minds back to the Imperial Conference which met in London
two years ago in 1930. At that time
the Socialist Government held authority
in Britain, and notwithstanding that
Britain's open door invited all the world
to deluge the country with unwanted
goods, the unrelenting devotees of Free
Trade still refused to realise the portents
of economic and financial disaster which
even then were apparent to unbiassed
thinkers, and which culminated in the
financial and economic débâcle of last
year.
At that meeting in 1930, in London,
to which I have referred, Mr. Bennett,
the Prime Minister of Canada, invited
the Members of the British Commonwealth to meet in conference in Ottawa
in 1932, and, at the same time, boldly
came forward with an offer to increase
Canadian Empire Preferences by 10 per
cent., if corresponding and reciprocal
advantages were agreed to by Britain
and the other Dominions. This offer
was derisively spurned by the organs of
Liberal opinion in the country——
Mr. BEATTIE: Quite right, too.
Mr. POLLOCK—and rudely turned
down by Britain's Labour Government.
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: But the Canadian
Minister's invitation to all the units of
the Empire to meet in Economic Conference in Ottawa in 1932 was agreed to.
So long as the Labour Government continued in power in Britain, little hope
was entertained at that time of any
radical cure of the malaise which afflicted
the Empire and the world.
Mr. NIXON: MacDonald is in power
yet.
Mr. POLLOCK: But startling and
drastic events in the Kingdom soon began
to follow each other in bewildering rapid
succession, and it may not, perhaps, be
considered out of place if I shortly catalogue these momentous movements as a
prelude to the main story of the Ottawa
Conference. The first disturbing factor
was the country's dismal adverse balance
of trade resulting from our open and
Debate on the Address
23 NOVEMBER 1932
Debate on the Address
tempting markets. This was followed by
the threat of Britain's unbalanced Budget, which, in turn, developed distrust
and suspicion on the part of foreigners
as to Britain's financial stability, followed
by heavy withdrawals of balances lying in
London. This run on London banks
necessitated borrowing vast sums from the
United States and France to meet these
calls, an incident which is unprecedented
in modern British history.
Shortly after the presentation of the
Budget the Socialist Government resigned,
to be replaced by a National Government
with Mr. MacDonald as Prime Minister.
Then came the financial panic and the
dramatic
abandonment of the Gold
Standard, causing a terrible world disturbance of finance. Following this
came the general election and the overwhelming defeat at the polls of the
Liberal and Labour parties, the establishment of a strong National Government,
mainly Conservative-
Mr. NIXON : Under Ramsay
MacDonald.
Mr. POLLOCK and the death
blow to the Free Trade policy which had
obtained for one hundred years in
Britain. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
One of the first acts of the new Parliament was the imposition of the Abnormal
Importations Act, known as the antidumping law, whose effects are now seen
in the favourable balance of trade and
the rehabilitation of the financial strength
of Britain. All these important movements, following in quick succession
within a single year, served to prepare
a favourable seed-bed from which it was
hoped and expected to reap an abundant
harvest at Ottawa.
The establishment of a National
Government in Britain, pledged not to
rule out any expedient, even to the
extent of the imposition of such tariffs
as would firstly ensure a favourable trade
balance for the country and offer protection to industries afflicted by foreign
competition, offered the surest guarantee
that the approaching Ottawa Conference would not be a mere talkingshop engaged in academic and futile discussions on the relative merits of Free
Trade and Protection, but a businesslike gathering which it was
trammelled by any outworn fetishes and
determined to reach a practical objective.
I can bear testimony to that result.
un-
When the date of the Conference was
settled, our Prime Minister decided it
was necessary that a delegation should go
to Ottawa to represent the Province in
association with the United Kingdom
delegation. It was quite certain that
questions affecting our considerable
export trade would come under discussion, whilst, not less important, perhaps
even more important, agricultural matters
in which we have such a vital interest
would, beyond doubt, be developed by the
Dominions, whose concern for a privileged position in the British market was
public property. The Dominions have
never concealed their anxiety to have
free entry to the British market for their
cereals, their meat and live stock, with
a tax against foreign produce.
The British Government willingly and
cheerfully acceded to our request, and,
my name having been put forward, the
Canadian Government admitted me to a
very privileged position. Although part
of the United Kingdom delegation,
technically I occupied the position of
adviser on Ulster questions to that delegation. Arrangements were also made.
for my colleagues and assistants, whose
duties and services I will refer to later.
As hon. Members opposite have tried
to decry the value of our Ulster delegation, especially my own position in the
Conference, I would like to inform hon.
Members that the Canadian Government
treated me in every respect as a British
Minister. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. NIXON: Very decent of them.
Mr. POLLOCK: They paid all my
expenses at Ottawa, they provided me
with a motor car and military chauffeurs
for the full period of my visit, and in
other ways they showed their friendliness to me and the other members of the
Ulster delegation. (Hon. Members :
Hear, hear.) The Canadian Prime
Minister, Mr. Bennett, was especially
friendly to Ulster, and he gave me his
personal assurance that Ulster liner
would be admitted free to Canada. As
to my relation with the seven British
Ministers who were present at Ottawa, I
had the advantage of personal acquaintance with them prior to the Ottawa
meeting, and during the Conference I was
freely admitted to the daily meetings of
Ministers, when discussions arose on the
current problems of the day. My colleagues also were occupied from day to
day on the various committees discussing

[Mr. Pollock]
many subjects, and I can testify fully
to the appreciation of their services.
by all the members of the British
delegation. Therefore, I do not think
that hon. Members opposite have any
ground for decrying the value of the
delegation at that wonderful assembly.
on
The opening plenary session of the
Conference was held in the large Hall of
the House of Commons in the Parliament
Buildings of Canada at Ottawa,
Thursday, July 21. This meeting was
an inspiration. It presented a spectacle
sufficient to rouse the imagination and
fire the blood of anyone claiming citizenship of an Empire whose area covers onefourth of the habitable globe, and whose
population is similarly proportioned.
Assembled in that Hall were to be seen
men dwelling in lands under the Southern
Cross side by side with those who lived
under the cold glitter of the Northern
Star. Some there were whose darker
skins proclaimed their Eastern origin,
others from Colonies and from the islands
of the seas, but all sheltering under a
common flag, all speaking a
common
language, and, over and above everything, all owing allegiance to a common
Sovereign who, in his home in Buckingham Palace, listened to the expressions
of devotion from his subjects met in
conference.
A great deal of misconception has been
current in this country as to the real
objects of the Ottawa Conference. Many
people seemed to think that the meeting
was solely designed for the betterment of
conditions in the United Kingdom, and
concerned themselves little or not at all
with the anxieties and problems of the
Dominions, which were little better than
those at home. They were apparently
ignorant that if concessions or sacrifices
were to be made by the Dominions to
each other, or to Britain, these concessions were expected to be reciprocal
and distributed, as far as possible,
equally over the different units of the
Empire. Failure to appreciate this
important factor is, I am convinced, at
the root of much of the criticism and
some of the disappointments that have
been experienced in surveying the results.
of the Ottawa Conference.
Many people picture Britain as the
great industrial centre of the Empire,
as indeed it is, primarily concerned with
the production and export of manufactured goods with the other members
of the Empire, solely agricultural or
pastoral in their outlook. So far from
such being the case, some of these great
countries, and especially Canada, have
become highly industrialised communities,
with vast internal resources. They are
directing all their energies, not alone to
the manufacture of their own internal
requirements, but they also are ambitious
to become exporters to the outside world,
thus coming into direct competition with
our home industries.
But whilst all the members of the
different delegations were expected to be
animated by the common aim of consolidating the Empire by closer economic
relationship, it is not unnatural to
assume that each was inspired with the
hope of reaching conclusions which would.
directly benefit the country which he
represented. This is human nature.
The truth is the Ottawa Conference
came thirty years too late. Had such a
meeting taken place during Joseph
Chamberlain's campaign in 1902, before
the manufacturing activities of
Dominions had developed, the problems
awaiting solution would have been much
less complex.
the
May I say at once that I cannot enter
into any discussion as to whether the Imperial fiscal policy of the United Kingdom
delegation is good or bad. This is an
Imperial matter, with which our Government has no contractual or legislative
powers. Whether the fiscal policy of the
Kingdom of which we are a part is determined on a Free Trade or Protection
basis, Ulster must accept the common verdict, and share the common burdens and
benefits. This, however, does not prevent
us from fostering our industries to the
greatest possible extent within the limits
of the fiscal policy of the United
Kingdom.
The main purpose of the Conference
was set out in the words of the statement
issued by the British Government. It
was not in the interest of or to confer
benefit on any one particular unit, but
for all. The object of the Conference
was:
To lay the foundations of an economic
policy for the Empire that would ensure both now and in the future an
increasing volume of Empire trade.
brought about as far as possible by the
lowering of trade barriers as between
the several members of the Empire.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

23 NOVEMBER 1932
That was the aim and object of the
Ottawa Conference, and the House will
realise that if all the purposes and all
the ambitions of the different units of the
Empire were to be harmonised it would
have required a much longer time than
was occupied during the month at
Ottawa. Our Ulster delegation was received everywhere with the greatest
friendliness by the representatives of
Canada, Australia, New Zealand, India,
South Africa, Southern Rhodesia, and
Newfoundland.
Mr. NIXON: And the Free State.
Mr. POLLOCK: We established many
friendships, and were treated as one with
the United Kingdom delegation. To my
mind, this was not the least of our
achievements, to let the Empire at large.
know very definitely of our sympathies
and ideals, which are directed unswervingly towards unity within the Kingdom
and the Empire, which is the very kernel.
of our existence. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Having this in our minds, I will now
discuss as succinctly as I can the extent
to which our Ulster interests have been
benefited by the deliberations of the Conference.
Towards this end, it will be convenient
to take catergorically different Dominions
of the Empire with which our exporting
interests are concerned, and also the commodities in which we specialise here.
Putting aside for the moment agriculture, which we regard as mainly of local
interest, the following Ulster goods are
capable of development in the Dominion.
markets:
-
Linen,
Ropes, Cordage and Twine,
Shirts and Collars,
Readymade Clothing,
Machinery,
Whisky,
Mineral Waters, and possibly
Soap.
we
Those are the articles in which
specialise, and for which we hope to find
markets not only in the Kingdom but
abroad.
CANADA.
Taking Canada first, as our most important Dominion, it will be found that very
considerable amendments have been made
in her Customs. Among these we find
exceptional benefit has been conferred on
our linen trade. As I have mentioned
before, I had information directly from
Mr. Bennett, the Prime Minister who, in
the friendliest way told me that we
should have free entry for our linen into
Canada. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The original duty of 25 per cent. plus.
3 cents per lb., etc., equalling, approximately 45 per cent on fine linen and
linen handkerchiefs, has been entirely
abolished-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-
whilst the duty of 15 per cent. on linen
thread has also been removed. We have
thus secured practically free entry for
our important linen goods, and I need
hardly stress the immense importance of
this concession.
Furthermore, the Canadian Government have slightly reduced the duty on
cotton shirts and collars. This interests
Londonderry, which, as we know, has a
large business in these commodities; but
hon. Members will appreciate the great
difficulty in regard to this item in
obtaining concessions on protective tariffs
where there is a considerable industry of
a kindred nature within the country
itself, for obviously the Canadians, like
ourselves, are concerned with the protection of those industries which they
carry on and desire to increase.
AUSTRALIA.
Now, in regard to Australia, we participate generally in the adjustment of
preferences in favour of goods from the
United Kingdom, while the measure of
our advantage against the foreigner has
been increased; that is, the tax imposed
on foreign competitive goods has been
increased. I need not quote the scale of
preferences which has been fixed, but that
is the general effect. Hon. Members will
have in their hands a full note of the
schedules of the different commodities,
which they can study at their leisure.
But this is not all in regard to
Australia. The opportunity was taken
of re-opening the question of the tariff
restriction in respect of continuous weave
-a technical term common in the linen
trade-which was pursued by my right
hon. Friend, the Prime Minister, when
he was in Australia, but the amendment
of which, owing to a change of Government there, was not actually carried into
effect. This matter has now been satisfactorily settled, and Australia has
amended her Customs tariffs so as to allow
of the entry of single articles, so long as

Another important concession is that

NEW ZEALAND.
New Zealand, which is, perhaps, a
more purely English or Ulster colony
than of the Dominions, has withdrawn a tax of 4 per cent. on linen
goods, on ropes and cordage twines, and
on mineral waters, while the duties on
shirts, collars, and readymade clothing
are to suffer a reduction of one-third from
nearly 40 per cent. to 27 per cent.,
which, again, should assist Londonderry,
which has a very considerable manufacturing trade in shirts and collars.
INDIA.
Now I come to India, that wealthy
dependency which differs very materially
in character from the other Dominions
of the Commonwealth, but which has a
tremendous value from the point of view
of our export trade. India has agreed
to grant a preference of 10 per cent.
against the foreigner in respect of cordage and rope, shirts and collars, and
readymade clothing.
But not only have these important
definite concessions been made,
made, but
practically all the Dominions have undertaken that when their finances permit,
they will consider sympathetically the
abolition of various duties against British
goods, or the establishment of further
preferences. This applies to Canada,
Australia, New Zealand and Newfoundland.
Furthermore, Canada, Australia, and
New Zealand have agreed to consider at
the earliest opportunity a revision of
tariffs to ensure that they shall be based
on the principle that United Kingdom
producers will have full opportunity of
reasonable competition on the basis of
relative cost of economic and efficient
production.
In the consideration by the respective
tariff boards of these problems, United
Kingdom producers will be entitled to
make representations. I regard that as
one of the most important outcomes of
the work at Ottawa.
AGRICULTURE.
Now I come to a matter which is of
very great importance to us from a good
many points of view, namely, agriculture.
A great many opinions have been voiced
for and against the proposals which have
been made, but I might point out that
the difficulties in the way of the formulation of a policy have been very serious.
In the first place, it was necessary that
in return for the markets which the
Dominions were giving us, we had
to provide extended market for
Dominion products, and these were
almost entirely of an agricultural nature.
At the same time, it was necessary not
only to protect but to better the prospects
of our own farmers.
an
Let me just summarise in a few words
what has been done. There is to be a
gradual reduction over a period of eighteen
months, commencing 1st January, 1933,
of the imports of frozen and chilled beef,
mutton, and lamb. The proportion of
the home market fed by the home producer is to be maintained, and the
Dominions are to obtain their increased
markets by means of a quota being
granted to them as against the foreign
will
producer. This
mean that the
Dominions will obtain a reasonable price
for their products, and the market will
not be liable to a disastrous collapse such
as recently took place. Provided this
scheme can be brought to fruition, and I
see no reason why it should not, the
result ought to be a reasonable prospect
to the farmer of a price for his cattle and
sheep. A similar scheme has been
brought forward in regard to the importation of bacon and hams, as hon.
Members are, no doubt, aware.
These are the permanent proposals,
but hon. Members will be aware that
since 7th November various temporary
restrictions have been in force. Imports
of chilled beef have been cut by 10 per
cent., and foreign frozen mutton and
lamb imports have been cut by 20 per
cent. Only this morning the temporary
restrictions on the importation of bacon
and ham have been put into force,
effecting a reduction for the next two
months of over 15 per cent., as compared

them. The farmer also should benefit

are now specific-and this is important—
instead of being simply on a percentage

I must now refer to apples.
again, dumping has been the bane of
apple growers, but a specific duty of
4s 6d per cwt. on foreign apples should

Having recounted all the benefits, or
rather, I should say, the means by which
benefits may be obtained, it occurs to me
that there has been a fashion in certain
quarters of asking what are these benefits
worth. The reply has been given that
no one knows, at least not in pounds,
shillings and pence, but I should like to
say this: The concessions that have
been gained are concessions which were
urgently asked for by the leaders of the
industries themselves. But, perhaps,
most important of all, now that the
principle of protecting our home producers has been established, whether by
quotas or positive tariffs, it is only a
question of time and experience to enable
us to grapple with problems that are at
present largely experimental.
But, apart from the more material
advantages which may be expected to
accrue from Ottawa, I should like to
raise the question to a higher plane. I
am satisfied that our Empire problems
cannot be fully and permanently solved
by purely economic measures, however
great and important they may be. The
solution must be based on higher ethical
and spiritual standards, and I have no
doubt that the mutual understanding of
each other's problems and difficulties,
gained at Ottawa by the members of the
Commonwealth, will contribute more and
more, as time goes on, to weld all the
component parts of the Empire ultimately
into one great economic union.

consummation, the Ottawa Conference will

There is one matter I should like to
think the Government is considering, and
that is the problem of emigration.
I
certainly do not want to see the flower
of Ulster manhood leaving us, but we
cannot shut our eyes to the fact that
Ulster men and women, in good times as
well as bad, turn their faces to the west
and go abroad to seek fame and fortune.
We must recognise the fact that in the
years 1924, 1925, and 1926,
in
years
which the industrial depression was not
so acute, almost 30,000 left Ulster, the
greater proportion of these going to
Canada.
I am aware that emigration has ceased
for the present, but it will begin again.
Our great Dominions will want settlers of
the right type, and Ulster has always
supplied the best of these. I should like
to see some sort of organisation set up in
conjunction with the Governments of the
Dominions, whereby those who go out
from Ulster should be properly cared for,
given advice and assistance and not left
to shift for themselves. I believe such
an organisation would be of immense
benefit to both sides. Our people would
feel that we still had their interests at
heart, and such a connection would
strengthen the bonds that bind them to
the Empire. An organisation like this.
would help to get the right man for the
right job, and do away with attempting
to fill, if I may use the simile, a round
hole with a square peg. If it is felt that
this is too big a thing to attempt, might
I suggest that it be tried in Canada, as
it is to that Dominion the largest number of our people go, and then, if it is
found to work, I am sure the other
Dominions would only be too glad to try
it. But I do feel that the plans for such
an organisation should be got ready so as
to be in a position to deal with emigration
when it starts again.
Whilst I feel very strongly on the subject of emigration, there is another matter which need not be delayed until
better times. I refer to the canning industry. This is an industry which
recently has made very great strides in
England, where there are now 84 canning
factories. The demand for British
canned goods is considerable. For instance, in 1929 16 million cans of fruit
and vegetables were packed in Great
Britain; in 1930 that number had more
than doubled, over 33 million cans being
packed; last year the number had reached
the total of 83 million cans, 56 million of
which were vegetable, and this year well
over 100 million cans have been packed.
If this increase continues, and I think it
will, these canning factories will need very
large supplies of both fruit and vegetables. I know that the demand for
canned peas produced by English growers
is very great. I have been told that 1,000
acres of peas might be planted to replace
the peas that at present are being imported. Here, then, is an industry that,
if it were fostered, and encouraged, could
do a great deal to absorb a large proportion of the available labour of our
countryside who are only too anxious and
willing to work. I, therefore, hope that
the Ministries of Commerce and Agriculture will be able to devise some scheme
which would enable such an industry to
be started as soon as possible in order.
that advantage might be taken of the still
available markets.

taken place did not take place thirty
years ago, when Mr. Joseph Chamberlain was at the height of his power. If
they had this Empire would have been
much nearer to being self-contained and
self-supporting than it is to-day. There
were not so many vested interests then
to overcome but, unfortunately, the
differences of opinion at home made it
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
23 NOVEMBER 1932
impossible to get anything done in the
way of tariffs. Anything I say with
regard to Ottawa, of course, is not in
criticism of my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Finance, or his colleagues in
the Government, because they are in no
way responsible for the fact that things
have been done in a way that I am sure
a great many of us would not have done
them. Ottawa is certainly a landmark in
the history of Great Britain. It is true,
as Lord Hailsham said the other day in
another place, that we have only laid the
foundation. Well, even to lay the
foundation is something, and I hope, as
the Minister of Finance has said, that
the generation that is succeeding us will
see to it that a fine sound edifice is built
on the foundation that was laid this summer at Ottawa. So far the Colonies have
come out of Ottawa, and indeed out of
recent legislation, pretty well.
I have no intention of going back over
the fight last year. The one question at
issue in Great Britain was the question
of protection, and the Government was
given a free hand to apply that method
in such a way that the languishing
industries of the country would be
revived. The first thing they did was
to bring in an Import Duties Bill. At
any rate, to put it in a nut-shell, the
result of the legislation in Great Britain
and the result of the agreements at
Ottawa means that the manufacturers get
protection equal to 20 per cent. on all
imported goods. That is all to our
credit, and I think that if I wanted an
argument in favour of a tariff I would
refer to the King's Speech, according to
which the reaction in the linen industry
alone has been very quick.
I have a protest to make, and that
protest is in regard to the treatment the
farmers and labourers have received.
They are entitled to the same protection
as manufacturers and people engaged in
other industries, and yet what are the
facts? The facts are that the manufacturers are getting a 20 per cent. protection, and the unfortunate agriculturists are getting only a 2 per cent. protection. I say that is unfair and unjust,
and I cannot think that if the decision
had been in the hands of the Northern
Government they would ever have come
to a decision like that. It is not
necessary that I should go into the
causes that have led to that, to my
mind, foolish decision, but instead of
giving the farmers the 20 per cent. proit as
tection extended to the manufacturers
they give them the quota. I remember
that when the quota was first introduced
by the Socialists-because it emanated
from the Socialists-Lord Brentford,
who is better known to most people here
as Sir William Joynson-Hicks, described
a stupid piece of Socialism and,
indeed, that is what it is. It is inspired
by fear of losing votes at the next election,
and yet it ignores the justice of the case
put up for agriculture. The quota, with
its limitations, and impositions, and endless interference with trade in a manner
that would not be permitted in peace
times in any other country except this,
is going to be a source of weakness rather
than a source of strength to agriculture.
Of all the industries in the country
there is none that needs help more than
agriculture. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Agriculture to-day wants a
stimulus, and what we are offering to it
is a series of artificial restraints. I am not
a prophet or the son of a prophet, but I
have no hesitation in prophesying that
before we meet here this time next year
the quota will have disappeared
altogther, and anyone who has anything
to say in favour of it now will be glad to
forget all about it. It is the purest piece
of political quackery the country has ever
seen. If the manufacturer gets protection to the extent of 20 per cent., why
not the farmer? If the industrial
worker gets protection to the extent of
20 per cent. why deny the same protection to the farm labourer? I want
to know why we employ foreigners to produce our food when there are plenty of
idle people at home anxious for work,
who can do it if they get fair play.
Mr.
BEATTIE: It is because of
British capital abroad.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: British capital
abroad is important in its way, but there
is something much more important than
British capital abroad, and that is the
souls and bodies of British people at home,
and I cannot think of anything more soul
or body destroying than idleness and unemployment. I think it would be a great
advantage to this country if its unemployed, or even half of its unemployed,
were got back to the land again, and if
by putting on a simple straight tariff, instead of this complicated quota business,
we would get tens of thousands of people
back to the land where they would earn
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Robert Lynn]
a decent revenue. A tariff is a simple
business. You know exactly what you
are going to do and what you are going
to get. Think what this quota is really
doing for the country. I should say in
passing that the temporary arrangement
that has been made shows how ineffectual
was the settlement at Ottawa on this
question of agriculture.
Mr. NIXON: Flax.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I am coming to
flax, and I contend that those who grow
flax are as much entitled to a protective
duty against foreign imports as the man
who manufactures linen. Until the
people who administer affairs at Westminster recognise the justice of this claim
I do not see what is going to happen.
What is this quota going to do? There
are two classes who, I am sure, will benefit
from it. One, the foreigners who are
sending chilled meat to us, and the other
the huge army of civil servants who are
bound to be appointed to carry out the
scheme. The moment it was decided to
reduce by 10 per cent. imports from the
Argentine, what was the result? In one
night the value of the chilled beef stored
in England rose by £600,000. Under the
quota we are going to hand over
£8,000,000 a year to the Argentine,
£8,000,000 that might be used at home,
whereas a simple tariff of, say, 2d per lb.
on chilled meat would bring in a revenue
to Great Britain of £25,000,000 a year.
Then again, we are to have a pig
quota. The pig quota is to be managed
by eight boards. I believe seven is the
lucky number, but eight is most unusual,
I cannot think of anything that will lead
to a more speedy destruction of the pig
industry than eight boards with huge
staffs working against each other. That
shows you how things are done. I do
not know what the quota for Northern
Ireland will be, but the quota for Great
Britain has been fixed, and in two and a
half years Great Britain is to have a quota
of 1,500,000 cwt. of pork. What has
happened in the case of Canada?
Canada is sending into Great Britain
50,000 cwt. of pork at the present time,
and Canada gets a quota immediatelyshe does not have to wait two and a half
years of 2,500,000 cwt. Canada comes
out of the scheme fifty times better than
Great Britain. I presume Northern Ireland
will be put on the same basis as Britain.
Although we have no control over the
matter, surely this House must realise the
injustice and the folly of all this. The
Government in a simple way could have
put a tax on foreign foodstuffs just in the
same way as they have put a tax on other
goods. Why, the whole thing is too
absurd for words, and, as I said before,
it is a pure piece of political quackery
which is bound to come back on the heads
of those who are responsible for it.
There are many other subjects in the
King's Speech with which one might deal,
but I have no intention of taking up the
time of the House except to make a
passing reference to them. The Prime
Minister referred to the parlous condition
of the railways. I am not quite sure
what is in his mind or in the mind of
the Government on that subject, but I
do hope they are going to be very cautious
in regard to any steps they may take. I
have great sympathy with the railways.
They are certainly in a very bad way,
and the first step in the decline of the
railways took place when the Government
stepped in and began to control them.
The railways are suffering severely to-day
from Government interference, and I do
hope that the Prime Minister will think
twice before doing anything in the way.
of nationalising the railways, as the Member for Pottinger suggests. The Member
for Pottinger is very hard to please. He
has already got a good Socialistic bus
system. A monopoly was created by the
Government, and this House is the only
place in Northern Ireland where you
could get anyone to say anything in
favour of it. This monopoly has produced higher fares, and it is of no advantage to the community.
There is a Marketing Bill referred to
in the King's Speech. I remember there
was a Marketing Bill introduced into the
Imperial Parliament last year. That Bill
was fought from the first line to the last
by the Unionist party, and I do hope that
our Government is not going to go in for
a Socialistic Marketing Bill. If the
effect of the Bill is to help the farmers to
help themselves, then I have no objection
to it, but if the Government are going
in for another of these Socialistic schemes,
so far as I am concerned I cannot promise
them my support.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I would first
of all like to thank the Minister of
Finance for his kind reference to myself,
and I should also like to express my

Debate on the Address
23 NOVEMBER 1932
sense of the honour conferred upon me
in being given the opportunity to serve
with my other colleagues as a representative of Ulster at the Imperial Conference at Ottawa. In his speech yesterday the Prime Minister mentioned the
fact that opinion in England had completely changed from Free Trade to Protection. Now the reason for that change
was that prior to 1931 the exports in
England were paid for by countries with
raw material and foodstuffs, but the
situation in 1931 was such that instead of
the raw materials and foodstuffs paying
for our exports it was a question of our
exports plus an export of gold to make up
the difference paying for our imports.
The result of that was that gold, which
had been exported from England, was
being used in foreign countries with no
prospect of our coming to trade with those
foreign countries. Even Mr. Graham,
in the last Socialist Government, endeavoured to get a general agreement
with foreign countries in order to lower
the tariff walls. He was entirely unsuccessful, because he had nothing to
offer.

A curious situation has arisen. Since
the Ottawa agreement no fewer than five
countries have endeavoured to come to

had the honour of representing this
Province
the
on
Newton Committee,

Mr. NIXON: What about flax?
Sir BASIL BROOKE: If all the concessions which were made come up to
expectations flax will not be taxed to the

which was used by the British Government and the various Dominions in their
agreements. We naturally realised that

important point towards helping agriculture in Northern Ireland. Of the total
agricultural output from Northern Ireland it is 80 per cent., and in England
it amounts to something rather less than
70 per cent. It was obvious that unless

Tardieu, who was the French Minister
of Agriculture, made a prophecy as to
what would happen in France, as it

unemployment and failures, drive the

That gentleman foresaw what would
happen in France unless agriculture was
helped. Agriculture was not helped in
England, and that situation was very
nearly happening in this country. Even
at the present moment there are many
failures amongst agriculturists in this
country and in England, and repayment of a great deal of money which
has been lent by banks at the present
moment is not very sure, so that it was
quite obvious that agriculture should, if
possible, be helped, and helped substantially.
It was asserted by some hon. Gentlemen opposite that in fact those of us
who represented this country in Ottawa
did nothing. It was said that my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) remained
all the time sitting in his room. A new
heaven and a new earth were not contained within our terms of reference.
I can assure the House that the representatives of this country attended all
with
committee meetings which dealt
various points of interest. One of these
was the Primary Producers' Committee,

say, that this Primary Producers' Committee adopted practically in toto the
recommendations of the Newton Committee. In addition to that, the agricultural advisers were invited to attend the
Committee of the Federation of British

representatives of the Trades' Union

These Committees were all attended on

of this country.
The Federation of British Industries

future another economic conference was

Debate on the Address

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Debate on the Address
[Sir Basil Brooke]
It is the opinion of that Federation, which
I presume represents most of the industries in Great Britain and perhaps in
Northern Ireland, that owing to the
Ottawa Conference British industry can
capture £250,000,000 of trade. That is
surely something of value.
There can be no question about this,
that with a healthy trade, with trade in
a flourishing condition, agriculture is
bound to benefit to a very great extent.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) No matter what quotas or tariffs are put on in
order to help agriculture, unless trade is
flourishing the buyers of our goods will
be unable to buy them. It has been
argued that Protection is to a certain extent an artificial arrangement of trade.
It is unavoidable at the present time.
Take one country alone. Germany has
placed a quota against the importation of
foreign butter, and the result has been
that instead of the normal flow of butter
into Great Britain the butter which
should have gone into Germany has been
imported into England. When you have
this unnatural restriction in every other
country it is quite obvious that we should
not stand out and allow this dumping
which was killing our trade and ruining
the whole possibility of prosperity. It
is also argued that any form of Protection is an inducement to inefficiency,
either in agriculture or industry, but I
feel it is often forgotten that we have the
highest social services in the world. We
have the people in this country normally living a higher standard of life.
The money for these social services can
only come out of industry, and therefore
it is only right that industry and agriculture should have some protection
against those countries which have not
the same standard of life and not the
same social services. Further than that,
an argument against the agriculturists is
that food prices are put up, whether by
tariff or quota.
The position is this, that in Denmark
alone, at the present day, there are
20 per cent. fewer pure breeding
SOWS
than eighteen months ago, and
the number of cattle in Great Britain
is greatly reduced. No individual, be he
occupied in what industry he pleases, is
going to produce goods at an uneconomic
rate. The result will be that if this
chaotic state continues in a few years
there will be a definite shortage of food
for the people. It is much better to come
in now, not to put prices up to an
exorbitant height, but to keep prices at
an economic level to the producer, and
at a level at which the producer knows
he will get a fair price. I am satisfied
that with that object in view the Ottawa
Conference has accomplished something of
value to agriculture and industry.
One of the most important resolutions,
or agreements, arrived at in Ottawa
which, I think, govern really the whole
situation, is the admission by
by the
Dominions that the home producer has
first place in his own market. That
admission has shown itself at the present
time, because the home producer was
competing against dumping by foreign
countries, who were afraid of the results
of the Ottawa Conference. The result
was that a chaotic state of dumping
existed. Owing to that resolution, or
agreement, the British Government was
able to put the position before the
Dominions and say:-" You must
restrict your imports and allow us to
get an economic price for our products."
The Dominions have made a restriction,
I understand, to the extent of 10 per
cent. Instead of that restriction coming
on in January it has come on at the
present time. At any rate, whatever
restriction has been put on--and I would
point out to the hon. Member (Sir
Robert Lynn) that it is a restriction in
the nature of a quota and not in the
nature of a tariff-the price of cattle at
the present time has risen by 30s a head.
That is only a beginning.
Another very important admission was
that all meat was interdependent on any
other meat. Perhaps I can explain that
in this way.
The argument was that if
mutton and lamb alone were helped and
beef was left with no assistance whatever,
in the end beef would have become the
cheapest type of meat, and would have
brought down the price of mutton.
Exactly that situation arose only recently
in England in regard to pork. Owing to
the overproduction of pork the price of
pork stood at a low figure. In 1930 the
consumption of pork in Great Britain was
some 7,000,000 cwts. In 1931 the consumption had risen from 7,000,000 cwt. to
11,000,000 cwt., the difference being
something in the vicinity of 4,000.000
cwt., which simply means that 4,000,000
cwt. of some other type of meat was not
being consumed. The result of that was
that the cheapest meat was being eaten,
and, therefore, the price of the other meats,
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
23 NOVEMBER 1932
mutton and beef, for which there was no
demand at that time, descended to an
alarming extent. Therefore, that agreement that all meats were interdependent
the one on the other was of the very
greatest importance, because if only one
type of meat was assisted then the others
were of no value and would come down in
price.
Now, it is unnecessary for me to go
into the various points relating to agriculture because they appear in the White
Paper, but I think it should be
pointed out with regard to chilled
meat that this, as the Minister of Finance
has explained, comes from the Argentine.
The Argentine has been reduced to the
1931 figure, which, in fact, amounts to
7 per cent. less than the average for the
previous five years. The Argentine is the
only country in the world which can produce that chilled meat. They are in a
position to put their cattle on the alfalfa
from the moment they leave the cows.
There is no cost of feeding such as there
is in this country. Those cattle are
shipped killed at two years old and are
the type of beef which no Dominion and
no other country can produce.
I think the hon. Member for North
Antrim (Sir Robert Lynn) was wrong
when he said, as I understood him to say,
that we should ignore the amount of
capital in the Argentine, because if the
taxpayers in this country are unable to
pay owing to failures in the Argentine,
the British Government, by some means
or other, either by taxing industry or
agriculture, will have to get the money
with which to carry on. It will mean
there will be a deficiency and a very big
shortage. So those things cannot altogether be left on one side and ignored.
I admit as an agriculturist I should have
liked to have seen many more concessions
given to agriculture. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). After all, agriculture is
the primary industry. If agriculture as
an industry fails it does not matter
whether linen sheets are made or machinery is made, the food of the people will
fail, and then everything else must fail
as well. One naturally strove hard to get
the best that possibly could be got, but
the fact that something has been got and
that, as the Minister of Finance has said,
a foundation has been laid, is, to my mind,
one of the most important things. It was
hardly to be expected that a country which
was completely Free Trade, a country
such as England, in which I understand
only 10 per cent. of the population are
interested in agriculture, would do more;
and it is a big move, to my mind, for the
British Government to accomplish what
they did.
The Member for North Antrim rather
drew an analogy as between industry and
agriculture. I should point out to him
that in certain respects agriculture has
been helped by a purely tariff method,
mainly with regard to butter, which has
actually a 15 per cent. assistance. Eggs are
assisted to the extent of 1/- and 1/9 per
120, which means something round about
10 per cent. The great difficulty if you
adopt this was considered by the Newton
Committee. If you take merely a protective policy, that is to say, if you place
a tariff on these goods, and if there is a
surplus of supply in the exporting country
the tariff will be paid for by that country.
With a quota you have a definite means of
stopping further supplies coming in to
any extent you require, and actually the
Imports Act, which was passed after the
National Government took up office, set
up certain tariffs. The result was that
the price of agricultural produce dropped
still further. If they had been in a
position to put a quota the supply would
not have met the demand to the same
extent and prices, to my mind, would have
risen instead of falling.
It is most important-and this, I may
say, was acknowledged in the end by the
industries that agriculture is a primary
industry and the producer should get an
economic price for his products because
it is only from him and through him that
industry can be assisted. Nowhere else
can you start the wheels of finance rolling.
If agriculture pays, and the farmer is in
a position to buy goods you are starting
the wheel of freer finance throughout the
world. That was acknowledged, I may
say, by the Federation of British Industries, and a great many leaders of industry
agreed with that when they saw that if
there was a ruined agriculture their industries would suffer. Ulster, to my mind,
has been what I might call fortunate in
that most of her industries have been
assisted to a certain extent.
There is one point and it is a point.
on which one regrets in some ways that
we have not succeeded as we would have
liked, that is with regard to the importation of non-pedigree cattle. It was argued
that the importation of non-pedigree cattle

[Sir Basil Brooke]
into England would undo the work of the
various cattle improvement schemes.
was impossible to argue further when
Canada demanded the same rights as the
Irish Free State in importing those cattle
into England. It is an argument which
I do not think anyone in Northern Ireland could refute, as Canada is a loyal
Dominion, a Dominion which has always

In one of the newspapers which represent the views of the leaders of the Opposition, a gentleman stated in regard to
Ottawa that in his opinion neither tariffs,
bounties, loans, nor quotas would be of
the slightest assistance to agriculture, and
some remarks of mine in which I expressed
moderate opposition were placed alongside. The question was put whether the
people should believe me or the others. I
can hardly think that that particular
paper intended to believe what I said. In
fact, what that paper said was that there
was nothing to be done to help agriculturists and that our minds were entirely
sterile. We believe we have laid the
foundation of a future to which we can
look with some hope.
In addition to these material gains
Ulster took no small part in cementing
the bonds of friendship amongst the
various countries or Dominions. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) We understood
their position and they understood ours,
and it has been said on the other side of
the water that even if nothing else had
been accomplished the co-operation
amongst the various English-speaking
races, representing nearly a quarter of the
world, was a very important matter. The
Dominions understand that we have an
intense loyalty and devotion to the Crown,
and they understand also that we have a
determination to remain in the Empire
of which we form a part. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Major McCORMICK: I desire in the
first place to congratulate both the
mover and the seconder of the Address
in reply to the Gracious Speech. The
inauguration of this session, amid such
magnificence as marked its opening by
his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales,
has been fittingly referred to by the hon.
Members. I join heartily in the tribute
to one who has graced those proceedings
and conducted them to such a successful
and satisfactory issue. Indeed, I might
say that the aspirations and prayers of
our people have been gloriously consummated by these acts, all tending to
give us a closer connection with those
Imperial ties we have always held so dear
and to give reality, if that were needed,
to our fealty to the Crown and kinship
with our Imperial neighbours. Whilst
we have never altered in those attributes
of a loyal and proud service, this noble
building stands out as the outward and
visible sign of a people strong in traditional and unswerving adhesion to Empire
ideas. We are, if possible, stronger and
more unassailable in our ties with the
Empire.
In the envisaged legislation which has
been forecasted in the Gracious Speech
one regrets an omission which is vital to
the sentiments I have just expressed, and
that is, that the unwritten law of loyalty,
backed by public opinion, requires legislation whereby the national flag shall be
in use where State grants are given. I
am happy to say that in very few cases
would this law require to be exercised.
I do not wish to speak on this matter
with any narrow view, but rather in a
broad, tolerant way, believing, as I do,
that it is the duty of the citizens of any
country to uphold their national flag.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The
national flag of any country-I care not
whether it be Timbuctoo, a South
American Republic, or the Irish Free
State-should be, and is, a treasured
emblem, and it is right for that particular country to hold it dear.
I say let
no one insult the flag of their country;
let them be proud to protect it as it
protects them; let no one say but that it
symbolises liberty as well as tradition.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I will
not go into the matter of the insult to our national flag at Newry.
That was a question of the taking
down of a flag; I am speaking now
of the flying of a flag, and there will be
a later occasion on which that matter will
come up on a Motion, which I understand will be before the House. The
matter is only in abeyance, but no doubt
all these things epitomise and illustrate
the spirit which, to use the wording of
the Gracious Speech, demonstrates our
undying devotion to the Throne.

Surely not. I am expressing my own

matter when I say that I feel that a
Certain unfairness has been done, and that

men who have gone out there without any
definite object so far as knowing what
they were going to do was concerned.
Possibly being young men, some of them
almost boys, they went out on a kind of
picnic, but one thing they did do, and it
was very similar to what is happening in
this old land, was to crowd into the cities
and towns, believing that those places were
the Mecca of all their hopes and wants,
whereas if they had gone into the broad
agricultural lands they would have found
work to their hands and something
which, at the end of a term of years,
would have well repaid them. Ulstermen, I might say, are very popular and
successful in Canada. In fact, I remember having a conversation with the right
hon. Mr. Motherwell, who was then
Minister of Agriculture, and who is a
County Antrim man. He said that the
best class of settlers they got were Irishmen, and naturally he preferred Ulstermen; and he instanced to me many
successes that had been achieved by
Ulstermen. Canada is a great country.
It is one of our greatest Colonies and I
see a great future before it and before
anyone who goes out there in the right
spirit.
I do not say that there is anything
very ambitious in the outline of legislation contained in the Gracious Speech,
but perhaps that is all to the good. I
rejoice to know that legislation is to be
introduced to enable schemes for the
marketing of agricultural produce to be
promoted. I believe that will do much
to help out the farming industry.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I hope so.

Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Major MCCORMICK: Agriculture is
our basic industry; indeed it is the basic
industry of any country, and I do feel
that through these Ottawa Agreements a
great hope is held out that there will be
something solid behind them and that we
will see our prosperity coming back once
more. The Ottawa Agreements indeed in
this respect are already operating very
well. I was told just to-day that so far
as the price of pork is concerned there was
an advance of 10/-. Whether that is due
to the Agreements or not I do not know,
but time being the essence of all things I
believe the change will be gradual, and
that time will show that the Agreements
are well founded and that they will have
good results.
It will be a great thing,
indeed, to think that there are more prosperous times ahead for the farming community.
It is also stated in the Gracious Speech
that a Moneylenders Bill is to come up in
this Session of Parliament. Whilst in
these days of a stringent money market it
is rather nice to think that there are people
who have money to lend, it puts me in
mind of the sayings of Poor Richard, one
of which was:
"Those who borrow go in sorrow."
But I find that the revised version of that
saying would be more like this:
"If you would know the value of
money go and borrow some."
A great number of these moneylenders
lend money at an iniquitous rate of interest, which, in many cases, is the ruin
of the people to whom they lend it. I do
hope that when this Bill comes before the
House we may have a chance of seeing if
something cannot be done whereby a low
or, at any rate, a moderate rate of interest
will be charged.
Mr. ELLIOTT: No rate at all.
Major McCORMICK: That would
hardly be fair. There are certainly people
who are in such circumstances that they
have no other resource but to go to moneylenders. They cannot help themselves,
and it would be a very fine thing if those
people who lend money could be made to
do so under such conditions that a moderate rate of interest would be charged. I
understand that the last Moneylenders
Bill that went through the Imperial Parliament contained such a Clause, and that
it has operated very well. We might
well follow along the same lines in this
matter. I feel, indeed, that the Government should seek to fix a rate of interest
that would help these people by saying
that whilst they could enter into any
agreements they liked they could take
advantage of a certain Clause whereby
they would be protected.

can say to-day that I feel thrilled to stand

There has been considerable criticism

The scheme has been criticised not only by

from a political point of view, I look upon
this building as the foundation stone of
our political liberty and the rock of our
political salvation. I think I could not
sum up the situation better than by using

to the activity in the linen trade.
should like the House to hear some of the

many other trades are there which, in

ALLEGED RIOTING IN BELFAST.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
