(Sir Dawson Bates.)
Mr. NIXON: I gave notice to the
Attorney-General yesterday and this
morning that I would raise a question this
afternoon relative to a report of a riot
appearing in the "News-Letter" on the
14th July, 1932, when in fact on the
authority of the police there was no riot.
And I cannot conceive anything more
calculated to lead to a breach of the peace
than for a responsible newspaper to report
a riot where there is no riot, and, as a
matter of fact, in this particular case
following this report there was rioting,
and several loyal people out of my constituency were arrested and haled before
a crimes court, consisting of two resident
Adjournment-
Alleged Rioting in Belfast
23 NOVEMBER 1932
magistrates, under an Act which was
passed 40 years ago, and practically all
convicted and put under a rule of bail,
and I am proud to say that I am the
bailsman.
Now I will just read the report of the
"News-Letter" and the reply of the
"Telegraph" of the same day. This is
from the "Belfast News-Letter" of

Thursday, 14th July, 1932. The heading
is "West Belfast Riot. Barrage of
stones in Cupar Street. Police baton
charge."
Trouble broke out last evening in
Cupar Street, which lies between the
Shankill and Falls Road, Belfast, and
a large force of police had to be called
out to prevent Roman Catholics and
Protestants from getting into grips. As
it happened, however, there was a barrage of stones thrown over the heads of
the police, who were compelled to draw
their batons and charge the rival
parties.
It is estimated that there were two
or three hundred rioters on either side.
The trouble arose about 10-30 p.m.
when a cyclist, John Johnstone, of
Ashmore Street, was cycling down Conway Street towards the Falls Road. He
was pulled from his machine and badly
beaten, having to go to hospital to receive treatment.
Reinforcements.
When the news of his attack reached
Upper Cupar Street, which adjoins
Ashmore Street, the people of the district were naturally indignant, although
they made no attempt to carry out a
reprisal.
Shortly afterwards, however, a band
of youths approached from the Falls.
Road end of Cupar Street, and at the
point where the first Orange arch is
erected the rival crowds met.
The police, in charge of District-
Inspector Ferris, interfered, but so large
were the crowds that they could not
deal with them without assistance.
Reinforcements were immediately summoned from Musgrave Street, and a
strong force with three "cage" cars
soon arrived on the spot and getting between the rival gangs they separated
them. Batons had to be drawn, and
both crowds were charged.
A Regular Battle.
There was a regular battle with stones
lasting for an hour, and it is stated
that one policeman was slightly injured.
Shortly after midnight, when the
disturbance had been quelled, the police
continued to patrol streets in the vicinity
and the "cage" cars could be seen waiting in readiness for any further trouble
that might break out.
Feeling in the district has been running high since the morning of the
"Twelfth" when a party of men from
the Falls Road attempted to pull down
an Orange arch which had been erected
in Cupar Street.
Now this is the reply of the police as
published in the "Belfast Telegraph" of

Thursday, 14th July, 1932. That appeared
in the morning and the reply came in the
evening:
No Riot, says Police.
Verbal and Vocal Exchanges in Belfast
Borderland,
Described as "Serious Trouble."
The reported outbreak of serious
trouble in the West Belfast district on
Wednesday was officially denied by the
police authorities to-day.
Exaggerated accounts of the occurrence were published in the morning
newspapers, but a "Belfast Telegraph"
representative was informed at Springfield Road police barrack that there was
no foundation for some of the statements, and there was absolutely no
danger of rival crowds coming into
conflict.
The trouble appears to have originated.
in a reported assault on a young man
named John Johnstone, of Ashmore
Street (Conway Street to Canmore
Street).
It was rumoured that Johnstone had
been pulled from his bicycle in Conway
Street and badly beaten, and it was
stated at the Mater Hospital this morning that the youth had received treatment for a lacerated lip caused by a
fall.
At all events, the supposed outrage
aroused the indignation of the people of
the district, and although no attempts
at reprisals were made, it was not long
before rival crowds assembled in Cupar
Street at the border of the Protestant
and Roman Catholic areas.
The two crowds made no effort to
come into closer contact, and contented
themselves by shouting and singing
party songs, but as a precautionary measure a force of police, under District-
Alleged Rioting in Belfast 92
Adjournment-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Inspector Ferris, assembled between the
crowds.
There is no doubt that the incident
would have passed off peaceably but for
the activities of some irresponsible
youths on the outskirts of the crowds,
who flung stones and other missiles at
the police.
The situation was handled with the
greatest of tact, and eventually both
crowds were dispersed when the police
drew their batons.
After about an hour the danger of
trouble was averted, although the police
remained on duty in the vicinity for
some time after midnight.
The complaint is that according to the
report of the "News-Letter" there was a
riot lasting an hour, and according to
the official report the police gave to the
"Telegraph" there was no rioting. There
is a contradiction between the two papers.
I take it that when the "Telegraph"
published that contradiction they were
satisfied that the information given to the
reporter was correct. And although the
"News-Letter" is the pet of the Government, I do not see why they should be
allowed to spread false reports any more
than any other paper. Why even the report of what occurred here yesterday is
absolutely misleading from the way they
put it, and I do not see why there should
be flesh of one and fish of another. At
all events, in this particular area there
was trouble later on for which a lot of
people that I have an interest in and that
I stand by, and will stand by, suffered
severely and were denied the right of
trial by jury.
I protest against that here and now.
When that Act was originally passed for
resident magistrates to try cases of rioting, it was passed because the Government of the day could not depend on the
magistrates and jurors in certain parts of
Ireland. As a matter of fact, they were
intimidated and they could not do their
duty. I never knew of a slight being put
on Belfast jurors before until this. And
Woodvale is not the only constituency.
that complains in that respect. I saw
several cases in County Down of people
brought before a court, and the only
evidence was they were going along a
road after something happened, and they
got outrageous sentences of two months.
I say this, that any responsible paper-
I do not care what paper it is that
publishes a report calculated to excite the
people and calculated to lead to a breach
of the peace or throw extra duty on the
police, that paper should be prosecuted
under this Civil Powers Act, and let them
take the consequences. Next time let
them make sure before putting in any
report that the report is correct.
As a matter of fact, it should be the
duty of the papers instead of exaggerating to do the reverse. I want the
Attorney-General to tell me now what he
proposes to do with the "News-Letter."
The report of the police as published in
the "Telegraph" states there was no riot
and the "News-Letter" said there was
a riot.

very little difficulty in answering the

Letter," which he says is an exaggerated
account-

Although the hon. Member seemed to

MARKET TOLLS IN NORTHERN
IRELAND MARKETS.
2. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Agriculture whether it is the
intention of the Government to introduce
legislation to deal with the inequality of
market tolls at present in force in the
various markets of Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I have been asked
by my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Agriculture to answer this question.
I have received no representations on
this subject and am not aware that there
is such a marked inequality of market
tolls at present in force in Northern Ireland as to warrant or justify legislation.
The circumstances in regard to markets
vary considerably in the different towns,
and it is by no means clear that a uniform
rate of toll would be justifiable or desirable.
In any event, having regard to the
circumstances under which many of these
markets have been constituted, legislation
on the lines indicated by the honourable
and gallant Member would present considerable legal difficulties.

of the answer given by the right hon.
Gentleman, may I ask him has he read

as I have stated in the question, of inequality and anomalies; and, further, is

Error in a Division.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member for
Woodvale (Mr. Nixon) raised a matter
in the House yesterday, which reflected
on the administration of my Department.
I have, therefore, gone carefully into the
matter. I find that the error occurred in
the printing of Hansard, and not in the
Votes of the House. Perhaps the House
will allow me to make the position clear,
as there is obviously some misapprehension. The Votes of the House constitute
the official record of the proceedings of
the House, for which I am personally
responsible, and can be produced as evidence of what actually has taken place
in the House. If, therefore, a mistake
were to occur in a Division list in the
Votes, I should take official action to have
the matter put right the moment my attention was drawn to it. Hansard, on
the other hand, is the verbatim report of
what takes place in the House. As this
verbatim report is produced at very high
pressure while Parliament is sitting in
order that it may be in Members' hands
at the earliest possible moment, it is the
custom for Members to draw the attention
of the Editor of Debates to any inaccuracies, so that they may be corrected in the
reprint. I should like to say that, in
my opinion, the Hansard of this House
is produced with marvellous accuracy.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

Mr. GRANT: In rising to support the
Motion before the House, I would like
to take the opportunity afforded of
offering my sincere congratulations to the
mover and seconder of the Address on
the very capable manner in which they
performed the onerous task allotted to
them. I would also like to join in the
congratulations offered to the Prime
Minister and members of the Cabinet on
having secured such a magnificent building for this Parliament to assemble in.
When the Parliament of Northern Ireland was opened some eleven years ago
by His Majesty the King, the critics,
representing many different political
views, stated that it would not be a lasting Parliament, but, like the building in
which we met in College Green, would
be of a temporary character.
It is with a great deal of satisfaction
that hon. Members on this side of the
House, and I am bound to say some on
the other side of the House, assembled
here on Wednesday last when His Royal
Highness the Prince of Wales declared
this beautiful building open, and when
it was handed over to the custody of the
Prime Minister for all time as the Parliament House of the people of Northern
Ireland. The critics must feel in a very
peculiar state of mind at the present
moment. Some of them felt it so much
that they could not see their way to
attend here when His Royal Highness,
representing the King, came to open our
new buildings; and it appears from the
empty benches on the other side of the
House that they are going to continue
their campaign of boycotting this Parliament. I should like to remind hon.
Members that for the first four or five
years of the Parliament of Northern Ireland we were able to do without their
presence, and we shall try to carry on
if they continue their absence from this
House. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The magnificent reception accorded to
His Royal Highness did not come as a
surprise to the loyal people of Northern
Ireland. But there is one thing we are
all delighted with, and that is, that
through the splendid offices of the Press

realised that there was a force of loyal

Mr. McNEILL: I feel that my first task
in addressing this House to-day is to pay

It gave me a great deal of pleasure to see

Corkey) addressing this House, and adopting the very optimistic tone whch he did.
It also gave me a great deal of pleasure

Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. McNeill]
really must express the sense of pleasure
which I feel at being summoned to sit in
a Parliament adorned with such consummate beauty. It is not the language of
exaggeration to say that this building, in
which we are now assembled, would do
justice to any State in the world, having
regard to its beauty and its magnificence.
It is a great tribute to the architect; it
is a great tribute to those who toiled
specifically to bring it to completion; and,
at the same time, it is a great tribute to
the Noble Lord the Prime Minister-
(hon. Members: Hear, hear)—and other
Members of the Cabinet for having, during the past ten years, exerted their
utmost powers to supply the Parliament
of Northern Ireland with a suitable
habitation.
Coming to the Gracious Speech from
the Throne I feel that it is my duty not
to take too optimistic a note in addressing this House to-day. I feel that we
are confronted with enormous difficulties,
difficulties of the very first magnitude,
and when I review our present position
to-day and compare it with the position.
which existed ten or eleven years ago,
when we first received our Parliamentary
institutions, I feel very dubious as to
whether or not we are in a sounder or
better position than we were at that
time. Look at what has happened.
Every hon. Member of this House from
the Prime Minister downwards knows
that we are living in a state of economic
catastrophe. We, like other countries
in the world, are suffering at the present
time from the almost total stagnation of
trade and industry. A kind of paralysis
has seized upon the whole economic system of the world, and when we assembled
in our little Parliament House in College Green ten years ago not one hon.
Member could have foreseen what was
going to happen. For that reason I say
we are up against enormous difficulties,
political difficulties which I am not going
to mention, and economic and financial
difficulties which I feel it is my duty to
mention and to state frankly to this
House.
Two days ago the noble Lord, the
Prime Minister, stated quite correctly
that since our autonomous life began we
had contributed a sum of £25,000,000 to
the Imperial Exchequer by way of Imperial contribution. That is quite correct, but the noble Lord, the Prime
Minister, did not at the same time inform this House that had it not been
for the generosity of the Imperial Parliament at Westminster we should today have been in the position of debtors
and not of creditors. In other words, if
we had fulfilled and paid that absurd
contribution of almost £8,000,000, which
was imposed upon us by the Act of 1920,
by this time, instead of having contributed £25,000,000 to the Imperial Parliament, we should have contributed
£80,000,000, or in the neighbourhood of
that figure.
And the noble Lord did not state,
although the noble Lord is perfectly well
aware, that year by year this Imperial
contribution is dwindling. I find on
looking up past records that in the first
year of our Parliamentary life we contributed a sum of £6,000,000. Last
year we contributed a sum of £412,000,
and that sum is not an Imperial contribution but, in the words of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, is earmarked
towards the Imperial contribution.
During the present year, according to
the Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock),
our Imperial contribution will amount to
something like £20,000. I feel that it
is my duty to put these facts not merely
before this House but before the public,
because the moral that I am going to
draw is that, as an integral community
here in Northern Ireland, we are not an
asset but a liability so far as the Imperial Parliament is concerned. In that
connection I have fortified myself by
resort to Hansard, volume 13, column
2754, to a statement made by the Minister of Finance on the 14th December of
last year. This is an excerpt from Han-
The Minister said:
sard.
In the earlier stages of our career
we agreed to give a large contribution
towards the Army, the Navy, and the
gigantic debt which is borne by the
United Kingdom, of which we
part. Little by little, as we extended
our servicesmeaning thereby our social servicesare
our expenditure increased automatically, and our contributions to these
services I have mentioned decreased.
That has continued until now our contribution has practically disappeared.
We are a thirty-fifth part of the
United Kingdom, and yet we do not
contribute a single penny to the burdens that are borne by the people of
Great Britain.-(Official Report, 14th
December, 1931, vol. xiii., col. 2754).

only mention it in order to impress upon

Coming to the question of unemployment, which is also mentioned in the
gracious Speech from the Throne, a great
deal has been said about unemployment
in connection with this Government, and
the Government have been severely

Having investigated and read very carefully what the Government have done I
am of the opinion that they have done
their utmost to alleviate the inevitable

a remarkable fact that, out of a total

last year cost us no less a sum than
£3,368,000, and in addition to that sum
of £3,368,000 I find, when I consult the

how the Government could have done

to the Government as well as to all parties
in this House.
In
But there is another aspect of this unemployment problem which fills me with
alarm. Hon. Members are perfectly
aware that since 1926 the parity agreement between Great Britain and
Northern Ireland provides, in certain
events, for certain payments by the
Imperial Parliament towards our Unemployment Fund. It causes me some
misgiving when I learn that those payments are dwindling year by year.
the first year, 1926, we received a sum of
£850,000 from the Imperial Parliament
towards our Unemployment Fund. Last
year we received a sum of £201,000 from
the Imperial Treasury towards our Unemployment Fund; and the estimated
contribution for the present year is only
a sum of £97,000. So that the very

if they have read Hansard or if they have

to maintain the balance of our Unemployment Fund. For every year, up to the
present year, we have borrowed from the
Treasury. Last year we borrowed the
sum of £1,600,000. This year we cannot even borrow and we must maintain
our unemployed out of revenue.
How is that going to be done? What
new source of revenue can we tap? In
reading through the last Budget statement of the Minister of Finance I noticed
that he was of the opinion that the new
import duties levied in Belfast and Derry
would bring in a revenue of £600,000.
I sincerely hope that his wishes will be
fulfilled, but even assuming that they
brought in a revenue of £600,000, how
are we going to maintain this huge army
of unemployed, which we must carry
along with us in the same manner as
every other country in the world at the
present time? Our Unemployment
are

Fund is in debt to the extent of

The Prime Minister dealt on Tuesday
with the question of our railways. He
referred to the plight of the railways and
the need for co-ordination of transport.
I very much doubt if the public fully
realise the services rendered to the community at large by the railway companies,
and I will instance the railway which I
know best, that is, the Belfast and
County Down Railway. Last year they
carried 121,000 tons of goods, 45,000 live
stock, and 3,313,000 passengers, that is
not including 3,700 season ticket holders,
and that without the loss of a passenger.
I will now ask the House to consider the
state of our roads in County Down and to
consider the loss of life and chaos that
would ensue if that railway came to an
end. The traffic would be enormous and
the road cost to the ratepayers incalculable.
There is another side to this question,
and this should interest people who represent labour both on this side of the House
and on the other side. The wages bill
of this company comes to £128,000 per
annum. They employ 925 men. No
man who represents labour wants to see
those people thrown on the dole and,
therefore, the time is coming when the
matter will be urgent, and when the
transport problem will have to be solved.
It will only be solved by co-operation and
co-ordination.
In conclusion, there is one small matter
-it is not really a small matter-I wish
to refer to the note in the gracious
Speech from the Throne regarding our
estimates. I recall the fact that last
year we over-estimated, for when the
Minister of Finance came to open his
Budget he found that our supply services
were all too high and a mistake was made
of £50,000. The revenue was not equal
to the expenditure. What is the lesson
to be learned from that? It is that
before estimating expenditure we should
estimate our revenue, and to do this the
estimates should follow the Budget and
not precede it. At present Parliamentary
control, here and elsewhere, in the
Imperial Parliament is practically nonexistent. The estimates come up and are
passed. Whether or not there is money
enough to meet them the Members have
not the slightest knowledge at all. The
Government certainly have, but after all
is said and done, everyone of us who
votes for the estimate is responsible for
it. So again I think the time is coming
when the financial procedure will probably have to be recast. Before I sit
down may I join the Member for the
University in urging the necessity for
caution and economy in the future.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

sent their produce to the

able to get the best prices obtainable.

believe that if propaganda of that kind

If the Ministry of Agriculture tried I

caused

It is a great shame that these moneylenders should be allowed to use these

24 NOVEMBER 1932
Debate on the Address
Mr. CRAWFORD: For many reasons
which I do not propose to give now, but
so far as my experience goes nationalisation has not proved very satisfactory in
the past.
According to the gracious
Speech the bankruptcy laws are going to
be re-modelled. I thoroughly agree with
that. I sincerely hope the Bill will prevent many of the abuses that have been
possible in the past, and that those who
are trying to make themselves rich at the
expense of the people will be punished in
a very severe and drastic manner. I
notice that county officers and courts are
going to be overhauled. Might I suggest
that the Ministry of Home Affairs could
easily make arrangements to hold
Resident Magistrates' Courts in such a
way that the present number of resident
magistrates could carry out the work
more satisfactorily. It is too bad that
one resident magistrate should be ordered
from one end of the county to the other,
and I am sure an arrangement could be
made whereby two Resident Magistrates'
Courts could be held on one day.
Might I say that I am sorry there is
not more in the King's Speech. If the
law against bookmakers and gambling
dens is strong enough I would like it to
be properly and effectively enforced, and
if the law is not strong enough the
Government should not hesitate to bring
in legislation to strengthen it. People
may say it is not wrong to gamble. I
am not questioning that. A thing may
be right in itself and wrong in its consequences, and I defy any man to say
that betting and gambling are not wrong
in their consequences. If gambling is
wrong in its consequences we should try
to repress it in every way we can.
I
believe the Minister of Home Affairs has
the power to do a great deal more than
he has done, and I contend that those
magistrates who are bringing contempt
on the law, by fining bookmakers only 5/-,
should be struck off the list of magistrates. The owners of property in which
gambling takes place also should be
prosecuted. When it becomes known
that a place is being used as a gambling
den the owner should be proceeded
against. I have often said I would give
Ministers no more powers, but if the
Minister of Home Affairs has not the
power to do what I have suggested I
would give him that power with great
pleasure, and I hope he will exercise it.
I trust that the Government will give
local authorities power to acquire land
for improvements and building purposes
more cheaply and expeditiously than they
are able to do at the present time. At
present, if a local authority wants a
portion of ground for the purpose of
widening a corner or building a school it
is a very expensive matter to get it. I
was talking to a farmer one day and he
thought the farmers were treated very
badly. I confess I led him along that
line, and he said that farming was no
good. I told him I was there to try to
get half an acre of land on which to build
a school. In five minutes that land
gained tremendously in value, and for
that piece of land the committee had to
pay much more than it was worth.
If we
had tried to acquire it compulsorily it would have taken us months
to do it. I sometimes have not a great
admiration for our legal friends, and we
could not have compulsorily acquired that
piece of land without a great deal of legal
costs. The result was that the committee
decided to give more than twice the value
of the land to get it quickly, and even
then we got it more cheaply than we
would have done by compulsory means.
I think the Government should empower
these bodies to acquire land in a much
cheaper manner than is possible at the
present time. It could be done quite
easily by appointing an arbitrator to
decide the value of the land. In conclusion, I appeal to the Government to
make every effort to find out those parts
of the country where the shoe is pinching, and if there are certain districts
where things are not as they should be,
the legislation necessary to put them
right should be introduced and passed.

Distress Committee.
I wish to remind the House, particularly the Opposition, that it is not within.
the power of this Government alone,

to this effort by holding up the gold of

insisting upon Europe paying, paying,

In the Gracious Speech, as well as in

that this Ottawa Conference, as the
Minister of Finance has said, has come
thirty years too late. The Ottawa Conference, and its results, must necessarily
be viewed as a beginning and, in my

I also recognise the fact, in connection
with these alterations in tariffs, that not
merely is half a loaf better than no bread,
but that a very important principle has
been agreed to by the Dominions. I refer
to the fact, as stated in the White Paper,
that the
Dominions are to revise the protective duties as soon as practicable on
the basis that United Kingdom producers will have full opportunity of
reasonable competition, having regard

That appears to me to be a very valuable
principle. If that principle is applied
in the near future it seems to me it is

efficient and which can still maintain
themselves, though it is very hard to do

City of Derry, as hon. Members know,

for a revival of shipbuilding in a place

Looking at the figures some little time
ago I noticed that in 1913, the year before the war, out of the total number of
ships then being built in the world-968
-no fewer than 508 were actually being

HOUSE OF COMMONS

built in Great Britain and Northern

the total ships being built in the world were

And it is under those circumstances that

Might I make this suggestion for the

it may be impossible actually to give a
direct subsidy for the building of ships,

in conjunction with the Imperial Government. I recognise the difficulty of
applying a subsidy to any particular industry, but, as many hon. Members have
noticed, within the last six months Germany, as to the bankruptcy of which one
hears so much as one reads in the daily
Press, has not merely completed the two
fastest liners in the world, but she is also
subsidising the breaking up of ships. If
we cannot get new ships to fill the stocks
in our great shipbuilding yards, surely
with the assistance of the Imperial Government something might be done to
assist those ship-owning and shipbuilding
companies who have a fleet laid up and
literally rusting away.
Every person interested in the shipbuilding trade recognises the fact that
there are ships totalling, I think, nearly
2,000,000 tons laid up in our various
ports and harbours, and that the vast
number of those ships will never take
the sea again. They will be completely
out of date and entirely uneconomic.
And what bankrupt Germany can do
might be done by the greatest shipowning and shipbuilding country in the
world. I would respectfully suggest to
the Government that something on those
lines might possibly alleviate, at least
temporarily, this depression in our shipbuilding yards.
I have nothing to add to the speeches.
that have already been made with regard
to the other matters dealt with in the
gracious Speech from the Throne. I
merely would add an expression of hope
to those expressions which have come
from both sides of the House that we have
at length turned the corner, or are at
least turning the corner, and that this
wave of industrial depression may at long
last be at an end.

in the year 1928 there were 134,000

135 Debate on the Address

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Debate on the Address
[Mr. Minford]
During the past five years the farmers
have passed through a most deplorable
time, and I do hope that this Ottawa
Conference has laid a foundation upon
which the Imperial Parliament and ourselves will be able to build in a way which
will speedily bring prosperity to our
farmers. When you consider that
147,000 people are working on the land
in Northern Ireland surely they are entitled to a fair crack of the whip. As
the hon. Member for North Antrim (Sir
Robert Lynn) said yesterday, other trades
have got a 20 per cent. tariff to protect
them, but we are left at the mercy of
foreign competition.
In conclusion, I may say that the
Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock) and
the Junior Whip (Sir Basil Brooke)
deserve credit for going to Ottawa with
the British delegation, but I can assure
you that if it had not been that the
farmers of Great Britain and Northern
Ireland took these firm steps the prospect
for the farmers to-day would have been
very poor. It certainly may help them
in two years to come, but the position was
so bad that they were unable to wait for
those two years. What they want to-day
is cash for their goods. What they
demand is a fair price for their products.
If you give us that we ask for nothing
more. I am not unmindful of the great
boon derating has been, and on behalf of
the farmers of Ulster I am most thankful
to the Government for that, but the price
of potatoes is down to 25s per ton, the
price of oats is as low as £4 10s per ton,
flax is a thing of the past, and the price
of cattle has dropped to a lower level
than at any time during the last forty
years.
I have painted a black picture in
regard to agriculture, but I hope this is
the last time I will have to employ such
a pessimistic tone. I am perfectly
certain that the Members of this House
are willing and anxious to do all they can
for agriculture; but sometimes I am
afraid some of the representatives in this
House do not realise the darkness of the
outlook. When I read the King's Speech
delivered at the opening of the Imperial
Parliament, I observed that for the first
time one half of it was devoted to the
deplorable state of agriculture. I believe
that, after all, you do realise that agriculture is the basic industry of our
country. If agriculture is prosperous,
then the other industries will be prosperous too; certainly the prosperity of
agriculture will not retard the prosperity
of other industries. I would be delighted
to see shipbuilding and the linen trade
enjoying their old prosperity. No man
would take a greater pride in seeing the
looms working and the shipbuilding yards
fully occupied than I would.
As the representative of an agricultural
constituency, however, I must point out
that the agricultural community looks to
this House to help it during the period
of depression through which it is passing.
Agriculture is passing through a time
without parallel, and shipbuilding is in
the same straits. For the greater part
of our shipbuilding and linen orders we
have to depend upon the foreigner, but so
far as agriculture is concerned we have a
market at our own door, and yet we do
not contribute nearly one half of its
requirements. Foreigners should not be
allowed to send in their produce at a
price below the economic cost of production. Why should our men be unemployed and our people be living on foreign
food? We want to see our men employed
and our fields filled with bumper crops.
When that is accomplished Northern
Ireland will have regained its prosperity.

REGULATIONS OF MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION.
1. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether the regulations of the
Ministry, dated 4th instant, and referred
to in the Votes, Proceedings and Records
of this House of the 23rd instant as
having been laid upon the Table, create
a right on the part of transferors
and former managers of schools to make
recommendation for appointment to
school committees; whether this right is
not in contravention of the Education
Acts; and whether the Ministry have
power to issue regulations contravening
Section 3 of the Education Act (Northern Ireland), 1923, as amended by
Section 2 of the Education Act (Northern Ireland), 1930.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): These
regulations do not, in the Ministry's
opinion, create any new rights of the kind
referred to in the question, such right
being already implied in the language
of the Section; the object of the regulations is to define the procedure necessary to give full effect to the provisions
of the Act in this particular, and these
have been made under the powers conferred upon the Ministry to that effect
in Section 99 of the Education Act (Northern Ireland), 1923.
The answer to the last part of the
question is in the negative.
POSITION OF MICHAEL MCGRATH,
SCHOOL TEACHER, DROMARA.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he is aware that
Michael McGrath, of Mahagoot, Sessiagh, Dromara, Co. Tyrone, was a
school teacher for 19 years and 7 months,
serving last in Cranagh, Plumbridge,
Omagh, and retired in September, 1907,
owing to mental weakness; whether his
condition was certified by Dr. Evans; and
whether he is prepared to pay him either
a retiring gratuity under the old system
or a disablement pension.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I am aware of the case to
which the hon. Member refers.
The position is that no evidence has
ever been produced that Mr. McGrath's
resignation in 1907 was due to his having
become mentally incapacitated for duty
while serving as a teacher. In point of
fact, Mr. McGrath intimated in October,
1907, that he was seeking re-employment,
and he did subsequently obtain nonpensionable employment in three schools
as a substitute teacher between 1907 and
1910.
In 1927, a medical certificate was produced to my Ministry to the effect that
the teacher was permanently incapacitated from carrying out his duties as a
result of an accident in 1910. In that
year he was serving in a non-pensionable
capacity, and, therefore, the certificate
was useless for pension purposes. The
certificate from Dr. Evans to which the
hon. Member refers, though dated 3rd
September of the present year, reached
me only on Saturday last, and is couched
in such guarded language that it is
obviously useless for pension purposes.
In the circumstances, the hon. Member will understand that whatever my
sympathies may be for the present unfortunate position of this ex-teacher, it
is not in my power to award either
gratuity or pension.

3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the number of working hours per week and wages
paid to the outside staff of Stormont
Estate.
Mr. POLLOCK: The ground staff on
the Stormont Estate work 44 hours per
week, and are paid a wage of 35s.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman is the Government satisfied that this is keeping up
the standard rate of wage for the class
of work done; whether he is aware that
rangers in the public parks in the city
of Belfast receive £2 6s 3d for a 44-hour
week, and whether, in view of that, he
is prepared to reconsider the question of
wages paid to the workmen on the Stormont Estate?
Mr. POLLOCK: I am not prepared
to admit the accuracy or otherwise of my
hon. Friend's statement, but, perhaps,
if I read a very short sketch of the
circumstances under which the arrangement was made it may satisfy the hon.
Member. The casual staff employed at
the outset on the Stormont Estate in the
work of seed sowing was paid at the rate
of 1s hour.
per
This in a full week gave
the men a wage of £2 4s, but as they
were paid only for time actually worked,
the weekly amount earned was reduced
if the weather or other cause interfered
with the operation of seed sowing. When
the rate of pay for the regular ground
staff came to be settled two alternatives
presented themselves, first, to continue
payment at an hourly rate of 1s, or to
fix a weekly rate which, while taking
into account the possibility of the men
not being fully employed from time to
time, would secure them against constant
fluctuation in wages. It was finally
decided to adopt the latter course, and
the weekly wage was fixed at 35s, payable
generally to agricultural labourers in
the district. The three gardners absorbed
into the staff from the Cabinet Secretariat, are paid a little more highly,
namely, 45s, 38s 9d, and 41s 8d per week.
With regard to the wage of the ordinary
labourers or rangers in the Stormont
Estate, we regard 35s as a natural and
proper remuneration.
Mr. BEATTIE: In view of the unsatisfactory answer to my question I

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS

HOUSE OF COMMONS
ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW
INDUSTRIES.
8. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Prime Minister whether he can state what
steps the Government have taken to
secure new industries since the passing
of the Industries (Development) Act, and
whether he can state the names and
addresses of any firms who have applied
to the Government for grants of free
sites.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): I have been asked by
the Prime Minister to reply.
Since the passing of the Act to which
the hon. Member refers, my Ministry
has endeavoured to make known its provisions both in the United Kingdom and
overseas by means of the dissemination
of publicity in various forms and through
various agencies.
Not only has publicity been given to
the fact that the Government is prepared to place sites on a rent-free basis,
at the disposal of industrialists and that
local authorities are similarly empowered
to grant freedom from local rates, but
copies of the regulations governing the
proposed grants have been sent to all
parties known to be interested.
I may
also mention that the occasion afforded
by the ceremonial opening of our Parliament Buildings was used to communicate a note on free sites for industry to
all correspondents of the cross-Channel
Press attending that function.
Although a number of inquiries have
been received, up to the present only two
concrete applications have been lodged
with the Ministry. The hon. Member
will appreciate, however, that such applications must of necessity remain confidential, at least until such time as a
definite decision has been reached as to
the making of a grant.
Mr. HENDERSON: In view of the
Prime Minister's statement over a year
ago that there were to be free sites, I
think something should be done, and I
hope that the right hon. Gentleman,
who speaks on behalf of the Prime Minister, will not let this matter drop. The
Government should take some definite
action-
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: The hon.
Gentleman must confine himself to asking a supplementary question.
Mr. HENDERSON: I would like to
ask if it is the intention of the Government to take some more effective steps
than advertising in the cross-Channel
papers. The Government should take
more drastic action if they want new
industries started in Northern Ireland.
RELIEF WORK FOR FARM
LABOURERS.
9. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he is aware that a
large number of farm labourers are now
unemployed, and what means, if any, he
proposes to take to relieve their distress;
and whether he proposes to organise such
relief work by repairing lanes, constructing footwalks along roads which have
none, reclaiming turbary wastes and
planting trees on mountains.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I have been
asked by my right. hon. Friend, the
Minister of Labour, to reply to this
question.
more
My Ministry has no information to
show that there are fewer permanent
agricultural labourers employed than in
previous years. On the contrary, the
increase in the area of land under tillage
this year would indicate that
labourers were required. Owing to the
agricultural depression throughout
Northern Ireland, however, farmers are
doing their utmost to reduce expenses,
and, as a result, there is, no doubt, some
decrease in the employment of casual
labour.
In reply to the second part of the
question, I would refer the hon. Member to the scheme operated by my
Ministry for the relief of unemployment
in rural areas. This scheme has been in
operation since the year 1929, and provides for grants and loans to farmers for
land improvement works, such as land
drainage, the improvement of ditches and
watercourses, the improvement of river
and sea embankments, the making of
farm roads, fencing and agricultural
improvements generally.
The Ministry's scheme of re-afforestation, by means of which 1,000 acres are
planted with trees each year, also provides employment for men in clearing
the ground, fencing, drainage, planting,
and other forestry operations.

Legislative Procedure Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Mr. POLLOCK: Hon. Members will
find a brief explanation of the object of
this Bill embodied in the printed note
accompanying the Bill. I propose to
amplify this slightly.
Under Sections 6 and 9 of the Northern Ireland (Miscellaneous Provisions)
Act, 1932, which was recently passed by
the Imperial Parliament, the Parliament
of Northern Ireland may, in certain
cases, legislate on matters which would
otherwise have been outside its powers, as
specified in the Government of Ireland
Act, 1920, provided that the consent of
the Treasury, the Board of Trade, or
the Commissioners of Crown Lands, as
the case may be, is previously obtained.
The Act provides that a statement in a
Northern Ireland Act that the necessary
consent has been given is conclusive
evidence that the consent has, in fact,
been obtained.
155 Legislative Procedure Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading
[Mr. Pollock]
The present Bill is designed to regulate the procedure in connection with the
insertion in a Northern Ireland Bill of
an intimation that the consent of one of
the above-named Departments has been
given. It has been found necessary to
legislate to this end owing to the fact
that the Imperial Department concerned
cannot give its consent till the Bill has
reached its final form, whereas the Chairman of Committees here may decline to
let the Bill proceed through its stages
here unless the Imperial consent is first
produced. Thus a position of stalemate
might well arise.
This Bill will prevent such a situation.
It proposes in Section 1 that where the
Clerk of the Parliaments of Northern
Ireland certifies that the consent of the
Treasury, the Board of Trade, or the
Commissioners of Crown Lands has been
obtained to any Bill of the Parliament
of Northern Ireland, the preamble to
the Bill shall state that this consent has
been obtained. Sub-Clause (2) of
Clause 1 of the Bill then provides that
the words of this statement may appear
in the preamble of a Bill at any of
its stages in either this House or at
Westminster, but that they shall not be
treated as part of the Bill until the certificate of the Clerk of the Parliaments
has been duly given.
Thus the Bill, while not affecting the
powers of either House to discuss, amend,
or reject a Bill at any stage, secures that
the recital of the statutory consent may
be inserted in a Bill independently of
the ordinary stages of legislative procedure, provided that the Clerk of the
Parliaments certifies that the appropriate
consent has been given.
I may add that it was carefully considered whether the same object could not
be achieved by the amendment of Standing Orders in this House and at Westminster, but the conclusion was reached
that the method now proposed is more
effective. I beg to move.

PARLIAMENTARY
This Bill, which is mainly of a
technical character, is based on the
Imperial Act, which received the Royal
Assent on the 24th March, 1932, and is
designed to give effect to the Convention
held at Geneva in July, 1931, for the
purpose of supplementing the provisions
of previous International Opium Conventions and to provide for the more
rigorous control of the traffic in dangerous
drugs.
The Imperial Act, like all other
Imperial Dangerous Drug Acts which
have been passed since the date of the
principal Act in 1920, applies to
Northern Ireland only in so far as it
relates to matters with respect to which
the Parliament of Northern Ireland has
not power to legislate, namely, matters
affecting import and export. In order,
therefore, that the law in Northern
Ireland may continue to conform with
that in Great Britain, it is necessary to
introduce this Measure into Parliament
corresponding in its provisions to the
Imperial Act in so far as these relate to
matters which are within the legislative
competence of Northern Ireland.
Clause (1) of the Bill is to the same
effect as Section I of the United Kingdom Act. It enacts a revised list of
drugs to which Part III of the 1920 Act
is to apply, and is achieved by substituting a new section for Section 8 of
the Act of 1920. Two special preparations, commonly known as codeine and
dionin, are excluded from this provision
in order to be dealt with by Sub-Section
3 of Clause 2 of the present Bill.
Sub-Sections 1 and 2 of Clause (2) deal
with new derivates of opium or the coca
leaf. The method is by prohibition of
such derivatives, followed by a power to
lift the ban if they are proved to be
scientifically or medically valuable and,
at the same time, to obtain from the
League of Nations a report whether or
not the drug is one of a habit-forming
character. Sub-Section 1 follows the
corresponding United Kingdom enactment, except that under the proviso the
Governor of Northern Ireland, instead of
making an Order of substantive effect,
merely declares that His Majesty has
made such an Order, and thereupon the
Sub-Section will cease to apply. Sub-
Section 2 enables the Governor to make
the necessary Orders in Council, where
His Majesty has done so upon the result
of communications received from the
League of Nations, and Sub-Section 3, as
already stated, follows the United Kingdom Act, enabling codeine and dionin,
the drugs excepted from the amended
Section 8 of the 1920 Act, to be brought
into Part III thereof. This Clause has
been included in the Bill because the
United Kingdom Act, although it contains a corresponding provision referring
to the United Kingdom, contains also a
provision to the effect that the Act is not
to extend to Northern Ireland, except in
relation to matters outside the powers of
the Northern Ireland Parliament.
I now come to Clause (3) of the Bill.
The United Kingdom Act of 1923 contains two provisions creating offences in
Great Britain, which depend for their
definition upon the state of law existing
in countries outside Great Britain whose
Governments are enforcing the various
International Conventions for the suppression of traffic in dangerous drugs.
These provisions are as follow:-
(a) A provision giving to Justices of
the Peace powers of search and seizure
as respects documents connected with
transactions or intended transactions
outside Great Britain which were, or
would be if carried out, offences against
corresponding laws in the place outside.
Great Britain;
(b) A provision making a person
guilty of an offence against the Act of
1920 "who in Great Britain aids, abets,
Dangerous Drugs Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Hanna]
counsels, or procures the commission,
in any place outside Great Britain, of
any offence punishable under the provisions of any corresponding law in
force in that place."
An Act similar to the United Kingdom
Act of 1923 was passed by the Northern
Ireland Parliament in 1924 (14 & 15 Geo.
5, c. 4). The Northern Ireland Act,
however, did not reproduce the provisions
as to offences against corresponding laws,
because the question of the constitutional
power to do so seemed to require a fuller
consideration than was at that time
feasible. That question has now been
fully discussed with the Home Office,
London, and that Office and the various
legal advisers concerned are in agreement
that provisions similar to the United
Kingdom enactments of 1923 should find
a place in the present Bill. Such provisions are, accordingly, embodied in this
Clause.
Clause (4) enables Orders or Declarations made by the Governor in Council
to be varied or revoked by subsequent
Orders or Declarations, and follows
Section 4 of the United Kingdom Act
of 1932, which gives similar power to His
Majesty in Council.
Clause (5) follows the previous Northern Ireland precedents, namely, Section
3 of the Dangerous Drugs and Poisons
(Amendment) Act (N.I.), 1924, and
Section 6 of the Dangerous Drugs Act
(N.I.), 1925. Sub-Section 2 is in effect
a saving for the provisions of the United
Kingdom Code, which apply
to
"excepted" matters in Northern Ireland.
Sub-Section 3 will enable uniformity of
administration to be achieved as between
Great Britain and Northern Ireland. I
beg to move.

Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I beg
to
"That the Bill
move,
be now
read a Second time." The musk rat
or musquash, an animal valued on
account of its fur, is a menace to the
agricultural and other interests in any
country in which it becomes established
in a natural state. The animal burrows
under river and canal banks, roads,
bridges, and railway embankments, thus
seriously undermining these structures.
Very serious damage has been done in
Central Europe by these animals, and in
Germany the Government is spending
considerable sums of money in endeavouring to eradicate the musk rat. Numbers
of these animals are, it is understood, at
large in England and Scotland, and in
the latter country in particular, the
position has, I understand, given ground
for some anxiety. For example, the
musk rats have burrowed under the banks
of the River Allan and are also believed
to inhabit at least two of the main rivers
-the Tay and the Forth. I am informed
that in America the damage done by the
floods at St. Louis some years ago was
greatly aggravated because the banks of
the river had already been undermined
by these pests. A feature of the animal
is that it multiplies with extraordinary
rapidity. I will quote the following from
a recent issue of the "Glasgow Herald":
The trouble began in Central Europe
near to Posen in the year 1905, when
three pairs of rats escaped from
captivity. What is the position to-day?
In the past twenty-five years millions
of musk rats have been killed, yet
Germany to-day, with all her skilled
scientists, can only hope to keep the
pests within reasonable limits by persistent trapping and so protect important waterways, such as the Rhine-
Danube Canal, by the exercise of
ceaseless vigilance.
The Measure before you takes power
to regulate the importation and keeping

It will be observed that Clause 8 gives

were

With regard to the cost of adminstration, I am hopeful that the passage of this
Measure will enable us to secure continued immunity from the musk rat as a
pest, and if this anticipation should prove

Cabinet Ministers and Directorships.
Mr. HENDERSON: I beg to move:
"That in the opinion of this House
Cabinet Ministers should resign all
directorships of public companies during their term of office."
It is with regret I bring forward this
Motion. We had a good example in this
House to-day of the way the Government follows in the footsteps of the
British Parliament. Now the position in
Northern Ireland, I regret to say, is this.
I believe there is not another Parliament
in the world would tolerate this, and I am
absolutely certain that the British Parliament, which we try to imitate, would not
allow Cabinet Ministers to remain
directors of private companies when they
accept that office. You may remember
the discussion that took place in the
British Parliament when Mr. Winston
Churchill was brought to book for writing
for various newspapers throughout the
world. We have seen it stated that when
Mr. Winston Churchill was a Cabinet
Minister in the British Parliament he had
to give up an income of anything from
£20,000 to £30,000 a year, which he
derived from writing for newspapers and
magazines. Was that a right or a wrong
thing for the British Parliament to insist
upon? When Sir Robert Horne became
a Cabinet Minister he was a director of
number of companies, and those
directorships brought him in from £20,000
to £25,000 a year. He had to give up
those directorships before he could take
up office as a British Cabinet Minister.
Is the Mother of Parliaments rights in
doing that, or is she wrong? With all
due respect. I say that the British Parliment did the right thing.

The PRIME MINISTER: I trust the
House will not in any way be influenced
to pass this Resolution. Indeed I hope,
before I have finished, that the hon.
Member will decide to withdraw
Motion. When the Government of
Northern Ireland was established this
question naturally, with many others of
importance, arose. After very careful
consideration, so far as I was concerned,
I came to the conclusion that it was
essential in a small community like ours
to enlist the very best brains in the community to help us. We did not wish to
have "has beens'; we did not wish to
have those who had no experience in
regard to matters of the greatest concern
affecting the whole of Ulster's business
and agricultural community.
I can
safely say, standing here at the end of
some eleven and a half years, that I know
of no single instance where any of my
right hon. Friends, who happen to be
directors of companies, found that their
ministerial duties clashed in any way with
the carrying on of the business which they
established or which had been established
by those who went before them.
It has to be borne in mind that,
whereas, in Great Britain you have a
population of some forty-five millions,
from which Members of Parliament are
chosen, we here have only one and a
quarter millions and, whereas, in the
Imperial Parliament there are some 700
Members, here there are only 52, and
whoever happens for the time being to be
Prime Minister is bound to select his
Cabinet Ministers from those who are
returned to this House and to the Senate.
Therefore, the choice here naturally is
much more limited than it is on the other
side of the water. It is found of great
benefit to the Government to have real
business brains in it-such as are
possessed by the Minister of Finance to
an
extent that is hardly appreciated.
Where even in this House to-day, without
casting any aspersion on any Member,
could we get a man who could conduct
the finances of our country so faithfully
and so satisfactorily as in the case of my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock)? (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Are we to say
because he is a director of a company-
Mr. NIXON: Several companies.
The PRIME MINISTER: The reason
why, I presume, he is a director of
several companies is because the public.
trust him. (Hon. Member: Hear, hear.)
It is because they want the best men.
We also want the best men, and I think
in the case of anyone who is making a
large sum of money outside the Government altogether in years to come it might
be difficult to get them to drop that
business and ask them to come in here
and give us the benefit of their ripe
experience. I came to the conclusion
some eleven years ago that Ulster would
be the sufferer if we confined ourselves
only to those who were too old for business, or so young that they were not
qualified to act. I doubt very much if
the hon. Member is correct in saying that
this is a principle which is carried out
throughout the Dominions. I believe I
am right in saying that the Dominions
are only too anxious, like ourselves, to
have the best of their business men in
their various administrative departments.
I doubt if the hon. Member is correct,
but my information at the moment is
such that I cannot contradict him. I
believe from my experience and I have
been in every Dominion Parliament and
in one of the Federal Parliaments in the

But I think it right for me to state
the policy of the Government in regard to
the use of the Union Jack, which we
loyalists all revere. The policy is that on
all public buildings which are used and
occupied by the Government and the
police the flag is always flown on National
holidays. But what is asked by certain
individuals is that all local authorities,
whether they are loyal or disloyal, should
be compelled to fly the Union Jack. I
ask have those people taken the trouble
really seriously to consider what such a
step means. To suggest that grants might
be withheld from local authorities if they
did not fly the Union Jack savours to me
very much of paying a man to appear to
be loyal.
I may be old fashioned, but I have been
brought up with the idea that it was a
privilege and not a penalty to fly the
Union Jack. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I was brought up to believe that
it is the duty of every loyalist to respect
and revere the flag, and take all the
necessary steps to ensure that the flag
would never be placed in such a position
that it would be reviled.
I could understand people coming to
the Government and demanding that the
flag should not be flown unless there was a
guarantee given that such flag would
receive respect. I can understand that,
but I cannot understand anyone suggesting that the Government should compel
disloyal people to fly the emblem of our
country. After all you cannot make a

individuals' heads. The Admiralty, as

HOUSE OF COMMONS

Wednesday, 30th November, 1932.
The House met at Three of the Clock.
The Clerk at the Table informed the
House of the unavoidable absence of Mr.
Speaker from this day's sitting.
Whereupon Mr. MOLES, the Chairman of Ways and Means, proceeded to
the Table, and, after Prayers, took the
Chair as DEPUTY-SPEAKER, pursuant to the Standing Order.
Paper Presented to Parliament.
Ministry of Home Affairs:
Report on the Administration of Home
Office Services, 1931. (By Act.)
Oral Answer to Question.
ROAD FUND AND UNEMPLOY-
MENT RELIEF.
Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state the
total amount paid from the Road Fund
since April, 1931, for work in relief of
unemployment.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): The total
amount paid out of the Road Fund from
the 1st April, 1931, to the 30th November, 1932, in respect of works on roads
promoted for the relief of unemployment
is £102,884. No payments have been
made in respect of any works other than
road works.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I would like to ask
the Parliamentary Secretary whether the
grants referred to were not paid in the
past by the Minister of Labour; whether
they are now being paid out of the Road
Fund, and, if so, has this House
authorised such payments?
Mr. HANNA: I must ask the hon.
Gentleman to give me notice of that
question.
KING'S SPEECH.
GOVERNOR'S ANSWER TO THE
ADDRESS.
The PRIME MINISTER (at the Bar)
reported that His Grace the Governor,
having been attended with the Address
of 29th November, has been pleased to
give the following answer:
I have read with great satisfaction the
expression of your thanks for the Speech
with which I opened the present Session
of Parliament.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Transitional Payments (Determination
of Need) [Money].
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
(Mr. Moles in the Chair.)
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient-
(a) to make provision that, in determining under the Unemployment
Insurance (Economy) (No. 2) Order
(Northern Ireland), 1931, questions as
to whether the circumstances of applicants for transitional payments are
such that, whilst unemployed, they are
in need of such payments, the following rules shall be complied with:-
(i) wounds or disability pensions
(as enumerated in section sixteen of
the Finance Act, 1919) which are
taken into account, shall be treated
as if they were reduced by one half;
(ii) weekly payments by way of
compensation under the enactments
relating to workmen's compensation
in force in the United Kingdom,
which are taken into account, shall
be treated as if they were reduced
by one half;
(iii) money and investments
treated as capital assets and taken
into account shall, in so far as the
value of all such money and investments considered in the aggregate
does not exceed twenty-five pounds,
be disregarded, and, in so far as that
value exceeds that amount but does
not exceed three hundred pounds, be
treated as equivalent to a weekly
income of one shilling for every complete twenty-five pounds;
Transitional Payments-
Committee
30 NOVEMBER 1932
(iv) in taking into account the
value to any person of any interest
in the dwelling-house in which he
resides, any sum which might be
obtained by him by selling or by
borrowing money upon the security
of that interest shall be disregarded;
(v) any benefit under the enactments relating to national health
insurance in force in the United
Kingdom shall not be taken into
account except so far as the benefit
exceeds seven shillings and sixpence
a week;
and to authorise the expenditure, out
of moneys provided by Parliament, of
such expenses as may be incurred by
reason of the provisions aforesaid.".
(Governor's recommendation signified.
-Mr. Barbour).
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): I beg to move the Resolution
standing in my name, as a necessary precedent to the presentation of a Bill, which
is intended to standardise in certain
important directions the methods of
assessment to be adopted by public
assistance committees throughout Northern Ireland in determining the amount
which they will recommend for transitional payments to the various claimants.
The Bill will be little more than the
embodiment of the Resolution, and will
be almost identical in terms with an Act
which has just received the Royal
Assent in Great Britain.
I shall leave it to my right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Labour, to explain in
detail, after the Motion is put from the
Chair, the precise effect of these arrangements. In regard to the effect on the
Exchequer, which is my more immediate
concern, it is impossible to say at the
moment precisely what the financial
effect will be, but it is expected to be
small in comparison with the cost of transitional payments as a whole which, for
the present year, is estimated at £845,000.
As hon. Members are aware, this type of
unemployment expenditure now falls on
the Exchequer instead of the Unemployment Fund. As a rough guide, I should
place the maximum expenditure, consequential on this Resolution, at a figure
of £10,000.

a
there is a doubt in the minds of claimants

On the contrary, I feel, speaking generally, that they have acted in a most

believe, therefore, that it is one of the

always to be found coming forward
willingly and voluntarily in order to discharge duties of this character.
Transitional Payments-
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
The public assistance committees, as
I have said, have a difficult task, and
there has been one form of criticism which
the Bill is intended to meet, that is in
certain essential matters there has been
some lack of uniformity, owing to the
scheme, as it existed in the past, permitting of inequalities in administration,
which is always objectionable and gives.
cause for justifiable criticism and dissatisfaction. The Bill, in connection with
which this Money Resolution is submitted,
will meet that criticism, and in connection
with certain essential features of the
scheme it will lay down rules for the
guidance and, in fact, for the control of
public assistance committees, which, I
feel, will ensure that equality of administration which is desirable.
In future public assistance committees
will ignore at least 50 per cent. of a
disability pension or workman's compensation allowance, or they can ignore the
whole or any part of the balance they
may think necessary in any particular
case. They will be controlled as regards
50 per cent., and they will be left a
discretionary power as regards the other
50 per cent. In the case of savings,
statutory protection will be given to
claimants whose assets do not exceed £300.
The first £25 will be disregarded, and
each subsequent complete £25 will be
treated as the equivalent of a weekly income of 1s. At the present the committees could insist on all savings being
taken into consideration in connection
with transitional payments, and this
statutory safeguard which is going to be
given to claimants gives a very considerable concession in order to meet the
situation.
A dwelling-house will also be disregarded if lived in by the claimant, and
the Public Assistance Committees will
also ignore in future at least 7s 6d of
any health insurance benefit that is paid.
These statutory protections will extend
not only to the income and savings of
claimants for transitional payments, but
also to the income and savings of members of the household which fall to be
reviewed for the purpose of assessing the
claimant's need. It is very difficult to
arrive at an estimate of what the cost of
these concessions will mean, but it is estimated that £10,000 per annum will cover
the liability. The Bill itself will be a
temporary Bill expiring at the end of
June next, but as hon. Members know,
this whole problem of unemployment
insurance is receiving a great deal of
attention, not only by the Imperial
Government, but by our Government
here, and it is the intention of both
Governments to introduce Bills dealing
with many features of outstanding importance relating to unemployment insurance.

Mr. POLLOCK: The subject matter of
this Bill falls naturally into two divisions,
and by reference to the draft of the
Measure which is in the hands of hon.
Members, it will be seen that Clauses 1-4
deal with the administration of the Stormont Estate, while Clause 5 deals with
the acquisition and disposal of land for
the public service generally. The Bill
is almost entirely administrative in
character and is simple in its language
and objects and requires no elaborate
explanation on my part.
The Ministry of Finance has been
advised that in order that it may be in
a position to regulate the use of the
Stormont Estate by the general public,
it must be armed with certain statutory
powers for the purpose, and the principal
object of this Bill is to confer the
necessary powers on the Ministry of
Finance. Similar provisions have been
enacted by the Imperial Parliament in
the various Parks Regulation Acts,
which empower His Majesty's Commissioners of Works to regulate parks
under their control, such as Bushy Park,
Hampton Court, and other such places.
Clause 1 of the Measure empowers the
Ministry of Finance to make regulations.
governing the admission of the public to
the Stormont Estate, and specifying the
times when the public may be admitted
and the parts of the Estate to which they
can have access. The regulations may
also make such provision as
may be
necessary for securing proper supervision
of the Estate, the prevention of any
abuse by the public of the privileges
afforded them, and also to take care that
those who offend against their interests
are brought to book, and in order that
adequate publicity may be given to the
regulations it is enacted that they must be
conspicuously displayed in suitable places
on the Estate. Any regulations made
under this Bill must be laid before each
House of Parliament, and if either House
resolves that any regulation shall be
annulled
Mr. POLLOCK: These rangers may,

ranger." I hope hon. Members do not

Clause 3 provides that prosecutions and
the recovery of penalities under the Bill
shall be governed by the Summary
Jurisdiction (Ireland) Acts, as also any
appeals against convictions for offences
under the Bill. Any penalties recovered

or any servant of the Ministry apart from
the Bill, and provides that any powers
conferred by the Bill are to be in addition
to and not in derogation of any such
existing powers.
Clause 5 provides for the acquisition.
and disposal of land generally for the
public service. The Ministry of Finance,
as successors in Northern Ireland to the
Commissioners of Public Works in Ireland,
have under the existing law the control

It has been found, however, that the

the Irish Commissioners in connection
with the disposal, as distinct from the
acquisition, of such land, are inadequate
and are not, in fact, as wide as those
vested in the corresponding British Department.
that regulation immediately
becomes void.
Clause 2 provides that uniformed

with all the powers of police constables.

week!
Moreover, in some cases the

which hold land under certain Statutory

The Clause, therefore, proposes to confer

merely to acquire but also to dispose of

(1) The Ministry of Agriculture may

keeping within Northern Ireland of any
animal of the species designated Fiber

absolutely.

My opinions are supported by a section of

In one or two years those animals that

miles. To my mind it is far better to
prohibit them altogether.

The House met at Three of the Clock.

Speaker from this day's sitting.

ABSTENTION OF MEMBERS OF
PARLIAMENT.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Finance whether Members of Parliament who absent themselves from this
House, thereby disfranchising their constituents, are entitled to draw their Parliamentary allowances.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The conditions under which
Members of the House of Commons are
entitled to draw their Parliamentary
allowance are set forth in the Resolution
of this House, dated 29th March, 1923,
which reads as follows:

CADETSHIPS FOR THE R.U.C.
3. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state how
the recent vacancies in cadetships for
the Royal Ulster Constabulary were
filled; whether applicants were invited to
present themselves for examination, and
if not, why this couse was not adopted.
Mr. HANNA: Two vacancies for
cadets in the Royal Ulster Constabulary
arose early this year, and it was considered necessary, in the public interest,
that they should be immediately filled.
It was accordingly decided to fill the
appointments by selection from the list of
applicants already before the Ministry
and Police Authorities.
Having regard to the fact that eligible
and suitable candidates were available,
it was not considered necessary to make
these appointments on the basis of
examination.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Arising out of the
hon. and learned Gentleman's reply may
I ask him what special qualification the
last two candidates appointed had for
such a position, and whether it is not a
fact that the only two qualifications one
of them had was, first, that he was a
Bachelor of Science and Engineering and,
secondly, that his people were personae
gratae with the Government,
Mr. HANNA: Both gentlemen
appointed for these two offices satisfied
the Minister of Home Affairs and the
Inspector-General that they were, and
proved themselves to be, excellent and
suitable for the positions they now hold.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Further arising out of
the hon. and learned Gentleman's reply,
can he give the House this assurance that
any further appointments to cadetships
will first of all be duly advertised and
applicants selected entirely on their
merits?
Mr. HANNA: I am not prepared to
give an undertaking that applicants will
be appointed as a result of advertising.
As to the second part of the supplementary question, that has always been
the guiding principle in the making of
appointments under the State.
Mr. NIXON: Is it not a fact that the
father of one of these candidates got a
bogus job under the Northern Government?
Mr. HANNA: No, that is not a fact.
Mr. NIXON: It is a fact.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it a fact that duly
qualified members of the R.U.C. do not
get the opportunity to go in for the
examinations for cadetship in the
R.U.C.?
Mr. HANNA: No, by arrangement
officers of the R.U.C. are now taken in
equal proportion from cadets and from
members of the Force.

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): : During the
period, 1st September, 1932, to 26th
November, 1932, approximately 20,737
tons of potatoes were exported from

During the months of September and
October, 1932, 10,075 tons of potatoes
were imported into the United Kingdom.

The figures for the corresponding imports

available, but during the three weeks
ending 19th November some 3,562 tons
of potatoes were imported.

Supplementary Estimate, 1932-33.

CLASS I. No. 4.
VISIT OF HIS ROYAL HIGHNESS
THE PRINCE OF WALES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum, not exceeding three thousand, eight hundred and
eighty pounds, be granted to His Majesty
for the service of the year ending on the
31st March, 1933, to defray such of the
expenses in connection with the visit of
His Royal Highness the Prince of Wales
to open the Parliamentary and Administrative Buildings at Stormont, as fall
to be defrayed by the Government of
Northern Ireland."
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): Hon. Members will not, I am
sure, expect me to dilate at any length
upon the events which have led up to the
submission of this Estimate. During the
debate on the Speech from the Throne
hon. Members have expressed their
appreciation of the arrangements made
in connection with the opening of this
building, and it is to meet the expenses
incurred in connection with this ceremony that this Estimate is now presented
to the Committee.
The occasion of the opening of this
building was, as the noble Lord, the
Prime Minister, pointed out, a unique
and memorable one in the history of
Northern Ireland as a self-governing
unit within the United Kingdom, and it
was, therefore, essential that the arrangements made should be in keeping with
the importance and dignity of the
occasion. Moreover, the fact that the
opening ceremony was performed by a
member of the Royal House added lustre
and distinction to a ceremony which,
even without that added honour, would
have been a notable event in the history
of the Province. The spontaneous
enthusiasm and expressions of loyalty on
the part of our people, which marked the
visit of His Royal Highness showed,
beyond all doubt, their desire that, subject to the express wish of the Prince that
no lavish expenditure of money should be
involved, every effort should be made by
those in authority to ensure that the
ceremonial and the arrangements generally would be in keeping with the
occasion. I believe that I am correct in
saying that those responsible for the
arrangements did achieve success in this
respect and that their efforts received
general appreciation.
Turning to the Estimate itself, hon.
Members will, I feel sure, consider it
extremely reasonable, and I think I may
say without fear of contradiction that
the sums expended were used to the best
advantage.
I should, perhaps, mention that provision for a substantial sum had been
made in the Government Hospitality
Estimate, approved by this House earlier
in the year, for hospitality expenses in
connection with the opening ceremony,
but in view of the general desire for
economy, the provision then made has
not been availed of.
As regards the individual items of the
Estimate, the largest is the expenses, etc.,
of the constabulary, naval, military, and
other units which were responsible for
providing the Guards of Honour and for
lining the route from the Quay to Stormont. It has been clear from the
speeches made by hon. Members that the
fine appearance of these forces was a matter of considerable gratification to the
people of the Province. The services of
these units were of incalculable value,
and I have no doubt the expenditure incurred under this sub-head is fully justified.
Sub-head B refers to the arrangements
for the safety and comfort of spectators
at Stormont, including the provision of
loud speakers to enable those outside to
follow the ceremony in the central hall.
Sub-head C_refers to stationery, and
here I think I would be expressing the
feeling of hon. Members if I were to
congratulate those responsible on the very
handsome and beautifully produced
official programme which was provided.
This programme will furnish those who
obtained it with a very worthy memento
of a historic occasion. I do not imagine
that hon. Members will wish to question
this Vote, but I shall be happy to elucidate any details which may be of interest.
I beg to move.

Just
Another thing, in coming to this
function the Lord Mayor of the City of
Belfast, the capital of Northern Ireland,
had to come up the back way.
imagine the Lord Mayor of London if

in Westminster having to go by the back

say that it was an insult to the dignity
of the Lord Mayor. Somebody said the

this House.

know whether the invitations were included in the expense of printing, but I

the representatives of the people, and by
all means let the party with the greatest
number have the greatest number of delegates on that committee when it is set up.
With that protest I close.

DEPUTY-SPEAKER: If you

to the House. That is to say, that in
