HOUSE OF COMMONS
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 6th December, 1932.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
RELIGION OF CIVIL SERVANTS.
1. Major MCCORMICK asked the
Minister of Finance whether, in view of
the claims made by the minority in Northern Ireland, he can state the numbers or
the percentage of Roman Catholics and
Protestants employed in the service of the
Northern Government.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The official records do not disclose the religious persuasion of the civil
servants employed in the several Departments.
GRADES IN THE CIVIL SERVICE.
2. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Finance if he can state
whether the grades of the Civil Service
in Northern Ireland are the same as those
in the Imperial Civil Service and what
are the reasons for setting up a class
known as "junior male clerks" established
in 1928 at a maximum salary of £200.
Mr. POLLOCK: The grades of the
Civil Service in Northern Ireland are not
in all cases identical with those in the
Imperial Civil Service, but it may be
taken that in those classes (usually designated "Treasury Classes') common to two
or more Departments, the rates of remuneration and general conditions of service approximate closely to the
corresponding grades in the Imperial
Service.
The question of the establishment of
certain ex-Service temporary clerks on a
salary scale with a maximum of £200 per
annum was the subject of a special investigation in consultation with the British
Legion in 1928. A White Paper was
then circulated to hon. Members, and I
shall be pleased, if the hon. Member so
desires, to provide him with a copy of
that document.
I hope, however, that the hon. and
gallant Member will not press me any
further on this subject, as any increase
in salary would make it necessary for me
to re-examine the question of the replacement of ex-Servicemen by female writing
assistants in many cases where the employment of highly-paid male clerks can
hardly be justified.
ALLOCATION OF ACCOMMO-
DATION FOR OPPOSITION.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): On a point of Order, I wish
to ask whether it is not the custom for
an hon. Member before tabling a Vote
of Censure on Mr. Speaker to raise the
question at issue by a question to the
Chair, and whether under the present circumstances you, Sir, could inform the
House regarding any correspondence which
may have passed on the subject of the
allocation of rooms within the building
in order that hon. Members before embarking upon a debate may be fully informed.
Mr. SPEAKER: As regards the first
part of the question, it is the usual custom for an hon. Member to raise the
question with the Chair before taking
the extreme step of tabling a Vote of
Censure on Mr. Speaker. I hope that in
this case it was merely a question of
ignorance and not of deliberate intention.
As regards the second part of the question,
I propose to place upon the Table of the
House the correspondence which gave
origin to the Vote of Censure upon the
Order Paper.
Mr. Speaker laid on the Table the
correspondence between the hon. Member
for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie) and himself
relating to the allocation of accommodation for the Opposition.
Ordered, That the said correspondence
do lie on the Table.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
The following Motion stood on the
Paper in the name of Mr. Beattie :-
"That this House views with regret the
refusal of Mr. Speaker to allow Members
of the Opposition to have the use of the
rooms set apart for the Opposition."
Motion not moved.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): We propose, in
this Bill, to lay down general rules for
the guidance of Public Assistance Committees in adjudicating on claims for
transitional payments. Although we may
not have gone as far in the provisions of
this Bill as some hon. Members would like,
let me remind the House that this is
a temporary Bill to meet present conditions and will expire at the end of
June of next year, when it is hoped to
introduce new legislation revising the
whole scheme of unemployment insurance,
based on the recommendations of the
Royal Commission.
In this Bill we have gone a long way
in removing an obvious grievance. It is
difficult to secure uniformity in examining
applications for transitional payments.
There is always bound to be criticism as
between payments made by different
Public Assistance Committees. This
Bill will remove a great deal of dissatisfaction and make the work of the
committees easier and less susceptible to
the criticism levelled against it. I would
ask the House to follow me while I
proceed to explain who are affected by the
proposed change in legislation. It is
only those contributors who have
exhausted their insurance qualification.
Under the Economy Order of a year
ago it was laid down that an applicant
for unemployment insurance benefit was
only entitled to draw 26 weeks' benefit
in any twelve months. At the end of
that period if his needs were such that
he required further benefit he became
entitled to transitional payments-the
full amount of which is paid by the
Exchequer, but if the home income was
such that the committee formed the
opinion he was not entitled, then transitional payments were refused. It is
inherent in a system of this kind that
there should be some lack of uniformity
between one Public Assistance Committee
and another, and we are asking the
House to give statutory authority to
rules which will make for uniformity as
between all Public Assistance Committees.
Hon. Members will have the rules
governing the procedure before them
and will observe that these new conditions will affect five classes or types
of resources. The general argument laid

some very

This resolution, if it does not demand
the resignation of the right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Home Affairs,
certainly demands the head of Major
Harris upon a charger. We are fully
aware that the composition of the Newry
Council is largely of a Nationalist-Communist character to-day-as it was eleven
years ago. History does not alter in this
respect, and eleven years hence it will
probably be the same. This explains
how it is that the Newry people are misrepresented in this matter, and yet the
Loyalist community pays fully 80 per
cent. of the rates. Personally I received
nothing but courtesy from the people of
Newry whilst I acted as Administrative
Commissioner there.
But this whole question raises a point.
which I fear you will not allow me to discuss now, that is, that legislation will be
required to enforce the flying of the
national flag by Councils such as this, who
get Government grants; in this case many
liberal grants. Newry has been
exceptionally well treated. What I wish
to maintain is that, as matters stand now
-to-day--I suggest to the Minister-he

the flag on stated occasions. I put this
forward-I suggest to him that he has
this power, and that he did not use it in

The purpose of your whole Bill, in my

the purpose of making the poor pay to
relieve the rich. That cannot be disputed. The savings under a Bill of this
kind are between £8,000,000 and
£10,000,000 per annum. If the Government in Great Britain had continued

Major MCCORMICK: I beg to support
this Transitional Payments Bill, and I
would like to congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary on his introduction of
it. I should like to say that I do not
follow at all the dire description which the
Member for Pottinger gave of what would
follow from this Bill. Neither do I agree
with the remarks which the Member for
Woodvale made with regard to this Bill.
So far as I can gather, this Bill places our
unemployed on a parity with the people
in Great Britain. Indeed I think that is
a thing to be desired. It also makes for
uniformity, which is badly wanted.
Regarding the Means Test, I think
there are different views that might be
taken of the principle. I wish to say that
I think there is great justification for the
Means Test in this specially depressed
time. As I contend, all legislation is
brought into effect for the particular needs
of that particular time, so I think that
there is need for this Act. I think that
these times of industrial depression call for
it. When everyone, rich and poor, worker
and workless, is feeling the pinch, it requires, what I might call a pooling of all
resources in order that ends may be made
to meet. We are in times of extraordinary depression and, what is to my
mind worse, we cannot see the end of this
thing. There seems to be no gleam of
hope, although we are urged to be
courageous and we will go forward. I
submit that we cannot do anything else
but go forward.
And
We find that the funds of different
bodies and different societies are all
brought into a pool in order that the main
body may survive. We find that one
department is paying for the costs and
losses of another, and so must we.
in the end, what is the great object aimed
at in many businesses? To keep the
worker employed, to keep him from getting into the lists of the workless. I
know mills that are kept going for the
sake of the employment for those people.
In many cases I know they are run at a
loss. The idea is that we will survive
through this time and that the time of
prosperity will come.
Mr. BEATTIE: Will the hon. Member mention one of those firms that are run
for the sake of the people.
Major McCORMICK: There is one
firm that I know, Jennymount Mills, in
which one part is paying for the losses of
the other part and the whole place is
going busily. They say we must keep
going, and this is a great help to that
firm. I say when that sort of thing is
done in a firm why not in a family?
Surely a financial crisis in national life
must find its repercussion in the family
life. I suggest that family life will be
strengthened, because the very root of
everything in our British national life is
the family. I submit that all persons
with families, whether they have the
advantage of unemployment benefit or not
-and there are many families that have
not that advantage and that cannot take
advantage of it-are forced in these times,
by the very nature of their circumstances,
to adopt this principle of the Means Test.
In my own family I myself am making
use of the Means Test, and yet I have
never got benefit, and I hope I will never
have to get it. But I would venture to
say that in the case of many Members of
this House a Means Test is being
operated. I, myself, have to make use of
a Means Test. Let us look at this thing
in a commonsense way. I suggest to the
hon. Member for Shankill (Mr. Henderson) that in employing a workman-he is
doing his best, I know, to find many a
man work, and has done a lot of good for
the working man, and speaks up for himwhen he is trying to make a job for a man
-and he knows what I mean by making a
job, trying to put a man into a place in
his own works where there is really no
work for him but he wishes to make a place

per cent.

I think it is a very good thing, and I am

fifty per cent.
Again this is not a general plan.
The merits are different in individual
cases, and when the matter come before
the public assistance committees I take
it that they treat each case individually.
That is a great safeguard and I am glad
to see it. At the same time I make this
statement, that the intention or basis of
pensions for wounds was that these were
given apart from any other consideration.
And I beg again to differ from my hon.
Friend from Woodvale. Pensions for
disability were given not for service but
for the fact that a man when he came
into the labour market was depreciated
to a certain percentage owing to his
wounds. Would I get a pension for my
services in the war for services only?
Would anyone? I say it is because that
man's worth in the labour market is
depreciated that he has got that pension
which is worked on a scale of percentages.
I would conclude by saying that I dissociate myself entirely from the hon.
Member's statement that the Government have exploited the ex-Servicemen.
On the contrary a great amount of money
has been placed in their way by employment and other means. I myself, as the

part in many stages of this employment,
and, if I may say so, I know the extent

also knew the difficulties of applying it.
Yet instead of helping us with constructive advice to make the new system
work as smoothly as possible they ran

Preferential Payments in Bankruptcy
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): Hon. Members will recollect the legislation in 1929
designed to modernise the Bankruptcy
Code as it applied in Northern
Ireland. The Act passed at that time
gave legal sanction to the majority
in
of the recommendations of the Departmental Committee appointed
September, 1926, to consider the question. It did not, however, deal with the
Committee's recommendation to limit,
in England, the absolute priority over
"Statutory period " means a ordinary debts hitherto enjoyed by the
period comprising five days at least Crown in the distribution of the property
as
385 Preferential Payments Bill-

7 DECEMBER 1932
Second Reading.
of a bankrupt. Action was deferred at
that time because the Parliament of
Northern Ireland had not power to deal
with the matter so far as it affected reserved taxes and such Crown debts as
were reserved matters.
The requisite powers have now, however, been secured from the Imperial
Parliament through Section 6 of the
Northern Ireland (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1932, which empowers the
Parliament of Northern Ireland, with the
consent of the Treasury, to regulate the
priority in bankruptcy administration of
Crown debts and certain debts due to
Trustee Saving Banks.
the
The Bill now before the House is a
consolidation measure re-enacting
relative portions of the existing law in
regard to preferential payments in bankruptcy, but with the addition in Clause 1
(9) of the provision that all debts proved
in a bankruptcy, including Crown debts,
shall be paid pari passu. The effect of
this will be that, instead of the whole
balance of a Crown debt being recoverable as at present, the Crown will only
be entitled at most to one year's debts in
full and afterwards to a dividend along
with the other creditors.
The opportunity afforded by the introduction of the present Measure is also
taken to bring the law in regard to the
priority of certain debts due to Trustee
Savings Banks into line with existing
law in Great Britain, and to effect some
minor textual clarification of the
Preferential Payments in Bankruptcy
(Ireland) Act, 1889, rendered necessary
by the passage of successive Acts of Parliament. I beg to move.
Question proposed: "That the Bill be
now read a Second time.'
Mr. BEATTIE: This Bill, I presume,
is a very technical one. I understand
from the remarks of the hon. and learned
Gentleman (Mr. Robb) that the Crown
has, at present, the preference of claiming 100 per cent. of the amount due.
Now he wants to put the Crown in the
same position as an ordinary individual
and subject to the same limitation in the
case of a bankruptcy. As a democratic.
assembly and as representing the people,
who on the whole, are the big items as
far as claims are concerned, I think the
privileged position which the Crown enjoys is justified. I take the Crown to
mean the people, and that is why I think
the Crown should have first claim on the
goods or money at the disposal of the
people against whom they are proceeding,
just as I would advocate that the Crown
should own the land, transport, and all
the things essential for the well-being of
the community at large.
I do not know why this change is made
in Northern Ireland so as to set the
Crown on a par with the ordinary
individual, except that it is to suit the
requirements of the supporters of the
Government. Perhaps some of the
Government supporters outside the House
have had the difficulty of meeting the
position where the Crown had claimed all
and nothing was left to divide amongst
them, and I presume they have made
representations for parallel treatment
with England. I still stand for the
Crown taking precedence in these matters
and having first claim on all goods and
chattels. Getting down to the origin of
the individual's right to property and to
money, it all, first and foremost, came
from the Crown in some way. It may
have been taken under a legal enactment
or under a statute, but it firstly had its
origin in some individual who took certain
rights illegally.
That is

Thursday, 8th December, 1932.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
GRADING
OF
ARCHITECTURAL
ASSISTANTS.
1. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Finance whether he can state
what arrangements were made in March,
1929, with the architectural assistants in
the Board of Works as to grading
parity with His Majesty's Office of Works
salaries; whether the architectural assistants and Class I and II architects early
in 1931 requested the Ministry to concede
the question of parity, and what was the
result; and whether the Ministry, in view
of the long and satisfactory service of
these civil servants, will consider the implementing of any undertaking made in
accordance with terms of appointments.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The reply to the first part of
the hon. and gallant Member's question
is that no arrangements were made with
the members of the architectural assistants grade as to parity in the matter
of salary with any officers of corresponding designation in His Majesty's Office of
Works.
With regard to the second part of the
question, it is a fact that the members
of the grades referred to did put forward
representations broadly in the sense
stated in the hon. and gallant Member's
question. After a careful examination of
the duties of the officers concerned, the
conclusion was reached that the salary
scales already in existence were reasonable in relation to the duties and responsibilities attaching to the posts, while at
the same time bearing a fair comparison
with the salaries which men of similar
qualifications can command in civil employment, and also with the remuneration of professional officers in other Departments of the Service. I am not
aware of any failure on the part of my
Ministry to implement any undertaking
given to any officer as part of his terms
of appointment.

the Imperial Board of Works-

PARLIAMENTARY BUILDINGS—
COST OF UPKEEP.
6. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the entire annual cost of upkeep of
the Parliamentary Buildings at Stormont, including the grounds, etc.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have been asked to
take this question.
The estimated costs for the current
financial year of the upkeep of the
Parliamentary and Administrative Offices
at Stormont are set out under various
heads on page 30 of the Estimates for
1932-33. The aggregate estimated cost
is £7,655, which sum includes £897 for
wages and £2,600 for rates. If wages of

wages.
THE GIANT'S CAUSEWAY-
CHARGE FOR ADMISSION.
7. Mr. HENDERSON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he is
aware that an English syndicate is exploiting the nature and beauty of the
Giant's Causeway; whether the Government is prepared to introduce legislation
to stop this growing practice all over
Northern Ireland, and SO encourage
visitors and Ulster citizens to visit and
view nature's work without payment.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As I pointed
out to the hon. Member for Woodvale on
the 30th April, 1931, I have no jurisdiction with regard to this or any other
places of historic or scenic interest
situated on private property, and am not,
therefore, in a position to answer the
various queries contained in the question.
With regard to the last part of the
question. I see no justifiable grounds for
interfering with the private rights of the
owners of the property concerned, as suggested by the hon. Member.
Mr. HENDERSON: Would the right
hon. Gentleman not think it necessary to
introduce legislation in the near future
to put a stop to this exploiting of the
works of nature, and are the citizens of
Northern Ireland not entitled to walk on
their own land?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I suggest to
my hon. Friend that if the particular
place he refers to had not been fenced
in it would be in America to-day.
Mr. HENDERSON: How could they
take it over the ocean to America?

Sir DAWSON BATES: Major
McCallum was, prior to his appointment.
as Resident Magistrate on 6th May, 1920,
a solicitor of standing, practising in
Belfast. During the war he had a distinguished military career as a senior
officer in the Royal Irish Rifles.

salary, including bonus, amounting to
£940 68; travelling allowance of £100 in
respect of journeys within ten miles of his
station, and a stationery allowance of £8
-making a total of £1,048 6s.
During the same period he received
fees amounting to £42 for acting as
chairman of Courts of Referees under the
provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1930.

Adjournment of House 404
Adjournment of the House
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Adjournment of the House
(Christmas).
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House, at its rising this day,
do adjourn until twelve noon on Tuesday, 20th December, and that after the
report of Royal Assent to Acts agreed to
by both Houses, Mr. Speaker do adjourn
the House without Question put, until
Tuesday, the 28th of February, 1933,
provided always that if it appears to the
satisfaction of Mr. Speaker, after consultation with the Government, that the
public interest requires that the House
should meet at any earlier time during the
adjournment, Mr. Speaker may give
notice that he is so satisfied, and thereupon the House shall meet at the time
stated in such notice, and shall transact
its business as if it had been duly
adjourned to that date. (The Prime
Minister).
Mr. BEATTIE: I feel that the
adjournment of this House until Tuesday, 20th December, is uncalled for. I
would like to make an explanation of
why I say that. I am sure the Government are not so deaf nor yet are they
so blind that they do not realise the
serious position of over 100,000 people in
Northern Ireland. If they go away till
the 20th December, after being separated so
long from the end of the last Session until
the opening of this one, it will be very
callous conduct on their part and will
amount to neglect of the 100,000 people
of whom I have spoken. I would suggest that the House should continue in
session and endeavour to put into operation some of the ideas that the Minister
of Labour (Mr. Andrews) propounded
yesterday to the conference of local employment committees. If it were possible through any idea to employ even
half-a-dozen men the time of the House
would be well spent in thinking that
matter out.
We are coming to a time of the year
that is very important in the world's
history. It is a time for the children.
Unfortunately many thousands of
children will be greatly disappointed this
Christmas, and we as a Parliament and
the Government as a Government must
endeavour in some way, however small it
may be, to make what promises to be a
dark Christmas into a bright Christmas.
In my own area the people are bearing up
under a heavy strain with spirit and with
a hope that at long last something may
be done, but if the Government disappear from this House until Tuesday, 20th
December, and if on that date the House
adjourns without debate, then that Merry
Christmas, of which we have all heard
in our younger days, will not be a merry
one for the people for whom I speak.
I would also like to make my protest
against this adjournment from another
direction. If the Government endeavoured to centralise the amount given
in charitable subscriptions throughout
Northern Ireland, to bring them all into
a central fund, and to prevent political
parties from abusing charitable subscriptions by bringing in a Charities Act
similar to that in force in Great Britain,
it would tend towards a better distribution of those charitable donations
which liberal-minded people are giving
at the moment. Although I do not agree
with the charity basis, under the present
régime the people can do nothing but
either accept or allow themselves to
starve. That is the comment I wish to
make to the Government on this Motion.
If I were in Government circles I would
certainly pursue that course, keep this
House active, and make the Members of
it think out the best possible solution in
order to make a dark Christmas into a
merry one for the people who are
clamouring for food.
Mr. HENDERSON: It is with a great
deal of apprehension that I view the Government's policy of adjourning so suddenly. A short time ago when His Royal
Highness the Prince of Wales opened this
building the Prime Minister said we had
now got a Parliament. We all admire
this Parliament House, but the unfortunate part of it is that right hon.
Gentlemen opposite love their Parliament
so much that they are in undue haste
to get away from it. In my opinion this
is a wrong policy for the Government to
adopt. We were away last time for very
nearly seven months, doing nothing.
During those six or seven months great
industrial unrest took place in Belfast.
Lives were lost and hundreds and
hundreds of pounds worth of property
was destroyed. Had the Government
kept this House sitting I believe that in
all probability many of those things
could have been averted. But they were
not sitting, and in my opinion the Government's laxity in that matter was
405 Adjournment of the House

Adjournment of the House 406
responsible not only for the loss of life
but for the destruction of property.
I also protest on behalf of the single
persons in Northern Ireland. To-day we
had a glaring example. No later than
to-day the Minister of Labour-whether
he did so purposely or not I cannot
say tried to evade the question. He
told this House he had absolutely no
record of the number of single persons
unemployed in Northern Ireland.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member
may give his reasons for opposing this
Motion, but of course he could not be
permitted to go into details on the
questions he is now discussing.

Mr. HENDERSON: Instead
adjourning the House, the Prime Minister
and the Cabinet should get together to
propound a policy, and should introduce
legislation for the purpose of absorbing
the thousands and thousands of single
young men who, to-day, are a great
burden to their parents. Many of these
young men will have to carry on the
work that we leave undone; they will
have to make Ulster prosperous when we
are gone.
Yet thousands of them have
done nothing since the Great War concluded. Those boys are signing on at
the Employment Exchange, and
thousands are not signing on at all, for
the simple reason that the Ministry of
Labour has rightly decided that ex-
Servicemen and married men should get
the preference when any openings occur.
Does the Minister of Labour realise
that some married men have been signing on for the past four or five years, and
have not received a job yet? One case in
point is that raised by the hon. Member
for Woodvale (Mr. Nixon) and by myself
in the other House of a man who had
been signing on for eight years without
having obtained a job. If this House
adjourns until the 20th December, and
then until the 28th February, the parents
will still have to carry the burden of
feeding and clothing these young people.
whereas, you ought to be preparing a
programme to absorb them into useful
employment. Many things could be
done. The agricultural Members could
suggest many things to the Minister of
Agriculture whereby thousands of these
young men could be absorbed into
employment on the land. The Minister
of Home Affairs could find employment
for thousands in the reconstruction of
roads, and for hundreds more in the
repair of dilapidated bridges. You have
only to go to various parts of Northern
Ireland to see how much requires to be
done in the way of improving the roads.
I say it is clear unadulterated madness
to adjourn until the 20th December and
then until the 28th February. We have
sat only three weeks in this palatial
building. The Members of the House
know so much about the building that
when they go through that door they lose
themselves in the corridors. They have
not got to know their new House yet, and
still the Government propose to adjourn
until the 28th February. I say it is a
crying out shame that the Cabinet should
be so lax, and should close their eyes to
the fact that from 10,000 to 20,000 young
men are anxious to get work but cannot
succeed. Those boys are standing about
the street corners.

Mr. NIXON: I really think the House

certainly should be adjourned, but I

Mr. MINFORD: I beg to move:
"That in the opinion of this House
agriculture in Northern Ireland requires
every assistance the Government can
afford."
I think that no Motion that ever came
before the House has had to a greater
extent the sympathy of every Member
on both sides than this Motion. At the
beginning, I would like to draw a picture of the present hopeless plight of the
farmer in Northern Ireland. I think
every Member agrees that his plight is
a serious one. Everyone will agree that
the 'eighties were deplorable years, and
at that time the Government of Britain
induced the landlords to help the farmers. I may quote the prices of farm
produce in those days. Pork was some-
Agriculture--
Government Assistance
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Minford]
thing in the neighbourhood of 40s a
cwt., beef was 25s a cwt., and potatoes
something between £2 and £2 5s a ton.
Then take into consideration the cost of
production. A farm worker got about
£40, and the cost of a joiner about a
farm was 6d an hour. If you contrast
those prices with the prices ruling today, you will agree that the plight of
the farmer is hopeless.
We come on to the year 1914, when
the war broke out. From 1914 to 1917
the farmers tilled every inch possible,
but in the year 1917 Mr. Lloyd George
made a strong appeal to the farmers in
that great speech he made at the Claxton Hall. His words were:
Produce the food as you did during
the war. If you do that I shall never
let you
back into that state of despondency from which you came.
Unfortunately politicians have let the
farmers down on many occasions.
Mr. NIXON: Hear, hear.
Mr. MINFORD: I was delighted to
see what Mr. Baldwin, the leader of the
great party in England, said a few nights
ago.
Mr. NIXON: Second fiddle.
Mr. MINFORD: He said:
The policy of the National Government must be changed. The farmers
have been ignored for 90 years, and
we must pay more attention to agriculture and more attention to imports.
That came from the lips of a man who
knows, I am sure, more about the State
than any
other man. You must consider
that agriculture is the basic industry in
this country. To-day we have under
tillage one million acres, one and three
quarter acres in grass land, and half a
million acres in hilly and poor grass land.
Then consider that the total output of
agricultural products in Northern Ireland in 1930 was somewhere about
£15,000,000. In that year the linen output was £5,750,000, and shipbuilding
£5,500,000. Agriculture proved to be
more than double the value of those two
most important industries. I was
astounded to-day when I heard that
£20,000,000 was paid out in unemployment benefit. What was it paid for?
Has trade improved? It was paid to keep
the workers from starving. I am standing here to-day, and all I ask the Government to do is to give an assurance that
they will give the farmers a helping hand.
Mr. BEATTIE: What about derating?
Mr. MINFORD: Consider the fact
also that 147,000 people earn their daily
bread from agriculture. To-day the fact
is a deplorable one that there are 10,000
farm workers unemployed. What is
going to be the result? These 10,000
men and their families must get support
from the Government in some shape or
form. Surely it is better to help the
farmers before they are shipwrecked than
to make an attempt to salvage the wreckage.
The Ottawa Conference was looked
forward to with great hopes. I have no
doubt as a result of the Conference that
some trace of prosperity will be seen in
two years' time, but the difficulty to-day
is that the farmer wants immediate relief.
The price of pork to-day was 40s per
cwt. The Lane Fox Commission stated
that the figure should be 64s, a loss on
a 2-cwt. carcase of 43s. Who can stand
that? Potatoes to-day are worth £1 per
ton, and yet when we made an application to the Imports Advisory Board for
an increase in price, they said, in reply,
that there were no grounds to justify such
an increase. The sooner mentality_of
that sort is stopped the better. The
Minister of Agriculture will bear me out
that it takes £3 per ton to grow potatoes.
I am not blaming the Ministry of Agriculture or this Government at all. I
know that the Leader of this Government
would do anything for any industry
which is humanly possible. I would like,
however, to know what is going to happen
to the agricultural industry. In 1921
there were 110,000 acres of flax grown;
to-day there are only 7,000 acres. What
is the result? We used to make Ulster

I am
exceedingly sorry to think that any man

Surely an industry, the output of which
is more than double that of shipbuilding

this: The whole idea of farming was

enable the district to turn to mixed

Farmers could purchase

Government creamery was built and run

were to take shares. I myself sold
1,000 dollar shares among neighbouring

The result, after a number of years, was
a prosperous district, and indeed it is
pointed to as the premier mixed farming
district of Western Canada. Any hon.
Member wishing to read of the details of
this vast change-over, will find the book
in the Library of the House. I submit

idleness, and the Parliamentary Secretary has said it produced happy homes.
If less than half of that amount had been

to the people. I do not give this as a
perfect scheme. I plead that it is worth.
a trial. The times demand it.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I should like to
say, at the very outset of my remarks,
that I deeply sympathise with the unfortunate position of the agricultural community in Northern Ireland to-day. I
realise to the full the depression which
prevails in almost every branch of the
industry, but I also realise, perhaps
somewhat better than other Members who
have spoken to-day, that bad as the position of our farmers may be, it is not
worse, and in many respects a great deal
better, than the position of farmers in
many other parts of the world. I do not
make that statement as an excuse for
doing nothing to relieve the depression
which exists, and I hope to show later in
my speech that a very great deal has been
done, and is being done to improve the
position of agriculture in the United
Kingdom, and that since the commencement of the present depression there has
probably been no period at which the
outlook for the future has been more
favourable or more promising of a definite
improvement in agricultural prices. But
it is important that we should realise that
the problem is not a local one, and that
the depression which affects us in Northern Ireland is merely a reflection of the
world-wide depression which exists not
only in agriculture, but also in industry.
As hon. Members are aware, the market
for a great part of the agricultural produce which is produced on our farms is
found in Great Britain, and what is the
position of the market there? With
almost three million persons unemployed,
it is inevitable that there should be a
great curtailment in the demand for agricultural produce. The same is true of the
United States, where the number of unemployed is, perhaps, ten or even twelve
million, and of Germany, where another
four or five million persons are unemployed. Under conditions of industrial
prosperity all these people would be purchasers of agricultural produce on a very
much greater scale than is the case to-day.
It is true that so far as wheat and
potatoes are concerned, these may be little
affected by unemployment since they are
probably the two cheapest foodstuffs that
can be obtained; but the decline in the
prices of meat, butter, eggs and other
livestock products is due, in a very large
measure, to the tremendous mass of unemployment which exists, and to the
curtailment in the purchasing power of
the industrial community.
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Sir E. ARCHDALE: In face of a
position, such as I have described, only
two courses are open. Either a recovery
in industrial prosperity must be brought
about in order to stimulate the demand
Agriculture-
Government Assistance
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Edward Archdale]
for agricultural products up to the level
at which it existed a few years ago, or
else a reduction in the supply of agricultural produce thrown on the market must
be effected, so as to limit supply in
accordance with the effective demand
which exists at a reasonable price. I think
I may claim that the National Government in Great Britain and our Government in Northern Ireland are both doing
all they possibly can to restore prosperity
along these lines.
Mr. NIXON: What about flax?
Sir E. ARCHDALE: I do not propose
to deal with the steps that have been taken
to aid the return of industrial prosperity,
but I do propose to show that the restrictions which have been imposed on the
imports of agricultural produce are likely
to lead to a very substantial improvement
in the position of the farming community
by restricting supplies in accordance with
demand and preventing the dumping of
surplus produce from abroad.
The first step which was taken by the
National Government with a view to
restricting the import of livestock products was the appointment of a Reorganisation Commission for pigs and pig products, charged with the preparation of a
scheme for the reorganisation of the home
industry, coupled with the regulation of
foreign imports by quota. Then at
Ottawa, arrangements were made for the
restriction of the quantities of foreign
meat, which were to be allowed into the
United Kingdom as from the beginning
of 1933. It was found, however, that the
imports of meat and bacon which were
reaching the United Kingdom in the
autumn of this year were so great that an
immediate restriction of supplies was
necessary. Consequently, a series of conferences were held with representatives of
the principal exporting countries, and in
the course of a few weeks arrangements
have been made to introduce a voluntary
scheme of import restrictions in anticipation of the legislative restrictions which
will come into force next year.
As a consequence, we find that to-day
there is in operation a working scheme
for a reduction of from 10 per cent. to 20
per cent. in the imports of South
American chilled beef, of 20 per cent. in
the case of South American frozen
mutton and lamb, of 10 per cent. in the
imports of New Zealand and Australian
mutton and lamb, and of 20 per cent. in
the imports of bacon and ham from
foreign sources. The effect of these restrictions, which have been made on a
voluntary basis, should soon begin to
make itself felt, although in view of the
large imports which were taking place
just prior to the introduction of the restrictive scheme it may take a few weeks
before accumulated stocks are depleted
and an effective rise in prices is secured.
But that a rise in price will take place is
fully apparent. In view of the apparent
rapidity and ease with which the negotiations with the importing countries have
brought about an agreement to restrict supplies, some hon. Members may suggest that
this step should have been taken earlier.
To suggest this, however, ignores the
fact that a determination to introduce
restrictions on imports in 1933 by means of
legislative action had already been taken
by the Government. If it had not been
that this fact was known by the representatives of the importing countries, I
do not think that they would voluntarily
have agreed to the curtailment of their
exports to this country which they have
now sanctioned. Knowing that compulsory curtailment of their imports
would be required in 1933, they were
therefore prepared to anticipate that restriction on a voluntary basis in order
to secure the goodwill of this country.
It will be appreciated, however, that
the voluntary restriction of imports
which has just been introduced is an offshoot of the new long-term agricultural
policy of this country, which has been
hammered out at countless discussions
and at numerous commissions during the
past year. In the course of these discussions and at the various commissions,
I am glad to say that Northern Ireland
has been constantly represented. For
many years past I have been convinced
that the best policy which can be pursued
by the Imperial Government is a policy
designed to encourage the development of
the livestock industry within the United
Kingdom. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
So far as Northern Ireland is concerned,
my Ministry has consistently fostered the
development of livestock production,
which constitutes fully 80 per cent. of the
output of our farmers. It is apparent,
therefore. that the adoption of a livestock policy by the Imperial Government
is in our best interests, and I welcome
the recognition by Major Elliott that the
crux of the agricultural situation to-day
Agriculture-
Government Assistance
8 DECEMBER 1932
is to be found in the prices of livestock.
It is recognised, however, that it is not.
sufficient simply to impose a restriction
of imports from abroad and exercise no
control over production at home. If
supplies are restricted from abroad, the
consumer must
the
be assured that
agricultural industry at home will make
up the shortage which is thus created so
long as a reasonable price is assured.
Moreover, it would obviously be of little
consequence if supplies from abroad were
cut off and the home producer proceeded
to increase his production so rapidly that
over-production must occur and prices
slump.
I think I can make this clear by reference to the position of potatoes. The
quantities of potatoes imported into the
United Kingdom this autumn have been
negligible, and yet I suppose that never
before have potato prices been worse
than they are at present. This slump
in the prices of potatoes, however, is
not due to foreign competition, but overproduction at home, and it becomes
apparent that, until the British and
Northern Ireland farmer so organises his
marketing that he has effective control
over the quantity of produce which is
thrown on the market, excessive slumps
in prices are always liable to occur.
Accordingly, I am glad to know that
steps are being taken to organise the
home producer so that he will have
greater control over the marketing and
disposal of his produce. In the early
summer of this year the British Government appointed a Reorganisation Commission for pigs and pig products.
Northern Ireland were represented on
that Commission, and the chairman,
Colonel Lane Fox, made a special visit
to Belfast early in August to study the
situation here and to interview representatives of bacon curers and producers.
The fact that my Ministry was represented at Colonel Lane Fox's Commission meant that we were able to prepare
a scheme, differing in several material
respects from the scheme which was ultimately adopted by Colonel Lane Fox
and his colleagues as applicable to
Great Britain, but which was yet suitable for the special conditions which
prevail in Northern Ireland.
I am glad to say that the Commission
agreed to the modified scheme which was
submitted for Northern Ireland, and I
think I may claim that we have secured
for the Northern Ireland producer all the
advantages of the British scheme,
together with the exemption of our small
farmers from some of the conditions with
regard to the making of contracts, which
would have proved difficult to put into
operation here.
A similar Reorganisation Commission,
dealing with milk, is at present sitting in
London, and on this Commission again
Northern Ireland is represented. It is
anticipated that the Commission will
issue its report in a few weeks' time, and
already my Ministry is engaged in the
preparation of a scheme which, it is
hoped, will fit in with the British proposals, while at the same time the special
circumstances of production in Northern
Ireland are safeguarded.
In order to put into operation the
schemes for the better marketing of pigs
and milk to which I have referred,
legislation will be required. Hon.
Members will recall that in the speech
from the Throne His Grace delivered at
the opening of this Parliament, it was
indicated that an Agricultural Marketing
Bill would be introduced. I hope to be
able to introduce this Bill when the
House reassembles in March, and the Bill
will be framed so as to enable schemes for
the better marketing of pigs and of milk
to be introduced in Northern Ireland, so
that we shall secure the advantages in
connection with the marketing of these
commodities which I hope will accrue
from the adoption by the British Government of the recommendations of the Reorganisation Commission, to whose work I
have just referred.
The scheme of voluntary restrictions
upon the imports of meat and bacon to
which I referred earlier provides us with
a breathing space during which to make.
arrangements for the introduction of
schemes for the better marketing of our
produce. Although pigs and milk are
the first two commodities for which marketing schemes have been prepared, there
is no doubt that similar schemes will be
put forward for other products-notably
for fat stock, for potatoes and for eggs.
I fully anticipate that marketing schemes
for these commodities fat stock,
potatoes, and eggs-may be brought forward in Great Britain at an early date
and it will be necessary for us to keep
step.
These schemes may require a considerable degree of reorganisation on the part
Agriculture-
Government Assistance
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Edward Archdale]
of our agricultural industry, but I am
confident that our farmers will not hesitate to make that reorganisation when
they are assured of a progressive limitation of foreign supplies. In the case
of pigs, Colonel Lane Fox's Commission
has recommended that the quantities of
bacon and hams imported should progressively diminish with the expansion of
home production, and that production
in Great Britain and Northern Ireland should be organised so as to
increase by 10 per cent. every four
months. This production will, of course,
be subject to a guaranteed minimum
price which will be based on the cost of
feeding stuffs so as to afford a reasonable
profit to the farmer. In the case of meat
also, the maximum quantities which will
be allowed to be imported into the United
Kingdom will progressively decline until
in the second quarter of 1934 they will
amount to only 65 per cent. of the imports during the twelve months ended
30th June, 1932.

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON :

Motion, one concerning agriculture,

The policy which has been enunicated by
the Imperial Government may be divided
into two parts-what are called the shortrange policy and the long range policy.
The short range policy is dealt with by
the wheat quota and also by the Pig
Commission. I understand that the
recommendations of the Pig Commission
come into force in July, and that by
means of the control of imported bacon
the price will be fixed at about 60s per
cwt. This will vary according to the
prices of feeding stuffs. What is most
useful to the farmer-in fact, the whole
point of the scheme is that the farmer
will have four months' guarantee. That,
I think, is the main point in the Pig
Commission's recommendations.
The long-range policy deals with livestock. That was fully covered in the
debate we had a week ago and by the
Minister of Agriculture to-night. I do

Lieut.-Colonel Gordon]
not propose to deal with that, but I wish

We export to England. We are linked

before the House.
After all is said and done, this is a
Motion which could only be dealt with by
the Imperial House with any hope of

proposal to the Minister of Agriculture or
the Junior Whip (Sir Basil Brooke), who,
I believe, will answer for him, and I hope

The next point I want to deal with

the Northern Government.
The plain
fact of the matter is, they cannot.

affecting the land annuities is reserved by

hold out any hope that this Parliament
can deal with land annuities is a mistake.

They have to pay very much higher

Under the
Ashbourne Act for 49 years a farmer here

absolute owner, under the 1925 Act 43
per cent. over 66 years, while under the
English Act over 60 years a farmer pays

place between the Ministry of Agriculture
in England and other countries with regard to restrictions. It should be borne

market. Therefore, you had those two

that the primary producer was to get an
economic price, and second, that he was

There can be no fault to find with the

acknowledged that demand, and the

Mr. NIXON: A Member on your own

I see Northern Ireland cattle sold in

Allam's yards, and yet I can remember
ten or fifteen years ago when no one
would buy an Ulster beast, because he
was was a miserable looking animal.
Again and again you saw on the other
side of the Channel cattle from Southern
Ireland making pounds more than cattle
from Northern Ireland. Let me tell you
that I ship quite a considerable number
of cattle to England. I put fifty Ulster
cattle and fifty Free State cattle together
on one farm, and after a year the Ulster
cattle brought a better price than the
Free State cattle. That is a tremendous
change from the old days. Then we find
that cattle bred by the hon. and gallant
Member for South Derry (Captain
Chichester-Clark) are beating in the prize.
ring the best cattle in the world, and
even taking the chief prizes from that
part of the country where the "Soldier's
Song holds sway. When I visit agricultural shows in England I find that
Ulster butter, eggs, and potatoes are the

Captain DIXON: I am glad to see the

Mr. MINFORD: When I put this

Captain NIXON: I do not say it is

Mr. MINFORD: I quite admit that
no farmer has received more encouragement from a Government than the Ulster

We know that Ulster eggs are the best

this Motion purely and simply with the

I was
born in the farming industry, and I know

will not, perhaps, try to lash me because

Agriculture in England the distressing
state agriculture was in to-day.
Sir BASIL BROOKE: I want to
assure the hon. Member that I had no

Mr. MINFORD: I said we ought to
take the opinion of experts, and the
Junior Whip cited me as an expert. I
said I knew farming from A to Z, but
my point was that the Government ought
to have consulted experts in the cattle
trade. At that time prices were falling
tremendously, and we did what we could,
as ordinary members of the farming community, to suggest means of stopping that
fall. We went there to help the Government and not to hinder them. I do not
want doles for the farmers. I want this
Government to assist the farmers to get
an adequate price for their produce.
Mr. BEATTIE: Abolish the middlemen.
Mr. MINFORD: There is no denying
the fact that farming to-day is in a very

do that. I know that in England the
farmers are in a very bad position, much
worse even than we are. That is one of
the reasons why I wanted the whole position discussed in this House, to try to
discover if we could keep our place at the
top.
With regard to the results of the
Ottawa Conference, a reduction of imports
of 35 per cent. in two years from now
is too far in the future to be of any real
assistance to the farmers now. You have
got to make up your minds to do something now. We are paying twenty-three
millions away in unemployment benefit,
and I say rightly so, but I also say that
as long as the people of Ulster and the
people of Great Britain cannot get the
necessities of life you cannot say there is
over-production. I believe we shall have
to turn to agriculture to solve the industrial problem, because I do not believe
we shall be able to absorb all our workers
in industrial concerns. I brought this
Motion forward with two objects; first, to
help the farmer, and, second, to help
employment. I do feel that in such a
perfect agricultural country as we possess, we could increase our production by
at least 33 per cent. if the country was
properly developed. I would like to see
the people who rave about Ulster and
preach about it putting what they preach
into practice. I would like to have an
answer to my question as to whether there
is any hope, during the next twelve
months, of the British and Ulster farmers
getting an economic price for their products. Could a farmer have run his farm
this year and squared his expenses?
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: I am quite
willing at any time to show the hon.
Member my books for the past year. They
show a loss of at least 35/- per arable
I have kept very careful accounts,
and I have gone into all the details, and

acre.

what was for the good of all concerned

I hope this debate will at least put some

century. The year 1847 was a bad year

I was very glad to hear the hon. and
gallant Member for Down suggesting that
a Committee of this House should cooperate with the Ministry of Agriculture
here and with the Ministry at Westminster to try to thresh out a policy for
the good of all concerned. In the war
years we raised more than we are doing
to-day. Why not raise the same amount
to-day My motto is, British first,
Colonies second, and the foreigner last.
I hope I have created no ill-feeling in the

say at once that it has always been
the policy of this Government in respect
to the imposition of land annuities that
where it can be shown that any individual

annuities, consideration has been shown

security for payment of the annuities.
There can be no charge levied against
the Government of any hard dealings
with these people.
the
Let me remind the House that this is
an annual appeal which has been made

always been raised in this Parliament and
arguments have always been the same.
The
year in question has almost been
the worst year on record, and while I do

Ireland, still, at the same time, all the

those behind in their payments. I

to meet their obligations.

Mr. POLLOCK: As I say, the Government is prepared to consider any special

HOUSES ERECTED.
2. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the total number of subsidy houses
built to date under the Housing (Grants)
Act, 1932.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): I have been
asked to answer this question.
Since the 7th June last, the date on
which the Act came into force, the plans
for 173 houses have been approved, of
which eight have been completed to date.
REVISION OF BETTING LAWS.
3. Major MCCORMICK asked the
Prime Minister whether it is the intention
of the Government to take steps to amend
the betting laws on the lines of the Bill
recently before the Imperial Parliament.
Mr. HANNA: As the hon. and gallant
Member is no doubt aware, a Royal Commission is at present inquiring into the
whole question of the law relating to
betting and gambling and cognate
matters, and it is considered that it
would be premature to contemplate any
revision of the betting laws until the
Government has had an opportunity of
examining the conclusions arrived at by
that Commission.

529 Late Captain Chichester-Clark
Legislative Procedure Bill .530
28 FEBRUARY 1933
The late Captain Chichester-Clark.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon) (speaking with emotion): It
is my melancholy duty to intervene for
a few moments in order to voice the
sentiments of the House in reference to
the sad loss that we have sustained by
the death of our old and valued friend,
Captain Chichester-Clark.
In coming
up just now I could not help feeling the
gap in the ranks of this Assembly.
Captain Chichester-Clark's career in the
Royal Navy was very distinguished, and
his services to his country when he retired
from that Force earned for him the
praise and the thanks of the people of
Ulster. We here were accustomed to his
figure in the House, we were attracted
by his personality, and we know that his
death has created a loss which it will be
very hard to fill.
The last opportunity I had of conversation with him was in relation to the new
hall for the Royal Ulster Agricultural
Society. He had set his heart on improving that organisation. He had farreaching ideas as to the benefit it would
confer upon the Ulster people, especially
upon those engaged in agriculture. He
had also a long view with regard to those
matters with which he himself was particularly familiar. I hope nothing will
happen in the vears to come which will
interfere with the development which he
had in view. I have lost not only a
valued parliamentary colleague but a
very close and affectionate friend. Το
his widow and his family there goes out
from this House the deepest sympathy,
profound and sincere, at the loss of a man
so well known and highly esteemed in
the Ulster area.
Mr. NIXON: I should like to join in
the expression of sympathy to
should stand for a moment in respectful
silence.
All hon. Members stood accordingly.

railway companies have always set up a

Take the case of the chairman of the
Irish Council of the R.C.A., Mr. O'Donnell, an active trade unionist, a man who
always carried out his duty faithfully and
well to the company, and who organised
excursions on behalf of the company.
After 35 years' service they select him,
as an active trade unionist worker, to go
outside with a lorry loaded by blacklegs.
When their attention was drawn to it
the company eased the situation and
brought him back. But he had not long
re-started until he was ordered to do the
same work, to act as a blackleg against
his fellow workers who were out on strike.
If he did not comply his wife and eight
of a family could starve. He refused to
blackleg and was compelled to walk the
streets; he is walking the streets at this
moment. That is pure victimisation by
the railway company because of his trade
union activities.
I can quote 33 other cases of a similar
kind. The only part of Ireland in which
that is taking place is Northern Ireland.
There has not been one case in the Free
State, because neither the Government
nor the unions there would permit such
a thing. The Northern Government are
allowing that state of affairs to continue,
and are allowing the people who remained
at work to be persecuted and intimidated
into undertaking the role of blacklegs.
I say that the Government will have to
step in
and take immediate action,
because such things will, perhaps, lead
to a very serious upheaval in the internal
affairs of the railways concerned.
There is another thing to which I take
objection. For fifteen years I have pursued my activities as an official of a union.
When any disputes occurred the employers
with whom I dealt never took individuals
into their offices; they always dealt with
the men collectively. But in this strike
we find this form of persecution-every
individual who has something to lose is
intimidated to such an extent that if he
had not his principles at heart he could
not resist the overtures made by the company. The 33 men who are walking
about in Northern Ireland are the victims
of this terrorism and persecution, and I
ask the Government to call upon the
railway companies immediately to have
it stopped.
I would also like to refer to signal
cabins. No man is allowed into a signal
cabin unless he is highly efficient. I
would ask the right hon. Gentleman is
it true that the work in the Magherafelt
signal cabin, for a period of time, was
carried on by a member of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary. I want him
definitely to make that a point in his
reply, and to give some information in
regard to that incident. I would also
ask, is it true to say that the railway
companies were using the police as
messengers from the railway offices to the
homes of ex-employees in delivering
circular letters with the object of getting
the men to return to blackleg?
I do not want to speak too long, but
before I sit down I would say that

whether this Government thinks the railways are justified in their demands, or

That is the side that has first and foremost to be considered. If they fail to

then, as Statesmen, they have failed in

that the workers are putting up an unequal fight, but right is might. Their

employed in any industry.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.

made an application to the Wages' Board

There is a misunderstanding here, and

must necessarily be followed. On the

presented their cases to the Board, there

findings.
The recent decision of the Board was
that the pay of all grades embraced in
the scheme shall be reduced to the level

is important to remember that to-day because it is an important factor in the
matter. The finding was carried by the

representatives on the Board objecting.
It will be seen that the dovetailing of
these two awards in connection with this

position. Therefore, I feel it necessary
that I should tell the House what the
finding of 9th May, 1931, was in order
that hon. Members may know the effect
of the recent and disputed finding.
The finding of 9th May, 1931, was as
follows: A reduction of 43 per cent. off
the earnings of men in the conciliation
grades, with the proviso, however, that
the reductions should not operate so as
to reduce any man's earning below 40s a
week. As regards stationmasters, clerks,
and supervisors the reduction was 2 per
cent., with a further reduction of 1 per
cent. in respect of earnings in excess of
£100 per annum. The net effect, therefore, of this recent award would be that

The Railway Strike
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
the lower paid men would be reduced
by the full 10 per cent., the stationmasters and clerks by 7 per cent. and
6 per cent. according to salary, and the
general body by 5 per cent., all in
addition to the previous cut to which I
have referred.
The finding was not acceptable to the
trade unions. On 6th December the
Ministry for Industry and Commerce in
the Free State wrote to the Irish railway
companies proposing, with a view to preventing a strike in the Free State, to give
a subsidy to the companies if they would
agree in effect to defer the putting of the
finding into force so far as it affected
railway employees in the Free State until
1st May of the present year. I understand it is to come into operation in the
Free State on that date, unless in the
meantime an agreement modifying it
shall have been arranged or a new finding
given by the Board.
The companies, in accepting this offer,
stated that they intended to regulate
wages in accordance with the finding, but
that they were willing to make good to
their employees in the Free State the full
amount of the reductions due to the finding, provided that they receive the
necessary funds from the Free State
Government. I met the unions, at their
request, in Belfast, on 13th December
last, and I stated very definitely and
finally on behalf of the Government that
we could not agree to give subsidies, because we felt that to do so would be unfair
to the general taxpayers, that it could
not be a basis for permanent peace, and
it would create obvious embarrassment in
the future in dealing with other industrial troubles which might arise, because
of the fact that both employers and workpeople if once the principle was established would look to the Government to
bridge the difficulty.
Obviously the effect would be to place
upon the Government in the years that
lie ahead a burden which no Government should be asked to bear on behalf
of the taxpayers of the country. Now at
the same time, when I met the representatives of the unions and told them
what I have related I admitted that the
granting of a subsidy in one part of
Ireland-I could not do otherwise than
admit it-and not in the other created
an embarrassing position beyond all
doubt, but I pointed out that it was not
of our making, because of the fact that
we were not consulted before the subsidy
was offered and accepted by the Free
State employees and the companies concerned. I pointed out, however, that the
conciliation scheme contemplated joint
consultations, and I suggested to the
representatives of the unions that they
should get into touch with the railway
companies direct. The unions' representatives took my advice, and a conference was held in Dublin on the 16th
December, but no agreement was found
to be possible.
On the 17th December I met both
parties in Belfast when, what I may call
a truce, was arranged, which I hoped,
and had some reason to hope, would lead
to permanent peace. Between the 21st
December and the 4th January I was in
frequent touch with the parties. On the
12th January I met the representatives
of the unions again and arranged that a
further conference would be held between
the parties concerned. This took place
at the York Road Station, Belfast, on
the 20th January, and was continued
on the following day, but again, I
regret to say, the parties concerned were
unable to accommodate with each other
to the extent of arriving at an agreement.
A further conference was held between
the parties on the 27th January, and
again with no result. On the following
day I met the representatives separately
and I again saw the unions on the 30th.
The strike commenced at midnight on the
30th. The Railway Clerks' Association
decided not to take part in the strike.
Since then I have been in frequent touch
with the railway companies. An informal
meeting, I understand, took place
between the representatives of the
LMS and the two unions on the 21st
November, but again with no outcome.
