carefully to every word spoken here in
the hope that I should find some constructive proposition. One question that
ought to be asked is, what can the
Government do?
Mr. BEATTIE: Nationalise the railways.
answer
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I can
that if Mr. Deputy-Speaker will allow
me to do so. I think the Minister of
Labour has done all he possibly could to
bring about an amicable settlement. He
has got no powers to do anything else. In
my judgment there are only two courses
open to him-first of all, to induce his
friend, the Minister of Finance to put up
a subsidy. I do not know whether this
House would agree to that or not. The
other solution is that which the hon.
Member for Pottinger proposes, but the
Minister of Labour has no statutory
power to take over the railways, nor does
this House, I fancy, want to take them
over. The Member for Pottinger has
been allowed to refer to this, and I only
mention it in connection with the strike.
I do not believe that the nationalisation
of the railways would prevent strikes.
Some other countries-Australia, for
example have tried it. Australia has
been losing eight millions a year on the
State railways, and it has not been able
to prevent strikes. Australia has got
what the Minister of Labour here has not
got, compulsory powers to prevent strikes,
but even with those powers strikes occur
in that country. How can the Minister
of Labour and the Government do anything more than they have done to bring
this unfortunate dispute to an end? The
Minister of Labour said that he hoped
Ulster was not going to be made the cockpit for fighting out industrial battles that
really should be fought in Great Britain. I
am afraid there is a suspicion abroad that
it is the British battle that is being fought
out on Ulster soil on this occasion. That,
I am sure, is one of the things we do not
want. We do not want to see a fight
even in Great Britain.
As one with friendly feelings to both
parties, I realise the desperate position
in which the railways find themselves.
To some extent that unfortunate position
is due to Government interference in the
past. If the Government had kept out of
dealing with the railways in Great Britain
just after the war I do not think the railways would be in the terrible plight in
which they are to-day. I would do two
things. The first thing is to warn the
two parties to the dispute that there is a
third party, a more important party, than
the two involved in the dispute, and that
is the general public. The general
public are getting very tired of these railway strikes. The second point I wish to
make to those people is this: that the
general public to-day are not depending
on the railways to the same extent as they
depended upon them thirty years ago. I
am not going to apportion the blame
either to one party or the other, but I
think that if the two parties would sit
down calmly and quietly and think the
thing out they would realise that they are
driving another nail into the railway.
coffin. The railways have suffered quite
enough.
They have been driving away
their best customers; they have been
driving to the roads people who formerly
used the railways, and do they think that
a strike like this is going in the end to
help either the railway companies or the
workers? I for one think it will not.
I do say this: you can never effect a
compromise where there is a spirit of
bitterness abroad. I hope there is not
very much bitterness abroad in this strike
Adjournment-
The Railway Strike
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Robert Lynn]
yet, and I think that before that spirit is
engendered the parties to this dispute
should meet together, possibly under the
chairmanship of the Minister of Labour.
But, at any rate, they should meet together and try in the most friendly way
to find out whether it is not possible to
bridge over the gulf-or rather the stream,
because it is not a gulf-that separates
them. Time is important in this matter,
and as one who is friendly to both parties
I appeal to them to cast off their fighting
garments; to get rid of all their fighting
paraphernalia, and to sit down in a
friendly and businesslike spirit to see
whether they are not able to find a solution
to this difficulty. That is the only way in
which this thing can be settled.
The hon. Member for Pottinger said
that the strike might go on for a month or
for two or three months longer. If it
does, some members of the general public
will suffer, but the people who will suffer
most are the people connected with the
railways. I think it is in their interests
that this strike should be brought to an
end at once.
Mr. NIXON: At the outset, I want to
congratulate the Prime Minister on giving a further exhibition of his contempt
for the working people of Northern Ireland by his exit from this House during
this debate on this afternoon. One of the
unfortunate things; one of the scandals,
in connection with the industrial trouble
in Northern Ireland is that Cabinet
Ministers hold directorships in these companies and are thereby a party to the
dispute.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: I must remind the hon. Member that if he wishes
to assail Cabinet Ministers there is a
definite procedure that must be adopted
for that purpose.
In the meantime, he
should deal with the Motion before the
House, which is an entirely different
matter.
Mr. NIXON: I am glad to hear your
reminder, and if spared and well I shall
have the pleasure of acting on the hint on
a future occasion. I do not like tyranny,
and the treatment of the clerks of the
G.N.R. is nothing more or less than
tyranny. A bully, a tyrant, and a coward
is usually covered by the one hat.
Minister of Labour said one thing that I
agree with that he did not want Ulster
to be used as a cockpit for these fights. I
think that is being done in the present
The
case by the directors of the G.N.R. in their
treatment of their clerks in Ulster. How
is it that it is the clerks in Belfast and in
Ulster that are being singled out and
compelled under threat of dismissal to act
the blackleg? I will tell you the reason,
because the chairman of the directors of
the G.N.R. would be afraid to do that in
Dublin. He selected the loyal Ulster
clerks, and through his agents he asked
them to do what he would not be allowed
to do in Dublin, thereby showing his
appreciation of their loyalty.
I am glad the Prime Minister is back
in the House, and I want to draw his
attention to the fact that over and over
again the loyal workers of the Northern
Counties Railway, down at York Street
and at Larne, organised receptions and
demonstrations of welcome for the Prime
Minister himself on returning from Great
Britain and other places. I want to tell
the Prime Minister that to my own
personal and individual knowledge many
of the men associated with those demonstrations in his honour are now amongst
the strikers, and, while I do not know
all about the merits of the case, from
what I know of the men I do not think
they would be on the streets to-day unless
they had been driven to it by stress of
circumstances.
When the Prime Minister comes to
deal with this matter-because it will
have to be dealt with at some time-I
want him to remember that amongst
these strikers who are threatened with
the loss of their livelihood, and whose
wives and families are threatened with
starvation, are many men who have often
cheered him on his return, and men whom
he was proud to shake hands with. I
know some of the men on strike, and
there is not an hon. Member on the other
side of the House who would not be
proud to shake hands with them if he
was engaged in an election and was looking for votes. I know some of the clerks
who had been persecuted and brutally
turned from their work, although they
did not go on strike. So far as the
victimised clerks in Belfast are concerned
it is the duty of the Government to say
to the directors of the railways,
"Hands
off them." It is not necessary to say it
publicly, because you will be talking to
them in your clubs to-night, and when
you are doing so you can say to them
quietly, "I think it is better to reinstate
those clerks, because we can find no sin
in them. We can find no fault in them."
Adjournment-
The Railway Strike
28 FEBRUARY 1933
Do not play the part of Pontius Pilate,
who, when he could find no fault in our
Lord, washed his hands in an endeavour
to clean himself, but he did not succeed.
It is your duty to tell your colleagues
to reinstate those clerks forthwith. Do
not for a moment imagine that their
treatment is as just as you seem to believe
it is. I did not think myself that there
is so much power behind the clerks as
there is. The Minister of Agriculture is
looking at me. He knows some of thera
too. Get that breach healed, and then
proceed as quickly as you can to heal the
other breach.
I am quite satisfied that there is gross
mismanagement on the part of the
directors of the Great Northern Railway,
and anybody who looks at the useless stuff
they purchase, which is lying ready to rot,
will agree with me in that. With regard
to the Northern Counties Committee Railway, you would imagine that Sir Josiah
Stamp was going to rule England, Ireland, and Scotland. He is supposed to be
a great Britisher, but if that is sc it is very
strange to me that he does not put one
hundred per cent. tyres on the buses of
the company in Northern Ireland.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: I must
point out to the hon. Member that we are
not now discussing the question of buying
British.
Mr. NIXON: I wish we were, because
the unfortunate thing is that the people
who
say "Buy British" do not buy British
at all if they can get something else
cheaper. At the risk of repeating myself
I want to again ask the Prime Minister to
tell the railway directors to stop persecuting the clerks and to reinstate them. With
regard to the other part of the dispute,
there has been a genuine strike.
I am
sorry the Minister of Labour is not in the
House, but his representative is here.
I
was told this afternoon-I am not pledging my word as to the truth of this-but
I was told this afternoon that the Ministry
of Labour sends men to fill vacancies of
the men on strike.
Mr. GORDON indicated dissent.
Mr. NIXON: I am not stating that
definitely-I am only saying I was told so,
and if it is not so I would ask the Parliamentary Secretary to deny it, and if it is
so to stop it, because I am quite sure the
Minister of Labour would not be a party
to that. When you are settling this strike
remember these men of other days, and
remember that you will want them again.
In conclusion, see that the Belfast clerks
are as well treated as the Dublin clerks.
Mr. GRANT: I had not any intention
of taking part in this debate at all, but I
think I should make an appeal to the
Government to see if something cannot
be done to bring the representatives of the
railways and the railway workers together.
I myself have some experience of strikes,
and I know the settlement of a strike is a
rather difficult question to tackle. I do
not think that any good purpose will be
served by using language such as has been
used in this House this afternoon. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I do not think it
helps matters at all to introduce personalities about the Frime Minister or
anyone else. It is recognised by all classes
of the community that if one man in
Northern Ireland deserves well of the
community it is the right hon. Gentleman
who presides over the Ministry of Labour.
He has done all he possibly can to bring
about a peaceful settlement between the
representatives of the men and the railway
companies.
In making my appeal to the Government this afternoon I realize the difficulties of the Government butting in on this
particular question, but I also recognise
that if this strike is allowed to drift without anyone taking any apparent notice of
it except those immediately concerned, it
is going to create such bad feeling amongst
the people of Northern Ireland that
sooner or later the Government will probably be compelled to take some action.
I would much prefer that action was taken
voluntarily by the Government at this
It does not matter
particular stage.
whether or not the question of pride
enters into it.
The Prime Minister could easily ask
the representatives of the men and the
companies to meet together and talk matters over. I have no vested or invested
interest in the railways, good, bad or indifferent. All I am interested in is the
welfare of our community, and to see that
the people who have to use the railways,
either for transport purposes or otherwise,
are considered. We do know that the
railways serve a very important purpose
in the community. I do not agree with
those hon. Members who have said this
afternoon that the railways are finished.
I do not think they are finished, and the
Adjournment-
The Railway Strike
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
. railway workers do not believe they are
finished because they take a pride in the
railways and in the work they perform in
connection with those railways. I do not
intend to labour this subject, but I would
appeal to the Prime Minister and to those
on the Government benches to see if they
could not possibly bring the interested
parties together at the earliest moment
and let us have this unfortunate strike
settled, because if it continues it will not
help other industries in Northern Ireland.
Therefore, I hope my suggestion will be
accepted in the spirit in which I make it.
Mr. MINFORD: I think the time
has arrived when the Government should
try to bridge this gulf or gap between
the railway companies and the men. I
am quite satisfied that the dispute can
be settled, but if it is going to drift on
it will injure our industries. The time
is approaching when the farmers will require artificial manure, and one of the
big factories in Belfast, in fact the
biggest factory in Belfast, is becoming
alarmed at the situation, because if they
do not get away the thousands of tons
of artificial manures which will help to
grow food for our people next year
it
will become a very serious matter.
I do not think it is beyond the power
of any person to bring about a settlement, and I believe action should be
taken by the Prime Minister and the
Minister of Labour. I have great faith
in the Prime Minister in regard to the
settling of disputes. I have never seen
him beaten at it yet. I would like, on
behalf of the railway companies and
the workers, and the Members of this
House, to urge that something should be
done immediately. I support the suggestion put forward by the hon. Member
for Duncairn (Mr. Grant) that
Prime Minister with the Minister of
Labour should approach both parties.
If they did so I feel they would be doing
something for our people.
the
It is sad to think that the strike should
be carried on. Other industries are
suffering, but the people who are the
principal sufferers are the wives and
children of these workers. It is quite
true, as the hon. Member for Duncairn
says, that the railwaymen take a pride
in their railways. I agree with him also
when he says that the words passed from
the other side of the House will go no
length to ease the situation, but, in fact,
will inflame it. I would appeal to the
Prime Minister to go with the Minister
of Labour and meet both parties, and I
feel sure a settlement will be arrived at.
Mr. BEATTIE: Would the Prime
Minister not think it desirable, as the
Leader of this House, to make a statement on the railway situation? I think
it is an outrage that he is sitting silent.
.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER The hon.
Member knows he cannot make a second
speech.
Mr. GORDON: There were one or
two points raised in the discussion to
which, in the absence of the Minister of
Labour, it is necessary that I should
refer. Suggestions have been offered by
Members of the Opposition and by Members on this side of the House that an
effort should be made to bring both
parties together for the purpose of effecting a settlement. A strike is never
entered upon hastily. When men determine upon a strike it is only after
exploring every avenue that it is possible
to explore, and when there is dissatisfaction with the offer made. A lockout also is never decided upon hastily.
Every avenue of escape, again, is examined, conferences are held, discussions
take place and, finally, when no other
decision can be arrived at the lockout
takes place.
Arising out of suggestions put forward
by hon. Members opposite, I would like
to say that every effort has been made
by the Minister of Labour. Conferences
were arranged and representatives of the
railway unions and representatives of the
railroads met the Minister of Labour on
many occasions, and, as has been admitted by the hon. Member for Shankill
(Mr. Henderson) and by the hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie), eulogies
have been showered upon the Minister
of Labour.
Mr. BEATTIE: I make no admission
of that kind.
Mr. GORDON: Probably the hon.
Gentleman is too ungracious to make that
admission. However, since he will not
make that admission, let me say that it
has been made by representatives of
the great trade unions connected with
the railways. They have showered en-
Adjournment-
The Railway Strike
28 FEBRUARY 1933
comiums upon the Minister of Labour
because of the great efforts he has put
forward. The hon. Member for Pottinger
made one suggestion, and it is possible,
Mr. Deputy-Speaker, that you will not
permit me to enter into an examination
of the proposal that he put before the
House. If you did, I think I could
advance figures to show that the proposal
he made has been tried in many countries
with financial disaster to the industries
concerned and also to the countries. He
suggested nationalisation. I always feel
that a debate of this character gives an
opportunity to men to express their
political opinions. Many times they go
beyond the matter before the House and
are anxious to put forward a political
suggestion. The next suggestion came
from the hon. Member who represents
the Shankill Division (Mr. Henderson).
He suggested compulsory arbitration.
Mr. NIXON: He repudiated it.
Mr. GORDON: All awards that have
taken place in connection with the railways have been voluntary. They need
not have been accepted by the railway
trade unions or the railway directorates.
On this occasion a voluntary award was
made and the men after due examination
refused to accept it. Neither the Prime
Minister nor the Minister of Labour can
for a moment admit that the directors
should submit to certain dictation, or that
the railway employes should accept certain
dictation. The Minister could call a conference in order to build a bridge, as has
been suggested by some hon. Gentlemen
on this side of the House, but as to
dictating terms he could not stand for
that. On this occasion the Minister of
Labour has held many conferences. We
are prepared to hold one this evening; we
are prepared to enter into a conference
to-morrow.
The conferences which were held proved
abortive. On many occasions we felt we
were nearing a solution of the whole
difficulty when the matter fell through.
The Minister of Labour has in season and
out of season endeavoured to find a solution for the difficulty that has arisen, and
is still prepared to find a way out of the
difficulty with which the railways are
faced to-day. The hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Nixon) raised a point, and I should like
to say that the Labour Exchange never
orders a man to go to a particular place
where a strike exists.
Mr. BEATTIE: What about Sinclair's
pork factory?
Mr. GORDON: If the Labour Exchange
suggested that there was employment to be
found at a certain place and the applicant
for work said, "There is a strike going
on at that place and I refuse to go," that
is perfectly all right. The man need not
go and he is entitled to draw his unemployment benefit. The Labour Exchange
never has been used, and I rather think
that during the period of life of this Government never will be used in the interests
of any particular section of industryeither the leaders of industry or leaders
of the trade union movement. My final
word to hon. Gentlemen on both sides of
the House is that we are anxious to effect
a settlement.
Mr. NIXON: What about the clerks?
I
Mr. GORDON: We are prepared to
meet both sections at any time in order to
arrive at a solution of the difficulty.
repeat that if the trade unions and
directors of the railway companies are

prepared to meet them in order to try to
find a way out of the difficulty.
Mr. NIXON: What about the clerks?

NON-CIRCULATING BOOK
YD 08452

Tuesday, 8th March, 1932.
The Fourth Session of the Third Parliament of Northern Ireland, appointed to
meet 8th March, 1932, in the Twentysecond year of the Reign of King George
V, was opened by the Governor (His
Grace the Duke of Abercorn, K.G.,
K.P.) in person.
The House met at Ten Minutes before
Twelve of the Clock, Mr. SPEAKER
(Right Hon. H. G. H. Mulholland, M.P.)
in the Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod
(Major T. Dalby Hackett, D.S.O.) was
announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman Usher said:
His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the
Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Three
of the Clock, and then resumed.

and delivered to the Librarian of the

Sessional Orders.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are
returned for two or more places in any
part of Northern Ireland do make their
Election for which of the places they will
serve, within one week after it shall
appear that there is no question upon the
Return for that place; and if anything
shall come in question touching the
Return or Election of any Member, he is
to withdraw during the time the matter
is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw
till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath been elected or returned
a Member of this House or endeavoured
so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt
practices, this House will proceed with
the utmost severity against all such persons as shall have been wilfully concerned
in such Bribery or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any persons hath been tampering with
any Witness in respect of his evidence to
be given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath
endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing or giving evidence,
the same is declared to be a high crime or
misdemeanour; and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against
such offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in
any case before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered:
That the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary do take
care that, during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets
leading to this House be kept free and
open, and that no obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members
to and from this House, and that no
disorder be allowed in the precincts of or
in the passages leading to this House,
during the Sitting of Parliament, and
that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant at
Arms attending this House do communicate this Order to the Commissioner of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND
RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings,
and Records of this House be printed,
being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and
that he do appoint the printing thereof;
and that no person but such as he shall
appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered: That a Committee of Privileges be appointed.
OUTLAWRIES BILL,
""
for the more effectual preventing
Clandestine Outlawries read a First
time and ordered to be read a Second
time.

King's Speech
King's Speech
8 MARCH 1932
KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to report that
the House has this day attended in the
Senate to hear his Grace's Speech, on behalf of His Majesty, to both Houses of
Parliament; of which I have for greater
accuracy obtained a copy. The Speech is
as follows:
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I view with concern the repercussion
of the world economic crisis upon those
major industries of our Country which
are dependent upon international commerce. Nevertheless, the textile trade
has benefited to a certain extent by
the recent change in the fiscal system
of the United Kingdom of Great
Britain and Northern Ireland. I trust
this improvement may be maintained,
that its sphere may be extended to
other industries in the near future, and

The King's Speech, which we have
just heard, is in some ways rather remarkable, as it takes up so much space
with the present economic crisis. This
crisis has crowded out nearly all other
subjects from our thoughts, and those of
the world. It is in every Ruler's mind,
in every Government's Exchequer, and
has got into all our pockets.
I am safe in saying that no Government in the world except our own will
balance its budget this year. In our
case it has been made possible only
by the patriotism shown by all the
British people in such a crisis as
this. They have shown themselves
to be truly an imperial race, and
one to be relied upon in time of trouble.
Our people have displayed to all their
determination to pay their debts, and to
sacrifice their all for their country's
cause. This spirit must be supported by
our leaders and rulers, and
effort
made by the Imperial Government and
our own to second the effort made by the
common people of this land.

I am glad to see in this respect, the

economies foreshadowed. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I trust that the Government will be ruthless in economy where
necessary, and that they will not hesitate
to cut down expenditure. I think the

crisis, should be helped, and we call upon

I have always been of the opinion that

"up against it," I will welcome, and I

such is

I rejoice, with the King's Speech, in

[Mr. John Johnston]
I cannot stop without referring to the
great change in the fiscal policy of this
country, which has just taken place. It
will profoundly affect all of us in Northern Ireland, and none more so than
the farming community. For the first
time in over 80 years the farmers' produce will get some protection, and not
be liable to the disastrous flood of foreign
importation as hitherto, particularly
potatoes, oats, eggs, poultry, and dairy
produce. This will give our people a
preference in the home market, and a
similar boon is foreshadowed for the
bacon industry.
This Speech winds up on a subject in
which I have personally taken a great
interest, the development of electricity.
This, if properly done, will mean everything to Northern Ireland when industry revives. It puts power and light
into every small town and village, and
makes the establishment of new industries an easy matter. It will improve
the amenities of the country side out of
all knowing. I have not seen eye to eye
with the Government in this matter. I
felt it would have been better to develop
along the lines of private ownership
rather than under Government control,
but the Government in their wisdom or
unwisdom, have decided to do both.

The world economic depression of the

I want to take this opportunity of tendering to the Prime Minister the thanks
of the Ulster farmers for the conspicuous
services he rendered to them in connection
with the import duties on certain classes
of agricultural commodities. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). I had the
honour of attending upon the Prime
Minister with different deputations, and
at all times the noble Lord, with grace,
courtesy, and wise diplomacy, succeeded
in finding a practical solution of most of
our difficulties. I would like also to
thank the Minister of Finance and other
Members of the Government who helped
to put our interests on a more satisfactory

Speaking as one with a practical
knowledge of agriculture I feel that what
has now been done should only be considered a step in the right direction. I feel
it will be found necessary, if the required
protection is to be given to farmers that
an Import Board should be set up, composed of practical, well-informed men,
to control the imports of all agricultural
products so as to stabilise the market,
and thus ensure to the farmers an economic return for their labour. I am
convinced that had this step been taken
some time ago the balance of trade would
not have gone so much against us. The
uneconomic prices which farmers were
obliged to accept made it impossible for
them to carry on.
Thus a considerable
amount of our food had to be supplied
from foreign countries, which meant that
we were sending money abroad, which
should have been kept at home. Every
acre of land going out of cultivation must
necessarily call for extended foreign markets for manufactured goods and if our
home grown food supplies fall away faster
than we can create fresh markets, the
balance of trade must go steadily against

this great victory was to leave the farming community as they were. One would
have thought from the Belfast Press that
some great achievement had been reached,

this
famous Westminster battle. But,

There was one single omission, I think.
The Prime Minister ought to have advised
the Government on that occasion that the
farmers of the Six Counties wanted a

resolutions of the County Derry farmers
that if a tariff of 20 per cent. were imposed on flax, it would practically reestablish that great industry in the Six
Counties, but I knew at the same time

predominated. Flax is admitted free,

may starve and die for all they care.
There was expressed in the Gracious
Speech a pious hope that something may

Border a little closer they would have

heavy tariff they are excluding foreign

thought that the Prime Minister would

and I say he has neglected it. It is

The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): May I add my hearty congratulations to the hon. Member for
North Armagh (Mr. John Johnston),
and the hon. Member for Antrim (Mr.
Minford) on the very excellent speeches
which they made in proposing and
seconding this Motion. I have listened to
a great many speeches in my time, and I
am glad to say they were fully up to the
high reputation of the speeches of
gentlemen to whom this particular duty
was entrusted. The hon. Member (Mr.
John Johnston) said that this was our
last meeting in this building, and therefore, perhaps, I may take the opportunity
of saying that that is so, and that when
we meet again it will be in the new
Parliament House at Stormont. What
the Government propose doing is to have
no Autumn Session
this year,
but to
clear up all the work that has to be done
before we rise, keeping the House alive,
if hon. Members will realise what I mean,
by not proroguing there and then,
finishing the business and proroguing at
later date when
we are definitely
certain when it will be convenient for the
ceremony of opening the new House to
take place. Then when we meet at
Stormont we will begin the Session of
1933, reply to the Speech from the
Throne and get over the Address, because I feel, and I am sure every Member
will feel, that it would be inappropriate
to wind up the Session after having the
a
opening ceremony. We would prefer to
open the new building at the same time
as we open the new Session of Parliament. I think it will be more appropriate for the distinguished member of
the Royal Family-whom I hope and
trust we will have, although I cannot
say so definitely to-day-to open the new
Session when he opens the new building.
Mr. DEVLIN: Would it not be well
and more appropriate if we had a dissolution first before we open the new
Parliament House?
The PRIME MINISTER: My experience of the Ulster people is that they
do not care for a great many changes.
They are quite satisfied to carry on as
they are. I know that the hon. Member is very anxious to have a Nationalist
Government, but as we are practically
two to one in the House, representing the
country, I think we will be able to manage quite well without dissolving Parliament. We will prorogue it in the
ordinary way.
Now, I come down here at the opening
of each new Session with a certain amount
of trepidation. I have never known
when I sit here what the chosen Leader
of the Opposition is going to attack the
Government upon. It is kept a dead
secret up to the last moment, and no
one knows what heavy guns will be
trained on us by the champion of the
Opposition. We shiver to think of our
past misdeeds, our sins of commission and
omission, and therefore I was somewhat
relieved to find that the first shot of the
Session is a complaint against apples.
After all, when one thinks of a community which is a very live one, occupied
with subjects of varied interest and great
importance, and finds that the combined
brains of all these clever men opposite can
only just bring up the question of apples,
or something about pottery works, and I
think a reference to loans, it provides a
barometrical index of the state of Ulster
at present.
Mr. HEALY: And Soviet flax.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am going
to deal with the question of flax. At any
rate, it gives me relief to know that we
cannot be attacked on anything of a
really serious character.
Mr. DEVLIN: Wait and see.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
The PRIME MINISTER: I presume
that the hon. Member (Mr. Devlin) will
admit that his party chose the hon. Member (Mr. Healy) to fire the heavy guns,
even if he himself comes along afterwards
as the infantry or some other arm of the
force. May I first deal with what the
leader (Mr. Healy) on this occasion has
said. He says we ought to be more
generous in our loans to the farming
community. I can guarantee that no
Government or Minister has been as
generous to the farming community as
my right hon. Friend (Sir Edward
Archdale). Bring a just case before him.
and he will treat it with the greatest
generosity as far as the limit of the financial resources of our country will admit.
But behind all this has been the consistent policy of the Government since we
took office to get the farming community
out of debt, and, if possible, to see that
they would never get into debt again.
I think all those who have lived in the
country and who realise the life of the
farmer know that there is nothing he
dreads more than being in debt, either
to the Government, or to a bank, or to
his neighbour. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). I think it is an awful thing to
have debt hanging over his head all the
time.
What have the Government done?
With the assistance of the Exchequer on
the other side, land purchase has been
practically completed. There is hardly
a holding that has not been vested in
the tenants, and that means that the
reduction from the rents to the instalments that are paid is a considerable
advantage to the farming community.
Nobody who is honest can deny that.
Then, on top of that, the Government
provide a sum of £900,000 a year in order
to relieve the farmers of rates on agricultural land and farm buildings. That is
no small matter. Coming on the top of
that is the £450,000 spent by the Government on social services, which the farmers in the country generally enjoy just
as much as the Corporation of Belfast or
any of the other local authorities. Those
two sums alone are of the utmost assistance to the farming community. Over
and above that, I find that £150,000 has
been availed of for special cases which
have been brought before the notice of
the Ministry. The hon. Member (Mr.
Healy) therefore, can rest quite satisfied
and not be so gloomy in the future when
he knows that no effort will be spared
to help the farmers along the very
difficult road which they are travelling.
Mr. HEALY: Will you supply them
with seed potatoes?
The PRIME MINISTER: My right
hon. Friend will go into that. I am not
prepared for all the various shots fired.
My right hon. Friend will deal with that
later on. The hon. Member objected
very strongly to putting into sanitary
condition the barracks of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary. I am sure he will
not get much sympathy in that connection. I am quite satisfied the desire is
that those who protect the lives and property of the people should live in decent
surroundings. I have dealt with this
matter on many occasions. I repeat that
after we took over in 1921 I inspected a
large number of barracks personally for
the purpose of ascertaining the true facts
of the case, and some of them I found
miserable in the extreme and not really
fit for decent men to live in. We have
set ourselves to improve those buildings
and make them fit for those who perform
important public duties.

The PRIME MINISTER: All the

I say
now that had it not been for co-operation

as I am concerned, I am trying to get on.
The next point was flax. The hon.
Member knows that we have done all we
could in regard to flax. The feeling was,
and still is, of course, that the linen industry is one that we must do everything
we possibly can to foster, because so many
of our people are engaged in it. It
helps all round with employment, and
gives that class of occupation to our
trained women which is a great factor
in the financial life, not only of our city
but of our whole Province. Therefore,
it was our duty to do all we could to
meet the wishes of those engaged in that
particular trade.
When the gift of the new National
Government-I call it that to flaxspinners and the trade generally was
announced, I immediately got into communication with both sides of the flax
industry. We had a conference, and out
of that conference a great deal of good is
going to take place. Hitherto there has
been rather much cutting of one another's
throats, if I may say so, in the business
from the sowing of the seed to the production of the finished linen article.
There has been too much inharmonious
communication, if I may put it in that
way, and now these sensible businessmen,
and farmers, and scutchers have shaken
hands. They met round a table and
agreed mutually among themselves for a
better understanding in future. I have
every authority for saying that in the
long run the promotion, extension, and
betterment of flax, growing are even
better assured than they would have
been by a mere 10 per cent. duty. After
all, when a crop varies between, I think,
£40 and £80 a ton, 10 per cent. is a
mere bagatelle compared with better
treatment in Ulster itself by Ulstermen
engaged in the trade. Therefore, I hope
that this agreement will mean far more
than appears on the surface.
Then the hon. Member, as usual, drew

I suppose we can hardly say legally that

Now, the two most important points in

housing of the
the working class, and,

Pending the introduction of the proposed
Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
Measure I cannot, of course, enter into
any details beyond saying that it is the
intention of the Government to focus
attention on the smaller types of houses,
and, as heretofore, to grant to local
authorities power to supplement the Government's efforts in the encouragement of
the building of these houses.
We have decided in all the circumstances, and especially in view of the
reduced cost of building material, to fix
the subsidy at £25 per house, which we
hope will be an incentive to local
authorities and private builders to continue the erection of workmen's dwellings.
In considering the proposals which we
will lay before the House, we have had
to bear in mind that the efforts which
have already been made to meet the
housing shortage have entailed the expenditure of a great deal of money, and have
placed upon the Exchequer a heavy
burden, which must continue for some
years to come, and however much we
may desire to hasten the building of more
houses we must exercise caution in placing
too severe a strain upon our resources.
Since the matter was taken in hand
by Parliament and the Government,
upwards of 25,000 houses have been
erected under the Housing and allied
Acts, and a sum of not less than approximately 23 millions has been contributed
out of State Funds to secure the erection
of these houses. The figure for Belfast
is £1,400,000, and that for the rest of
Ulster £1,390,000. For the current year
the burden upon the Exchequer in respect
of this expenditure is £156,000, a figure
which will be appreciably increased in the
coming financial year. In formulating
our proposals we have had to bear these
figures in mind, and the assistance which
we suggest should be given for the next
two years is, in our opinion, the most
generous that is possible, having regard
to financial considerations.
The Government has given anxious
thought to the question of rents in connection with houses built with the assistance of a subsidy, but we are still of
opinion that this question of rents in such
cases cannot be adjusted by governmental
action, and that the only means by which
satisfactory results in this connection can
be obtained is by encouraging the building of these smaller workmen's dwellings.
In other words, we feel there must be
an encouragement of building, and to
hamper in any way the freedom of those
who are prepared to undertake the task,
whether it be the Belfast Corporation or
any other local authority, or private
enterprise, would be to do irreparable
damage. If we lay down restrictions
about the rent to be charged afterwards,
or if we do anything which will make the
money invested in the building of houses
fly out of the country the financial extension of the City of Belfast and of
other towns is bound to suffer, and our
successors will find themselves in a great
difficulty owing to the want of foresight
on the part of their predecessors. Therefore, we feel it quite impossible, as I
say, to do anything more than to hold
out a hand of assistance to those who are
less able to help themselves.
As I said, there are two points, housing
and pork. My right hon. Friend (Sir
Edward Archdale) and I have agreed to
invite to a conference every person in
Ulster directly or indirectly connected
with this important trade. Every representative chosen will be welcome. We
both feel after long and anxious consideration that the new arrangements which
are being at the moment worked out by
the Imperial Government will be of a
very far-reaching character. I think
there is no doubt there will be a revolution in the pork trade. What we are
anxious about is that we should not be
behind the fair.
Mr. HEALY: This time?
The PRIME MINISTER: I do not
remember being behind.

about maize.

What we propose to do is to call this
meeting for the purpose of having a plan

We have not exhausted our progress by

only be accomplished by hard work. I do
not believe there is a harder worker to be

He works from morning till night.
Why, some of the people in the city here,
hard and all as they think their tasks are,
do nothing compared with what is carried
on by the farming community, and we
are all delighted to think that they are
pulling through and succeeding, and we
wish them all possible success.
Now there is only this to be said:
That both those engaged in commerce and
trade as well as the farmers themselves

with them, and to help them as far as

financial resources. We have never denied

In regard to the general question, I

these bodies as is shown across the

charitable sources. I say it is a regrettable

more outrageous state of affairs one could

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Henderson]
To save £200,000. The Minister of
Labour was told in this House that
if he saved that money thousands
of men and women would be automatically cut off. And the Minister
of Labour, obeying, I dare say, the
orders of his general, who is the Minister of Finance, immediately puts that
into operation, with what result? It is
pitiable. There is starvation everywhere
in Ulster, or at least in part of Ulster,
because I cannot get away from the fact
that this is only part of Ulster. None of
you like to be reminded of that, but as the
son of a gentleman born in County
Monaghan, I remember my father feeling
very sorely that Monaghan should be
thrown into the Free State.
I believe that this part of Ulster is being
very badly handled. You have cut down
the grants for the building of houses, and
then we hear the Prime Minister talking
about what will be done for housing, and
how they are going to house the working
people of Northern Ireland. You will
never house the working people of Northern Ireland if you reduce the subsidy from
£50 to £25. It would have been far more
honourable if you had said you have not
the money.
Instead of all this talk about
balancing your Budget, if you got down
to brass tacks and told the people the
exact financial relationship between Ulster
and the Imperial Government, we would
know where we are. But no one seems
to know where we are, not even the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Commerce. I do not believe there is a
member of the Cabinet who knows our
exact financial relationship with the
British Empire. The sooner a new policy
is adopted the better for the people of
Northern Ireland.
It is a regrettable thing that for all
time right hon. Gentlemen opposite are
going to rule this Province, for we never
can have any advancement or prosperity
or new ideas brought into operation as
long as we have such antiquated politicians
on the other side of the House.
Much as
they may have been successful in their
own businesses they have not been very
successful up to the present time as politicians beyond holding on to their very
handsome jobs. If there is anyone who
should talk about Ulster being a paradise
it is the Cabinet and their secretaries.
But I can assure you that not many of
the unemployed with whom I come in contact find it a paradise. And I come in
The
contact with thousands who are in utter
starvation and destitution due entirely to
the apathy of the Government. I have
always told the people that they get the
kind of Government they deserve.
working people of Northern Ireland have
got the Government they deserve, and the
Government they deserve is the one that
is punishing them in many ways. The
Minister of Labour very diplomatically
transferred his work to the guardians. If
£200,000 was going to be saved at the
expense of the unemployed, he should
have done the dirty work himself. Instead of doing that, he placed on the
shoulders of the guardians throughout the
country the responsibility of taking the
unemployment benefit from the people
who were entitled to it. I think that was
one of the most cowardly and one of the
meanest acts ever perpetrated by a
Cabinet Minister. If I had been a Cabinet
Minister I would have risen to the occasion
myself, and if the money was going to be
cut off I would have done it myself.
Instead of doing so, the Minister of
Labour put that responsibility on the
shoulders of the guardians. Some of
them are very human men and women;
others are very inhuman. In fact, quite
recently one of the ladies in a particular
board-I do not want to mention the

because he had three of a family and had
to seek relief from the Board of Guardians. Not so long ago the right hon.
Gentleman and his friends were advocating huge families; now they are telling
people who become unemployed that they
should not have a family at all. That is
a deplorable state of affairs, and some day
it will react on the right hon. Gentleman
opposite. I say that you have made a
blunder in regard to the cutting down of
the subsidy. What you are going to save
in the curtailment of the subsidy you are
going to pay out in unemployment grants.

cease work of that kind, when they know
that in Belfast, and in every hamlet in

poverty, and that the people are starving?
The local authorities were carrying out
work of great public utility to the

any man with a knowledge of

be employing anything from 12,000 to

I ask the Minister of Labour to lay

years, yet the umpire lays it down that

Then we come to the new Act passed

that side. The Minister of Labour
smiles. I will show him an anomaly
to-day. There is an anomaly between the
Minister of Labour and myself, and between him and the unemployed. He
could sit down to a very hearty dinner,
but there are many hundreds of people
who have not a dinner to sit down to.
I am not saying this personally, but that
is an anomaly that should be removed.
Take the case of a married woman.
Her husband is working and she is a
little longer on the exchange than they
desire her to be because she is in the
position of having two incomes. They
call that an anomaly and disallow the
married woman. That is not an anomaly
at all. The reason she goes out to work
is to assist the family income in order to
maintain a decent standard of life in the
home. The Anomalies Act was placed on
the Statute Book to remove one kind of
anomaly, that is, the high wage earner
within a period of a week. It was stated
that numbers of men were working on
Saturday and Sunday in the printing
trade and earning £5 or £6, and that
during the remainder of the week they
were drawing unemployment benefit.
Miss Margaret Bondfield made that statement. It was also said that dockers were
drawing unemployment benefit after
working two days in the week, for which
they were paid anything from £3 to £4.
Those statements were all exaggerated.
The Committee investigating the statements found that the practice was not as
extensive throughout Great Britain and
Northern Ireland as appeared from the
Press. The Press is solely responsible
for the position to-day. It has poisoned
the minds of all those decent people who
think for themselves, because when they
interpret the Anomalies Act to-day the
majority of people believe it really means
what the Press says. I want to try to
disabuse the mind of the Minister of
Labour in regard to that.
The object of the Anomalies Act has
been lost sight of, and where it was not
intended to be applied it is being applied.
Imagine a man working in a shipyard for
30 years. Last year he got a job walking
greyhounds round Celtic Park. He does
that all summer, and when he comes forward in the winter to claim benefit the
Minister of Labour puts him under the
seasonal clause, Clause 2.

in the Plaza, in Belfast, two nights a

I do not know how they could say that,
because I do not think a waitress is a
seasonal worker at all. The waitress who
resides in a seaside town and who never
leaves that town to look for any other
class of employment is a seasonal worker,
but a girl who lives in Belfast and goes
to a seaside town to get employment during the summer months and then returns
to a district where work of her kind is
available cannot be graded as a seasonal
worker. Nor did the framers of the
Regulations ever intend her to be included within the scope of Section 2.
The whole thing is being misinterpreted
and mismanaged to the detriment of
those justly entitled to receive benefit.
The other Section I hoped to have seen

says if a person is employed for one or

Insurance Acts. I that No. 3 of the

have given the public assistance committees a free hand and you know the

Another point. Why do you take war
pensions into consideration? When war
pensions were given we understood that
they were not to be taken into account
in any matter of this kind. But every
class of income is taken into account now.
I should like to hear the Parliamentary
Secretary or the Minister trying to justify
the taking of pensions into account. It
was stated in Great Britain that pensions
were given for services rendered on fields
other than the industrial field. A man
may have been disabled, but that disablement only increased his financial
responsibility, and he was granted a
pension. To-day, when that pension is
taken into account, he is being penalised
under the means test. He is asked to
keep, not only himself but his wife, on
the pension. I will give as an illustration
the case of a pensioner with 28s a week,
a married man with no family. If he
comes under the means test he has more
than the amount laid down in the
regulations, and that means that he has
to provide for his wife out of his pension,
whereas the pension was given to him by
the pension authorities to provide for
himself.
You should try to remove the anomaly
of including pensions in the family
income, and of including other things
which have no concern with anyone.
What right have you to say that because
a lodger in my house is earning £2 10s a
week the income of my house is £2 10s?
The lodger may be giving me only 30s.
When I say what the lodger gives to the
house, the official says it is not what he
gives, it is what he earns, that matters.
The official goes to the place where the
lodger works and inquiries what his wages
are, and the amount is taken into consideration by the committees on the
ground that the people of the house are
living in common. That class of intimidation should be stopped immediately.
To
say that people who are not related are
living in common is an outrageous thing.
That is the basis of calculation and the
mentality that has always applied on
the Lisburn Road. They did it when I
was there, and I presume they still continue it. They also ask particulars of
every little thing, such as co-operative
savings, national savings certificates.
Everything is included, and the applicant
is faced with a string of questions which
he could answer only with the advice of
a lawyer.
I think that in view of the misinterpretation of the Acts of Parliament that
is prevalent, this Amendment of mine

The Government should bring in some

poverty and destitution which are rampant throughout the Six Counties, and
thereby save the assets of the nation.
Money is not an asset of the nation.

remember very well quoting at an

Il fares the land, to hast'ning ills
a prey,

When once destroy'd can never be
supplied.

9 MARCH 1932
Mr. O'NEILL: It may be, but your own
figures in the supplementary estimate do
not bear the interpretation you put upon
it because if you had less unemployment you would have less cost. You will
have an opportunity of explaining how
that occurred.
I will give you an instance of how I
believe the officials of the Ministry go to
the very extreme in order to put people
off unemployment insurance benefit. A
couple of years ago in this House I raised
a particular case regarding officials employed in the municipal baths at Warrenpoint, and the same state of affairs exists
to-day. There are probably not more
than half a dozen persons employed in
those baths, but the Ministry of Labour
have been guilty of a most indefensible
act in holding that while some of these
officers have to be insured, others have
not. For instance, the boilerman has
not to be insured under the Unemployment Insurance Acts, while the superintendent of the baths, who is a full time
officer, has to be insured. This question
has been before the Ministry before now,
and an explanation of their action has
been given by the Ministry which I think
this House would hardly care to endorse.
However, the view taken by the Ministry,
or by officials of the Ministry, has deprived certain of these officers of benefits
that otherwise they would be entitled to.
This is an extract from a letter from one
of the officials of the Ministry of
Labour:
I have to inform you that the boilerman, female attendant, washerwoman,
and the boy who cleans the boxes, etc.,
are not required to be insured under
the Unemployment Insurance Acts.
Contributions under these Acts are,
however, required to be paid in respect.
of the Baths Superintendent and the
ticket collector.
That seems to me to be cutting the
thing very fine. The baths superintendent is a full time officer and never has
received unemployment benefit. The
other officers referred to are not full time
employees, but are what are called
seasonal workers, and yet they are not
required to be insured, and are therefore
not elegible for benefit. I think that
such a decision on the part of the Ministry
is indefensible, and it only goes to show
the extremes to which the officials of the
Ministry will go in order to prevent people
receiving benefit. In a further letter
from the Ministry the official says:-
I have to inform you that the reason
the boilerman at the Municipal Baths
is excepted from the scope of the Unemployment Insurance Acts is because
his duties are of a domestic character.
The Superintendent of the Baths is,
however, required to be insured, as his
duties are other than of a domestic
character.
Both these persons are in the same
employment, and while one is never unemployed, and never receives unemployment benefit, he is required to be insured,
while the other, who is only seasonally
employed, is not required to be insured
and therefore is never entitled to receive
unemployment benefit. I say that this
is a typical example of the effort of the
Ministry of Labour to employ every device
possible to prevent people from securing
the benefits which Acts like this are designed to give them. There surely can
be no difference between the case of a
boilerman who is employed for six months
in the year at the baths, and a man who
is employed as a boilerman in any other
firm during the winter months. I have
mentioned this case to show that some
alteration should be made in the conditions necessary to secure unemployment
benefit. This practice of simply cutting
people off benefit cannot be justified in
the present state of affairs. My own
impression is that the Ministry of Labour
could administer the present Acts with a
good deal more advantage to the insured
people, and that no new legislation is
required to remedy these grievances.
However, if any new legislation is considered necessary the Minister should come
to the House and ask for it, because you
cannot allow people to remain in a state
of absolute starvation. Therefore. I think
it is the duty of the House now, at the
beginning of their new Session, to alter
their Unemployment Insurance Acts so as
to secure that no person will be allowed
to die of want.

There is another industry which was
started in Northern Ireland. This will
be of interest to the agricultural Members
who sit on the county boards as well as
to the Prime Minister. A local firm
last year started a new industry which
gave a great deal of employment. They
were able to supply the Belfast Corporation with a certain commodity at
27s 3d a ton. Their competitors, who
thought they had a monopoly of this business, were charging £3 3s a ton. What

reduced their price to 23s 6d a ton the
cross-Channel firm, which was out to
destroy any attempt by this local firm to
establish a footing in Northern Ireland
and to create work here, sent word that
they would supply the commodity from

a ton the year before. That is what we

the suggestion put forward by the Prime
Minister with regard to creating new industries is bound to fail. There is no

1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the order prohibiting Mr. De Valera, President of the
Irish Free State Executive Government,
from entering any part of Northern Ireland, except County Antrim, is still in
force.
SECRE-
The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): No, sir.
Mr. HENDERSON: Arising out of
that reply, may we take it for granted

Northern Ireland on any occasion he

Mr. HEALY: Also arising out of that
will the hon. Gentleman tell us what the

SHORT LEAVE IN THE ROYAL
ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether short leave granted
to members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, under Barrack Regulation 11,
has in some cases been curtailed by an
order made on May 3rd, 1931, which enjoins that any such leave already granted
would be cancelled when an inspection
by the Commissioner or District Inspector
was notified, except leave granted for
urgent reasons; whether such order causes
inconvenience and hardship to men who
have made arrangements before the inspection was notified and who have not
time to cancel those arrangements.
Mr. HANNA: Short leave is a
privilege, the taking of which involves
no elaborate previous arrangements, and
is granted only subject to the condition
that it does not involve interference with
or absence from any particular duty.
Apparently the impression appears to
have prevailed in certain quarters that
this short leave was a right rather than
a privilege, and the directions issued by
the Commissioner of Police in May last
were intended to correct this wrong
view.
There are no grounds for the suggestion that attendance at inspections causes
inconvenience or hardship to the men,
who are fully aware that the granting
of the privilege of short leave is contingent on the due performance of such
duties as may be necessary.
MARKETING OF AGRICULTURAL
PRODUCE.
3. Mr. DEVLIN asked the Prime Minister whether he is prepared to set up a
committee, representative of all parties
in the House, to devise an agricultural
policy for Northern Ireland, with special
reference to the marketing of agricultural
produce.
The PRIME MINISTER: The Government is confident that the far-sighted
policy which my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Agriculture, is pursuing
adequately meets the requirements of the
farming communtiy, and that as a result
of the various Acts prescribing the
marketing of agricultural produce already
on the Statute Book, satisfactory progress
is being made. I am not convinced that
any advantage would be gained by adopting the suggestion of the honourable Member. However, needless to say, if any
Member can put forward constructive
suggestions they will be carefully and
sympathetically considered by my right
honourable Friend.

Question of Privilege.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member for
Woodvale (Mr. Nixon) has raised a question of privilege. I understand it relates
to a question which he sent into my office
and which has been disallowed. The
ordinary procedure under circumstances
where a question has been disallowed is
to convey to the hon. Member concerned
at the earliest moment an intimation
of the fact that the question has been
disallowed. In this case no discourtesy was, of course, intended, but,
unfortunately, through inadvertence the
hon. Member was not notified. It was a
pure mistake for which I take full blame
and responsibility, as it is my duty to
see that intimation is conveyed to the
hon. Member that his question has been
disallowed. I hope that under the circumstances the hon. Member will accept
my apology.
Mr. NIXON: Having regard to the
way you have tendered it, I certainly
do accept your apology. This is not the
first time this has occurred, but I am
sure it will be the last.

Now I have charged the Government

That is what the Roads Tribunal really

be paid by the people using the roads.
And that was all got up by the Northern

and making the country poorer than it is.
and creating unemployment. To do that
we have in this country the highest road

Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
10 MARCH 1932
The Northern Government would not
have that because they apparently want
to create unemployment. They put a
duty on that no ordinary man can pay,
and which swallows all his earnings before he starts. Many a man with a little
bit of money or with a few sons, if
allowed, could get a charabane or a bus,
employ his sons and earn a living by
charging what would pay him and keep
him going.
But the Northern Government say "No. You cannot do that. We
have passed an Act of Parliament by
virtue of which we traffic in the sale of
the King's highway." It is no longer
free. There is only one freeman in Ulster
now, as I heard the hon. Member for
Shankill say a short time ago. I heard
the Parliamentary Secretary standing
where he is now say-and the Minister of
Labour will not laugh when he hears itin bringing forward an Insurance Bill that
one of the reasons for bringing forward
the Bill was owing to the starvation-the
expression he used was "owing to the
people being under-fed"-they were not
able to work, and the Insurance Bill was
brought forward for the purpose of relieving them. Could there be a greater
indictment of any country?
Could anything graver come from this side than
came from the Parliamentary Secretary
on that occasion-that in this advanced
age in this great city, the capital of Northern Ireland, a city we are proud of, a
city we delight in and put before any
other city, that a Gentleman after being
eleven years in office, and after taking
£11,000 for looking after the unemployed,
gets up here and tells us that these people
are so badly under-fed that they are not
able to carry on work?
The Minister of Labour often tells us
about being up on that famous hill at
Comber when he begins to get despondent
and surveying from its height his great
army of unemployed, where he can look to
Hillhall, which, a short time ago, was the
scene where a man named Truesdale died
of starvation. There is many a one who
dies of starvation that there is not a word
about. I say we can boil it all down to
this one point. We can do away with
the six points we heard about yesterday,
and the one point is this: the Government
may not be able to solve the unemployment problem, notwithstanding the
numerous promises they made. Notwithstanding that four or five months ago they
covered every gable of the walls in West
Belfast with placards "Vote for Browne
and Employment;" they are not able to
solve the unemployment problem. There
is one thing they can do, and that is, they
can make provision, by legislation or
otherwise, whereby no family will be left
destitute or without an income. There
are thousands of families in this city at
the present time with only 10/- or 15/-,
or perhaps £1 a week to live on. That is
a disgrace to the Government; it is a disgrace to Northern Ireland; it is a disgrace
to the Empire, and it is a disgrace to
civilisation.

listened with great attention to the speech

He referred to the public assistance

Debate on the Address

[Mr. Byrne]
Sometimes they continue the grant the
applicant was formerly receiving and
sometimes they reduce it. I have known
cases where people, two days after being
granted benefit for four or eight weeks,
have had to go before a court of referees
and their benefit has been disallowed.
Before I left home to-day a man called
on me and handed me a form showing
that he had been cut off unemployment
benefit on the ground that he was not
normally in insurable employment. I
asked him what he usually worked at,
and he said he had worked practically all
his life as a builder's labourer. He had
been out of work for almost two years
and now his unemployment benefit had
been stopped.
After getting benefit for two years he
was told there was no more money for
him, and he wanted to know what he
would do. He had a wife and three of a
family, and I say it is most unfair that,
when a man has worked practically all
his life as a builder's labourer and has
been receiving unemployment benefit,
that that benefit should be discontinued
on the ground that the man is not in
insurable employment. We on this side
of the House have made the best case we
can for these poor people, and I maintain
it is the duty of the Government-I do
not care where the money comes fromto see that they do not starve. It is
deplorable when a person like myself has
to meet these people day after day, hear
the strong case they make, and feel that
one is unable to do anything for them.
It has been stated, and I repeat it, that
there are people who have been signing
at the Labour Exchange for six and eight.
years. I know houses where three single
men are living. They have to keep the
house, and in some cases a mother and
perhaps a sister, and although all three.
men are out of employment not one of
them is receiving benefit.
These young men are going about the
streets day after day, and what is to be
done with them. Some provision should
be made for people of that sort, and I say
it is the duty of the Government to ensure
that they do not starve. I am not one
of those who would encourage people to
do anything rash, but a man to whom I
was speaking the other day, who had been
treated in the way I have tried to convey
to the House, said, "What am I to do?
I have a wife and three children, and I
am going home. If I steal I have to go
"
to gaol, and I cannot starve.' I must
say that I was very sorry for this poor
man. The Government should form some
committee away from the Labour
Exchange where such people as these
could register, disclose their circumstances, and obtain some relief.
There is another matter I desire to
refer to regarding seasonal workers. If a
man works for only six months in the
year, in what is termed seasonal employment, although he has to stamp his card
for twenty-six weeks, he does not get a
single farthing in benefit in respect of
those stamps when he is unemployed
during either the summer or winter. I
do not say that these people should be
entitled to receive benefit for six months
when they have worked for only six
months, but I do contend that they should
receive benefit for some period, say two
months, in respect of their contributions
for twenty-six weeks. In conclusion, if

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I think it will be admitted

In the first place, he asked me what was

It is that as regards unemployment benefit, both in

Britain so that equal conditions should

exist throughout the whole of the United

What are the facts? As regards unemployment benefit alone, approximately

and threequarter millions was paid last

and old age.
When the Government representing this small area is putting up
that huge sum, almost half of our total
income, towards the relief of distress, I

Mr. ANDREWS: I come a little further. The public assistance committees
have been referred to at considerable
length. It has been suggested that their
administration has been harsh and cruel.
I am not responsible for their administration because Parliament has decided that
they, and they alone, shall have the charge
of deciding not whether a person is entitled to benefit but, if the courts of referees and umpire decide that the person
is entitled to benefit, they decide the
amount the person is to receive weekly
having regard to his actual need. Now,
why was that change made? Simply because the Unemployment Fund in Great
Britain had got into debt to the extent
of £115,000,000. An hon. Member said
a few minutes ago that the Northern
Government should not have been afraid
to pledge our resources in order to help
the unemployed. He evidently forgot
that our Unemployment Fund is overdrawn to the extent of approximately
£5,000,000, so that the two funds taken
together, were overdrawn to the extent of
£120,000,000-a
-an enormous sum which
was affecting the whole financial structure
of the Kingdom. Borrowing could not go
on indefinitely; there had to be a change.
What was the change that was made?
It was decided that insured persons should
receive the statutory benefit to which they
were entitled on the contributions which
they had paid upon an actuarial basis,
and that meant that the maximum amount
in any one year, which an insured person
was entitled to receive as standard benefit
was for twenty-six weeks. It was recognised in Great Britain and here as well,
that when the twenty-six weeks came to
an end the position of many homes might
be serious if some further provision was
not made. How could that provision be
made most justly and most fairly? By
what was called the means test? That
means test was to be applied with the object
of placing in those homes where there is
the greatest need, such money as is available, and I want to say here clearly and
frankly, that I feel that the public assistance committees have, without fear or
favour, and with a great deal of public
spirit, undertaken this duty. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). They are not
acting harshly, and I can prove that is so,
for the position is simply this. In all,
the public assistance committees have
reviewed 24,463 cases. They have not
deprived everybody of payment, quite
the contrary. They have given full
benefit to 9,218 persons or to 38 per cent.
of the entire number reviewed. They have
given reduced benefit to 10,718 persons,
or 44 per cent. of the cases reviewed, and
there have been "nil" determinations in
only 4,529 cases or 18 per cent. What of
those cases that have got benefit on a reduced scale? On the average, they have
got two-thirds of their statutory allowance
We come a little further along. We
have heard a great deal about the
Anomalies Act and how harshly that has

Debate on the Address
Debate on the Address
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
In the first place it was the Socialist
Government which introduced the Anomalies Act, not the present National
Government.
Mr. BEATTIE: You accepted it.
Mr. ANDREWS: Under the Anomalies Act the number of claims in the
whole of Northern Ireland which have been
disallowed up to the present has only been
2,590. It is true that we accepted the
Act as the hon. Member (Mr. Beattie)
has said. Why? Because it has been,
as I have already indicated, the considered policy of the Government since
we came into power, that the best we can
do for our people here is to preserve in
this connection British standards. Hon.
Members cannot have it both ways. If they
do not approve of the Reinsurance
Agreement which means parity throughout the whole of the United Kingdom,
let them have the courage to say it and
we know where they stand, but if they
accept the Reinsurance Agreement, which
since it was entered into has brought
to our Fund on the average three-quarters
of a million a year, and which I look upon
as the charter of our working people for
all time as regards these social standards
-I say if they accept the Reinsurance
Agreement as the best possible, then they
must admit that the conditions under
which that Agreement exists must be
adhered to, and that is parity in all
things with Great Britain.
Therefore, it is perfectly futile for hon.
Members to get up in their places day
after day in this House and say, "You
ought not to do this, you ought not to
have public assistance committees at all,
you ought to have the courage to do this
job yourself, you ought to appoint a
dictator in the form of an insurance
officer to settle who is to get benefit, you
ought to do away with courts of referees
and umpire and have the courage to act
in all these matters as the Minister of
Labour should." Of course, that position
is absurd. Furthermore, when my Department had a discretionary power-it
has none now-I was criticised day after
day because it was suggested that I was
using that discretionary power, and that
the insurance officer was also using it
against the interests of claimants. I
take it as a compliment that hon. Members wish that power restored to me, but
the law does not provide for it, and as
long as the Minister of Labour in Great
Britain is not charged with that grave
responsibility I will take jolly good care
that I shall not be charged with it here.

It may occur, after a public assistance committee has decided that the

he is not entitled to get anything at all

Mr. ANDREWS: Excuse me for a

There has been a great deal of talk also

reasonably near correct. Why do they
continue to register? In the first place
it is one of the ways of obtaining employment, and the exchanges have actually
last year, notwithstanding the depression
in trade, found work for 33,891 persons,
so that if a person is not registering at
the exchange he is not taking one of the
ways of obtaining employment.
But there is another reason why a
person who is unemployed should continue to register. As the hon. Member
for Pottinger knows very well, he does
so in order to get his health insurance
card franked, so that if sickness falls
upon him he will be able to obtain benefit.
Supposing I admit that the 62,496 persons
at present registered as unemployed may
be a few thousands out, it does not follow
at all that the number of 13,651 persons
who are employed now who were not
employed a year ago is incorrect. For this
reason, if the figure of 62,000 odd is not
right now the corresponding figure of a
year ago was probably inaccurate
the same extent, and, as the figure quoted
in his Majesty's Gracious Speech was the
difference, the difference, therefore, is
certainly annroximately right.
to
I want now to give another reason why
I feel these figures are approximately
correct. The reason I am speaking on
this subject at length is that the question
of the incorrectness of the figures is continually being raised. We know very
closely the number of people actually in
work, because we know there are in
Northern Ireland 270,000 insured persons,
and if we take from the 270,000 insured
persons the number of books lodged at
the Exchanges, and if we add to that
4 per cent. to cover those who are sick,
and who may not be registering, we find
that the number of those insured persons
at present in employment is 190,000 odd.
Last year the figures made up on exactly
the same basis showed about 174,000, a
difference of 16,000, and if you make an
allowance for the fact that the insured
population has risen during the past year
by a few thousands, this way of arriving
at the decreased number of unemployed
checks the figure of 13,651 within a few
hundreds.
The hon. Member for Central (Mr.
Devlin) went on to ask me what the
Government had done to help to provide
employment for our people. One thing
we have done is that we have provided
security for capital, and that is the very
foundation upon which capital must rest.
We have done our best to encourage shipowners to place orders with our shipyards,

I suggest that one of the first ways is

Then there is another aspect of the
question to which the Prime Minister
has referred on more than on occasion.
That is the development of the whole
system of agriculture on scientific lines.
I have the greatest possible sympathy
with him in regard to that, but I would
remind him of this fact that the country
that has made the greatest progress in
agricultural development inside the last
eighty years or so less than that, the
last sixty or seventy years-Denmarkhas done so not through legislation but
through education. Denmark was practically down and out in 1864 when the Germans took the two duchies from them, but
they started to educate the people, and
through education the great farming cooperative movement grew. It is due to
that, and to that alone, that the agricultural condition of Denmark is what it
is to-day.

I
want to face the hard stern facts that are

we can extricate the country from the

For the past eight years we have heard
a little but not enough about the Prime
Minister's prophecies. He burkes, I
always notice, reference to those prophecies very naively, but it is common
knowledge that the Prime Minister over
and over again said that given a proper

paradise he began, I saw, to qualify the
