paradise compared with the internal conditions that exist in other countries.
But what has been told us from day to day
from month to month and from year to
year is that the conditions are improving.
That is what I consider Couéism.
There was a Professor Coué who said if
you kept on suggesting to yourself that you
were getting better if you were financially
embarrassed you would be made financially affluent. If you had some serious
disease you should forget about it and say
you were better. That is what the Prime
Minister has been dishing up to the unfortunate people of the Six Counties for
the past eight years. Day by day, was
the formula of Professor Coué; day by
day in every way I am getting better
and better. The Prime Minister of the
Six Counties is the one outstanding
memorial of Professor Coué. Day by
day in every way we are getting better
and better, but every day it is getting
worse and worse.
I want to refer particularly to a certain aspect of the discussions in this
House. The Parliamentary Secretary
yesterday said that the ideal State was
the State that was prospering industrially.
Now we are not dealing with an indus
trial State. We are dealing with a State
that is preponderatingly agricultural, and
I say that, notwithstanding that a number of back benchers represent agricultural constituencies and are fully in sympathy with every movement that can be
put on foot to bring to good health and

Government as represented by the front

the ideas and ideals of agriculture more
about the streets of Belfast and about

aspirations, than we hear about the agricultural community from year's end to
year's end.
So long as the agricultural community
of the Six Counties, who like the agriculturists of every country are the mainstay of the industry and the very basis
of the wealth and stability-so long as
they are ignored by front benchers and
shoved aside by the mentality of Belfast,
you will deserve the ignominious title
this Government has got of a Belfast

ignominiously known as the Belfast

Government and their supporters rush

falling.
I was very much surprised to find to-day

Professor Corkey) uttering a tale of woe

I have seldom heard, to the effect
that the world was whirling headlong to
decay, that rationalisation of the most
drastic kind
was apparently the only
remedy, that we did not exactly know
where we were, and that they would be
wise men who could evolve any remedy for
the state of affairs that exists. I have
never heard such a piteously doleful and

the Member for the University. The only
thing that puzzled me while he was delivering it was how the hon. Member
could reconcile that doleful prophecy and
that expression of inability to see any
cure for the present state of affairs with
the basic principles of Christianity. I
only hope that on his return to this holy
place he will develop a more Christian

world. If he wants to find a remedy for
these things that he and we all deplore
so much I would suggest that he should
read the Encyclical on Labour issued
some years ago by Leo XIII.

Major McCORMICK: I should like to

may be, it is clearly the duty of the
Government to give effect to such legislation, and to see that, whilst these

were let

Mr. DEVLIN: A few days ago I ventured to raise .in the House the, to me,
all-important question of the marketing
of agricultural produce, with special
relation to transit, and the Prime Minister-I think he was impressed with the
importance of the matter at the timethen said he would discuss the matter with
me. I waited for the invitation to discuss the matter from then until now, but
the invitation has not been extended. I.
therefore, put a question upon the Order
Paper to-day. I notice the Prime Minister has entirely changed his attitude. I
do not know why he has done so, because
in my judgment if we had less talk in this
House and elsewhere of our interest in
the farmers and in agriculture, and more
practical work for the farmers and agriculture, it would be far better for us.
I had not before me at the time the
fact that I have since discovered-and
which I discovered largely because the
matter was mentioned by the Prime
Minister-that this question has already
been dealt with. The question I am
raising now is a matter of pressing public
importance and is most vital to all our
interests. It was really so vital and
important six years ago that the Prime
Minister set up a Committee for the purpose of taking evidence and of coming to
conclusions upon the basis of that evidence as to the best way in which this
matter could be dealt with. That Committee, I gather, was composed of a
number of political and other supporters
of the Prime Minister. Its chairman
was Mr. John M. Mark, M.P.; the next
inost important member of it was Mr.
William Grant, M.P., and the other
gentlemen whose names are here are, with
one exception, I understand, strong poli
tical supporters of the noble Lord.
That Committee was appointed, and
the terms of reference were very simple;
in fact, they were practically on the same
lines as the question I put to the Prime
Minister. It was a Committee to inquire
into---
(a) The cost of transit of farm
produce;
(b) the causes of the difference in
prices obtained by producers and the
prices charged to consumers; and
(c) the methods of marketing agri.
cultural produce generally..
If the government, of which the noble
Lord, the Prime Minister, is the head,
thought it important six years ago, when
agriculture was in a less parlous condition
than it is to-day, to set up a Committee
of this character to explore the question
and submit recommendations as to the
result of their explorations and inquiries,
surely it is rather a contemptuous thing
for the Prime Minister to treat my suggestion in the way he has done, at the
end of six years, during which time agriculture has passed through a period which
has caused much disquietude to those engaged in that occupation?
That Committee sat and heard evidence,
and I would like to read to the House
one of the paragraphs in their Report.
The Committee animadverted upon the
fact that several vested interests refused
to be represented or to give evidence befor it. They seem to be a very powerful
body. They seem either to have stupefied
the Government or prevented them from
making a single improvement. After
animadverting upon the action of several
public bodies who refused to give evidence
or be represented before the Committee,
the Report states:
-
"The Committee have, however, received general evidence from reliable
and very varied sources to the effect
that the present costs of transit, even
if they can be shown to be compatible
with working expenses are nevertheless
so high as to constitute a very grave
impediment and, in some cases to which
we shall refer later, a virtual bar to
the marketing of Northern Ireland
farm produce."
Adjournment-
Agricultural Produce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Devlin]
That is a very serious statement for a
Committee appointed by the Government
to deal with agriculturists and those engaged in agricultural matters to make.
They go on to say:
"The need for cheap transport was
never greater in connection with the
agricultural industry than it is to-day."
That is in 1927. Five years have come
and gone since then.
"The need for cheap transport was
never greater in connection with the
agricultural industry than it is to-day.
Our Northern Ireland farmers are now
faced with the keenest possible competition in the British markets which
constitute the main outlets for their
produce. Apart from other factors
which are enabling overseas exporters
to obtain a firm footing in British
markets, is the fact that frequently it
costs them much less for the conveyance of their produce to those markets
than their North of Ireland competitors
are compelled to expend for the same
service."
Then they go on to give examples.
Would the House listen to the examples.
"Apples.
I hope the Prime Minister does not mind
my mentioning apples-
"Apples in barrels are carried from
New York, Boston, Nova Scotia, etc.,
to any port in the United Kingdom for
3s 9d per barrel; while apples in
barrels from many stations in the
County Armagh cost 4s 5d per barrel
to London.
"Eggs from Enniskillen to Liverpool
cost 65s per ton, whereas eggs from
Hamburg to Liverpool cost 50s per
ton."
They go on to say that similar examples
could be multiplied. They proceed:
"So keen has this competition become
that it is now a very obvious and
urgent fact that, unless something can
be done to enable our producers to
compete in British markets on equal
terms with overseas exporters, there
is a grave danger of a serious diminution in Northern Ireland of agricultural
exports. It is unnecessary to labour
the disastrous consequences which such
an eventuality would entail not only
for our farmers but also the carrying companies."
Since I got this report I was going to
ask for a whole day to discuss the matter,
because this is a very valuable document.
It has given in simple language to the
public and to all who are interested in
the question a very clear and explanatory
statement not only of the conditions that
existed but also of the dangers that lay
ahead of agriculture owing to the deficiencies, if I may use the term, in regard to transit.
case.
Now the furamental fact of the
situation is this: As I said before, I
am not an agriculturist. I am no
authority on agricultural matters, though
I trust, and it is the only thing I claim,
that I have some commonsense and power
of observation. What struck rue in reading the other day statistics compiled by
a very important person engaged in a
large way in agriculture in England-and
the same applies here- -was that he
pointed out the one irresistible fact that
for every £10 paid by the consumer for
agricultural produce the farmer only receives £3. And then he went on to say
that if the farmer could get £1 additional
for what he produces it would put the
farmer in a very strong and firm position.
I take that as the foundation of my
In the first place, if that is the
case and it is incontestable-then I say
that it is a grave situation that people
in the towns and cities, whose food will
be taxed to a greater extent later on,
have to pay £10 for what the farmer only
gets £3. There is a margin of £7. This
Government have been dabbling in legislation, carrying vexatious measures which
have caused resentment amongst our
farmers. I am not going to say whether
the Government are right or whether
the apple growers are right on this
question. I have taken a certain view
upon that apple question, and it is that
before you begin to tamper with people's

it a first consideration to bring those
people into conference and consult them,

as to the methods by which their trade
could be improved. If somebody comes
to me and says: "You cannot conduct
your business at all. I will go in, conduct it for you, and show you more profitable methods by which you can carry on
your business," I would say to that man:
"Well, show me how it can be done."
You have passed Measures of which the
Prime Minister boasted to-day. Whether
they are good Measures or bad Measures

I do not know, but this I do know that

a Committee to which anybody on that

I respectfully say to the Prime Minister

really desirous of giving the practical men
an opportunity of bringing forward their
policy.

The PRIME MINISTER: With regard to the building of the Royal Courts
of Justice as I prefer to hear them
called-in Belfast, the question of the

to present us with a brick building. All
Public Works and Buildings 208
Supplementary Estimates-
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[The Prime Minister]
the plans were prepared and the Estimates were obtained along that line. My
right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, and myself went over to London
entirely in the interests of the City of
Belfast, because we felt that, with such a
magnificent building to be erected, it
would be appropriate that it should be
built in stone instead of brick. We felt
that the dignity of the city and the
harmony of the City Hall, and many other
fine buildings in the town would be rather
marred if there were to be established
such a large building as the Royal Courts
of Justice in brick, which was more or
less alien to the fine erections in the city.
It was nothing to the Government, so far
as that was concerned, because, of course,
a large brick building would have been
very fine, but we did have the feelings of
the citizens generally in mind and, therefore, we pressed the British Government
of the day to accommodate us by putting
in stone instead of brick
It has to be borne in mind by hon.
Members of this Committee as well as by
the outside public-and we cannot repeat
it often enough—that the British Government are making us a present of
both our Parliament House and Administrative Buildings and the Royal Courts of
Justice, and it is somewhat delicate and
somewhat difficult to approach those who
are making a present to tell them exactly
what you want in that present. In other
words, the whole thing was a delicate
operation. We had to treat the donors
as making a very gracious gift to our area
and not interfere too much with the way
in which they carried out this present.
In the ordinary course we had very little
to do with the form the gifts would take,
and I think, with the single exception of
asking them kindly to put in stone instead
of brick, we have left the whole matter
very largely in their hands, except where
they were good enough to consult my
right hon. Friends and myself as to the
accommodation required and the proper
way in which the rooms should be
allocated. And, in reply to the hon.
Member for Pottinger (Mr. Beattie) and
also to the criticism of the hon. Member
for the Central Division (Mr. Devlin), it
has to be borne in mind that the Parliament House will hold the whole of our
Civil Service; that is to say it is not only
a Parliament House but the home of our
Civil Service, plus some accommodation
in the Royal Courts of Justice
Now we came to this arrangement with
the Imperial authorities. They said, "It
is really asking a good deal for us to
change our plans from brick to stone.
However, as you have made certain concessions in regard to the other building
which have saved the Treasury in Great
Britain a very large sum of money, we
will at least help you in order to save the
amenities of the City of Belfast.
"" And
they were so sympathetic that, although
the additional expense would amount to
£27,500, they said they would divide that
with us, so that our share would be just
one-half of £27,500, and they would add
to their gift the remaining portion of
that sum. That was generous. It was
difficult for us to do more than call
attention, as we frequently did, to our
magnificent granite here in the Mourne
Mountains. In the case of the new Parliament and Administrative Buildings
they met us to a large extent, and hon.
Members, when they go up there, can see

local granite. So far as the main buildings are concerned they had to import a

it technically, that, although it was easy
to obtain blocks of granite for the purpose of the steps and the basement work,
it was almost impossible to get out of
any quarry the large quantity that would
be required for the facing of the building.
Not only that, but the cost would have
been very much greater. I understand
it would have been doubled, so that, instead of having to divide the sum of
£27,500, we would have had to divide

all the circumstances we thought the
generosity of the British Government was
such that it would ill become any of us
to criticise unduly what they inteded to

Mr. CRAWFORD: I should like to

the Criminal Injuries Act, should the

the premiums? It would look to me as

Committee had this matter under consideration on various occasions, and they
were assured by the respective Ministries
that everything was o.k. so far as insurance was concerned. I hope the
question of the hon. Member for Mid-
Antrim (Mr. Crawford) will be answered,
and answered clearly. I should like to
know why the Government had not this
wardress insured.
Mr. JOHNSTON: The County Council
by law is liable for criminal injuries, and
the
Government elected to pay the
amount instead of having the County
Council made liable for the expense. The
insurance company does not come into it.
There was a law passed here that civil
servants who were injured should be able
to make the council of the county in
which they were injured liable. The
Government has come to the rescue of the
County Council of Armagh, and I think
the question of insurance does not arise.
Mr. BEATTIE: I should like to know
if the Government are running risks as a
result of which they may be called upon
at times to make payments of this kind.
You should set up immediately a scheme
of national insurance whereby you could
have your own insurance fund for cases
like this. The sooner you establish such
a scheme under State management the
better. We are running risks, and our
whole assets may go by the board and we
may be left penniless as soon as England
ceases to give financial assistance to Northern Ireland. We must get an
assurance from the Minister that the
Government are prepared to set up a
State insurance scheme for purposes of
this nature.
The CHAIRMAN: I am afraid that
is asking a good deal more than can be
given under this Vote.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Surely the question
as to whether wardresses are insured can
be answered? If they are insured, surely
the insurance company is liable.

Sir DAWSON BATES: There appears

entitled to pensions. If they are injured

way with their rights as citizens to make
a claim for injury under the Malicious
Injury Acts. Insurance has nothing to
do with it.

policy of encouraging the provision of

NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum, not exceeding £2,400, be granted to
Majesty for the service of the year ending
on the 31st of March, 1932, to defray the
grant-in-aid of the cost of Benefits and
Expenses of administration under the
National Health Insurance Acts."
Mr. GORDON: I feel that I will have
the support of every Member of the Committee in presenting this Supplementary
Estimate, and more especially will I have
the support of my hon. Friend (Mr.
Beattie) who sits on the Front Opposition
Bench.
Under the National Health Insurance
Act, 1931, provision is made for the prolongation in health insurance of certain
classes of persons who would otherwise
lose their health and pensions rights.
The additional charge on the funds of
approved societies resulting from this prolongation is met by the Exchequer, which
pays over to the approved societies a sum
representing the value of 36 contributions
for each member benefiting by prolongation. The total charge on the Exchequer for these contributions is now
estimated at £2,400-the amount shown
in the Supplementary Estimate.
This sum will meet the cost of prolongation up to 31st December last the
date fixed by the National Health Insurance Act (Northern Ireland), 1931.
The cost of the further prolongation to
31st December,1932, under the National
Health Insurance (No. 2) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1931, is included in the 1932-33
Estimates for Health Insurance. I beg
to move.

ELECTRICITY IN EAST DOWN
AREA.
1. Lieut.-Colonel GORDON asked the
Minister of Commerce whether he can
state in what areas in East Down will the
Electricity Board operate, and give an
approximate date when current will be
available.
The
MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): My hon. and gallant
Friend will appreciate that the Electricity
Board is an independent entity and not
under the control of my Ministry. I
have, however, had inquiries made and
am informed that work is at present proceeding on the construction of a 33,000
volt line which will link Belfast with
Newtownards and Comber, and thereafter
form a junction with the existing Belfast,
Holywood, and Bangor line at Bangor.
The Electricity Board propose to put in
hand very shortly the construction of an
11,000 volt main transmission line
to connect Bangor, Groomsport, Donaghadee, and Millisle, and also a 33,000 volt
line connecting the Board's system at
Poyntzpass with Newry.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
A contract has also been placed
for the provision of low tension distribution systems in Newtownards,
Comber, Groomsport, and Millisle, and it
is anticipated that supplies of electricity
will be available in these centres before
the winter of 1932-33.
The Board is not at the moment in a
position to give an exact date when its
main transmission system will be extended to the remainder of the eastern
portion of County Down. I am informed,
however, that the necessary surveys are
being gradually undertaken.
The question as to the extension of the
Board's supply system to particular areas
is largely dependent upon the extent of
the load available. If, therefore, my
hon. and gallant Friend has in mind any
particular area where a supply of
electricity is urgently desired, I would
suggest that the residents in that area
may assist to expedite consideration of
their claims by furnishing to the Board
statistical data as to the potential demand
in their area obtained as a result of a
canvass.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Arising out
of the first part of the reply, is the
Minister not responsible under Section 4
of the Act of 1931 for collecting the information?
Mr. BARBOUR: I will endeavour to
do so in this case.

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-

Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONE
Mr. POLLOCK: My attention has
been directed to this resolution, and I
would take this opportunity of informing
the hon. Member that the matter has
been somewhat exaggerated.
It is the normal practice of this
Government to ensure that such printing
requirements as can be entrusted to, and
undertaken by, the printing industry in
Northern Ireland shall be so allocated,
and in pursuance of this policy, I may
state that 97 per cent. of the total printing orders for this Government, during
the last financial year, were assigned to
Northern Ireland firms and executed in
Northern Ireland. In the instance which
has given rise to this question, it was
decided to produce certain lists, which
had previously been printed, by a duplicating process in London, in order to effect
substantial financial economy, a course
which will, I think, commend itself
generally, and this accounts for the printing of those particular lists not being
continued.
It might, perhaps, be of interest for
hon. Members to know that, as I am informed, printing firms in Northern Ireland are not excluded from participation
in, and, as a matter of fact, have secured
orders for Government printing for
United Kingdom requirements.
Mr. McCARROLL: Do I understand
the Minister to say that this work has
been done in London?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes, at a saving of
£140 out of a total of £300. They have
a peculiar duplicating plant which is not.
in existence here. It is not printing.
Mr. McCARROLL: Do the same rate
of wages apply?
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not know.
Mr. COLLINS: Oh!

there any definite progress in connection
with a labourers' cottages scheme at the
time it was decided for financial reasons
to suspend the operations of the Act.
In that case the council had actually
formulated a scheme involving the
erection of 333 houses.
In several other cases, councils had
contemplated the formulation of schemes
and some of them had taken steps to
invite applications for cottages, but
beyond these, preliminary steps, no
definite progress has been made.

bill ejectments; whether the arrears in

Sir DAWSON BATES: I understand
that legal proceedings have been taken
by the landlords in certain cases, in the
areas referred to in the question, against

but, as stated in my reply to the hon.
Member's question of the 18th ultimo, I
have no jurisdiction to interfere in matters of this character, and have no
definite information on the points referred to in the hon. Member's question.
With regard to the last paragraph of
the question, it is not the intention of
the Government to set up a committee to
inquire into the rents of these recently

I have received with great satisfaction the expression of your thanks for

present Session of Parliament.

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): In considering the
present proposals which are now before
the House, in regard to the future of
housing in Northern Ireland, the Government took into their earnest consideration
the views expressed in the Report of the
Select Committee presented to the House
in the month of December last dealing
with the question of rent restriction. It
is proposed to bring in a Bill dealing with
this matter at an early date and, therefore, I propose to refer only to one paragraph of that Report in this connection.
Towards the end of their Report the
Committee used these words: :-
"In referring to this matter of. the
shortage of houses the Committee desire, even at the risk of overstepping
their terms of reference, to suggest
that the greatest need at the moment
is for houses which can be let at low
rents, i.e., not exceeding 6s per week,
and housing subsidies in future,
whether made by the Government or
by local authorities, should be made
conditional upon a rent not exceeding
a certain limit being charged for a
prescribed period."
I may say at once that the Government
concur in the first part of that Report.
Indeed, it has been, and is, the policy of
the Government, since they introduced
their first Act dealing with the question
of housing in 1923, and it was with the
object of trying to get the type of house
within the means of the working man that,
in 1927, the Government, when introducing the Bill in that year fixed the
minimum area of houses qualifying for
subsidy at 650 superficial feet. We had
found at that time that the practice of
the builders was to build to the maximum
allowed under the Acts, and therefore
the attitude of the builders defeated to a
large extent the object the Government
had in view of providing a type of house
within the means of the working man.
It will be within the recollection of
hon. Members that, in deference to the
wishes expressed from all parts of the
House, the Government agreed to increase the maximum area to 700 superficial feet, but the result of the working
of that Act has been that this Amendment hinders the supply of houses which
the Government regarded as most urgently
needed. I would like hon. Members to
take a note of these figures relating to
houses built by private builders between
1930 and 14th March, 1932. In regard
to houses between 500 and 550 superficial feet only 1 per cent. built under
the Acts came under that description.
When we come to the next stage, houses
between 550 and 600 superficial feet, the
proportion was 27 per cent., then between
600 and 650 we find it was 32 per cent.,
and within the last limit 650 to 700
307 Housing (Grants) Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Sir Dawson Bates]
superficial feet it was 46 per cent. Those
percentages show that the contention I
put forward is the correct one.
As will be seen when I come to explain
the proposals we are now putting forward,
the Government have come to the conclusion that a still greater limitation in
the maximum size of the houses eligible
for subsidy is necessary.
With regard to the second part of
the recommendation of the Committee,
namely, that the payment of subsidy
should be dependent upon a condition
limiting the amount of rents charged,
we have examined this proposal from every
angle, and we have come to the conclusion that any such condition would
defeat the main object which we have in
view. We are convinced that conditions
of this kind, limiting the user of the
house, or restricting the sale of the house,
would prevent our obtaining any houses
at all. After all, builders are not philanthropists, and people are not prepared to
invest their money in houses which are
subject to restricting conditions of this
kind.
I have said over and over again at
this box that there is only one way of
reducing rents satisfactorily, and that is
by obtaining an adequate supply of
houses, and by encouraging people to invest their money in houses, and unless
we can succeed in getting people to put
their money into houses, a shortage will
always be with us. As I have often said,
we, in Belfast, are very much more fortunately situated in regard to housing
shortage than any other city in the three
Kingdoms.
There was at one time in the recollection of many Members of this House,
a surplus number of the working-class
type amounting to something like 10,000
in Belfast. We have always enjoyed,
and I venture to say we are still enjoying, the fact that we are the cheapest
housed city in the three Kingdoms, and
that is all due to the fact that in the
days that are passed one of the most
favourite forms of investment, especially
for the small investor-including many
workingmen-was the erection of houses,
but unfortunately owing to the restrictions in regard to the use of building
materials, and the abnormal shortage that
took place, restrictions were put on the
rents to be charged on the existing
houses, with the result that even after
the war had terminated, it was found
that building operations as an investment had absolutely ceased, and an
enormous shortage of houses had resulted.
The Government had then to come to
the rescue with the object of encouraging
people to again go in for building operations, and, as a result, in Northern
Ireland we have no fewer than 25,320
houses completed with State financial
assistance. It is a peculiar fact that
although generous assistance was available between 1919 and 1923, both under
the Housing Acts, and under the Unemployment Relief Funds, a period of four
years, only 498 houses were erected by
private builders.
These earlier Acts, for which this Government were not responsible, imposed
certain restrictions in regard to the user,
and the sale of these houses, and the
refusal of the investing public to put
their money into bricks and mortar was
due entirely to the restrictions contained
in those Acts.
The first Act of this Government was
the Act of 1923, and those Acts have
been followed by similar Measures.
Under those Acts, the subsidies to
builders did not impose any restrictions
whatsoever, except as to the type and
size of the house. When I tell you
that between 1923 and the present time
21,318 houses, apart from houses built
by local authorities, had been built
by private individuals, it must be
admitted that the policy of the Government in refusing to place restrictions, had
the result, at all events, of getting
houses which the earlier Acts did not
achieve.
It might interest the House to know
what burden has been imposed on the
State in connection with the financing of
these various Acts. Under the Housing
of the Working Classes Act, 1908, we
paid subsidies amounting to £12,730;
under the Housing (Additional Powers)
Act of 1919, we have paid subsidies
amounting to £58,850. The House will
remember that under the Housing Act of
1919 the Government of the day undertook to pay annual subsidies in respect of
houses erected under that Act. Some of
the annual subsidies to the local
authorities have been commuted by payment of a lump sum, whilst in other
cases, the payment of the annual subsidy
is being still continued. Under this Act.
309 Housing (Grants) Bill-

15 MARCH 1932
Second Reading
the amount to date is £280,899. Disbursements from the Unemployment Relief Funds account for approximately
£200,000, and the payments under the
Housing Acts passed by this Parliament
amount to £2,080,000, making a total of
State assistance of
approximately
£2,633,000.
These figures, large as they are, do not,
I think, fully represent the assistance
which has been given from public funds
towards the erection of houses. Many
local authorities have given further assistance by means of supplemental grants
in respect of the houses built under the
Housing Acts, and in some cases, local
authorities have embarked on schemes
themselves towards which they have got
assistance from the State, but which,
even with this assistance, entail charges
upon the rates. The Belfast Corporation
have been paid something in the neighbourhood of £520,000 towards schemes
which they themselves undertook, and I
understand that even with this help,
these operations have entailed an appreciable charge upon the ratepayers of the
city.
Up to the end of February 9,500
houses have been built in the City of
Belfast by private builders, which were
eligible for subsidy at varying rates, and
the Government have paid in respect of
these houses, £873,580. The Corporation
have paid by way of subsidies £319,000,
and have made advances by way of
interest-free loans to the extent of
£119,000. In the case of these interestfree loans the principal will, of course, be
repaid, but the Corporation will have to
find the interest on the loans during their
currency out of City funds, but so far as
the Corporation is concerned, there is
another side to the picture. The housing
accommodation has been increased by
9,500 houses, and this cannot but have
had a great effect upon the health of the
city, and it cannot but have lightened
to a very appreciable degree the responsibility of the Corporation in this direction.
There is, of course, very direct financial
benefit to the Corporation also involved,
because I think we may safely take the
average valuation of these houses at £9,
and it is not unreasonable to assume that
in respect of each of these houses the
Corporation collects a sum of at least
£4 10s Od per annum in rates. On the
basis of a 25 year loan at 5 per cent.
interest, the annual charge for interest
and sinking fund in respect of a loan for
the amount of a subsidy of £40 would be
£2 18s Od or thereabout, and, therefore,
there is an increase in revenue to the
Corporation in respect of each house of
£1 12s Od which, I venture to say, would
more than compensate the Corporation for
any extra services which they may be
called on to give. For the last year the
subsidy given by the Corporation has been
£20 and not £40, and, therefore, the
benefit in respect of the houses built
during the last year would be SO much
the greater.
Hon. Members will, therefore, appreciate that we have made large strides
towards meeting the deficiency in housing
accommodation, and that in doing so we
have incurred serious financial liabilities.
As I have already pointed out, our
liabilities in respect of subsidies under the
Acts passed by this Parliament amount
to over £2,000,000, and this will entail
an annual charge on the Estimates of
£169,000. In addition, we have to meet
annual sums amounting to £21,000 in
respect of liabilities incurred under
previous housing legislation.
In formulating our future policy we
cannot but have regard to these liabilities,
and to the present financial situation.
Our resources are limited, and we have
therefore to attach great importance to
the financial aspect of the question.
Balancing these various considerations,
we have come to the conclusion that the
utmost assistance that we can give in this
matter is a subsidy of £25. We have also
come to the conclusion that the maximum
area under the existing Acts of 700
superficial feet is too high-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear) and we therefore
propose that the subsidy shall only be
granted to houses between a minimum of
500 superficial feet and a maximum of
550 superficial feet. That decent and
comfortable houses can be provided within
these limits is proved by experience.

considered it necessary to lay down that

The power of local authorities to make
supplemental grants will be continued,
and as the Government grant is now being
reduced to £25, we think that this is a
reasonable maximum for the supplemental grant by local authorities. In any
area, therefore, in which a local authority agrees to supplement a Government
grant it will be possible for the builder
to earn a subsidy of £50, and we think
that this amount should be sufficient to
enable him to build economical houses
which could be let at a price which will
be within the means of the ordinary
working man. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
I should point out that we make provision to ensure that where a house has
been commenced before the 9th March
under the existing Housing Acts, but is
not completed until after the 31st March,
this house will be eligible for subsidy at
the reduced rate even though it does not
comply with the conditions now laid down
as to size and so forth.
It has hitherto been our custom to
legislate in regard to housing for one year
only, and this has had the disadvantage
of leaving builders in a state of uncertainty towards the end of the year and
thus slowing up the preparation of plans
for new buildings during that period.
For these reasons we think it better to
legislate for a period of two years, and
accordingly if this Measure is accepted
the Act when passed will remain in force
until the 31st March, 1934. I beg to
move.

""

Here is a letter from the

"Grants from the Road Fund,"
and here is the circular:
Minstry of Home Affairs,
Stormont,
Circ. No. R179.
Belfast.
25th January, 1932.
Sir, I am directed by the Minister
of Home Affairs to state that the
question of the grants to be paid from
the Road Fund in respect of the programme of work for the financial year
1932-33 by local authorities has been
receiving his earnest consideration in
the light of the fact that the reserves
in the fund have been completely exhausted and of the growing demands
on the Fund.
In these circumstances, the Minister
was at first constrained to feel that it
would be necessary for him to reduce
the percentage of rates of the grants
in respect of the three classes of roads,
but, after most careful and anxious
consideration as to the effect of such
change on the finances of local government authorities, particularly having
regard to the fact that in the majority
of cases the Estimates have already
been prepared in the expectation of
receiving the grants at the existing
rates, it has now been decided to retain
for one year more the present scale of
grants, i.e., 60 per cent. on 1st Class
roads, 30 per cent. on 2nd Class roads,
and 15 per cent. in respect of certain
3rd Class roads.
The retention of these rates for a
further year, which, as has already
been explained, has been decided upon
in order to avoid any dislocation or
disturbance of the accounts of local
authorities, will inevitably have the
effect of producing a very substantial
deficit in the fund during the course of
the year.
Accordingly, the Minister feels that,
while the grants at the above rates will
be paid, it will be necessary, as far as
possible to effect economies by curtailing, where practicable, the road programmes of the various local authorities
on the different classes of roads, i.e
by deferring works which are not of
really essential and urgent character
for a year at least, and by reducing, or
in special cases by abandoning the works
altogther for the present.
In particular, the Minister feels
constrained to impose a reduction in
the amounts of the grants which nor-

I cannot see how any hon. Member can
vote against this Amendment which I
have proposed, because it simply means
that this House expresses its approval of
the way in which the Government has cooperated with the local authorities in the
past as regards the promotion of schemes
of public value, with the object not only
of improving our cities and country towns
and districts, but also of finding useful
employment for some, at any rate, of
those whom industry cannot employ in
these difficult days. The continuance of
the friendly and helpful co-operation
which has existed between our local
authorities and the Ministry of Labour
is the only fitting way by which these
schemes, mainly of local importance and
value, can be promoted and carried out.
The suggestion that the Government
should embark on schemes on their own
would be interfering with the duties and
responsibilities of the local authorities in
the various areas and would involve the
engagement of large staffs for the purpose
of carrying out what are, after all, local
improvements.
In all, schemes involving an expenditure of almost eight million pounds have
been approved since the Government came
into being, and the grants sanctioned
from Government sources have been over
2 millions. Surely what is wanted is a
continuance of this policy, and no legislation is necessary in order that it should
be continued.
I think that a word of praise should
be given to the Government, and especially
to the Minister of Labour, for what they
have accomplished by assisting local
authorities to carry out these schemes of
utility, and also by giving employment
to those who are not able to secure it
themselves.

revenue-
There are two sorts of schemes, revenueproducing schemes and
producing schemes. I think we must all
admit that we have, unfortunately, come
to the end of any useful revenue-producing schemes. The only schemes we
can produce now would be non revenueproducing schemes, and if we consider the
ordinary finances of non revenue-producing schemes we find that a man would
have to earn £190 before the scheme
would be productive, that is after taking
into account the £60 which would be
saved in the Unemployment Fund. Then,
what do we have at the completion of the
scheme? An unproductive scheme.
Perhaps we have spent £200,000 of our
money, and the unemployed man is left
destitute. He is left worse off than when
the scheme started. We have spent on

The hon. Member does not seem very well

eighteen months of the time they were
in office, when they were solving the unemployment question, they instituted
3,716 relief schemes. They spent on those
schemes £69,906,000, and unemployment
increased from 1 millions to 3 millions
during that time. However, it is a very

aggravate the situation by destroying use-

all these ten years my Department has

Now, hon. Members opposite have indicated-I will not put it further than that
-that no schemes are going on. At the
present time there are in operation in
Northern Ireland, and the greater number in Belfast, 78 schemes, involving a
Government grant of £664,000. Actually,
at the moment, 2,110 men are engaged in

have not been started by the local
authorities and that involve a Govern.
ment grant of £131,000 odd. If these
schemes were started to-morrow, they
would provide for one year work for 2,700
people. So that I am justified in saying
that nowhere else is so much being done.
If there is any hold-up in this matter,
the hold-up is not due to the Government.

Minister made yesterday in introducing

much impressed by the figures given with

remainder of the Six Counties had cooperated to anything like the same extent,
I should not have a single word to say
to-day by way of criticism.
I differ from some of my hon. Friends

ever may seem
Probably it is unfortunate that the

Probably the work of economy would have

not the best way of carrying out a

Housing (Grants) Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Healy]
The Minister, however, made another
prophecy yesterday in addition to the
many prophecies made from the Government Benches. He prophecied that within
a reasonable time they would have a
sufficiency of houses. Well, that remains
to be seen. The worst of prophets is that
when they embark on a journey into the
future they do not take a return ticket.
I am afraid it sometimes happens that
hon. Members on this side fall into
exactly the same errors in this matter
of prophecy. However, I am not going to
prophesy on this occasion. My difficulty
is with regard to housing in rural and
municipal areas. I know that large sums
of money have been allocated for the
purpose of providing houses, but urban
councils have not used that money in
providing houses for the people who are
unable to provide houses for themselves
-that is the working classes. They
erect a sufficient type of house which is
occupied by the professional or semiprofessional class.
Sir DAWSON BATES: What size?
a
Mr. HEALY: Up to 750 superficial
feet, and the rents of these houses are
anything up to £1 a week. Anybody who
knows the conditions in the country towns
will realise at once that it is not possible
for any man earning tradesman's
wages to pay a rent of this kind. Therefore, we have the extraordinary spectacle
of the Government wasting money, spending large sums of money, to which the
working classes must contribute their
quota, to subsidise the building of houses
for people who ought to be in a position.
to build them themselves. At the same
time, in the urban area of Enniskillen,
with which I am particularly concerned,
there practically has not been a single
house erected that would fall within the
compass of a working man's dwelling.
That brings us again to another point.
Under the Labourers Acts for providing
housing accommodation there was an
element of compulsion. It was open to
the applicants to make representations to
the district council, and if they were unwilling to perform their obligations they
could appeal to the Local Government
Board. A like provision, I suggest,
ought to be inserted in this Bill with
regard to urban areas which have not
been carrying out their duties to the
working classes as the Legislature contemplated they should. I think there
should be an element of compulsion in
this Bill, and that working people in an
urban area, who cannot find housing
accommodation and for whom there is no
provision made, ought to be able to come
to the Minister of Home Affairs and, in
putting up a scheme, he ought to be in
a position to come to their aid.
Generally speaking, I am not in favour
of coercing local authorities where those
local authorities take a broadminded and
enlightened view of their responsibilities.
But we have to recognise the fact that
there are many public bodies, such as the
Enniskillen Urban Council, which will
never rise to their responsibilities in this
matter unless some element of compulsion
is added. It is unfortunate that all
public representatives do not take the
public-spirited view of the members of
the Belfast Corporation in regard to the
provision of houses for the working
classes, but we have to deal with facts
as we find them. In Enniskillen the
Urban Council have refused to vote a
single penny of money on their own
account to the subsidising of labourers'
dwellings, although they have been prepared to take all the money the Government voted, utilise it, and then charge
rents that will ensure that there will be
no loss on the rates. In other words, the
Urban Council of Enniskillen-and in
this respect, I suppose, it is not any different to many other urban councils—are
not prepared to do anything for the working classes. They are prepared to utilise
the Government grants for the erection of
dwellings provided the rent will bring
them in a sufficient return to cover depreciation and sinking fund interest. In
other words, there is no sympathy whatever with the working classes in that particular area. The result to-day is that a
working man living in Enniskillen has no
chance of securing a house, but he must,
as a taxpayer, contribute his quota to
provide houses for other people who can
afford a rent of £1 per week.
.

Major BLAKISTON-HOUSTON :
would like to congratulate the Minister

I was delighted to see that he had brought

comfortable, and that it will be impossible for people so to twist the Acts

The most important thing of the lot is

namely, the subsidy of £25. I can quite

of Finance has a certain amount of

his Department and others. I am afraid
that every builder, who will not build

and on to the Minister of Labour's Department. It is well known that if this
subsidy would encourage building it
would help to absorb an enormous
number of wage earners; that is, taking
the widest possible view of building

all classes of people are employed either

large amount of employment given. If the
Minister of Home Affairs could possibly
extract a little more out of the Minister
of Finance's Department, and
houses were to be built, it would probably
relieve the Minister of Labour's Department. I am not in a position to say what
one Department can do against another,
but I do know, and everybody knows,
that if the Government require money,
either for the Ministry of Labour or the
Ministry of Finance, it has to come out

more
The hon. Member for the University
(Rev. Professor Corkey) yesterday put
forward a very pretty picture of very few
houses being built to the acre. Would
he ask the Minister of Home Affairs to
start a Fortwilliam Park for the workers?
I doubt if they want it. I personally
have a house, and my garden, to my
mind, is far too large. It is not big
enough to employ people and it is
too big to do oneself. (Laughter.)
The hon. Member also spoke about slums.
For one cause or another I go into a great
number of houses in Ballymacarrett.
Many of these houses are built in narrow
streets, but they are kept extraordinarily
well by the housewives. They are clean,
neat, and tidy. Indeed, the thing that
always strikes me as extraordinary about
those houses is the enormous amount of
time spent by the women folk in polishing brass. I can assure the hon. Member
that there is no such thing as slums there.
Where slums do appear, in my humble
opinion, is in a district of big houses
which have become unpopular, and which
are turned into tenements of the worst
type with, practically speaking, no sanitary arrangements and no organisation
for the comfort of the women, and still
less of the children. The house built
genuinely for the purposes of tenements
or flats is quite a different matter, because
in that case adequate kitchen and sanitary arrangements are provided, but to
turn an old house of the type I am referring to into flats is perfectly ridiculous.
From the evidence we heard at the Rent
Committee, we found that on the Antrim
Road there were four- and five-storey
houses which could not be let. That
property has been converted into flats of
a sort, which are nothing else but slums
of the worst kind.
The hon. Member for South Fermanagh
(Mr. Healy), a few moments ago, criticised the Government for not doing anything regarding subsidy houses. I think
that if he had read the terms of reference
to the Rent Committee he would have
seen that subsidy houses were entirely excluded from the scope of its investigations.
The Committee had nothing to do with
subsidy houses. I hope the Minister of
House Affairs will do everything that is
practicable to see that the materials are
bought and manufactured in Northern
Ireland, and that those materials which
are not manufactured in this area will
be procured in the British Isles. We do
not grow timber that would suit this
class of job, but we could quite easily put
in a clause that timber must be imported
in bulk, and thus allow the builders and
owners of sawmills to have the work of
turning out the different classes of
material required. If that can be done,
and builders are encouraged in that way,

the speeches delivered from all sides of the
House on this Housing (Grants) Bill, and
I might say I am agreeably surprised at
the interest taken by all sections in the
provision of houses for the working class.
At the outset, I regret it is imperative
on the Government to reduce this subsidy
to £25. The Prime Minister, speaking
here last Tuesday week in connection with
this matter, stated that what was in the
mind of the Government with regard to
the proposed Rent Restriction Bill was
that they believed
that any
interference with those responsible for the
building of subsidy houses in the way of
fixing rents might retard the progress of
building operations. With that I strictly
disagree, because I think the action of
the Government in reducing the subsidy
is calculated to do far more harm to the
progress of building than any action they
might take in bringing in legislation to
control the rents of these houses.
There is another matter that I complain of. We have heard a lot from
Members who represent city constituencies in connection with the size of these
houses. Now, I represent a rural constituency, and I entirely disagree with
the views expressed here by many Members that houses of 500 to 550 superficial
feet meet the wishes of the people thev
are intended for. I do not know what is
felt in the City of Belfast, but listening
to the speeches by right hon. Gentlemen
and by hon. Members on both sides, one
would think the business of this Parliament was to legislate for the great City
of Belfast alone. (Hon. Members: No,
no.)
I want to put forward the rural contention. It is, generally speaking, that
the class of people who will occupy these
houses in the rural areas have large families, and that houses with a superficial
area of from 500 to 550 superficial feet
are not sufficient to meet their requirements. I think I am perfectly right in
stating that the superficial area is entirely
too small. On one occasion, I think it was
in 1929, when speaking on the Housing
Bill I complained, as I complain now,
that the Government in granting this

mission. In the old days we had commissions set up in this country to determine and fix the rents of tenant farmers.
I think that this matter of the rents on
subsidy houses should seriously engage the
attention of
the Government. This
question of the exorbitant rents charged is

There is just one other matter I am

I think it is the mind of the Government,

Major MCCORMICK: I would like

has been, through various causes, a longdelayed Measure, and although I believe
the Minister of Home Affairs has endeavoured in former Bills to give the industrial worker the benefit of grants
towards their homes, various things contributed to putting "out of the picture" a
proper Measure to ensure a plentiful
supply of working-class houses. One of
the causes was the size of the house called
for, and the insistent demand to increase
rather than decrease the superficial area
and cost. Consequently the rent was too
high for the ordinary workman.
The question of whether a house is to
be 500 or 700 feet in order to ensure
sufficient accommodation for a workman's
family is a matter of very divided opinion,
and whilst I am inclined to the view, that
the largest families being of the working
classes, the larger house should be more
necessary, yet that does not solve the
problem. For one must look at possibly
the most vital point involved and, that is,
what is a workman able to pay as
rental? I contend that of necessity we
must settle the question-the ability to
pay. If we take it that one-sixth of his
wages should go in rent, very likely it
would work out that a wage-earner,
having 40s to 50s a week, should pay 6s 6d
to 8s 6d in rent. I think that is fair
and reasonable on an average basis.

I am reminded of the story of "Alice
in Wonderland." In the course of her
many wanderings, Alice came to the door
leading to a beautiful garden. Owing to
her size, she was unable to enter the
door. I suppose in fairyland everything
is of a fairy-like nature, and so proportionately small that we mortals do not
understand it. However, Alice saw a
bottle on the table and she partook of
the magic elixir and found herself growing smaller and smaller, until she became
a little person of fairy-like appearance.
Being suited to the dimensions of the
fairy house she then entered the building. Unlike the story, the houses our
various Bills deal with, though small and
infinitesimal in room space gather
greatness in the size and immensity of the
rents demanded for them. I feel that
Alice would not even try to enter one of
them, but would prefer Wonderland and
the company of the Mad Hatter, to the
questionable luxuries of modern life and
the expensive rents and high taxation
prevailing on this mundane sphere.

It is a great scandal that since the introduction of this Bill the Belfast
Corporation, through its Finance Committee, have recommended to the Council
the discontinuance of payments of subsidies for houses affected by this Measure.
They will, therefore, cease to help the
class of people who are in the worst
plight in wanting this small class of house,
and whom the Belfast Corporation have
always contended they are out to help.
But the greater portion of the amount
which the Corporation claim to have
paid-something like £500,000-has gone
to speculative builders who are charging
through their agents these enormous rents.
I say the Corporation, by their act or recommendation, are deserting the very
class of people for whom these Acts were
primarily designed. Under this Bill the
people who will occupy these houses will
be working-class tenants primarily. In
99 cases out of 100 they will be workers,
and it is, therefore, most important that
a Clause safeguarding them to the extent
of reasonable or low rents should be inserted in the Bill. Only in this way can
the claim for reasonable rents be made
good. In support of this there
numerous instances quoted of this class of
house being erected by competent builders,
and let at low or economic rentals. Whilst
I understand that rents are coming down
slowly and normal conditions are coming
back, yet the protection of the class who
have no alternative to the demands of
rapacious property owners is long overdue.
Those people can be protected now under
this Bill. I say that is imperative in the
Bill before the House, but before a drastic
Clause is considered giving effect to it, it
might be wise to look into the question of
whether the amount of the subsidy given
would warrant a control or rent Clause
being inserted. In other words it means:
Can we induce good builders, by a grant
of £25 per house, to build ? Of course
that £25 will be augmented by local
authorities.

The census that was taken over three

These figures are pretty much the same

rooms are working-class people. I know

I have repeatedly had this question put
to me by many of my constituents, who
are largely working-class people, and
people very loyal to the Government.
They have voiced their deep disappointment that up to now, with all the Housing
Acts that have been passed, no serious
attempt has been made to assist the building of workers' houses at economic rents.
And I have been at a loss to defend the
Government's want of action in view of
the provisions made from time to time.
Why, every Bill on housing that this
House has passed was to be for the benefit
of those who could not afford to buy a
house. We were told that the subsidy
offered them the means of getting a house

say, has happened. But here is the

the rents or will he say that regulations
are called for?
I feel very strongly on this Bill, and I
wish to press with all the energy I possess

subsidy. And I say, with all due respect,

Another man owns a thousand houses in

I say that position is most illogical. It

Well, they are loyal, but there are two

Mr. MINFORD: I rise to support this
Bill, and I do hope local authorities will
take advantage of the subsidy. Although
a great deal has been accomplished under
previous Housing Acts there is still a
shortage. I would have preferred to
have seen the subsidy £50 instead of £25,
but at the same time I think the Government should be congratulated that in
these times of financial stress they have
granted a subsidy of £25. I believe it
will be an inducement both to local
authorities and private enterprise
to
build still more houses. I was of the
opinion expressed by some hon. Members
that the houses erected under this Bill
should be subject to control so far as the
rents are concerned, but after the explanation given by the Prime Minister I
have come to the conclusion that an
ample supply is the best type of control.
I sincerely hope that when times improve
the Government will be in a position to
increase the subsidy.
Every Member must realise that the
Government has always been a great
advocate of better housing conditions
for the working classes of Ulster. Our
workers deserve good houses because good
houses are essential to good homes. The
erection of houses under this Bill will provide work for the unemployed, and I hope
that before many more years have passed
the present restrictions on rents will have
been abolished, and that an ample supply
of houses of all types will be available at
a reasonable rent. It is true that there
may be some people who have taken undue advantage of tenants in the past, but
I think this subsidy of £25 will encourage
both local authorities and private builders
to erect all the houses that are required.
The hon. and gallant Member (Major
McCormick), referred to the fact that
some people are living in two rooms instead of in a house. I am afraid that
is not always the fault of the builder or
the landlord, because in many cases we
find that a higher rent is charged for the
two rooms than for the entire house. I
do not think that in all cases it was the
shortage of houses that made these people
live in two rooms, and the smaller type of
house that will be built under this Bill
will leave no excuse for people to live in
two rooms. In conclusion, I hope that
both local authorities and private builders
will take advantage of this Bill so that
sufficient houses will be erected to enable
the law of supply and demand to control
rents.

LOANS FOR FARMERS.
1. Mr. STEWART (for Mr. Healy)
asked the Minister of Agriculture
whether he can give the total number of
applications made for loans for farmers
since 1930, and the number in which the
applications were refused.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I take it that
the hon. Member refers to the scheme for
the issue of loans through the joint
stock banks, for the purchase of live
stock, seeds and manures, which came
into force in 1930. Under that scheme
1,069 applications for loans have been
received, and of these 419 have been refused. In addition, 62 applications for
loans from the Government Loans Fund
were received during 1931 of which only
one was refused.

Amendment is that it is equally important
that the layout of the site should be controlled, and I think the Government
would be the best body to do that. The
local authorities have used a good deal of
wisdom and discretion in the laying out
of sites for which they themselves were
responsible, but from what I have seen
myself I am convinced that they have
been too lax in regulating the layout of
sites on which other people were building.
These defects have been of several
kinds. First of all, very often the front
of the house has been set quite flush with
the street, thereby denying the people
the privacy to which they are entitled.
In a small house, particularly where
there is practically only one living room,
it is very undesirable that the house
should be right on the street. These
people have their little romances, their
little tales to tell each other, and sometimes their little squabbles, and it is not
reasonable to ask them to live so close to
the street as these houses have been
placed. In another respect the layout-

Mr. DEVLIN: In view of previous
controversies, I thought he could do anything if he was Parliamentary. We will

houses. As I say, the whole thing is
done deliberately to give the public the
impression that the Government are
giving some public funds to assist housing
when they are doing nothing of the sort.
It would be far better to withdraw the
Bill and introduce a new Bill and consult people who know something about
the people and the people's needs. Let

lines upon which something satisfactory
could be done. You offer a subsidy of

Railways (Valuation for Rating) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:

Mr. BARBOUR: The valuation of
railways in Northern Ireland is at present
ascertained by reference to the Valuation
Act of 1852, which fixes the valuation on
the basis of net annual value, that is to
say, the rent for which, one year with
another, the same might in its actual state
be reasonably expected to let from year
to
year, the probable average annual
cost of repairs, insurance, and other expenses, if any, necessary to maintain the
hereditament in its actual state, and all
rates, taxes and public charges, if any,
except tithe rentcharge, being paid by
the tenant.
The valuation of a railway must,
therefore, be based on the rent which a
hypothetical tenant would normally pay
for the land and buildings comprising
the railway's property, but the definition
of value cannot be applied to ascertain
the annual value of a railway in the same
way as it is applied in finding the value,
Railways Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
for example, of a shop. In valuing a
shop there is usually no great difficulty
in finding sufficient evidence of rental
value, but in the case of a railway there
is no such evidence, as the companies who
occupy railways are also the owners.
A special method-usually referred to as
the "revenue principle"-has therefore
been devised for applying the statutory
definition of value in the case of railways
and other properties, such as gas and
electric light undertakings. The method
is the outcome of numerous law cases
which have been before the courts for
many years past, and it has become so
firmly established that it possesses almost
the same legal sanctity as the statutory
definition which it purports to apply.
This method of arriving at railway
valuations worked well so long as the
railways enjoyed a reasonable degree of
prosperity. Modern industrial depression and the competition of road transport have been severely felt by the
railways, and the resulting fall in their
revenue has been so great that if the railways were to insist on their strict legal
rights under the "revenue principle" the
result might in many cases be a nil
valuation. In recent years the whole
fabric of railway valuation has only been
maintained by makeshift informal agreements, having no foundation in strict
law.
This position is felt to be impossible,
and it is considered that the whole question of the valuation of railways should
be revised and put upon a clear statutory
basis, which, while securing fair treatment for the ordinary ratepayer, shall
not impose too harsh conditions upon the
railways. The fact that a railway is
actually working is an indication that it
is of some value to the company working
it, and this renders it inequitable that it
should escape altogether the burden of
rating which is levied to support those
services which it enjoys in common with
other ratepayers.
I should, perhaps, mention here that
unlike industrial hereditaments, a railway undertaking does not gain in actual
financial benefit from the derating legislation of 1928 and 1929. The threefourths relief which it obtains must,
under the statutory freight rebates
scheme, be passed on to users of the
railway.
It will readily be appreciated that
under the "revenue principle" of fixing
valuation, the larger the amount allocated to interest on tenant's capital, the
smaller will be the balance of receipts
which may be considered as landlord's
rent or valuation. Judicial decisions
have established that for the purpose
of calculating the interest on tenant's
capital, the capital value of plant, rolling
stock, stores, etc., is to be their present
value in terms of modern money values
and not their original cost. The result
is that, in addition to the rapidly shrinking revenue of the railways, the position
has been complicated by the fact that,
owing to the decreased value of money,
the allocations for interest on tenant's
capital have had to be very largely increased. Thus, rental value under the
present system entirely disappears and a
nil valuation is the result.
The first part of this Bill gives a statutory basis to the "revenue principle" interpretation of the Act of 1852, while
freeing it from the judicial qualifications
which have been grafted on to it, such
as the necessity for allowing fixed percentages for interest and profit on tenant's
capital. There are to be quinquennial
revisions of railway valuations. For the
purposes of such a revision, the Commissioner of Valuation is, in accordance with
Clause 5, to ascertain the average of the
net receipts of each railway company as
a whole for the first five of the six completed accounting years next preceding
the date on which such revaluation is to
come into force. Having arrived at this
average, he is to use it as the basis of the
letting value of the railway, and the
annual rent thus arrived at is to be the
valuation for the next five years.
It is possible however, and, if the
present decline in revenue continues, even
probable, that the foregoing formula may
still involve a nil valuation. The Bill
provides against such an eventuality, because, as I have already stated, so long as
a railway runs, it must be considered
to have some value. A minimum valuation is accordingly specified which is to
operate in the event of the receipts of
the railway companies falling beyond a
certain point. Clause 7 of the Bill details the method of arriving at such a
minimum valuation.
In the case of the actual railway track
itself, the minimum valuation is to be
the valuation which would have been
placed on the land under the Act of 1852
if it had not been adapted for use as a
Railways Bill-
Second Reading
21 MARCH 1932
railway. In the case of other portions of
the railway, such as goods sheds and so
forth, the minimum valuation is to be
arrived at on the annual basis of letting
value, but on 1914 standard and reduced
by two-thirds.
The
Having now, in language as little
technical as possible, described the general
aim of the Bill, I will reply to a question
which doubtless many Members have been
asking themselves, namely, is Northern
Ireland the only part of the British Isles
that has had to face this problem?
answer is that it was faced in Great
Britain in 1930, when the Railways
(Valuation for Rating) Act was passed.
That Act in the main corresponds with
the Bill before this House, save that it
does not provide for a minimum valuation. In the Irish Free State, a Bill
was passed towards the close of last
year,
and the present Bill corresponds more
closely with it than with the British Act,
by reason of the fact that the Irish basis
of valuation and case law on valuation
differ in many respects from that which
operates in Great Britain. Moreover, a
differing system of railway valuation in
the two parts of Ireland would be bound
to lead to confusion, owing to the inter-
State character of a number of the railways.
I have confined myself to the main
outlines of the Bill. The more technical
aspect of the various Clauses can best be
dealt with in Committee. I beg to move.

New Industries (Development) Bill.

Mr. BARBOUR: The prolonged industrial depression through which Northern Ireland in common with the rest
of the United Kingdom has been passing
has brought home to us in a most forcible
manner the greater vulnerability of an
industrial community like our own almost
entirely dependent on one or two major
industries. Although the depression has
affected all industries, without exception,
it has weighed most heavily of all perhaps
on shipbuilding, and almost as heavily on
the textile trades. Northern Ireland,
therefore, has been in an exceptionally
exposed position, and relatively she has
suffered more than a comparable area
possessing a broader industrial basis.
Accordingly, the Government has been
turning its attention to the special opportunities of broadening the Northern Ireland basis presented by the recent change
in the fiscal policy of the United Kingdom, and the Bill now before the House
represents an effort to take advantage of
those opportunities.
The Bill is very simple in character.
It empowers the Ministry of Commerce,
For the purposes of the Bill a "new
industry" means one devoted to the production of goods of a kind which were
not being produced in Northern Ireland
before 1st November, 1931. The maximum period during which the Ministry
of Commerce is empowered to continue
making the annual payments, and the
local authorities to continue exemption
from rates, is twenty years, reckoning
from the date which the Ministry's
annual payments began.
Hon. Members will appreciate the
necessity of restricting the benefits proposed by the Bill to industries concerned
only with goods of a kind not previously
being made in Northern Ireland. It may
be, of course, that the opportunities of
successfully establishing a factory for the
the production of something already
being made in Northern Ireland are quite
as good as those for the establishment of
one engaged in producing something
entirely new. The restriction of the
benefits to new industries, therefore, must
not be taken as implying that in the
Government's view the only industries
which stand a chance of successful development are those already existent here. By
confining the benefits to new industries
the Government avoids an injustice to our
existing industries.
In the exercise of its functions under
the Bill the Ministry of Commerce will
have the assistance of an Advisory Committee, to which it may refer applications
for the benefits allowable under the
Measure. The Ministry, however, will
itself make the decision on each application, and that decision shall be final. In
any case in which the Ministry considers
that an annual payment should be made
the Ministry will obtain the consent of
the Ministry of Finance before such a
payment is made.

The Bill provides that, in order to

other conditions attaching to the acceptance of an application as the Ministry

Shooting Affair in County Derry.
Motion made, and Question proposed,

Mr. McCARROLL: I desire to raise
a question in regard to the shooting that
occurred on St. Patrick's Day in a part
of County Derry, when two Catholic
young men, who were members of a procession proceeding to a railway station,
were fired upon and seriously wounded.
Most of the facts in connection with this
diabolical affair have already appeared in
the Press, and I should like to know what
steps the Government propose to take to
apprehend the perpetrators of this outrage, to ensure that there will not be a
recurrence of such a terrible affair, and
that adequate measures will be taken to
safeguard the lives of the Catholic people
in these parts and to allow them to live
in the enjoyment of their rights as free
citizens.
I do not know that there is at all an
adequate appreciation of the terrible
character of this outrage. These men,
members of a procession, were proceeding in a legitimate way in the morning,
in broad daylight, to the railway station
at Magherafelt, when they were fired
upon by a large party. I understand
that there were several members of a
party lying in ambush and they opened
fire in this murderous fashion on this
unarmed body. Those men could not
have congregated there, in my opinion,
without the knowledge of the police
authorities in that area. Moreover, I
am bound to say that it was within the
knowledge of the Ministry of Home
Affairs that there was in this area a
reign of terror that has existed for a considerable period. There has been a good
deal of shooting, and there has been a
the
good deal of interference with
Catholic people in that area.
These facts
were, I understand, brought to the knowledge of the Government, and I suggest
that the Government either ignored
entirely the representations that were
made to them in regard to this state of
affairs, or that they failed absolutely to
do anything to provide adequate protection for that procession which, as I
say, was proceeding, as it was entitled to
do on that particular day, to the railway station.
There can be no question as to the right
of members of that procession to congregate at their hall and proceed, on St.
Patrick's Day, to the railway station and
there entrain to participate in a demonstration. I do not think there will be any
question as to their rights in this respect
when they were proceeding in a peaceable
way, and when they were unarmed. When
they were doing so this, as I call it,
murderous attack was made on them.
Those men with rifles congregated on
either side of the road, along which this
procession was proceeding, could not have
dropped out of the air. The police must
know the conditions in the locality. They
must know who the persons are who
possess these rifles, and this assembly of
armed men could not have taken place
without the knowledge of some of those
who are supposed to be the guardians of
law and order in that area. I suggest
that it is quite impossible that these men
could assemble there in broad daylight
and commit this atrocious crime without
the knowledge of either the regular police
force or the Special Constabulary in that
area.
I regret exceedingly the necessity of
raising this matter. There has been
growing up in Northern Ireland a spirit.
of peace and goodwill. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). This and other
incidents of which we have had to complain in this House have a very serious
and disturbing effect on the peace of the
country, and create alarm and apprehension in the minds of the people we
represent. I do say that the Government cannot be absolved entirely from
responsibility for permitting to be created
the situation in which this attack was
made upon inoffensive and unoffending
