Rathkenny Creamery and Milk Producers
Mr. BYRNE: I want to raise a question in regard to a milk war in County
Antrim? May I do it now?
Mr. SPEAKER: Yes, the hon. Member is entitled to raise that question on
the Adjournment.
Mr. BYRNE: As many people are
aware, there is a milk war going on in
County Antrim. The suppliers of the
Rathkenny Creamery stopped supplies
about a week ago.
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps
the hon. Member would allow me to say
that it is customary, in raising a matter
of definite importance of this kind, to
give notice to the Minister concerned.
Mr. BYRNE: I did mention the matter
to the Minister of Agriculture.
Mr. DEVLIN: It is the business of
the Government to deal with a milk war
as well as a real war.
Mr. BYRNE: The price paid to the
farmers during the last year has been
3d. to 5 d. a gallon. The Rathkenny
Creamery is the only creamery outside the
association of creameries, and by price
cutting it is preventing other creameries
giving a reasonable price to suppliers of
milk. This is a very serious matter for
the farmers in that locality. The prices
that are paid are ridiculously low. I
think it is the duty of the Minister of
Agriculture to take some action in the
matter, so that the people concerned may
obtain decent prices. The noble Lord
took a very active part in settling the
milk war last year, and I should like the
Minister of Agriculture to do something
in this dispute. I have been asked to
raise this matter, which is a very serious
one, and I hope the Minister of Agriculture, in his reply, will be able to give
us some information and some hope of a
settlement being arrived at.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: Since
the house assembled to-day my hon.
Friend did come to me on this subject,
and I have managed to get particulars
of what is happening. The Rathkenny
Creamery purchases manufacturing milk,
that is, milk for making butter, and from
the returns which I have received I am
satisfied that the Rathkenny Creamery
pays its producers a price which compares
very favourably with the price paid by
other co-operative creameries for manufacturing milk. The trouble between the
creamery and its producers appears to be
due entirely to the fact that the Rathkenny Creamery is selling a portion of
its manufacturing milk at a cut price in
the Belfast liquid milk market, and the
producers contend that they should be
paid liquid milk prices. This dispute is
one between the management committee
and the suppliers. I can only add that
I regret the dispute, and that I am prepared, if both sides desire it, to give any
assistance I can to try to effect a settlement. They, of course, are supplying
liquid milk at a lower price than the
ordinary liquid milk suppliers. Therefore, they are cutting the prices from a
good many people who supply nothing but
liquid milk.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 22nd March, 1932.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
BILL PRESENTED.
Ministry of Home Affairs Provisional
Order Confirmation (Bangor and
County of Down Financial
Relations) Bill,
"to confirm a Provisional Order of the
Ministry of Home Affairs relating to the
Borough of Bangor and County of Down,"
was presented by the Minister of Home
Affairs, supported by Mr. Hanna, and
read a First time.
Ordered, That the Bill be referred to
the Examiner of Petitions for Local Bills
and be printed. [Bill No. 6.]
Business of the House.
Resolved: "That, notwithstanding any
Standing Order or Custom of the House,
the remaining stages of the Consolidated
Fund Bill may be taken at this day's
sitting." (The Prime Minister.)
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Consolidated Fund Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"" That the Bill be now read a Second
time." (Mr. Barbour.)
Mr. BEATTIE: I thought the Financial Secretary would have given a brief
to this side of the House, but unfortunately that duty is left to me. I think
the expenditure as a whole that has been
embarked upon by the Government has
not given any beneficial results to the
people of the Six Counties.
It is my
intention to criticise this expenditure in
certain directions, and I believe that if
it is accepted in the spirit in which it
is given economies can be brought about
without any injustice being done. One
of the questions I wish to deal with is
that of transitional payments. I disagree
entirely with the action of the Government in issuing regulations under which
this Exchequer grant is administered by
the poor-law board. We may be told
that that is a body elected by the people.
I wish to repudiate any such statement
so far as it concerns the public assistance
committees. The public assistance committee is a body elected, one part by the
people and the other part by co-option.
The members are the representatives of
the majority party of the poor-law board,
and in the case of the Public Assistance
Committee of Belfast it really consists
of the representatives of the Unionist
Party. This committee has not done
credit to itself so far as its administration
of transitional payments are concerned,
because it has decided that 8/- a week
is a sufficient amount to be granted to a
man or woman or a youth between the
ages of 18 and 21.
I claim that such a body is not competent to deal with the administration of
transitional payments to the unemployed,
and the Government would be well
advised to act on the powers conferred
by the regulations and abolish that
committee. They should then set up
another committee, with a new mentality
and with more humane instincts, a committee that is familiar with the trials
and difficulties of the unemployed people.
The Government are spending £5,000 a
year on public assistance committees, and
if they would curtail that expenditure
and devote the money to the unemployed
it would be economy in the true sense of
the word. The Government have set up
a service for investigation work, which is
a duplication of a service already existing, and I do not see why two similiar
services should be maintained at the
expense of the deserving poor.
Another point I want to bring before
the Minister of Labour is this.
You are
spending money on the payment of legal
gentlemen for their services as chairmen
of courts of referees. These gentlemen
receive from £600 to £700 a year as

On the question of housing the Government has spent large sums of money
for the purpose of assisting the local
authorities and builders with the object
of providing homes for the people who
require them. I think the Government's
policy on the housing question is wrong,
because it did not get sufficient houses
when you were giving £100 plus £40 from
the Corporation, and to-day you are only
giving £25 with no prospect of anything
from the Corporation. I think that £25
will be lost. It will really be futile so far
as the private builders are concerned. It
has been always claimed by myself and
the representatives of the party I have
the honour to represent in this House,
that no public money should be given to
any individual without a voice in its
administration. Now, in house building,
I think the Government when they make
subsidies should have a voice in fixing
the letting value of the houses, and until
the Government do that we will never
get houses fit for the working classes.
You will get them fit for living in, but
not fit for paying for. It is a paying
proposition the working classes are looking for at the present moment. There
are plenty of houses. There are houses
built by the Corporation. I was round
an
avenue last night where there are

being charged.

Mr. BEATTIE: Yes.
1932 we have built our normal supply

There is also the question of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary and the Special Constabulary. I am more particularly
concerned with the Royal Ulster Constabulary at the moment. There was a
rule in the old Royal Irish Constabulary
that the members of that force should be
in a position to administer justice as between one class of the community and the
other, and they were enjoined against
joining secret societies. When this Government took office a like rule prevailed
for a considerable period, but latterly I
understand the members of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary are allowed to join
the Orange Order, a secret political
society. How. I ask you, can a constable,
a sergeant, or a district-inspector of the
Orange Order do justice as between one
section of the community and the other
when he is sworn, cn the one hand, to be
a loyal brother to his friends of the Order
and, on the the other hand, to do his duty
to the State and to administer evenhanded justice to all. Such a man could
not possibly do his duty.
Mr. GRANT: Are you certain of that?
Mr. HEALY: I am certain of my
facts, though you are not often certain of
yours. It is a scandal that does not exist
anywhere else that a police force under
the Government should be in a position to
join the particular religious and political
organisation that is at the back of the
Government themselves. Probably the
Members of the Government are members
of this organisation too. I suppose they
are. But, at all events, they ought to
consider the interests of the remaining
members of the community. There are a
great many Protestants who are not

would like even-handed justice administered as well, but they are not likely to

constable being asked to do something

In the administration of old-age pensions I had frequent communications with
the Government. It is quite impossible
for people living in rural areas to get
proof of age, and the Government
will not grant an old-age pension now
unless actual proof of age is available.
The result is that there are many people
of 72, 73, and probably older who are
otherwise eligible but who cannot claim
an old-age pension. The Government
know quite well that the records in the
parish registers, schools, and otherwise,
are incomplete in some cases and nonexistent in others. If they were to
accept the recommendations of their own
courts or of their own inspectors of the
Ministry of Labour we should have no

has seen an old person he has a fair idea
to whether that person is of the
requisite age or not, and particularly
when he visits him in his home.
But someone sitting in an office in Belfast, who has never had an opportunity
of seeing the applicant or anyone connected with the hearing, gaily turns the
applicant down, and denies that person
a pension often for as long as two or
three years.

as

The other matter I want to raise deals
with the question of the provision of seed

land, and things of that kind, that were

Minister denied it, but here we have the

with the country farmers, and especially
the poorer people, in the crisis they are.
passing through to-day. In the Free
State seed oats and seed potatoes are
available for farmers in like circumstances,
and they were available in Northern Ireland as late as 1925, but for some reason
or other, perhaps the officials do not want
to be bothered, they will no longer give
grants of seed potatoes or seed oats.
•
They are giving small sums of money,
obtainable through the bank in the
ordinary way, to the people for the purchase of seed potatoes. Let the House
understand what that means. The
average loan for a small farmer is about
£3, and it takes two people along with

I never heard such a preposterous statement in my life from a Department
supposed to represent the interests of the

in the farming community. It is news

with Great Britain are concerned, the

That is the sum total of what we have

up to
1925, and on which they are

If I had known there would be a debate
to-day I could have brought a list of all
blind persons in receipt of an allowance
in the City of Belfast. We have been
thanked by the blind persons' organisation. There are no people more entitled
to sympathy than blind people. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Blindness is one
of the greatest afflictions anyone could
imagine or conceive. It is very remarkable that most blind people take
interest in football and every other form
of sport, and in politics and everything
in which an ordinary person takes an
interest. I remember spending a night
with the members of one of the blind
person's organisations, and, after we had
discussed their own grievances first, there
was no subject in which they did not
take an interest, or which they were not
competent to discuss. There is nothing
so terrible as to belong to the kingdom
of darkness, to know what is going on
about you, and to be able to take no part
in it.
It is humiliating to any country that
blind people should have to go out on the
street and beg or importune persons, or
hold out a can to get money. I do not
know how it comes, but I have seen some
of that in Belfast lately. I cannot
understand how it is necessary. We
have a rule in the Corporation that any
person certified to be blind whose allowances do not amount to £1 a week, shall
have them made up to £1. That is for
one person, and, of course, we consider
what is going into the house. Many will
ask, "How can they live on £1 a week?"
It is true it is very hard to live on £1
a week, but at the same time it is a great

Newry stating that any attempt to hold
a demonstration or to deliver an address
on Easter Sunday would be suppressed by
Governmental powers.
On only one occasion in Newry was
there any departure from the conditions
laid down by the Government or from
the general programme. On that occasion
the party who departed from it was
arrested. The Government can make up
its own mind what to do at any time, but
it should not create the innovation of
waging war on those who go out to pray
for their own dead and for nobody else.
In the next place, if it is an offence to
have this prayer meeting at all, and if it
is the duty of the Government's agentsthe police to prevent it, then there is a
way of preventing it. If it is to be
legally suppressed, then I say to sneak out
in the midst of the night and deface the
posters is a despicable way of dealing with
any object. I would draw the right hon.
Gentleman's attention to the fact that
these posters were scraped down in the
midst of the night. The point I want to
make out is that this is a meeting which
is being held in the cemetery after
ordinary Mass in the Church.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Mental Treatment Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Although in England
a comprehensive statute which in effect
consolidated and brought up to date the
law in regard to lunacy was passed in
1890, and a subsequent Measure-the
Mental Treatment Act was passed in
1930, bringing certain valuable reforms
into operation, lunacy law in Ireland
for all practical purposes has remained
unaltered since the passing of the Act of
1875. Although I am glad to say the
actual care and treatment of this malady
is no less enlightened and efficient in Northern Ireland than in any other part of
the world, the fact remains that our
legislation dealing with the question is in
some respects archaic and has not kept
pace with modern developments.
While, no doubt, the progress of medical
science and the growth of an enlightened
public opinion have revolutionised the
treatment of the mentally afflicted, there
is still a tendency to regard to mental
illness as something carrying an indelible
stigma, and although we may congratulate
ourselves that we are no longer living in
an age which considered fetters and a
straw pallet as the suitable equipment for
the treatment of the insane, the deepseated idea that persons of unsound mind
are to be regarded as lepers or pariahs to
be shut off from society still survives to
a certain extent. Consider, for example,
as evidence of this the existing procedure
for dealing with dangerous lunatics, to
which I shall again refer, which would
seem to imply that there is something
actually criminal in mental infirmity.
It is of the first importance that this
entirely wrong and cruel idea should be
got rid of. As has been well said in the
Report of the Royal Commission
Lunacy, which sat in 1926:-
on
"The keynote of the past has been
detention, the keynote of the future
should be prevention and treatment."
It is essential that mental illness should
be considered in its true perspective as a
serious malady requiring sympathetic
and specialised treatment, and one which
does not necessarily carry in its train
any greater reproach than any ordinary
physical disability. Mental disease, like
other forms of disease, is in many cases
curable and the chances of effecting a cure
are infinitely improved if treatment is
undertaken in the incipient stages of the
disease. Under existing conditions, and
as the law now stands, it is almost
inevitable that any disposition towards
mental disability will be concealed as
long as possible on account of the prejudice which unfortunately still obtains.
in regard to this malady.
To endeavour to combat this false impression and to provide for the early
treatment of sufferers is one of the main
objects of this Bill. Hitherto the specialised treatment provided in our public
mental hospitals has been confined to persons definitely certified as of unsound
mind, and the preventive value of such
treatment has been denied to those who
may be merely threatened
threatened with the
disease or who may be suffering from
some temporary form of mental instability which does not amount to actual
insanity.
Mental Treatment Bill-
Second Reading
23 MARCH 1932
The object of Part I of our Bill is,
therefore, to enable such cases of incipient
mental disease to be treated in mental
hospitals without any necessity for certification and without undue formality or
the intervention of anything in the
nature of judicial proceedings. The provisions in this respect have been adopted
with little alteration, from the corresponding provisions of the Mental Treatment Act of 1930 now operating in England. These provisions provide for
voluntary treatment and also for temporary treatment.
With regard to voluntary treatment,
it is provided that persons who are desirous of submitting themselves for
treatment for illness of a mental nature
may voluntarily avail themselves of the
benefit of treatment in mental institutions and may submit themselves to such
treatment without the necessity for
certification.
It may be interesting to note that, in
connection with this matter, evidence was
given before the Royal Commission, to
which I have already referred, of several
distressing cases of people who felt that
they were becoming mentally unstable,
and in whose cases rest and special treatment in a mental home would have been
invaluable, but who were unable to avail
themselves of this advantage until their
illness had progressed to the point when
they became certifiable. Had it been
open to them to receive the necessary
treatment in the initial stages of their
illness it is possible that its progress
might have been arrested and the necessity for certification might never have
arisen.
The provisions dealing with temporary
treatment are intended to meet the case
of persons suffering from some temporary
form of mental disorder which, in the
opinion of their doctors, would be likely to
yield to the specialised mental treatment
in a mental home. The patient in such
cases, although possibly suffering from some
purely temporary form of mental illness
may nevertheless be incapable at the
moment of volition and unable, therefore, to avail themselves of the provisions
relating to voluntary treatment to which
I have just referred.
The procedure proposed under which
such cases may be received in a mental
hospital provides for an application to
this effect being made by the husband,
wife, or relative, or, if made by some
person other than such relatives, the
application must indicate the connection
of the person making the application
with the patient. The application must
be supported by a certificate from two
doctors to the effect that the patient is
suffering from mental illness and is likely
to benefit by temporary treatment. The
patient may then be accepted for a period
not exceeding six months as a temporary
patient and this period may be extended
for further periods of six months with
the consent of the Ministry, if it appears
from medical evidence that recovery is
likely as a result of further temporary
treatment. It will be noted that, in this
case as in the case of a voluntary patient,
the patient is not certified to be of unsound mind, nor is the intervention of
a judicial authority required. The
reasons underlying these provisions for
voluntary and temporary treatment will,
I think, be fairly obvious.
It may be appropriate if I here refer
to proposals which are in the nature of
a logical corollary to this system of preventive treatment in the incipient stages
of the malady. I allude to the provisions in Part IV. of the Bill which
will enable public mental hospitals to
provide clinics at which extern patients
may obtain advice and treatment, and
which will also enable patients who have
been discharged from the institution to
receive advice and treatment which may
be of the greatest benefit in preventing
a recurrence of the illness.
Apart from these provisions the opportunity has been taken to effect various
amendments in the general law relating
to mental disorder, which will have the
effect of bringing the law in Northern
Ireland more into line with the more
modern English code, and which will also
simplify the existing procedure. I do
not at this stage propose to go into
elaborate detail, but I would like to mention a few of the more important points
where it has been thought desirable to
introduce such amendments.
It is first of all proposed, with the
object of removing anything which may
tend to keep alive the unfortunate prejudice which we know still exists in regard to mental disorder, to abolish
certain terms which have hitherto been
employed in connection with mental
illness, and which have acquired a sinister and objectionable significance. The
term "lunatic" will pass into oblivion, and
Mental Treatment Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Sir Dawson Bates]
the expression "person of unsound mind"
will be used to designate persons suffering from this form of illness. Similarly,
"lunatic asylums" will in future be
more accurately described as "mental
hospitals," and the objectionable terms
"pauper" or "poor" in relation to inmates of public mental hospitals will be
replaced by the expression "rate-aided."
It will be observed that a considerable
portion of Part II. of the Bill deals with
the procedure in regard to the admission.
to and discharge from institutions of
patients. With regard to admissionsthere are no fewer than 7 different forms
of procedure for the admission of persons
of unsound mind into mental institutions.
The most common method is that employed in the case of ordinary admissions
to public mental hospitals, and the conditions governing these are, strange to
say, not at present laid down by statute
but are prescribed in the regulations
made by each individual asylum committee
and approved by the Governor.
The
conditions so laid down by regulation are
in short an application supported by a
medical certificate on which a recommendation from a justice for the admission of the patient is obtained.
In the case of so-called dangerous
lunatics admitted under the provisions of
the Act of 1867, unfortunately a comparatively numerous class, although in
many instances the individuals are not
dangerous in the ordinary acceptance of
the term, the procedure laid down is entirely contrary to the whole trend of
modern opinion in regard to mental illness.
Under this statute, alleged dangerous
lunatics are, if I may put it in this way,
arrested, brought before two justices,
charged with being dangerous lunatics,
convicted and committed to an asylum.
They are, in fact, treated as criminals.
Mr. BEATTIE: Did you say alleged
lunatics?
Sir DAWSON BATES: May I put a
case to my hon. Friend? A constable
going along the street sees a man behaving
in a way that is more or less dangerous
to himself or to somebody else. The
constable arrests that man and brings
him before the Court, and, according to
the present law, on the evidence of the
doctors, he is committed as a dangerous
lunatic.
Mr. BEATTIE: He is not an alleged
lunatic.
Sir DAWSON BATES: In the case of
private patients, the procedure, laid down
by statute, is somewhat similar to that in
the case of patients admitted to public
mental hospitals, except that it is
necessary to have certificates from two
doctors instead of one.
I need not refer to other special
methods of admission as those under the
Army Act, under the Acts relating to
Criminal Lunatics, or in the case of
lunatics so found by inquisition, as these
will not be affected by this Bill.

common
It is, therefore, now proposed, following
the practice which has obtained for many
years in England, to adopt a
procedure for admission under which persons of unsound mind may be received
into mental institutions on a simple order
of a J.P. supported by a
medical
certificate.
In order to provide for cases where it
may be desirable that the patient should
be removed at once to a mental institution,
provision is made that, if the doctor
certifying the patient is satisfied that he
should be removed forthwith to the
asylum, this may be done in anticipation
of the justice's order. In such cases, however, the authority to detain the patient is
limited to seven days unless, meanwhile,
the full procedure for admission has been
completed.
There is also the further type of case
where a person of unsound mind is found
actually behaving in such a way as to
constitute a danger to himself or to
others, and to meet such cases machinery
is provided, as in the English Act, which
will enable the patient to be placed under
restraint, pending certification and completion of the necessary formalities to
enable him to be received in a mental
institution. The proposed provision,
which, as I have said, follows that in
the English Act, gives power to the
police to bring such persons for safe
custody to a workhouse, pending the completion of the order for their admission
to a mental hospital.
It has also been thought desirable to
adopt provisions which appear in the
English Act whereby cases of persons of
unsound mind, believed to be cruelly illtreated or neglected, can be brought under
notice of a justice, who can then set
machinery in motion to have the matter.
553 Mental Treatment Bill-
23 MARCH 1932

Second Reading

investigated, and, if necessary, to have the
person of unsound mind removed to a
mental hospital for proper care.
It will be observed that a somewhat
important alteration has been made in
regard to the period of duration of
reception orders as compared with the
duration of certification under the existing
law. As matters stand at present, there
is no limit to the period during which the
certification of unsound mind enabling a
patient to be detained in an institution
remains in force. Consequently, apart
from the possibility of a case coming under
the observation of the Inspectors of
Mental Treatment in the course of their
inspections, a person who had become
cured might, nevertheless, as the result
of some oversight on the part of the persons in charge of the institution, continue
to be detained in the institution.
re-
Such a contingency is no doubt most
unlikely to arise in institutions so admirably conducted as our present day mental
hospitals, but it was, nevertheless, considered necessary when the English Act
of 1890 was passed to insert provisions
safeguarding beyond a possibility of
doubt patients in mental institutions
from being detained after recovery. It
has been thought well to include in this
Bill provisions corresponding to those in
force in England. Under these, a
ception order, which will in future be
the authority for the detention of the
patient, will remain valid in the first
instance for one year only, and thereafter for successive periods of 2, 3 and 5
years. Before the termination of each such
period the medical officer of the institution must certify that the patient is
still of unsound mind, and sanction must
be obtained from the Ministry for the
continuance in force of the reception
order for the subsequent period. This
procedure ensures that every individual
case must be brought up for examination
and review at comparatively frequent
periods.
The existing provisions in regard to
discharge, as in the case of admission,
are partly governed by regulations and
partly by statute, and show a similar lack
of uniformity. Provisions similar to
those in the English Act of 1890 have,
therefore, been incorporated in the Bill
and while no radical change in principle
is effected, this arrangement will, it is
believed, prove more convenient in
operation and for purposes of reference.
Part III. of the Bill deals mainly with
a proposed alteration of the system under
which private establishments are authorised to receive persons of unsound mind.
The existing arrangement is that laid
down in the Private Asylums Act of
1842, and, as may be imagined, can
hardly be regarded to-day as entirely up
to date.
The system of licensing laid down in
that Act under which proprietors of
private asylums must apply annually at
Quarter Sessions for licences has been
subjected to criticism. So far back as
the year 1846 the inspectors of lunatics.
in their annual report stated that the
procedure was found to be attended with
inconvenience and was open to objection.
Such decision must necessarily depend
mainly upon medical and technical considerations, and it is, therefore, now proposed to substitute in place of the system of licensing at Quarter Sessions a
system of registration by the Ministry,
who will be advised by their inspectors.
Part IV. of the Bill comprises various
amendments of the law relative to public
mental hospitals.
I have already dealt with those relating to extern treatment and after-care,
and I hardly think that it is necessary
at the moment to refer to any of the
other Clauses save those relating to the
parliamentary grant in aid of the maintenance of persons of unsound mind in
public mental hospitals and the settlement and chargeability of rate-aided
patients.
With regard to the parliamentary
grant, I may explain that, prior to the
establishment of the Northern Government, the parliamentary grant was made
by way of a capitation grant of half the
net charge of maintenance subject to a
maximum of 4s per week. These grants
were payable out of the Local Taxation
Account, but for many years the funds
in this account were insufficient to meet
the entire amount of the required charge,
and the actual payments did not amount
to the authorised maximum.
On the establishment of the Northern
Government, when the Local Taxation
Account was wound up, it was decided
to stereotype the grant at the average
amount paid during the three financial
years from 1918 to 1920, and this
Mental Treatment Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Sir Dawson Bates]
arrangement was embodied in the Local
Government Act, 1923. Owing, however, to the increase in the number of
patients in the asylums, the fact that
the amount of grant was thus fixed and
did not fluctuate in proportion to the
increase of the patients has, no doubt,
thrown an increased burden of charge on
the local authorities.
As hon. Members are no doubt aware,
the question of the amount of this grant
forms one of the matters on which a
recommendation has been made by the
Committee which recently sat to consider
the relations between State and local
expenditure, whose Report is at present
under the consideration of Government,
and while it seems clear that the time
has come when a change in the existing
system of fixed grant is called for, the
House will, I am sure, appreciate that,
until a decision has been arrived at in
regard to this, together with the other
important questions dealt with by that
Committee, it is not possible specifically
to lay down in this Bill the details of a
new system of grant. I have the permission of the Minister of Finance to
state that the grants in future will not
be less than at present.
I now turn to the very complex
question of the Law of Settlement. There
has hitherto in Ireland been no such law,
and as a result the asylum of the district
in which a person of unsound mind is
found must receive and maintain such
person. This, in some cases, presses hardly
upon asylums which may thus have
to maintain an undue proportion of persons really belonging to some other part
of the country. In England and in
Scotland a Law of Settlement does
obtain, but in its operation is of an extremely complicated character. Members
will, I am sure, realise that, in the case
of persons who may have lived at various
places for comparatively brief periods
during their lifetime, the fixing of
liability for their maintenance on any
particular district is a matter of no small
difficulty. Great difficulty in enforcing
the Law of Settlement exists in England.
We do not want to introduce an arrangement which will give rise to a similar
difficulty. We have, therefore, endeavoured to produce a method for fixing
chargeability which will be comparatively
simple in operation, and our proposal will
go far to meet the difficulty.
We propose that, in the first place, the
mental institution of the district where
the person of unsound mind is found will
prima facie be responsible for his maintenance. If, however, the committee of
that institution can show that the patient
has not been resident in their district for
a period of three years and has been continually resident in some other district
for three years, the liability will then be
thrown on to that other district, and the
patient may be transferred to the mental
hospital thereof, or a suitable financial
arrangement entered into between the two
districts.
I have not endeavoured to give a detailed résumé of the contents of all the
various Clauses as, I think, this is
scarcely necessary at this stage of the Bill,
more especially as many of these are selfexplanatory and a substanial number,
moreover, are really re-enactments of
existing law with minor amendments, a
course which has been followed to avoid
the necessity for legislation by reference.
so far as possible. By this means
substantial part of the Act of 1875 and of
the Act of 1842 has been repealed, which
will, I think, help to clarify to a certain
extent the very involved code of law which
deals with lunacy and will prove, I hope,
a stepping stone to a complete codification
at some future date.
a

to the preparation of the recommendations.
on which this Bill is based. I beg to
move.

ing that prevention is better than cure.

I would also like to deal shortly with

I am sure no man is going to go to a
certain district because he is mentally deranged. That is one of the things everybody tries to hide. The worst case I came
in contact with affected me so much that
he thought I was the mentally deranged
man. A mentally deranged man always
thinks the man beside him is the one who
is mentally deranged. I heard a story
about a prominent leader of the Unionist
party visiting Purdysburn. He was going
through a ward with the doctor and the
doctor said to him: "That gentleman is
going out to-morrow." He said: "I
would like to speak to him.' He went
over to the man and said: "Good-day,
my friend."
The patient said: "Goodday; who might you be?" "I am Lord
Hugh Cecil," he replied. The patient
said: "You will not be long here till they
will cure you of that disease. When I
came here I thought I was the Duke of
York." I had the experience of being
an orderly in attendance on cases of this
kind. I was in Netley Hospital, to which
some very serious cases of mental trouble
came from India. I had an experience
there that taught me that the mentally
deranged man always thinks that he is
normal and that the normal man is
mentally deranged.

should like to congratulate the Government, and especially the Minister of
Home Affairs, on having brought forward this Bill. I should like to congratulate the Minister on two counts.
In the first place, because the Bill is the

being brought into force in Northern

I am heartily in accord with all that

there are one or two points which I

one of the main objects of the Bill is to
""
do away with the term lunatic."
That is a most praiseworthy aim, I am
but while the actual lunatic still
sure,
continues to exist-and I am afraid there

The hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr.
Beattie) expressed grave suspicion and
grave mistrust about this Measure. He
thought very much advantage would not
be taken of it. I can assure him he is
quite wrong. There is already an
extern department for mental treatment

staffed by a very capable and eminent

advantage is taken of that department
to a very considerable extent. He sees
quite a number of patients there and is

hon. Member, perhaps, has not as much

can assure him there are quite a number
of people who are afraid of one thing,

and that is that they are going off their
heads. They come to a medical man in
order to try to get some form of treatment which will keep them from becoming insane. They feel themselves that
their brains are going wrong, and they are
exceedingly anxious to be treated by
somebody who will be able to give them
such instructions and such directions as will
prevent them from becoming insane. That
is just the type of people whom it is most
essential not to send to a lunatic asylum,
or, as it is now called, a home for mental
treatment, but to a mental hospital where
their cases can be looked into.
I hope
that under this Bill it will be possible for
mental homes to be established which
have not at all the same accommodation
as an ordinary mental hospital or a
lunatic asylum, homes where patients
can be taken in and detained for a fortnight, perhaps, or a month, or even three
months, if necessary, without the stigma
of a mental home or of mental treatment
being attached to them, or without it
being said that they have ever been inmates of what I am afraid will still be
called a lunatic asylum, despite this Bill.
I am also very glad that the possibility
of people being put into such a home without any certification, should have been
recognised under the Bill, and I hope that
one of the beneficial effects of it will be
that such a home as I have visualised will
very shortly be established in Northern
Ireland.
The second point which I want to make
is that the regulations both for the admission of patients to homes for mental
treatment, and for their discharge from
those homes have been very well regularised under this Bill. From the point
of view of the general public, as the hon.
Member for Pottinger has already emphasised, one of the most important things is
that the general public should be satisfied
that there is no possibility of a perfectly
sane man being shut up in a lunatic asylum, or in a home for mental treatment.
That is admirably safeguarded under the
Bill. There is no possibility of patients
being admitted to these homes without
adequate inquiry being carried out, and
the mental condition of the patients being
a matter about which there can be no dispute.
In connection with the patients in these
hospitals, I am very glad to see a
Clause in the Bill which gives the medical
officer in charge power to prevent their
discharge. In the past it has been possible for the relatives of a person of unsound mind to take him away from the
mental hospital, and to undertake to take
charge of him themselves. I am quite
certain that that privilege has been abused
in the past, and that harm has undoubtedly been done by taking out of
mental hospitals patients who were not fit
to be at large. I am, therefore, glad to see
that the medical officer in charge is being
given power to say that those patients
should not be at large. It is possible
that they would be a danger either to
themselves or to their friends and neighbours, and therefore, they are going to
be kept under control.
Another provision which I am glad to
see from the purely professional point
of view, is that the certifier that a man
is of unsound mind is to be protected
against vexatious actions at law. It will
be necessary for the High Court to give
leave for such an action to be brought.
It will no longer be possible for a man
who considers that he has been unjustly
certified to bring an action, without first
of all showing that he has reasonable
grounds for believing that the certifier
did not act in good faith or with proper
skill. This provision will give considerable protection to the medical certifier.
In regard to the settlement Clause,
which gives an authority power to have
a patient transferred to the district from
which he came, I think the provision in
the Bill is a fairly good one, but this
question of settlement is a very difficult
matter on which to make up one's mind.
When the Local Government Commission was sitting we received a great
amount of evidence in regard to Acts of
Settlement from the various
various public
authorities who appeared before us, and
the opinions among those authorities themselves were very diverse. Some authorities wished the Acts of Settlement to be
made much more drastic much more stringent, and much more easily applicable,
than they are at present. Others had
come to the conclusion that Acts of Settlement really cost more than would be required to keep the patient or the pauper,
as the case might be, in the institution to
which he had been admitted. However,
I think the suggested arrangement contained in the Bill is quite a good one, and
one which may be taken advantage of by
the different public authorities, without
putting them to very much trouble or
expense.

On a perusal of the various Clauses of
the Bill, and also of the Schedules, one
cannot but be impressed by the vast improvement that has taken place in the
treatment of those unfortunate people
who suffer mentally. I was reminded
very forcibly of the state of affairs, and
of the manner in which pauper lunatics
left many years ago, when I was
acting as commissioner in charge of a
large workhouse. In a place apart from
the main building there was a series of
kennel-like sheds or cubicles, very dark
and insanitary, and altogether calculated
to make people madder, if that were possible. Of course those places had ceased
to be used, but I was informed that that
was where the "poor loonies" were kept
not a great while ago.
Medical science, and up-to-date
methods of hygiene and sanitation, have
made for great changes in this respect.
Practically every person, even the poorest
of our people, can have recourse to institutions which before were closed to
them on account of the charges.
I observe that as far back as 1821,
when we had the first Lunacy Act, and
down to recent years, all the various Acts
described these people
as lunatics,
criminal lunatics, and pauper lunatics.
These terms might be described as household words. I hope Members of the
House will not take this in a personal
way. We are well aware how these terms
are created, and sustained. I am glad
they are now, happily, to be done away
with, and we hope never to hear them
again used. In the same way the lunatic
asylums are to be termed public mental
hospitals, and so on. We cannot but
look on these changes as synonymous with
the better treatment of the patients who
are in these institutions. While we are
sorry for those afflicted persons and the
suffering they undergo, we take it as a
timely and healthy sign of the progressive times we live in. Let us also hope
that it is a sign of a proportionate decrease in the numbers of mentally afflicted
persons.
There is no doubt, and no one can
deny the fact, that the various Lunacy
Acts required overhauling and revision,
in order that these unfortunate people
should be more sympathetically treated,
and their particular needs understood,
and for this reason I heartily welcome
the Bill and hope for its satisfactory
operation. I hope that the financial

made more secure. I feel this is most

and the want of which would not have
been any serious inconvenience to any
person in Northern Ireland for a very
considerable time to come. I think the
reason for the introduction of this
Measure is not that anybody here wants
it-the Government do not want it-but
that a similar Measure was introduced in
the Imperial Parliament, and this craze
that you have got of walking step by
step with Great Britain impelled you to
introduce legislation on almost identical
lines. If I may say so, the need for such
legislation in Northern Ireland is not at
all comparable to the need in Great
Britain, because there have been several
instances of scandals in connection with
the committal of lunatics to private institutions in England, but there have
been none of that type, so far as I know,
in Northern Ireland.
Therefore, the need in both areas is
not identical, but the policy of keeping
step with Great Britain must needs be
pursued to the detriment of the most
deserving class in the community, namely,
the farmers. It is far more essential
that there should be brought in some
Measure dealing with agriculture than
that the time of the House should be
taken up dealing with the treatment of
mentally afflicted people. It is curious,
too, in respect of this that the Northern
Government are walking in the wake of
the Free State. At a very early stage
in the administration there they changed
the old terms of "lunatic" and "lunatic
asylum," and substituted the term
"mental hospital" and "mental home."
You are now copying, in what I regard
as a most vital department, from the
Irish Free State. You are adopting this
Measure here not because of any special
need, but because a similar Measure was
introduced in another place. I notice,
too, that the Government Front Bench
was remarkably well filled for a Measure
of this kind. I noticed also that the
hierarchy in another place were occupying
the seats in the gallery for the Senate.
Apparently the question of mental
treatment excites the Government far
more than any ordinary measure, and
I leave it to the imagination of the
House to interpret the significance of
that.
There are confined in the ordinary
mental institutions in this country today a large number of people who, I
think, if their relations were desirous,
could be discharged immediately without
any harm to themselves or to the community, but it is pretty well known.
that after an individual has spent a
considerable time in a public institution,
whether an improvement has been noted
in the case or not, the relatives do not
want him back. It implies a certain
stigma on the family. That is particularly so if there are young persons,
especially girls, behind who do not want
their relatives back in the old home.
Therefore, there are many people who
to-day could with safety be discharged,
and who are at present a public charge
on the rates. There is no attempt made
in this Measure to ensure that a matter
of that kind may be made right.

HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Black]
The other Clause to which I referred
is Clause 54, which deals with the financial assistance to be given to the local
authorities. That has already been dealt
with by a number of Members who have
spoken, but I think it is a matter of some
importance. The provision of finance as
between the Exchequer and the local
authorities commenced as far back as
1875. The original idea was that half
the expenses of the maintenance of rateaided patients should be borne by the
Exchequer and the other half by the local
authorities. The idea was that the total
cost per week was a matter of 8s, 4s of
which would be borne by the Exchequer
and 4s by the local authority.
That was all very well at the time,
but owing, as the hon. and gallant Member for East Down (Lieut.-Colonel
Gordon) has mentioned, to the failure of
the Local Taxation Account the amount
which was contributed by the Exchequer
got less and less-that is, after the passing of the Local Government Act-and
eventually in 1923 the matter was compromised by this block grant which has
been referred to. It was no longer a
capitation payment, but a block grant.
The hon. Member for the University has
referred to this block grant as the beginning of the local authorities' trouble.
I do not believe it was the beginning of
the trouble at all. I think that it was
merely to put a brake on the tendency
which had gone on for years and years
by which the Exchequer contributed a
smaller and smaller proportion and the
local
authorities were forced to contribute a larger and larger proportion of
the cost of the patients.
The local authorities have naturally
objected to a system which has been
gradually raising their contribution
from 50 per cent. to 80 per cent. or 90
per cent. of the cost of maintenance.
The House will recollect that in the report of the Financial Relations Committee, presided over by the hon. and
gallant Member for South Derry
(Captain Chichester-Clark), there was a
recommendation that this grant should
be very substantially increased. Nothing has been done towards increasing the
amount, and in this Bill we have the
provision in Clause 54. Now, the Minister of Home Affairs has given the House
the assurance that it is not intended to
decrease the amount of the block grant,
but the wording of Section 54 is surely
very alarming to the local authorities.
The wording is as follows:
"The Ministry shall, by regulations
made with the approval of the Ministry of Finance, provide for the payment out of moneys provided by
Parliament, to each council of a county
or county borough, in respect of the
expenses of the council on account of
the maintenance of rate-aided patients
in the public mental hospital established for such county or county
borough, of annual grants of such
amounts and subject to such conditions
as may be prescribed in the regulations,
and such regulations may provide for
the discontinuance of grants payable to
such a county or county borough council
under section ten of the Local Government Act (Northern Ireland), 1923 (as
amended by subsequent enactments),
and for the application of any provisions of that section to grants payable under this section.'
Therefore, instead of having what they
have at present, an Act of Parliament,
a statutory provision, entitling them to
a certain block grant every year what is
in this Bill, as it is now drafted, is a
provision by which the Minister of Home
Affairs and the Minister of Finance may
by a stroke of the pen decrease or wipe
out this grant altogether.
I quite agree it would be a mistake to
attempt to stereotype for ever the amount
prescribed by the Act of 1923. That
has worked out rather unfairly in effect
for this reason, that the amounts were
lump sums while the number of patients
in asylums in every county has increased,
with the result that the local authorities
since 1923 are progressively getting a
smaller and smaller amount per head
from the Exchequer in respect of patients.
But while I do not think there should
be anything in the nature of stereotyping
the block grant so that the Exchequer
can contend that it is the maximum the
local authorities can get, I think some
provision ought to be inserted in the Bill
to show that the Exchequer intend to
pay not only the amount they pay at
present, but that they should pay a
fairer proportion of the contribution on
the lines, I would suggest, of the recommendations in the Report of the Financial Relations Committee.
I realise it is difficult to provide all
this in a Bill until the financial relationship between the local authorities and

homes.
I do not like this policy of imitation
of either England or the Free State,
but so far as mitigating the stigma
upon people who suffer from mental
diseases and their relatives is concerned
I think everybody will welcome the departure from the expression "lunatic" to
that of mental patient. Hitherto, as is
very well known, the fact that a person
suffered from a mental disease was
very serious reproach on the family. The
family generally tried to disclaim him.
or her, and in many instances the word
a
"lunatic" became the butt of ridicule and
the subject of gibes and jokes. This
sprung to a large extent from the manner in which the law itself regarded him.
It is not so very long ago since the provincial newspapers used to publish details regarding the committal of a lunatic
in exactly the same way as they published
details regarding the committal of a thief
or some other type of criminal.
It is a grand thing to be able to get
away from that, and I should like the
use of the word "lunatic" to be abolished
in every respect, even in the description
of the lunacy laws. I should like to see
it laid down under Part II., of the Bill
that in all references to regulations
under the Lunacy (Ireland) Acts these
Acts shall be known as the Mental
Diseases Acts. The farther we get away
from this gross description the better it
will be, because the word "lunatic" is
one that is very easily perpetuated notwithstanding all the efforts of the law in
the opposite direction. With regard to
the committal of mentally diseased persons, they should certainly not be brought
up as criminals are brought up, and when
they are being removed to a mental hospital, if police assistance is necessary, as
it generally is, the police should be plain
clothes policemen and not uniformed
officers of the law.

Regarding the remark of the Member
for South Fermanagh as to the contrast
between the provision made in this
Measure for the alleviation of mentally
diseased persons and for the farmers,
statistics furnish proof that from the
farming community more than from any
other part of the community the greatest
number of mentally diseased persons is
drawn. The moral is very obvious. If
the conditions of the farming community
were much brighter and happier and the
farmers were more prosperous than they
are to-day, it is inconceivable that they
would furnish such a large proportion of
the inmates of mental hospitals. So far
as the farmers of the Six Counties are
concerned, I do not think they will find
any encouragement from the Government
Benches to believe that the time when
they will cease to send so many people to
these mental hospitals is approaching.
On the contrary, they may justifiably be
forced to the conclusion that the present
Government is not only a menace to the
physical health of the farmers, but a
menace also to their mental condition.

24 MARCH 1932

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 24th March, 1932.
The House met at Twelve of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
BANK RATE IN NORTHERN
IRELAND.
Mr. DEVLIN asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state why the
Bank rate in this country is one per cent.
greater than in Great Britain, and
whether the Government is prepared to
make representations to the banking
authorities to have the same rate made
applicable here as across the Channel.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I cannot state why the Irish bank
rate is, at the moment, precisely one per
cent. greater than the Bank of England
rate.
I would suggest, however, that international considerations have much to do
with the fixing of the Bank of England.
rate, and obviously, such have little significance in Ireland. Moreover, it must
not be assumed that the English Banks
charge their borrowers merely at the
English Bank rate.
Having regard to these considerations,
the answer to the second part of the question is in the negative.
Mr. DEVLIN: If we are to have the
step by step policy in regard to other
matters surely, in view of the fact that
we are an integral part of Great Britain,
we ought to have the same terms in the
banks as Great Britain.
to
Mr. POLLOCK: We have no evidence
that we do not follow the English practice. While I do not wish to be very
assertive in the matter, I am perfectly
satisfied that no English bank is willing
to accept the official English bank rate
for advances made
customers in
ordinary trading. If the advances are
made against Government securities it is
a different matter. Here our banks would
be willing to treat customers quite as
fairly as the banks do in England. So I
am advised.
Major HALL-THOMPSON: Surely it
is a fact that for an overdraft, which,
unfortunately, is necessary in commercial
affairs at the present time in many cases,
the banks of Northern Ireland do charge
one per cent. more than do the banks on
the other side of the Channel. Is that
not to the disadvantage of the development of business in this country?
Mr. POLLOCK: The Irish banks here,
I think, would answer that question by
saying that their arrangements are on
an entirely different basis in regard to
overdrafts, that interest is charged from
day to day by Irish banks upon the exact
overdraft, whereas in Great Britain it is
charged on the amount pre-arranged, and
that, therefore, the position of the Irish
banks is quite as favourable to their
customers as is that of the English banks.
Mr. DEVLIN: Would it not be within
the province of the right hon. Gentleman to have these banking arrangements
made similar as between Northern Ireland and Great Britain?
Mr. POLLOCK: That is a matter for
the banks. They are not national
banks.
Mr. DEVLIN: I wish they were.
Major HALL-THOMPSON: It is possible, and it is the practice for the English
banks to allow overdrafts on exactly the
same terms as overdrafts are allowed in
this country, with the exception that one
per cent more is charged.

Motion made, and Question proposed:

to 1901, and for other purposes connected therewith," it is expedient to
authorise the payment out of moneys

maintenance of rate-aided patients in
the public mental hospital established for
such county or county borough."-
(Governor's recommendation signified).
(Mr. Barbour).
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): Hon. Members will observe
that the Resolution which appears on the
Order Paper is general in form, and in
this connection I would refer to the statement by my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Home Affairs, when moving
the Second Reading of the Bill. He then
pointed out that the basis of the Government grant towards the maintenance of
rate-aided patients in mental hospitals
was one of the subjects of consideration
by the Committee which recently sat to
consider the relations between State and
local expenditure. The recommendations
of this Committee are still under consideration, and although hon. Members.
may feel some disappointment that the
Resolution does not lay down the actual
basis of grant for future application, it
would, I suggest, be unreasonable to
press my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Finance, to deal with these grants in
a piecemeal fashion. It is the intention
of the Government to give serious and
early consideration to the recommendations contained in the Report, and at
the moment it will, I think, suffice if I
give an assurance that until that Report
has been fully considered in consultation
with the local authorities, it is not contemplated to alter in any way the
amounts now being paid to the several
local authorities as laid down in the
Local Government Act of 1923. I beg
to move.

Mr. BYRNE: I would like to join

That sum is altogether inadequate with

Asylum. Since the lump sum of a grant
was given, about 400 additional patients

when we had about 1,000 patients in

CLAUSE 1 (Power to receive voluntary
patients).
Question proposed: "That the Clause
stand part of the Bill."
Mr. CRAWFORD: Clause 1 makes
provision for the authorities of mental
hospitals to receive voluntary patients.
I would like the right hon. Gentleman to
explain how voluntary patients are to be
received when the institutions are overcrowded. Even if there were room it
would be a pity to have voluntary
patients with the ordinary patients in a
mental home. Suppose some unfortunate person lost his mental balance for
a time, it would be a good thing to have
some place in which he could be kept
separate from the ordinary patients, so
as to give him a chance of recovering.
It would not be going too far, I would
suggest, if something in the nature of
what the Government are doing for
mentally defective children should be
done in this connection.
There are scarcely enough of these
patients to justify a separate place for
each county, but surely there could be
one place for the whole Six Counties. I
think I have said enough to make myself
clear. I know a number of people who are
patients in mental hospitals, and if they
had had an opportunity of being treated
a few weeks earlier they would not be
there now. At present, as far as I can
see, there is no room for such patients
in the mental homes. This Clause makes
it permissible for them to go in, but
there is no room for them. It would be
a good thing if the Minister could
arrange in some way to have a proper
place for those people. It is entirely in
the interests of people of that class that
I am speaking.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I quite appreciate the object of the remarks of my
hon. Friend. One of the most important
objects of this Bill is to enable individuals
who are temporarily deranged to go into
a home without at the same time being
dubbed insane. My hon. Friend's difficulty is that at the present the mental
homes are not big enough to accommodate
this class of patient, and he suggests
there should be one new institution
started for Northern Ireland. I would
be rather opposed to the idea, because it
would tend to extravagance, but I think
one hospital might arrange with another
to take the patients, in any event, so far
as this Bill is concerned. I hope that
with modern treatment the number of
insane persons in Northern Ireland will
be less than it is at present, and I do
not think anything I could put into the
Bill would help the object my hon.
Friend has in view.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Would it not be
more expensive to have five or six homes
instead of one? To have one place in
the Six Counties to which we could send
these persons would be a much more
economical way of providing for them.
I think it would be more economical to
buy one of the large houses that are
vacant at the present time. This would
be more economical than to have five or
six institutions with a matron and staff
in each.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not set
myself up as an expert in mental treatment. My hon. Friend, in this connection, has a great deal more practical experience than I have, but I would have
thought the erection of a villa in the
grounds of one particular hospital might
serve for the whole area. The result of
that would be that you would not have
to appoint extra officials or extra doctors
to deal with the cases in it. Each
county would pay its own share of the

cost.
Clause ordered to stand part of the
Bill.

Sir DAWSON BATES: If the Government were to accept the Amendment proposed by my hon. Friend it would defeat the very object he has in view. My
hon. Friend seems to have misunderstood the effect of this Clause. Under
the Clause, for the protection of the
patient, the medical officer has to send in
at the end of one year-that is from the
date of the admission of the patient-and
then after two and three years, and thereafter every five years, his report on the
condition of the patient. What my hon.
Friend proposes should be done is that
on the 1st January of every year all the
medical officers connected with these
institutions should send in reports on all
the people under their care. There are
something like 4,600 inmates in mental
homes in Northern Ireland, and that
would mean that for a period of about
three months the superintendents in
these institutions would be busy writing
a report on each particular case.
these 4,600 reports would come into the
Ministry of Home Affairs which, although
it is suggested that we are overstaffed, has
only two medical inspectors. Would my
hon. Friend tell me when these medical
inspectors could deal with these 4,600
reports? What we want is to get these
reports in from day to day, that is to
say that if a patient is admitted on the
1st January his report will come in on
the 1st January following, and if on the
2nd January then on the 2nd January
following; in other words that the reports will flow in daily to the Home

Mr. CRAWFORD: Might I ask the
Minister will any constable of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary have power to arrest
a person, take him to the workhouse, and
have him examined there, and, if so, is
that not going just a bit too far?
I
would ask the right hon. Gentleman to
give this power to no one of less rank
than head constable, or, as an alternative,
to make it that the constable must take
the person arrested before some police
authority. One can understand that
there might be a dispute in the house,
sometimes even a man and his wife might
fall out (laughter)-and some statement
might be made to the constable, who has
not the experience of a head constable,
as a result of which, without any great
reason, a man might be arrested, taken
to the workhouse, and kept there for a
certain time. If the Minister could see
his way to change the "constable" there
to "head constable" it would be an improvement. He might even give the
power to persons of the rank of sergeant,
or make it that until the constable reported the matter to his authorities there
should be no arrest.
Sir DAWSON BATES: One of the
great objects of this Bill is to take away
the criminal taint from those who are
mentally afflicted. It was with this
object that this Clause was framed. If
my hon. Friend looks at the Clause he
will find that these powers are not given
unless an officer or constable of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary is satisfied that their
exercise is necessary for the public safety
or for the safety of a peon alleged to
be of unsound mind. If people have to
look for a sergeant, a head constable, or
a district inspector, or even a county inspector, it might be that the poor
individual would have committed suicide
or killed somebody before he is removed.
It surely is better that he should be
treated as mentally unsound and taken
to the infirmary, which, after all, has
not the pauper taint, rather than that
he should be taken to the cells and treated
as a criminal. If my hon. Friend can
suggest any other way to meet such a
situation as I have described I will be
only too glad to consider it.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Why take him to
the workhouse?
Sir DAWSON BATES: We must take
him somewhere. I hope the term "workhouse" will disappear in course of time,
but, after all, the infirmary is the proper
place to which to take these mentally
afflicted persons.
Mr. STEWART: I was going to suggest to the right hon. Gentleman that he
should delete the word "workhouse" here
and insert "infirmary."
Sir DAWSON BATES: There may be
a technical difficulty about that, but if
I can do it without any difficulty I will
be only too glad to fall in with the suggestion of the hon. Member.
Question put, and agreed to.
Clause, accordingly, ordered to stand
part of the Bill.

their duty. Somebody must do it.
do not want to ask the police to interfere
in cases like this, and we think the proper
person is the relieving officer, who, after
all, is there for the relief of the sick.

position to make up their
their budget

Minister of Finance at the time. To

situation.

the same grants as they have had in the

The British Note
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Nixon]
Prime Minister on the Adjournment of
the House if he wished to make any
statement in respect of Paragraph 4 of
the second British Note, dated 9th April,
from the Secretary for the Dominions to
Mr. De Valera, the President of the
Executive Council of the Irish Free State.
The paragraph in question reads:-
"It is true that the 1921 Settlement
did not result in the establishment of a
united Ireland, but the Treaty itself
made the necessary provision for the
union at that time of the two parts of
Ireland if both had then been ready to
accept it.
"As to the future, His Majesty's
Government in the United Kingdom
feel it sufficient to state that, in their
opinion, there can be no conceivable
hope for the establishment of a united
Ireland except on the basis that its
allegiance to the Crown and its
membership of the British Commonwealth will continue unimpaired."
It is particularly with reference to the
last part of the paragraph that I, and I
think the House, and the country, would
like to hear the Prime Minister, if he
can see his way to make a statement this
afternoon. Without any comments from
me, I think that very clearly implies
that the Imperial Government might
contemplate a united Ireland under
certain circumstances.
The PRIME MINISTER (Viscount
Craigavon): I have had very short notice
of the intention of the hon. Member to
raise this question in the House this
afternoon, and I would prefer not to
have it raised just quite so soon.
Mr. NIXON: To-morrow.
The PRIME MINISTER: If the hon.
Member will be kind enough, perhaps
next week I can make a statement. That
will give me an opportunity to inquire
into the whole matter in the meantime.
I will only say this, that by the action
of the British Parliament, and by the
action of the Free State Parliament, as
it then was, the position of Ulster was
made abundantly clear. I had no knowledge whatever of the terms of the communication with the present Free State
Government, and I have hardly had time,
as I was travelling up this morning from.
a distant part of County Fermanagh,
even to digest the exact meaning of the
words used in the communication.
Therefore, I think it would be better not
to make any pronouncement at the
moment, except to say that we here in
the Ulster area stand to-day exactly
where we stood through the past eleven
years. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
No change has taken place in the desire of the people, no change has taken
place in the determination of the present
Government of Northern Ireland to remain an integral part of Great Britain
and the Empire. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). No change has taken place
-I reiterate that and, therefore, if
some words have been used which would
give a different impression they must
have been made under a complete misapprehension. I do not think it would
be proper for me to go further than that
to-day because, as I say, I really have
not had an opportunity of either consulting my colleagues or even of analysing the
exact terms used, but I will carry on
with my colleagues exactly the same in
the future as I have done in the past.
Nothing can change my attitude towards
our feelings of loyalty to the King, to the
Constitution, to Great Britain, and to the
Empire-nothing under any circumstances whatever. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Mr. NIXON: I thought it was a question the Prime Minister might have been
able to answer right off the reel and
without making up his mind, but, of
course, he is the judge, and since he
would like to make up his mind as to
how he should answer that question I can
offer no objection.

The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): If hon. Members will
refer to the summary as set out on page
131 they will observe that there is an
increase in these Estimates of £5,875,
as compared with those which I placed
before the Committee for the year
1931-32. The increase is, however,
mainly in respect of grants in aid of
works which had been actually com.
menced, as in the case of the Newry Ship
Canal, or of expenditure on works to
which the Government had already agreed
to contribute part of the expenditure
involved, as in the case of the Ballycastle Harbour. Apart, however, from
the increase on those items I am glad to
be able to inform the Committee that the
Estimates now presented show a reduction in most items as compared with
those for last year, which, as hón. Members may remember, represented a total
reduction of 27 per cent. as compared
with those in 1930-31.
In reviewing the various functions of
my Ministry, I shall first deal with those
touching what I may call the commercial
aspect. The services afforded to the
commercial community, with the details
of which the Committee are already
familiar, have been freely utilised during
the past year by our exporters, and many
of these have received effective assistance
in building up their selling organisations
abroad. In addition, much useful information regarding trade conditions,
calls for tenders, commercial openings,
and the like, has been issued to firms
to whom the information was likely
to be of most practical service. The
utility of the services thus afforded by
the Ministry can, perhaps, best be
gauged by the increasing frequency and
confidence with which Northern Ireland
firms are, after ten years' experience of
the Ministry's work, taking advantage of
the service afforded. My Ministry also
is in close and cordial relation with the
Imperial Departments in London, and it
is largely due to this that it was possible
to give effective assistance to the com-
Estimates-

mercial interest affected by recent legislative proposals before the Imperial
Parliament.
It is gratifying that within the last
six months signs of improvement have
become manifest in the linen industry,
but the continued depression in the shipbuilding industry, and the consequent
heavy unemployment, have served as a
stern reminder of the dangers inherent
in the concentration of our activities upon

fiscal policy of the United Kingdom
affords incidentally an opportunity of
broadening our industrial bases. Following the imposition of the general tariff
there is every likelihood that new concerns will in due course be formed to
manufacture in Northern Ireland goods
formerly produced abroad, and foreign
firms will establish branch factories
within the United Kingdom.

reduction which it has been possible to
make in the provision for grants to Conservators is really an encouraging sign.
In recent years the Boards of Conservators
found it difficult to make ends meet with
the revenue secured from licence duties
on fishing gear, and from grants-in-aid
by the Government, and in introducing
former Estimates I have always had to
bear in mind the possibility that certain
increases might have to be made in the

The revenue of the Boards, however,
now bears a more satisfactory and
healthier relationship to essential expenditure, and not only has it been possible
to avoid increasing the grants, but, in
one case, a Board was able to dispense
last year with the grant normally made
to it. A contributing factor has been
the increased revenue from salmon rod
licences since the passage of the Fisheries
Act in 1928. Hon. Members who participated in the debates on that Act will
recollect the fears then expressed that the
raising of the salmon-rod licence duty
from £1 to £1 10s per annum would
seriously discourage salmon angling.
am happy to say that, possibly owing to
the condition of our rivers, very few
anglers have been able to resist the appeal
of the sport, and the resulting increase
in revenue has, as reflected in this Estimate, done something to bring nearer
the conditions contemplated in
middle of last century, when the Boards
were brought into existence a state in
which the whole cost of protection would
be borne by those deriving benefit from
the fisheries.

the
The Committee will also notice that
for the first time since my Ministry took
over the administration of fishery services in 1926, no provision has been included for grants to hatcheries. In the
absence of any public hatcheries in Northern Ireland our predecessors considered
