Ministry of Commerce
13 APRIL 1932

it in the public interest to encourage the
establishment of commercial hatcheries at
Kilrea and Newtownstewart, by making
to the proprietors an annual grant based
upon the output of the hatcheries. When
my Ministry became responsible for
fishery administration I considered it undesirable to depart from this principle
without adequate experience and consideration, but I have now reached the
conclusion, which I have communicated
to those concerned, that in continuing
the grant until last year the Government
has done all that could reasonably be
expected to assist in the firm establishment of the hatcheries, and that in
future the cost of the salmon hatcheries
must be borne by the owners themselves.
I can
assure hon. Members that my
Ministry maintains an active and sympathetic interest in all fishery matters
throughout and around our territory.
The executive action in regard to the
enforcement of fishery laws is, of course,
taken in the main by the Boards of Conservators constituted for this purpose.
There are, however, many matters of detail which come at some stage directly
before the Ministry, and the fishery bylaws, which from time to time appear
on the Table of the House, are in every
case the sequel to careful investigation
and consideration. I have no doubt,
also, that hon. Members have seen
references in the Press recently to
attempts that are being made to establish Portrush as a fishery centre. I do
not wish at this stage to say anything
on this subject beyond expressing the
hope that the efforts will be successful,
and that Portrush, and Northern Ireland
generally, will ultimately benefit.
Hon. Members may be interested to
know that the issue of fishery loans from
the Government Loans Fund continues,
twenty-six further loans to the amount
of £709 having been issued during the
calendar year 1931, bringing the total
advanced since April, 1926, to £5,650.
These loans have been a definite help to
our inshore fishermen, and it is greatly
to the credit of the borrowers that, notwithstanding the difficult years recently
experienced, they have, with few exceptions, met their obligations in the matter
of instalments. The summer herring
season last year showed considerable improvement over its predecessor, and our
fishermen being now adequately equipped
to take advantage of any opportunities
offered, there is ground for hope that,
given favourable conditions, the coming
season will bring increased prosperity in
our fishing centres.
In introducing these Estimates in
previous years I have spoken of the
participation of Northern Ireland in the
exhibitions which are organised in
London and large provincial centres by
the Empire Marketing Board. The
public interest in these exhibitions does
not appear to flag, and the demand for
samples of Northern Ireland produce
with which we have been met in the
"Empire Shops" in which we have
participated during the past year has
been a matter for astonishment as well
as gratification. The exhibitions are
now tending to fall into two definite
categories on the one hand trade shows,
aimed at the trade buyer rather than the
general public, and on the other Empire
shops, the primary appeal of which is to
the retail purchasing community.
The Ministry has taken pains to include in each exhibition, in addition to
our staple exports, new food products
of Ulster origin and valuable initial
publicity for these products has been
obtained. Through the medium of the
trade shows we were able last year to
introduce to important trade buyers,
amongst other commodities, liquid eggs,
which Ulster is now canning in competition with China and other foreign
countries.
The success which has attended the
shops, at which samples are sold direct
to the public, has caused the Empire
Marketing Board to concentrate more
and more on this type of advertisement,
as it has been found that these shops, in
addition to selling thousands of samples
direct to the consumer, attract the retailer, and, through him, the wholesaler.
On last year's figures, the average cost
of each exhibition was some £70, a cost
which, in my opinion, is almost negligible
in comparison with the value of the
publicity obtained. Moreover, I would
remind the Committee that it is not
merely trade publicity which we are
getting from these exhibits. They have
served to make familiar to our compatriots throughout the length and
breadth of Britain the name of our
Province and the place we hold within
the United Kingdom. I am confident
that the Committee will approve the continuance of this work.
Estimates-
Ministry of Commerce
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Barbour]
With regard to the census of production, hon. Members will recollect, from
my observations under this head when introducing last year's Estimates, that this
work was undertaken here in Northern
Ireland, rather than in Great Britain
under an agency arrangement with the
Board of Trade, as was the case with the
previous census in 1924. The work of
the census has been proceeding smoothly,
the tabulation has been practically completed, and the task of drafting the
report commenced.
Before I leave the subject of trade and
commerce I should like to refer to a
factor which is exercising a rapidly increasing influence upon our economic and
social life, and that is the development
of tourist traffic. The competition between the countries of the world to
attract visitors to their shores is becoming
more intense from year to year, and it
would be a calamity if our Province,
with its natural attractions, failed to
receive the attention which it so well
deserves.
Hon. Members will, I feel confident,
agree with me that an expression of our
gratitude is due to all those members of
the Ulster Tourist Development Association who devote so much of their time
and energy to the organisation of tourist
traffic. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Each succeeding year provides abundant
proof of the utility of the Association's
work and of the necessity of widening
its scope.
The Government proposes,
accordingly, to continue their support of
this body financially to the same extent
as last year.

weights and measures, and the various
registrations of companies, friendly
and industrial and provident societies,

The financial and administrative liabilities incurred by the Ministry in respect
of the building of electric main transmission lines last year have been
transferred to the Electricity Board
which was established on 1st June last.

The principal duty which continues to
provide a considerable burden of work
consists of the settlement of the disputes
referred to the Industrial Assurance Commissioner by policy-holders or by the
companies and societies carrying on the
business. In 1925, which was the first
year of the operation of the section which
imposed arbitration duties on the Commissioner, the number of disputes referred
to him was 155, while in 1931 the figure
827. The work is proceeding
smoothly and I have had many indications of the confidence with which the
arbitration court set up by the Act of
1924 is regarded both by insurers and
insured and of the gap it fills in this
important thrift service. Provision is
made in the Estimates for continuing the
appointment of the practising barrister
who acts for the Commissioner in hearing

cases which reach the stage of a formal
hearing.

spread difference of opinion, and ideals,

That is, that these grants have served a

I would like to contradict another statement, this time made by the Member for
Woodvale (Mr. Nixon). His last remark,
as I understood it, and I think I am
quoting him accurately, was that he was glad
the Minister had recognised the mistake
the Government had made in connection

grant that would be made, and that you

Woodvale and I am speaking of something I know-that as a result of the
assistance that the Northern Government
and the Government of the Irish Free
State have given to this little railway, and
thanks to the superhuman efforts that
have been made by many prominent
citizens in Londonderry, not merely is
there every prospect of this railway
carrying on in the future, but I personally believe that that very important
little railway will manage to weather the
storm, and will manage to serve in the
future, as it has served in the past, the
interests of the County of Donegal in
the Irish Free State, and the interests I
am more particularly concerned with,
the interests of the City of Londonderry.
I say, speaking from a knowledge of the
situation, a knowledge of the place, and
a knowledge of the commercial importance of that little line, that this grant
that has been made from year to year,
and this final grant that is now being
made by our Government, has served a
most useful purpose. It has enabled this
line to weather the storm up to the
present, and I believe it will enable it
to weather the storm in the future.

CLASS VI. No. 1.
MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £49,989 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending on 31st March, 1933,
for the salaries and expenses of the
Ministry of Agriculture (15 and 16
Geo. V., c. 3, s. 4 (N.I.); 16 Geo. V.,
c. 4 (N.I.))." (Note-£17,000 has been
voted on account.)
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I am in the
happy position of presenting Estimates
for my Ministry which for the second
year in succession show a substantial if
not a large saving. If hon. Members
will refer to Vote I. they will find that
in all but two items economies have been
effected. The net increase in Vote I. of
approximately £2,400 is accounted for by
the necessary increase in our veterinary
staff and consequential travelling expenses. No one regrets this increase more
than I do, but, unfortunately, we have
no option in the matter. Following the
regretted outbreaks of foot-and-mouth
disease in the Downpatrick area in June
of last year, the Ministry of Agriculture
and Fisheries issued an Order requiring
the mouth of every animal leaving Ireland to be examined by a veterinary
surgeon before shipment. The net increase in Vote I. is more than accounted
for by the requirements of this Order.
I should like to take this opportunity
of paying a tribute and expressing my
gratitude to the veterinary staff of the
Ministry and to all those who helped
them for the extraordinarily able manner
in which this outbreak was handled.
Similar outbreaks in Great Britain have
cost millions of pounds to suppress,
and
I attribute the fact that this serious outbreak, which might well have spread over
the country, was put down at a total cost
of £14,500, mainly to the able manvery
ner in which our chief veterinary officer
and his staff handled a most difficult and
dangerous situation.
Before I leave this aspect of the
question I should like to acknowledge our
great indebtedness to the police for the
very efficient manner in which they cooperated with us in this difficult task.
But for the very able and tactful manner
in which they controlled the movement
of animals in this district it might well
have been impossible to prevent the
spread of the disease over the whole
Province. Northern Ireland has long
been free from this plague, and I sincerely hope we may never experience
another outbreak.
The sources of infection have always
puzzled veterinary surgeons and perhaps
the
most disturbing feature of the
numerous outbreaks in Great Britain has
been the failure, owing to the great
difficulties in the way, to trace the
probable source of infection. I am,
therefore, particularly glad that we were
able, after a most exhaustive inquiry to
trace the source of infection. It was
found to be due to Dutch broccoli or
cauliflower, imported through the port of
Leith, the refuse from which was, unfortunately, thrown on a rubbish heap
to which the cattle at the farm on which
the first outbreak occurred had access. As
hon. Members already know, Holland is
never free from foot-and-mouth disease.
Whilst there is a certain amount of
satisfaction to be derived from being in
the position to present to the House
reduced Estimates for two years in
succession, I should be failing in my duty
if I did not point out that the services
for which I am responsible cannot be
further curtailed without serious injury
to their efficiency. Moreover, I must
emphasise the fact that if we in Northern
Ireland are to take full advantage of
the opportunities which may arise through
the change in the fiscal policy of the
United Kingdom a material increase in
agricultural expenditure is inevitable in.
the immediate future.
The agricultural situation has loomed.
very prominently in the Press during the
past few months and, whilst I do not
desire to review the situation in detail,
there are one or two important aspects
to which I should like to refer before I
sit down. The greatest difficulty our
farming community in Northern Ireland
has had to face during the past few years
has been the almost catastrophic fall in
the price level of agricultural produce.
Fortunately for Northern Ireland this
Ministry of Agriculture 686
Estimates-
14 APRIL 1932

fall in prices has been much more marked
in the case of cereal than in animal
products, and the fact that 80 per cent.
of our agricultural income is derived
from stock and stock products has enabled
the Northern Ireland farmer to weather.
the storm in a much more satisfactory
manner than farmers in other parts of
the world. I am very happy to think
that all the signs indicate that the removal of the pound from the gold
standard, together with the operation of
the 10 per cent. tariff imposed by the
Import Duties Act, has definitely checked
the fall in the price level of agricultural
commodities. Without being unduly
optimistic, I think I can with confidence
express the view that prices have touched
bottom, and that the agricultural situation
is definitely on the mend. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
Even to the lay observer it must be
obvious that the agricultural industry is
on the threshold of a new era. I am
sure the Committee will be glad to know
that we have played our part in the efforts
which have been made to shape a new
policy for agriculture. I am under a
great debt of gratitude to Sir John
Gilmour for agreeing to an officer of my
Department acting as a liaison officer
between me and the Imperial Cabinet on
agricultural policy. By this means we
have been able to keep in close touch
with developments, ensure that
interests have been properly understood
and, in particular, play a not unimportant part in securing the recognition
of the fundamental importance of live
stock and live stock products in United
Kingdom agriculture.
It is too soon to speak with any degree
of certainty, but I am not without hope
that the promise to limit quantitatively
the import of foreign bacon will in due
course be extended to foreign beef and
mutton. If we are to secure such important concessions to agricultural development it is essential, owing to
complicated treaty obligations, that there
should be a high degree of organisation
amongst Northern Ireland producers,
and on that task my Department is concentrating all its energies. Our task has
been simplified by the lead we have
taken in stock improvement and marketing legislation. I am aware that these
developments have given rise to a certain
amount of criticism amongst the less enlightened members of the community. It
is a curious fact that all progress brings
in its train a band of irresponsible critics
whose main contention is that everything
has been perfect, is perfect, and will be
perfect, if only no change is made, and
the good old methods allowed to continue
indefinitely.
Mr. COLLINS: Hear, hear.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: The way
of the reformer is not an easy one, and
I am in the rather peculiar position of
seeing the efforts which we have made
extolled in the agricultural Press of
England and Scotland as
our
model of
The imposition of a 10 per cent. tariff
on certain agricultural produce, together
with the duties which have been imposed
on
foreign potatoes and horticultural
produce generally under the Horticultural
Produce Emergency Duties Act, have
been an advantage, but I attach more
importance to what may be described as
the long-range policy in connection with
which His Majesty's Government in the
United Kingdom has undertaken to limit
the importation of pig products if a satisfactory scheme for the re-organisation of
the bacon industry is brought into
operation in the United Kingdom.
Progress has already been made and
officers of my Department are working
in close collaboration with the Ministry
of Agriculture and Fisheries in the
elaboration of an acceptable scheme of reorganisation.
a
progress and efficiency, whilst a very
vocal, but, I am glad to think, small
minority at home attribute to them all
the ills and misfortunes which have beset
the agricultural industry. Be that as it
may,
I am convinced that the agricultural situation is definitely on the mend.
Improvement may be gradual, but it
will be none the less certain and beneficial, and I sincerely trust that I may
continue to count on the whole-hearted
support of the vast majority of the farmers in Ulster in the efforts which are
being made to ensure that Northern Ireland secures its full share and, if possible,
more than its full share of the opportunities which will arise through the
quantitative limitation of the imports of
foreign agricultural produce. It will, as
I have hinted, entail a still higher degree
of marketing organisation than we have
yet reached and closer combination and
concentration of action amongst producers. But the prize is well worth
striving for, and I am confident that
the farmers in Northern Ireland will rise
to the occasion. I beg to move.

That is what is wrong with the
country, and what is wrong with every
country as well as this. That is what is
wrong with Great Britain, that is what
is wrong with Australia, with America,
and all those countries. The country is
run by inspectors and officials and bosses
of all classes, and it seems to be useless
to protest here, because when an Estimate
may appear to be reduced the reduction,
generally speaking, is a reduction of
services, and not a reduction of staff. The
staff always seems to be increasing. It
is so here; it is so in this Vote No. 1.
The Minister talked about his reforms,
and about the difficulty he was meeting
in his measures of reform, and he said
that all reformers meet with difficulties.
Weil, that is true. Anyone out for reform certainly will meet with difficulties.
A reformer has to stand alone very often.
I recollect that an hon. Member said that
when he walked into the smokeroom the
other Members walked out. He had to
stand alone because he stood for reform.
He told the House that financially this
part of the country was heading straight
for disaster. He told the House that two
years ago, and they had found out that
it was true. They made an effort to
was not
correct that, but the effort
enough. It will never be corrected until
there is some big change, and the half
of these overlapping services are dispensed
with.
I know of services carried out by the
Ministry of Agriculture that are perfectly useless. Take, for one thing, the
collection of statistics. That is useful
up to a point-I admit that—but what
happens? The police go round, I think
in the month of June; they collect a
great lot of unnecessary details, and they
bring them in. The statistics are then
compiled and sent forward to the Ministry, and I think a staff of clerks work
on them the whole year round and bring
them out in the form of a blue book.
Who reads them? Who is interested in
them? I do not object at all to the
collection of statistics in a useful manner,
but when you go into so many details
as that there are so many hens a year
old, so many hens two years old, and
occupy a big staff all the year round
in compiling them, then I say the whole
thing is overloaded with details. By the
time the blue book is issued the next re-
We are speaking of the Ministry of
Agriculture at the moment, but the Department is no worse in this respect than
any other Ministry either in this or in
any other country that I know anything
about, and the sooner the people's representatives put their heads together, and
instead of trying to score debating points
across the floor of the House and to put
one another in the wrong in the Press
and before the public, stop all this nonsense the better for the country and the
better for the people who sent them here
to represent them. I really have said
more than I intended to say; the reason
I did not intend to say so much is that
I look upon it as useless and hopeless.

the money,

Oxford tests?

Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I hope
that when the new tariff on bacon comes
into force the live pig will become the
greatest trade, and that the dead pig
trade will go out altogether.
In regard to the egg trade, the prices
are very small, but so long as they are
not smaller than they are in other
countries-they are as high as the best
prices in England-I think that is about
the utmost that can be expected.
The hon. Member for Mourne (Mr.
O'Neill) is very interested in flax. We
are all rather interested in flax, but you
cannot get a farmer to grow what does
not pay him, and every year flax has
been going down. No matter what
variety we have the imports are coming

The
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE:
hon. Member does not seem to think we

more prosperous, but until the farmers
are prosperous we cannot expect the farm
labourers to be sure of getting work.
Mr. COLLINS: What about the man
in England? Could you not speak to

Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: There
was a small tariff put on flax, but the
majority of people in this country would
like cheap flax. The mills would
naturally all look for cheap flax, and,
therefore, there is no use in encouraging
the farmer to grow a product that does
not bring him in money.
The hon. Member also mentioned the
question of loans. All a man is required
to have is two sureties; who must be
reliable men. I do not fancy the hon.
Member or anybody else would give
money when a man was in debt already
and had no goods that could be seized.
The Ministry make it as easy as they
possibly can for a man to get a loan.
If those two sureties are responsible men
-they need not be big farmers—we give
the loan at 4 per cent. Those terms
are a great deal better than those in the
Free State or any other country at the
present time.
My hon. Friend (Mr. Beattie) is very
interested in the state of the farm
labourers. They are far worse off than
the unemployed, because they have no
chance of getting anything when they
are unemployed.
Mr. BEATTIE: My contention is
that they get nothing when they are
working.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: As my
hon. Friend, the Member for Antrim

they get very good wages in that county.
I think it will be found that in some
places they get very fair wages. In my
part of the country, and that of the hon.
Member for South
South Fermanagh (Mr.
Healy), not one farm in sixty employs
any labour at all, but it will be found
that the labourers employed on most of
the big farms there are quite satisfied.
On my own farm the men I employ are
grandfathers and fathers, so that does
not show they are badly off.
Mr. BEATTIE: Tell me the wages

away.

SCHOOL ACCOMMODATION IN
AUGHNACLOY.
1. Mr. ELLIOTT asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether the Ministry is fully
aware of the serious condition which has
arisen in the town of Aughnacloy owing
to insufficient school accommodation for
the pupils of that district; and whether,
in view of the fact that the Regional
Committee for that area has approved of
a new school to replace two existing unsatisfactory buildings, he will see that
the Ministry expedite the building of the
proposed new school, and if any inquiry
is necessary see that it is held at the
earliest possible moment.
SECRE-
The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF EDU-
CATION (Mr. Robb): The Ministry is
fully aware of the urgency of the need
for a new school in the town of Aughnacloy, and it has already approved the
sketch plans of the proposed new building, with a view to the preparation by
the Regional Education Committee's
architect of the detail of the plans. The
erection of the new school is a matter for
the Regional Education Committee.
Objections have been received by the
Ministry from certain bodies of ratepayers
in the area to the application of the
County Council, as the Education
Authority, for sanction to the raising of
the necessary
loan. Some of these
objections were subsequently withd. 2wn,
but as some still exist it will be necessary
to hold a public inquiry into the application. Arrangements are being made
to hold this inquiry at the earliest possible date.
REGIONAL EDUCATION COMMIT-
TEES AND THEIR OFFICIALS.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he can state which
Regional Education Committees have decided to dispense with the services of
schoolmistresses, female school doctors,
and school nurses on the occasion of their
marriage; which committees have decided
to dispense with the services of the former whilst permitting the latter to continue in office after marriage; whether
he can state if the discrimination in the
latter case has the approval of the Ministry; and whether, instead of leaving this
matter to the discretion of these Committees, the Ministry will issue a general
rule on the question which will conserve
vested interests from the date of its
enactments.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
19 APRIL 1932
Mr. ROBB: None of the committees
have decided to terminate, upon
marriage, the service of women school
doctors, but the Belfast and County Down
Committees have so decided in the case
of teachers and nurses. The Antrim,
Ballymena, Larne, North Antrim, Fermanagh, Colerainę, and Limavady
Regional Education Committees have decided to terminate the employment of
women teachers upon marriage, but have
taken no action in respect of doctors or
nurses. The practice followed by the
Ministry is identical with that followed
by the former Commissioners of National
Education in the case of teachersnamely, to leave the question to the discretion of the local managers, who are
the employers.

integral part of the remuneration for
registration work, and, in my opinion,
are not excessive.
Provision has been made by various
enactments for the issue of copies of
birth entries for certain specific purposes
at cheap rates, but the resulting loss of
remuneration to the issuing Officers has
not been made good, and I cannot view
with favour any extension of the system
of cheap certificates. Moreover, I do not
regard a single payment of 3s 7d as a
hardship on parents.
BELFAST CORPORATION SEWER
CONNECTION AT DUNDONALD.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
for a considerable time past the proposal
to have a connection made with the Belfast Corporation sewer at Dundonald has
been before the Castlereagh Urban
Council and the Belfast Corporation and
a charge struck of 17s per house;
whether up to the present anything has
been done, and, if not, whether he will
endeavour to have this work expedited,
in view of the present system of drainage
being a serious menace to the health of
the inhabitants of this district.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I am aware that
negotiations are going on between the
Castlereagh Rural District Council and the
Belfast Corporation in connection with
the sewerage of Dundonald. Some rather
intricate questions regarding the share
of the cost to be borne by each authority,
the size of the sewers to be constructed,
and other matters have to be determined.
These have been referred to the engineers
to the two authorities, and a report is
expected at an early date.
I am satisfied that the authorities concerned are fully alive to the importance
of the matter, and that they are anxious
to find a solution to this somewhat
difficult problem. If necessary, my
Ministry will render every assistance in
their power to bring about agreement.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Rent and Mortgage Interest
(Restriction) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: I cannot but
regret the necessity for introducing
further legislation dealing with this very
difficult question of Rent Restriction.
In 1923 I appointed a Committee,
which was representative of all shades of
opinion, to advise as to the course to be
pursued with regard to this subject. The
members of that Committee differed on
many aspects of the problem, but on one.
proposition they expressed themselves as
unanimously agreed, namely,
"that
control of rents should be removed at the
earliest possible date." With that conclusion most of us will agree, because it
is generally recognised that rent restriction-the artificial control of rentsis in itself an evil, and we are only
justified in promoting legislation of this
kind on the ground that it is the lesser
of two evils.
In considering this matter, it is important that hon. Members should keep
clearly before them the course of events
which has led up to the present situation.
The control of rents was instituted, as
hon. Members are aware, in 1915. All
building of dwelling-houses had come to
an end owing to the exigencies of the
Great War. Prior to that date, rents
for dwelling-houses in Northern Ireland
and particularly in the City of Belfast
were extremely moderate; in fact, our
city enjoyed the position of being the
most moderately-rented city in the United
Kingdom. In 1915, however, partly
owing to the cessation of building, and
partly owing to other causes, the demand
for houses here and elsewhere began to
exceed the supply, and, as there was no
means of catering for the increased demand, rents began to rise. It was
found necessary, therefore, to control the
letting prices of houses in the same way
as in the case of the prices of many other
commodities at that time.
The control imposed by the Act of 1915
was limited to the cases of houses of £26
valuation and under. This legislation
remained untouched until 1919, when the
limit of control was extended to £52, or
just twice the original figure, and this
Act was followed in 1920 by further
legislation, which is the foundation of
our present code extending the limit to
£78 or three times the original figure,
while the permitted increase on the rents
was fixed at 40 per cent. of the standard
rents, a figure at which it still stands in
Great Britain.
The members of the Committee which
considered the matter in 1923, while
agreeing as to removing control at the
earliest possible date, differed amongst
themselves in their estimates as to the date
at which control should be completely removed, and it is instructive to bear in
mind that the furthest limit was that
suggested by Mr. Harry Midgley,
Secretary of the Irish Textile Trades'
Federation, who thought that the date
for all classes of houses should be fixed
as the 1st July, 1930, while the majority
of the Committee were of opinion that
the 1st May, 1926, should be the date.
It must, of course, be remembered that
the Committee was reporting in 1923, at
a time of great uncertainty.
The Government thought it wise to
allow a little more time to elapse before
embarking on a definite policy with regard to decontrol, and consequently the
Rent Restriction Act of 1920 was renewed from year to year until 1925, when
the Government decided to make a start
to proceed by three stages. The Act
passed in 1925 prescribed that:-
(a) Houses of a rateable value of over
£52 were to go out of control on
1st November, 1926.
(b) Houses exceeding £26 and not exceeding £52 were to go out of control on 1st May, 1928, and
Rent Restrictions Bill-
Second Reading
19 APRIL 1932
(c) Houses not exceeding £26 were to
go out of control on 1st May, 1930.
It was further provided that in the
case where any house exceeding £8 valuation came into the possession of the landlord that house should become decontrolled. At the same time the permitted
increase of rent was reduced from 40 per
cent. to 30 per cent. The houses falling
within the first two categories went out
of control on the dates named, without
causing any undue hardship, though, of
course, there may have been isolated
cases of inconvenience.
a
Admittedly the problem of houses of
valuation of £26 and under has been
much more difficult. Although in the
interval there had been a great deal of
building, the demand for houses of this
type remained in excess of the supply
in the year 1928, and towards the end
of that year it became evident that control could not be taken off in 1930 without creating undue hardship amongst the
occupiers of houses falling within this
category. Accordingly, the Government
felt bound to ask Parliament to extend
the period of restriction until the 1st
May, 1933. We hoped that by that time
sufficient houses would have been built
to enable us to dispense with further restriction altogether, or, at any rate, to
dispense with restriction in the case of
houses exceeding £8 valuation.
though 16,545 houses have been built
since 1st April, 1928, with the aid of
subsidies, and although a very appreciable number of houses have been built
in the same period without any such
aid, we have to face the fact that there
is still a deficiency, and that the demand
is in excess of the supply, and that,
therefore, if we take no action to extend the period of control, there will be
a general and severe rise in rents.
Al-
It is important to consider the causes
which have prevented the realisation of
the hope which was generally entertained, that by now there would have
been sufficient houses to enable us to allow
the ordinary economic laws of supply and
demand to operate. As I have already
pointed out, many new houses have been
built, but there have been other causes
operating to prevent this augumented
supply of houses from having the expected
effect.
In the first place, the intense economic
depression which has afflicted this area
in common with other places has tended
to induce many of those who occupied
the larger type of houses to seek less
expensive accommodation, and this has
resulted in more pressure on the supply
of houses having a lower valuation, and
in this respect we cannot lose sight of
the effect of the higher rates and taxes.
In the cities and towns many of the
houses are of the large terrace type of
three storeys, and houses of this type
have become unpopular. Owing to the
greater cost of maintaining them and the
difficulty of obtaining servants, there is
an increasing reluctance to occupy such
houses, with the result that it is becoming increasingly difficult to find tenants.
for them even at pre-war rents, and there
is a strong tendency for people who formerly occupied these houses to move into
the smaller and more easily worked
houses of two storeys and of the bungalow
type. This again put pressure, direct or
indirect, upon the supply of new houses
which are being provided.
The advent of the cheap motor-car,
which is now within the reach of an increasingly large proportion of the population, has increased enormously the
demand for small houses with garage
accommodation, and has further accentuated the unpopularity of the terrace
house.
The cost of building, while it has
fallen considerably, has not gone down
to the extent that was hoped, and the
requirements of local authorities for a
higher standard with regard to streets
and other allied matters has tended to
keep up the cost of building.
There is another very important cause,
and it is one of the evils inherent in
legislation such as rent restriction. Many
houses which are at present subject to
control, particularly houses approaching
the upper limit of £26 are occupied by
persons who could very well provide
accommodation for themselves, especially
having in view the facilities now offered
by local authorities under the Small
Dwellings Acts, and the assistance which
can be obtained from building societies
and other organisations of that kind.
These people are, however, content to
occupy houses at a controlled rent, even
though they could easily make other
arrangements, and indeed it is hard to
answer the argument that it is inequitable that such people should be protected
from the operation of the ordinary
economic law of supply and demand,
759 Rent Restrictions Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading.

[Sir Dawson Bates]
especially as in many cases the owner is
less well off than the tenant. A case was
reported in the Press the other day of
a man in England who was in receipt
of an income of several thousands a
year who was in occupation of a controlled house. The Rent Restriction
Acts undoubtedly lead to inertia
amongst such people, and if they were
to do as they ought to do and arrange
to provide accommodation for themselves
the problem of rent restriction would be
brought within much narrower limits.
Another cause which, undoubtedly,
has tended to restrict the supply of houses
is the feeling of unsettlement and insecurity which is engendered by the
agitation which is raised from time to
time to extend rent restriction beyond its
present limits. We should encourage as
much as possible investors to put their
money into houses, to build houses and
to purchase houses, so that capital may
be provided for the building of still more
houses. If, however, we threaten investors with control and restriction, we
definitely discourage the investment of
capital in this kind of property, and we
restrict the supply of houses and thus
promote the continuance of the present
state of affairs of high rents of houses
where the rents are not artificially controlled.
For my part I am determined, and the
Government are determined, to keep rent
restriction within the narrowest possible
limits and to get rid of it as soon as it
can safely be done without undue hardship. It is an artificial state of affairs
and, in our opinion, the housing position
will never be really satisfactory until restriction and control is abolished. We
have, however, to balance two evils
against one another. On the one hand,
we have the evil of restriction with all its
disadvantages, but, on the other hand,
we have the hardships that would be
created by an immediate cessation of
control. On the whole, therefore, we
have come to the conclusion, after giving
the most earnest consideration to the recommendations of the Select Committee
appointed by this House to report on
rents, that restriction must be continued
for a further period.
We are not prepared to extend control
to
houses which are not now in
any
control. We think that such a course
would be contrary to the public interest.
It might confer a temporary advantage
upon some individuals in the community.
but we are convinced that it would be
definitely detrimental to the interests of
the community in the long run.
to
We have been told over and over
again of the great fortunes that are, or
were, being made out of the building of
subsidy houses. If there were these
great profits, how is it that more people
did not take advantage of the subsidies
obtain them? The subsidies were
available for local authorities, public
utility societies-in
societies-in fact, they were
available for everybody-and if there
were these vast profits to be made, I cannot conceive how it is that local authorities did not go in for much more extensive
building programmes than they have
done. In almost every case-if not,
indeed, in every case-building schemes
of local authorities, after crediting the
subsidies, have had to be assisted out of
the rates.
In finally deciding on the provisions of
the Bill, which I am now submitting to
the House, the Government have carefully considered all the recommendations
made by the Select Committee. In the
first Clause of the Bill we give effect to
their recommendation that the Rent Restriction Acts should be extended to the
1st May, 1936.
As I have already pointed out, houses
between £8 and £26 valuation, which
come into the possession of the landlord,
become decontrolled. The Committee
recommended that this provision should
be abrogated, and that not only should
control be continued on houses within
this category which have not become decontrolled, but that control should be reimposed in respect of those houses which
have gone out of control. The hon.
Members of that Committee realised
that to re-apply control in all cases would
give rise to a new set of injustices, and,
accordingly, they suggested that in any
case where a person had, since the passing of the Act of 1925, purchased a
house that had become decontrolled or in
the belief that it would, on his obtaining possession become decontrolled, provision should be made that where the
ownership of the house has changed
between the date of the passing of the
1925 Act and the publication of the
Report, the owner might appeal to the
County Court to fix a rent for the house
in excess of the statutory rent which
would be reasonable, having regard to the
purchase price paid.

I do not think that the Committee
can have fully realised the confusion and
difficulties which would arise in attempting to put into force a recommendation
of this kind. Having regard to the
evidence which was put before the Committee as to excessive increases in rent,
we feel bound to propose that houses
which are now in control should remain
there, but we do not think we would be
justified in re-imposing control where
houses have already become decontrolled.
We think it would be impossible to arrive
at any rule whereby the belief of the
owner could be ascertained, and
think that the proposal of the Committee
would impose on the County Courts a
problem which would be almost insoluble.
we
The effect of Clause 2 of the Bill will be
to prevent houses of from £8 to £26
valuation, which come into the possession
of the landlord after the 12th instant,
from becoming decontrolled.
Clause 3 of the Bill is one which will,
think, meet with general approval.
Mr. BEATTIE: Not altogether.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I hope it will
meet with general approval. The evidence before the Committee disclosed that
some owners and agents had sought to
evade the provisions of the Acts in the
case of controlled houses under £8 valuation, by making agreements which
have been generally described as "Hire-
Purchase Agreements. Such agreements have taken various forms, but the
one object is common to all, namely,
evasion of the provisions with regard to
rent. These agreements purport to be in
the nature of sale agreements, but I have
no hesitation in saying that they were
not bona fide and there was no real intention of carrying through a sale. I
am glad to think, for the credit of the
landlords and agents in this Province,
that such agreements were used by only
a very small minority, and that the use
of such means of evasion is condemned
by every decent landlord and reputable
agent. The agreements of this character
which were brought to the notice of the
Committee were most discreditable, and
showed an utter disregard for fair dealing as between landlord and tenant.
It
is quite clear that they were mere tricks
designed to extort exorbitant rents from
tenants who were unable to protect themselves. We do not desire to prevent
genuine sales of houses where arrangements are made to have the purchase
money paid by instalments, but we are
determined not to allow unscrupulous
persons to evade the Acts by documents
that are really lettings disguised as sale
agreements.
The Committee made a general recommendation on the subject, without, however, suggesting a means for countering
the evil. The problem has not proved an
easy one, but I think that hon. Members
will agree that we have produced Clauses
which, while not interfering with genuine
cases of sale will, at any rate, make it
extremely difficult for anyone to frame
agreements such as those quoted in the
Committee's report.
The Clause is divided into three parts,
and I hope that hon. Members will
clearly bear in mind that the provisions
of this Clause relate only to houses which
are subject to the Rent Restriction Acts.
In the first Sub-Clause we provided
that in any case of a sale of a dwellinghouse where the purchase money is to be
paid by instalments with interest, the
rate of interest is not to exceed 7 per
cent. This provision is necessary mainly
to prevent a loophole of escape from the
provisions of Sub-Clauses (2) and (3),
and we have fixed, as a maximum rate
of interest, one which will cover every
legitimate case. This rate of interest is,
of course, merely a maximum, and I
should think that there are not many
cases in which it would or could be
charged.
Sub-Clause (2) deals with the case
where an option to purchase is given with
the provision that the purchaser is to be
allowed to occupy the premises pending
the exercise of the option, and is to pay
for the use of the house during that
period. It is laid down that the amount
of the purchase money is to be stated
expressly in the agreement which is to
be executed by all parties. It seems
almost incredible that it should be necessary to make a provision of this kind,
but actually experience shows that it is
Further, no greater sum is to be
charged by way of rent or otherwise for
the use or occupation of the dwellinghouse during the period than the amount
of rent which the owner would, under
the Rent Restriction Acts, have been
entitled to charge if the dwelling-house
had been let. If the owner makes any
excess charge the Sub-Clause makes it
recoverable. Again, if the option to buy

sure that most hon. Members will

I pass now to another point dealt with
by the Committee. Hon. Members will
recollect that, where a landlord pays the
rates on a house to which the Rent Restriction Acts apply, he is entitled under
the Act to pass on any increases of rates
to his tenant, and, conversely, if the
rates fall, the decrease should be passed
on to the tenant. It has been found in
a certain number of cases that, whilst
landlords have not failed to add the increases, they have forgotten to give the
tenant the benefit of the decreases, and
the tenant, through ignorance or some
other cause, has omitted to claim the
benefit. By this Clause an obligation is
placed on the landlord to notify the
tenant of any decrease, and he is made
liable to a penalty for failure to do so.
Clause 5 deals with a matter which
occasionally has given some little trouble.
There is already a remedy at common
law, but we think that possibly a definite
provision with specific remedies may be
more advantageous and may put an end
to what is a most objectionable practice.
Firstly, the Clause deals with the case

As hon. Members will appreciate, we
have gone very far to carry out the recommendations of the Committee. In
two particulars we have not been able to
follow their recommendations. One of
these is the re-imposition of control on the
houses which had actually come out of
control. This I have already dealt with.
The second point related to sub-letting
of rooms in controlled houses. If hon.
Members will look at the Report of the
Committee they will see that the recommendation is couched in very general
terms, and there is no hint as to the
method by which this recommendation
should be carried out. I am not surprised
that the Committee abstained from entering into particulars, because, after a very
careful study of the subject, I have come
to the conclusion that there is no effective
means of dealing with it. Any provision
landlord
giving a
power to resume
possession of the house, if his tenant is
sub-letting rooms at an exorbitant price,
would, of course, be quite inoperative.
No landlord is going to the trouble and
expense of resuming possession of the
house merely to re-let it at the same rent
simply because his tenant is charging exorbitant rents. If the provision that, on
the landlord obtaining possession, the
house went out of control remained, it
might be a different story. This might
have a deterrent effect in the case of
houses between £8 and £26 valuation,
but this provision will be gone if the
House passes this Bill, and, therefore, the
power of resumption of possession by the
landlord gives no remedy. In any event,
it would be extraordinarily easy to evade
any provision with regard to sub-letting
of rooms, because the Committee themselves state that the recommendation was
not intended to apply to furnished rooms
as defined by the Rent Restriction Act
of 1927.
We have spent much labour and thought in
trying to meet the Committee's views with
regard to this matter, but I and my
advisers have been unable to evolve any
satisfactory method for dealing with it.
I am, however, quite open to suggestions
in the matter.
May I before sitting down reiterate my
firm conviction that the real and permanent solution of the question that we
have been considering does not lie in restrictive legislation. Legislation of the
character which I have introduced this
afternoon may be necessary as a temporary
expedient in spite of its manifest and
manifold disadvantages, but, in my
opinion, and I may say in the opinion of
the Government, the only true and the
only satisfactory solution to the problem.
of rents is that every encouragement
should be given to people to invest money
in house property, so that more and more
funds may be provided for the building
of houses until a sufficiency is provided to
meet all reasonable needs of the community. When the supply of houses is
equal to the demand, there will be no
further necessity to introduce Rent Restriction Bills, and I would appeal to
every Member of this House to do nothing
and to say nothing which will discourage
enterprise in the building of houses, and
thus promote confidence and enterprise
in the building industry. I beg to move.

The Rent Restriction Acts were introduced for a particular purpose.
In
1915 men left their homes to fight in the

exploiting class, who invest their money
in house property in order to get a large
return at the expense of the sweat and
labour of the industrial masses of Northern Ireland.

Albertbridge Road.

clamour for the

Rev. PROFESSOR CORKEY: I wish
to congratulate the Government on introducing this Bill. I think it will go a
long way to meet the complaints made in
regard to overcharging in the way of
rents for houses that have been decontrolled. It is a very thorny subject.
People are very sensitive where their interests are touched, and I feel that the
Government deserve thanks for the way
in which they have tackled it. They
have gone a long way to introduce a Bill
which will do away with many of the
things which people justly complain
about. I support the re-introduction of
control, because I think the owners of
these houses are in fact, in possession of
a monopoly. A great deal has been done
to build houses, but all the ingenuity of
the builders has not enabled them to
erect houses which could be let at a rent
comparable to the rent charged for the
working classes prior to the war.
Before the war rents ran from 3/- to
6/- for houses of £8 valuation, and these
houses constituted about half the number
of houses in the whole community. The
rents charged for houses from £8 to £26
valuation ran from 6/- to 12/-, and these
houses constituted one-third of the total
number of houses in the whole country.
If these houses were allowed to become
decontrolled, and the rents were increased, the houses which would have
been available for the workers would have
become increasingly less. I think, therefore, there is reason in the action which
the Government have taken, in bringing
in this process of decontrol so far as these
houses are concerned. It is really the
working-class houses which constitute a
monopoly.
Further than that,
it appeared
to those who were members of the Committee that the controlled rent gave a
fairly reasonable return on the money

average case. Here, for example, is a
typical case, one of many which came
before the Committee. A house was
built at £150. The supposed value of
the house at present is £250, and the
poor-law valuation is £10 10s. The controlled rent for that house was £25.

Rent Restrictions Bill-

[Mr. Connellan]
there is a difficulty in finding tenants

Those conditions handicap not only the

chaotic state of industry in the Six
Counties. People do not know exactly
where they are, what they should invest
in, or whether it is safe to remain in the
Six Counties at all or not. That is
attributable to this Government's incompetence and selfishness, and its want of

this other issue, that in the rural districts
you have got poverty of a very abnormal
kind. You have got an extraordinary
amount of depression, and people are
flying to the cities and towns in abnormal
numbers, thinking they will there escape
from the conditions of starvation with
which they are confronted. They come
into the towns to compete with the townspeople in regard to labour and make the
housing conditions infinitely more chronic
than they have ever been.
That, in brief, is how I would answer
the question asked by the Minister of
Home Affairs, when he was moving the
Second Reading of the Bill. He asked
how was it that greater advantage was
not taken of the subsidies. My reply is
that greater advantage is not taken of the
subsidies because of the chronic conditions
that exist in industry, amongst the working classes, amongst the employing
classes, amongst all sections of the community, that they are alarmed, that they
feel that insecurity is so great. That is
daily demonstrated by the removal of industries from this territory to the Free
State. They are afraid to put any stake
whatever in the country, and they have
merely become quiescent and submit to
whatever conditions prevail. My contention is that as these inequalities
began at the very beginning of this Government, they can only end by the fall of
the present Government from power.

Prime Minister's Visit to London.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Captain Dixon).
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask
the Prime Minister to state the order of
the business to be taken during the
remaining portion of this week. I also
want to ask him has he any statement to
make with regard to his recent visit to
London. I understand that was a
political mission with which the question.
of unemployment was coupled. As I am
interested in the question of unemployment in Northern Ireland I hope that if
he makes a statement it will contain the
promise that a grant, equal to the amount
of the surplus which the Budget of Great
Britain is showing at the present moment,
is to be returned to the unemployed of
Northern Ireland. I hope he has some
announcement of that nature to make.
on
I would also like to ask the Prime
Minister why he rushed to London, on
whose authority did he embark
expenditure of that kind, and what
danger the Six Counties were in because
of the attitude adopted in the Notes
sent to the Free State by the National
Government, which is a Unionist Government. It proves to me that the right hon.
Gentleman has no confidence in the
National Government. Many people are
to-day waiting to hear what was the real
object of the Prime Minister's visit to
London. The unemployed worker is waiting to have restored the ten per cent. that
was last year deducted from the amount
of his benefit. I hope the Prime Minister
will be able to justify the expenditure
incurred by his mission with the Attorney-
General to London on what I would at
the moment call a fool's errand. Surely
if the National Government is worth
supporting it is worth reposing confidence
in, and I would not lose many nights'
sleep over some document that passed between another Government and the British
Government. Those are points on which
I want some explanation from the Prime
Minister. I want to know if he can
justify the heavy cost entailed by a deputation of this kind proceeding to London,
and whether the work done is of such a
nature as to benefit the masses of the
people of the Six Counties.

granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1933, in
respect of Public Works and Buildings,
including expenses of dredger and

(20 Geo. V., c. 20 (N.I.), and 21 and 22
Geo. V., c. 5 (N.I.))."—(Note-£63,000
has been voted on account.)
The FINANCIAL SECRETARY OF
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): This Estimate is to be found
on pages 23 to 33. Hon. Members will
note that, as explained in paragraph 5
of the general foreword to the Estimates,
the abolition of "duplicate voting" now
takes effect in the case of all works
services, and not only in the case of headquarters of Ministries, and that this
change has necessitated certain alterations
in the form of this Estimate. Works
expenditure incurred on behalf of Northern Ireland Ministries is now borne
finally on this Vote, and is not recoverable
from Departments. Two works items do
not appear here, however, namely, expenditure on ancient monuments and on
harbours, the reasons being clearly set
out in the foreword mentioned. There is
a decrease in the Estimate this year as
compared with 1931-32 of approximately
£126,000, of which £116,000 is under
Section I and is due mainly to the fact
that the buildings at Stormont are nearing completion.
The anticipated expenditure (Sub-head
D) in connection with the portion of the
new Law Courts which will house the
Ministry of Commerce and other sections
of Departments remaining in town,
accounts for an increase of about £14,000,
and this may be regarded as indicative
of the acceleration of work on that building. It is anticipated that the transfer
of staffs to the building will take place
towards the end of the current financial
year. The increase in Sub-head B for
furniture and fittings is accounted for by
the provision required for the fitting out
of the new Parliamentary portion of the
Stormont Building as well as the cost of
furniture for the Departmental offices in
the Law Courts. It will be recollected
that under Section 34 of the Government of Ireland Act all the above expenditure is repayable to the Exchequer
of Northern Ireland from Imperial
Funds.
Expenditure under Section II shows
a gross decrease of £13,000, new works
expenditure being down by £18,000. It
will be observed that provision is made
for the payment of the balance of the
contribution due from Northern Ireland
funds in respect of the provision of
accommodation for staff at Stormont surplus to the agreed numbers for whom the
British Government has provided accommodation. The estimated total provision
under this head is £30,000. An item of
£1,250 in connection with the new Law
Courts Building reappears here too, owing
to the fact that the Northern Government
agreed to contribute from Northern Ireland funds towards the increased cost of
the Law Courts, due to the use of stonework externally. A balance of £1,250,
Estimates-
Public Works and Buildings

[Mr. Barbour]
as I said a moment ago, is here provided for. There is also a sum of £1,045
provided for the cost of the accommodation for the Incorporated Law
Society. These two works account between them for a reduction of £10,000
on the 1931-32 figures.
One of the largest increases under this
sub-head is £2,000 for the erection of
four cottages at Stormont. These are for
the use of the ground staff, as difficulty
would otherwise be encountered by them
in finding suitable accommodation in the
neighbourhood. Undoubtedly, it will
be advantageous to have some of the staff

a provisional estimate only, and £1,000
is a re-vote as there was no expenditure
in 1931-32.
Under the heading of Maintenance,
Repairs, etc., there is an increase of
about £6,500, which in the main is due
to anticipated expenditure for the

Royal Ulster Contabulary barracks built
two or three years ago, and to increased
dredging which it is proposed to perform
in connection with the navigation on the

Drainage Trustees, and a gradual reconditioning of the navigation channel is
being undertaken on the work, spread

Bann drainage contract.

year the

amount provided in the Estimate each

conditions last
year accentuated by
abnormal winter floods.

beg to move.

Stormont has no greater ability than a
boilerman employed at the Labour Exchange, and therefore why should there
be a difference in their wages. I find I
made a mistake. It is at the administrative offices at Belfast- -no name is
given that two boilermen receive 40/6,
and 48/- a week respectively, while the
boilermen employed at the Houses of
Parliament at Stormont each receive 55/-
a week. How does the Government justify this difference in wages, because the
most up-to-date heating and boiler system has been installed at Stormont, which
means labour saved, whereas in the
administrative offices somewhere in Belfast the boilerman is probably looking
after an old set of boilers that require
more labour. I disagree that even 55/-
a week is sufficient, but I think it is time
there was a levelling up process and all
boilermen were paid 55s a week.
There is another matter that has been
a bone of contention in Newtownards.
The Government are employing at Newtownards Camp handy men who are doing
all classes of tradesmen's work. Representations have been made to me on the
question, and I think the Government
should officially recognise the different
classes of work involved, and allocate a
tradesman to carry out the work of each
class. A shipwright for a shipwright's
job, a joiner for a joiner's job, and a
blacksmith for a blacksmith's job that
is the recognised rule of trade unions at
the present moment.
Mr. NIXON: And a lawyer for a
lawyer's job.
Mr. BEATTIE: We sometimes do not
want lawyers. There are too many
lawyers at the moment. The trade union
lines of demarcation are very well defined,
and no mistake can be made if you will
follow the procedure laid down by them.
You want at least three tradesmen in
Newtownards Camp.
The PRIME MINISTER: Newtownards Camp is being given up shortly, and
this question will not arise.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am sorry I did not
raise it sooner. It was only in the past
twelve months I got to know that instead
of recognising the crafts of the various
workmen, who were walking about unemployed, you employed a handy man.
Short and all as the period might be I
ask you to have the matter remedied,
even at this late hour. I believe a
carpenter is the class of man that should
be employed, and work from this to the
end of June would be very serviceable to
a carpenter, and there are plenty of them
unemployed.
The other point I ask is has this
caretaker at Enniskillen a free house. If
he has not a free house, does 31s 6d per
week compensate him for the amount of
work he has to perform. I am not conversant with the conditions at Enniskillen,
other than seeing them on the march each
12th of July. I want to know is 31s 6d
the Enniskillen district rate, or is that
amount added to a free house. I notice

Another point raised by the Member

school. This school came under review

said about it downstairs, but I would
like to point out to the House that this
appeared on the Estimates in 1927-28 as
£4,200, of which £900 was spent. Next
year the Estimate was for £2,000 and
none was spent, next year £2,000 and
none spent, next year £2,000 and none
spent, and now £4,460 which includes a
revote of £2,000. It seems to me we are
living in hard times, and if this school
could have been done without in the past,

it will be all to the good of the taxpayer.
It is not a practising school. The

school children. The delay the Parliamentary Secretary has explained is due to
waiting for the embankments or boulevards to settle. But the new building is
not to be at the back on the loose
ground; it is to be put at the side.
Surely it could have been at the side four
or five years ago.
The point is whether
this amount could be held over without
undue hardship.

tioned the question of the rates at Stormont. I understand when the building

say that subject to correction—and I am

Mr. HEALY: When I stopped speaking on the last Estimate I was dealing
with the question of policy, and I would
like now to remind the Prime Minister
that on this particular Estimate he ought
to give an indication to the Committee
and to the country as to what policy he
is going to adopt to meet the very altered
needs and circumstances of the moment.
He knows-I think nobody knows better
-that the position is not as it was even
a year ago. He must be aware that large
numbers of people who hitherto were in a
position to pay their land annuities are
now obliged to come to the Government
to borrow for the purpose, or to go to
the joint stock banks, sometimes without
any result. Therefore, he ought to make
up his mind, and I suggest that the
right moment has now come for him to
make a gesture of goodwill and friendship
towards the people who have stood behind him since 1921.
When a Government starts economies
it really ought to start them in the right
place, namely, at the top. When the
Government of the Free State started
their policy of economy they began with
their own salaries. Every man from the
President of the Executive Council down
through the various Ministers had their
salaries reduced; in some cases,
£1,000 and other salaries in proportion.
The President of the Executive Council
in the Free State to-day receives £1,500.
The Prime Minister of Northern Ireland,
I suggest, receives considerably more than
£4,000, which is the salary of the Prime
Minister of Great Britain. There is here
by
an opportunity for the Prime Minister of
Northern Ireland to show the people
that, when he speaks of sympathy with
them and with the country, he really
means what he says.
There are approximately 318,309 male
people between the ages of 20 and 65 in
Northern Ireland. If you take the
salaries due to this administration you
will find that every one of those people
is obliged to pay the sum of approximately £9 to keep this Government running.
I suggest that that figure is far too high.
Even in a prosperous year, even at a time
when money is plentiful, and when employment is good I suggest that figure is
too high. Whatever it may have been in
the year 1921, in the year 1931 I respectfully suggest it is absolutely abnormal. It
is not that the reduction of the salaries
of the Prime Minister and other Members
of the Cabinet would succeed in bridging
the gulf between prosperity and poverty,
but, at all events, it would be an indication to the people who are starving that
the Government at least are in sympathy
with them. The Prime Minister's salary
has been quoted at £4,200, I think-
£4,208. It is made up of £2,700 for
salary, £1,488 allowance for contingencies
of office, in addition to which he has his
official residence, free fuel and light, and
so on.

[Mr. Beattie]
I say that if the Prime Minister has to
bear the cost of all the hospitality of the
various Ministers, then those Ministers
should return to the general fund the
£425 which they receive in pursuance of
an office, which in their case, does not
exist, a Cabinet Office. The Prime Minister got £1,750, now £1,488 for contingencies of office. I understand from
reading the newspapers, that the Speaker
of the House, who also lives within the
precincts of Stormont, has to extend a
very large amount of hospitality to distinguished visitors to this city.
If the Prime Minister's salary, with
allowances, is too small, what grant is to
be made to the Speaker in regard to the
hospitality extended by him? I do not
stand for a low basis of calculation, but
I say that the Prime Minister is taking
too much for contingencies of office from
the general fund. He should be compensated for the hospitality which he extends, and the high upkeep by those
Ministers on whose behalf he extends hospitality. If a Minister is receiving £425
plus his Ministerial salary, and is imposing all the hospitality on the Prime
Minister, he is not doing justice to the
Prime Minister. Therefore I say the
whole thing will have to be gone into.
We are spending more money than we
are able to spend, and I believe we can
make a saving. We can take from those
who can afford to give it away, and give
it to those who are bearing more of the
financial burden than it is possible for
them to bear.
The cost of Cabinet Offices and contingency grants should be taken into
consideration by a Select Committee of
the House, and the onus of responsibility
for the spending of the Hospitality Fund
should be placed on some one individual
who would know what was necessary to
keep up the dignity and prestige of the
office of Prime Minister. I also want you to
consider the cost of the upkeep of the
office of Speaker. I do not know what
his salary is at the moment. I want all
the heads to be taken into consideration,
and readjustments made. By those readjustments I believe we can make a very
good saving to the general fund of Parliament. In regard to the fixing of
salaries for the respective offices, I want
to say here and now, as I have said previously, that from the reading of "Hansard" I am quite satisfied that if the

to time. But from the reading of "Hansard," I have come to the conclusion that

by those Members who sat either on these
Benches or on the Benches behind the
Government. You cannot say that those
are the actual salaries recommended by

Oral Answers to Questions.
UNEMPLOYMENT-BENEFIT
CLAIMS REJECTED.
1. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he will state the total
number of claims for unemployment
benefit rejected during the past twelve
months by Courts of Referees and
umpires, including deputy umpires, on
the grounds that the claimants were
"not normally in insurable employment"; and whether he will state if there
is any legal or other definition of the
expression or formula quoted.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): In the twelve months ended on
the 31st March, 1932, the Courts of
Referees disallowed 21,891 claims to
benefit on the grounds that the claimants
had not proved that they were normally
in insurable employment and would
normally seek to obtain their livelihood
by means of insurable employment.
During the same time and on the same
grounds the umpire disallowed 2,977
claims, but he allowed 1,641 of the claims
disallowed by the Court. The total disallowance, therefore, during the period on
these grounds was 23,227.
The umpire has not given any definition.
such as is asked for in the question. He
has, however, various decisions laid down
principles upon which the words are to
be interpreted and applied.
Mr. NIXON: Can the Minister explain to the House how any human being
could prove that in future he would be
engaged in insurable employment?
Mr. ANDREWS: It is not my duty to
explain that to the House.
MR. T. J. KINNEAR, CHAIRMAN
OF COURTS OF REFEREES.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Labour whether he will state when Mr.
T. J. Kinnear was appointed to act as
chairman of Courts of Referees, and how
he was employed prior to being
appointed.
Mr. ANDREWS: This gentleman was
appointed to act as chairman of Courts
of Referees on the 6th January, 1931.
He is a barrister-at-law who was engaged
for many years in several departments of
the Civil Service, and he retired in
October, 1930.
Mr. NIXON: Am I right in saying he
is a retired pensioned civil servant?
Mr. ANDREWS: Yes, there are many
such persons retired on pension.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it a fact that this
gentleman was a servant in the Ministry
of Labour for many years prior to his
retirement, and that it was owing to the
position he held in the Ministry of
Labour that the Minister appointed him
as chairman? Is there any case of a
similar kind in England?
Mr. ANDREWS: It was not because
of that fact; it was because of his
fitness for the position, and similar
appointments have been made. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).

reducing the wages paid to their er-

CONDITION OF ULSTER EMI-
GRANTS IN THE DOMINIONS.
4. Mr. NIXON asked the Prime
Minister whether reports of the destitute
condition of Ulster emigrants
in
Australia, Canada, and New Zealand have
reached him, and whether, in view of the
encouragement given to emigration by the
Government he will take steps to rescue
these unfortunate people from their unhappy surroundings.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have been asked
by the Prime Minister to reply.
It is the case that in consequence of
the depression in Australia and Canada
complaints have reached my Department
with regard to about ten young men from
Northern Ireland who chose to avail
themselves of the facilities provided under
the Empire Settlement Act for migration
from the United Kingdom to those
Dominions, and these cases have been
taken up with the authorities concerned.
On the other hand, I have received
reports from many young men thanking
the Department for what has been done
for them, and stating that they are in
good positions and doing well.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is it a fact that
several of the young men who were encouraged to go out by the Minister are
now in destitution in those countries to
which he took them, and is he prepared
out of his own private purse to send their
fares to these young men and restore
them to their homes?
THE TRUSTEE ACT, 1925.
5. Major McCORMICK asked the
Prime Minister whether the Government
proposes to introduce legislation corresponding to the Trustee Act, 1925, as
passed by the Imperial Parliament, which
does not apply in Northern Ireland, and,
if so, when will it be introduced.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The position has not altered
since my reply to a similar question by
the hon. and gallant Member on 28th
November, 1929. Owing to more urgent
legislation, final consideration of this
question has had to be postponed.
THE MARKETING OF PORK.
6. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Agriculture if he has sanctioned the
appointment of a Committee in COoperation with the National Pig Breeders'
Association on the question of the marketing of pork, and if he will press the
importance of a guaranteed minimum of
60s per cwt. as the policy best suited
to Ulster requirements.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): I have constituted a Committee to advise the Ministry
on the question of developing pig and
bacon production in Northern Ireland
so that, when the time comes, we may be
ready to co-operate in any quota scheme
promulgated by the Imperial authorities.
This Committee will naturally be in a
position to make recommendations on any
matter connected with the pig industry,
and, of course, any such recommendations
will receive my earnest consideration.
The Committee will naturally keep in
close touch with the National Pig
Breeders' Association in Great Britain
and the Pig Industry Council.
Mr. HEALY: Will the right hon.
Gentleman consider the suggestion made
in the latter part of my question as
being the most important question that
has come before his Department yet?

ULSTER FRUIT GROWERS'
ASSOCIATION.
7. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he has seen the
statement of the Ulster Fruit Growers'
Association that they were obliged to
cancel orders from Britain by reason of
legislation here, and were selling Bramley
apples here at 20s per barrel less than
they could procure across the water; and
whether he will introduce amending legislation in view of the unpopularity of the
recent Marketing of Fruit Act.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: I have
seen the statement referred to by the
hon. Member, but I cannot accept as a
fact the suggestion that orders were cancelled because of the Marketing of Fruit
legislation in operation here. The price
obtainable this year for Bramley apples
in Northern Ireland and the Irish Free
State compares favourably with prices in
cross-Channel markets, when allowance is
made for the cost of transport. It is well
known that the demand and price of
Bramley apples in British markets has
been below normal this season because
of heavy imports of apples from overseas.
The answer to the latter part of the
hon. Member's question is in the
negative.
Mr. HEALY: Is the right hon. Gentleman aware that, to-day and for some
time past, the price of extra fancy apples
in Belfast is 25s to 28s per barrel, and
that the price of ordinary Bramleys in
the English market is to-day 52s per
barrel and the cost of carriage between
