ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Loans Guarantee (Money).
Considered in Committee under Standing Order No. 65.
[Mr. MOLES in the Chair.]
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That it is expedient to amend the Loans
Guarantee Acts (Northern Ireland), 1922
to 1931, by extending to the 31st day of
March, 1933, the period within which
the Ministry of Finance may give
guarantees under the Loans Guarantee
Act (Northern Ireland), 1922."-(Governor's Recommendation signified.-Mr.
Barbour).
Mr. BARBOUR: The Government
have decided to recommend Parliament
to adhere to its policy of keeping alive
the Loans Guarantee machinery, and this
Resolution has, accordingly, been tabled
as an essential preliminary to the introduction of the requisite legislation. The
activities of the Ministry under this
machinery during the past year have
necessarily been limited owing to the
stagnation in industry, and hon. Members will have observed from the returns
which have been tabled from time to time
that they relate to two transactions only,
namely, a supplemental guarantee to the
Oceanic Steam Navigation Company to
enable the "Georgic" to be completed,
and a guarantee in connection with the
construction of a fruit boat. Satisfactory security has been obtained in each
case.
Looking to the future we find in the
realm of shipping an unhappy prospect.
In Northern Ireland-a community
boasting the biggest shipbuilding concern
in the world-the yards have not a single
slip occupied at the present time. In
this, of course, we are not alone. The
yards in Great Britain are suffering in
the same way, and although subsidised
contracts continued to be placed long
after British shipowners had ceased to
place orders for new tonnage, the
shipping depression has now reached a
point at which even foreign shipbuilders
are experiencing almost complete
paralysis of their activities, despite the
At
operation of out and out subsidies.
such a time as this our Government is
called upon to consider its future policy
in regard to the grant of credit facilities
under this Act. The issues are threefold-Firstly, the employment position;
secondly, the nature of the security that
can be offered by the applicant, and
thirdly, the difficulties which already face
the Exchequer in respect of past loans
guarantee commitments.
It is quite obvious that, looked at from
the employment position alone, the need
for credit facilities is as great as, if not
greater than, in the past. Unemployment
amongst shipyard workers is in the
region of 60 per cent., and with the completion of the "Georgic" in two months'
time we fear that matters will be worse.
The Committee will appreciate that the
Government do not claim that the continuation of these facilities will of themselves restore to any appreciable extent
the activities of our shipyards in the
coming year. British and foreign shipowners have been temporarily forced to
retire from the new tonnage market as a
result of the serious shrinkage in revenue
from passenger traffic, illustrated by
drastic cancellations of liner sailings, and
by a grave curtailment of the staple
cargoes on which merchant shipping de-
883 Loans (Guarantee) Money- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee

[Mr. Barbour]
pends. The fact that 4 million tons of
deadweight capacity were still out of
commission at the end of last year provides
eloquent testimony to the loss of cargo
traffic.
One comforting thought, however,
emerges, namely, that much of this laid
up tonnage has become obsolete, so that
when indications of improvement appear
on the horizon shipowners must undertake commitments in the way of new
tonnage. The Government desires, therefore, to retain the statutory powers so as
to be able to give some assistance when
this time comes, bearing in mind that
even to-day there are to be found
prosperous shipping concerns which are
maintaining and even developing their
trading position. We must not imagine
that these Acts are only of interest to
shipowners and shipbuilders, and that
ships are the only form of capital undertaking likely to be constructed in Northern Ireland. If the hopes held out
that new industries may be started here
as a result of Britain's new tariff policy
come to anything, the existence of our
Loans Guarantee Acts may be of considerable assistance in determining the
locus of such new factories, and prove to
be complementary to the Bill relating
to free sites now before Parliament.
The security offered must be tangible
and will be closely investigated by
the Advisory Committee, which
voluntarily rendered such valuable service
in the past.
I now turn to my third point, namely,
the position of this Government under
the scheme of arrangement proposed in
regard to the Royal Mail group, to which
more than one-half of our guarantees has
been given. The Royal Mail scheme has
now received consideration at the hands
of the various groups of creditors, and
although the approved scheme has not
as yet received judicial sanction, there
can be no objection to a reference to it in
general terms. It will be within the
knowledge of the Committee that during
the last fifteen months the Royal Mail
voting trustees have been grappling with
the task of salving the biggest shipping
group in the world, comprising one-sixth
of the British Mercantile Marine, and
their work has been made progressively
more difficult by the world depression.
I should like to, say, on behalf of the
Government, how deeply we are indebted
to them and all those associated with
them for their work in this connection.
The scheme proposes a sort of moratorium for three years, during which
time the various groups of secured
creditors, including Governments, are
asked to withhold their rights of foreclosure. In the meantime the relative
rights of these parties are preserved
essentially unaltered. It provides for a
reorganisation of management, both at
home and abroad, involving substantial
economies more important still, it introduces a new spirit of co-operation.
The Government is to remain liable under
its guarantees, but the income from its
specific securities is to be available for
the service of the guaranteed loans. In
this connection it should be pointed out
that even under the present depressed
conditions the group
companies
general are not losing money so far as
direct trading expenses are concerned.
in.
The Ulster Government and the
British Government, who are jointly
concerned in most of the transactions,
have been in consultation with the
sponsors of the scheme from the time of
the very first draft, and both Governments are satisfied that on general principle the scheme is sound, and that it
provides a satisfactory solution of the
problem. In the opinion of this Government, given some improvement in
world shipping conditions, taken in corjunction with the substantial economies
and improved management, there is no
reason why ultimately any serious sacrifice should be entailed on the part of
this Government. As a temporary
Measure the Government will, in all
probability, be called upon to make advances under its guarantees in any cases
where net earnings for the time being
prove to be insufficient to meet the service of the guaranteed first mortgage
loans, but if such should be the case the
scheme provides that such payments
shall rank in the preferential position
which is given under the scheme to those
who, like the Government, are fortunate
enough to be covered by first mortgages
on the assets in question.
These payments, therefore, would be temporary
payments and the Government would be
entitled to recoupment in respect of such
out of earnings in the same preferential

way.
The alternative to acceptance of the
scheme could only be an attempt by an
army of receivers to realise the assets,
and, although the Government Guaran-

teed Loans are, in the main, strongly

group of creditors would only
brought about a collapse of the

Harland & Wolff are so closely related.

en-
I am glad to note that the main body
of principal creditors, as well as the two
Governments, have shown, by their
acceptance of the scheme, not only that
they have appreciated the national interests involved, but that they consider
the scheme a fair one in that it provides
a framework within which the principal
creditors, including the Governments,
may handle the assets which are available
for payment of the outstanding loans
without disturbance of the existing
relative rights.
The Government have come to the
conclusion that the outcome of having
provided guarantees in the past is not
such as should debar us from future
action under those Acts. I have also
shown that from the point of view of
employment and of capital expenditure
the continuance of the legislation is desirable, and, accordingly, the Government
recommends this Committee to approve
the Resolution now before it.
Before sitting down I should like to
place before the Committee one important consideration. At the Ministry's
request the actual wages disbursed by
our shipbuilders in connection with ships.
financed under our Loans Guarantee
Acts have been taken out. The result
shows a total saving to the Unemployment Fund since 1923 of approximately
£3,200,000, which excludes the indirect
employment which has been given, and
also takes no account of the saving to
the British Unemployment Fund in the
production of the raw material. I beg
to move.
Mr. HEALY: In this matter the
Government probably were on the horns
of a dilemma about ten years ago. It was
then a question of throwing on to the
Unemployment Fund a great deal more
members than the finances of the time
justified or of giving these guaranteed
loans, which were not expected at the

time to have the serious consequences
which they really have had. The Government, however, even ten years ago,
ought to have been aware of the fact that
shipbuilding was one of the industries for
which there was no immediate future.
That they have gone on continuing these
guaranteed loans in the interval shows
that they did not realise their responsibilities to the taxpayers as they ought to
have done.
The large sum at present outstanding,
namely, £9,250,000, is a very serious
matter for the taxpayers of the Six
Counties considering the taxable capacity
of this area, and, therefore, I do not
think the Government, or their financial
advisers, approached the matter from the
proper angle, namely, as to whether it
was justified from the point of view of
the taxpayers generally. I think they
looked at it entirely from the standpoint
of employment in Belfast, and, as Belfast
will not bear the major portion of their
responsibility, I think their outlook
ought to have been a little wider. I do
not know whether the optimism of the
Minister of Finance or the Minister of
Commerce is going to be justified but, if
the report of the shares which I saw

exactly of the same opinion as the Minister
of Finance or the Minister of Commerce,
and believe that there is not the same
future for the Royal Mail Steamship
Company and the allied Kylsant groups
as the Government believe.

Sir WILSON HUNGERFORD: I am
delighted that the Minister has made
that point quite clear. There is no doubt
that if these guarantees had not been
given very many of our people would have
been walking about the streets, and
under the system now in operation
might not be in receipt of unemployment
or transitional benefit. It is exceedingly
hard, to get people to realise what a
serious thing it would be if our shipyards
were closed.
Through the Loans Guarantee Acts no
fewer than 53 ships of first-class type have
been built here. That should not be
forgotten and one can easily realise the
amount of work thus provided. I cannot
agree with the suggestion of the hon.
Member (Mr. Beattie) that all the work
should be executed in Belfast. There is
a certain amount of work that cannot be
done here and we do not begrudge any
benefit which the depressed steel industries
across the water received as a result of
these orders for ships.
Not only have
the workers in Belfast been helped, but
also the small shopkeepers. They provide the food which has to be purchased
by these workers' families, and supplies
have to be obtained from the country.
In that way the money paid in wages is
widely distributed with beneficial results.
The Government should, therefore, be
commended for the policy which they have
adopted in regard to guaranteeing loans.
Mr. POLLOCK: I pass away from the
detail matters referred to by my hon.
Friend the Member for Pottinger (Mr.
Beattie) because they are hardly germane
to the principal subject under discussion
to-day, that is, the propriety or otherwise.
of continuing the principle of loan
guarantees, but there is one point I
would like to refer to. He mentioned
one particular case in which the work was
done on the Clyde, by Harland and
Wolff, I presume, under our guarantee.
As a matter of fact, he is correct up to a
point. If my recollection is correct the
hull was built on the Clyde, but we received a very important offset in the case
of a Union Castle boat which was given
to us in Belfast without any guarantee
because of the fact that that hull was
built on the Clyde. Therefore, there was
no loss to the workmen in Northern Ireland.
Touching on the main subject, hon.
Members opposite seem to be under a
misapprehension. I suppose it is not
competent or proper for me to make any
imputations, but if they are not under
a misapprehension they are certainly
misinformed in regard to the whole operation of the Loans Guarantee Acts and
the possible ultimate issue. If we could
view this subject in its proper perspective
we must carry our minds back to 1922
when we decided to follow the British
Government in passing a Trades Facilities
or Loans Guarantee Act in accordance
with the policy which they had carried on
for some years, and in connection with
which they had guaranteed sums amounting to £75,000,000.
We at that time saw the necessity of
applying ourselves to the question as to
whether our shipyards here were to continue in full work, but above all to see
that our splendid workmen here were to
be assured of continuous work. The hon.
Member for South Fermanagh (Mr.
Healy), has made very disagreeable insinuations that the action of the Government was influenced, because there was
some person whom most Members will
recognise associated with one of the companies concerned. There is not the
slightest ground for, or a scintilla of
truth in, that statement. The Government was actuated by one motive, which
was the welfare of our working men.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
But remember that the conditions existing in 1922 form a very remarkable
contrast to those existing to-day, when
the whole world is sunk in depression,
when there is an economic avalanche, the
like of which was never known in history.
Conditions were very different in 1922,
when the directors of the Royal Mail
Company approached us to assist them in
providing capital for the purpose of building ships in Belfast. Was there a single
man in the whole of the Three Kingdoms
at that time who would have questioned

Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: This is
a small Bill, which I hope will not take
up much of the time of the House. At
the outset it may interest honourable
Members if I give some facts which will
enable an accurate appreciation to be
made of the immense and growing
economic importance of the poultry
industry to the agricultural community.
The following figures for the year 1928
indicate the annual value of the output
from the leading agricultural commodities:
-

It will be seen from these figures that
the poultry industry is worth 3 millions
sterling a year, almost as much as the
cattle and pig industries combined.
Further, poultry production is capable
of almost unlimited further development.
In this connection it may be pointed out
that the United Kingdom imports
annually poultry and poultry products
to the value of about £20,000,000. That
shows the possibilities, more particularly
now that at last home produce looks like
obtaining a favoured position in the
British market.
Although poultry rearing is important
to the farming community of these islands
generally, it is of vastly greater relative
importance to the small farmers of Northern Ireland, and the development of the
industry in this country in recent years
has been remarkable. For example, in
1904 the poultry population of Northern
Ireland was estimated at 4,351,344, but
in 1930 it had risen to 8,807,516. The
number of poultry in proportion to
acreage is also considerably higher in
Northern Ireland than in Great Britain
or even the Irish Free State. The following figures in this connection are
illuminating:-

At present I regret to say that this
valuable industry is menaced by serious
disease. Bacillary White Diarrhoea at
the moment constituted the gravest
danger to our poultry flocks. The effect
of the disease is that within three weeks
of hatching the young chicks die off
rapidly, the rate of mortality being anything from 90 to 100 per cent.; consequently where outbreaks occur practically
the whole of the young stock is lost.
Moreover, surviving birds, although
apparently healthy, act as carriers of
the disease, the germ being transmitted
in the eggs and thus hatches in subsequent years are reinfected.
917 Poultry Diseases Bill-

21 APRIL 1932
Second Reading.
Unfortunately, there is no known cure
for this disease. The only method of
coping with it is to determine its presence
by bacteriological examination and then
to weed out the reacting birds. The
Ministry has done much in recent years
to prevent the spread of this disease
within Northern Ireland, and the results
on the whole are satisfactory. Poultry
stations under the schemes of County
Agricultural Committees are obliged to
have their flocks tested and, in addition,
we have a voluntary scheme whereby
private breeders can have birds tested at
a small charge.
Private breeders are fully alive to the
advantages of the scheme, and are having
birds tested in increasing numbers. For
example, in 1927-8 the number of blood
samples tested for private breeders was
2,606, whereas in 1930-31 the number
was 22,851.
I am glad to be able to say that many
breeders who found it impossible to rear
chicks in 1928 have, as a result of our
scheme, had no difficulties in this connection in 1932.
All our efforts and expenditure in endeavouring to eradicate bacillary white
diarrhoea disease within Northern Ireland will, however, in the end be nullified unless steps are taken to exercise
some control over the imports of breeding
poultry, day-old chicks, and hatching
eggs. It is futile to stamp out disease
one day if we allow it to be introduced
the next. I may say in this connection
that practically all outbreaks of bacillary
white diarrhoea in Northern Ireland can
be traced directly or indirectly to such
imports. All the important poultryproducing countries in Europe have now
regulations in force to prevent the introduction of disease, and as these countries
are our chief competitors on the British
market we are going to be seriously handicapped if we simply fold our hands and
look on without taking similar precautions.
It seems to me quite extraordinary that
while the Diseases of Animals Acts give
ample power to protect other live stock,
such as cattle, sheep, swine, etc., from
contagious disease, no provision has heretofore been made for the safeguarding of
our poultry flocks which are of at least
equal importance from the financial point
of view. Probably the explanation is
that when the Diseases of Animals Acts
were first contemplated poultry were regarded as of little economic importance
and, consequently, they were left outside.
the scope of that splendid legislation
that has freed us from such scourges as
pleuro-pneumonia, which within living
memory was a very serious disease in this
country. It is also to the Diseases of
Animals Code that we owe our comparative immunity from such diseases as
foot-and-mouth disease, swine fever, etc.
All I now ask for. is authority to protect
similarly our poultry industry and, if this
proposal is approved, I look forward to
equally satisfactory results. Members will
observe that the Bill is what is known as
an enabling Measure, that is, that it gives
us the necessary powers to make Orders
without specifying in detail what those
Orders shall be. In that respect it
follows precisely the lines of the Diseases
of Animals Acts already referred to, and
it is difficult to see how a question of
disease could otherwise be efficiently dealt
with legislatively. However, in case
hon. Members desire to know what
Orders we have in mind at the moment,
I may say that we propose, in the first
instance, to secure as far as practicable
that breeding poultry, day-old chicks, or
eggs imported for hatching, are not
carriers of bacillary white diarrhoea. It
is not at present proposed that disease in
poultry should be made notifiable, or to
schedule areas on account of disease, because the measures we are already taking
are reducing the incidence of disease, and
are adequate to cope with the position so
far as the internal situation is concerned
at present. Disease might, however,
suddenly get out of hand, and a particular district might become a plague spot
In that
contaminating a whole area.
case it might be necessary in the interests
of the industry to resort to drastic
measures, but we do not contemplate such
action at present, and I am hoping that
it may not be necessary. At the same
time, as in the case of the Diseases of
Animals Acts, we must be prepared to act
if, unfortunately, an emergency such as
we have indicated should arise. I beg to
move.

apple industry by legislation? Remember
the apple industry attained its position
entirely by the unaided efforts of the
people.
Sir EDWARD ARCHDALE: No.
Mr. HEALY: The Government did not
legislate as to apples until a year ago.
There were plenty of apples in the
English market until a year ago. Your
legislation effectively closed that market.
You legislated for pork and the pork industry has been hampered. Now you are
legislating for the egg industry, Ulster's
greatest industry, and the one that has
made its way without legislation; the one
that has gone to the very peak of success
without legislation. (An hon. Member:
What about grading?) It achieved its
greatest success before even the grading
restrictions came on. The Minister gave
us figures about 1928 with regard to egg
exports. Surely an up-to-date Ministry
would have figures for 1930 and 1931.
The figures he has given here for 1928
represent the very peak and the very
maximum for eggs in the country. If he
takes the figures for 1931 he will probably find a decrease. Surely he ought
to tell the truth about the industry and
give us the figures for 1931. As the restrictions become closer and closer the
value of eggs and egg products becomes
less. If the Northern Government
cannot help agriculture in the Six
Counties they at least should not hamper
it. They ought not to impose restrictions
on industries that have come to the forefront without any help from the
Government.
There is another matter, and I think
it is the most serious matter of all. Every
piece of legislation introduced into this
House presupposes the appointment of
new officials. I can already see quite a
number of young gentlemen favourable
to the Government up and down the
country looking for positions. Probably
they are promised. It is the easiest way
in the world for a Government to remain
popular to have jobs here and there to
allocate. But what about the taxpayers?
Is there not going to be some finality in
the cost of administration? Is there
going to be no end to the burdens imposed on that patient beast of burden,
the taxpayer? The Minister of Agriculture will next seek to appoint a number
of officials, and the taxpayer is going to
pay them, and at the end of the year
we shall find that the exports of eggs
are not increasing at all in proportion
to the amount of money expended.
In other words, the people themselves
know better than the Department of
Agriculture how to manage their industries. They know better how to manage
their eggs, pork, butter, and potatoes.
They had to get markets for these things
before the Government began legislation.
The industry is not prospering in proportion to the legislation and increased
number of officials. Therefore, although
I am not prepared to go the length of
moving the rejection of this Bill, I think
really the House should consider very
seriously whether they are likely to advance the interests of agriculturists by
means of legislation which the people
mainly concerned do not ask for.

Although a great many people think the

throughout the agricultural community
would be in favour of this Measure.

I rose particularly to say that while I
can recognise there may be cases of emergency in which the Minister of Agriculture should have the power of deciding
promptly on some course of action, I
notice that in this Bill, as it is, it is in
the power of the Minister to do absolutely
what he pleases. I have again and again
drawn attention to the fact that it is a
very imprudent thing to put the power
in the hands of any Minister to do what
he pleases by regulation. I think the
Government should see their way to add
to this Measure a Clause which would
not take the power out of his hands in
a case of emergency, but would preserve
the rights of this House to have the
regulations that he makes laid on the
Table. He will do something some day
which perhaps I or some other person
will find fault with and which we never
heard of at all, and he will say that on
such an evening you passed a Bill giving
me power, and I can do what I please.
I think the representatives of the people
have a perfect right to see that all regulations of every description are laid on
the Table so that they can find fault
with them if they think fit. I would
give the power in an emergency, but to
give these wider powers is neither wise
nor prudent.

Blood-testing gives a certain amount of

Often readers appear to be under the

Further, the disease is infectious as well

So infectious is this disease that I think
it well to also quote from a leaflet which

lot of chicks is suspected of being
diseased this lot should be attended to
by another person or, if only one person is available, left until last. Incubators, brooders, hovers, houses,

It is to be observed on every hand that
large numbers of persons are going into
the poultry industry for egg purposes,
and I know personally that many of these
people are keeping poultry for the first
time; therefore the greater is the necessity for the prevention of disease.
I am not a keeper of poultry myself
and I do not know a great deal about
Estimates
Adjournment
21 APRIL 1932
them, but I am fond of eggs and I think
it would be a dreadful thing, indeed, that
we should have bad eggs through disease,
or that we should run the risk of contracting this disease through a hen having
bacillary white diarrhoea. I hope we will
not have a great army of inspectors under
this Bill, but the question arises, can
you avoid having inspectors? There is a
great outcry against inspectors but, I say,
we must have inspectors, and if we pass
this Bill we are in the hands of the
Ministry, and all I can say is, if we must
have them, let them be a few women
who have a thorough knowledge of their
work.

PREPARATION OF DOG LISTS.
2. Mr. McCARROLL asked the Minister of Finance whether he has received
a communication from the Derry Branch
of the Typographical Association renewing the protest against the transfer to
London of printing work hitherto done in
this country; whether, before the decision
referred to was arrived at, opportunity
was given to firms in this area to tender
on an equal basis; whether it is not contrary to statutory provisions to have the
printing of the lists of dog licence holders
executed outside Ireland; and whether,
in view of all circumstances, it would not
be desirable to revert to the former position, under which the employment was
provided at home.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The communication to which
the hon. Member refers has been received
and answered.
Since the hon. Member persists in referring to this work as printing, might
I again point out that, as I explained
fully in a reply given to him on the 14th
ultimo, the printing of the lists has been
discontinued, and they are being copied
by duplicating process in the Stationery
Office, London. As a result of the
change, the Exchequer has made a
saving estimated at more than 40 per
cent. of the previous cost.
I am not aware that there are any
firms in Northern Ireland which could
compete for work of this nature, but if
there are, I am prepared to undertake
that they will be given an opportunity
of tendering for future contracts.
There is no statutory provision which
prohibits the printing or duplicating of
these lists outside Ireland.
The answer to the concluding portion
of the hon. Member's question is in the
negative.
Mr. ELLIOTT: May I ask whether
it is a fact that by Statute these dog
lists must be delivered by 15th April
each year; whether the right hon. Gentleman is aware that under the new
arrangement these lists have not yet
been delivered, and what steps he proposes to take in regard to this matter?
Mr. POLLOCK: It is a fact that
under an Act of 1865, the date mentioned
by the hon. Member, 15th April, is in-
Icluded as the date on which these lists
should be prepared, but it has never been
the case, or has not been the case for
many years, at any rate, that that has
been complied with. It is regarded as
an archaic Act. The period between 13th
March and 15th April this year, whether
on account of the number of dogs I do
not know, was quite insufficient to prepare the lists.
That is the answer to my
hon. Friend from Tyrone. There is no
special obligation as to date, except that
contained in this archaic Act of 1865.
Mr. McCARROLL: May I ask the
Minister, having regard to the use to
which these dog lists are put, if the proposed method is considered a correct one?
They will be used very extensively by the
people, and will they be as suitable for
the purpose as the old ones? May I also
ask whether the decision of the Government in respect to this is consistent with
the desire to maintain employment in
Northern Ireland?
Mr. POLLOCK: It has been found in
practice that there has been no difficulty
in respect of the circulation of these lists.
They are intended for the police and must
be posted up at the doors of petty sessions
courts, police barracks, and such places.
No one will want to examine these lists
except someone to see about his own dog.
No inconvenience has really been caused
by the method adopted.
Mr. HEALY: Is it a fact that the
paper suitable for cyclostyle work is not
suitable for posting up?
Mr. POLLOCK: That is a technical
matter which I am not prepared either
to accept or to deny.
Mr. HEALY: Can the right hon.
Gentleman tell us what the actual cost
previously was?
Mr. POLLOCK : Yes. The actual
cost was £340, and it has been reduced
to £200 by the change.
THE MEANS TEST.
3. Mr. McCARROLL asked the Minister of Labour to state the total number
of cases in which, since the regulations
under the Economy Act came into force;
the means test for transitional payments
has been applied, up to and including
the 31st March; the total number in
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. McCarroll]
which full rates have been allowed and
are being paid; the total number in which
partial rates were paid and are being
paid, and the numbers in which no
allowance has been made; and also
whether any steps will be taken to secure
greater uniformity in administration, and
in
the amounts allocated by public
assistance committees.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The total number of determinations received from public assistance
committees up to the 30th March last
(the latest date for which figures are
available) was 31,197. Of these 11,668
were allowed at normal benefit rates,
and 14,415 at rates lower than normal
benefit rates, while in the remaining
5,114 cases the needs of applicants were
held not to justify payments.
A conference was held to co-ordinate
views in administration in certain areas
where discrepancies existed. Allowing
for the variation in local conditions I am
not now aware of any serious lack of
uniformity in the administration.

of Labour whether he can state the basis
upon which the rank or grade of
manager
of employment exchanges in Northern
Ireland is determined.
Mr. ANDREWS: The rank of the
manager of an employment exchange in
Northern Ireland is determined according
to the importance of the exchange.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to ask as
a supplementary question whether Derry
Employment Exchange managership is
lower than that of Belfast in grade, and
whether that of Bangor, with borough
status, is lower than that of Lurgan, with

the Order Paper.

Gentleman tell the House the reason why

EMPLOYMENT EXCHANGE SER-
VICE-PAYMENT OF
OVERTIME.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state the total
number of hours of non-payable overtime including qualifying hours for payable overtime performed by the members
of his staff in the employment exchange
service during the two years ended 31st
March, 1931 and 1932.
Mr. ANDREWS: There is no actual
record of the total hours of non-payable
overtime performed in the employment
exchange service during the years referred
to. Overtime, whether payable or nonpayable, is restricted to a minimum.
STAFFS OF EMPLOYMENT
EXCHANGES.
6. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state if the
staff provided for the work performed by
the employment exchanges is based on
the unemployed register, and, if so,
the number of unemployed persons
counted for the purpose against each
member of the staff; if this basis is of
uniform application throughout the employment exchanges service in Northern
Ireland, and if it is identical or otherwise with that in operation in Great
Britain.
Mr. ANDREWS: The employment
exchanges are staffed according to the
total amount of work to be performed.
The number of persons on the unemployed register is only one factor. Conditions vary from office to office and an
identical basis, whether as regards offices
in Northern Ireland or offices in Great
Britain, is not possible, particularly as
the Exchanges in Northern Ireland perform work in connection with the administration of the contributory and noncontributory pensions schemes and other
matters which is not carried out by the
Exchanges in Great Britain.

7. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister of Home Affairs whether he would
consider the advisability of issuing an

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): Such an order as
is suggested would not be within the

1926.
Major McCORMICK: Arising out of

Sir DAWSON BATES: Even if I had
the power,
that would be an insult to

Mr. CRAWFORD: Arising out of the

MENTALLY DEFECTIVE
CHILDREN.
asked the
8. Major McCORMICK
Minister of Home Affairs whether any
arrangements have been made in regard
to the treatment of mentally defective
children of a non-educable kind; and
whether the Government proposes to introduce legislation dealing with these
children on the lines suggested by the
various public bodies in Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The question
of the treatment of mentally defective
children of a non-educable kind engaged
the most earnest consideration of the
Government prior to the introduction of
the Mental Treatment Bill at present
before this House, but it became clear
that the establishment of an institution
or institutions for the treatment of these
children would involve heavy public
expenditure.
Having regard, therefore, to the existing financial situation and the necessity
for rigid economy, it was decided with
regret to postpone further consideration
of the matter for the moment.

9. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of

Sir DAWSON BATES: The answer to

Mr. ANDREWS: A friend of mine
suggested to me this forenoon that this
was my big day.
Mr. BEATTIE: Your pay day.
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
26 APRIL 1932
re-
Mr. ANDREWS: My reply was that I
did not look upon it as that, that I looked
upon it as the big day of the Opposition.
However that may be, it is the one
occasion in the year when I have the
opportunity of referring to the general
policy of the Department and its many
activities in a great number of directions.
I think I should, in the first place, remind hon. Members how greatly the work
of the Deparment has increased during
the last few years. When we took over
our powers from His Majesty's Imperial
Government more than ten years ago we
became responsible for industrial
lations, trade boards, the factory and workshops code, the Truck Acts, and workmen's compensation. In addition to that
we had dual control with the approved
societies in connection with health insurance matters, and we became responsible for the employment exchanges and
for the unemployment insurance. Since
then there has been added to the duties
of the Department, old age pensions (contributory and non-contributory), widows'
and orphans' pensions, employment services, such as relief schemes, juvenile
training centre, etc. Our control over
health insurance matters has been
strengthened and medical benefits have
been added to this scheme. This, of
course, has involved an increase in our
Estimate, and in addition to that it has
involved the Department in a great many
additional duties of a very important
kind in the public interest.
May I say that the general policy remains what it always has been, namely,
that in connection with these four great
social services which my Department is
charged with the responsibility of dealing
with, to remain in step or in parity with
Great Britain. That was the policy
which the Government decided upon when
we took over our powers more than ten
years ago, and from that policy we have
never varied, either as regards administration or legislation. Of course the Department is frequently criticised, very
often from two very different standpoints
at the same time. I am told that we
cannot afford the great expenditure involved, that we are a poorer part of the
Kingdom than that which lies across the
Channel, and that we ought to cut our
coat according to our cloth. The reply
of the Government I think is very convincing. It is that because we have for
certain services a Parliament of our own
that is no reason why our working
people should suffer as regards benefits
and privileges which their fellow countrymen in Great Britain enjoy, and which,
if we continued to be governed from
Westminster, they would also enjoy.
Besides, if the Government were to do
less in connection with these matters, I
do not think it would involve any saving,
because it would simply mean that the
local authorities would have to bear a
heavier burden as the rates would have
to make up the difference. The attack
on the other side is that the Government are not doing half enough to
deal with the situation as it now exists.
In fact, hon. Members opposite have
stated from time to time that the Government is doing nothing.
Mr. BEATTIE: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: And I observe that
a Member of a local board the other day
said the same thing. Well, of course, a
statement like that is really foolish, as
almost every sentence which I utter to-day
will show. There is the less extravagant
statement made that we are not doing
enough. The answer to that is that we
are doing everything which has been done
in Great Britain, and more than is being
done in any other country in the world,
and that we cannot afford to do more.
May I say at this stage that I particularly desire to-day to remove a misunderstanding which, I fear, is too
general, namely, that the Ministry of
Labour Estimates show an actual increase
in State expenditure this year of £217,703
against last year. This is, however, only
part of the story. It is true that we ask
the Committee to vote under all heads, as
shown on page 83 of the Estimates,
£4,002,411, as against £3,784,708 for the
previous year. It should be remembered
in this connection that last year the Unemployment Fund borrowed £841,000,
while this year we are estimating on the
basis of paying our way. In other words,
instead of borrowing to make up the
deficiency as between the income of the
Unemployment Fund and the actual expenditure as happened last year, the State
is to make up such difference as there may
be. A correct comparison, therefore, discloses a reduction of £623,297, less certain
adjustments, under the Re-insurance
Agreement, which can only be correctly
ascertained at the end of the financial
year.
Ministry of Labour
Estimates-

HOUSE OF COMMONS

Mr. Andrews
In addition to the £4,002,411, to which
I have referred as the State's contribution
to these social services, the Ministry will
be responsible this year for collecting
from 48,000 employers and 360,000 employees a sum estimated at £1,645,000.
The total amount, therefore, paid to the
beneficiaries this year, will be approximately £5,380,000. Yet some people are
ungenerous enough to say that the Government are doing nothing. The importance of this figure is that nothing at
all is included in it for administration.
The Committee will be interested to know
that the administration cost of all the
services of the Ministry of Labour, about
which we hear so much in these days
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the highest in the
world.
Mr. ANDREWS- -is only 6.9%.
Mr. BEATTIE: The highest in the
world.
Mr. ANDREWS: Sometimes my hon.
Friend speaks too quickly. It is only 6.9,
which is very moderate. Some trade
unions are not able to administer as
cheaply.
Mr. BEATTIE: You are the highest
administration.
Mr. ANDREWS: And that figure includes the health insurance scheme,
which, owing to its dual control, is an
expensive scheme to administer, I admit.
Pensions, for instance, as regards administration, only cost 2.7%. The whole cost
of the administration of our pensions
scheme is met out of the financial resources of the scheme itself, and I am
glad to be able to tell the Committee today that the same applies for the first
time as regards our unemployment scheme
and our health insurance scheme. This
is the reason why the net figure for administering the services of the Ministry
of Labour will only be £22,240 this year,
the decrease of £76,214 being mainly due
to increased appropriations in aid and
certain staff and other savings.
On this occasion it might interest the
Committee if I reviewed as briefly as
possible the various activities of the Department and their importance to the
people generally in Northern Ireland. The
first service to which I desire to refer is
that of our industrial relations branch,
in other words, the preservation as far as
possible of industrial peace. It is always
a pleasure to me to refer to the harmonious relations which exist between
the workers and their employers in Northern Ireland and the few strikes and lockouts which we have. We are much more
fortunate in that direction than they are
in Great Britain. During the past year
important questions arose affecting both
the spinning and weaving ends of our
staple industry. Through the machinery
of conciliation and negotiation, which
was established some years ago by my
Department in connection with the
spinning branch of the trade, and with
the goodwill of both employers and
workers in that branch, certain differences
were adjusted; and wage reductions also
resulted from the negotiations, it being
recognised by all concerned that the state
of the industry at that time required.
that some sacrifices should be made by
the workers in order that we might be in
a better position than we were to compete with the fierce foreign competition
to which we were subjected.

In the weaving end of the trade it is
true that a strike occurred and lasted
for a few weeks in Lurgan. I am glad
to state that it did not spread to other
districts, and after a few weeks' time,
under the auspices of the Department,
matters were adjusted on a satisfactory
basis. In the building trade, under the
auspices of the Department again,
settlements were arranged of a good many
outstanding difficulties. At our docks,
quite recently, there was a certain trouble
associated with our cross-Channel trade.
Here, again, the Department was successful in bringing about a settlement.
think I am entitled to say that I am
particularly gratified that our chief conciliation officer, by his patience, tact, and
ability in dealing with matters of the
kind, has earned the confidence of both
employers and employees to a very remarkable degree throughout Northern
Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Largely owing to the influence of the
Department, therefore, I think I can
claim that we have averted strikes which,
if they had occurred, would have cost
our Province many hundreds of thousands
of pounds.
I need only refer briefly to Trade
Boards. There are in Northern Ireland
eighteen of these Boards, composed, as
they are, of representatives of employer
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
26 APRIL 1932
and employee, with a neutral appointed
member as chairman. They exist for the
purpose of settling wages and conditions,
and they affect 3,000 firms and 50,000
of our employed persons. When I became Minister of Labour I remember in
this House I was very frequently attacked
on the ground that these Boards were a
perfect pest, that they never should have
been established, and that they were unacceptable both to employers and work-.
ing people. We legislated on the matter
in this House, and owing to reasonable
administration I am glad to think that
these Boards are now looked upon by both
employers and employed as a very satisfactory way of dealing with labour matters in those industries to which the
Boards are applied. At any rate, there
has been absolutely no trouble in those
industries since we here became a Parliament.
There are one or two things I would
like to say about our Factory and Workshop code. Our employers have been cooperating in a most generous way with
the Ministry in this connection, with the
result that, I am glad to be able to
state, through improved ventilation,
sanitation, lighting, etcetera, and the
shorter hours which they now enjoy, the
health of our industrial workers in Northern Ireland has improved to a remarkable degree. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). But there is one thing which I do
not look upon as satisfactory, and that
is that there are in Northern Ireland far
too many accidents. Many of these
accidents, I believe, are avoidable. There
were no fewer than 1,195 last year, and 13
persons were fatally injured. These accidents involved payment by employers
during the to the average amount per
week of £1,000. My Department has been
urging for some time that employers
should to a very great extent protect moving parts of their machinery in such a
way as to lessen the probability of
accident, and that their foremen and
workers generally should be instructed as
to the importance of not taking unnecessary risks. In our shipyards safety committees have been established and have
been most useful in this respect.

I now come to the question of pensions.
It may surprise hon. Members to know
that in this little area of ours we have no
fewer than 94,297 pensioners receiving
pensions every week.
Mr. BEATTIE: How many paid for
them?
Mr. ANDREWS: They range from
under one year to over ninety, and I can
assure the Committee it is no light task
to see that the conditions which Parliament has laid down are fulfilled when
these pensions are granted, and work is
rendered more difficult through the everchanging circumstances in the lives of the
pensioners. These pensioners are scattered
all over Northern Ireland. They live in
our city streets and they live high up on
mountain sides. They reside in the
island of Rathlin and also on the islands
of Lough Erne. Administration under
the circumstances is, therefore, a very
difficult matter indeed. My inspectors
from time to time hear funny statements
made. For instance, the other day a
woman was asked to try to think of
some evidence with regard to her age
which she could give to qualify her for
the old-age pension. Her reply was:
"Well, I cannot get my birth certificate,
and I cannot get my baptismal certificate.
I really cannot think of any evidence I
can give." Our inspectors are always
ready to help a claimant, and the inspector in this case said: "Well, now,
just think again, because if you cannot
give some proof, of course, you cannot
get the pension." "Well, she said, "I
remember when I was a little girl being
taken to the opening of an Orange Hall,
and above the door of that Orange Hall
there was a date." So the inspector said:
"Yes. That might be very good evidence.
He went and looked at the Orange Hall
and found the date on the stone was
1690. (Laughter.) Although that made
the woman rather over 200 years of age,
I do not know that it was taken as satisfactory proof of her actual age. Again,
when a claimant was asked to try to give
some proof of her age, she said: "Well,
the truth of the matter is, I have a very
bad memory for these things, but my
mother is inside, and she probably remembers the event better than I do. She
will, no doubt, tell you what my age is."
However, that may be, I can assure you
that every effort is made in order to ensure that justice is done in connection
with these matters.

Mr. DEVLIN: Are these the tests
that are applied to blind persons?
Mr. ANDREWS: I shall refer to that
later on. As regards health insurance
matters, I am sorry I cannot say that all
is well. The health insurance scheme is
giving great anxiety to the Ministry of
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Andrews]
Health in Great Britain, and it is also
giving a considerable amount of anxiety
to us here. I remember that, when I became Minister of Labour, the health insurance scheme was very often criticised
on the ground that the reserves were far
too large, and that it was a foolish thing
to go on creating these immense reserves.
My answer always was: "Well, we are
in close contact with the best actuarial
authorities in the Kingdom on these
matters, and they assure us that the reserves are necessary to liquidate the contingent liabilities which are certain to
occur from time to time, especially as the
scheme goes on to function.'
Now, nobody makes an attack on the
ground that the reserves are too large;
no one suggests that the benefits should
be increased or that the contributions
should be lowered, because I think everyone realises that the liabilities upon the
scheme in these days have been increasing
beyond what was first expected. As hon.
Members know, there is a valuation of
the assets and liabilities of the approved
societies made every five years, and the
last valuation which was reported upon
some months ago disclosed the fact that
the societies' financial position had gone
back a good deal. That is exactly what
is causing the anxiety at the present time.
I may say, however, that I should be
much more anxious about the position if
it were not for the fact that we are so
closely associated with the British scheme,
and therefore we are on a much sounder
foundation than if we had to depend on
our position here alone.
The demands on the approved societies
have increased, I think, largely owing to
the fact that when the scheme was started
it was the first contributory scheme of
the kind which was launched. A great
many people did not know very well how
to make a claim. They had never made
claims of the kind before; they hesitated
to make them, and if they could carry
on for a short period without making a
claim upon the health insurance funds
they did so. Now they have come to
realise and nobody can blame themthat, as it is a contributory scheme to
which they are paying when they are
working, they are entitled to get benefit
when they are ill, and so the claims have
vastly increased.
In addition to that, due to unemployment, the contribution income has fallen
off to a very considerable extent, so that
the approved societies have been hit both
ways to a rather startling degree at the
same time. The claims of married
women have mounted up to an alarming
extent, as the following figures disclose.
The expenditure in 1931 upon men was
£1 2s per head. The expenditure upon
single women was £1 5s 1d per head,
while the claims for married women
amounted to no less than £3 4s 10d per
head. In other words, married women
paid into the fund 17s 4d per head, and
during the year to which I am referring,
namely, 1931, they drew out on the
average no less than £3 4s 10d.
The general position, however, has improved as between the year 1929 and
1930. The claims upon the approved
societies in 1929 amounted to £681,359,
and last year they amounted to £623,092,
or a reduction of approximately £60,000.
So far, so good. Of course, the great
difficulty in health insurance matters is to
be sure when a person is really entitled
to draw benefit and when a person is not
entitled to do so. We are largely dependent on the certificates which are given
by the local doctors, and in recent years
our medical referees' service has been
greatly strengthened, with the result
that the approved societies-and they are
paying for this scheme themselves-can
have a second opinion when they so desire. In addition, this service is of a
consultative nature, because when the
medical referee finds something wrong
with the patient which the local doctor
may not have discovered, he communicates his views to the local doctor, very
much, I am sure, at times to the advantage of the patients who are the insured
persons.
I am very pleased to acknowledge the
very helpful way in which the Central
Insurance Practitioners' Committee cooperate with my Department in connection with this very important social service.
As hon. Members know, a year or so ago
there was attached to this service a medical benefit scheme, and I am pleased to
say that that scheme is working very
smoothly and satisfactorily, and that
complaints are few indeed. Only six
complaints of sufficient importance to
necessitate their being considered by the
Medical Benefit Council have been received since the scheme was started.
Four hundred and ninety-nine doctors,
and 405 chemists are working the scheme,
and I am confident that it is of incalculable value to insured persons, due to
Estimates-

the fact that there is brought within the
reach of the insured person when ill, medical advice, which, no doubt, in many instances, shortens the duration of the
illness, and in other cases actually saves
human lives.
I come now to unemployment insurance. We have so frequently discussed
this matter in the House-and quite recently that I am afraid there is not
much new that I can say upon the matter.
But, at the same time, if I did not refer
to the scheme and its working at some
length I probably should leave myself
open to the reproach that I had run away
from it. That is not just my way.
I
should like to say at the beginning of
my remarks on this subject that last year
we estimated on the basis of 25 per cent.
unemployment. As a matter of fact, it
worked out at 26.8 per cent., and I venture to suggest that it was a very close
estimate, having regard to the fact that
the year was an abnormal one. How
abnormal it was will be gathered from the
fact that during the financial crisis of
August last unemployment rose in our
area to 28.5 per cent., but on the suspension of the gold standard and the
adoption of the abnormal importation
duties it fell again towards the end of
the year to 24.1, and it is rather less
now, I am glad to say.
.
However, we are estimating on the
basis of 25 per cent. unemployment for
this year, which, unless something unexpected happens, we think is a conservative
estimate. The reason we are budgeting
for 25 per cent. unemployment is thisalthough, as I have said, it is rather
lower at the moment-the whole world's
industrial and financial position is very
uncertain, indeed, and in addition to
that our shipyards, I admit with great
regret, are in an unfortunate position at
the present time, through no fault of
those controlling the destinies of those
yards, of those who work in the yards, or
of the Government. As I have already
said, we are not borrowing for this year.
We are paying our way-with the result
that our Estimates are apparently increased by £260,000.
In
Several changes have been made in the
scheme, as hon. Members know. The
contributions income has been increased
from each of the three contributors.
addition to that, it was necessary to reduce the benefits paid by approximately
10 per cent., and even then it was found
that the expenditure would be largely in
excess of the income if benefit were paid
under the old conditions. Therefore it
was considered necessary that the standard
benefit should be limited to 26 weeks, and
that, after that, if the claimant found
that a further payment was necessary he
could receive it provided that he was able
to show in the first place that he was
normally in insurable employment, and
would normally seek to obtain his livelihood thereby. And the second condition
is that he can show to the public assistance committees that he is in need of what
is, after all, not insurance benefit but a
free State grant. Now a great deal of
criticism has been directed against this
needs test, but the object of it can be
(defended, and it is to conserve what
funds there are for those who need them
most.
As regards the scheme, the first condition to which I referred is adjudicated
upon by the machinery of the Department,
and as regards the latter condition,
namely, the needs test, that is applied by
the Public Assistance Committee. And
although there may be features connected
with that form of administration which
are not acceptable to many of us, yet at
the same time I am entitled to say that
I think these public assistance committees all over Northern Ireland have
played a very honourable part. They
have shouldered a heavy burden and I
believe that they are discharging their
responsible duties with great care and in
a purely public-spirited way. Their
duties are unpopular. They knew they
would be unpopular from the start, and
I think they deserve all the more credit
for shouldering what they were aware
would be an unpopular task to perform.
And how are they performing their
task? Just let me tell the House. Up
to the 30th March they have reviewed
31,197 cases. They granted full payments to 11,668 claimants. They gave
assistance to 14,415 claimants and they
found in 5,114 cases that public assistance was not necessary.
Now, on the
average, therefore, they have given twothirds of the benefit rates to those who
claim this form of State grant. How can
it be said fairly or with truth that these
public assistance committees are not endeavouring to do what is right in the
public interest by conserving the money
available, as I have said, for those who
are able to show that they require this
form of help, after having exhausted the
benefit which they were entitled to receive on the actuarial basis from the Unemployment Fund itself?

United Kingdom of which we form a

people between the ages of 16 and 18 are

tween the ages of 16 and 18, and I do

Now, we hear also a good deal about
new industries. Some people say that
the efforts of the Government to bring
new industries into our midst will be

We hear of a good many inquiries for

I shaved myself with a razor-blade which

do

I
wish to say that from the senior right

T
that the conditions which prevail in the
United States of America are infinitely
worse than the conditions which prevail
in Great Britain.
Then I asked myself a second question.
Having regard to the position in which
we are placed in regard to Great Britain,
are we in a position to deal with the
problem of unemployment in a comprehensive manner? I am of the opinion
that no State which is not a Sovereign
State can do other than, at the very best,
tinker with this great subject. Even if
this were a Sovereign State I doubt
whether as a Sovereign State we should
be able to provide a remedy to deal with
this great problem. I am inclining to
the view that the problem of unemployment is not a problem for a Federal
State such as this, nor for a Sovereign
State, but that it is a collective problem
which must be tackled and dealt with by
a combined council of civilised countries.
There is one thing, I think, which
strikes the casual observer in looking at
these Estimates, and in comparing these
Estimates with the Estimates of 10 years
ago, and that is, the enormous increase
in the cost of the social services. In
1923, I notice, the Estimates of this
House for social services amounted
approximately to two million pounds.
To-day, not including education, they
amount to substantially over four million
pounds. These social services include,
as the Minister pointed out, all branches
of social service in our midst. They
include unemployment benefit; they
include transitional benefit; they include
health insurance; they include widows'
and orphans' pensions, and they include.
the contributory pensions which are now
paid to the insured persons who attain
the age of 65.
This cost is enormous. Ever since I
entered this House, some three years ago,
the cost has been increasing year by
year, and it is only during the past year
that an attempt has been made to arrest
this somewhat startling tendency. We
had last year, if I remember aright, an
attempt I believe a perfectly sincere
attempt by the Prime Minister and by
the Members of the Cabinet to reduce
the cost of administration, and at the
same time to reduce the cost of social
services. I myself, so far as I have been
able to study the subject of economics,
do not agree with the postulates of such
a policy. I do not believe that we are
I going to solve the problem of unemployment, if it can be solved at all, by any
cheese-paring policy. By saving £20,000
or £30,000 a year we cannot deal with
the subject or even deal with the fringe
of the subject, no matter though our
intentions are of the very best.
I am somewhat concerned, when I reflect upon what this House did last year
with regard to unemployment benefit. I
am somewhat concerned that not merely
did we reduce the unemployment benefit,
the weekly benefit, by 10 per cent., but, as
the Minister himself pointed out to-day,
we also increased the contributions from
the State, from the employer, and from
the employee. In addition to the reduction of 10 per cent., we compelled the
insured population to subject themselves
to what was in reality a far greater reduction. Hitherto they had been allowed
to draw benefit for several years, but we
fixed a limit to the period of time during
which benefit might be drawn, a limit
which, if I remember aright, was six
months, so that it seems to me to some
extent that we are all responsible for
having imposed upon the working population a greater burden than we imposed
upon ourselves. We imposed upon ourselves the burden of a reduction of 15
per cent., which I am glad to say was
carried out pretty well universally and
without exceptions, but we imposed upon
the employed population, the industrialists, a far heavier burden, and I am
sorry now to reflect that in my opinion
that burden was somewhat heavier than
they could be expected to bear.
burden, which is not estimated by a reduction of 10 per cent., has deprived them
of such material advantages under this
great system of legislation which began in
1911, these National Insurance Acts, that
I should say their total loss amounted at
least to 25 per cent. or 30 per cent.
This
There are other aspects of the Estimates
to which I should like to refer; in fact,
there are so many that I find the question
of a choice very difficult. The question of
new industries was raised by the right
hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Labour.
I doubt very much whether this policy
of new industries is going materially to
help new industries here in Northern
Ireland. I am afraid that the Government and the House generally-or perhaps
the Cabinet-act upon the assumption
that the function of industry is to provide
employment. I have never looked upon
industry as necessitating such a function.
Estimates-
Ministry of Labour
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. McNeill]
In my opinion the purpose of industry is
to produce goods and to render services,
and the purpose of every Sovereign Parliament in the world to-day is to enable
those goods and services to be distributed.
And when I reflect upon the material
wealth of the world in civilised countries,
and it must be remembered that the
world is all one single market-and when
I reflect that there is a superabundance of
raw material, and a superabundance of
manufactured articles, and that there is
an unlimited capacity to produce_whatever articles the community needs, I come
to the conclusion that what we want in
Northern Ireland and elsewhere in other
countries, is not new industries, but the
distribution of the goods and services which
have been brought into being by existing
industries.
And even with regard to new industries
I do not think it is a proper policy to
take a country which is primarily agricultural, like Northern Ireland, and which
is situated within easy reach of the world's
greatest industrial markets-I do not
think it is a sound policy, considering the
particular genius of this country, to try
to convert it into an industrial country.
I would be sorry to see cities scattered
about the midst of County Tyrone and
other parts of Northern Ireland. I would
rather see rolling fields of grain and long
drills of potatoes. And I believe that
what we want to-day in Northern Ireland,
if we are to exist as a separate entity, is
to devote our energies very largely to
fostering what is at hand, namely, agriculture.
With regard to industries in agricultural districts I may tell this House that
I have been very favourably impressed by
the existence of smaller industries in certain agricultural districts. I do not know
if hon. Members have ever visited Belleek
or the pottery there. I spent some time
there last summer, and I was immensely
impressed by the potentialities of the
small industry operating there within
narrow limits. That industry has not
converted Belleek into an industrial city.
It provides employment; it provides
goods and services; and yet the character
of the place remains as it always was.
And I was also impressed with a visit
to West Donegal by such local industries
as that at Ardara. And when we talk
about fostering industries in Northern
Ireland by giving free sites to persuade
industrialists to come across, my own
opinion is that small industries are the
only industries which we should seriously
attempt to implant here in Northern
Ireland.
There are not many other points that I
can conveniently raise at the present
time, because we must make certain concessions to time which never loses time,
but I should like whole-heartedly to compliment the Minister and the Department upon one particular branch, and
that is the Juvenile Employment
Department in Alfred Street. And I
should like to ask every hon. Member
here to visit that Department and to see

I would like also to have some further

employment in Northern Ireland. It
is due largely to the fact that so many

is shown to-day in the public Press, that
you are transferring your responsibilities
for the working classes from the Government to the Boards of Guardians.
The Lord Mayor of Belfast stated yesterday that the Corporation were paying
£1,000 a week to the Board of Guardians
for outdoor relief. The burden has been
so great that he also has got into a state
of hysteria. All our settled politicians,
civic and national, are constantly getting
into a state of hysteria. The Lord
Mayor got into a state of hysteria the
other day and told us that if this thing
went on they would be municipally bankrupt, and that is because they are paying £1,000 a week, £50,000 a year, for
outdoor relief to people who ought not
to have to be given outdoor relief, but
who ought to be treated out of the Unemployment Fund. You are saving
that. You are getting additional funds
from the additional impost put upon the
workers and employers-a dual burden
first of all upon those who are working
as employees, and upon the employers in
the industries which are carrying on.
Therefore, I say that the right hon.
hon. Gentleman was quite right when he
set himself to the task of meeting this

cold and rigid facts and figures with that

Now, I want to say that I still go

wrong here all along is that there has

community to the discussion of this
problem. A committee of public safety
was the last proposal made by leading
merchants and business men in Belfast.
I think this committee of public safety
should consist of men of goodwill of all
parties to see if we can get out of these
difficulties in which we find ourselves.
We are not going to get out of them by
the new methods adumbrated in the
British policy with regard to economics.
I do not think we will. I think our
difficulties will become worse. Northern
Ireland is faced with an impost of
£200,000 imposed through the wheat tax.
Bread will become dearer. Every article
manufactured in England that we have
to buy, including agricultural implements, will become dearer. The cost of
living will become dearer; everything
will be costlier here in Northern Ireland,
and I see no signs of a revival of industry. If that is a policy of which this
Government feel proud, I do not think
that the people of Northern Ireland will
be satisfied, when we come to the real
adjustment of these things, as the right
hon. Gentleman was in the closing part
of his speech.

A full court consists of the chairman, a
representative of the employers, and a
workers' representative. A person going
before the court is entitled to a full court
if he demands and claims it. But, unfortunately, I would say of these 23,000
persons there were not 20,000 who understood that. When they come into the

and that form is that they will take the
court that is there whether it is complete or not. They think if they do not

they sign, and the minute they sign their
doom is sealed. They have only to wait

added to the 23,000. That is the general
rule, and that is the general policy.
I would have given the Minister time

The thing I am concerned about is the

There are many hungry days and nights

I have time to make a point about the

problem is going to be more acute as
time goes on.

Sir WILSON
HUNGERFORD:
I
desire to ask the Parliamentary Secretary
of the Ministry of Home Affairs for some
information of which I have given him
notice. I supplied him the other day
with a statement from tenants of subsidy
houses in the Oldpark district. Those
tenants are dissatisfied with their houses
and they feel that the conditions under
which the subsidy was granted have not
been carried out. The Parliamentary
Secretary was good enough to promise
me that he would investigate the matter,
and I shall be glad to know if that investigation has been carried out and if
he has got the inspector's report.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): The question
in regard to complaints in connection
with these houses was first raised by
the hon. Member for Pottinger (Mr.
Beattie), and in answering his question
I promised to make an investigation into
those complaints if I could have particulars of specific cases. By the help of my
hon. Friend behind me (Sir Wilson
Hungerford) a number of particulars were
sent to my Department. I am pleased
to say that in many cases the complaints
are entirely without any foundation, and in
most of the cases have only a slight foundation. At the time the matter was first
raised in the House a complete and full investigation had been made by the Corporation officials. I was not aware of that, when
I undertook to make a fresh investigation. However, having promised
across the floor of the House that I
would
have an investigation made,
I secured a report.
It is most unfortunate that complaints
should be addressed to us in such extravagent and grossly exaggerated terms.
I do not say that the hon. Member
opposite or my hon. Friend behind have
any responsibility in that regard. By
way of illustration, there was a suggestion that plumbing work in one of the
houses was very defective. All that was
required was to screw the tap in the
exhaust pipe. That was all that was
needed. In most of the other cases a
similar state of affairs existed-a slight
defect. The result of the examination
proved that the houses are not defective,
and that they have been built strictly
in accordance with the rules and regulations governing subsidy houses. It is
a pleasure to be able to state that, but
it is a great pity that persons of responsibility, such as the secretary of an
association, should lend himself to such
gross exaggeration.
Again, in reference to the presence of
the police at a distress in connection with
one of the subsidy houses, it has been
represented that the police were there
for the purpose of terrorising the
tenants. May I take this opportunity
of making perfectly clear that the police
were there for no such purpose. It having been intimated to the police by the
landlord that he intended to carry out
a distress in that neighbourhood, it became the duty of the police to attend,
not to help in the work he was doing,
but to see that the proceedings would
be held in circumstances where there
would be no breach of the peace.
That
was the sole purpose of the presence of
the police, and that was the only duty
they performed. It is a pity that we
have been put to so much trouble and a
considerable amount of expense in
getting the particulars. If my hon.
Friends who have interested themselves
in these matters are anxious to make any
further inquiry I will be only too glad
to give them the information we have
been supplied with.

Mr. HANNA rose.
Mr.
SPEAKER: The Member for
Larne has already spoken once
on the
Adjournment.
Mr. HANNA: By leave of the House
I would like to correct what might be
a very erroneous impression. In the
case the hon. Member (Mr. Nixon) refers
to, the mistake was made in the actual
carrying out of the distress. It is one
of the principles of our law that if a
man abuses an authority or licence given
to him by law he becomes a trespasser
from the very beginning. If a man sets
out to carry out a warrant of distress,
which was a perfectly good warrant, but
in carrying it out he does something that
is irregular, his whole entry is a trespass.
The presence of the police is, as I said,
for the purpose of preventing anything
in the nature of a breach of the peace.
That is their constant duty. They do
not go to help in the carrying out of
distress, but for the protection not only
of those engaged in the carrying out of
the distress but of all other interested
parties. They are not on one side or the
other.
Mr. NIXON: Do they protect a man
in an illegal act?
Mr. HANNA: No. They have no responsibility for any illegality. It must be
understood that a man is entitled to police
protection from others even though he is
engaged in a transaction that is not a
worthy one.
