The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): In moving the Resolution
which appears on the Order Paper in my
name, it is necessary for me to give to
the House an explanation of this somewhat unusual procedure. When the
Money Resolution of the 12th April,
which was precedent to the inclusion of
Clause 54 in the Bill, was taken, and
again when the Clause itself was
sidered in Committee, questions were
raised by the hon. Member for Mourne
(Mr. O'Neill), and the hon. and gallant
Member for East Down (Lieut.-Colonel
Gordon), the effect of which was to
challenge the propriety of leaving the
existing lunacy grants at the mercy of a
Departmental order, even though that
order is under the Bill required to be
laid before this House. My hon. and
gallant Friend had tabled a Motion with
the object of ensuring that, at any rate,
the existing grants would not be diminished, in an endeavour apparently to
embody in statutory form the assurance
which was given by me in moving the
Money Resolution, namely, that until
the Report of the Financial Relations
Committee had been fully considered in
consultation with the local authorities, it
is not contemplated to alter in any way
the amounts now being paid to the
several local authorities as laid down in
the Local Government Act of 1923.
My right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, found difficulty in accepting the
Amendment tabled by the hon. and
gallant Member, but undertook to
examine the question in collaboration
with himself, and this discussion has
taken place. As a result of this discussion and subsequent Departmental
1007 Mental Treatment (Money)-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Resolution Rescinded

[Mr. Barbour]
consideration, the Government has come
to the conclusion that as this whole
question of the grants to local authorities
and the recommendations of the Financial
Relations Committee in regard thereto
must very shortly come up for consideration in consultation with the local
authorities, and any results that flow
from that consultation will require to be
embodied in a Bill to be brought before
this House, it would be more satisfactory
to all concerned if the Government grant,
known as the grant in respect of pauper
lunatics, remained for the present untouched. This result can best be
achieved by leaving this Bill silent on
the subject, and this object can be
attained by a very simple Amendment,
but one which, owing to the fact that the
Bill is now in the Report stage, is a little
complex to bring about.
If the present financial Clause, No. 54,
is removed from the Bill automatically
the financial provisions in the 1923 Act
become reinstated. Section 10 of that
Act provides, in effect, that "until
Parliament otherwise determines "-I
wish to draw the attention of hon. Members particularly to those four wordsthe Ministry of Home Affairs are to pay
annually out of voted moneys an amount
equivalent to the average of the grants
paid in respect of the three financial
years ending 31st March, 1918, 1919, and
1920. A reversion to that position will
give the hon. Members the assurance that
they sought in a tangible form, and will
leave over for debate in this House, in
connection with some later Bill, a more
scientific method of calculating not only
these grants but, I trust, grants paid to
local authorities in respect of other
services.
The procedure, therefore, to attain
this object will be, firstly, to rescind the
Money Resolution of the 12th April;
secondly, after that rescission has been
accepted, to move that the Bill be recommitted to a Committee of the Whole
House in respect only of this particular
Clause 54. When that Clause is excised
by a Motion, which I will make at the
appropriate time, the Bill, as so amended,
will then be reported to the House.
As a preliminary to this machinery,
therefore, I now beg to move formally,
"That the Resolution of the House of
Tuesday, the 12th day of April, be hereby
rescinded."
Mr. NIXON: I am sure the House
greatly appreciates the very full, clear,
and elaborate statement made by the
Minister of Commerce in regard to this
matter, because it is not very often the
Government in this House rescind
Resolutions duly passed and recently
passed. This Resolution was passed on
12th April and it will be rescinded today, but if the Government had
accepted the Amendment proposed by the
hon. and gallant Member there would
have been no necessity to rescind this
Resolution. But the Government never
like to accept anything in a direct,
straightforward manner, hence the
necessity for this Resolution. I dare
say that so far as the Government, not
the Minister, is concerned it could all
be explained by referring to it as a
purely mental matter.
Mr. BYRNE: I agree with the rescinding of this Resolution, because I
take it that it means we are going to get
a grant, and that is better than getting
no grant at all. I say that this block
grant should be given pro rata to the
different institutions in the Six Counties.
I believe that in some of the mental
hospitals the numbers have decreased,
and that in others they have remained
stationary. In Belfast, since this block
grant was given, the number of patients
has increased by about 400. The grant
has been unfair so far as Belfast was
concerned. If you are going to give the
block grant, and that grant only, I say
it should be pro rata for all the institutions in the Six Counties. When this
grant was given it meant about half the
cost. The cost at that time was much
less than it is to-day, and it meant that
the Government was contributing about
half of the cost. To-day the cost is
about 16s. I think I am right in saying
that the Belfast Mental Hospital is receiving about 2s 63d per patient in the
institution. That is most unfair.
do not know whether the Government
will reconsider the matter or not, but
it is unfair to Belfast, where the numbers have increased so enormously. They
have increased about 33 per cent. since
this grant was given. While it may be
fair to the institutions outside Belfast,
it is most unfair to Belfast, and I hope that
the Government will reconsider this matter and give justice all round. If you
are giving a small grant, let it be pro
rata for all the institutions in the Six
Counties.

The Government are making a great

reason for disliking the Clause is this.

Rev. Professor CORKEY: I beg to
move, in page 2, line 10, after "full"

exceeding twenty-five years and".
This Amendment of mine is suggested
for the purpose of limiting the time over
which annuities may be paid for a house.
People when they want a house only
think of the amount which they will have
to pay week by week, and nothing else
interests them. That became very
1039 Rent Restrictions Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Committee

[Professor Corkey]
apparent during the sitting of the Committee of Inquiry. We found the people
were prepared to buy houses on forms of
agreement which were absurd and
onerous simply because there was a
desperate need of houses in their case
and they were prepared to do anything
to get the house. Now this Bill is
intended to protect people of that sort
and I introduce this Amendment simply
for the purpose of further protecting the
people who, on admission and by the
very fact that we have got this Bill
before us, are not able to take care of
themselves.
First of all, a house is a thing with a
limited term of life. It does not last
for ever. The occupant will find he is
not in the house very long-not a great
number of years-until it begins to show
signs of deterioration, and if the payment for the house is spread over an
excessive number of years the purchaser
may find when he has completed his payments that there is no house for him to
possess. The stairs have become shaky,
the slates have blown off the roof and
the floors are untrustworthy. Take, for
example, a house fifty years old that is
being sold. The seller of the house is
unreasonable and makes a provision that
the annuities be paid over a period of
forty years. That is to say, when the
purchase will be completed the housea working-class house is 90 years old.
Is there any reason in a man making an
agreement of that sort? He has this
justification, that he wants to obey the
Rent Restrictions Acts and he wants to
get a rent for the house in the name of
purchase annuities as long as his house is
habitable.
That is one reason why I think the
time ought to be limited. We found
some people are absolutely unscrupulous
when dealing with people who were in
great straits for houses. I do not say
that all owners are of that type, but
there are some, and people should be
protected in this time of scarcity. There
is one other point I wish to make. It is
sometimes said that if you extend the
time during which the payments are
made for the house the actual payments
become increasingly small. That is so
up to a point, but when you pass a
certain point there is practically no
difference in the amount of the weekly
annuities. Here are one or two facts
which I have taken-

think 30 years would be more reasonable.

Money Resolution which was the natural
precedent of this small measure was SO
very exhaustive, and I hope illuminating,

object of the Measure is to ensure the

Guarantee Act for another year, to 1933
-as a matter of fact to 31st March, 1933.
It is a one-clause Measure, and is to enable the Ministry of Finance, that is, the

the security is sufficient. I do not think
I need offer any further comments. I beg
to move the Second Reading of this Bill.

HOUSE OF COMMONS

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 28th April, 1932.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
PRIVATE BUSINESS.
Hall's Divorce Bill.
The following Report was made from
the Joint Committee on Divorce Bills:
That they had considered Hall's Divorce
Bill, and that the averments in the
Preamble had been proved to their satisfaction, and that they had gone through
the Bill and made an Amendment
thereto.
Oral Answers to Questions.
"CUTS" IN SALARIES OF P.E.
TEACHERS.
1. Mr. McALEER asked the Minister
of Finance whether he has seen the many
resolutions adopted by county and district meetings of the teachers in public
elementary schools in Northern Ireland
complaining of the "cut" in salaries
which took place last year, and whether
it is the intention of the Government to
give special consideration to the many
strong appeals made for the restoration
of the amount deducted from the salaries
of this very useful body of civil servants.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have seen a number of such
resolutions, but regret that in the present
state of public finance the Government
is unable to reconsider the question of
the reductions made in teachers' salaries
last year. I might add that the position.
of teachers is not by any means unique
and that many classes have suffered from
the prevailing economic depression to a
greater extent.
LAND ANNUITIES-SUGGESTED
REDUCTION.
2. Mr. McALEER asked the Minister
of Finance whether, in view of the widespread depression in the farming industry, and the many public meetings of
the Ulster Farmers' Union and other
agricultural organisations which voiced
the troubles of the farmers, the Government will see its way to recommend a
reduction in the annuities of fifty per
cent. and extend the period for payment,
or, as an alternative, not to press for
the payment of the May and June instalments until November, 1932.
Mr. POLLOCK: In reply to the hon.
Member, I regret to say that as the land
purchase annuities form a most important part of the revenue of the Province,
it would be impossible to accept the suggestions contained in the question.
DEFAULTING LAND TENANTS.
3. Mr. HEALY asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can give the total
number of tenants who were in default
with their rent annuities at December,
1931, as well as the number of decrees
granted for the year ending March, 1932.
Mr. POLLOCK: The information required is not available in the precise form
set out in the question, but the following information will probably satisfy the
requirements of the hon. Member.
The number of cases referred to the
local solicitors in respect of the November
and December, 1931, gale days was
3,783.
The amount of arrears outstanding on
31st March, 1932, was approximately
£15,000, out of a total sum collectible of
£918,000, representing 1.6 per cent.
Mr. HEALY: The right hon. Gentleman has not answered the last part of
my question about the number of decrees
during the year ended March, 1932.
Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: Is it not a
fact that the abnormal amounts outstanding on 31st March, 1931, that is
where two or more half-yearly instalments are overdue, was only £4,223, a
decrease of £500 on the previous year?
Mr. POLLOCK: That is correct, I
believe.

Mr. HEALY: Will the Minister of
Finance make some effort to procure the
information I require? It ought to be
very easily obtainable.

MAGISTERIAL SYSTEM.
4. Mr. McALEER asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether it is a fact that
the Northern Ireland Incorporated Law
Society made a recommendation to abolish
the magisterial system and appoint
magistrates or district judges of legal
standing and experience; and whether it
is the intention of the Government to
introduce legislation next year to bring
this recommendation into effect.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): No such recommendation has been received.
Mr. DEVLIN : Is the right hon.
Gentleman aware that a recommendation
was made at the Irish Convention,
approved by the Ulster representatives
unanimously and by representatives from
all Ireland, in favour of the abolition of
these justices of the peace, and, in view
of that fact, would it not be well to
abolish them altogether?
Sir DAWSON BATES:
I think my
hon. Friend is correct. I am not in a
position to say what the intentions of the
Government are.
Mr. DEVLIN: Now that we have got
a sort of partial sympathy for the declaration, may I ask the right hon.
Gentleman whether he will carefully
consider the idea of giving concrete
expression to the sympathy he has
expressed?
CALEDON A.O.H. BAND—
ST. PATRICK'S DAY PARADE.
5. Mr. McALEER asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he can state by
whose authority the sergeant in charge
at Caledon refused permission to the local
president of the Ancient Order of
Hibernians for the band to parade the
town on the morning of St. Patrick's
Day; why they have been prevented on
other occasions from parading the town
by the only route to the railway station;
and whether it is a fact that fifty per
cent. of the inhabitants are Catholics and
supporters of the band.
Sir DAWSON BATES: As it was
apprehended that the band parade in
question would give rise to a breach of
the peace, the responsible organisers were
warned by the police that the parade
could not be permitted to take place.
A dangerous riot was narrowly averted
on the 13th August, when a similar
parade took place.
I am informed that, except in this
instance, no such parades have been held
in Caledon for some fourteen years, and
no question of preventing them therefore
arose.
With regard to the latter part of the
question, I am informed that about onethird of the inhabitants of Caledon are
Roman Catholics, but I have no information as to the number of these who are
supporters of the band.

Mr. HEALY: What about Ballinderry?
AMENITIES OF COAST ROADS.
6. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state what is the position in relation to
preserving the amenities of the Antrim
and other coast roads under the Planning
and Housing Act, 1931.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Under the
Planning and Housing Act, 1931, the
county council of any county can formulate a scheme for planning the area under
its jurisdiction or any part of it for the
purpose of preserving amenities.
The
council may, at the request of a rural
district council, delegate their powers
under the Act to the rural district
council concerned.
No schemes have so far been submitted
to the Ministry. This is not surprising
having regard to the short time that the
Act has been in force. Such schemes
require a considerable amount of preliminary consideration and preparation, and,
in view of the financial stringency at
the present time, local authorities have
to be cautious in entering into fresh
liabilities.
Mr. DEVLIN: Did the right hon.
Gentleman not issue a circular from the
Home Office advising these local
authorities to put the Town Planning
Act into operation? The beauties of our
coast scenery have been absolutely desecrated by individuals being allowed to
build where they like until a whole
scheme of ugliness seems to destroy the
appearance of the real beauties of Northern Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: That may be
so, but my hon. Friend will appreciate
that even a local authority cannot take
away the rights of people without compensation.
BOROUGH AND URBAN PLANNING
SCHEMES.
7. Major MCCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the number and nature of schemes
submitted by borough and urban authorities under the Planning and Housing
Act, 1931.
Sir DAWSON BATES: No schemes
have as yet been submitted to the Ministry by borough or urban councils.
For reasons which I have already given
to the hon, and gallant Member, it could
hardly have been expected that any
schemes would have been ripe for submission at such an early date.

During the year the Ministry lost the
services, through retirement, of Mr. W.
H. Welply, the senior chief inspector of
schools. Mr. Welply was 36 years in the
public service as inspector of elementary
schools, during the last 15 of which he
held the posts, first of divisional inspector and then of chief inspector in
Belfast. In these posts he performed
most valuable work and his assistance and
genial presence are much missed in the
Ministry.
The second Vote for Educational
Services amounts to £1,892,860. The
Committee will observe, in the first
place, that the amount of this Vote is
practically the same as last year, there
being a slight increase of £249 in the
actual figures. At first sight it might
seem that no economies in education had
been effected, but it is to be remarked
that the main savings were made in last
year's Vote, which was less than the
amount in the Estimates of the preceding
year, 1930-31, by £51,412.
Last year
the 7 per cent. cut in teachers' salaries
produced a saving of £93,470, of which
£90,170 came from the teachers of the
public elementary schools. The savings
attributed to the cut in the present year
amount to £125,350, of which £108,000
is ascribed to elementary, £12,100 to
secondary, and £5,250 to technical schools
respectively. That is to say, the gross
amount which I should be asking the
Committee to vote to-day would be larger
by £125,000, had not the general reduction of 7 per cent. been made last
year.
The figures I have just given would
seem to show that the total saving this
year as compared with last is greater
in respect of teachers' salaries by £31,880.
As a matter of fact, however, the savings
under this head for elementary secondary
and technical education in 1932-33 are
only £15,700. Where, then, is the
difference in these two sums, amounting
to £16,180. It is accounted for by the
normal growth of this expenditure during the past year, principally under the
head of increments to teachers' salaries,
but partly on account of additional
teachers required by an increase in the
pupils' attendance and increased capitation grants due to the same cause.
The extent of our savings is further
disguised by the fact that this year
the amount estimated to be granted for
the building of new voluntary elementary
schools under the recent Act of 1930 is
£30,000, an increase of £20,000 over last
year's estimate. No portion of the
£10,000 voted last year was, however,
actually expended, and this sum is again
included in this year's Estimate.
Another item of expenditure which is
continuously growing in amount is the
cost of teachers' pensions. In 1930-31
£30,000 was spent on this, last year
£59,000 was the Estimate, and in the
present year we are asking for £63,000.
These sums are needed to supplement the

Each elementary school pupil in Northern
Ireland is estimated to cost £9 9s 6d a
year to educate.
When the present Ministry took over
from its predecessors in Dublin in 1922,
the average daily attendance of pupils in
our public elementary
elementary schools was,
approximately, 152,000; it is now close
upon 172,000, which means that there are
20,000 more pupils present in our schools
every day of the year. This increase is
due chiefly to the effect of the Education
Act in tightening up the regulations for
compulsory attendance an addition of
some 2,000 pupils was caused also by the
taking into connection of six schools
taught by the Roman Catholic community
of the Christian Brothers.
The addition of 20,000 pupils to the
daily attendance might have been expected to require about 640 new teachers
to cope with the larger numbers, but
thanks to the policy of amalgamation of
small schools steadily followed by the
Ministry, the teaching strength has
actually been increased by only 258.
This policy was greatly assisted by the
efforts of our local education authorities
in building new central schools, without
which the amalgamation of schools on
any considerable scale would have been
impracticable in a large number of cases.
Besides the amalgamation of boys,
girls' and infants' schools under the same
roof, which was extensively effected by
the Ministry, the most useful form of
amalgamation is the combination of two
or more schools in the same urban centre,
and this has been carried out in many of
the towns as well as in Belfast, and the
In such cases
process is still going on.
The corresponding
average rate in England and Wales was
last year £13 2s 6d.
In considering the cost of education it
is interesting to note that, notwithstanding the very considerable improvements
made in our educational system and the
great extension of educational facilities
provided by our local education authorities, the Estimates now presented to
Parliament do not differ much in amount
from those put forward eight or nine
years ago. To-day we are spending from
Parliamentary funds nearly £1,960,000;
in 1923-24 our Estimates under the two
Votes were £1,914,000, and in the following year (1924-25) £1,971,000, actually
£11,000 more than to-day. It is true
that the salaries of our elementary
teachers have been twice reduced in the
interval, but let us glance for a moment
at some figures of the substantial progress that has been made.
the need for new premises is imperative,
as usually none of the existing houses is
large enough for the combined attendance
of all the schools involved in the amalgamation, and in any case most of such
existing buildings are crowded and unsuitable and far below modern standards
of school architecture.
Up to the present date 55 new schools
have been built and opened for use by
the Education Committees. Eleven of
these schools, with accommodation for
over 10,000 children, have been erected
in Belfast, and 44 are situated in the
rest of the area of Northern Ireland. In
the nine years, between 1922 and 1931,
the number
separate elementary
schools in Northern Ireland has decreased
by 199, from 2,066 to 1,867, that is to say,
about 260 old schools have been struck off
the roll, and some 60 new schools, allowing
for some under voluntary management,
have come into operation.
Ministry of Education
Estimates--

HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Robb]
Most of the schools struck off the roll
are small schools with only one or at most
two teachers, schools which are, of course,
extremely costly to maintain relatively to
the numbers of pupils in attendance. The
number of schools of this type has
diminished since 1922 by 188. There has,
on the other hand, been a welcome increase of 62 in schools sufficiently large
to maintain a staff of four or more
teachers.
While I am referring to this matter,
I might remind the Committee of the
great saving in cost of staffing the schools
which is secured by the policy of eliminating small schools in favour of large ones.
It will be realised that as two schools of
50 pupils each are entitled to employ
four fully qualified teachers, and as a
single school of 100 pupils needs only
three teachers, the building of a new
school which enables an amalgamation of
this kind to be carried out results in the
saving of a teacher's salary, at an
average cost of £317 for a man teacher
and £238 for a woman teacher. This
saving is not always realised immediately
on amalgamation as the existing teachers
are usually retained as privileged assistants in the amalgamated school, but on
the retirement or resignation of a member
of the staff normal conditions are restored and a saving is effected. As a
rule, redundant members of the staff tend
soon to disappear.
While the effect of amalgamation in
producing economy is greatest in the
smaller schools, substantial savings are
secured in nearly all cases, and it is for
this reason that in the Ministry's opinion
the expense of new buildings, which some
people consider an extravagance in these
days of financial stringency, is really recovered through the saving in salaries,
and, in the long run, proves a really
economical measure. And the advantages
secured in this way to the pupils' health
and educational efficiency are so selfevident that, even were there no saving,
the work would be worth doing for its
own sake. A careful line is drawn by
the Ministry in these matters between
what is essential and what can be done
without, and the pros and cons in each
case are very carefully weighed.
I have already referred to the fact that
£30,000 appears in our Estimates this
year for building grants to voluntary
school managers under the provisions of
Section 10 of the Amending Education
Act of 1930. £10,000 of this money is
a revote from last year, as no portion of
the grant was actually expended last
year. Grants amounting to £39,000 on
an expenditure of double that amount
have been approved by the Ministry, but
in no case were the works sufficiently
advanced before the end of last March
to enable any part of the Ministry's
moiety to be disbursed. Under the
statutory regulations for disbursement of
the grant the Ministry is not called upon
for a contribution until one-fifth of the
amount to be raised by the manager has
been expended. Owing to the amount of
time absorbed in preliminaries, such as
inspection and the vesting of the site in
trustees, the preparation and examination
of plans, advertising for tenders, and
other details, which are tedious and
necessarily take up a considerable time,
actual building operations were not
far advanced when the last financial
year terminated. It is likely that considerably accelerated progress will now
be made, and it is expected that the
present Estimate of £30,000 will be fully
required in the present year. Two large
schools, the grants for which amount to
£18,500, are in active process of erection; in three other cases, involving
grants totalling £20,500, contracts are
being placed, and, in addition, further
schemes involving grants amounting to
£8,000 are under consideration. Many
other applications have been received in
the last few months, the examination of
which is proceeding. In view of the fact
that the building of voluntary schools
had practically ceased in recent the
years
Ministry considers the expenditure on

May I be allowed to develop this point?
It might be supposed that the Ministry
has sufficient data in its possession over
a long term of years to enable it
accurately to estimate the number of new
teachers required every year. But on
examination of the figures of teachers
leaving the service it is found that these
figures vary considerably from year to
year, and are subject to substantial
fluctuations which are not always easy to
explain and are generally very hard to
foresee. Deaths and retirements on pension are accountable for about half the
teachers leaving the service; the number
of deaths is small, from 10 to 15 a year,
but the retirements have been affected by
changes and reductions in the salary
scales, which have been not infrequent in
the last dozen years and which influence
materially the rates of pension. The
increasing of salaries to such a substantial
extent just after the war caused many
teachers to retire prematurely before
serving the full term of years; recent reductions in the scales have had a somewhat
similar effect on teachers wishing to be
pensioned before the lower rates of salary
took effect. These factors have made a just
estimate of the demand for teachers that
might exist three years ahead rather
difficult, but the problem is rendered still
more difficult through uncertainty in the
number of resignations on marriage of
young women teachers, and also through
the fact that many teachers who resign
their positions return later to the service
and form portion of the still available
supply. Then, even supposing that
officers of the Ministry can form, in spite
of these uncertain factors, a fairly
reliable estimate of the number of
teachers leaving the service annually, the
problem of the requirements of the
schools is further complicated by the fact
that school attendance is improving in
most places, which, of course, requires
more teachers, and, on the other hand,
that beneficent process of amalgamation
of schools to which I have already referred diminishes the need for teachers,

an
We now proceed to consider the
general question of a standard programme for all schools. A point which
has been raised in evidence in relation
to the inspection system is that through
fear of a lowering in rating a teacher
is loth to depart from the rigid lines
of the programme and follow his own
initiative and that, as a result, his
individuality is stifled to the detriment
of his pupils and of their general proficiency. If this is true to any considerable extent it is a very serious
matter. The real value gained from
education depends largely on the personality of the teacher, and while a
public system cannot be left entirely
to individual inclinations, the importance of freedom within limits is well
recognised. Indeed, there is even
opened up the whole question whether
the continuance of
official programme is advisable. In England the
Board of Education, as the central
authority, prescribes no standard
syllabus and only publishes a general
handbook of suggestions for the guidance of teachers; the head teachers
are permitted to frame their own programme in accordance with generally
understood principles. We are not
certain, however, that this is found to
be an entirely satisfactory solution,
and in any case it does not follow that
it would be the right course to pursue in the comparatively small area of
Northern Ireland with its centralised
system, so far as the oversight of the
curriculum is concerned. We recommend that a standard programme
should remain, but
that every
couragement should be given to principals of schools to submit for approval
such modifications as they may conensider desirable, either in the direction
of omitting subjects or by curtailing
the extent of the present courses, having regard to local conditions and
their own considered opinions. This
course is already open to them and they
are invited to adopt it, but we understand that, for various reasons, very
few avail themselves of the invitation.
If it is through fear of what might
happen to their rating, we trust that
such fears can and will be removed.
We suggest that inspectors should encourage the more progressive principals
to lead the way in this respect. We
would even go further and recommend
that the inspector should be directed
to confer with principal teachers as to
the best programme for their schools,
and that they should assist those who
may be more nervous or unambitious
to study their own local conditions
and environment and to frame such
modifications in the curriculum as are
suitable. If this is carefully supervised, we have no fear that the trust
will be abused.
The recommendations of that paragraph
have the full concurrence of the Ministry,
and we hope a number of teachers will be
encouraged to consider seriously and
intelligently the requirements of their
particular school, and that we shall not
hear any more complaints that the freedom of the teacher to try out original
ideas of his own is unduly curtailed,
though, of course, he must convince his
inspector and the Ministry that what he
proposes has in it the seeds of progress,
and is not merely the peculiar plan of an
educational crank. I have not gone into
any of the details of the Estimates, but
I shall be happy to answer any questions
that hon. Members may wish to put on
the details. I beg to move.

Minister's pronouncement. The words
which I quote are these, and I may say
to the Members of this Committee that
I entirely agree with the words which I
am just about to quote:-
The demand of the clergy, shortly,
is this, that although Stranmillis
Training College is owned and maintained by the general body of taxpayers, nevertheless clergymen, merely
as clergymen, should be represented on
that committee, though they would
neither be appointed by the public,
nor answerable to the public, nor removable by the public.
There can be no doubt that this involves a question of principle, and to
such an extent did it involve a question
of principle that the entire committee of
nine, the
the committee who had been
appointed by the Minister of Education,
and who were responsible to this House
for the conduct of an institution built by
public funds and maintained by public
funds-that committee, rather than
agree to the terms sought to be imposed
upon them by the United Committee of
Protestant Churches, resigned. And the
House will remember that the chairman
of that committee was a Member of the
Cabinet of Northern Ireland.
So I say there can be no doubt that
a question of principle which operated on
the minds of the Government and the
mind of the Prime Minister in September
of last year has been changed, has been
overthrown, and a new principle substituted in its place, and no reason whatsoever given. I do not wish it to be
thought that in any way I am attacking
the clergymen of Northern Ireland. I
am not. I raise this question in this
House in this way because I am concerned not merely with the interests of
education, but also with the religious
future of Northern Ireland. And I
cannot conceive that it is in the interests of Northern Ireland that clergymen, merely as clergymen, should be
appointed upon such a committee. They
are not appointed by this House. They
are not appointed by the Minister of
Education. They are appointed by
three, and by three only. And I say it
is an extraordinary thing that three
members of the one profession, or of a
sacred calling, should be entitled to go
upon a committee which looks entirely
after the material and secular interests
of the students and teachers in Stranmillis College.
Before the clergy were appointed, the
Minister had, I think, very properly
given every facility to the clergymen to
see that religious education was being
imparted in that institution. Clergymen
of the different denominations were
allowed to go to that institution daily,
or so many hours a week, to impart
religious instruction at the appropriate
hours. They were paid for their services,
and I have no doubt they performed
those services admirably and with perfect
sincerity.
But what is the position to-day? Not
merely do the clergy look after the
spiritual interests of the students of
Stranmillis College, but they claim to be
entitled to operate as ordinary Members
of a committee simply because they are
clergymen. Now that they are on the
committee, they would have the power
to appoint teachers to that institution.
They would have the power to dismiss
teachers. They will have all the powers
proper to a management committee, and
I have looked in vain in the records of
Great Britain and Ireland in connection
with Protestant education for a similar
precedent and I cannot find any.
I have in my hands a Government
pamphlet issued by the Department of
Education in Scotland, and it is very interesting to note that in connection with
Scottish primary education, the national
committee which looks after the training of
teachers is composed entirely of members
from the different education authorities
throughout the length and breadth of
Scotland. It does not include in its
membership a single member of the
clerical profession acting as such. Nor is
there on the central executive committee

I think that this is a very important

misgiving in the minds, not merely lay
minds, but the religious instincts of the
Protestant Ulster people in Northern
Ireland. As I said before, I trust that a

that he will explain to this House how it

principle in September, in October, in
November, ceases to be a question of
principle six months later.
I do not know whether I should be
justified in prolonging discussion along

account for this sudden change of front.
I have heard it said, though I do not

going back on a question of principle he

credit such a policy. I should like to
give the noble Lord, the Prime Minister,
credit for being a statesman, but I
of
cannot conceive
a statesman who
changes a question of principle from day

that we are going to upset and bankrupt

Education surely must be the very best

We cannot afford to go on increasing expenditure year after year on particular
services while the nation's revenue is

It is generally thought in this House,
or, at least, that is how I have gauged
the feeling of Members, that as long as
money is spent recklessly education is
being improved. That is not always so.
The most expensive house is not always
the best to live in. The most expensive
stock bull does not always rear the best
calves. The most highly dowered wife
may not be the most suitable. There are
many people who think if you spend
money you get the best results. I have
noticed in this House a feeling that as
long as we are throwing money in all
directions we are doing the right thing,
even if we are bringing the country to
the verge of bankruptcy. Again, this
education is having a tendency, I think,
to lead people into professions to which
they are not suited, into professions
which, in spite of the Parliamentary
Secretary's assurance, are overstaffed and
will continue to be overstaffed. We are
inclined, through this system of education, to attempt to get them away from
the paths they should follow. We can
see the day, and it is not very far distant, when the ploughman may be a good
deal more useful than the professor,
because we must have the ploughing of
land and the hewing of wood and the
drawing of water for all time. We
should let our expenditure on education
be reasonable, efficient, and suitable to
what we can afford, otherwise it is only
a question of a few years before this
country goes down in general bankruptcy.
Now, I cannot help referring to the
Estimate in detail. True, the Estimate
for this year is actually down by the
immense sum of £249 out of £2,000,000,
compared with last year, but the Committee should remember that that reduction is due entirely to the cuts in
wages and reductions in salaries. Obviously, therefore, the Estimates otherwise must have very considerably increased compared with last year.
Yesterday the London County Council
were considering their Estimates for the
coming year, and it is not uninteresting
to notice the reductions they made.
They have made a reduction in their
Estimates for the coming year of
£1,500,000 out of a total of £10,000,000,
a very big proportion, and only half of
this reduction is due to the 10 per cent.
cut in teachers' salaries. These salaries
actually represent two-thirds of the total
expenditure, so we can see that the
London County Council have certainly
shown that efficiency and economy, even
without reducing salaries, can still go
hand in hand. When I remind you that

the whole of the children of England and

Here are we, unfortunately, with what
is practically an increase in our Estimates. The Parliamentary Secretary did
refer to the fact that we spent considerably less per head on education. The
only answer I have to that is that the
income per head of the population in this
country is two-and-a-half times smaller
than the income of the people in England.

only a part-time officer-I am not questioning whether he is paid too much or

They seem to me to be doubling up in

The fees I have quoted represent in

If this sort of thing is going to continue

from income-tax and death duties will, it
is computed, fall by between 25 per cent.

a number of lean years in front of us,
that this fall will not continue.
If we do not face up to realities
as they are and as they are going
to be in the future, we shall find
our expenditure on education up; we
shall find our whole educational
edifice crumbling to the ground, and,
what is much worse and more important,
we shall find that these highly educated
children will have their future mortgaged,
and will be brought up in a bankrupt
inheritance to live on the dole.

Rev. Professor CORKEY: I would
like, first of all, to congratulate the Parliamentary Secretary on the interesting
statement he has given us. I always
enjoy the statements made by the Parliamentary Secretary on this subject. They
are always lucid, and they are always
concise and informative. To begin, I
would like to say that all legislation is
Every law 19 an exexperimental.
periment and has to be tried out in actual
experience. The politician or the statesman legislates not blindly, but in the
light of all the facts which are at his
command, and he may find that in spite
of all his wisdom the law which he designed was not at first perfect. Even
the 1920 Act, the Act by which we
operate here, was found not to be perfect and has been modified once or twice
to bring it into conformity with the circumstances which have developed since
1920.
The chief critics of the educational
policy of the Northern Government seem
to forget that, and they seem to imagine
that in regard to education the Government should have been able to establish
a Utopia which would have been perfect
from the first and which would not have
demanded the slightest modification from
then until now. But that is not how
laws are framed. That is not how satisfactory educational systems are developed. I have great confidence and
belief in the educational system which
has been developed during the last ten
or twelve years in Northern Ireland. I
think it suits Northern Ireland, and is
about as wise a system as any man could
devise for the education of the people
here. It has been modified from time
to time, but it has been modified in the
light of facts which have emerged in the
actual working of the system, and it
seems to me, therefore, that there is very

Coming nearer to the point, may I ask

injure the cause of education in the community It has not been explained to
us how they are going to act as grit in

these men ought to know something about
education. They are educated
themselves. Not only that, but these are

the last hundred years. They may not
be perfect, but I venture to say the
average minister of religion, be he Protestant or Roman Catholic, knows a great
deal more about education than ninetynine out of every hundred men in his
parish. It would seem to me a very remarkable thing that these men should be
ostracised in regard to education, and
that they should be allowed to take no
part in the training of the children of the

I want to point out that there were
weighty circumstances to be considered in
this matter. First of all, my hon. and
learned Friend has not pointed out that
possibly more than half the Protestant
schools in Northern Ireland are
provided schools, schools that are actually
managed by clergymen. They have not
been transferred. Possibly, in some cases,
they cannot very well be transferred. It
does not seem to me very unreasonable on
that account that the institution in which
the teachers are trained for work in those
schools should have some representatives
of this great body of managers on its
committee of control. That is a matter
the effect of which I think ought to be
taken into account.
In addition to that, when the Government decided that the system of education
in Ulster should not be for Protestants a
secular system-when they came to that
decision, which they did very soon, there
was no point or reason in making the
training college an exception to the rule.
No great harm was done, I understand,
by the appointing of a number of representatives of the transferrors on the regional committees, which was done by the
Act passed in 1929. They are the most
useful men, I am told, on the committees
at the present time, and their advice is
sought on difficult matters in spite of the
protests that were made by men who at
that time, and prior to it, had secularistic
ideas in regard to education. It seems
to me the same will prove to be the case
in regard to this particular institution.
The complaint has been made that this
is a public institution. If that is so, is
the same not true of the regional committees and of all the institutions which
they govern, and is that not so also of
many of the particular and individual
primary elementary schools scattered up
and down the country? Many have
been built by public money, but the Government have made provision for the appointment on the local management committees of representatives of the churches.
When the Government has gone so far it
would have seemed somewhat illogical; it
would have seemed to me more like a
disregard of the principle to have kept
Stranmillis College estranged from the
whole system, and to have attempted to
maintain a secularised institution at the
very heart of what was not to be a purely
secular system of education.
May I say with regard to this particular
matter one further sentence? It is very
difficult to maintain
a purely secular
system of elementary education, and I
must say that in later years I have come
more and more to sympathise with the
position in this matter adopted by my
Roman Catholic fellow-countrymen for
the reason that a purely secular system is
very likely to become not merely secular
but anti-religious and positively dan-

leader in this matter a man of the type of

We are distinctly denominationalists. We

term the mellow atmosphere of the Committee, in which the hon. Member for
Central Belfast (Mr. Devlin) in his most
persuasive way has been endeavouring to
obtain some concessions from the Minister
of Finance. I was rather pleased to find
the Committee in that agreeable frame
of mind in which they would be able to
come to agreement on something. I desire
to add my tribute to the Parliamentary
Secretary (Mr. Robb) for the manner in
which he brought forward the Estimates
in this Committee, and for the clear explanation he has given of many points.
Whilst a certain duty devolves on one to
support this Estimate, the enormous
amount which we are spending upon
educational services at the present time,
especially in these days of hard economic
facts which stare us in the face daily and
even hourly, makes us pause to consider

if the results are in consonance with the
expenditure. I am not picking out the
Education Estimates only in this respect.
The Prime Minister has just said that
instead of being small and parsimonious
in the Education Estimates he would
rather be at fault in going too far. I
say that there is a mean between the two
extremes. I do feel that we have gone
from one extreme to the other; we have
not attempted to follow the middle line.
As far as elementary education is concerned to-day, I for my part cannot see
that there is such a great improvement
as would warrant the enormous increase
in the Estimates. I am generally in
agreement with the hon. and gallant
Member for South Derry
(Captain
Chichester-Clark) in what he has said
regarding this expenditure. If we allow
the means by which we are to attain the
result to get so far ahead of us, we are
very liable to ruin ourselves and those
children and young people generally
whom we desire to help. After all, the
great result aimed at in education is that
the youth of our country should turn out
useful citizens, useful to themselves and
useful to their country.
On the subject of economy and
efficiency, from time to time I have compared the various Departments of our
Government. Take, for instance, the
Ministry of Agriculture, where a sum of
less than £200,000 to be accurate,
£181,000-is involved. I have indeed felt
that economy there was misplaced. The
Ministry of Education require a sum of
almost two millions, which I say is largely
for the future. I am not against it, I
am not against the future well-being of
our youth, but there is, I fear, the risk
that if we do not conserve our resources
there may be no work in the future for
our people. Architects' fees form a glaring instance. I feel that the amount involved there is deplorable. If all the
items of expense are in keeping with
those, I say that a halt should be called
not only in this Department but in all
Departments of the Government.
Professor JOHNSTONE: Before you
put the Motion to the Committee I
should like to say a few words. I should
like to congratulate the Parliamentary
Secretary of the Ministry of Education,
my Colleague in the representation of the
University, on the admirable and delightful way in which he has put the Estimates before us. There are one or two
points in connection with this Estimate
that I should like to say something
about. One of these is in reference to
the statement he made in regard to the
curriculum which, I believe, is now
practically finished, and which is likely
to be laid down in the future. I have
long felt that one of the greatest risks at
present in education-and I am not
speaking now purely and simply of Northern Ireland, but of education everywhere especially primary education-is
the fact that there is a tendency to make
it too much hidebound.
There is a tendency to lay down a
specific course, and to make every teacher,
no matter what his capabilities may be,
no matter what his predilections may be,
stick to that particular course, and,
finally, to have his pupils inspected on
the results so far as that particular
course is concerned.
Nothing in the
whole speech of the hon. and learned
Gentleman (Mr. Robb) pleased me more
than the statement that in future
teachers are going to be encouraged to
use their own individuality and to strike
out more or less on original lines of their
own. I think that nearly everyone concerned with education realises that the
great risk in all education is the fact
that it has a tendency to stifle that individuality and to make us all more or
less conform to the same type. Anything which would militate against a
tendency of that kind is something which
I think ought to be encouraged.
There is another point in connection
with the curriculum on which I wish to
say a few words, the question of the inspectors. I usually read the reports of
the meetings of the various national
school teachers' associations, and it is
very seldom they do not contain an outcry against the present system of inspection. I am sure that the Ministry
have devoted considerable thought to the
question of inspection, and I hope that
they will be able to bring about such
changes in the system of inspection as
will ensure that instead of the national
school teachers looking upon the inspectors as their natural enemies, they will
come to regard the inspectors as their
friends and advisers. I think that is
really the attitude which the inspectors
ought to have towards the teachers. The
inspector ought to be there to advise the
teacher, to act as a sort of liaison officer,
to let him know what is being done in

seems to me to be the last shadow of the

education, I think, is one of the most

mean general adult education. Everyone

Mr. HEALY: At this late hour of the
evening I do not think there are more
than one or two matters I want to raise.
I have often heard that the Prime
Minister is a master of political subtlety,
and certainly we have never had a better
example of it than this evening. The
hon. Member for the University (Mr.
McNeill) read out an extract from a
speech the Prime Minister made some time
ago in which he laid down a definite policy,
and nothing could be clearer to my mind
than that that policy has been absolutely
departed from, and yet the Prime Minister stands up here and tells us he stands
to-day where he stood then. Well, if the
Members of the House of Commons
believe that, then I think the Prime
Minister must be a magician.
But the matter that concerns us is very
vital. In 1923 when you set up the Committee, out of which your Education
Acts have grown, the policy then was
definitely a secular one. The hon. Member for the University, who has just sat
down (Professor Johnston), described it
as a mixed system of education. I think
there can be no doubt that what was in
the mind of the Committee and the mind
of this House was, that you wanted a
definitely secular system in the Six
Counties. We protested against it, and
I was very pleased to note as time went
on that the various Protestant churches
likewise protested. To-day the secular
system is gone, but the penalties you imposed on Catholic schools in consequence
of the adoption of this secular system will
remain. That is the bitter injustice of
the whole proceeding, and it is one to
which neither the Prime Minister nor any
Member of the Government has so far
directed himself.
What is the position? We, as ordinary
taxpayers, contribute to the erection of
the schools under the regional committees
and at the same time we must erect our
own schools. The system has broken down.

There can be no question of that. Out
of practically 2,000 schools in Northern
Ireland less than 500 have been transferred, and probably you have reached
the point now when the transfer of
schools is about to cease. The clergy who
desired to transfer their schools have
made up
their minds on one side or other
before now. Therefore, I take it that
the slowing down, as I think it is described in the report of the Ministry of
Education, has come to a definite point.
Therefore, there is all the more reason,
I think, for the Minister of Education
and the Cabinet to reconsider the injustices that they have imposed upon the
Catholic body, because we are the people
more interested in religious education
than any other religious denomination in
the Six Counties. We built our schools
at a time when the proud Presbyterian
body were refusing to fulfil their obligations in that respect. Anybody who
reads the report of Mr. McNeill, chief
inspector of schools in Belfast, in 1911
will see there disclosed the lamentable
apathy of the Presbyterian body in regard to schools, and he gives the explanation. The Presbyterian Church system
was different from the Episcopal or the
Catholic. They neglected their opportunities at that time, and now when they
have probably provided themselves at the
public expense with all the schools they
need are we going to be denied equal
facilities?
I
The hon. Member for Derry was advocating a policy of retrenchment.
was just wondering how many schools
have been erected at the public expense
in his constituency, how many in County
Down, and how many in County Antrim.
Now that the richer people, who ought
to have a greater interest in education,
have provided themselves with all the
schools necessary is it to be said that you
are going to call a halt, and that there
will be no further money for the building
of Catholic schools, particularly in rural
places where the people are poorer and
are not in the same position to provide
themselves with educational facilities that
you ought to have provided. In this
matter we do not speak for any insignificant minority of the people. We
represent the largest body of schoolgoing children in the Six Counties. We
are the majority. We have 72,000 children on the school rolls. We have more
children on the school rolls than the
Church of Ireland, the Methodist, and
other bodies, excluding the Presbyterians.
And yet we are treated as you would not
dare to treat any of the other bodies.
I know the Prime Minister probably
will say, "We made an education system
and you do not conform to it." Well,
if we had conformed to that system the
Treasury of Northern Ireland would today be several thousands of pounds
poorer than it is, as the Minister of
Finance will admit. We did not conform, because we cannot conscientiously
conform, and that is the point the
Protestant churches have now taken up.
Therefore, I say, in justice we ought not
to be penalised, as we are penalised in
the building of our schools, and the
cleaning, heating, lighting, and equipment of our schools.
The other day in Enniskillen there was
erected a beautiful intermediate school.
It cost the religious body which put it
In the same locality
up some £14,000.
there are two other schools built at the
public expense, not one penny of which
have any of the churches subscribed. I
I think that is such a disgraceful transaction, and it shows such favouritism. It
is a violation of the 1920 Act, which says
no penalty should be attached to such
matters. The Prime Minister is driving
a coach and four through the 1920 Act.
He is driving a coach and four through
all ideas of equity. Now that he has
been obliged to recede from the position
he took up in 1923, I really would ask
him in the spirit of justice and in the
spirit of fair play to reconsider this whole
matter-now that he has surrendered the
original principle for which he stood,
namely, secular education.
Mr. ROBB: I want to reply to one
or two things that have been said. With
regard to what my hon. Friend and
colleague (Professor Johnstone), who
sits on my right, says about the
teaching of adults, I might remind
him and the Committee that in the 1930
Act there is a section which empowers
education authorities to help in any way
they see fit, and approved by the Ministry, classes for adults. The Ministry is
quite prepared to consider any scheme put
forward for the development and exercise
of the powers of the education authorities under that section, but the initiative
must come from the authorities themselves. It does not lie with the Ministry
to initiate these things, and I may say it
is with some regret that the Ministry has
seen the evening schools formerly carried
Estimates-
Ministry of Education

[Mr. Robb]
on by many national school teachers
growing fewer and fewer as time goes on.
We do not know whether it is the
attraction of other and more popular
things in the evenings that has led to less
concentration or less willingness on the
part of the pupils to attend these evening
schools, but the fact remains that the
Ministry does make grants to evening
schools. That the amount of the grants
is diminishing the Minister regrets.
With regard to what the Member for
Derry said, touching the general expenditure, might I point out to him that
out of the total amount expended,
£1,900,000, almost £1,663,000 goes in
payments to teachers, and I think he
would be a bold man who at the present
moment would suggest that now another
cut should be made in the emoluments of
teachers. That seems to be the only
direction in which possibly the Education
Estimates can be reduced in any way
worth doing.
As to the fees that were paid to the
architect in County Down, may I say that,
so far as the Ministry is concerned, no part
of that expenditure comes upon this Vote,
and our Vote has not been increased,
even if County Down has been extravagant in the payment of fees to the
architect, because for some time we have
been paying County Down the limit of
the eightpenny rate. But I might point
out to the hon. Member and to the Committee that these fees did not cover
simply and solely the personal remuneration of the architect. These fees covered
the amounts he had to pay for draughtsmen and others whom he has had to
employ. The whole of that money does
not go into his own pocket, and it is
rather an accident that in this particular area these fees amount to such a
large sum.
Captain CHICHESTER-CLARK: I
just want to say, I tried to make it
perfectly clear, that I only cited this as
an instance. I had no intention of
criticising the architect of County Down.
That would be completely outside my
business. I have no reason to suppose
that he has not earned his fees.
I was
only citing the fees as increasing in
geometrical progression in the last three
years, doubled, doubled, and doubled. If
we go on doubling and doubling while the
income of the country is going down and
down, I am not very far wrong in assuming that bankruptcy would be the result.
Mr. ROBB: I see the hon. Member's
point, but the answer is very simple.
This is non-recurring expenditure. It is
not going to happen this year. County
Down is building under a scheme. It
took some time to frame a scheme and
did not do, what many regional committees did, start here and there piecemeal. It took its own time and made a
programme of building. It started that
programme of building about three years
ago, and it has reached its peak at the
present time. The expenditure of £60,000
referred to by the hon. and gallant
Member was made last year, and the
large fees of the architect were earned
last year, but that expenditure is being
repaid over a series of 35 years by means
of a loan from the Government. Further,
it is non-recurring expenditure. We are
not going next year to erect another
school at Newtownards costing £15,000,
and another one costing £30,000 or
£40,000 at Bangor. Those schools that
have recently been built in those towns
are going to last for a hundred or two
hundred years. Their cost will be spread
over whatever period the loan was granted
for.
I think the hon. and gallant Member
is looking at this question from a wrong
point of view. I would like to ask him
if he has gone about the country and
examined the hovels in which the children
were taught. Does he not think that
almost any expenditure and any sacri
fice would be worth while if it improved
those wretched hovels? The new schools
that have been erected and those that
have been renovated ensure that for the
next two generations at any rate our
children will be educated in well designed, sunny, and well ventilated
buildings, and in cheery, healthy, and
stimulating surroundings, instead of in
the wretched hovels that were formerly
such a great blot on our educational
system in the North of Ireland.
When I first took up the position
which I now have the honour to hold
I was, of course, interested in education
generally, but I did not know much
about the buildings in which our children
were being educated, except a few in
Belfast. I have taken it as part of my
duties to investigate, as far as the oppor
tunities presented themselves, the state
not only of the curriculum, but especially
of the school buildings. I started with
a sort of luke-warm enthusiasm for the
provision of better buildings, and if

bes
to a

there is one thing that will give me more
satisfaction than anything else when I
come to vacate my present office it will
be that during my connection with the
Ministry the buildings in which our
children are being educated have been
revolutionised. They are being revolutionised, and no better work could any
man put his hand to.
Both the Member for Central (Mr.
Devlin) and the Member for South Fermanagh (Mr. Healy) have said that in
their view the system of education that
was inaugurated by the 1923 Act has
failed. In the most emphatic manner I
challenge any such statement. The Act
was passed in 1923, and it came into
operation only in 1925. That is seven
years ago. We have had only seven years
in which to set up local education authorities and get them started on their work.
Already in those seven years one-third of
the total pupils in elementary schools in
Northern Ireland are working in schools,
either provided or transferred, controlled by the Education Committees. I
think that is a very good result for the
time we have been at work. We hope
that this result, which we regard only as
a beginning, will mean the dawn of a
new era not only for the pupils I have
referred to but for all the pupils in
Northern Ireland.

Oral Answers to Questions.
GLENONE SCHOOL, COUNTY
DERRY.
1. Mr. LEEKE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he is aware that the
Manager of Glenone School, County
Derry, has reconstructed the building in
accordance with the Education Act and
has been refused the grant; and whether
he will see his way to reconsider the
matter and allow the amount to which a
manager is entitled.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): One of the
conditions of a grant under Section 10 of
the Education Act (Northern Ireland),
1930, is that the school shall be vested
in trustees, appointed with the approval
of the Ministry, for the purpose of maintaining and carrying on the school.
The manager of Glenone Public Elementary School has carried out certain
much-needed works of repairs and reconstruction but, notwithstanding these
works, the Ministry is advised that the
school building is defective in most essential points and not suitable for vesting
as required by Section 10 of the Act referred to.
In the circumstances, the Ministry has
been obliged to refuse a grant and I am
unable to reverse this decision.
Mr. LEEKE: I should like to ask is it
not a fact that the inspectors approved
of these alterations and were highly
pleased with them. In view of that fact
I think he should revise his decision.
Mr. ROBB: As I said, the manager
has executed certain much-needed works
and repairs, but the technical advisers of
the Ministry report that the building,
even with these works and repairs, is
not suitable to be taken over by trustees
and vested.
Mr. LEEKE: I will raise this matter
again.

GATE LODGE KEEPERS AT
STORMONT.
2. Mr. NIXON asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the names
of the lodge keepers recently appointed to
the gate lodges at the two entrance gates
to Stormont Buildings, and what remuneration is attached to these posts.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): One of the lodges is occupied
temporarily by the head messenger
attached to the Cabinet Offices, whose
rate of remuneration is in accordance with
the general scale seen on page 1 of the
current Estimates. The second lodge is
vacant, but it is the intention to make
it available for the recently-appointed
park keeper of Stormont Estate.
Mr. NIXON: Have you the name of
the messenger?
Mr. POLLOCK: Dalgliesh.

THE SHOOTING AT
BALLINDERRY.
4. Mr. LEEKE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is aware that
a statement has been made and duly witnessed by Mr. Henry O'Neill, President
of the Ballinderry Ancient Order of
Hibernians, denying having told the
local police that the band would leave at
9-30 a.m., but clearly indicated to the
constabulary authorities that they would
leave at 8-30 a.m., and that if the
authorities had requested them to travel
by an alternative route they would have
done so.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have seen a
statement, signed by Mr. O'Neill, which
is substantially to the effect as indicated
in the hon. Member's question. It is
not, however, borne out by the statements
of other parties, and I am not prepared
to accept it as accurate.
Mr. LEEKE: Does that mean the
Minister suggests that this man is making
a false declaration ? He must either
accept it or not.
Mr. HEALY: Does the Minister
always accept the statement of a person
who is involved rather than that of a
disinteresting person?
Sir DAWSON BATES: What I was
particularly thinking of were the statements made by individuals who see eye
to eye with my hon. Friend.
Mr. LEEKE: This statement was duly
witnessed by a magistrate. You must be
suggesting he was swearing a lie.
AIRCRAFT REPAIRS IN
NORTHERN IRELAND.
5. Major McCORMICK asked the

Sir DAWSON BATES: In presenting
to the Committee the Estimates of the
Ministry of Home Affairs, I am glad to
be in a position to refer to the fact that
we have been able to effect substantial
reductions in the various services for
which the Ministry is responsible, the
total of the reductions being £21,146. It
is a fact, of course, that on the contrary
we have an increase of £22,658 in connection with our grants to local authorities, the net result being that while we
are increasing our grants to local authorities, we have reduced the cost of our own
administration by substantial amounts.
As regards the Estimate for the Department of the Ministry of Home Affairs,
it will be observed that the decrease is
£940, which is due to the fact that we
have been able to effect a substantial reduction in the number of our staff. It
will be observed on page 52 that, for the
current financial year, the total number
of staff attached to the Ministry is 140,
as against 150 for the year 1931-32, but
it should be explained that this gross
reduction of 10 includes 3 officials who
were formerly attached to the Ministry
when it was located at Ocean Buildings
but who are now transferred to the
general pool, the result being that we
have a net reduction of 7 officials.
The fact that it has been possible to
effect this substantial reduction in
numbers and consequent expenditure, in
Ministry of Home Affairs 1124

HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Sir Dawson Bates]
spite of the increasing responsibilities
and duties imposed upon the Ministry by
new legislation, will, I feel sure, demonstrate to the Committee that every care
is being taken to reduce the work of the
Department as far as possible, consistent
with efficiency.
on
Turning to the general work of administration, I have pointed out
several occasions of a similar character
that our work generally falls under two
heads-Home Office Administration and
Local Government Administration. Home
Office Administration is a wide comprehensive term, involving police, prisons,
law and order, asylum administration, as
well as a multitude of other minor but
still important services, such as Wild
Bird Protection, Reformatory, Industrial
and Borstal Schools, the Pharmacy Acts,
Explosives, the Petroleum Acts, and so
forth.
All these services-in fact, one might
say the main activities of the Home Office
division of the Ministry of Home Affairs
resolve themselves into a consideration of
the question of law and order, and in
this connection I am glad to be able to
say that in Northern Ireland there is
much reason for satisfaction in connection
with the prevalence of crime, although
there has been a slight increase in the
number of cases specially reported by
the police, yet these are mainly attributable to what one might regard as less
serious crimes, such as petty larcencies,
etc.
The Judges of Assize, on their visits
to the various counties as well as in the
City of Belfast, have been able to report
that a normal state of affairs has existed
during the past year and that, from the
calendars that came before them, they
had no cause for anxiety. In fact, the
presiding judge at the opening of the
Down Summer Assizes stated that
an
unusual and unprecedented state of peacefulness " existed, and at the Spring
Assizes at Derry the judge made special
reference to the decrease which he
noticed in charges arising out of drunkenness.
Another important aspect of administration in connection with crime during
the year is the fact that the percentage
of persons made amenable for crimes
committed during the year was 68.7.
This is the highest percentage reached
during the past five years, and reflects
the utmost credit on the Royal Ulster
Constabulary who have continued to
carry out their duties in a thoroughly
efficient and satisfactory manner, in
spite of the fact that, on the grounds of
economy, the strength of the Force is
being steadily reduced.
I will now turn to the question of
drunkenness, which I have already referred to, and I submit that the judges'
remarks are fully borne out by the
following figures, which show clearly that
the lurid pictures which from time to
time are given by certain enthusiasts in
the cause of temperance have no real
foundation in fact. The number of convictions for drunkenness in Belfast has
decreased from 2,326 in 1927 to 1,642 in
1931, which is a reduction of as much as
33 per cent. The number for Northern
Ireland, excluding Belfast, has decreased
from 2,423 in 1927 to 1,984 in 1931.
It
During the year 1931, 2,356 prisoners
were committed to prison, as against
2,283 in 1930, and 2,661 in 1927.
will thus be seen that the numbers, while
slightly more than last year, are considerably less than the numbers five years ago.
At the same time, although the numbers
committed last year were slightly more
than the year 1930, there were a greater
number of short-term cases, the result
being that the
average number of
prisoners in custody for the whole of the
year 1931 was only 307, as against 336 in
the previous year. These figures in themselves speak volumes for the improved
conditions in Northern Ireland, and show
clearly that, while troubled and unsettled
conditions may prevail elsewhere, the
people of Northern Ireland are becoming
on the whole more law-abiding.
While I am dealing with the question
of our prison population, I think it well
to state that the expenses of maintaining
our prisons is being kept down as low as
possible. Our cost per head for the year
1930 was £67 7s Od as compared with
£63 7s Od for 1929, and £67 16s Od for
1928. These costs are, as I have explained on a previous occasion, somewhat
in
excess of the comparative English
figures, i.e., £53 19s Od for 1928;
£50 8s Od for 1929; and £49 2s Od for
1930, but it would be unfair to our prison
administration to attempt to draw hasty
conclusions from a comparison between
these figures, having regard to the exceptional conditions under which the
administration is carried on in Northern
Ireland. It is an established principle

in prisons administration, as well as in
the administration of other institutions,
that the per capita cost tends to decrease
as the numbers increase, or, in other
words, the cost is lowest in the case of
large institutions.
As the Committee is aware, fortunately
the numbers in our various prisons are
comparatively low, and, accordingly, in
the interests of efficient supervision we
are compelled to maintain a staff which
would be capable of dealing with considerably larger numbers. In addition
to that we are not able, as in Great
Britain, with our limited resources to
maintain a series of institutions of a
specialised character for the various
classes of prisoners. In point of fact, on
the contrary we are compelled in Belfast
Prison to cope with several different classes, each of which class requires separate treatment and consideration. In other words, we are endeavouring in Belfast Prison to carry on work
which in Great Britain would be dealt
with in many different institutions, such
as first offenders, prisoners on remand,
short-term prisoners, old offenders, convicts, who are divided into different
categories. While we cannot go to the
same extent in the way of segregation in
different institutions, we endeavour to
put into effect, so far as is possible, this
very desirable and indeed necessary principle, and we must therefore maintain at
Belfast Prison a larger staff than if the
institution were used for one class only.
The same principle applies also in the
case of the Londonderry Prison, which, as
the Committee is aware, is used not only
as a prison for short-term prisoners committed from the north-west areas, but
also as a criminal lunatic asylum.

I have taken a special interest in our
prison administration, and I am satisfied
that our prisons are being run efficiently
and economically, and I am glad to have
this opportunity of expressing my appreciation of the manner in which the prison
staffs, from the governors downwards,

other countries the Governments have

The years that have gone by have been
full of difficulties in connection with
prison administration, not only in Northern Ireland but in other countries, and,
on the whole, great credit is due to
our prison staff, and, if I may be invidious.
for a moment, I would like to refer to

to say has seriously impaired his health
and caused him and us very considerable

The various prison industries continue
to be maintained, and some months ago
we were able to make arrangements under
which prisoners were afforded a longer

than had been possible previously. The
new workshops, to which I have already
referred, are giving complete satisfaction,
and the industries are now being carried
out under the healthiest possible conditions, under light and airy circumstances.

cannot speak too highly of the continued

The number of inmates at present
under detention is 71, as compared with
30 a few years ago. This increase may,
perhaps, seem alarming and may indicate
an increase in juvenile crime, but it
would be wrong to arrive at any such conclusion. The real meaning of the increase is that the courts are taking greater
advantage of a system of disclipinary and
technical training which the Borstal
Institution provides, and while we have
not had, perhaps, sufficient experience of
the system in Northern Ireland to enable
us to judge accurately the value of this
principle, yet from our limited experience
we are satisfied that the principle is a
sound one and tends on the whole to make
better citizens of the boys who have completed their period of training than the
old system of sending them to prison,
which tended on the contrary to make
criminals of them.
I have been afforded opportunities
from time to time of coming into personal contact with the boys, and I have
followed their after-history with the
utmost care. I am glad to be able to
state that a substantial number of them
have justified the training and discipline
which they have received at our training
school, and that only a small pro-
11 proportion-about 30 per cent.-have come
unfavourably under the notice of the
police since their return to ordinary civil
life. Even in these few cases the offences
were, for the most part, of a trivial
nature and did not indicate a return to
criminal habits or tendencies.
The expenses of running the Borstal Institution
have been controlled with the greatest
care, and the figures for 1930 show a
very substantial reduction over those for
1929, the cost per head for 1930 being
£52 9s 6d, as compared with £66 8s Od
for 1929. In England the comparative
figures were £65 14s Od and £68 8s Od.
The educational and, moral welfare of
the boys continues to be looked after
satisfactorily, and, in addition to the
teaching afforded by the staff, we have
a considerable number of voluntary
teachers and lecturers who go to the
school in their spare time and interest and
instruct the boys on all manner of
subjects, from boxing to architecture. I
am sure I am expressing the view of this
Committee when I say that the Government and the whole community are indebted to these ladies and gentlemen, and
also to the ladies and gentlemen who
have, at their own expense, provided
entertainments and excursions. The
kindly human touch which is brought
into the lives of the boys by these ladies
and gentlemen cannot but have the
utmost effect on the boys' minds. Finally,
I must refer to the work of the Visiting
Committee of this school. It is largely
owing to their efforts and the efforts of
their welfare officer that employment is
found for the boys on discharge, and I
must once again publicly extend my
heartiest thanks to all the members of
the committee for their interest, not only
in the boys while at the school, but also
on leaving.
Although the Reformatory boys at

the activities of the school apply equally

I think I have already satisfied the
