the last few years, we are becoming a
more law-abiding people. That satisfactory process is due to several causes- -it
is perhaps inherent to ourselves—it is

one could have ever contemplated under

it is due to several causes.
In the first place, our regular police
force is drawn from our own people; it

people, who have sympathy with our
people, and who know our people.
The
old antagonism between the police and

people now assist the police, whereas the

To a large extent the constitution of

last
As was explained in this House during
the course of our debates on economy
year, recruiting for the Regular Constabulary has been suspended and will continue to be suspended for some time yet,
until we have effected a substantial reduction in the strength of the force as a
whole. We have also suspended our
general barrack reconstruction scheme,
and are confining ourselves at present to
reconstruction of a few cases where the
existing circumstances call for immediate
amelioration.
While we are, in the essential interests
of economy, effecting a reduction in the
strength of the Royal Ulster Constabulary, I am satisfied that we are not impairing the efficiency of the force, and the
Committee may rest assured that no steps
will be taken which will in any way
prejudice the maintenance of law and
order.

Turning to the Local Government Department of the Ministry, I think that,

in Northern Ireland, and to their organisation, a Memorandum setting forth the

was

Only a few days ago the Newtownards
Board of Guardians were in a position to
open their new district hospital, and I
must congratulate that Board on the
vision and courage with which they faced
up to this problem, and with the excellent results that they have obtained.
A hospital is now provided for the inhabitants of the Newtownards Union
which will rank as one of the best hospitals
in Ulster, and I would particularly like
to refer to the care and attention which
the Board of Guardians gave to the
subject of securing a proper medical and
nursing staff.
The Banbridge Board of Guardians
have also, with our approval and encouragement, converted their old workhouse into a district hospital of excellent
Estimates-

Co

design and properly fitted
up and
equipped to deal with the needs of their
Union. As I have already said, there
are other proposals under consideration
at the moment, and pending a solution of
the difficulties which usually arise in these
cases, I do not think it expedient to
express any views regarding the proposals.
Perhaps the most important aspect of
local government administration is that
relating to roads and road traffic. The
Committee is aware that for the last few
years we have by financial assistance been
steadfastly encouraging the road authorities in Northern Ireland to face up to the
problem of improving the road systems
in their various areas.
As the Committee is aware, our road
systems were in a most unsatisfactory
condition following the war and it became necessary to spend large sums of
money on making up the various classes
of roads to that standard which is
warranted by the traffic passing over
them. I am glad to be able to say that,
with the hearty co-operation of the local
authorities and with the substantial
grants which we decided to accord to
them, our road systems now compare
favourably with those in other countries
of similar character.
Our difficulties were not made any
easier by reason of the fact that the
number of motor vehicles in the Province
continued to increase year by year at
such a substantial rate-in fact, we
found that it was difficult for us to keep
pace with the increase in motor traffic,
but from the reports which I have
received I am inclined to think that we
have now reached a point at which the
work we have done in the past will enable
us to keep abreast of the traffic in so far
as the maintenance and improvement of
our roads services are concerned.
Owing, as I have said, to the poor condition of the roads and the necessity for
meeting the situation at once, at all
costs, we found it necessary during the
last few years to encroach heavily upon
the resources of the Road Fund in order
to accord to the road authorities the
utmost financial assistance possible. I
would remind the Committee that we continue to contribute 60 per cent. in respect
of first-class roads, 30 per cent. on secondclass roads, and 15 per cent. on thirdclass roads, which are used for motor
traffic.
As a slight index of the expense of
road reconstruction work in Northern
Ireland, in connection with which we have
in the past been giving grants of 72 per
cent. on Class I. roads, I would like to
point out that this special reconstruction
work has cost no less than £1,063,000.
On the other hand, it has enabled us to
provide on the more important roads in
Northern Ireland 100 miles of new
foundation, 70 miles of reinforced concrete
roads, and 22 miles of asphalt macadam
surfaces. The result is, as the Committee
will appreciate, not only better roads but
lower future maintenance costs.
Apart from the improvement and reconstruction of our road systems, considerable attention has been devoted to
the cutting of hedges and the roundingoff of corners and the improvement
generally of vision at such corners.
of
In addition to these measures which
have been taken with the object of improving traffic conditions and of lessening
the risk of accidents, a forward step has
been taken, particularly in Belfast, in
connection with the establishment
automatic road signals. The Belfast Corporation have cordially co-operated with
the Ministry in the establishment of these
signals, and have received grants from
the Road Fund amounting to 50 per cent.
of the cost of setting up and of maintenance.
I saw it stated in one of the papers
this morning that no saving has been
effected by this system as regards the
utilisation of pointsmen. I think that is
wrong. I have had the figures taken out,
and they may be of interest to the Committee. I find that, to provide for
interest and sinking fund, cost of operation, maintenance, and general supervision involves an annual sum of £134.
As against that, to work a point where
you place an automatic signal would
require the equivalent of the services of
one and a half policemen per day, which
would work out at a cost of £480 per
annum, which means that there is a
saving of £346 per annum at every point.
But, apart altogether from the economical
side of it, I think it will be admitted
that these signals have proved a great
boon and blessing and that their development not only in Belfast but in other
centres is strongly called for.
I would like now to say a word or two
on the question of accidents. While the
number of accidents reported for the

[Sir Dawson Bates]
year 1931 shows an increase on the
number reported for the previous year,
I am glad to say that they have not
increased as much as might have been
expected, having regard to the additional
number of vehicles now using the roads
and the greater extent to which motor
vehicles are used.
For the year 1928 the number of
accidents reported was 1,457, the number
of persons killed being 114, and the
number injured 1,592. For the year
1931 the number of accidents reported
was 1,582, with 114 persons killed, and
1,724 persons injured. It is to be noted
that while the numbers of deaths in the
two years were the same, there was an
upward tendency in the number of
accidents and the number of injuries, but
in this connection it must be remembered
that between the year 1928 and the year
1931 the number of motor vehicles using
the roads increased from 31,000 to 36,000,
and I think it must be admitted that were
it not for the steps taken to lessen the risk
of accident, and for the other measures
of traffic control which we have adoptedincluding the provision of mobile police
patrols in motor-cycle combinations and
motor-cars-the number of accidents and
injuries would have been considerably
greater. It might be of interest to hon.
Members to know the number of accidents
in England and how they compare with
the number here. I find that Great
Britain, with a population of 47,790,000,
had 11.7 accidents per 1,000 vehicles.

Mr. NIXON: What does the expression
"accident" include? Does it mean
accident involving death or bodily injury?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not quite
follow what the hon. Gentleman means.
Mr. NIXON: I will try to put it
more plainly. Some people might call the
wrecking of a motor car an accident, but
what I want to know, and what I think
the Committee will want to know, is
when the Minister uses the expression
"accident" does he mean to convey that
something happened involving death to
some person or bodily injury to some
person.
Sir DAWSON BATES: That is the
point I am dealing with. The Government are not concerned if a man drives
his motor car against a stone wall and
smashes it up.
Mr. NIXON: That is what I wanted
to have made clear.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I thought it
would have been clear to the ordinary
individual. I find that in Great Britain,
with a population of 47,790,000, the num
ber of accidents per 1,000 vehicles works
out at 11.7, while in Northern Ireland,
with a population of 1,256,000, the number of accidents per 1,000 vehicles works
out at only 4.4. And with regard to
accidents to the population, I find that
in Great Britain the number of accidents
to the population per 1,000 works out at
.4, while in Northern Ireland it is only
.12.
Mr. HEALY: Is not the population in
Great Britain a little more dense than
in Northern Ireland?
Yes, but
Sir DAWSON BATES:
Great Britain also has its rural areas in
addition to its industrial centres. In
this connection I think it only fair to the
motoring community to state that according to the reports submitted to me, almost
half of the accidents that occur are caused
by the carelessness of pedestrians.
Another very important feature in connection with road traffic administration
is the fact that so few accidents occur
in which drivers of omnibuses and motor
coaches are concerned, and when we take
into consideration the fact that these
vehicles are constantly on the road I think
that this circumstance constitutes a strong
tribute to the care and skill of the drivers
of these vehicles. I could only wish that
the drivers of ordinary private vehicles
would show the same skill, care and
courtesy which is displayed from day to
day by the drivers of these public service vehicles. Out of a total of over
1,500 accidents only 32 were caused by
motor omnibuses and motor coaches.
The use of the double-decked motor
omnibus has proved very popular in Northern Ireland, and it is prehaps unfor
tunate that we have not found it possible,
up to the present at any rate, to extend
the operation of this class of vehicle, but
we feel it to be only prudent to wait and
gain more experience of the use of these
vehicles, particularly from the point of
view of the safety of the passengers and
traffic, as well as the effect that they have
on the road surfaces.
I feel that I have detained the Committee too long. I have tried to cover
the main points dealt with in the Estimates, and I now beg to move.

Mr. HEALY: Although we may have
to complain of a good deal in these Estimates, in other respects I do not think
anyone in this Committee will cavil at
the minuteness with which the Minister
has gone into the details of his Department. He has made the most of the

taken an hour and ten minutes
practically to deal with the activities of
the Department of Home Affairs, and I
am afraid that we shall be in the position,
in which we sometimes find ourselves in
this Committee, that when we have
spoken, which we do at no great length,

Committee.
The Minister has discovered, not I think
for the first time, that the Ulster people
are law-abiding. That is a discovery that
even the Opposition made a good while
ago, so that I think the Minister is just
a little belated. It is rather curious that
the Minister records a steady decrease in
crime just in direct ratio to the decrease
in the Royal Ulster Constabulary and the
practical elimination of the Specials.
We have always been told that the existence of the Specials was our assurance
of the security of the people of the Six
Counties. But they have disappeared for
all practical purposes from the Estimates.
-that is, excepting the officers—and, notwithstanding that, the peace of the Six
Counties not only remains unimpaired,
but continues to improve day after day.
Therefore, it will be of the greatest interest for hon. Members of this Committee
to turn back to the speeches of the
Minister of Home Affairs in introducing
his Estimate for former years and compare them with his speech to-day.
But I find that, notwithstanding the
Minister's congratulations, he has still on
his pay roll 2,846 persons at headquarters
costing the country about £635,000.
That is a fairly large figure for a comparatively small area such as the Six-
Counties. I do not think if there were
a referendum of the people taken they
would stand for anything like a charge of
that kind. I do not think they can afford
it, and I do not think it is necessary.
Therefore, the first thing to which the
Minister should devote his attention is the
reduction of those figures at the earliest
possible moment.
We are as much interested in the preservation of peace in the Six Counties as
any Member of the Government can be,
because in the past when there has been
any departure from that peace we have
been the people who have suffered, and
I have no doubt that if there should be
any similar happening in the future we
would be in exactly the same position.
But we have a right to call the attention
of the Committee to what I think the
Minister has rather carefully skimmed
over, namely, the administration of law
and order in the Six Counties. I would
like to direct the Minister's attention to
two particular incidents in this connection.
The first is that which occurred at a place
called Annahugh in County Armagh
some years ago, and which was repeated
on subsequent occasions down to last
year, namely, the destruction of a hall by
armed men in a district where the population are all of the political faith of the
Minister, and where one-half of the ablebodied men of from twenty-one to sixty
years of
age are in the Special Constabulary and, therefore, presumed to
have arms. In that district an outrage
which meant the demolition of a public
building on no fewer than three successive
occasions took place, and on each occasion
the ratepayers had to pay.
If the police force had been half so
efficient as the Minister 'has indicated he
would have had no difficulty in putting
his finger on the guilty person or persons,
because there was a whole set of circumstances in connection with the affair
which pointed clearly to the probable
source. I need not weary the Committee
by going over the details. They were
pretty familiar a short while ago, but
one notable fact was that the people who
came to destroy this hall knew the local
surroundings and also knew fairly well
whether they were likely to meet with any
opposition. It was noticed, too, I think,
by some people whose information was at
the disposal of the Ministry, that on the
night of the outrage lights were seen in
some local halls at an unusually late hour.
The Parliamentary Secretary at the
time told us that no efforts would be
spared to bring the guilty people to
justice; in fact, he almost indicated that
if we kept silent and did not do anything
to upset the equilibrium of the specialists
of the Home Office, who were investigating the matter, we would have the
culprits by the leg in a day or two. And
so we have kept silent all these months-
I might say all these years but the
people who perpetrated these outrages are

yet walking about, I have no doubt still

The second outrage to which I want
to draw attention occurred at a place

people who came armed to attack a peaceful procession going to the train, were
able to walk across the country past farmhouses of loyal supporters of the Government and "B" men, and make their
escape. Does the Minister contend that
the Royal Ulster Constabulary, who live
in the surrounding districts and townlands, did not see the people passing by
after such an extraordinary event as a
succession of shots? If they saw them
passing by, why is the Minister not in

This is a part of the country that is
intensely loyal. They had to pass the
doors of members of the Special Constabulary. They must have known who
the men were. Therefore, it is futile for
the Minister to come into this Committee
and say there is anything like impartial
administration of law and order in the
Six Counties. There is not. This constitutes a scandal. My hon. Friend, the
Member for Mid Derry (Mr. Leeke), had
a question on the Paper to-day setting
out the statement of a respectable local
resident. He says he conveyed to the
police force an intimation that the procession would start at 8-30 rather than 9-30,
the hour originally arranged, because the
plea of the Constabulary is that they were
unaware that the original plans had been
changed, that is, the hour of starting had
been changed from 9-30 to 8-30.
This man makes it quite clear that he
gave them information to this effect.
What I suggest is that the Royal Ulster
Constabulary probably forgot about the
change. They ought to have been there
to guard this procession, having in mind.
what had previously occurred and the
objections urged against its passing that
way, and taking into consideration the
whole circumstances, but they were negligent of their duty. And more than
that. Some people in the locality, who
probably are members of the Special
Force, knew of the circumstance too, but
did not take advantage of it.
These are two incidents-I could give
more-that have been figuring a good deal

there are people with arms in the Six

with impunity tumble down a hall in

occasions, for which the ratepayers have

The Minister referred to reformatories, and anything I say about that

years,

There is another class of person I would
like to put a word in for, and I know
that it will be very hard for the Government to do much, and that is the discharged prisoner. For example, if a
person is discharged to-morrow morning
from Belfast Jail after serving his sentence for some crime which he committed,
he is not entitled to unemployment benefit, and he will not get work. How would
he get work when there are 30,000 ablebodied men totally unemployed in Belfast at the present time? He would not
get it. He would not get unemployment
benefit. He would get a little assistance
from the societies that look after such
cases, but they have very limited means
for that purpose.
What is that prisoner
to do? There is nothing in the world he
can do after the little assistance he got
is exhausted but commit another crime
and get in again for another period.
That is why we have habitual criminals.
I know myself it would be a very difficult
problem for the Government to tackle. I
appreciate that it would, because if they
cannot find employment for men who have
never been in trouble, how can they do
so for men who were? Yet they should
think about it and endeavour to make an

beyond description.

A matter I would like to bring before
the Committee is the operation of the
Betting Act. Whilst in no way would I
encourage gambling, yet I feel that the
scandal of the manner in which batches
of bookmakers are brought before the
Courts and summarily fined, calls for
action on the part of the Government.
It seems to me indefensible-and I am only
speaking for fair play all round-that
these men should be brought up indiscriminately and fined according to the
constitution of the Bench at the moment,
sometimes a large fine and at other times
a small fine; the fine having no relation
to the offence. That is the worst part

Nobody knows! There are periodical
raids; the feature of the raid being by
surprise to catch as many as possible. I
am not one of those who believe that all
these people are innocent, nor do I
believe they are the only guilty ones. It

what is possibly worse, that they have

are always telling us that that money is

I come now to another matter to which
I do not like to refer because I hate to
mention personal matters in this House,
but I do it as a matter of principle. I
refer to the appointment of Rear-Admiral
Archdale to the position which he now
occupies in the Ministry of Home Affairs.
I would have liked the Minister to have
told us his reason for appointing Admiral
Archdale. If there is one thing about
which the public are jealous it is the civil
service. Since I came into this House I
have made it a point never to attack a
civil servant or the civil service. I know
this much about them, though I have
never had anything to do with them
officially, that if it were not for the civil
service the governments of these countries
would be in a worse position than they
are. The Members of the Government,
not only here but everywhere, are very
often merely the gramophones of the civil
service. It is the civil servants who, by
their thought, their efficiency, and the
care they give to all these questions, prepare the minds of the Ministers, and,
mind you, Ministers require to have their
minds prepared, any of them that I have
ever seen, and they require to be well
briefed. Therefore, I am jealous of any
interference with the civil service, and I
object altogether to Admiral Archdale,
excellent citizen, and, no doubt, militant
and impartial admiral though he was in
his day and generation, being brought in
and placed, not in an ordinary position
in the Home Office, but in one of the
highest positions. Is it not one of the
highest positions?
Mr. COLLINS: It is a good one.
Mr. DEVLIN: It is a good one, any.
way. In each department of the civil
service when promotions come along those

branches. If you had wanted to give a

there would not be any necessity for a

not an active admiral but a sort of
specialised agent who would advise us as
to the best way in which the Southern
navy could be prevented from attacking
Northern Ireland, or something like that.

before the magistrates, and dozens of

The Post Office makes its profits out of

I say the Government ought to stop
this system of petty persecution. I do
not think it is fair. These people could
be fined once for an offence and then left
alone. Why is the law only put into
operation against the poorer classes of
citizens? Why is the right hon. Gentleman dealing with only one branch of
betting and not with every branch of it?
I was told the other day of a magistrate
who, on the bench, was insisting on a
fine of £10 or £25 being imposed on a
bookmaker, although he owed a bookmaker £200 himself for bets made on the
telephone. I am sick of that sort of
thing, and every citizen ought to be sick
of it having magistrates prepared to
impose these penalties on these poor
people while they were engaged in betting
themselves. I would like the Home
Secretary or the Parliamentary Secretary
to tell us if they propose still to continue
persecuting these people.
Now I come to the question of policemen joining political organisations. I do
not believe that a policeman ought to be
allowed to join a political organisation of
any sort or kind. A policeman is human
like everybody else and will naturally be
guided, if not by his opinions, by his
prejudices. I think it would be much
better to have the police force free from
association with any organisation, Orange
or Green. If the administration of
justice is to compel the respect of all
sections of the people those who are
administering the law, whether as policemen or as judges, ought to be free from
party partisanship or political organisations. I hold that view very strongly.
Those are the only observations I have
to make on these Estimates. I wish to
say, in conclusion, that while I have been
very critical of the Home Secretary and
his administration I trust that when he
comes to do the right thing, as he is
doing in regard to prison administration
and the Borstal Institution, he will get
adequate recognition from this as well as
from every other section of the community.

Mr. HEALY: I gave notice earlier in
the day of my intention to raise a matter
on the Adjournment. The other day I
got a reply from the Minister of Agriculture dealing with the price of apples in
the cross-Channel market, to which I took
some exception. I had better read the
question, so that the Members of the
House may be in possession of the facts.
I asked him whether
the price of extra fancy apples in Belfast is 25s to 28s per barrel, and the
price of ordinary Bramleys in the
English market is 52s per barrel, and
the cost of carriage between the two
places is only 3s or 4s per barrel.
The Minister of Agriculture informed me
that
the prices in January and February,
1932, for Bramleys in the English market was 278 10d per barrel. The price
at Covent Garden was 34s per barrel,
but the cost of carriage to Covent
Garden is 7s. Therefore, the price in
Belfast is a shade higher.
I have in my hand documentary evidence
to prove that the statement that Bramleys
in Belfast were 27s 10d was not a real
quotation, for the best of all reasons on
earth, that apples are not quoted in anything but shillings and sixpences.
Therefore, the sources of information
must be very meagre, and they must be
very poorly informed, when the Minister
quoted 27s 10d per barrel. There never
was such a quotation in the Belfast market. He can take the newspapers, to
which his own Department supply the
official figures. He can go back as far as
he pleases, and he will not find
quotation of 278 10d, I think. I hold
that the figure of 27s 10d is more correctly given as 28s. If the Minister
adopts that figure, I am prepared to
accept it-28s for extra choice Bramleys
in the Belfast market. But my point
is the difference between the price that
the grower can secure in the Belfast
market, and the price that he can obtain
in the English market. I said on

There is another question too, namely,
the commission of salesmen. As a matter
of fact, the commission in Belfast market
is 12 per cent., and in London, in the
Covent Garden market, it is 7 to 10 per

apples out of the country, but must put
them in bags and sell them as boilers
for an insignificant amount.
I would ask the Minister of Agriculture, therefore, to consider the position
of this industry seriously. It is one of
the few industries in Northern Ireland
that has been able to make its way apart
from any Government help or interest.
It has built up the reputation which it
holds to-day on the London, English, and
foreign markets entirely on its merits. It
is true that there may be on each of
these apples a blemish slightly larger
than is permitted under the Ministry's
grading system, but the people in
England who buy these apples understand that perfectly well. Irish apples
are better keeping apples than the
English Bramleys, and they command as
good a price as the very best Bramleys
on the English market. All the growers
ask you to do is to allow them to ship
these apples to the people who want to
buy them and who know their quality.
And they want to be able to do that unhampered by your restrictions.

the Department intended to wage war on

CLAUSE 15 (Restrictions on receiving
patients upon orders, etc., of interested
persons.)
No person shall be received or detained as a person of unsound mind in
an institution, or as a single patient,
where the reception order has been
made by or on the petition of, or the
medical certificate in respect of the
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I beg to move, in
page 14, lines 28 and 29, to leave out
the words "the institution" (in paragraph c) and insert the words "a registered institution or house to which the
patient is admitted."
This Amendment is introduced as a
result of representations made to me by
an hon. Member, and I am sure that it
will greatly assist in the administration.
Under the Clause, as it stands at present,
it is not possible for the resident medical
superintendent of a public mental hospital, or the medical officer in charge of
a registered institution or house, to sign
the medical certificate of a person being
admitted to such institution. It has been
pointed out to me, however, that while
this restriction is a very desirable one in
the case of registered homes, yet, were the
resident medical superintendents of a
public mental hospital not allowed to
examine and certify patients who may
later be admitted to their own institutions, considerable difficulty, delay, and
expense might ensue. In practice, I am
aware that the services of the resident
medical superintendents in Northern Ireland are called upon frequently in connection with the examination of many
persons who must ultimately become inmates of their institutions. I think it
is only natural that these gentlemen who
have wide experience of mental illnesses
should have an opportunity of certifying
when it becomes necessary.
Amendment agreed to.

CLAUSE 25 (Discharge of paying
patients recovered).
(1) The resident medical superintendent or person in charge shall, upon
the recovery of a paying patient, send
notice thereof within three clear days
next after the recovery, to the person
on whose petition the reception order
was made, or by whom the last payment
on account of the patient was made.
(2) The notice shall state that unless
the patient is removed within seven
days from the date of the notice he
will be discharged.
(3) In case the patient is not removed
within seven days from the date of the
notice he shall be forthwith discharged.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move
in page 21, line 2, leave out from the
word "shall" ("in charge shall") to the
word "send" ("send notice thereof") in
line 3, and insert the words "as soon as
he is satisfied that a paying patient has
recovered."
Clauses 25 and 27 relate to discharge
of patients. Under these Clauses the
onus of deciding when a patient is
sufficiently recovered for discharge is not
definitely fixed on any one person, and it
has been pointed out to me that this may
give rise to difficulties. Accordingly,
the Amendments which I now move make
it quite clear that this onus rests on the
resident medical superintendent who is,
of course, the only person who is in a
position to give such a decision.
Amendment agreed to.

Exported Animals (Compensation) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be read a Second time."
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): The Slaughtered
Animals (Compensation) Act (Northern
Ireland), 1928, passed by this House
four years ago provides for the payment
of compensation in respect of animals exported from Northern Ireland ports and
slaughtered in British landing places by
reason of the requirements of the British
authorities in consequence of foot-andmouth disease. The fund from which
such compensation is payable is constituted by a small levy as follows paid by
shippers on each animal exported:-Each
head of cattle, 24d; each sheep, d; each
pig, 1d. The arrangement is therefore
a very sound form of insurance to which
the State is not asked to contribute.
For a considerable time past the cattle
trade associations have been pressing for
an extension of the legislation, so as to
provide compensation not only for
slaughter but also in respect of the
extra lairage and feeding charges payable
in British landing places whenever,
owing to foot-and-mouth disease or
suspected disease, whether in Great
Britain or Northern Ireland, animals
sent through our ports are detained in
British landing places beyond the usual
detention period of ten hours. For
example, last June animals consigned
from Northern Ireland were held in cross-
Channel landing places for prolonged
periods, during which the owners had to
pay considerable extra sums in respect of
lairage and feeding. It has been estimated that in consequence of the June
outbreak, such additional charges falling
to be borne by exporters through Northern Ireland ports amounted to about
£2,000. This Bill will enable that
amount to be paid to the shippers concerned from the insurance fund. Further,
the measure protects traders against
similar risks in the future.
Section 13 (1) of the Act provides that
whenever the compensation fund amounts
to £5,000 the Ministry may make an
order for the suspension of payment of
the export levy per head on each animal
shipped. In view of the increased
liability now proposed to be placed on the
insurance fund, it is the intention that
the sum of £5,000 referred to should be
raised to £10,000. This increase has
been approved by the trade interests
concerned.
After careful consideration, I am of
opinion that this proposed legislation is
sound and I have, therefore, great
pleasure in commending the Bill to this
House. I beg to move.
Mr. MINFORD: I rise to support this
Bill. I think that any Bill brought in
by the Minister of Agriculture deserves
the support of both sides of the House.
This Bill will clear away many difficulties
in regard to the shipment of cattle.
Last year the shippers of cattle experienced great delay for a considerable
period at the English and Scotch ports
owing to the outbreak of foot-and-mouth
disease which cost the exporters a sum of
£2,000. The Insurance Fund, which
amounted to £5,000 and which has not
been spent, was contributed to by the
exporters, who had to pay hundreds of
pounds extra for serious losses incurred.
Any loss derived by cattle shippers is a
direct loss to the farmers. Might I
mention two items in regard to the landing of cattle on the other side. When
cattle are landed on the other side the
shippers have to pay 4d per head for
inspection fee and 3d per head for
tagging. I would like some explanation
in regard to that. It may be a small
sum, but in the aggregate the amount
concerned between 1924 and last year was
£152,000 for all Ireland. Last year the
total for Ireland was £24,720. I consider
that these fees should be paid by the
English people themselves, because on
this side they have no veterinary fees
to pay at all. The only charge here is
4d per head for hay and 3d per head for
lairage. When you consider that the
Irish shipper has to pay a total of 7d per
head, and that these tags cost only 3d

DISTRESS IN NORTHERN IRELAND
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn.'
(Sir Basil Brooke).
Mr. O'NEILL: I wonder if it would
be possible to get any reply to a question
I raised yesterday during the debate on
the Estimates of the Ministry of Home
Affairs with regard to the position in
Castlewellan and Annsborough. I do not
see either the Minister of Labour or the
Minister of Home Affairs in the House.
The House will remember that I brought
forward cases of great hardship and want
in this district. I understand that some
of them are cases of almost absolute
starvation. The Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs did
state in reply that he would have inquiries made, and probably the time has
been too short to make those inquiries
or to have had a reply to them. There
is no doubt that in this district for some
time past there has been a good deal of
distress due to unemployment in the mills
at Annsborough and to other causes, and
there are a lot of people on the brink
of starvation, if not in absolute starvation. I think when such distress occurs
on a scale like this it is the business of
the Government to inquire into the matter immediately and to afford instant
relief. The complaint I have received
not only in regard to outdoor relief but
in regard to the Ministry of Labour is
that people have been cleared off unemployment benefit wholesale, with the result that both those who are insured and
those who are not are in dire distress at
the present time. I would like to know
what has been done, because this is not
the first occasion I have raised the question in this House, and things have not
improved in the meantime. Perhaps the
Parliamentary Secretary would tell us
exactly what the position is.
Mr. BYRNE: In the City of Belfast
there are a great many cases of distress
as bad as those to which the Member for Mourne has referred. Those of
us who are mixing with the working
people encounter nothing but the direst
distress wherever we go. We know that
under recent Acts of Parliament an unemployed person can draw unemployment
benefit for only six months, and then he
has to go before a public assistance committee which, I am sorry to say, is not
very sympathetic towards him. When
they have drawn four or eight weeks'
benefit their case comes before a Court of
Referees, and their claim for further
benefit is turned down entirely. This is
a very serious matter for the working
people of this city. Some time ago there
was a prospect of an improvement in the
linen trade which we hoped would relieve
unemployment considerably, but I am
sorry to say that according to reports I
have heard within the past week hundreds
of people have been paid off. I am told
that this is due to the reduction of the
tariff on linen from 50 per cent. to 20
per cent.
During the whole of my public life I
never heard of more distress than exists
in the city at the present time.
Something should be done for these people at
once, because there is nothing but starvation staring them in the face. When
their transitional benefit is exhausted the
only thing left for these unemployed
people is to go before the Board of
Guardians, and everyone knows that
decent working people, who are unemployed through no fault of their own,
are very reluctant to be mixed up with
pauperism. If they are granted outdoor
relief they have to perform a certain
amount of work, and people have told me
they would starve rather than apply to
the guardians for relief. I sincerely
hope the Government will take some
effective steps to promote employment for
the large number of people who are now
practically in a state of starvation.

What is in the minds of these people?
When the Great War broke out they

Oral Answers
5 MAY 1932
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 5th May, 1932.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
JUVENILE EMPLOYEES OF
JOHNSTON & CO., BELFAST.
1. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state how many
boys of the age of 15 years have been
engaged through the Juvenile Exchange
by the firm of Johnston & Co., Ravenhill
Road, Belfast, and what are their periods
of employment; whether these boys have
been employed as labourers by this firm
on municipal and Government contracts
at a wage of from 6s to 7s per week;
whether he is aware that this firm has
been blacklisted by the Belfast Corporation; and whether he will see that no
more contracts, subsidised by public
funds, will be given to this firm until they
receive a clean bill of health from the
National Union of Operative Heating
and Domestic Engineers and General
Metal Workers.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE
(Mr. Barbour): In the unavoidable
absence of my right hon. Friend I have
been asked to reply. The Ministry of
Labour's available records show that in
the last three years the Belfast Juvenile
Exchange filled vacancies for apprentices
or helpers in the case of ten boys of about
the age of 15 years with the firm in
question. Of these one has been employed
for ten months, while two others reregistered at the Exchange after seven
months and three weeks respectively.
The Department has no information as
to the actual wages paid to the boys or
as to the work on which they were engaged.
With regard to the latter part of the
question, the matter is at present under
consideration between the representatives
of the Union and of the Government
Department concerned.
CARCASES OF PIGS CONDEMNED.
2. Mr. GAMBLE asked the Minister
of Agriculture whether he can state how
many carcases of pigs have been condemned by the Inspectors of Pork since
the introduction of the Act.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE
(Sir Edward Archdale): The Agricultural
Produce (Meat Regulation) Act (Northern Ireland), 1930, came into operation
on the 1st May, 1931. During the
twelve months ended 30th April, 1932,
274 carcases of pigs were condemned
under the provisions of the Act.
REVALUATION OF
AGRICULTURAL LAND.
3. Major MCCORMICK asked the
Prime Minister whether the Government
propose to introduce legislation for the revaluation of all agricultural land now outside the scope of the Revaluation Act.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have been asked to take this
question, the answer to which is in the
negative.
LANDLORD AND TENANT
LEGISLATION.
4. Major McCORMICK asked the
Prime Minister whether it is the intention of the Government to introduce
legislation on the lines of the Imperial
Parliament's "Landlord and Tenant Act,"
and in accordance with the recommendation of the Departmental Committee set
up to consider this question.
SECRE-
The PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME
AFFAIRS (Mr. Hanna): In the absence
of my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson
Bates) I have been asked to reply.
I have to refer the hon. Member to the
answer given to a similar question asked
by the hon. Member for Mid-Londonderry on the 28th April, to which I have
nothing to add.

a return showing the number of accidents

mention one matter of interest in connection with the work of the Registrar-
General's Department, that is to say,
during the past year, in addition to the
normal publication of the Registrar-
General's weekly, quarterly, and annual
reports, a review of vital statistics has
been published, with which are incorporated life tables based upon the census
of population taken in Northern Ireland
in 1926. This review covers a period of
time extending backwards 80 far
records are available and in so far as it
embodies the results of the Census of
population taken in 1926 it may be said
to round off and complete the material
which the Registrar-General was required
to prepare and publish in accordance
with the provisions of Section 6 of the
Census Act (Northern Ireland) 1925.
The life tables incorporated in this report are the first scientific attempt to
prepare for Northern Ireland as a separate entity tables of the rates of mortality
and consequent expectation of life in this
area. Such tables were never before
prepared for Ireland separately from
Great Britain, but are now available for
each part of this island.
Under Subhead M the increase of
about £4,500 in the Receipts Appropriated-in-Aid Subhead is due chiefly to
the additional receipts expected to accrue
from the Imperial Government in respect
of staff engaged on what are called Reserved Agency Works Services, such as
the erection of the automatic telephone
exchange. I beg to move.

the licence duties are to be increased

man wants to refuse a suitable position,

It is the decision of the Cabinet. When

that boy should be given the same preference as ex-Servicemen, many of whom

The Clerical Union say that the

a settlement with the ex-Servicemen. The
Cabinet are now giving a large percentage

Next, I want to refer to the motor

Another thing I want to take exception
to is the ruling out of ordinary civil
servants from the higher positions, the men
who pass the examinations and who get
the marks. I see the Permanent Secretary here at a salary of £1,886, or something like that. He never passed a Civil
Service examination in his life. He was
not a civil servant, and had no training
whatever in business. A few years ago
most people were inclined to bow to a
gentleman, no matter where he was, if
he had a great financial reputation. But
events in Great Britain and elsewhere
have dissipated that idea once and for
all. We know that a great many financial reputations are spurious, and there are
several people in this House at the present
moment who know that to their cost.
It would be a very big job, indeed, for
me or anyone else to commence reading
out the numerous and well-paid posts
created by this Department. At the
present time I think that would be rather
superfluous in view of the fact that there
is a very good book on the subject which
I had not the pleasure of reading yet
and which is published at twopence. It
is a book, I believe, from what I hear,
that is making an impression. I remember raising a question to which I still
take exception. When young men pass
the Civil Service examination and have
their marks allotted to them, I think after
they pass the doctor they should be
appointed in order of merit. I have every
reason to believe that the examinations
as conducted by the Civil Service Commissioners are fair and above board. I
have every reason to believe that the
marks given are fair, but I object
absolutely to candidates after they have
got good marks from the Civil Service
Commissioners being brought before
another board and questioned, and being
knocked up or down or off the list.
That is not to be taken as reflecting
on the members that form that board.
I know some of the gentlemen, and I am
not reflecting on them in the slightest degree, but I do say that no man can sit
here or in a room, and after asking a
candidate a number of questions then
decide on the ability of that candidate.
If it is a question of physical appearance
or something like that, then there should
be a medical test set up. Candidates
have to be medically examined, and that
is quite proper, but for a number of
gentlemen to call themselves an investigation committee and hurl all sorts of
foolish questions at the candidates brought
before them is absolutely absurd, because
some of the candidates might be nervous.
I am sure they would be. What would
make them more nervous is that this Committee and, again, I mean no personal reflection on the gentlemen of the Committee-have the reputation of knocking
off people that should not be knocked off,
and of putting people on whose marks
did not warrant them being put on.
That in itself would make candidates
coming before them nervous.
I suggest that it would be more honourable and above board to appoint the

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £1,790 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the

the year ending 31st March, 1933, to pay
certain miscellaneous expenses, including
certain Grants in Aid."-(Note-£500
has been voted on account).
Mr. BARBOUR: There is little that
calls for comment in this Estimate.
Grants-in-aid have been fractionally
reduced in accordance with the general
economy cut principles that have been
applied all round. Sub-head I calls for
some more detailed comment. The explanation of the proposed grant is that
the former Clones Union was partly in
County Monaghan and partly in County
Fermanagh. On the setting up of the
Northern Ireland Government, the Union
was divided, about one-third of the area
being attached to Lisnaskea Union in the
North, but no division of assets and
liabilities was made. The failure of the
Imperial Government to have such an
apportionment made has not, however,
been of material consequence, as items
such as superannuation allowances have
been accepted as a final charge by the
body where the office of the former
guardians was situated, while matters
such as the adjustment of payments due
for treatment of inmates from transborder areas have been left to settle
themselves on the assumption that assets
and liabilities in general cancel out.
The present case, however, is in a
different category. It is a case of a bank
overdraft which the former guardians
owed but which now, owing to severance,
cannot be legally accepted or legally enforced, so far as one can judge. For a
considerable time past the bank concerned has made representation that it
was not equitable that it should be
penalised merely because the three Governments concerned had left a transborder problem unsettled. My right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Home Affairs,
and myself have accordingly come to the
conclusion that in equity the bank should
not be left in this position. On the
other hand, only one-third of the former
Clones Union is situated in Northern
Ireland, and our normal liability should
be confined to that proportion of the
debt. Technically this amount might be
held to be owing by the Lisnaskea Union,
but it cannot legally be imposed upon
them, and, in any event, if the amount
were paid from the rates, it would, in
all probability, owing to derating, be
paid as to 80 per cent. by the Government in the long run.
the long run. The grant,
therefore, is an ex-gratia payment in
respect of a moral obligation arising out
of the establishment of separate Governments in Northern Ireland. I beg to
move.

Oral Answers to Questions.
BUILDING PROGRAMME FOR NEW
SCHOOLS.
the
1. Major McCORMICK asked
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry
of Education whether, in view of the
heavy expenditure in the building and
equipment of schools, he proposes to curtail or stop the building programme for
new schools other than those already in
hand.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRE-
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The answer
is in the negative, but I may explain that
as a result of personal representations
made by the Minister in December, 1930,
the building programme has, in view of
the financial stringency, already been curtailed or delayed.
Except where they merely replace
existing unsuitable schoolhouses, the
building of new schools results, through
amalgamation, in the concentration of
pupils in larger school units, which can
be more efficiently and economically
staffed, and I may add that the consequent saving in teachers' salaries is much
greater than the annual loan charges on
the money borrowed for new or enlarged
schools.
INCREASED BUS FARES.
2. Major MCCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether, in
view of the increased bus fares put into
force on almost all routes, he will make
representations to the Bus Fares Tribunal to have the scales reconsidered.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The hon. and
gallant Member appears to be under a
misapprehension regarding the activities
of the Tribunal referred to in suggesting
that the Tribunal has put in force increased bus fares on almost all routes.
The facts are that after considering
the representations made by certain
operators and formal objections lodged by
local authorities and other interested
parties, and having weighed up carefully
expert evidence tendered by persons of
experience and knowledge in connection
with the operation of motor omnibus
services, the Tribunal has formulated certain basic principles on which they consider bus fares should be regulated in
Northern Ireland in future.
The practical application of these principles to various routes is at present under
consideration, and a further session of the
Tribunal has been arranged to consider
and decide as to the practical working out
of their general principles in connection
with these specified routes which all interested parties can attend and be heard.
The Tribunal is an independent body
and in connection with its activities must
be guided by the evidence placed before
it by applicants and objectors, and it
would be out of place for me as Minister
of Home Affairs to make any general
representations to the Tribunal of the
nature suggested by the hon. and gallant
Member.
Major MCCORMICK: May I ask the
Minister if he is aware that these increases inflict great hardships upon many
people who have gone to live permanently
in the country?
Sir DAWSON BATES: As I have
already pointed out, these applications
will come before the Tribunal, when, no
doubt, my hon. and gallant Friend's
friends will be present and will put forward their views.

NUMBER OF BETTING

3. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
give a return of the number of betting
prosecutions for the year ending 31st
December, 1931; the total amount of
fines received and the number of persons
prosecuted.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The number
of betting prosecutions in Northern Ireland for the year ended 31st December,
1931, was 2,367; the number of persons
convicted was 2,359; and the total
amount of fines received was £8,300
approximately.
DISTRESS SCHEMES IN BELFAST
-WORKMEN'S INSURANCE CON-
TRIBUTIONS.
.
4. Major BLAKISTON HOUSTON
asked the Minister of Labour whether it
is a fact that men employed on distress
schemes undertaken by the Belfast Corporation in conjunction with the
Guardians do not have insurance contributions paid in respect of them, and, if
so, whether he will take steps to have
such contributions paid.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Section 15 of the Unemployment Insurance (Northern Ireland) Act,
1928, which corresponds to a provision in
the Imperial Statutes definitely makes the
class of employment referred to in this
question non-insurable so far as Unemployment Insurance is concerned and unemployment contributions are not, therefore, payable. Contributions are, however, payable under the National Health
Insurance and Contributory Pensions
Acts.
EMPLOYMENT REGISTER.
the
5. Major MCCORMICK asked
Minister of Labour whether he can state
the number of persons formerly signing
the employment register and who have
ceased to do so without obtaining work
through the Exchange.
Mr. ANDREWS: There are no records
kept of the number of persons who cease
to sign the register without obtaining
work through the Exchange.
However, between April, 1931, and
April, 1932, there were 32,764 vacancies
filled by the Employment Exchanges.
During the same period the number of
persons in Northern Ireland in employment insurable under the Unemployment
Insurance Acts increased by approximately 16,000.

NEWSPAPER REPORTS.
Mr. NIXON: Would I be in order in
asking you, Mr. Speaker, if it is competent for newspapers or others to report
or publish proceedings of this House, or
exchanges between hon. Members, incorrectly, or to make such reports incorrect
by way of addition, omission, alteration,
evasion, or otherwise?
Mr. SPEAKER: It would be a matter
of privilege which the hon. Member could
raise. Any newspaper has a perfect
right to publish any extracts it pleases
from debates that take place in this
House, and provided the report does not
maliciously misrepresent any hon. Member
of this House a newspaper is quite entitled to print or to leave out what it
pleases.

separate the children from the father and

mother, and also separate the father from

the bus from Newtownards, in the second

fare. That is proof of the statement that
there is destitution in County Down.
I contend that facilities should be given
to the people who use the buses.
We
all realise the terrible condition of industry in the country districts. It is
almost impossible in towns like Carrickfergus and Newtownards to get a living.
Even when work is obtained the people
do not get much money. I hope the
Minister will take immediate action in
regard to putting a stop to any suggestion of increasing the bus charges for
people travelling to and from outlying
country districts.
In regard to the roads, I contend that
the Government are not doing the proper
thing in regard to them. The Ministry
of Home Affairs, which should be looking
after the health and wellbeing of the
people, has been responsible for sending
out circulars curtailing the expenditure
in regard to the construction of new roads.
The Ministry of Labour asked the local
authorities, through circulars, to cut
down the expenses in regard to the reconstruction of roads. That, in the first instance, creates unemployment, and
employment is necessary at the present
time. It means that the roads that require attention now are going to be in a
dilapidated state and will eventually cost
fifty per cent. more to repair them. It
means that sewers which should be put
in will not be laid, and the earth will
be permeated with matters that will be a
menace to the health and wellbeing of
the people.
In connection with the policy of the
Government in regard to town planning,
the Minister of Home Affairs was asked
seven years ago by Members on all sides
to bring in a Town Planning Bill, but it
was not introduced until recently. If
the Bill had been introduced when it was
demanded first it would have resulted in
a saving of millions of pounds for the
taxpapers. I would like to ask the Parliamentary Secretary what action the Ministry proposes to take to compel the local
authority in Dungannon to introduce a
sewerage scheme there. Such a scheme
would mean the employment of hundreds
of men for a number of months, and yet
the Minister allows the health of the
people there to be sadly neglected. The
same thing applies to other parts of Northern Ireland where the Ministry has
suggested doing away with necessary reforms. I would instance a case. In
Trooper's Lane, County Antrim, 19
houses are taking water from a river that
is polluted with all sorts of nuisances.
Can you realise that the people there have
to go to an old drain, put a bucket in and
draw water from that river for their
personal use?

I do not know whether the Ministry of

who drive motors know that if you have

Home Affairs, so that they may be

drove from Dublin to Belfast this morning. It is something like 108 miles, and
I can assure you that once you have
driven it you do not want to turn round
and drive back again immediately.
Some two or three years ago I remember a case brought before the Grand Jury
of County Down in which a bus driver
near Banbridge actually fell asleep at the
wheel of his bus, and by doing so drove
over a man and his wife and killed them.
I only mention that to illustrate the
danger which can arise through people
being asked to drive for longer than
nature will allow. Therefore, I would
like to support the hon. Member for Pottinger in asking the Minister of Home
Affairs to regulate the working-hours of
these bus drivers so as to ensure that the

would like to add that from my experience the bus drivers in Northern Ireland are very much improved during the

of giving way on the road. The driving
in general is greatly improved, and we do
not want to go back to the old days.

he thought it an idea well worthy of

hon. Member for Pottinger and the hon.
Member for Shankill were pointing out
the excessively long hours these bus
drivers have to work. As far as the
railways are concerned, as we all know,
all railway servants have only an eighthour day.
The traffic on the roads is so complicated
and so dangerous that really I would
imagine it is an easier job to drive a
steam locomotive on a railway line than
it is to drive a bus on the public road.
After all, all the engine driver has to
look out for are the signals, and that is
not nearly so hard a job as that of a bus
driver looking out for traffic on the road
and not knowing where it is going to or
where it is coming from. An engine
driver has to be at his shed half an hour
before his engine leaves the shed, and his
time is counted as beginning from that
hour; and he is allowed another half hour
when he arrives back at night. All that
is included in his eight-hours day. If by
chance his run during the day exceeds
eight hours he is paid overtime, and, as
far as possible, the railway companies try
to keep him reasonably near the eight
hours. Another point is that if a driver
exceeds 120 miles in a day he is paid
overtime.
As I listened to the figures quoted by
the hon. Member for Pottinger I realised

I have tried to impress on the House
time and again, namely, that the railways are suffering under most unfair competition from road traffic. We have heard
to-day about the bus fares. Candidly-
I may be saying an unpopular thing-I
think these fares were far too low. They
were far below economic reason or business common-sense. I have got hold of

There is no difference in the

betting laws in relation to the rich man

Mourne put to me. Could I deny that

The hon. Member is perfectly right.
There is a constant and incessant demand
every day in the week, every hour of the
day, and nearly every minute of the
hour by our good temperance reformersthey want the licensing law changed.
Other people who are more or less interested want the law changed. Everybody wants a change in the licensing law.
If it be true that the facilities for
getting intoxicating liquor in a country
attracts tourists, then the only advertisement that our area gets along those lines
are the speeches of ardent temperance reformers, who constantly proclaim from
the street corners and pulpits and everywhere else that in Northern Ireland you
can get a drink on Sunday at any time
you like. Then we have it from hon.
Members opposite that this is the driest
place in the world for a visitor on a
Sunday. Neither the temperance advocates
of that kind nor the hon. Members
opposite truly or accurately represent
the facts. Although we consider that in
our temperance legislation we have gone
farther than most other places still, I
believe, this is the most comfortable
place for a visitor to be on any day of
the week, whether on Sunday or Monday,
because from ten o'clock to ten o'clock,
except in small places where the hours
are from ten to nine, he has a constant
opportunity of getting a drink at any
time between those hours.
If it is reasonable refreshment that is
required I think-and I speak with some
modesty, of course, and with some little
experience that the man who could not
find reasonable refreshment on a Sunday
from ten o'clock in the morning until ten
o'clock at night is the sort of a visitor
who should not be here at all. (Laughter.)
Surely nobody connected with the trade
or opposed to the sale of intoxicating
liquor wants to go back to the days of
the old bona fide traveller. That was
always an anomaly and did an enormous
amount of harm. I rather believe it
moulded the opinion of the people and
made them take a stronger view against
the liquor trade than they would have
entertained but for the abuses of that
old law. I can promise no change in
the licensing law, but I would like, as
far as my words will ever reach those
who intend to visit our shores, to tell
them that the hospitality they may expect
is not so lavish as the temperance advocate,
would suggest, and is not so restricted as
those who sit opposite would lead them
to believe, but that, on the whole, they
will find this a comfortable and convenient place to be in on a Sunday.

know that very well. If times

were
The people have only one remedy, and

per

Mr. ANDREWS: Notwithstanding
the long period which has elapsed since
these people worked, there are still 104
persons in Annsborough and 38 in Castlewellan drawing benefit. The hon. Member for Mourne (Mr. O'Neill) suggests
that I have got some discretionary power
in connection with this matter, that I can
override the decisions of the court, and
that I can override the decisions of the
umpire. Of course if I were to do so,
the Public Accounts Committee would
find fault with my Department to a
serious extent, and probably the Comptroller and Auditor-General would do so
too. Parliament is responsible for
making the law, and I am responsible
for administering it. Within the law
my Department is administering not only
this service of unemployment insurance,
but all the social services, in my opinion,
as sympathetically as it is possible for it to
do.
As regards the question that has been
raised about blind persons' pensions, I
wish to say that no one would be sorrier
than I would be if any person who is
blind within the meaning of the Act was
deprived of the pension, but thank goodness, it is not my duty to decide what
the degree of blindness is.
There is a
doctor for that purpose. He examines
the claimants, and decides whether or not,
in his opinion, the degree of blindness
entitles the person to a pension. Suppose
that the Department on the advice of the
doctor disallows a claim. The claimant
has a right to appeal to the local
pensions court, and, in most instances, to the umpire.
the umpire. Again, the
Department has neither the first word
nor the last word in connection with the
matter. Parliament has set up the
courts to adjudicate in these matters,
and the responsibility rests upon those
courts, and not upon me.
The hon. Member for Mourne went on
to say that people who had got the pensions some years ago were now being deprived of them. In some instances, that
is so. But the degree of blindness very
frequently changes. Eyes may get worse
or eyes may get better. In very few
cases do eyes remain stationary, as I, for
instance, know. Sight may improve in
one direction, and may get worse in
another. The fact that a person gets a
blind person's pension one year does not
mean that that person is necessarily entitled to a blind person's pension as long
as that person lives.
The proof that my Department is administering these social services sympathetically is to be found in the enormous
amount of money that the Department
is spending. I am budgeting for over
four million pounds of State money for
these social services, and in addition to
that, speaking from memory, the contributions which the workers and the employers pay amount to a million and a
half more, so that my Department is
spending the huge sum of five and
a half millions on these social services.
That being so, can anybody reasonably
say that the Department's administration is cruel and harsh, as is sometimes
said by hon. Members opposite. That is
the position as clearly expressed as I am
capable of doing it.

The reason I am interested in this

said he would not because we were getting

THE OTTAWA CONFERENCE.
NOMINATION OF DELEGATE FOR
NORTHERN IRELAND.
Mr.
MCBRIDE asked the Prime
Minister whether a representative of the
Northern Government will accompany the
United Kingdom Delegation to Ottawa?
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes, sir; I
have to announce that the Secretary of
State for the Dominions through the
Secretary of State for the Home Department has invited me to nominate a delegate to act in an advisory capacity on the
Delegation, and I am pleased to say that
my right honourable Friend the Minister
of Finance has kindly consented to act.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. COLLINS: Will this delegate act
in an advisory capacity, because under
the Government of Ireland Act we are
prohibited from having any relations
whatever with any other part of his
Majesty's Dominions? Could you not get
the Government of Ireland Act amended
before you send a delegate so as to give
you some power?
The PRIME MINISTER: I think the
answer to that is that we are all perfectly
satisfied with the Government of Ireland
Act.
Mr. DEVLIN: In view of the fact that
the Ottawa Conference is to discuss matters in which the interests of the Colonies
and Great Britain are concerned, and in
view also of the latest performance of the
present Government in reducing the tariff
of 50 per cent. to 20 per cent. in regard
to Northern Ireland linen, is the Prime
Minister not aware that there is no consideration whatever given to Northern
Ireland?
The PRIME MINISTER: It is in
order just to protect such interests I am
so delighted that the Government on the
other side have invited us to nominate a
representative to advise them in matters
particularly affecting Ulster.
Mr. DEVLIN: Can the right hon.
Gentleman tell us precisely what is the
meaning of advisory capacity? Is it to
stand out on the mat until the delegate is
called in? Is that what is meant ?
The PRIME MINISTER: My right
hon. Friend is very good at getting
the door opened when he wants it. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)

hon. Gentleman is going across to Ottawa
to confer with the Free State, does the
Prime Minister not think it would be
better to confer with them at home than
at Ottawa?
Mr. NIXON: Will the Minister of
Finance take advantage of the occasion
to ask the representatives of the Colonies
to endeavour to give effect to the promise
made by the Prime Minister standing
there about a year and a-half ago that he
would request them to assist him in solving the question of unemployment in
Northern Ireland?

The Budget-
Minister's Statement
11 MAY 1932

י
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
THE BUDGET.
Financial Statement, 1932-33.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That this House approves the proposals
of the Government for meeting the
financial requirements of the year.'
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Hon. Members will, no doubt,
recall the depressing conditions existing
a year ago, when it was found necessary
to resort to unusual expedients directed
to balancing the Budget of Northern
Ireland for the year which then lay ahead
and which closed on 31st March last.
To accomplish that result, important
sacrifices on the part of all those in receipt
of public money were demanded, and in
the main cheerfully conceded as a patriotic
necessity and duty. The figures of the
past year, which are already in the hands
of Members, and on which I propose to
comment later on, bear witness to the
success which has followed this act of
renunciation, and afford the satisfaction.
which always follows the consciousness of
right-doing, that Britain and our little.
Province almost alone of all the countries
in the world have faced the situation with
courage and success. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
The year 1931 will long be remembered
as a year fraught with momentous,
political, economic and commercial consequences to the Kingdom and Empire.
It will be written in history as the year
of the resurrection of our people from the
grave of apathy and indifference, and may
well prove a turning point in the fortunes
of the Kingdom in its relations to that
great confederation of nations and peoples
which we call the British Empire.
Furthermore, from the point of view
of commerce and industry, the year 1931
must be reckoned as in some respects one
of the blackest in our history. In its
earlier months all hope of recovery seemed
abandoned, and a feeling amounting to
despair had taken the place of expectation
and confidence. However, the very
acuteness of the economic and financial
situation was, beyond doubt, something
in a nature of a blessing. It aroused the
British people to a sense of the serious
danger to the entire structure of the
Commonwealth, and in its rebound overthrew all the fiscal traditions of one
hundred years, and opened up possibilities
of a new and prosperous era in the life
story of Britain.
In such extraordinary circumstances,
involving radical changes in the whole.
political, fiscal and financial outlook of
the country, it could not be expected that
our Province could be free from its
natural reaction on every feature of our
Provincial life, but especially in the
domain of finance.
The House will, I am sure, appreciate
the difficulties and confusion resulting
from these changes, and feel that it is
matter for congratulation that we have
emerged from this fateful year of 1931
with our current obligations met, and a
margin of contribution to the Imperial
Services greater than we undertook to provide in our Budget calculations. The
House has had presented the figures
relating to the revenue and expenditure
for the past year, and it may be thought
that these figures require little further
explanation.
But, following my usual practice in presenting our annual accounts, I feel it will
be convenient if I analyse these figures of
income and expenditure, and call attention
to some interesting comparisons between
the estimates made in the Budget of last
year, and the ultimate outcome as shewn
on the Financial Statement issued on the
last day of the financial year, 31st March.
If hon. Members will turn to Table I of
the White Paper, which has been circulated, they will find statements comparing
the estimated with the actual outturn of
last year's finance.
EXPENDITURE, 1931-32.
Dealing first of all with the expenditure
during the year 1931 we find that Consolidated Fund Services, apart from the
Road Fund, accounted for £289,000, or
£91,000 in excess of the estimate. The
details will be found in Table II, and are
as follows:-Interest on borrowings,
£145,000; sinking funds, £90,000; and
other items, £54,000. The exceeding of
the Budget Estimate arose on two main
heads (1) the high rate of interest paid
in respect of temporary borrowings,
following the departure from the gold standard in September last, when the bank
rate was as high as 6 per cent., and consequently money was considerably dearer
for bills of the character we use for our
temporary borrowings, both in Great

amongst "Other" Consolidated Fund

I come to the supply services of last

less than their Budget Estimate.

In all, then we find that the total expenditure of the Province last year amounted
to £11,577,000, and I shall now examine

REVENUE 1931-32.
The first source of revenue which I will
touch upon
is the transferred taxes, that
is, those taxes which produce revenue
which are imposed by us and collected by
These amounted to £1,008,000; that
is £30,000 less than the Budget Estimate.
The details are:-Estate duties, or death
duties, as they are generally called
£676,000, realising £9,000 in excess of
the Estimate; stamp duties, £201,000, or
£36,000 less than was estimated, and excise duties (that is income tax and licences
of various kinds) £131,000, or £3,000 less
than the Estimate.
I cannot but wonder at the fact that in
a year when the value of all securities has
been depressed to a level which a few
years ago we would have regarded as
phenomenally low, the yield of estate
duties has not only fulfilled, but has exceeded our Estimate by £9,000. May I
remind the House that estate duties are a
very variable and uncertain method of
raising revenue as it depends entirely
upon the rate of mortality during the
period. It happened that we were fortunate in receiving an item of £30,000 late
in the month of March. We regarded
that as a sort of windfall.
The yield of stamp duties reflects only
too truly the chaotic state of the world
and its reactions on business transactions
of all kinds. Hon. Members will realise
that the great bulk of our stamp duties
arise from stamps on transfers of securities
and from the buying and selling of securities. There is no doubt that until world
confidence is restored, the returns from
this duty must continue to show a shrinkage, and perhaps give us reason for
thought. Motor taxation, as I have stated
above, produced £559,000.
Still keeping to last year, I would
remind hon. Members that the Budget
Estimate for reserved taxes was
£6,945,000. In September, however, I
was informed by Mr. Snowden, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, that as a result
of the additional taxation imposed by his
Supplementary Budget, combined with

the results of the first half of the year,

£43,000; tobacco, £37,000, and oil,

In regard to Inland Revenue-that is

The total original Estimate for reserved

As against this, the actual amount to be

provided us last year with £3,580,000, and

An examination of the figures given for

is to be found in the continuous and rapid
decline in the consumption of alcoholic
liquor

As an important feature of our numerous social problems it is impossible not
to dwell, in passing, on the consistent
and persistent decline in the
sumption of alcoholic liquor in
Province, and the consequent loss

last year. In other words, we have to

two million pounds in revenue from this
source, or considerably more than 50 per
cent.

Amongst the items of non-tax revenue

may be of interest to hon. Members to

The Budget-

HOUSE OF COMMONS

of £14,000 on the working of the Post
Office, from which we receive £890,000
revenue, as against £876,000 expenditure.
A significant part of my comment is that
this is the first time in our autonomous
career that the Post Office has paid its
way, and the occasion is surely worthy
of more than a mere passing notice,
having regard to the importance of the
service.
I have watched this commercial
department of our public life from year
to year with more than ordinary interest.
I can recall in one of my Budget statements, some four or five years ago, congratulating the House that the loss on
the working of the Post Office had been
reduced at that time from a considerably
larger figure to £20,000. At any time
I had hoped and expected that we were
approaching a period when that loss on
the Post Office Service would be turned
into a profit, but the depression of recent
years falsified that hope, until to-day,
when we find, as I have said, that we
have turned the corner, and can report
a profit, however small, having regard to
the magnitude of the service, on the
operations of last year. This result is
all the more remarkable when we call
to mind the year of general commercial
difficulties through which we have passed.
I think it is possible to regard the Post
Office as a very important barometer in
respect of the conditions of trade, and
although in these depressing times it is
hard to see any blink of sunshine yet
the Post Office, if it do give any indication of trade, would show that we are
not so bad as perhaps some of our neighbours in respect of economic conditions.
The other items of non-tax revenue

and a very important tribute in regard
