In all, then, the non-tax revenue, the
items I have read, amounted to
£3,032,000, bringing the total revenue
available from all sources last year to
£11,989,000. If we deduct from this the
total expenditure for the year, namely,
£11,577,000, we are left with a balance
of £412,000 as the amount available for
surplus and Imperial contribution. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) Of this sum,
£11,000 was the balance remaining in our
Exchequer at the 31st March last,
£401,000 being held by the Imperial
Treasury as the balance of our residuary
share. So that the balance last year of
income over expenditure, I repeat, was
£412,000. That finishes last year.
have said good-bye to it so far as the
figures and accounts are concerned, and
I think we may congratulate ourselves,
having regard to the conditions prevailing in every country in the world, that
we came so happily through.

I

Now I come to the year that lies ahead.
Hon. Members will be anxious to learn
the results of my investigation into the
prospects for the year, and the steps which
I
propose to take to ensure the continuance of the solvent position in which, I
am happy to say, despite world-wide depression, we completed the year which has
passed.
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
11 MAY 1932

SUPPLY.
The House has already had the Supply
Estimates under detailed examination,
and I need not, therefore, take up very
much time on this subject. A certain
amount of disappointment has been expressed at the fact that the total
£8,937,000 is in excess of last year's total
by some £108,000. To those people who
have expressed dissatisfaction at any increase, I should like to point out that in
the current year our Supply Estimates
make provision for meeting in full from
revenue the cost of unemployment insurance. We borrowed last year £840,000
for current unemployment needs for which
no provision whatever appeared in our
Estimates. But this year we have provided out of the Exchequer the necessary
money to provide for the transitional
benefit outlay. I am sure the House will
agree that it is wiser and sounder policy
that a matter of this kind should be
covered from year to year out of revenue
rather than that a huge debt should be
piled up. (Hon. Member: Hear, hear.)
The Consolidated Fund items of last
year were:-Interest, £133,000; Sinking
Funds, £195,000; Road Fund, £570,000,
and other Consolidated Fund charges,
£160,000, making a total of £1,058,000.
The interest charge contains £95,000 for
Treasury Bills and £38,000 for Ulster
savings certificates. This figure is a net
amount after the appropriate withdrawal
of £24,000 from the Interest Sinking
Fund. The gross interest to be paid on
Ulster savings certificates during the year
is estimated at £62,000. The House will
understand that it is necessary that we
should provide from year to year for the
payment of interest and also the increase
in the value of these savings certificates
as years go on.
The Sinking Fund payments, it will be
seen, are £105,000 in excess of last year.
£85,000 is due to the restoration of the
normal allocation to the Land Purchase
Sinking Fund established for the purpose
of preserving in perpetuity the annual
value of the existing land purchase
annuities. The House will remember
that it was necessary in the exigencies of
the position a year ago to utilise a sum of
£85,000 by withholding for a year the
contribution to the Sinking Fund on our
land purchase annuities. The excuse for
that was that we were ahead in regard to
the necessary provision for extinguishing
the land annuities at the time we expected they would expire, and we argued
from that that it was a perfectly justifiable
withdrawal, having regard to the necessity
of balancing our accounts. But this year,
on the other hand, I propose to make the
ordinary provision, amounting to £85,000,
and the restoration of that will keep the
fund in its proper condition.
The remainder of the increase is due to normal
growth in the allocations to the Sinking
Fund for meeting the interest payable in
respect of Ulster savings certificates.
in
The figure of £160,000 for other Consolidated Fund issues contains provision of
£150,000 to meet possible liabilities
connection with loan guarantees.
Although, as I have stated in the House
on previous occasions, the Government is
convinced that the reorganisation scheme
which has recently been adopted for the
future management of the Royal Mail
group of companies has reasonable prospects of success, I feel that, having regard
to the fact that this will be the first year
of the scheme's working, and to the continued depression in shipping, it is only
prudent to make this provision against
possible losses, not only on Royal Mail
guarantees, but on guarantees to any other
companies on which losses may arise. It
is simply an Insurance Fund.
RESERVED SERVICES.
Having dealt with the expenditure in
regard to our own operations and for our
own requirements here, I come now to the
cost of operating the Reserved Services.
The total required for the Reserved
Services is £1,766,000. I do not propose
to weary the House with details, as there
is nothing to which I need specially direct
the attention of hon. Members. Full
details will, of course, be found in the
completed White Paper. I think it right,
however, to call attention to the expenditure on the Post Office, amounting to
£891,000, to which I have already referred
in my statement with regard to last
year.
Our total expenditure for the current
year I estimate, therefore, as follows:-

Now I come to the revenue which
should be available to meet-this expenditure. The first item I take is what
the House understands as transferred
revenue, that is to say, revenue that we
collect and control ourselves.
I cannot expect the Estate Duties to
continue the high yield of past years,
and I do not, therefore, rely on this
source for more than £600,000 in place
of the £676,000 realised last year.
Stamp Duties are estimated to yield
£211,000, a figure £10,000 in excess of
last year's receipts, but appreciably below
the normal yield of these duties. I feel
that, having regard to present unsettled
conditions of the Kingdom, and of the
world, my estimate cannot, with prudence, be placed any higher.
Excise Duties will, I anticipate, realise
the same amount as last year, namely,
£131,000.
I expect motor taxation to produce
£570,000, that is, £11,000 over the
£559,000 yielded last year. There is a
continual movement in the results of
motor taxation from year to year in an
upward direction, and I do not think
there is any reason to apprehend that the
coming year will be any exception to that
rule.

Now I come to the reserved revenue.
In Customs and Excise, we expect to
derive substantial additions this year in
three directions. Firstly, there is the introduction of the new tariff policy by the
Government of the United Kingdom.
The new duties thereby entailed will add
to our Revenue an amount estimated at
£590,000. Secondly, the changes in the
Tea and Sugar Duties, will, we hope,
provide an additional £63,000 net; and
thirdly, the return to normal collection
of the Tobacco Duties-it will be remembered that last year our revenue suffered
severely by the premature withdrawal of
large quantities of that commodity from
Bond in anticipation of adverse Budget
changes-leads us to expect in the current
year an additional amount under this
head estimated at £340,000.
As against these increases, we are
forced to reduce our expectations from
the liquor duties, in view of the continuing decline in consumption.
And now I will give a summary of the
total amount of Customs and Excise

INLAND REVENUE.
The prospects of the Inland Revenue
show, unhappily, a very different state of
affairs. I have already mentioned that
the abnormally large collection in 1931-32
was in large measure due to the fact that
payments had been made by numbers of
taxpayers at an earlier date than usual.
Although this factor influenced last year's
revenue substantially to our advantage,
hon. Members will readily realise that it
has a converse effect on the revenues of
the present year. I need not enlarge
upon the general shrinkage of incomes
suffered by all classes of taxpayers last
year on account of the appalling state of
industry and trade. Clearly we must,
on that account, apprehend a substantial
reduction in the yield of Income and Sur-
Tax this year, which is assessed on last
year's incomes.
From these two causes, I am unable to
rely upon the Inland Revenue, which last
year produced £3,810,000, for more than
£3,250,000.
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
11 MAY 1932

The yield of the individual duties is
expected to be as follows:-Income tax,
£2,800,000; sur-tax, £440,000; corporation and excess profits duties,
£10,000; making a total of £3,250,000.
In addition to these amounts to be
collected within the current year, I am,
however, expecting to receive certain
adjustments of our residuary share of
reserved taxes for the past two years
(which will shortly come before the Joint
Exchequer Board for their consideration),
the payment of which will fall within this
year, and which will amount to approximately £350,000, thus bringing the total
amount of reserved taxes to be brought
to credit up to £8,203,000. The total
tax revenue for the current year is therefore estimated at-transferred taxes,
non-tax revenue, £1,870,000.
There are no special considerations to
affect my estimates of the various items
of non-tax revenue. They are very short
and easily understood. The amounts are
as follows:
-
Transferred: "Existing " land purchase annuities, £658,000; church temporalities, £19,000; interest and miscellaneous, £283,000; making the total
transferred, £960,000.
Reserved: Post Office, £910,000; total
non-tax revenue, £1,870,000. A total of
£1,870,000.
I am now in a position to construct my
complete Estimate of the income and
expenditure account for 1932-33.
Mr. HEALY: Before the right hon.
Gentleman leaves that, will he explain to
us whether the "interest and miscellaneous" includes the borrowing on the
Unemployment Insurance Fund
I
Mr. POLLOCK. I presume it does.
I have been engaged in so many figures
that at the moment I cannot answer the
hon. Member with definiteness. It is
easily discovered, but I believe it does.
have shown that the total receipts from
revenue may be taken at: Tax revenue,
£9,365,000; adjustment of residuary
share, £350,000; non-tax revenue,
£1,870,000. To these must be added
grants from the Imperial Government in
respect of public buildings, £149,000;
unemployment equalisation, £97,000; and
the self-balancing items of local loans repayments, £75,000; and "new" land
purchase annuities, £287,000. The total
income for 1932-33 is therefore estimated
at £12,193,000.
The total charges against this amount
consist of our local expenditure,
£11,761,000, to which must be added the
self-balancing items in respect of local
loans and "new" land purchase annuities
to which I have just referred, £362,000,
giving as our total charge against income,
£12,123,000, leaving a balance available
for surplus and Imperial contribution of
£70,000. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I do not,.however, regard this balance
as sufficient, and I propose, therefore, to
ask my colleagues to join with me in
taking steps to ensure, by special measures
of economy, a saving of at least £50,000
on the Supply Estimates. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). It will not, I am
aware, be easy to achieve this, but the
task should not prove impossible, granted
the good-will of our people, and a recognition by all of the fact that in times such
as the world is experiencing to-day,
measures of economy must be adopted
and services curtailed to an extent which
in times of normal prosperity could not
be regarded with favour.
By effecting this saving of £50,000, 1
shall increase the balance available for
Surplus and Imperial Contribution to
£120,000, and although this amount will
only make it possible for us to pay a contribution towards Imperial Services considerably less than I should like to be
regarded as our normal responsibility, I
feel some satisfaction that in times such
as the present we are able to balance our
accounts and to provide for even a small
contribution without the adoption of revolutionary methods.
Some disappointment may be felt in
certain quarters that I have been unable
to lessen the burden of taxation. I have
received strong representations regarding
the incidence of both the Entertainments
Duty and Motor Taxation. The figures
which I have to-day presented to the
House themselves provide the answer to
these applications.
Before I close, there are two matters on
which I should like to dwell for a moment.
The first has relation to the necessity for
economy. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
As I have said, I have undertaken to discover savings to the extent of £50,000
within our Departmental Estimates s
submitted. Not only is there no room for
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Pollock]
Supplementary Votes, but we must cut
down the existing provision. Therefore,
I would strongly advise those who have
schemes on hand, or who are thinking of
undertaking even desirable schemes, to
endeavour to stand on their own feet for
a change, and not rely on the Government. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
This is apart, of course, from the distress
and relief schemes, of which information
has already been given to the public and
which must appeal to all. The value of
practically any scheme is its ability to
support itself, and one of the most
valuable qualities, in my judgment at any
rate, to acquire and develop is that of the
old spirit of Ulster self-reliance.
The second has reference to ouc
Imperial contribution. It is right I
should give information in regard to how
that has been treated during the last ten
years of our life. Notwithstanding that
we have not by any means been immune
from the adversity which has overtaken
the world, we have been able to
pay approximately £25,000,000 to the
Imperial Exchequer since we took over
financial responsibilities in November,
1921. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Furthermore, there are, in addition,
several hidden sources of contribution to
the Imperial Services, which do not
appear in our accounts, by reason of the
financial limitations imposed by the
Government of Ireland Act. I reckon
that these amount to not far from
£500,000 annually.
In addition, I would like to point out
that our contribution is paid after we
have met all our charges for land purchase, including bonus and excess stock,
to the extent of £250,000 annually. We
have provided the farmers of Northern
Ireland with the fee simple of their
property to a considerable extent, at any
rate until it is finally extinguished.
I cannot think, therefore, that the
worst enemies of Ulster can successfully
cast any aspersion on the soundness of the
financial position of the Province, seeing
that our real contribution to our great
Imperial Services is not by any means inconsiderable.
I am happy to say, finally, that our
credit on
the London Market stands
deservedly high, as always, and we have
now a keen competition for any Treasury
Bills we may require for our temporary
needs.
I think we may congratulate ourselves,
having regard, as I say, to the conditions.
of the world, that we have been able in
this little Province removed from the
heart of affairs, but still not immune from
the difficulties and reaction resulting from
world-wide conditions-we may congratulate ourselves that we have come happily
through our difficulties so far. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. HEALY: I think it is customary on
occasions of this kind to offer some congratulation to the Mover of this Resolution. It is customary in another place to
have a statement of this kind,. very
intricate and very elaborate as it is, and
involving a great number of figures, discussed on the day following. In this
House, however, it has been the custom
to discuss the matter right off the reel as
it were, and that does put, I submit,
Members of the Opposition in rather a
difficulty, because, to-morrow, when we
have had the opportunity of going through
these figures at our leisure many matters,
no doubt, would call for criticism and
inquiry that probably will have escaped
in the mere listening to or reading of the
very intricate statement of the Chancellor
to-day.
I notice that the Minister of Finance
is very much more hopeful of the future
than the Imperial Chancellor. Mr.
Chamberlain, speaking the other day,
declared that this country was not yet out
of the wood, and I think probably he
could not have put the position better in
those few words, so that people everywhere might realise the gravity and
seriousness of the position which is confronting this country to-day. The Chancellor took some pride in the fact that so
far he has contributed a sum of
£25,000,000 by way of Imperial contributions to Great Britain. I do not know
what view the people of the Six Counties
may take of that, but I would say, at all
events, that. it is a tremendous decline
from the original sum provided for in the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920. This
Government was established in 1921, and
if the Imperial contribution of £7,000,000
had been paid all these years, I can quite
see that instead of standing on its feet
to-day it would have vanished. The
Minister of Finance for a moment also
dwelt upon the question of alcoholic
licence duties. It seems to me we have
approached a period when we are about

to kill the goose that laid the golden egg,
that carried the Northern Government
along all these years.

Mr. JOHN JOHNSTON: I rise to
congratulate the Minister of Finance on
the very excellent Budget statement he
has made. I am sure he is quite pleased
that, with the British Chancellor, he has
been able to record a surplus, a thing
which we did not think would be possible
last year.
I am sure he is surprised and
delighted to know that, along with the
British Chancellor, he is the only Chancellor up to the present who can face a
House of Commons with a surplus. There
are increases in taxation, but we on this
side of the House are prepared to pay
those taxes if the end is achieved, and
if Great Britain and Northern Ireland
will thereby be enabled to pay their
way.
There is one section of the community
to whom, I think, the Minister of Finance
might have paid a tribute, that is, the
taxpayers of Northern Ireland, because
it was the taxpayers of Northern Ireland
who gave the Minister his surplus. It was
the taxpayers who paid up on last January
and enabled the Minister of Finance to
balance his Budget. I think a tribute
is due to them for their patriotic action
in doing so.
On thing we very often hear in this
House is that Northern Ireland is too
small an area to have a Parliament, as
the expenses would be too great on
account of its area and the size of its
population. That view is often put forward by the Opposition, which is nonexistent at present.
I wish they were
here. I myself was under the impression
that Northern Ireland was a very small
and a very insignificant place when I
looked at it on the map, but on making
enquiries, to my amazement I found that
seven of the thirteen New England States
which formed the Federal Government
of America were comparable in area with
Northern Ireland. They are Vermont,
New Hampshire, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Delaware and
Maryland. Of those seven States only
one at the present time has a larger
population than Northern Ireland, that
is Massachusetts.
That fact fortifies the opinion that Northern Ireland has an area big enough,
and is populous enough to govern itself,
and I am sure that we will not listen to
any more of these stories that Northern
Ireland is too small an area to have a Government. That brings me to a point which
I think the Chancellor of the Exchequer
touched upon rather lightly, that is,
the crisis through which this world is
passing and which is not over yet. He only
touched on it lightly, because of the fact
that happily we are linked with the
finances of Great Britain.

Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Mr. JOHNSTON: The right hon.
Gentleman when there is nothing in one
pocket can put his hand into the other.
This time he has done so to nearly the

It is so small that the Minister thinks it

in consequence, determined, if it is possible, to add another £50,000 to it. That

I believe that our Government and the
Government of Great Britain will be
compelled, whether they like it or not,
to economise much more than they have
done. I want to make sure the Government are going to do this.
No matter what Government are in

they did last year. The limit of taxa-
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
11 MAY 1932
tion has been reached (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). If any more taxes are put
on, or if the existing taxation is increased, instead of the Government getting more money they will get less
money. Therefore, I say that the Governments of Great Britain and Northern
Ireland will have to economise in both
expenditure and salaries. I would not
be surprised to see this Government very
shortly following the example of Great
Britain in appointing a Commission to
go into the expenditure of the various
Departments.
I can quite see that is coming on the
other side, and I hope this Government
will not hesitate to take that course too.
It is high time they did it. I am of the
opinion, and have been of the opinion for
many years, that the savings effected in
Northern Ireland could be very much
greater without in any way interfering
with the efficiency of our splendid Civil
Service. There is one thing you can have.
You can have too much of a good thing.
The Civil Service is a splendid organisation, but you can have too much of a good
thing. I believe the curtailment of some
of the operations of the Civil Service
could very well be effected without loss of
efficiency.
Captain CHICHESTER-CLARK: I
would like to add my tribute of congratulation to the right hon. Gentleman, the
Minister of Finance, for the able and
lucid way in which he introduced the
Budget for the coming year. If I may
say so, with all respect, he brought it in
with all the pep, and energy, and dash of
a very young man. But the curious
action of the Opposition has rather left
us dumbfounded. I feel I would not be
wrong in congratulating that party on
having done the best thing they have ever
done, that is retiring and letting us get
on with the debate.
I know that a few years ago it would
have been thought, and perhaps it is still
thought, a very presumptuous thing for
a private and humble back bencher to get
up and criticise, or even talk upon, the
nation's Budget. But times have
changed since then, and the people upon
whom we looked as kings of finance have
faded away.
A few years ago if a man's
name began with H-Harrison, Horne,
or Hatry-or even if it had been Kylsant
or Kreuger, we should have listened to
him with great reverence, and we would
have tried to follow out the financial
schemes he was recommending. But, as

There can be no doubt-and I feel that
perhaps I am wasting my eloquence, as
the Opposition are not here-that legislation in the past ten years has been
legislation for one class only. I am not
disagreeing with that. I am glad to see
the sort of legislation which has been
passed and which has so greatly improved
the lot of the poorer people of the world,
but there can be no denial that legislation
has been for one class only. During the
history of the British Empire we have
seen legislation first of all by the feudal
class, then by an absolute monarch, then
a limited monarch, and in recent years
and the years during which Great Britain
has made wonderful strides to prosperity,
the ruling classes have been the middle
class, and it is through their wise rule that
Great Britain is now the country it is
to-day.
Unfortunately the rule of the middle.
classes is passing away. and the country

These are the direct results. The indirect results are much greater and spread
much further, but I want to stick strictly

results were. The action on the labour
market and the action on unemployment
of these death duties suddenly operated
have been exactly the same as a catastrophe like the fire on the Bermuda. I
think from the calculations I have made
that every thousand pounds collected in

unemployment register or it keeps one
man on who otherwise might come off.
By every thousand pounds of death duties
we are adding one more man to the Minister of Labour's troubles.
The reason I raised this question so
definitely at the present time is this.
During the years preceding the war, and
I might even add a few years after the
war, there was a certain prosperity in the
land, and there was a chance for the
thrifty and hard-working to replace
capital that had been snatched from the
country by the operations of these taxes.
There was a chance for every man during
his lifetime, if thrifty and saving, to be
able to put back a little of the capital
previously taken away. Now, and here
is the point, there is no possibility in the
days of bad trade for replacement, and
nobody can save anything. Apart from
the complete destruction of any incentive
to thrift, most people, most firms, and
most industries are living on their
capital. There will be no hope of any
real saving for several years to come. In
the meantime, if this depression goes on
it is only an actuarial calculation to say
that the country will be dispossessed both
of capital and income in the course of
five or six years. For that reason I
would ask the Chancellor of the Exchequer when he comes to make the
Budget in future years to bear these
points in mind. I do not want him to
answer me now. I know the answer he
will give me, because I have read in

I had not intended to rise to-day. I

These figures are in many respects

Reference has already been made by the

the fact that, for the first time since the

That is a matter for congratulation-
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-because, if

estimate or understand, has been changed

But there is one factor in this Budget
to which I think it would pay to draw
attention, and that is that, in spite of all
our lip service to economy in the past, our
estimated expenditure for the year upon
which we have just entered is slightly
higher that it was for the year which has
just passed. I have the exact figures here
for the past three or four years since I
had the honour to become a Member of
this House, and I think they are somewhat significant. I find that for the year
1928-29 the expenditure of this Parliament amounted to £9,861,000, that in the
following year it increased to £11,109,000,
that last year our expenditure was
£11,411,000, that for the past year our
expenditure was slightly higher at
£11,577,000; and for the year to come,
taking down the figures which have been
supplied by the Minister, I find
that our estimated expenditure amounts
to £11,760,000.
I mention these figures with some degree
of apprehension. I do not blame the
Minister of Finance. That is not his
duty. His duty is, in accordance with
the financial decisions of this House and
in accordance with the Votes in Supply,
like a prudent accountant to arrange if
possible for a balance on the credit side.
But the figures are somewhat significant
of the tendency of what we may call the
modern state. That tendency has already
been referred to by the hon. and gallant
Gentleman (Captain Chichester-Clark)
who has preceded me, that tendency
towards socialisation, towards the increase
of the Supply Services and the social services. That tendency, it seems to me, is
a dangerous tendency unless there is some
prospect of a check somewhere.
I am not for one moment criticising

the widows and orphans for whom we now

a permanent basis. I say that for

afternoon. I hope sincerely that his ideas
will be carried out, and that he will be
able at the end of this year to show that
this saving has been effected. I think the
greatest compliment ever paid to the
Minister of Finance since this House was
established was the fact that the Members of the Opposition marched out of the
House without a word of criticism or
congratulation. No greater compliment
could be paid to the Minister of Finance.
I want also to congratulate him on the
fact that he made a statement which
amazed me, that was, that he and his
Colleagues in the Cabinet are the best
temperance advocates in Northern Ireland. I am delighted to have it on the
authority of the Minister of Finance that
he and the other Members of the Cabinet
are our greatest temperance advocates.
He had some scathing criticism to make
of extravagant statements made on this
question outside. I am a temperance
advocate, but I have never made an extravagant statement. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
I think it is just a question whether
the pulpit and the platform, which the
Minister referred to, have not been as
useful and as helpful in bringing about
temperance feeling in the country as even
the actions of the right hon. Gentleman,
the Minister of Finance. I heartily congratulate him on those actions, but I
assure him that pulpit and platform have
helped him very considerably in this particular matter. I have absolutely no
sympathy with extravagant statements,
and I think it is a matter for congratulation that there is a stronger temperance
feeling throughout the country to-day
than there has been for years past.
I join in congratulating the Minister
on the fact that he is introducing no new
taxes. If new taxes were needed I think
I could suggest one or two, but this is
not the occasion for doing so. I would
like to refer to what the hon. and gallant
Member for South Derry (Captain
Chichester-Clark) said regarding death
duties. I think the £500,000 he put
down is a very large amount, and that
he must expect a great number of people
to die, which I hope will not happen, if
he is to get that sum. I would appeal
to the right hon. Gentleman to try to be
a little easier, if he can, on those estates.
I had to do with a very small estate
recently, and it became absolutely_necessary for the people left behind to borrow
money to pay the estate duty. That left
them in a very awkward position so that
they can scarcely keep their heads above
water. Every hundred pounds taken in
estate duty has a tendency to reduce the
working capital both in business and
estates, and makes it more difficult for
them to carry on. That, in its turn,
brings down income-tax, and the result
is a vicious circle. I appeal to the right
hon. Gentleman to try to have these death
duties reduced in futurę.
I notice that he believes there will be
£1,023,000 more received from Customs
and Excise and from the tariffs that are
being put on imports. I did not get the
exact amount that he attributes to tariffs
and the amount he attributes to Customs
and Excise. I hope the greater part of
this is not-

matter

any further, except to say

The Budget-
Minister's Statement
11 MAY 1932

I join with the other Members who
have spoken before me in saying there is
an urgent and clamant need for economy
in every sense of the word. I think the
time is coming when this Government will
have to set about reducing its salaries on
a much larger scale than they have
attempted in the past. I hope that it
will be realised that the income of everybody in the country, the taxpayers and
the ratepayers, is being reduced tremendously. Agriculture, shipbuilding,
and linen are in a bad way, and so I join
with the hon. and gallant Member for
South Derry in saying that the time
has come when we must exercise the
strictest possible economy, and when
everybody has to try to bear his share of
the burden.
Mr. BEATTIE: I would like to extend
my congratulations to the Minister of
Finance on the manner in which he presented his Budget. In saying that I
would like to concentrate on the policy
now being pursued by the Chancellor of
this Parliament and the Chancellor of
the Imperial Parliament, that is, the
policy of undoing direct taxation and
introducing indirect taxation, which has
been the policy adopted by the Conservative Government in the past, a
policy that was responsible for dragging
out of the poorer classes an amount of
money far in excess of their capacity to
pay. I
am opposed to the indirect
taxation policy on the ground that the
equalisation of the nation's productive
wealth is not based on the same percentage as-
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Indirect
taxation is touching upon what is in the
purview alone of the Imperial Government, as the hon. Gentleman knows.
Mr. BEATTIE: I know that tea,
sugar, matches, and all those things are
essential for the upkeep of the working
man's home. On those articles have been
reimposed taxes to the extent
£30,000,000, which were taken off by the
Labour Government.
of
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: The hon.
Gentleman cannot, as I have been pointing out, discuss them, because they represent services not within the control of
this Parliament.
Mr. BEATTIE: I am not going to
discuss them at the moment, but I am
against that policy.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: The hon.
Gentleman cannot refer to that.
Mr. BEATTIE: I object to that
policy of indirect taxation.
Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: The hon.
Gentleman knows he cannot object here.
It is outside our purview.
Mr. BEATTIE: I object to that
policy, and I agree with the hon. and
gallant Member for South Derry (Captain
Chichester-Clark). He condemned the
Government for living in the clouds.
Yes, they are living in the clouds, because the system under which we are
living has now fallen into decay, and it
is going to fall round about us unless
some new generation of thought comes in
to reconstruct it. Therefore, the Government have got to the clouds for fear
of that great crash that is coming about.
The ideas of the ancients have got to
pass away, and the standards that have
been cruelly brought about have got to
take a quicker step in the future than in
the past.
That means that a greater revenue must
be obtained for the upkeep of that
higher standard for the people. But it
must be derived from this angle. The
Chancellor of the Exchequer must bear
in mind that 80 per cent. of the productive wealth of the nation is at the
moment divided between 20 per cent. of
the nation, and that 80 per cent. of the
nation is living on 20 per cent. of its
wealth. That unequal distribution in
itself has caused this decay, this enormous
amount of disorder, and this enormous
amount of starvation and poverty in our
midst. That has all got to be changed,
and the sooner the better. Hon. Members may talk about Socialists and Communists, but those are the new ideas and
they are bound to come. The hon. and
gallant Member may not be here when
they come into operation, and I may not
be here either.
Captain
CHICHESTER CLARK:
They did not come at the last election.
Mr. BEATTIE: We do not bring
them in a day or in a month, but they
are irresistible, and as sure as night
follows day they will come in the future,
because the system we are living under
has failed to provide a living for the
worker. We have in Northern Ireland,

HOUSE OF COMMONS

out of a population of a million and a

If a properly organised system of society
were in existence, would those 70,000
people be denied the right to work?
I think

""

Mr. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: The mental thoughts of the hon. Member or those

Mr. BEATTIE: I am opposing the
policy of the Government on the grounds
that the policy they have been pursuing
in the past and are endeavouring to follow
in the present twelve months is bound
to bring disaster in the end. That being
so, I am entitled to pursue my arguments

The hon. and gallant Member said he was
not decrying the taxation of the people
for the social services. Out of the total
revenue of Northern Ireland, do the
social services take away more than they
are entitled to? I say no. Who are the
people the social services cover?
The
hon. and gallant Member was in a State
service for many years, and he did honour
to himself, perhaps, in the rank he filled.
He has been compensated by the State
for the services rendered. I do not
object. But we are only compensating
the industrial soldier on condition that he
has attained the age of 70, and that he
has not a sufficient income to maintain
himself in any comfort and decency.
That is a State service paid for by the
State. Old age pensions do not take
away very much income.
Mr. POLLOCK: A million and a half.
Mr. BEATTIE: A million and a half
out of, possibly, £12,000,000, is not a big
amount. Now we come down to the
contributory pension, the pension at 65,
and the widows' and orphans' pensions.
You must remember that extra taxation
was placed upon the working men to
qualify for these pensions. I have not
forgotten that the State pays part of these
pensions.
Mr. POLLOCK: And the employer.
Mr. BEATTIE: And the employer.
The whole contribution, I entirely agree
with the hon. Member, is paid out of
industry. Out of the State comes a
portion; out of wages comes a portion; and out of industry comes a portion, so that the whole, from the broad
point of view, comes out of industry.
Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Hon. MEMBERS: No, no.
Mr. BEATTIE: Yes, it does. Industry is the workshop of the producer, and
the producers are the payers of the contributory system of pensions. I put it
this way to Members opposite, that without the producer you have not a farthing
of income.
Mr. POLLOCK: Who is the producer?
Mr. BEATTIE: All men who work by
hand or brain.
Mr. POLLOCK: The hands have
nothing to do with it. It is the brain.
Mr. BEATTIE: The right hon. Gentleman says the hands are nothing without
the brain. The Lord gave us all brains
to use. Some are not as highly efficient
as others. We have highly efficient brain
work and we have highly efficient hand
work. I tell you that with the 100 per
cent. efficient brain you possess, if you
had not a hand you could not produce
anything. I want to say the whole producing classes are the real asset of the
nation. We derive all from that class.
Therefore, those who bemoan or criticise
expenditure of the kind we are giving in
providing for the social services for the
class, who actually produce the wealth for
the Parliament to carry on really, should
not be Members of a State of this kind.
There is nothing good enough in the land
for the producer.
Mr. CRAWFORD: What about the
farmers?

so ably mentioned by the hon. Member

Mr. POLLOCK: May I interrupt the

debt was incurred subsequent to our
taking over control of our own matters,

Mr. BEATTIE: Let me explain my
position. From 1912 to 1920 we were
contributors to the central fund under the
Imperial Government. This period from
1912 to 1920 was a prosperous period,
and the fund actually showed millions of

we took upon ourselves the responsibility
of running a separate and distinct fund.
Mr. POLLOCK: It was bad luck.
Mr. BEATTIE: It was bad luck; it
was an uneconomic proposition from the
Northern Ireland point of view, because
you had not an insured population at
that period equal to the demands of the

Therefore, I say, this £3,400,000 that was
created during the period of taking over
and the period of the agreement being
arrived at and which was created by the
aftermath of the war-that liability does
not rest on the Unemployment Insurance
Fund of Northern Ireland, but on the
Unemployment Insurance Fund of Great

Mr. BEATTIE: As I was saying, in

the Minister mentioned with hopes of

point to which I wish to refer is that of
the motor duties. I have contended all
along that the basis of the taxation of
motors is not right or proper. The basis
of taxation on which we are at present
working was a war-time Measure. The
war has now been terminated for fourteen
years, but we are still working on the
war-time Measure. Do I understand that
the reason for the continuation of that
basis is that the Chancellor of the Exchequer feels that he can drag more out
of the motorists of Northern Ireland in
that way? I may tell him that if there
were a fair tax based in accordance
with the consumption of petrol in Northern Ireland he would derive more money
in that way than from the horse-power
tax.
Mr. CRAWFORD: What would be the
tax?
Mr. BEATTIE: The basis would be a
tax similar to what is in force in England.
As the years pass the consumption is
getting greater, and the right hon.
Gentleman would always be in the
position of having an increased yield of
taxation because of the increased consumption. I believe that a change in the
basis of motor taxation to a petrol tax
would be welcomed throughout Northern
Ireland.
Mr. ELLIOTT: Hear, hear.
Mr. BEATTIE: Not only would it be
of service to motorists in the carrying
trade but it would be of service to many

cars and who, because of financial stringency only use them at the week-ends.
Under present conditions they cannot
afford to keep a motor car for week-ends
only. Therefore, I believe the right hon.
Gentleman would realise more in that way
than he does under the present system.
Now, the Chancellor of the Exchequer
made a statement to the effect that we had
paid £25,000,000 in the last ten years to
England. I do not know whether he thinks

not.

Mr. POLLOCK: I do.
Mr. BEATTIE: I do not. I feel that
if that £25,000,000 had gone towards the

connection. The Imperial connection at

you can stand by in any way and say you
are quite safe for all time.
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes.
Mr BEATTIE: You may say "Yes,"
but I am rather doubtful, and I know

no matter who gets you.
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not agree.
Mr. BEATTIE: You do not agree, but

You have not met your obligation to the extent that was originally

Mr. POLLOCK: No.
be
Mr. BEATTIE: It is all right saying
that from the loyalty standpoint. Personally, I do not care if there were four
Parliaments in Ireland. I would
dominated no more by a Parliament in

I would always stand for Ulster. (Hon.

Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member is

Mr. BEATTIE: Any way our present

Lieut.-Colonel GORDON: In rising to
speak on the Budget so admirably introduced by the Minister of Finance,
one feels the disadvantage of not
having had a day to digest it and to go
through the figures which, though they
were most clearly given, it is impossible
to keep in one's head. It is a great pity
that the Opposition took the childish and
silly step of walking out of the House,
instead of, as usual, making one or two
speeches and then adjourning the debate,
so that those who are really interested in
the finances of the country could have an
opportunity to study the Budget and be
in a position to come to this House with
a clear idea of what they would like to
say about it. As it is we have to do our
best, and I will try to bring to the notice
of the House some of the points that
struck me in the course of the Minister's
speech.
The first point is that the Minister said
we have in fact over-estimated, that we
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Lieut.-Colonel Gordon]

have actually passed in this House
Estimates for the supply services which
now we find we cannot maintain, and
this is shown by the fact that we have
to economise on the supply services
already passed by this House. It seems
to me that it would be far, far better and
a more businesslike proposition for the
Chancellor of the Exchequer to come to
the House and open his Budget as soon as
possible in the financial year and prior
to the Estimates for the supply services
being taken. Then we would not be in
the position of passing Estimates for
which, in fact, there is not enough money.
I think that is the businesslike view, and
is what most business firms would do.
They would begin to study their expenditure when they knew what their
revenue was to be. To illustrate this
view, may I recall that in the debate on
the Education Vote I criticised the expenditure of £4,600 for a new school at
Stranmillis. I was told by the Front
Bench that this was necessary and the
money had to be voted. Well, if Supply
had come on after the Budget and we had
seen an item like that, which could
possibly have waited for four or five
years, it would probably have disappeared.
In dealing with Supply prior to the
Budget statement we are bound to be
working in the dark.
The hon. and gallant Member for
South Derry (Captain Chichester-Clark)
dealt very fully with the heavy burden
of death duties and estate duties.
Curiously enough, I also was going to
deal with that subject and had worked
out the exact figures which had been
taken from capital in this Province from
1922 to the date of this Budget. In 1922
the sum of £171,000 was taken in death
duties, and for the last six years over
£650,000 has been taken every year. The
exact total taken from 1922 is £6,761,000.
As the hon. and gallant Member so
clearly put it, this is a drain on capital
and the resources of industry and must
ultimately have an effect upon employment and industry. No State can go on
living on its own back. It is bound to
come to an end, and the end is that you
get a lean animal unable to support those
depending on it.
I am glad to see that the Minister has
set aside in the Consolidated Fund a sum
of £150,000 for liabilities, which I hope
will not have to be met, under the Loans
Guarantee Act. I would like to ask has
any consideration been given to, or has
any conference taken place, as to the
current debt on the Unemployment Fund
of £2,500,000, and whether, this year or
in the future, proposals will be made to
this House for funding that debt.
That the Sinking Fund provision has
been resumed for the land annuities is
all to the good. Last year,
as the
Minister has said, we put nothing aside.
At the time he introduced his Budget
last year the proceeding was perfectly
sound in view of the financial crisis. We
might have found ourselves in rather a
bad way if we had not got a fund to
meet these land annuities when they die
out. I hope that the procedure of letting
the Sinking Fund provision lapse will
not occur again, and I am glad to see
that it has been resumed for this year.
The hon. and learned Member for the
University (Mr. McNeill) also asked what
was the balance standing to the credit of
our various sinking funds. These figures
were given last year by the Minister who
opened the Budget, and I would like to
know how the figures for this year compare. They were then given in detail, and
I would like to have them given in detail
again.
Another point that comes straight to
the eye in reviewing the figures in the
White Paper and in the Budget speech
is that, while our population here is about
1,250,000, our revenue is £11,761,000.
That is the revenue taken from that
population of 1,250,000, and it works out
at something like 9.5 pounds per head
of the population. For England, according to the last figure that was given by
Viscount Snowden when he was Chancellor of the Exchequer-and that is the
last figure available-the revenue was
£16 3s per head of the population. This,
I think, shows that this country is not so
wealthy and has not the same resources
as England, and, therefore, as the hon.
and gallant Member for South Derry has
said, what we want is plain finance.
These figures certainly support that view.
Another point is that if you analyse the
figures you will find that we are spending
on insurance and pensions four million
pounds and on education two million
pounds. Under the heading of Ministry
of Home Affairs, Constabulary, etc., after
deducting what is given for derating and
adding on certain items, you have seven
millions for social services. The total,
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
11 MAY 1932
after deductions, is somewhere about ten
millions, out of which we are spending
seven millions on social services.
It is
certain that taxation has reached a peak
and it is a burden that can no longer be
borne at its present rate. I would remind the hon. Member (Mr. Beattie) that
it is on taxation the social services depend. Taxation comes out of industry.
The social services depend on the wheels
of industry turning round. If you cog
those wheels and hinder the machinery
of industry by over-taxation you are
travelling in a vicious circle. Industry
cannot go on carrying a burden which is
stopping it working.
In the past this country, I think, was
known and had a reputation far and wide
for a characteristic, and that characteristic was thrift. On that thrift was
built our agricultural, linen, and shipbuilding industries. I think we want an
example from the Government in order
to bring back this thought that used to
be the leading point in our social life.
We have built up here in Northern Ireland a structure which, I think, in years
of plenty can be carried on, but this
structure is too heavy for these lean years.
I think it is somewhat top heavy, and
we have got to come down to plain finance
and thrift to get back so that the wheels
of industry may turn faster in the future.
This can only be done when all in Northern Ireland realise that the Government
has no inexhaustible supply of money.
The limit of taxation has been reached,
and to get back to our old position of
work and thrift we must realise that
sacrifices have to be made by all who live
in this country. May I say that the basis
of the social structure-economy, thrift,
industry and commerce-depends on one
thing, and that is social security, and so
long as we maintain and have our connection with the British Empire we have
that social security which we on this side
all stand on.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I rise to support the
Budget statement introduced by the
Minister of Finance. May I add my congratulations to those speakers who have
preceded me and say with what pleasure
we listened to the statement made by the
right hon. Gentleman, a statement which
I think should please and satisfy most,
if not all, Members and residents in this
area. First of all, I like the Budget
statement, because in it there are no new
taxes and, secondly, because I see in it a
decrease of expenditure. At first sight
it would look as if our expenditure was
going to be rather more for the present
year than it actually is, but on analysing
it I find that a sum of £733,000 represents a decrease in expenditure for the
current year.
That in itself would be
most commendable, and I congratulate
the right hon. Gentleman on it, but that
coupled with the fact that the Minister
hopes to save a further £50,000 during
the year makes it even more acceptable.
I hope that when the right hon. Gentleman comes to present his Budget statement in the new Parliament House he will
be able to tell us that he not only reduced
the expenditure by £50,000 contemplated
to-day, but that he was able to do it by
at least twice that amount. I feel, like
other hon. Members, and like a great
many in this area, that our expenditure
must be very considerably reduced, and
any efforts the right hon. Gentleman may
make in that direction will have my
whole-hearted support.
May I say how glad I am that we are
not without some Members on the
Opposition benches this afternoon. I am
glad we have at least two hon. Members
who had the courage to remain in their
places and did not get angry and run
away. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
While I do not agree with all that was
said by these two hon. Members, may I
say that I agree with at least some of
their statements. I do not agree, however, with the hon. Member (Mr.
Beattie) that this £50,000 which is to be
saved is going to be saved from the poorer
classes. I hope in respect of those who
are best able to bear deductions the Government will look to them for deductions.
I feel that there are many avenues of
expenditure in Government Departments
that might very well be considerably reduced without impairing efficiency or
doing any of the officials concerned much
harm. I am sorry that the hon. and
learned Member (Mr. McNeill) should
think so hardly of the agricultural community. He is rather sorry that the
Government should have embarked on
the derating scheme. I want to tell the
hon. and learned Member something perhaps about agriculture he does not know,
and that is, that the agricultural community are the most deserving community in this whole area.

very little
for their produce.
If the tax was

put on petrol I believe many more small

this area.
As the hon. Member for Pottinger has said, I believe that as a result
of this change of taxation the Government would lose no money. I hope something will be done in this connection so
that those who use the roads most will
be compelled to pay most of the motor

Mr. BEATTIE: That is their own

Mr. ELLIOTT: It may be their own

and that coupled with unsatisfactory

of profiteering. I am sorry to say that
even with derating and I congratulate
the right hon. Gentleman on that very
comprehensive Measure agriculturists, as
a whole to-day, are not in a very satisfactory or sound condition. It would look at
first to the hon. and learned Member
that derating was some preferential treatment that the agricultural community
had got. What is the fact? The agricultural community to-day are just put in
same position as the hon. and learned
Gentleman. They are asked to pay rates
on the houses they live in, but they are
not asked to pay rates on stock in trade.
We never hear of a draper or grocer
being asked to pay rates on stock, but
they are asked to pay rates on their
dwelling-houses or shops. The farmer
still has to pay rates on his dwellinghouse, but he is no longer, I am glad to
say, through the generosity of the Government, asked to pay rates on his stock
in trade, on which he never should have
been asked to pay rates. I am glad the
Government at last realise that, and that
the farmer is no longer expected to pay
rates on his stock in trade.
Mr. McNEILL: Land.
Mr. ELLIOTT: That is his stock in
trade, his plant. He derives his livelihood from it. He is only now put in the
same position as any ordinary citizen and
is still compelled to pay rates on his
dwelling-house. I agree in part with
what the hon. Member for Pottinger
(Mr. Beattie) said about motor taxation.
I feel that a more equitable distribution
of this tax would be secured by putting
it on petrol. There are many people in
a small way in the country who would
like to have a car as they do not live in
the favoured resorts of County Down or
convenient to the City of Belfast, but because the tax is on the car they have to
May I say in connection with the Post
Office that I am glad to hear the right
hon. Gentleman is able to make a profit
out of it. I hope the time has come when
he will have a return to the penny postage
for this area.
Mr. SPEAKER: The hon. Member for
South Tyrone, I think, knows this is a
reserved service. I have already ruled
that reserved services cannot be discussed
under any circumstances in this House.
I hope he will not refer to them again.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I was not quite sure
that that was a reserved service, but I bow
immediately to your ruling. May I say
that I congratulate the right hon. Gentleman on the fact that the Post Office is
now a paying proposition, and, if I am
not trespassing outside the bounds of the
Rules of Procedure, may I express the
hope that the time is not far distant when
the right hon. Gentleman and the Government will take over the control of the
Post Office for this area.
Coming to another question, which I
am afraid is rather a thorny one, I should
like to say that I agree with the right
hon. Gentleman when he says that the
Government are ardent temperance reformers. Certainly by their temperance
legislation here they have done a great
deal to make this area of ours a more
sober place than it would have been, and
I have on more than one occasion congratulated them on the steps they have
taken. In fact, I have gone so far as to
say to the Government, "You have done
so well with the legislation you have
enacted and it has been so effective that
the time has come when you might go
another step and entirely purge this area.
of this vexed question of intoxicating
liquor." In connection with Excise
duties, and now I am coming to a point
which-
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
11 MAY 1932

Mr. SPEAKER: I think the hon.
Member for South Tyrone will be well
advised to leave Excise duties alone, because they are a reserved service, and I
have ruled that they cannot be discussed
in this House. I am sure he understands that.
Mr. ELLIOTT: I quite understand it,
but I was only going to say that I never
made any appeal to the right hon. Gentleman for a reduction in liquor taxation.
I was not one of those who did that. I
only say, as far as Excise duties are concerned I hope I am in order in saying
this that I have no regrets at all to
express in this House for the fact that
the right hon. Gentleman finds himself
to-day receiving less revenue from intoxicating liquors than he did in previous
years. I hope I am in order in saying
this.
Mr. BEATTIE: How will he make
it up?
Mr. ELLIOTT: I can only say in
reply to the hon. Member for Pottinger,
if I am allowed to say it, that according
to the Budget statements presented here
year by year by the right hon. Gentleman this revenue has been decreasing,
and I have never yet in this House had
to listen to the right hon. Gentleman
expressing the opinion that taxation
should be put on any other commodity to
meet the decreased receipts from intoxicating liquor. So the time has not
arrived for any new taxation in order to
meet the deficiency on the taxation on
this commodity.
I can only say what I am very glad
indeed to be able to congratulate the
Government on their legislation dealing
with this question, and I dissociate myself, although I am a strong temperance
reformer, from the many extravagant
statements made. One was that this is
a drink-sodden area. I do not agree
with that. I do not think it is fair even
to the people of the area, because anyone
who looks at the statistics as presented
by the right hon. Gentleman must see
that we are gradually getting nearer and
nearer to the goal that I, at any rate,
look forward to, that is, the time when
he will have no revenue from intoxicating
liquor in this area.
May I say again that I am in entire
sympathy with the Government and with
the right hon. Gentleman in the proposals made for a decrease in expenditure.
I hope the appeal which has been made
by the hon. and gallant Member for
South Derry (Captain Chichester-Clark)
and the slogan he adopted here to-day,
which I take up very heartily, that is:
"Plain finance for plain people," will be
adopted. I might go a little farther and
say, let us cut our coat according to our
cloth. I am glad that up to the present
we have had presented to us every year a
Budget which has balanced. I hope that
may long continue.
In conclusion, may I congratulate the
Prime Minister on his selection of the
right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of
Finance, as our representative at the
Ottawa Conference. I feel that the
rights and privileges of Northern Ireland are quite safe in the right hon.
Gentleman's keeping, and I hope that
when that Conference is over there will
dawn for Northern Ireland a brighter
day than has yet dawned for her.
Mr. POLLOCK: By leave of the
House, I should like not only to reply to
some of the remarks that have been made
on both sides of the House, but also to
give some information that was specifically
asked for, namely, figures relating to
different subjects. May I say that the
discussion has ranged over a very wide
field, and I fear the time at my disposal
is not sufficient for me to enter, with any
great prolixity at any rate, into the
matters discussed so exhaustively by the
different Members, but, if I may take
them categorically and deal with each as
shortly as I can, it will perhaps serve to
shorten the discussion.
The hon. Member for North Armagh
(Mr. John Johnston) was concerned that
a Commission should be appointed by the
Imperial Government to examine the
whole question of expenditure, and that a
corresponding Commission should undertake a similar duty here. When that
takes place in Britain we may give it
some consideration, but I am afraid that
it would lead to no useful purpose at the
present moment.
I come now to my hon. and gallant
Friend from County Derry (Captain
Chichester-Clark), and also his neighbour,
the hon. and gallant Member for East
Down (Lieut.-Colonel Gordon), who dealt
with the question of estate duties. These
duties, of course, are under our own
control, but I am not going to join issue
The Budget-
Minister's Statement
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Pollock]
with the views expressed by the hon. and
gallant Members in regard to the danger
that has arisen to the capital of the
country through the imposition of this
method of taxation. We got it as a
legacy and, unfortunately, we cannot
rule it out as a very important part of
the revenue of the country.
When the death duties were introduced
originally by Sir William Harcourt it
was intended deliberately to create a
greater distribution of wealth for the
country, but it has had, I admit, the
misfortune of draining the capital of the
country to a very enormous extent. I
am certainly not going to join issue with
my hon. Friends in respect of the vast
sums of money taken from the capital of
the country by the imposition of these
duties. However, we, as I say, have them
as a legacy and we must go side-by-side
with Great Britain in regard to a matter
of that kind.
I come now to my hon. Friend from
the University, whose very exhaustive
speech covered a very wide area, and
would require a considerable amount of
time to deal with in detail. But I may
reply specifically to some questions he
asked. The first was with regard to the
It
Sinking Fund for land annuities.
amounts to-day to something about
£1,100,000, and the Sinking Fund of the
Ulster Savings Certificates amounts to
£650,000. These are the specific questions that were asked by my hon. Friend,
and I am glad to be in a position to
provide him with the information. He
advocated, if I took him up accurately,
a contribution on the permanent basis.
A permanent basis would be a very unfair
position for Northern Ireland to occupy.
The very flexibility and variation of the
contribution has been one of our great
safeguards (Hon. Members: Hear, hear)
--because the contribution is based on
our fitness to pay.
When it was originally instituted and
conditions were very materially different
from what they are to-day, we were able
to pay in the first year and, as a matter
of fact, paid £6,100,000 contribution.
But just in proportion with our inability
through lower taxation-just as that went
on from year to year our contribution
decreased, and, as a matter of fact, at
the present time it is not an unsafe proposition to submit that Northern Ireland
is exactly getting all her revenue to
spend in her own Province. When the
revenue
was high a large part of it
was going towards the Imperial services
and to the Imperial Exchequer. But
now, from the figures I presented, it must
be observed that we practically use all
our revenue. It is distributed among the
different traders of all kinds, and that
money goes into circulation in Northern
Ireland. Surely we must admit that it
benefits the farmers, and, therefore, I
suggest to my hon. Friend from the University that a contribution on some permanent basis would certainly not redound
to the advantage of Northern Ireland.
My hon. Friend also asked me in regard to the remission of entertainment
tax on dramatic entertainments. The
great difficulty in respect of offering remissions for any individual or definite
institutions that are in the nature of entertainment, presents itself at once. I
quite sympathise with the idea of
encouraging dramatic or literary culture.
No one possibly has a greater sympathy
with that than I have, but how is it
possible to discriminate between all the
various amateur performances which
could claim they were on exactly the
same basis. They were intended for the
development of culture and education,
whether music, literature, or the drama,
such as the hon. Member referred to.
So I am afraid I cannot give any encouragement at this moment in regard to
special treatment.
I was also asked a definite question
with regard to the liability in connection
with the new unemployment insurance
debt. That debt is being provided for
by a method which will extinguish it
in a certain number of years. It stands
at £2,700,000 to-day, and was originally
£3,400,000. The new debt which has
accumulated, amounting to £2,500,000
approximately, is a debt on the Unemployment Fund, and it is right perhaps
that I should inform the House that this
deficit is exactly on a par with the British
deficit, and that when Great Britain
undertakes, as we believe, and, in fact,
know that the Government there propose to undertake a method of dealing
with the deficit it will be our duty then
to confer with the British Government in
regard to the treatment of our own deficit. That is the best answer I can give
to the specific question asked.
I do not think there were any other
specific matters. I do not propose to
enter into the generalities discussed by

Oral Answers to Questions.
EMIGRATION FROM NORTHERN
IRELAND.
2. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Finance whether he can state the
number of persons from Northern Ireland
who emigrated to the United States in
the last three years; whether he is aware
that for the majority of the young people
who would emigrate but are obliged to
remain at home, there is no employment,
and whether he can state what steps the
Government proposes to take with the
view to providing them with employment.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The numbers are-3,996 in the
year 1929, 5,198 in 1930, and 130 in the
year 1931.
I am not prepared to agree that there
is no employment for the majority of
those who stay at home.
With regard to the last portion of the
question, the hon. Member is himself
fully aware of all that the Government
has done, and is doing, in its endeavours
to relieve the lot of the unemployed;
having regard to the many opportunities
which have been given to this House to
debate the unemployment question recently, I do not propose in this reply
again to enter into its details.
PUPILS LEAVING PUBLIC
ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS.
3. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the
number of pupils who in 1929, 1930, and
1931, left public elementary schools of
Northern Ireland respectively; how many
proceeded in each of these years to
secondary and technical schools, and
whether he is aware that in the vast
majority of cases there is no satisfactory
employment for ex-pupils of public
elementary schools.
The
SECRE-
PARLIAMENTARY
TARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
EDUCATION (Mr. Robb): The number
of pupils who ceased to attend public
elementary schools in 1929 was 26,073,
and, of this number, 5,077 went to
secondary or day technical schools. The
Ministry is not in a position to say how
many others became students of evening
technical schools.
In 1930 and 1931, 21,520 and 20,617
pupils respectively ceased to attend public
elementary schools and, of these, 4,431
and 4,096 respectively went to secondary
or day technical schools.
to
The reply to the last part of the
question is in the negative. According
the latest available information
supplied, annually by the teachers, about
87 per
cent. of the children who left
school and did not go to other day schools
went to work or were employed at home..
UNDERTAKING BY KING'S
SCHOLARS.
4. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the
number of years a King's Scholar undertakes to teach in a public elementary
school under the Ministry of Education
for Northern Ireland; what payment has
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Beattie]
to be made if he or she fails to implement this engagement; what payment is
exacted from a schoolmistress who is
married before that period is completed,
and is on account of her marriage dismissed or compelled to resign and is
thereby rendered incapable of earning
money as a teacher; and whether he can
state if married schoolmistresses were employed in some of the model schools
directly managed by the late Commissioners of National Education.
Mr. ROBB: As a condition of admission
to a recognised training college, a King's
Scholar is required to enter into an agreement to serve to the satisfaction of the
Ministry, within a reasonable period after
completion of training, for five years as
a public elementary teacher in Northern
Ireland if afforded an opportunity of such
employment, or, in default to refund to
the Ministry the full amount paid by the
Ministry in respect of training. In the
case of a man who has undergone a twoyear course of training this may amount
to about £140, in the case of a woman to
about £125. The amount varies with
the particular years in which trained, and
with the number of years for which
trained.
Where a woman teacher is married and
leaves the service before the five-year
period of service is completed, she may be
called upon to refund the full cost of her
training, but the Ministry is always prepared to consider the special circumstances
of each case.
Married women teachers were employed
in model national schools directly managed
by the late Commissioners of National
Education.
CLASSIFICATION OF PUBLIC
ELEMENTARY SCHOOLS.
5. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the number of public elementary schools now in
operation in Northern Ireland, and the
number of these placed in Class A, B and
C, respectively, for inspection purposes;
what conditions are required by the
Ministry for each classification; whether
teachers and managers have been furnished with the conditions; for how long
a period, in the case of a school lowered
from Class B to Class C, is such a school
to be retained in Class C, whether
teachers and managers of such schools
are informed of this; how many twoteacher schools where both teachers are
marked "highly efficient," have been
lowered to Class B within the past year,
and can he state why this has been done
and whether there is a distinction made
in such cases between transferred and
voluntary schools.
Mr. ROBB: On 31st December, 1931,
there
were 1870 public elementary
schools in operation. Of these, 321 were
in Class A, 1221 in Class B and 317 in
Class C, and 11 had not been classified.
The conditions of classification are set
forth in P. Circular 44, dated June, 1924,
a copy of which I am sending to the hon.
Member. This circular was issued to
managers and principal teachers of every
public elementary school on 3rd July,
1924.
When a school is lowered from Class B
to Class C it becomes eligible for a general
inspection in each school year, and the
question of readmitting the school to
Class B is considered on the results of
such inspection; this procedure is implied
in the terms of the circular referred to.
I am not aware whether any twoteacher schools have been lowered to Class
B in the circumstances mentioned in the
question, but the number (if any) would
be few, and if the hon. Member has
such a case in his mind and will send me
particulars, I shall have inquiry made
about it.
There is no distinction between transferred and voluntary schools as regards
determination of the classification.

Oral Answers
Oral Answers.
12 MAY 1932
Mr. ROBB: The present members of
the committee are Mr. J. S. Mahon,
Chief Inspector; Mr. C. A. Abraham, of
the Principal Teachers' Union, and Mr.
H. Magill, a retired teacher.
During 1931, there were seven appeals
to this committee with the result that in
three cases action favourable to the
appellant was taken, in three cases the
Committee recommended no alteration in
the original report, and one case has not
yet been settled.
I do not agree that the Appeal Committee does not enjoy the confidence of
the teachers, nor can I admit the
accuracy of the implications in the remainder of the question.
The inspection system is an essential
feature of our educational organisation
and a necessary safeguard in the application of public funds. The reports of
inspectors are valuable as a guide, not
only to the Ministry but also the
managers teachers and members
of
education committees.
The answer to the last part of the question is in the negative.

FEES FOR BIRTH CERTIFICATES.
8. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether the Clerks of
Unions write birth certificates during the
office hours for which they are paid;
whether they deliver the fees so received
to the treasurers of the Unions in relief
of the rates, or appropriate the money so
received to themselves, and are thereby
paid twice for the time so occupied.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have been asked to
reply.
I believe that the answer to the first
part of the question is in the affirmative.
The fees received by the clerks in respect
of the issue of birth certificates are retained by them as part of the emoluments
of their office, and no doubt this factor
is taken into consideration in the fixing
of the remuneration paid to them for
their services in connection with the administration of the Poor Law.
FEE FOR SEARCH OF REGISTER.
9. Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he is aware that
for birth certificates at reduced rates the
Clerk of the Coleraine Union charges, in
addition to the scheduled fee, a research
fee of one shilling; whether he approves
of this exaction; and whether he will
take steps to have it remedied.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am taking this
question also.
I am informed that in connection with
the issue of birth certificates at reduced
rates, the Clerk of the Coleraine Union,
in his capacity as Superintendent Registrar of Births, Deaths, and Marriages,
does not charge a search fee when the
information furnished to him by an
applicant is sufficiently precise to enable
the entry in the register to be found without prolonged search. In cases in which
it is necessary for the Superintendent
Registrar to search his register for a
period of more than five years, a fee of one
shilling is usually charged. The practice
of the Superintendent Registrar is within
his rights, and, in my view, cannot be
considered unreasonable.
I would like to add that in many instances, the Superintendent Registrar, in
his discretion, makes no charge for either
search or copy of entry, but makes a
gratuitous issue to the applicant.

Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS Mr. Speaker's Ruling
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would refer the hon. Member to the reply
given in this House on the 14th
March last to the hon. Member for

there been any definite progress made in
connection with a labourers' cottage
scheme at the time when it was decided
for financial reasons to suspend the
operations of the Acts.
In that case the Council had formulated a scheme involving the erection of
333 houses.
In addition, four other rural district
councils, namely, Ballymoney, Kilkeel,
Limavady, and Lisburn had schemes in
contemplation at the date in question
involving the provision of 106, 146, 144
and 52 cottages respectively.
Generally speaking, the Ministry is not
in possession of precise information as to
the number of houses of applicants for
cottages declared by medical officers of
health to be unfit for human habitation
until the respective schemes are formulated and the petitions in respect thereof
submitted to the Ministry for confirmation. As the schemes in the four cases
referred to had not reached that stage,
the information indicated in the question
is, therefore, not available.
With regard to the Downpatrick case,
333 representations had been considered
by the Council, including 108 made on
the grounds of insufficient housing accommodation, and 225 on the grounds that
the applicants were living in unsanitary
dwellings.

Land Law Bill-
