HOUSE OF COMMONS

administrative
[Mr. Pollock]
say, largely of an
character, and designed to Overcome
difficulties which have emerged in administering the powers in regard to land
law transferred to the Ministry of
Finance by the Government of Ireland
Act, 1920, and the Orders made under it.
As there may be some misunderstanding
in the minds of hon. Members, I desire
to emphasise at the outset that the Ministry is not taking to itself any new
functions. It already possesses these
functions, and has acted on them for the
past ten years, but for reasons which I
will more fully explain in dealing with
Clause 1, the Ministry considers some
amendment of the existing law desirable
in the interests of all parties concerned.
The first Clause relates to the distribution of the proceeds of sales of holdings
by the Ministry. In all cases the sales
are the consequence of default in payments of the land purchase annuity; a
decree is given by the county court, and
if payment is not made in a reasonable
time the decree goes to the Under
Sheriff to execute by distraint. If he
makes a return that there are no goods to
meet the amount of the decree, the
owner is served with a notice of sale and
in a great many cases this results in payment of the arrears. If it does not, the
only course left is to sell the holding by
auction, though before such final action is
taken every effort is made to persuade the
proprietor to
to make arrangements to
pay the arrears, if need be, by instal
ments. I should like to impress on
the House that the utmost consideration is shown by the Ministry, and the
proof of this is that during the past ten
years the total number of sales arising in
the last ten years only amounts to 79a negligible number, when it is realised
that the total number of holdings,
subject to Land Purchase Annuities in
Northern Ireland, amounts to about
120,000.
To turn now to the machinery set up
by the Bill for distributing the proceeds
of such sales, I should explain that prior
to the transfer of functions to Northern
Ireland, the Irish Land Commission
carried out these functions. The ordinary
practice was that an examiner investigated the title of claimants and a
lay commissioner allocated the proceeds.
The Ministry of Finance, as statutory
successors to the Commission, are not, in
fact, required by law to use legal
machinery at all, but obviously the
Minister has been solely guided by the
advice of his legal branch in distributing
the moneys.
The present Bill proposes to
make the solicitor to the Ministry the
statutory authority to examine and rule
on the claims. In difficult cases the
solicitor will have the help of practising
counsel. A responsibility, therefore,
which is at present indefinite will by this
Bill be fixed-the responsibility will
be placed
placed in the proper quarter,
namely, in the hands of
hands of the legal
profession.
The present Clause and the Schedule to
the Bill set out the proposed procedure in
detail, and have been drafted in consultation with my right hon. and learned
Friend, the Attorney-General. Briefly,
it is so drawn as to minimise expense to
parties, including the unfortunate proprietor himself, having claims to the
residue of the purchase money after payment of the amount due to the Ministry
for arrears and costs. The Bill proposes
that an appeal shall lie to the county
court from the decision of the solicitor
where the balance to be distributed
exceeds £30. There will be an appeal to
the county court where the person found
to be entitled to any sum over £15 is a
minor, or of unsound mind.
The amount available for distribution
is in most cases very small, the holdings
being generally those which are on an
uneconomic level or which have been
allowed by their proprietors to run to
neglect. In the 79 cases to which I have
referred, 61 involved amounts under £50.
Hon. Members will, I am sure, be in full
agreement that a disappointed claimant
should not be put in the position, in a
case involving only a few pounds, of
having such small amount frittered away
in court proceedings. In fact the court
fees would more than absorb the great
majority of balances which would be in
the hands of the Ministry.
The second Clause of the Bill should
present no difficulty. It is necessary
because, in order to recover the arrears of
land purchase annuities as each Quarter
Session comes round, a large number of
sealed certificates in proof of debtrunning perhaps into some 2,000-have
to be sent by the Ministry to the local
solicitors who act on behalf of the Ministry with a view to ensuring payment.
Hitherto, all these sealed certificates
have had to be authenticated-that is,
Land Law Bill-
Second Reading
12 MAY 1932
signed-by a secretary or assistant secretary personally, by reason of the provisions of the Ministries of Northern
Ireland Act, 1921. The present Clause
will allow the Seal to be authenticated by
officers of the Ministry of lower standing.
I may add for the information of the
House that although this very large
number of certificates is issued, the
greater part of them are never acted on.
The proprietors know with great exactitude the last day up to which it is possible
for them to make payment of the annuity
before the court proceedings begin, and
I understand that it is a long-standing
practice in many parts of the country to
wait until the last moment before making
payment. The certificates, therefore, in
many cases do not become court documents at all, but they have to be in
readiness with the local solicitor.
Clause 3 relates to tithe rentcharges.
The explanation for its necessity I propose to give in a few words. By the
Tithe Rentcharge and Variable Rents
Act (N.I.), passed by this House in the
year 1930, tithe rentcharges and variable
rents payable to the Ministry of Finance
were varied by a reduction of eight per
cent. below the then existing figure, this
percentage being in permanent and final
substitution for a variation to be calculated at every 15-year period by
reference to the fair rents fixed in each
county. But the Act of 1930 did not
dispose of the question whether a similar
reduction should apply to tithe rentcharges and variable rents payable to
private individuals, which are variable on
the same basis as those payable to the
Ministry. This matter was left open to
agreement between the parties.
however, the present position in regard
to these rentcharges, etc., is one of great
uncertainty, it has been thought well to
put it upon a definite basis. Accordingly
it is now proposed to legislate so as to
make the eight per cent. reduction a
general one, that is to include the Ministry of Finance as well as private persons.

decide, according to legal principles, who

Mr. BEATTIE: He has no right. It

Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon.
Member need not. The size of the allotments provided under the Bill will be
strictly limited, and only one allotment
may be held by any person. The work
involved in cultivating an allotment
would, therefore, be such that it could
ordinarily be carried out by a man in
employment outside his ordinary working
hours. Moreover, the profit from the
allotment could not possibly exceed the
statutory limit fixed in the Unemployment Insurance Acts as a bar to eligibility
for unemployment benefit. If my hon.
Friend has some doubt in accepting my
assurance, acting on the views expressed
by the Minister of Finance, I am in
a position to give a definite assurance
that no unemployed person need have any
hesitation in obtaining a plot, or in selling
any surplus produce of his allotment which
he may not require for the use of his
own family, provided only that he remains
ready to accept any suitable employment
which may be offered to him.
With regard to Clause 1, that indicates
the local authorities upon whom powers
are proposed to be conferred by the Bill,
that is to say, county borough, borough,
and urban district councils. These authorities, hon. Members will observe, do not
include rural authorities, the reason being
that I am informed by these authorities
that no need exists in rural areas for the
provision of such allotments, as it is the
object of the Bill to enable local authorities to provide. The remainder of the
Clause empowers local authorities, with
the approval of the Ministry, to take on
lease land for use as allotments or to use
for that purpose land already in their
possession. Land acquired under this
Clause need not necessarily be within the
area of the local authority. An urban
district council may acquire land in a
neighbouring rural district if no suitable
land is available within the urban district
itself.
Clause 2 sets forth the general conditions which must be observed by local
authorities in the letting of land in allotments under the Bill. For obvious reasons
it is necessary to limit the amount of land
which any person may hold as an allotment. The limitation proposed is oneeighth of an acre, and I am informed by
those who are experienced in these matters
that this limit is a reasonable
Another important condition is contained
in paragraph (c) of Sub-clause (1). This
paragraph will not, I believe, be found
by local authorities to be unduly restrictive, and will at the same time ensure

that allotments will be available only for
those classes of persons whom it is the
object of the Bill to assist. Clause 3
contains certain conditions applying to
tenants of allotments. These do not, I
think, call for any special comment.
Clause 4 enables local authorities, if
they so desire, to supply seeds, manure,
and agricultural implements to tenants of
allotments. Where this is done, the cost
of the articles supplied can be repaid by
the tenants by instalments. Such an
arrangement is practically necessary in
the case of tenants of very limited means.
Clause 5 requires local authorities which
provide plots to make regulations, with
the approval of the Ministry of Home
Affairs, for the cultivation of the allotments, the preservation of good order
thereon, and other such matters. Hon.
Members will observe that it is proposed
to prohibit the keeping of animals on
allotments, as experience has shown that
where no such prohibition exists the keeping of poultry, rabbits, and so on, is a
constant source of trouble.
Clause 6 provides for the recovery of
possession of allotments, or of sums due
to local authorities where tenants have
made default.
Clause 7 is one of the most important
in the Bill, and I desire to draw the special
attention of hon. Members to it. Throughout the rest of the Bill we are dealing
with the provision of allotments by local
authorities themselves. This Clause gives
local authorities an alternative method of
procedure. Instead of providing allotments themselves they may make grants
to approved voluntary organisations which
provide allotments for such tenants as
might receive allotments provided by
local authorities under the Bill. Some
of these organisations have been in
existence for a considerable time, and
have gained valuable experience in all
matters appertaining to the administration of allotments. Local authorities
may, therefore, find it prudent in some
cases, both on grounds of economy and
efficiency, to support voluntary organisations operating in their areas rather than
to provide allotments themselves, and it
is for this reason that we have inserted
this Clause in the Bill. Agencies which
may be assisted must be approved by the
Ministry of Home Affairs, and must be
non-profit making concerns.
I think the remaining Clauses of the
Bill call for little comment. Clause 8
authorises local authorities to accept contributions and gifts for allotments, while
Clause 9 enables them to appoint committees, which may include persons not
members of the local authority, to administer the Act. Clause 11 provides penalties
for persons causing damage to allotments,
or to any crops, fences. In order that
local authorities may not be debarred from
taking effective action this season Clause
12 has been inserted to legalise any steps
which, with the approval of the Ministry
of Home Affairs have already been taken
or which may be taken by local authorities
before this Bill becomes law. I believe
that in the exceptional circumstances the
House will agree with me that a Clause
of this kind is justified. I beg to move.

I would like in conclusion to say one

Motor Vehicles (International Race)
Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read the Second
time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Bill which
now comes before the House for consideration is a short one, and its purpose and
object need little explanation, but the
House is entitled to have an explanation
of the reason for its introduction.
As the House is aware, we in Northern
Ireland have been fortunate in that during the last few years we have been able
to secure for Northern Ireland the
Tourist Trophy Race organised by the
Royal Automobile Club. We are also
fortunate in having a course which is
eminently suitable for such a race and,
if I may say in passing, we are fortunate
in having local authorities such as the
Down County Council and the Newtownards Urban District Council, who realise,
as the Government does, the enormous
benefits and advantages to Northern Ireland which a race of this character brings
with it, and who, accordingly, have supported the Government in every way
possible in connection with the carrying
out of these races.
The races in years past have, from a
spectacular and interest point of view,
been eminently successful, and have attracted visitors from all parts of the
British Isles, and even from foreign
countries, while, in addition, they have
afforded interest and amusement to hundreds and thousands of our own people.
At the same time, the cost involved on
the promoters of these races is very considerable, and when the Government of
Northern Ireland last autumn issued a
formal invitation to the Royal Automobile
Club to hold the 1932 race in Northern
Ireland we were informed by the club that,
while they were most desirous of accepting
our invitation, they were faced with the
financial difficulties involved in the
organisation and conduct of the race.
The Club informed us that in connection with the 1931 Race they were faced
with a substantial loss, and that they
could not undertake to carry out a further race in Northern Ireland unless they
could be sure of a substantial guarantee
against contingent loss.
Under these circumstances the Government had several conferences with the
local Race Committee, with the object of
endeavouring to arrive at some method
by which sufficient funds could be raised
to guarantee the Royal Automobile Club
against any contingent loss in connection with the race.
After weighing up every possibility it
was finally decided that the most equitable solution of the problem was to ask
owners and drivers of motor cars attending the race to pay a nominal charge
not exceeding half a crown for the privilege of bringing their cars into the race
area.
en-
As the House is aware, the local Committee have, in connection with previous
races during the last few years,
deavoured to raise subscriptions to meet
their share of the expenses of the race,
but unfortunately it has become increasingly difficult to raise money by these
means, and although, undoubtedly, many
people and firms have contributed, the
amount so collected would not be sufficient to build up a fund to meet the situation.
The local committee also hope to raise
a certain amount of money by the sale of
badges to spectators attending the race.
I should explain however, that the purchase of these badges by spectators will
be on a purely voluntary basis, and that
there is no suggestion of requiring spectators on foot to pay anything in the
nature of an admission charge. On the
other hand, we feel that it is not unreasonable to ask motorists to pay this
small charge of half-a-crown.
Mr. BEATTIE: What are the
motorists to pay haif-a-crown for?
Sir DAWSON BATES: If my hon.
Friend had been listening to me, I have
been trying to explain that it is to raise
funds to cover the expenses of the race.
I should also explain that, while this
charge would be levied on spectators,
arrangements are being provided in the
Bill to exempt from the charge persons
entering the race area for purposes un-
Motor Vehicles Bill-

[Sir Dawson Bates]
connected with the race. For example,

Sir DAWSON BATES: I will explain

the Bill is not actually required towards

The generous action of Lord Wakefield,
who has done so much to encourage the
development of the British Motor Industry in all its branches will be within
the knowledge of the House. Lord
Wakefield presented the prize money,
amounting to £1,500, last year. This

Those are the main points in the Bill and,

PROSECUTIONS FOR ILLICIT
DISTILLATION.
2. Major McCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the number of prosecutions for
illicit distillation for the year ending
December, 1931.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): During the year
1931 proceedings were taken in fifty cases
under the Illicit Distillation Acts,
seventy-nine persons in all being prosecuted.
TUBERCULOSIS MORTALITY.
3. Major MCCORMICK asked the
Minister of Home Affairs whether he can
state the number of persons being treated
for tuberculosis in Northern Ireland and
the total deaths attributable to this
disease for the year ending December,
1931.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Statistics regarding the treatment of tuberculosis are
made up for the financial year. For the
year ended 31st March, 1931, the latest
date for which accurate information is
available, the number of persons treated
for tuberculosis in Northern Ireland was
10,381. The number of deaths during
that period was 1,465.

Order for Second Reading read.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I indicated when I introduced my Estimates a week or so ago the
fact that the payments from the health
insurance funds, both in Great Britain
and here, were causing anxiety to the
Ministry of Health in Great Britain and
to my Department. The chief difficulty
has been for some time that the claims
made by married women have been excessive, and, if allowed to continue, would
endanger the financial position of the
approved societies. Hon. Members will
appreciate that we are linked up with
health insurance across the Channel to
such a degree that the two funds are
really inseparable. We are represented on
the Joint Committee which controls
health insurance for the whole of the
United Kingdom. Many of the funds
are available for the support of our
societies, if in difficulties, just in the
same way as they are available for the
assistance of societies in Great Britain,
under similar circumstances.
The position is shortly this, that there
is a Measure at the present time before
the Imperial Parliament and it will be
necessary for the reasons I have already
stated that whatever decisions are come
to in the Imperial Parliament and whatever form the Bill takes when it leaves
the Imperial Parliament should be given
effect to here at the same time. This
Health Insurance Bill-
Second Reading
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
Measure, which I have the honour to ask
the House to give a Second Reading to
to-day, is, briefly, for the purpose of
giving the Government here powers
through Orders in Council to apply such
portions of the British Measure as are in
respect of services transferred to the Parliament of Northern Ireland. The benefits which married women receive at the
present time and it is their benefit that
will be affected by this Measure—are 12s
per week sickness benefit and 7s 6d disablement benefit. The British Bill proposes that the 12s shall be reduced to 10s,
and the 7s 6d to 5s. The savings that
will be effected by that change will it is
considered on an actuarial basis keep the
funds of the societies solvent.
I may say that the single women's
benefit is also affected. Sickness benefit
is not affected, but the disablement benefit will be affected to the extent of 1s 6d.
The 7s 6d benefit will be reduced to 6s.
Hon. Members may say that they do not
like the procedure by Order in Council,
but it is inevitable in this case, and we
are just following the practice which we
followed when we dealt with health insurance matters a few years ago. Our
Parliament will probably not be sitting
when the British Bill becomes law, and
if our Parliament were not sitting there
would be no way of dealing with the
matter except to call the House specially
together for the purpose of considering
it. As it is inevitable that we shall follow
Great Britain in connection with health insurance matters, it would seem to the Government quite unnecessary that we should
ask Parliament to meet specially to deal
with a matter which can be dealt with
equally well in the only convenient way
that it can be dealt with-by Orders in
Council. I beg to move.
Mr. NIXON: There is not much difficulty in catching the Speaker's eye to-day,
on this side of the House at all events,
but I do think if a Bill like this was
introduced in any other Parliament there
would be very severe criticism, because it
strikes me that this House is called on
to pass legislation which may apply to
Northern Ireland, Acts that have not
yet been passed in the United Kingdom.
Clause I reads:
(1) In the event of any Act (in this
Act referred to as "the United Kingdom Act") being hereafter passed in
the present session of the Parliament
of the United Kingdom to amend certain enactments relating to national
health insurance and certain enactments
relating to widows', orphans' and old
age contributory pensions and for purposes connected therewith, and enacting that the United Kingdom Act, so
far as it relates to matters with respect
to which the Parliament of Northern
Ireland has power to make laws, shall
apply to
.
And then one of the ways of applying
these Acts that have not yet been passed
is by a Special Order, without coming before Parliament at all. They are to apply
legislation to Northern Ireland that may
be passed in the United Kingdom on some
future occasion without coming into this
Parliament, and to proceed by way of an
Order or Proclamation signed by His
Grace the Governor. I do not think
such a proposal was ever made any place
before. The Clause also states:
(2) An Order in Council made for
the purpose of sub-section (1) of this
section may make such modifications
and adaptations of any enactments relating to national health insurance
and widows', orphans' and old-age contributory pensions as appear necessary
or expedient for the extension of the
United Kingdom Act to Northern
Ireland.
That is to say, that this Order in Council
will apply here the Act as passed by the
Parliament of the United Kingdom, but
they can alter it at any time.
Mr. ANDREWS: May I point out to
my hon. Friend that the Bill has already

to Northern Ireland in its final form, and,
further, that it is essential that the Bill
should apply to Northern Ireland at the
same time as it applies to Great Britain.
Mr. NIXON: The explanation of the
Minister only goes the length of the Bill
already before the Imperial Parliament,
but, I think, the reading of this Clause
shows that it would apply to any Act
hereinafter passed by the present Session
of the Imperial Parliament.
Mr. ANDREWS: Relating to health
insurance.
Mr. NIXON: But apart from that
altogether, why does the Government not
come into this House and table the Bill
and give the Members an opportunity of

debating it and expressing their views on

That Order in Council can modify or

""
Bus Fares Tribunal
Bus Fares Tribunal
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Nixon]
I wish to say at the outset that anything I may say is not to be taken as a
personal reflection upon the gentlemen
who form the Tribunal. They have been
appointed by the Government of Northern Ireland to administer an Act passed
by a majority of this House. They are
doing that, and my criticism in respect
of this Motion is not a criticism of those
Gentlemen.
There was a time when the railway companies had a monopoly of transport in Northern Ireland and in every other country.
After the war railway fares were prohibitive, but the Government of the day
never interfered with their fares or with
their monopolies. I am now talking of
the period subsequent to the war. But
there came a time when there was what
we may call a revolution in transport,
when motors in the form of buses commenced to compete, and to compete successfully, with the railway companies.
That was all to the advantage of the
travelling public all over the Six
Counties, and also to the advantage of
the dwellers in the cities, who had cheap
transport to go to the seaside places or
wherever they wished to go. At all
events, fares came down.
Like every
other thing, they would be and should be
regulated by the law of supply and demand, a great old law that is often
preached from those benches when it is
suitable. But in this particular case it
was not suitable, and a Bill was brought
forward. I had the honour of opposing
that Bill. I think I said that one of the
effects of that Bill would be to create
monopolies and to bring transport largely
back under the control of the railway
companies. My prophecy in every respect
has been confirmed. On the 10th of this
month I put down a question to the
Minister of Home Affairs and it was
answered on the 12th. The question was:
"To ask the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he can state the number of bus routes in Northern Ireland
which have been acquired by the various
railway companies to date."
The reply was:
"The Minister of Home Affairs: Up
to date the railway companies in Northern Ireland have acquired omnibus
services operated by 37 owners on 84
routes." (Official Report, 12th May,
1932; Vol. 14, col. 1385).
In this small area of six counties, with
the assistance of this Act, the railway
companies have control of 84 routes.
Then there are a few very large companies,
and the whole tendency since the smaller
companies were eliminated is to apply to
the Bus Fares Tribunal for an increase of
fares. Indeed, in one case I think I am
right in saying an application to reduce
fares by a bus company competing with
a railway company was refused by this
Tribunal.
Now when an application is made to
increase fares in any locality the unfortunate travelling public have either to
submit or they have to call meetings,
subscribe money, and fee counsel to defend their interests, to defend, if possible,
the use in Northern Ireland of the King's
highway. It is quite common now to
read in the papers about leading and
eminent K.C.'s being occupied day after
day for prolonged periods fighting, in
some cases, the cause of the railway companies and the existent bus companies,
and in other cases the cause of the unfortunate travelling public before this
Tribunal in a matter with which the Government should never have interfered.
To give the House an idea of the state
of public opinion in the counties I will
first read a resolution passed by the
Armagh County Council as it appeared
in the Press on the 13th May:
(
on
"At Armagh County Council
Tuesday a resolution was passed on the
motion of Mr. G. A. Locke, seconded
by Mr. J. Corkey, protesting against
the monopoly given to certain bus
owners in securing for them the excluive use of passenger traffic over
roads towards the upkeep of which
they contributed only to a very limited
extent.'
"The resolution added that the
precedent thus set up of guaranteeing
a profit to bus companies was a most
dangerous one, which, if followed to a
logical conclusion, would put an end to
all competition and result in a general
increase in the cost of all commodities.
They objected strongly to the State
guaranteeing profits to any person or
company."
Resolutions of protest were also passed at
Templepatrick, at Antrim, I think at
Newtownards, at Finaghy, Greyabbey,
and at various other places throughout
Northern Ireland.

law

Mr.
ignorance.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The right of
an individual to use a road is always
subject to the consideration of the rights
of others. This is not a new principle.
Road users, and particularly those who
ply for hire have from time immemorial
been subject to control or regulation of
one kind or another, and it has been laid
down by various Acts of Parliament that
individuals who desire to use the roads
for public gain must accept obligations as
to how their traffic is conducted and the
fares to be charged.
The King's Highway is for the use of
the people, but we cannot allow it to be
exploited for the benefit of certain
sections, and it was because of this exploiting by certain individuals, involving
risk of life, damage to roads, inconvenience to the public, excessive fares,
and the creation of uncontrolled monopolies that the Government stepped in in
1926 and brought the principle which had
already been embodied in previous Acts
into application to suit modern motor
traffic.
Now, what has been the result of the
policy of the Government? Contrast the
position to-day with the position a few
years ago. To-day, under our system,
every district in Northern Ireland- -even
though thinly populated-is catered for.
It has sufficient services for the local

traffic and capable of expansion from

In the year 1928, before the system had
been properly organised, there were no
fewer than 175 accidents directly attributable to motor omnibuses and charabancs,
as a result of which no fewer than 23
persons were killed and 208 injured.
In the year 1931, the number of accidents directly attributable to motor
omnibuses and charabancs was only 32,
as a result of which only two people were
killed and 39 injured. I ask this House
if the saving of 21 valuable lives in itself
is not sufficient answer, and I challenge

ments under pressure of the Whip, and
as the Whip is active on this particular
occasion I do not expect anything else but
that the Motion will be defeated by an

Mr. HANNA: I only rise to say a
word or two to try to dispel some of the
confusion of thought that may exist as
to the meaning of monopoly. The word
has been constantly used in this House,
and it is a feature of most of the resolutions that the hon. Member read or referred to. A peculiar construction is put
on the word monopoly. When I speak
of monopoly I mean that there is a
right or privilege given to a person or
persons to do certain things at a certain
place in whatever manner they like to do
it. Let us see if any of these characters
or qualifications exist in the relationship
of those who now run bus services under
our law. They are given a licence.
That lasts for one year on the terms that
they provide buses that are mechanically
fit, that they are driven by expert and
skilful drivers, that they begin their buses
on a route at a particular place, and
finish at a particular place, that they
begin at a particular time and finish at
a particular time, and that they only
charge those fares that a judicial body
appointed by Act of Parliament, which
passed its Second Reading in this House
without a division, fix. That is spoken of
glibly as a monopoly.
If we would only condescend to use
words in the ordinary acceptation of
terms, and if we made speeches knowing
what we were talking about, and used
only words we knew the meaning of, there
would not be half the resolutions that are
passed here, there and everywhere. What
has happened in relation to this matter?
Away back four or five years ago we
found a certain condition of affairs existing. Any man could bring out any
machine and call it a bus. It did not
matter so long as there were four wheels
and a seat it was a bus. He put any
men he liked on to drive it, the lame,
the halt, and the blind; he overcrowded
his bus to whatever extent he wanted;
there was no insurance for anybody.
Men without any means could get secondhand buses, as many of them did get
them, and when wrong and harm was
done to these poor people in Woodvale,
whom the hon. Member (Mr. Nixon) represents, what happened to them?
they brought an action at law and had
damages assessed they could not be paid.

Mr. NIXON: That is a misstatement.

ought really to subscribe, because, while

Mr. HANNA: The hon. Member does

has undertaken and is now about to hold

in relation to particular routes and
particular parts of those routes. And it
will be time enough-whether the hon.
Member opposite or any other hon. Member has met any disaffection in the
country or not-to make a great deal of
noise when the injustices that they fear,
or pretend to fear, are put into operation,
or when some attempt is made to put
them into operation. Up to the present
nothing of that kind has been done.
This Tribunal have given evidence of
their great interest and their desire in
the performance of their duties to
interpret the spirit of the law which we
passed, and there is nothing in any of the
circumstances which have arisen inside the
last month that should shatter the faith
of any person in the Tribunal or in their
performance of the duties which we
expect them to perform.

Slaughter of Animals Bill. [S.]
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. McNEILL: The Bill which is now
before the House, and which has already
received the approval of the Senate, will,
I am sure meet with the cordial approval
of all hon. Members, and it requires little
apology from me to commend it. A short
resumé of its aim and scope is appended
to the memorandum affixed to the Bill
itself. Briefly its object is that all
animals, except swine, slaughtered in
slaughter-houses and knackers' yards in
Northern Ireland, whether for human
food or otherwise, shall be humanely
killed. It will be seen that this Measure is
in line with the great humanitarian principles which are so prominent a feature of
the present age, principles which go 30
far as to assert that we owe a duty not
merely to our fellows but to the animal
creation, which exist either as beasts of
burden or as a source of food. Indeed,
one might be justified in saying that in
the Bill the prediction of the great English political philosopher, Jeremy Bent-
"The
ham, has been well-nigh fulfilled.
time will come," he said, "when humanity
will extend its mantle over everything
which breathes. We have begun by
attending to the condition of slaves; we
shall finish by softening the lot of all the
animals which assist our labours and supply our wants."
In its practical effect the object of this
Bill is to assimilate the law in Northern
Ireland to the existing law of Scotland,
where the Slaughter of Animals Act,
1928, has proved such a profound success.
And it is well known that but for the pressure of business during the past four years
in the Imperial Parliament, a Measure,
similar to the Bill in my hands, would
have found its way on to the Statute Book
dealing with the slaughter of animals in
England and Wales. Hon. Members will
remember that since the passing
of the great Public Health Act in Ireland
in 1878, the regulation and licensing
of slaughter-houses which in the
definition section includes knackers'
yards was committed to the various local
authorities, who were given power to make
by-laws dealing with the slaughter-houses
in their particular areas. Some years
ago, as is pointed out in the memorandum
to which I have already referred, the
Ministry of Health in Great Britain
issued model by-laws for slaughterhouses, which may be adopted voluntarily
by local authorities, providing for the use
of mechanical instruments. No fewer than
433 local authorities in Great Britain,
and seven in Northern Ireland have
adopted these model by-laws. For the
benefit of hon. Members I shall mention
the names of these seven enlightened local
authorities. They are, Belfast, Bangor,
Ballymena, Larne, Lisburn Urban and
Lisburn Rural, and Cookstown. Now
what local authorities have hitherto been
entitled to do voluntarily, the present Bill
proposes to make compulsory in Statutory
1497 Slaughter of Animals Bill-

is MAY 1932
Second Reading
form, with a view to uniformity in the
conditions of the 400 slaughter-houses
which serve a necessary though unpleasant
purpose.
Many thousand animals are slaughtered
every year in Northern Ireland, and the
great majority are despatched in the
Belfast abattoir, where the use of the
humane killer is obligatory. I have
visited many of our municipal institutions in Belfast, but I must own that I
have never had the courage to visit the
abattoir. Not many years ago one would
as soon have visited the Cyclops' cave,
but I am informed and believe that the
present abattoir is in every way a credit
to this great city, and that every precaution is taken there to ensure that the
minimum of pain is inflicted. Unless we
are prepared to adopt the advanced
theories of the vegetarian-the Pythagorean of these modern days-we must
admit that to kill animals fit for
human food is a necessary condition of
our existence. But to kill them painlessly by the introduction of the humane
killer is equally essential in the light of
our modern ethical notions with regard
to our duty to the animal creation.
Henceforth, if this Bill becomes law, the
humane killer will take the place of the
poleaxe, which is still used in many
slaughter-houses for the despatch of
larger animals. This is all to the good.
The use of the poleaxe requires consummate skill in the hands of the wielder.
The aim must be taken at a particular
spot, an area about as large as a golf
ball. The slightest error of aim means
an additional blow or blows. Statistics
are available to show that in many cases
repeated blows are necessary, involving
involuntary cruelty to the animal, though
if the first blow is properly directed immediate unconsciousness is the result.
In the case of the humane killer there
is no risk of misadventure. Its effect is
mercifully sudden, in fact instantaneous.
Having never seen the humane killer in
action, or even at rest, may I quote the
words of the distinguished Member of the
Senate who introduced the Bill? He
said:
"There are two kinds of humane
killers. There is the bullet-firing
killer, and the captive bolt killer. The
captive bolt killer fires a bolt which
cracks the skull and penetrates the
brain, and the bolt recedes into the
barrel again a moment after death is
caused. This kind is portable and
easy to handle and keep clean. It
eliminates all unnecessary suffering,
and involves no danger whatever to the
carcase. It means no danger to the
operator himself. It can be bought for
19s 6d, and the best type costs five or
six guineas."
I do not know how many humane
killers would be required by our several
local authorities, but I am safe in saying
that the cost would impose no additional
appreciable burden upon the rates. And
in connection with this question of cost
may I remind the House that, since this
Bill got its Second Reading in the Senate,
the councils of the two associations of
local authorities in Northern Ireland,
municipal and rural, have had the matter
under consideration, and have notified the
Ministry of Home Affairs that they
entertain no objection to the Bill.
It will be noticed with regret by hon.
Members that swine are excluded from
the purview of this Bill. They have also
been excluded from the Scottish Act of
1928, to which I have already referred,
and perhaps it is better that the law here
should conform to the law in Scotland.
The reason for their exclusion appears to
be that there is a prevalent belief,
whether well founded or not I cannot
say, that the flesh of swine slaughtered
in this modern humane way is injuriously
affected. This is a matter which properly
belongs to the science of the veterinary
surgeon, and I do not propose to offer any
comment beyond expressing the hope
that the theory may turn out to be illfounded. It will again be noticed that
this Bill applies only to places, namely,
to slaughter-houses and knackers' yards.
It has no application to individual
farmers, who are entitled to kill their
own live stock for their own consumption
in their own way. To attempt to make
the Bill a household word in such cases
would be impracticable and ill-advised.
The Bill again has no application to
members of the Jewish community, who
have their own peculiar methods of
slaughter in accordance with religious
rules, which are coeval with their most
ancient history. And following the
pattern of the Scottish Act there is also
an exemption in the case of Mohammedans, though I doubt whether there are
any followers of the prophet resident in
Northern Ireland, except an occasional
student at the University, and the
1499 Slaughter of Animals Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading

may be seen
[Mr. McNeill]
peripatetic lascars who
vending their wares daily in some parts
of this city. Yet the general principle
is sound that the Bill shall in no wise
conflict with the religious belief of any
member of the community or of the
stranger that is within the gates.
One important effect of the present Bill
will be, I believe, the elimination of the
element of fear which possesses the
victim as it is led into the slaughterhouse. We are familiar with the vivid
pictures in ancient writers of the terrified
and reluctant animal being led by the
priest to the altar amid an attendant
ritual of horror. The ritual connected
with the humane killer is short and instantaneous.
The captive bolt pistol is
held close to the head. It makes only a
slight noise, requires little skill in the
use, no injury is caused to the carcase,
and loss of consciousness is immediate.
Coming to
to the Clauses, Clause 1
provides for instantaneous slaughter or
instantaneous insensibility to pain by
stunning. The humane killer is to be
operated by a person who is licensed by
the local authority. Clause 2 provides
that the licence shall not be granted to a
person under the age of 18, and the local
authority must be satisfied that he is a
fit and proper person. The licence is to
be granted for a period not exceeding
twelve months, it is liable to be suspended,
and a fee not exceeding five shillings may
be imposed as a condition of holding such
a licence. Any person aggrieved by the
decision of the licensing authority may
appeal to a court of summary jurisdiction.
Clause 3 applies to cases where the local
authority have themselves provided
slaughter-houses, and Clause 4 is concerned with the obstruction of officers and
police, and other authorised persons, in
the event of their being hindered in the
carrying out of their duties or rights in
connection with the inspection of
slaughter-houses. Clause 5 takes into
cognisance existing by-laws, so far as they
are inconsistent with the Bill. Clause 6
makes the exemption to which I have
already referred in the case of members
of the Jewish persuasion, and provides for
the case of a Mohammedan applying to
a local authority in Northern Ireland for
a licence to slaughter animals, a very
remote contingency in my opinion, having
regard, inter alia, to the inveterate repugnance of Mohammedans to swine flesh.
But it is just as well in our domestic legislation to provide for all possible contingencies. Local authorities are defined
in Clause 7, and the object of Clause 8
is to prevent any clash of authority between local bodies and the Ministry of
Agriculture in the performance by the
Ministry of its duties under the Diseases.
of Animals Acts in what may be an infected area. There is nothing in the interpretation Clause which calls for any
comment. I beg to move.

Major MCCORMICK: I should like also
to congratulate the hon. and learned
Member for the University on the able
manner in which he introduced this Bill,
which, I understand, is his first Bill. I
beg heartily to support the Bill as I think
it a very fine thing that more humane
measures than we have at present should
be compulsorily adopted in regard to the
killing of animals for food. I feel there
will be a unanimous feeling in favour of
the Bill.
The Title of the Bill is to my mind
rather crude. It has a directness of
nomenclature which is very much to the
point. I am not critical of this, but I
am rather inclined to credit the framers
of the Bill with a candour which I am
sure the animals concerned would not
appreciate. But I say further that it
might be termed the "Slaughter of the
Innocents Bill" so far as any effort at
opposition to it can be expected from those
empty benches which I see opposite. For
instance, the hon. Member for Central
(Mr. Devlin), who is absent, brought in
a Bill for the protection of wild birds, and
was surprised to get it passed. I think
that event was the cause of thanksgiving
and evoked a pæon of praise from the
feathered world which we can hear to-day.
That was all to the credit of the hon.
Member. But we do not know what is
in the minds of the bovine race, how they
feel, or what rhapsody of criticism they
will employ towards those hon. Members
who are not here to support them to-day.
But if they could speak, or if they had
some other method of expressing themselves, possibly they would show they
hold the same opinion of the Opposition.
as we do. I do not want to be inviduous,
but I deplore the absence on this occasion
of the hon. Member for Central (Mr.
Devlin). I do not know where he is. He
may have taken his companions off with
him to a bird-nesting conference, possibly in Lisnaskea. As it is, they cannot be participators in a Bill which must
be helpful to the animal world. If these
hon. Members cannot be friends of ours
and sit in this House with us, they might
at least be friends of the dumb and inarticulate creation, and help those animals
which cannot help themselves. It is said
that animals in their affections never
desert man, but I regret to find that not
only will man desert man, but even forget
his fellows of the lower world, who provide him, by their sacrifice of life with his
very food.
I understand there is a general and
clamant demand for this Bill, and I feel
that it should be passed unanimously. I
hope that in the regulations that will be
put into force that accompany the Bill
severe penalties will be provided for

admitted to these yards. I have by
question to the Minister of Home Affairs
called attention to the driving of cattle
for shipment or some other point. The
same thing may be said to apply to the
animals that go to the slaughter yard.
It is remarkable the way in which many
drovers treat in a cruel way these dumb
animals. It is bad in moral ways,
and the loss entailed to the owners
in money is very large through loss of
weight. I suggest that these drovers
should wear a large and prominent badge
so that if they were guilty of cruelty any
citizen or policeman could take action.
This might have a deterrent effect.

This memorial, as you will all see, has
been signed by 2,191 fruit growers from
every one of the Six Counties of Northern
Ireland, representing 5,085 acres under
fruit. These are the genuine signatures
of commercial growers only. A look at
its pages will convince any unbiased person that the signatures are genuine, and
in addition, the acreage under fruit and
the address of each grower is given as a
guarantee of its bona-fides. Everything
about that memorial is straight and above
board.
The Ulster Fruit Growers' Defence
Association has now a great many more
members than are represented by this
memorial, as every grower's son who
works on his father's farm at fruit culture
is eligible for membership, although these
were not allowed to sign the petition, as
the owner only of the orchard was allowed
to sign, so that this memorial really represents upwards of 10,000 engaged and
financially interested in this very important industry, many of whom are entirely
dependent on it for their livelihood. This
industry employs more scientific labour
than any other industry on the land, and
provides continuous work for the twelve
months of the year to all those engaged
in it; and it has been initiated and
brought to its present up-to-date condition through the foresight and industry
of the growers themselves without any
aid, in any shape or form, from this
Government.
On October 7th, 1930, when this Apple
Bill was up for a Second Reading, a
petition signed by 1,454 growers having
3,670 acres of fruit, was presented to this
House by the hon. Member for North
Antrim (Sir Robert Lynn), who gave very
just and substantial reasons for the withdrawal of the Bill. The only sympathy that
appeal drew from the Ministerial Bench was
an unjustifiable comment from the Minister
of Finance, who ought to have more sympathy with the fruit growers in view of
his own experience of farming for a short
period in their midst at Loughgall, that
the petition was signed by growers "and
their families"; and the Minister of Agriculture's contention was that the signatories signed under a misapprehension.
That was a year and seven months ago.
In the intervening period this Act has
been discussed in this House, in the Press,
at public meetings and in market places
from every angle, and more than that, it
has actually been in operation for a
season, and now, instead of the Government's contention that only a
"small
noisy body" was opposed to the Act, here
we have the signatures of practically
every fruit grower in the Six Counties
who grows fruit for sale, wanting the Act
amended as they have found that their
apprehensions as to the injury it would
prove to their industry were well founded
and that if the Act continues to be enforced their industry will be wiped out.
We have only to look at the figures of
the exports from Belfast port since the
Act came into operation to show how
detrimental it has proved to the industry.
We will begin with October, 1931, and in
this connection it must be remembered
that October is never a heavy shipping
month as then growers are too busily
engaged pulling and storing their winter
apples, which are the main shipping
varieties. Last October 300 tons were
exported from Belfast. In November
the Act came into operation and in that
month 145 tons were exported. About
130 tons of these were for manufacturing
purposes and so not affected by the regulations. In December the total exports
of manufacturing and graded apples and
pears fell to 79 tons. In January they
fell to 40 tons. In February they were
45 tons. In March they were 49 tons.
So that, though October is normally one
of the lightest shipping months of the
year, there were almost as many apples
exported last October-300 tons-as the
total exported from November 1st, when
the Act became operative, till April 1st-
359 tons-the five chief shipping months
of the season. And when we take the
comparative figures for the previous
season we find that from November 1st,
1930, to April 1st, 1931, 9,469 tons of
apples were exported from Belfast,
whereas, in the same period for 1931 to
1932, only 359 tons were shipped, so that,
though last season's Bramley crop was
about one-fifth the previous season's, the
of the
exports fell to one-thirtieth
previous season's.
I have no hesitation in stating that this
drop in the tonnage exported was entirely
due to the impossible regulations made
under this Marketing of Fruit Act.
Under these regulations the growers were
not allowed to export their apples
honestly graded and packed to be sold on
their merits on the British markets in the
same manner and alongside English apples
similarly packed, which, as was proved
Marketing of Fruit Act 1508
Adjournment-
HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Mr. Nixon]
in the House recently, were realising
around 20s per barrel more than Northern
Ireland growers were able to get in the
home markets where they were compelled
to sell; and thus were denied their right
to take advantage of the highest prices
that have ruled for apples for twelve years
in the best markets of the world-the
British-that these growers built up
entirely on their own initiative.
The Minister of Agriculture told this
House last year that this Act was to raise
the standard of Irish apples in the British
market. But instead, the deliberations
of his officials and his Fruit Advisory
Committee resulted in branding the best
quality cooking apples in the world by the
most damning description ever conceived-
"imperfect" to allow of their being
exported at all under his Fruit Marketing
Act. No greater indictment of the
inability of his Department and his Fruit
Advisory Committee to make regulations
for the export of fruit is needed than that
"imperfect" grade, and this is the direct.
result of the breach of faith by the
Minister in failing to give the Ulster
Fruit Growers' Defence Association fair
representation on this Advisory Committee, as they speak for practically every
grower who sells fruit in Northern
Ireland.
The Minister stated recently that
"under one per cent. of the apples were
stopped" at the ports. What greater
evidence could be desired by the Government or by anyone that, therefore, this
Act and its inspectors are entirely unnecessary? The Minister of Agriculture.
has surely learned by this time the fallacy
of his contention that good apples can be
grown every year in Northern Ireland
irrespective of the weather, if only the
methods of fruit culture advocated by his
Department are carried out. The Members of this House saw eighteen months
ago a sample of the inferior apples produced under official guidance in County
Armagh. They were the worst specimens
of apples ever grown in this country or
any other, irrespective of culture, and
that in the best season there had been for
ten years.
Last year the results of their
work in County Armagh were SO
disastrous that they did not venture a
single demonstration in the premier fruit
growing country. And it is significant
that all the persuasive invitations of the
growers could not induce either the
Minister of Agriculture or his officials to
come and see for themselves the plots
which are sprayed by their officials from
Stormont, even though it is only one
hour's run in a car.
Over thirty years ago, when the second
judicial rents were being fixed by the
Land Commission, because these orchards
were beginning to bring in some reward
to the growers in County Armagh for
their foresight and industry and perseverance the landlords promptly took
advantage of it and the result was the
notorious "Pink Schedule," that caused
such bitterness and heart-burning in the
fruit growing district at the Diamond.
At that time the growers' rents were
raised about 15/- per acre on the orchards
they had planted and brought to production by their own toil and self-denial.
They are still paying that unjust impost
to-day in their annuities. They were
penalised by the landlords then for starting a new industry. They are penalised.
now by the Government, because, unaided, they developed a successful export
trade for that industry.
If the fruit industry had been down and
out, as flax is now, the Government would
not have looked at it. It would not have
yielded a happy hunting ground for
increasing Government officials. This
memorial includes practically every fruit
grower who sells fruit in Northern Ireland
and certainly all that export their fruit
from the counties Armagh, Tyrone and
Antrim.
The Ministry's agricultural statistics
give acreages under fruit in Derry, Down,
and Fermanagh, which the farmers living
in the rural areas in which the fruit is
reported to be grown, say do not exist.
For instance, although the Department
states that 595 acres of fruit are grown

since November last, when the Act came
into operation, they are offering their
apple trees to anyone who will stub them,
as they now consider them of no value.
This memorial, signed by practically
every commercial grower in Northern
Ireland, proves beyond all doubt that the
fruit growers do not want this Act. Their
British buyers do not want it.
And as
the people engaged in this industry know

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Slaughter of Animals Bill (S.).
Considered in Committee.
[Mr MOLES in the Chair.]
CLAUSE 1 (Provisions as to slaughter
of animals, etc.).
(1) No animal except swine shall be
slaughtered in a slaughter-house or
knacker's yard except in accordance
with the provisions of this section, and
it shall be the duty of the local
authority to enforce the provisions of
this Act within its area.
(2) Every such animal shall be instantaneously slaughtered, or shall by
stunning be instantaneously rendered
insensible to pain until death supervenes, and such slaughtering or stunning shall be effected by a person who
is at the time the holder of a licence
issued by the local authority under
section two of this Act by means of a
mechanically-operated instrument in
proper repair.
(3) If any person contravenes or fails
to comply with or causes or permits any
contravention or non-compliance with
any of the provisions of this section,
or attempts to slaughter an animal in
a slaughter-house or knacker's yard
otherwise than in accordance with the
said provisions he shall be liable on
conviction by a court of summary jurisdiction to a fine not exceeding five
pounds or on a second conviction to a
fine not exceeding ten pounds or on a
subsequent conviction to imprisonment
for a period not exceeding two months
or to a fine not exceeding ten pounds,
or to both such imprisonment and fine.

CLAUSE 4 (Obstruction of officers).
Any officer or constable of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary and any person
authorised in writing by a local
authority and the officers of any society
or institution for the protection of
animals authorised by the Ministry of
Home Affairs for that purpose may
enter any slaughter-house or knacker's
yard in the district of the local authority at any time when business is, or
appears to be, in progress, or is usually
carried on therein, for the purpose of
ascertaining whether there is or has
been any contravention of or noncompliance with the provisions of this
Act, and if any person shall refuse to
permit any such constable or person or
officer to enter any premises which he is
entitled to enter under this Act, or
shall obstruct or impede him in the
exercise of his duties under this Act, he
shall be liable, on conviction by a court
of summary jurisdiction to a fine not
exceeding five pounds.

Mr. BEATTIE asked the Minister
of Labour whether he can state if Exchequer grants are being used for the
payment of unemployment benefit owing
to the neglect of the Ministry in not
having immediate transfers made back to
unemployment benefit where the ten
contribution qualification has been fulfilled
for new benefit year.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): In the obvious interest of
insured persons to avoid delays in payment of claims whilst the application of
the "ten contributions " condition is
being decided, advances may on occasions
be made as transitional payments which
are subsequently found to be proper
charges on the Unemployment Fund.
Adjusting entries between the Unemployment Fund and moneys voted by Parliament are made periodically to cover cases
of this kind.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister aware
that he cannot juggle with the Estimates
of this House in such a manner as he has
done? Is he also aware that this irregularity of taking from one Class to support
another has been carried on over periods
of three months? I would ask the
Minister to give to the Comptroller and
Auditor-General some satisfactory answer
in regard to this irregularity which has
occurred.
Mr. ANDREWS: No juggling has taken
place and there has been no irregularity.
The matter is quite in order.
Mr. BEATTIE: The thing is irregular.
Is the Minister aware that there have
been repeated decisions of the Public
Accounts Committee to the effect that the
use of funds voted for one Class in support
of another Class is most irregular and not
acceptable to this House or to the Committee?
Mr. ANDREWS: I am quite satisfied
that the Public Accounts Committee and
the Comptroller and Auditor-General
will approve of what has been done as
being the only thing that can be done to
avoid delay in the payment of benefit to
insured persons.
Mr. BEATTIE: Is the Minister aware
that the payment of benefit is not the
principle involved at all, but that it is a
matter of continuing applicants
reduced rates of benefit when they should
be receiving full rates of benefit under the
Unemployment Insurance Act?

Mr. BEATTIE: I am not prepared to
give the landlord any exemption under
this Clause. We, as a Select Committee
of this House, went into this matter very
particularly, and we found that it would
take something very drastic to bring to
book those unscrupulous landlords who
had been evading the Rent Acts since
1925. By their financial jugglery, and by
these evasions, they have been able to take
pounds and pounds from poor people who
could not afford to pay. I admitted on
the Second Reading that there was
certain number of decent landlords, but,
in the majority of cases which I have
investigated, I have found that the landlords knew what they were doing and did
it deliberately to evade the Rent Acts.
By this new Sub-Clause you are going to
nullify the whole effect of the Measure
which this House so generously passed on
behalf of those tenants whom we were out
to protect and to guard, and to whom we
decided some compensation should be paid
for the exploitation of them that had been
carried out in the past.
I cannot see any good purpose that can
be served by this Amendment. The decent landlords do not require to go to the
court. It is the undecent landlord I
want to get at. By a decent landlord I
mean one who has fulfilled his obligations
in conformity with the Act of Parliament
and who has never endeavoured in any
way
to evade the Acts or to drag from his
tenant more than that to which he was
entitled. That is a landlord of a good
type, but he does not need to be covered
by an Act of Parliament, because he has
been guilty of no offence. The Bill, as it
stood, represented the unanimous decision
of the Select Committee. I hope the

therefor by the tenant under this section, or wilfully furnishes to the tenant a

Mr. BEATTIE: This is rather a

associations. I would like to know what

every company could not take on that

by the Ministry of Home Affairs. I want
to say that every company in the North

to explain what will be the qualifications

Ministry.

Mr. SPEAKER: Before the Parliamentary Secretary proceeds to reply,
perhaps he might find it advisable to
wait until any further criticism of the
Amendment is offered. There are other
hon. Members who wish to speak.
Major MCCORMICK: I think that
what is possibly in the mind of the
Member for Pottinger is that what he
considers to be certain undesirable
associations should not be allowed to
exercise the facilities granted under this
Bill, but that the particular people he
represents should be approved of by the
Ministry. I take it that this new subsection means that land should be let to
an association whose objects are kindred
to the objects set out in the Bill, as, for
instance, the Garden Plots' Association
or the Plot Holders' Association. These
associations have in the past done a great
deal indeed, particularly during the war,
to encourage the individual plot holder
to keep his plot tidy and in order. They
have certain regulations, no doubt, and
the point I want to bring out is this.
I fear that if these plots are let to
associations directly, the rights of the individual will be lost sight of. I have
nothing against these associations because, as I have said, they have done a
great deal to help and encourage plotholders, but on this occasion I stand for
the rights of the individual, who does not
want to be tied down by the regulations
of associations. There might possibly be
associations of a Socialistic tendency,
who might have a prior right as against
the right of the individual.
Mr. HANNA: The expression "approved association" is already defined in
the Bill, and has met with the approval
of the whole House. I refer the hon.
Member to Clause 7, Sub-Clause (2),
which says:
In this section the
expression
"approved association" means any
association of persons (not trading for
profit) approved by the Ministry of
Home Affairs, and being an association
whose objects include the provision of
allotments for persons qualified to be
tenants of allotments under this Act.
That is very wide and would include
all bodies, such as trade unions, if they
applied themselves to the objects of the
Bill.

Mr. SPEAKER: With regard to the
point of Order that the hon. Member for
Pottinger has raised, a controversial
Motion could not be put on the Order
Paper on the day of Prorogation.
Further, he should distinguish between
Government Motions and private Members' Motions. A Government Motion
can be put down on the Order Paper at
any time, and it is entirely within the
province of the Government to do so if
they think fit and right so to do. As to
a private Member's Motion, proper notice
must be given of it, and it comes
for debate at half-past Four o'clock on
Tuesdays or Fridays. As this is 8
formal sitting for one formal Motion of
thanks to the Lord Mayor and Corporation and the Prorogation of Parliament,
of course, the procedure for private
Members' Motions does not apply in this
case, and therefore the hon. Member's
Motion would not have an opportunity
of being debated at all, as the Prorogation will have taken place long before
half-past Four o'clock. Therefore, I
have no alternative but to inform the
hon. Member for Pottinger that his
Motion could not be accepted on the day
of Prorogation.

Order. Is it not a fact that Friday is

the custom of the British House
Commons, Parliament meets at an earlier

Is it not a fact that Private Members'

That being so, I am justified in asking

Mr. HENDERSON: I wish to raise a
point of Order. During the last sittings
of the House I placed a Notice of Motion
on the Table of the House. It is very
unfair and ungracious that we have not
an opportunity of discussing those two
Motions, of which notice was given in
the old House. The House has been
adjourned now for four months, and, now
that it has met, we thought we would
have an opportunity of discussing those
two Motions; but the two of them have
been ruled out of order, and we have no
opportunity of debating them here to-day.
I think this is a most outrageous attempt
by the Government to stifle any discussion
by the Opposition in this Parliament.
This procedure would not be followed in
any other part of the world; it could
happen only in Northern Ireland. May
I draw the attention of the Government
and Members to the fact that the Motion
I put on the Table of the House has
been lost, and that no one knows anything about it. Could that happen in
any other Parliament in the world? A
Member of Parliament puts a Motion on
the Table of the House; the Motion is
lost, and no one knows anything about it.
I want to protest in the strongest possible
manner against the outrageous treatment
meted out to the Opposition. We have
not met for four months and we are going
to adjourn for another two months; in
the meantime the starving people of Northern Ireland are to continue starving.

Mr. HENDERSON: The unemployed
will have to beg in the streets. I condemn the way the Government have

to civilisation.

Mr. SPEAKER: I think the hon.
Member is not quite clear on that

to do with the Government's arrangement of the business. It is the Speaker's

alternative but to say the Motion was
out of order, and, therefore, it could
not appear on the Order Paper. Beyond
that I cannot go.

Mr. SPEAKER: This House has this
day attended in the Senate, when the
following Proclamation proroguing this
present Session of Parliament was read
by the Speaker of the Senate:-
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR
OF NORTHERN IRELAND.
A
PROCLAMATION
For Proroguing the present Parliament
of Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by Section
eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
certain enactments amending the said Act,
that the Governor of Northern Ireland
shall in his Majesty's name summon,
prorogue and dissolve the Parliament of
Northern Ireland:
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that
this present Parliament of Northern
Ireland should be prorogued to the
twenty-second day of November, One
thousand nine hundred and thirty-two:
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, KNIGHT OF
THE MOST NOBLE ORDER OF THE
GARTER, KNIGHT OF THE MOST
ILLUSTRIOUS ORDER OF ST.
PATRICK, Governor of Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do publish
and declare his Majesty's Pleasure that
the said Parliament be, as from the
Prorogation
Prorogation
HOUSE OF COMMONS
reading of this Proclamation in the
Parliament of Northern Ireland, prorogued
to Tuesday, the twenty-second day of
November, One thousand nine hundred
and thirty-two.
AND I do hereby further declare his
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall on the said
twenty-second day of November, One
thousand nine hundred and thirty-two,
assemble and be holden at Stormont for
the despatch of divers
of divers urgent and
important affairs, and the Senators and
Members of the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland are hereby required to
give their attendance accordingly.
Given at Baronscourt, County Tyrone,
this twenty-ninth day of September, One
thousand nine hundred and thirty-two.
(Signed by his own hand)
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
End of the Fourth Session (opened

Tuesday, 8th March, 1932) of the Third
Parliament of Northern Ireland in the
twenty-third year of the Reign of his
Majesty King George the Fifth.
